full_text:
[Abstract]
Translation occurs not through isolated ribosomes but within dynamic mesoscale clusters called 'translation factories' or polysomes, where emergent properties arise from ribosome cooperation. This synthesis project investigates how ribosome clustering creates emergent translational behaviors—including enhanced processivity, coordinated protein folding, and localized mRNA regulation—that cannot be predicted from single ribosome properties. We will integrate cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) data from EMPIAR and EMDB revealing in-situ ribosome spatial organization, ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) data from GEO and GWIPS-viz capturing translation dynamics, structural data from PDB on ribosome-associated factors, and proteomics from PRIDE quantifying translation machinery stoichiometry. The central question is: how do spatial arrangements of ribosomes at the mesoscale (50-500 nm polysome structures) create emergent translational properties distinct from summed individual ribosome activities? Our computational approach combines spatial statistics analysis of cryo-ET reconstructions to characterize ribosome clustering patterns, kinetic modeling of translation dynamics informed by Ribo-seq pausing patterns, and agent-based simulations of polysome behavior. We will develop novel algorithms to segment and classify polysome architectures from tomographic data, then correlate these structures with mRNA-specific translation efficiencies from Ribo-seq. Machine learning will identify features of polysome organization predictive of translation output, protein folding efficiency, and co-translational assembly. Integration with protein-protein interaction networks from STRING and BioGRID will reveal how nascent chain interactions within polysomes enable emergent co-translational complex assembly. This project demands expertise spanning cryo-ET image analysis, translation biology, mathematical modeling, and machine learning—capabilities distributed across specialized laboratories. The data synthesis challenge involves reconciling structural snapshots with dynamic sequencing readouts across different experimental systems. Expected insights include principles governing polysome architecture, quantitative relationships between mesoscale ribosome organization and translation output, and mechanisms of emergent co-translational protein folding. Deliverables include open-source tools for polysome analysis, curated cross-referenced datasets, and predictive models of translation factory behavior. Understanding these emergent translation properties has implications for synthetic biology and diseases involving translation dysregulation.

[Background and Significance]
Protein synthesis represents one of the most fundamental and energy-intensive processes in cellular biology, consuming up to 50% of cellular energy in rapidly growing cells. While decades of research have illuminated the molecular mechanisms of individual ribosomes—from initiation and elongation to termination—an emerging paradigm recognizes that translation in vivo occurs not through isolated molecular machines but within organized mesoscale structures termed 'translation factories' or polysomes. These clusters of ribosomes, spanning 50-500 nanometers, occupy the critical mesoscale between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles, representing a frontier where emergent properties arise from collective ribosome behavior that cannot be predicted from studying single ribosomes in isolation.

The concept of emergent properties in translation factories encompasses several phenomena. First, ribosome cooperation within polysomes may enhance processivity through mechanisms including mRNA stabilization, reduced ribosome drop-off, and coordinated elongation rates. Studies using ribosome profiling have revealed that translation elongation rates vary dramatically across mRNA transcripts and even within single transcripts, with ribosome density patterns suggesting coordinated behavior rather than independent progression. Second, the spatial proximity of ribosomes translating the same mRNA creates opportunities for co-translational protein folding that differs fundamentally from post-translational folding. Nascent polypeptide chains emerging from adjacent ribosomes can interact, potentially facilitating the assembly of protein complexes through co-translational mechanisms. Third, the three-dimensional architecture of polysomes influences local mRNA regulation, creating microenvironments where translation factors, chaperones, and regulatory proteins concentrate.

Recent advances in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) have revolutionized our ability to visualize ribosome organization within cellular contexts. The Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) now contain hundreds of tomographic datasets capturing ribosomes in their native cellular environments across diverse organisms and cell types. These structural snapshots reveal polysome architectures ranging from linear arrays to circular configurations, with inter-ribosome distances and orientations that vary systematically. Simultaneously, ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) has generated vast datasets quantifying ribosome positions along mRNAs with codon-level resolution, available through the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and specialized databases like GWIPS-viz. These complementary data modalities—structural organization from cryo-ET and translational dynamics from Ribo-seq—have never been systematically integrated to understand how mesoscale architecture relates to translation behavior.

Critical gaps in our understanding persist precisely because existing studies examine either structural organization or translational dynamics, but rarely both simultaneously. We lack quantitative frameworks connecting polysome geometry to translation output. The rules governing polysome assembly—why some mRNAs form compact circular polysomes while others adopt extended linear configurations—remain unclear. Whether polysome architecture actively regulates translation or merely reflects passive consequences of ribosome loading is unknown. Most fundamentally, we cannot currently predict emergent translational properties from knowledge of individual ribosome behavior and mRNA sequence features.

The significance of understanding emergent translation properties extends across molecular and cellular biology. Translation dysregulation underlies numerous diseases, from ribosomopathies affecting ribosome biogenesis to cancer cells hijacking translation machinery for uncontrolled growth. Synthetic biology applications increasingly require precise control over protein expression, yet current models treating ribosomes as independent actors fail to capture the complexity of cellular translation. Understanding how mesoscale organization creates emergent properties will enable more accurate models of gene expression, reveal new regulatory mechanisms, and identify potential therapeutic targets.

The time is ripe for synthesis research addressing these questions. Publicly available data now spans sufficient diversity of organisms, cell types, and conditions to enable systematic analysis. Computational methods for analyzing cryo-ET data have matured, enabling automated ribosome detection and classification. Machine learning approaches can identify patterns across heterogeneous datasets that would be invisible to traditional analysis. This synthesis project will leverage these converging opportunities to establish quantitative principles governing emergent translation factory behavior, filling a critical gap in our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project addresses four interconnected research questions examining how mesoscale ribosome organization creates emergent translational properties. Each question generates testable hypotheses that can be validated through integration of existing publicly available datasets.

**Research Question 1: How does polysome architecture vary across mRNAs, cell types, and organisms, and what sequence/structural features predict polysome geometry?**

We hypothesize that polysome architecture is not random but follows predictable rules determined by mRNA sequence features, ribosome density, and cellular context. Specifically, we predict that: (H1a) mRNAs encoding subunits of the same protein complex will exhibit similar polysome geometries, facilitating co-translational assembly; (H1b) polysome compactness (measured as gyration radius normalized to ribosome number) will correlate negatively with mRNA length and positively with translation efficiency; (H1c) circular polysome configurations will be enriched for mRNAs with structured 5' and 3' UTRs that promote mRNA circularization through eIF4E-PABP interactions. These hypotheses will be tested by systematically analyzing polysome geometries from cryo-ET datasets in EMPIAR across multiple organisms (yeast, human, mouse) and correlating architectural features with mRNA characteristics from corresponding Ribo-seq datasets in GEO. Validation will use known positive controls—mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins, which are known to be highly translated and coordinately regulated.

**Research Question 2: Do ribosome spacing patterns within polysomes reflect coordinated elongation dynamics, and can Ribo-seq pausing signatures predict inter-ribosome distances observed in cryo-ET?**

We hypothesize that ribosomes within polysomes do not move independently but exhibit coordinated dynamics creating characteristic spacing patterns. Our predictions are: (H2a) inter-ribosome distances measured from cryo-ET will show non-random distributions with peaks corresponding to integral numbers of codons, reflecting synchronized elongation; (H2b) mRNAs with frequent ribosome pausing (detected as Ribo-seq density peaks) will show compressed inter-ribosome spacing upstream of pause sites in tomographic data; (H2c) the coefficient of variation in inter-ribosome spacing will be lower than expected from independent ribosome movement, indicating coordination. Testing these hypotheses requires developing novel computational methods to precisely measure inter-ribosome distances from cryo-ET reconstructions and correlating these measurements with codon-resolution Ribo-seq profiles. We will use mRNAs with well-characterized pause sites (e.g., those containing polyproline sequences or rare codons) as validation cases.

**Research Question 3: Does polysome organization enable emergent co-translational protein complex assembly, and can we identify structural signatures of nascent chain interactions within polysomes?**

We hypothesize that the mesoscale organization of polysomes creates emergent opportunities for co-translational complex assembly that would not occur with isolated ribosomes. Predictions include: (H3a) polysomes translating subunits of known protein complexes (from CORUM database) will show preferential orientations positioning nascent chain exit tunnels toward each other; (H3b) mRNAs encoding interacting proteins (from STRING and BioGRID databases) will show correlated translation efficiencies beyond what sequence features predict, suggesting functional coupling; (H3c) polysome architectures will show cell-type specific variations that correlate with the protein complex repertoire of each cell type. These hypotheses will be tested by analyzing ribosome orientations within polysomes from cryo-ET data, mapping nascent chain exit tunnel positions, and correlating with protein-protein interaction networks. Validation will use well-characterized complexes like proteasomes and ATP synthase, where co-translational assembly has been documented.

**Research Question 4: Can we build predictive models of emergent translation output from polysome architecture, and do these models outperform single-ribosome-based predictions?**

We hypothesize that incorporating mesoscale polysome features into translation models will significantly improve prediction accuracy compared to models treating ribosomes independently. Specific predictions are: (H4a) machine learning models incorporating polysome geometry features (compactness, ribosome number, inter-ribosome spacing variability) will predict protein output (from proteomics data in PRIDE) with higher accuracy than models using only Ribo-seq density; (H4b) the improvement from including polysome features will be greatest for mRNAs encoding large proteins or protein complex subunits, where co-translational effects are most important; (H4c) agent-based simulations incorporating ribosome-ribosome interactions will reproduce experimentally observed translation dynamics better than independent-ribosome models. Validation will use held-out test sets and cross-organism generalization to assess model robustness.

**Mechanistic Insights Expected**

Addressing these questions will yield mechanistic insights into: (1) the biophysical principles governing polysome self-organization, including the roles of mRNA flexibility, ribosome surface properties, and crowding effects; (2) the functional consequences of polysome architecture for translation fidelity, efficiency, and regulation; (3) the evolutionary conservation and divergence of polysome organization across species; and (4) the integration of translation with downstream processes including protein folding and complex assembly. These insights will establish polysome organization as a bona fide regulatory layer in gene expression, operating at the mesoscale between molecular mechanisms and cellular phenotypes.

[Methods and Approach]
**Overview of Synthesis Strategy**

Our methodological approach integrates four distinct data modalities—cryo-ET structural data, ribosome profiling sequencing data, protein structure/interaction data, and quantitative proteomics—to build comprehensive models of emergent translation factory behavior. The synthesis challenge involves reconciling data collected under different experimental conditions, from different organisms, and at different resolutions. We address this through careful data harmonization, cross-validation between modalities, and explicit modeling of uncertainty.

**Data Sources and Acquisition**

*Cryo-ET Structural Data:* We will systematically retrieve cellular tomography datasets from EMPIAR (Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive) containing visible polysomes. Initial analysis identifies >150 relevant datasets spanning Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Schizosaccharomyces pombe, HeLa cells, U2OS cells, neurons, and various bacterial species. Key datasets include EMPIAR-10304 (yeast cytoplasm), EMPIAR-10592 (HeLa cell lamella), EMPIAR-11001 (neuronal synapses), and EMPIAR-10988 (bacterial polysomes). Associated subtomogram averages and ribosome coordinates from EMDB will provide validated ribosome positions. We estimate accessing approximately 500 tomograms containing >50,000 individual polysomes for analysis.

*Ribosome Profiling Data:* Ribo-seq datasets will be retrieved from NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and the GWIPS-viz browser, which provides pre-processed ribosome profiling data with standardized annotations. We will focus on datasets with matched RNA-seq controls enabling calculation of translation efficiency. Priority datasets include GSE102720 (human cell lines), GSE52968 (yeast stress responses), GSE65912 (mouse tissues), and GSE134888 (ribosome collision studies). We estimate integrating >200 Ribo-seq datasets spanning multiple organisms and conditions.

*Protein Structure and Interaction Data:* Ribosome structures and ribosome-associated factor complexes will be retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), including recent high-resolution cryo-EM structures of polysomes (PDB: 6SGC, 7CPU). Protein-protein interaction networks from STRING v12 and BioGRID 4.4 will identify known complex subunits. The CORUM database will provide curated mammalian protein complex definitions. UniProt will supply protein annotations including subcellular localization and functional domains.

*Quantitative Proteomics:* Protein abundance measurements from PRIDE Archive and ProteomicsDB will provide ground truth for translation output. We will prioritize datasets with absolute quantification (e.g., PXD004452 for yeast, PXD010154 for human cell lines) enabling direct comparison with translation efficiency predictions.

**Computational Methods**

*Polysome Segmentation and Classification (Months 1-12):* We will develop deep learning algorithms for automated polysome detection and segmentation from cryo-ET tomograms. Building on existing tools (EMAN2, Dynamo, STOPGAP), we will train convolutional neural networks to identify ribosome positions with sub-nanometer precision. A novel graph neural network architecture will classify polysome configurations (linear, circular, branched) based on ribosome connectivity patterns. Transfer learning from well-annotated datasets will enable application to diverse tomographic data with varying contrast and resolution.

*Spatial Statistics Analysis (Months 6-18):* We will apply spatial point process statistics to characterize ribosome clustering. Ripley's K-function and pair correlation functions will quantify clustering at different length scales. We will develop novel statistics for oriented point patterns to capture ribosome orientation preferences within polysomes. Null models assuming independent ribosome positioning will provide statistical baselines for detecting coordination.

*Ribo-seq Processing and Integration (Months 3-15):* Ribo-seq data will be uniformly processed using established pipelines (RiboCode, Ribo-TISH) with standardized quality filters. Translation efficiency will be calculated as Ribo-seq density normalized by RNA-seq abundance. Pause site detection will use change-point algorithms identifying significant density increases. mRNA-level features (length, GC content, codon usage, predicted secondary structure from RNAfold) will be extracted for correlation with polysome architecture.

*Kinetic Modeling (Months 12-24):* We will develop stochastic kinetic models of translation incorporating ribosome-ribosome interactions. Models will be parameterized using elongation rates inferred from Ribo-seq and inter-ribosome distances from cryo-ET. Gillespie algorithm simulations will generate synthetic translation dynamics for comparison with experimental observations. Parameter inference will use approximate Bayesian computation to quantify uncertainty.

*Agent-Based Simulations (Months 15-27):* Agent-based models will simulate individual ribosomes as interacting particles on mRNA tracks. Interaction rules will be inferred from cryo-ET data (preferred distances, orientation constraints). Simulations will predict emergent properties including collision frequencies, nascent chain proximity, and translation completion times. Model validation will compare predicted polysome architectures with cryo-ET observations.

*Machine Learning Integration (Months 18-30):* Gradient boosting and neural network models will predict translation output from integrated features spanning sequence, structure, and polysome architecture. Feature importance analysis will identify which polysome characteristics most strongly predict protein abundance. Cross-validation across organisms will assess model generalizability.

**Data Harmonization Strategy**

Integrating heterogeneous datasets requires careful harmonization. For cryo-ET data, we will standardize coordinate systems, normalize contrast, and apply consistent resolution filters. For Ribo-seq, batch correction (ComBat) will address technical variation between studies. Organism-specific analyses will be performed first, followed by cross-species integration using ortholog mappings from OrthoDB. Uncertainty quantification will propagate measurement errors through all analyses.

**Validation Strategies**

All analyses will be validated using multiple approaches: (1) cross-dataset validation, testing whether patterns observed in one dataset replicate in independent datasets; (2) known positive controls, including well-characterized mRNAs with documented polysome properties; (3) cross-modality consistency, verifying that predictions from cryo-ET align with Ribo-seq observations; (4) held-out test sets for machine learning models; (5) comparison with published findings from individual studies.

**Timeline and Milestones**

Year 1: Data acquisition and pipeline development. Milestones: curated cryo-ET database (Month 6), polysome segmentation algorithm (Month 9), integrated Ribo-seq database (Month 12).

Year 2: Core analyses and model development. Milestones: polysome architecture atlas (Month 18), kinetic model framework (Month 21), initial machine learning models (Month 24).

Year 3: Integration, validation, and dissemination. Milestones: validated predictive models (Month 30), public tool release (Month 33), synthesis publications (Month 36).

**Team Composition and Expertise**

This project requires expertise in: (1) cryo-ET image analysis and structural biology; (2) translation biology and ribosome profiling; (3) mathematical modeling and simulation; (4) machine learning and data science; (5) software engineering for tool development. No single laboratory possesses all required capabilities, necessitating collaborative team science.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
**Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will generate five categories of deliverables that advance understanding of emergent translation factory behavior while providing lasting resources for the research community.

*Integrated Polysome Architecture Atlas:* We will create the first comprehensive atlas of polysome structures observed across organisms, cell types, and conditions. This atlas will contain >50,000 annotated polysomes from cryo-ET data, classified by architecture (linear, circular, branched, clustered), with quantified geometric parameters (ribosome number, spacing, orientation, compactness). Each polysome will be linked to organism, cell type, and experimental condition metadata. The atlas will be searchable and downloadable, enabling researchers to query polysome properties for specific contexts.

*Cross-Referenced Translation Database:* We will construct an integrated database linking mRNA sequences to their translation properties across multiple data modalities. For each mRNA, the database will contain: sequence features (length, codon usage, predicted structure), Ribo-seq metrics (translation efficiency, pause sites, ribosome density profiles), associated polysome architectures (where available from matching conditions), and protein abundance measurements. This resource will enable systems-level analysis of translation regulation.

*Open-Source Computational Tools:* We will release a suite of computational tools including: (1) PolysomeSegment—deep learning algorithms for automated polysome detection and classification from cryo-ET tomograms; (2) PolysomeStat—spatial statistics package for analyzing ribosome clustering patterns; (3) TranslationKinetics—stochastic simulation framework for modeling polysome dynamics; (4) PolyPredict—machine learning models predicting translation output from sequence and structural features. All tools will be documented, tested, and released under permissive open-source licenses.

*Predictive Models of Translation Factory Behavior:* We will deliver validated computational models predicting: (1) polysome architecture from mRNA sequence features; (2) translation efficiency from polysome geometry; (3) co-translational assembly likelihood from polysome orientation patterns; (4) ribosome collision frequencies from sequence and density features. Models will include uncertainty quantification and performance benchmarks.

*Curated Training Datasets:* We will create benchmark datasets for algorithm development, including manually annotated polysome structures for training segmentation algorithms, and curated positive/negative examples for co-translational assembly prediction.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project will establish quantitative principles governing how mesoscale ribosome organization creates emergent translational properties. We expect to demonstrate that: (1) polysome architecture is not random but follows predictable rules reflecting functional optimization; (2) ribosomes within polysomes exhibit coordinated dynamics distinct from independent behavior; (3) mesoscale organization enables emergent co-translational processes including coordinated protein folding and complex assembly; (4) incorporating polysome features significantly improves prediction of translation output. These findings will establish translation factories as a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, where collective behavior creates properties not predictable from individual components.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Understanding emergent translation properties has implications extending across molecular and cellular biology. For gene expression research, our findings will reveal a previously underappreciated regulatory layer operating at the mesoscale, complementing transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation. For structural biology, our polysome atlas will provide cellular context for interpreting ribosome structures, bridging in vitro and in vivo observations. For systems biology, our integrated models will improve predictions of protein abundance from genomic data, a persistent challenge in the field. For synthetic biology, understanding polysome organization will enable rational design of expression systems optimizing translation efficiency and protein folding.

**Enabling Future Research**

Our deliverables will enable multiple future research directions. The polysome atlas will serve as a reference for interpreting new cryo-ET studies, enabling researchers to compare their observations with established patterns. Our computational tools will lower barriers to analyzing polysome data, making this emerging field accessible to researchers without specialized expertise. Predictive models will generate testable hypotheses about translation regulation that can guide future studies. The integrated database will enable meta-analyses identifying conserved and divergent translation regulatory mechanisms.

**Dissemination Plans**

*Publications:* We anticipate 8-10 peer-reviewed publications including: (1) methods papers describing computational tools; (2) resource papers describing databases and atlases; (3) research papers reporting biological insights; (4) review/perspective articles synthesizing findings. All publications will be submitted to open-access journals or posted as preprints.

*Workshops and Training:* We will organize two workshops during the project: (1) a methods workshop training researchers in polysome analysis techniques; (2) a synthesis workshop bringing together translation biology and structural biology communities. Workshop materials will be made publicly available.

*Conference Presentations:* Team members will present findings at major conferences including ASCB, Biophysical Society, and RNA Society meetings, reaching diverse audiences.

*Community Engagement:* We will establish a project website with tutorials, documentation, and community forums. Regular blog posts will communicate progress to broad audiences.

**Long-Term Sustainability**

Ensuring long-term availability of project outputs is essential for lasting impact. Databases will be deposited in established repositories (Zenodo, Figshare) with DOIs ensuring permanent accessibility. Software will be maintained on GitHub with continuous integration testing. We will pursue integration of our polysome atlas with established resources (EMDB, GWIPS-viz) for long-term curation. Documentation and tutorials will enable continued use after project completion. We will identify and train community maintainers to sustain tools beyond the funding period.

[Budget and Resources]
**Personnel (Total: $720,000 over 3 years)**

*Postdoctoral Researcher - Cryo-ET Analysis ($180,000):* A postdoc with expertise in cryo-ET image analysis will lead polysome segmentation algorithm development and atlas construction. This position requires specialized skills in tomographic reconstruction, subtomogram averaging, and deep learning for image analysis—expertise essential for extracting quantitative polysome features from heterogeneous tomographic data.

*Postdoctoral Researcher - Translation Biology/Bioinformatics ($180,000):* A postdoc bridging translation biology and computational analysis will lead Ribo-seq data integration and biological interpretation. This position requires deep knowledge of translation mechanisms alongside bioinformatics skills for processing and analyzing sequencing data.

*Graduate Student - Mathematical Modeling ($120,000):* A PhD student will develop kinetic and agent-based models of polysome dynamics under faculty supervision. This training opportunity will develop the student's skills in stochastic modeling, simulation, and model validation.

*Graduate Student - Machine Learning ($120,000):* A PhD student will develop and validate machine learning models predicting translation output from integrated features. Training will encompass modern ML methods, feature engineering, and model interpretation.

*Research Software Engineer (50% FTE, $120,000):* A professional software engineer will ensure code quality, maintain repositories, develop web interfaces, and implement best practices for sustainable software. This investment is essential for producing tools usable by the broader community.

**Computing Resources (Total: $90,000)**

*Cloud Computing - AWS/Google Cloud ($60,000):* Deep learning training for polysome segmentation requires GPU computing beyond typical institutional resources. We budget for approximately 50,000 GPU-hours over the project. Cloud computing also enables reproducible analyses through containerized workflows.

*Data Storage ($30,000):* Cryo-ET data and intermediate processing results require substantial storage. We budget for 100TB of cloud storage with appropriate backup and accessibility.

**Travel and Collaboration (Total: $60,000)**

*Team Meetings ($30,000):* Quarterly in-person meetings bringing together the distributed team are essential for effective collaboration. Budget covers travel for 6 team members to 12 meetings over 3 years.

*Conference Presentations ($20,000):* Disseminating findings at major conferences (ASCB, Biophysical Society, RNA Society) requires travel support for team members presenting results.

*Collaboration Visits ($10,000):* Short visits between labs enable intensive collaborative work on specific project components.

**Workshops and Training (Total: $40,000)**

*Methods Workshop ($20,000):* A 3-day workshop training researchers in polysome analysis methods. Budget covers venue, materials, and travel support for participants from underrepresented institutions.

*Synthesis Workshop ($20,000):* A 2-day workshop bringing together translation biology and structural biology communities to discuss synthesis findings and future directions.

**Open Science Infrastructure (Total: $30,000)**

*Web Hosting and Database Infrastructure ($15,000):* Hosting the polysome atlas and translation database requires reliable infrastructure with appropriate bandwidth for data access.

*DOI Registration and Long-term Archiving ($5,000):* Ensuring permanent accessibility of datasets through DOI registration and repository fees.

*Documentation and Training Materials ($10,000):* Professional editing of documentation, video production for tutorials, and accessibility compliance.

**Supplies and Other (Total: $10,000)**

*Publication Costs ($10,000):* Open-access publication fees for anticipated 8-10 publications.

**Budget Justification Summary**

The budget emphasizes personnel because synthesis research is fundamentally a human intellectual endeavor requiring diverse expertise working collaboratively. Computing resources are essential for processing large cryo-ET datasets and training deep learning models. Travel enables the face-to-face interactions that build effective teams. Workshops extend impact beyond the core team. Open science infrastructure investments ensure lasting accessibility of project outputs. This budget is appropriate for a community-scale synthesis project that no single laboratory could accomplish independently, requiring sustained collaboration across multiple institutions and disciplines over three years.

We will integrate cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) data from EMPIAR and EMDB revealing in-situ ribosome spatial organization, ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) data from GEO and GWIPS-viz capturing translation dynamics, structural data from PDB on ribosome-associated factors, and proteomics from PRIDE quantifying translation machinery stoichiometry. The data synthesis challenge involves reconciling structural snapshots with dynamic sequencing readouts across different experimental systems. full_text:
[Abstract]
The nuclear pore complex (NPC) exemplifies mesoscale emergence: ~500 intrinsically disordered FG-nucleoporins create a selective barrier with transport properties unpredictable from individual protein behaviors. This synthesis project will develop comprehensive models of emergent NPC gating by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB capturing NPC architecture, molecular dynamics trajectories from GPCRmd and similar repositories, single-molecule transport kinetics from published studies compiled in curated databases, FG-nup sequence data from UniProt, and nuclear proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas defining cargo flux. The fundamental question is: how do collective FG-nup dynamics create the emergent selective barrier that simultaneously enables rapid transport of specific cargoes while excluding others? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from mesoscale FG-nup network properties—including collective conformational states, transient crosslinks, and cargo-induced reorganization—rather than simple additive binding interactions. Our analytical approach employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics informed by structural data to simulate FG-nup meshwork behavior, network theory to model connectivity patterns, and machine learning to identify collective states from simulation ensembles. We will develop Markov state models capturing transitions between emergent barrier configurations, correlating these with experimental transport rates. Integration of phosphoproteomics data from PhosphoSitePlus will reveal how post-translational modifications tune emergent barrier properties. Cross-species comparative analysis using orthologous NPC data will identify conserved principles of emergent selectivity. This project requires collaboration between structural biologists interpreting NPC architecture, polymer physicists modeling FG-nup behavior, computational chemists running simulations, and cell biologists understanding transport regulation. The synthesis challenge—connecting angstrom-scale structural data to nanometer-scale meshwork organization to micron-scale transport phenotypes—exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models of emergent NPC selectivity, identification of collective FG-nup states governing transport, and principles applicable to designing synthetic selective barriers. All simulation protocols, analysis code, and model parameters will be openly shared, enabling community refinement of NPC models.

[Background and Significance]
The nuclear pore complex (NPC) represents one of the most remarkable examples of mesoscale emergence in cell biology. Each NPC contains approximately 500-1000 copies of intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins (FG-nups) that collectively form a selective transport barrier within the ~40-60 nm central channel. This barrier accomplishes a seemingly paradoxical task: it permits rapid bidirectional transport of specific cargo-receptor complexes (up to 1000 translocations per second per NPC) while excluding non-specific macromolecules larger than ~40 kDa. The transport properties of the intact NPC cannot be predicted from the behavior of individual FG-nup proteins, making this system a paradigmatic example of biological emergence at the mesoscale.

Current understanding of NPC structure has advanced dramatically through cryo-electron microscopy and tomography studies. High-resolution structures deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) have revealed the scaffold architecture, including the cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic rings, spoke complexes, and membrane-anchoring elements. Recent integrative structures from the Bhattacharya, Beck, and Bhattacharya laboratories have achieved near-atomic resolution for scaffold components. However, the FG-nup meshwork that creates the selective barrier remains poorly resolved due to its intrinsic disorder, appearing as a low-density central mass in tomographic reconstructions. This structural ambiguity at the functional core of the NPC represents a fundamental gap that synthesis research can address by integrating complementary data types.

Single-molecule transport studies have quantified cargo translocation kinetics with millisecond resolution, revealing that transport is remarkably fast (typically 5-20 ms dwell times) and follows complex kinetic patterns inconsistent with simple diffusion through a static barrier. These data, compiled across numerous publications and partially curated in databases like the NPC Transport Database, provide kinetic constraints that any mechanistic model must satisfy. Meanwhile, molecular dynamics simulations of FG-nup behavior have generated extensive trajectory data exploring the conformational dynamics of individual and small groups of FG-nups. These simulations reveal that FG-nups can adopt multiple conformational states and form transient cohesive interactions through their FG motifs.

The fundamental gap in current understanding lies in connecting these disparate scales of information. We have atomic-resolution data on scaffold components, statistical mechanical models of FG-nup polymer behavior, and phenomenological transport kinetics, but no comprehensive framework linking FG-nup collective dynamics to emergent barrier properties. Existing models fall into competing camps—the selective phase model proposing a cohesive FG-nup hydrogel, the virtual gating model emphasizing entropic exclusion, and the forest model describing distinct FG-nup zones—without clear resolution. This debate persists partly because each model draws on different subsets of available data without systematic integration.

The mesoscale nature of NPC selectivity makes it particularly amenable to synthesis research. The relevant length scales span from angstroms (FG motif binding) through nanometers (FG-nup conformational states and meshwork organization) to tens of nanometers (cargo translocation paths), while relevant timescales range from nanoseconds (local FG-nup dynamics) to milliseconds (complete translocation events). No single experimental technique or computational approach spans these ranges, but the collective body of public data does. The Protein Data Bank contains structures of transport receptors (importins, exportins) and their cargo complexes. UniProt provides comprehensive FG-nup sequences across species, enabling evolutionary analysis of sequence-function relationships. The Human Protein Atlas and ProteomicsDB offer quantitative data on nuclear protein abundances that define the cargo flux the NPC must accommodate.

Understanding NPC emergence has significance beyond basic cell biology. The NPC serves as a model for understanding how intrinsically disordered proteins create functional assemblies with emergent properties—a widespread phenomenon in cellular organization. Principles discovered here may apply to other selective barriers, phase-separated condensates, and disordered protein networks. Furthermore, NPC dysfunction is implicated in aging and neurodegenerative diseases, and the NPC is exploited by viruses for nuclear entry. Mechanistic understanding of emergent selectivity could inform therapeutic strategies and inspire synthetic biology approaches to creating artificial selective barriers. The convergence of extensive public datasets, advanced computational methods, and the clear mesoscale nature of the phenomenon makes this an ideal target for NCEMS-supported synthesis research.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions about emergent NPC selectivity, each with specific hypotheses and validation strategies using existing data.

Research Question 1: How do collective FG-nup conformational states create emergent barrier properties that differ from predictions based on individual FG-nup behavior?

We hypothesize that the FG-nup meshwork exists in multiple metastable collective states characterized by distinct patterns of inter-nup cohesive contacts, and that transitions between these states occur on timescales relevant to cargo transport (microseconds to milliseconds). Specifically, we predict that: (H1a) Analysis of published molecular dynamics trajectories will reveal at least three distinct collective conformational states of FG-nup assemblies, identifiable through network clustering of inter-residue contact patterns. (H1b) These collective states will show different predicted permeabilities to cargoes of varying sizes, with state-dependent selectivity that cannot be explained by averaging over individual FG-nup conformations. (H1c) The energy barriers between collective states, estimated from trajectory analysis, will correlate with experimentally measured transport kinetics from single-molecule studies.

Validation will employ Markov state modeling applied to existing simulation trajectories from repositories including the Protein Ensemble Database (PED), MoDEL (Molecular Dynamics Extended Library), and published FG-nup simulation datasets from groups including the Bhattacharya, Hummer, and Rout laboratories. We will construct coarse-grained representations of FG-nup assemblies parameterized by these atomistic data, enabling simulation of larger-scale collective behavior. Predicted transport kinetics will be compared against compiled single-molecule data spanning multiple cargo types, transport receptor concentrations, and experimental conditions.

Research Question 2: What network properties of the FG-nup meshwork determine selective transport, and how do these properties emerge from FG motif sequences and densities?

We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from specific topological properties of the transient FG-nup interaction network, including connectivity, clustering coefficient, and path length distributions. Our specific predictions are: (H2a) The FG-nup network will exhibit small-world properties with high local clustering and short path lengths, enabling both local cohesion and global responsiveness to cargo. (H2b) Selective cargoes (transport receptor-bound) will navigate the network through paths that transiently disrupt local connectivity without collapsing global network structure, while non-selective molecules encounter topological barriers. (H2c) Cross-species comparison of FG-nup sequences from UniProt will reveal conserved features (FG motif spacing, charge distribution, cohesive domain length) that predict similar network topologies despite sequence divergence.

Validation will integrate sequence analysis of FG-nups across eukaryotes (from UniProt and OrthoDB) with structural predictions from AlphaFold2 (via the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database) and disorder predictions from MobiDB. Network properties will be computed from simulated and experimental contact data, then correlated with transport efficiencies measured for orthologous NPCs. The evolutionary conservation of network-level properties, rather than specific sequences, would strongly support the emergence hypothesis.

Research Question 3: How do post-translational modifications (PTMs) tune emergent barrier properties, and can we predict transport phenotypes from PTM patterns?

We hypothesize that phosphorylation and other PTMs of FG-nups modulate emergent selectivity by altering the balance of cohesive and repulsive interactions within the meshwork, effectively tuning the collective state distribution. Specific predictions include: (H3a) Phosphorylation sites mapped in PhosphoSitePlus will cluster at positions predicted to affect inter-FG-nup contacts based on structural modeling. (H3b) Cell-cycle-dependent phosphorylation patterns (from phosphoproteomics time-course data in PRIDE and ProteomeXchange) will correlate with reported changes in NPC permeability during mitosis. (H3c) Machine learning models trained on PTM patterns and transport phenotypes will identify specific modification combinations that shift the collective state equilibrium toward more or less permissive configurations.

Validation leverages the extensive phosphoproteomics data available for nucleoporins, including site-specific phosphorylation stoichiometries under different conditions. We will correlate PTM patterns with transport measurements from the same or comparable cell types and conditions, using data from the Human Protein Atlas and published transport studies. The mechanistic link between PTMs and collective states will be tested by incorporating PTM-dependent interaction parameters into coarse-grained simulations and comparing predicted effects with observed phenotypes.

Expected Mechanistic Insights: Successful validation of these hypotheses will provide a mechanistic framework for NPC emergence operating at the mesoscale. We expect to identify: (1) The repertoire of collective FG-nup states and their interconversion dynamics; (2) Network topology features that enable selective permeability; (3) Molecular determinants (sequence features, PTMs) that tune collective behavior; and (4) Quantitative relationships between mesoscale organization and transport phenotypes. This framework will explain how the NPC achieves selectivity through collective dynamics rather than static structural features, resolving long-standing debates in the field. The insights will be generalizable to other systems where intrinsically disordered proteins create emergent functional assemblies, including nuclear bodies, stress granules, and synaptic densities.

[Methods and Approach]
Our synthesis approach integrates heterogeneous public datasets through a multi-scale computational framework, progressing from sequence analysis through structural modeling to transport simulation and validation.

Data Sources and Acquisition:

Structural Data: We will obtain NPC scaffold structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), including recent integrative models (PDB: 7PEQ, 5A9Q, 5IJN) and component structures. Cryo-ET density maps from EMDB (EMD-14321, EMD-3103, and related entries) provide mesoscale context. Transport receptor structures (importin-β: PDB 1QGK; exportin-1: PDB 3GB8) and cargo complexes will inform cargo-nup interaction modeling. AlphaFold Protein Structure Database predictions for all human nucleoporins (available via UniProt integration) will supplement experimental structures for disordered regions.

Sequence Data: Complete FG-nup sequences for human and model organisms will be retrieved from UniProt (reviewed entries for NUP98, NUP62, NUP153, NUP214, NUP358, and others). OrthoDB will provide orthologous sequences across eukaryotes for evolutionary analysis. Disorder predictions from MobiDB and D2P2 databases will annotate disordered regions.

Dynamics Data: Published molecular dynamics trajectories will be obtained from the Protein Ensemble Database (PED), MoDEL database, and supplementary materials of key publications. We will systematically compile FG-nup simulation data from the Bhattacharya, Rout, Hummer, and Bhattacharya laboratories, totaling >100 microseconds of aggregate simulation time.

Transport Kinetics: Single-molecule transport data will be compiled from published studies, creating a curated database of translocation times, success rates, and cargo dependencies. We will integrate data from the Bhattacharya and Bhattacharya laboratories' transport measurements with broader literature values.

Proteomics and PTMs: Nuclear proteome abundances from the Human Protein Atlas (subcellular localization data) and ProteomicsDB will define cargo flux requirements. PhosphoSitePlus will provide comprehensive PTM annotations for nucleoporins. Cell-cycle phosphoproteomics from PRIDE archive (PXD004452, PXD006482, and related datasets) will enable temporal PTM analysis.

Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy:

We will develop a unified data model linking sequence positions across databases using UniProt accession numbers as primary identifiers. Structural data will be mapped to sequence coordinates, enabling integration of disorder predictions, PTM sites, and evolutionary conservation scores. A custom ontology will harmonize transport measurements across studies with different experimental conditions, normalizing for temperature, cargo concentration, and detection methods. All data will be stored in a relational database with programmatic access via Python APIs.

Computational and Analytical Methods:

Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics: We will employ the MARTINI force field and custom one-bead-per-residue models parameterized from atomistic simulation data. FG-nup assemblies of 50-100 chains (representing a realistic NPC channel segment) will be simulated using GROMACS and OpenMM. Simulations will span microsecond timescales, generating ensembles of meshwork configurations. Cargo translocation will be simulated using enhanced sampling methods (metadynamics, replica exchange) to estimate free energy barriers.

Network Analysis: FG-nup contact networks will be constructed from simulation snapshots, with edges representing transient cohesive contacts (FG-FG interactions, hydrophobic contacts). NetworkX and graph-tool libraries will compute topological metrics: degree distribution, clustering coefficient, betweenness centrality, and community structure. Dynamic network analysis will track edge persistence and rewiring kinetics.

Machine Learning for Collective State Identification: We will apply dimensionality reduction (UMAP, diffusion maps) to simulation ensembles to identify collective states. Variational autoencoders will learn latent representations of meshwork configurations. Markov state models (MSMs) built using PyEMMA will capture transition kinetics between states. Random forest and gradient boosting models will predict transport outcomes from collective state features.

Evolutionary Analysis: Multiple sequence alignments of FG-nups across eukaryotes will be constructed using MAFFT and analyzed for conservation patterns. Phylogenetic profiling will identify co-evolving residue pairs potentially involved in inter-nup contacts. Ancestral sequence reconstruction will enable simulation of hypothetical ancestral FG-nup properties.

Validation Strategies:

Cross-dataset validation will compare predictions against held-out transport measurements. Known positive controls include the well-characterized effects of specific transport receptor mutations on translocation kinetics. We will validate network models against crosslinking mass spectrometry data (from published studies) that provide independent constraints on FG-nup contacts. Predicted PTM effects will be validated against published perturbation studies (phosphomimetic mutations, kinase inhibition).

Timeline and Milestones (36-month project):

Months 1-6: Data acquisition and harmonization; database construction; team onboarding and training workshops.
Months 7-12: Coarse-grained model development and parameterization; initial simulations; sequence analysis pipeline.
Months 13-18: Large-scale simulations; Markov state model construction; network analysis implementation.
Months 19-24: Machine learning model development; cross-species comparative analysis; PTM integration.
Months 25-30: Validation against transport data; model refinement; synthesis of mechanistic insights.
Months 31-36: Documentation; publication preparation; tool release; community workshops.

Team Composition and Expertise:

The project requires: (1) Structural biologists with expertise in NPC architecture and cryo-EM interpretation; (2) Polymer physicists experienced in modeling intrinsically disordered proteins; (3) Computational chemists skilled in molecular dynamics and enhanced sampling; (4) Data scientists proficient in machine learning and network analysis; (5) Cell biologists understanding nuclear transport regulation; and (6) Bioinformaticians for evolutionary analysis and database development. We will assemble a team spanning four institutions, including R1 universities and a primarily undergraduate institution, with participants ranging from graduate students to senior investigators.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will generate multiple concrete deliverables that advance understanding of NPC emergence and provide resources for the broader research community.

Specific Deliverables:

1. Integrated NPC Data Resource: A curated, harmonized database linking structural, sequence, dynamics, transport kinetics, and PTM data for nuclear pore complexes. This resource will include standardized annotations, cross-references between data types, and programmatic access via REST APIs. We estimate integration of >500 structural entries, sequences from >100 species, >200 microseconds of simulation data, and transport measurements from >50 publications.

2. Coarse-Grained NPC Model Suite: Parameterized simulation models at multiple resolutions (MARTINI-compatible and custom one-bead-per-residue) enabling community simulation of FG-nup assemblies. Models will include validated parameters for FG-FG interactions, cargo-FG binding, and PTM effects. Pre-equilibrated starting configurations representing different collective states will be provided.

3. Markov State Models of NPC Dynamics: Quantitative kinetic models describing transitions between collective FG-nup states, with associated free energy landscapes. These models will enable prediction of transport outcomes for novel cargo types and perturbation conditions.

4. Predictive Machine Learning Tools: Trained models for predicting transport efficiency from cargo properties, FG-nup sequences, and PTM patterns. Feature importance analysis will identify key determinants of selectivity.

5. Cross-Species Selectivity Atlas: Comparative analysis of NPC selectivity principles across eukaryotes, identifying conserved and divergent features of emergent barrier function.

Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergence:

This project will establish quantitative principles for how collective dynamics of disordered proteins create emergent functional properties. By demonstrating that NPC selectivity arises from mesoscale network properties rather than simple molecular interactions, we will provide a paradigm for understanding other disordered protein assemblies. The identification of collective states and their interconversion kinetics will reveal how biological systems encode function in dynamic ensembles rather than static structures. Our framework for connecting sequence features to network topology to phenotypic outcomes will be applicable to diverse mesoscale systems.

Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology:

The methodological innovations developed here—integrating structural, simulation, and phenotypic data through machine learning—will be transferable to other mesoscale systems including: nuclear bodies and phase-separated condensates; synaptic densities and other signaling assemblies; cytoskeletal networks; and viral capsids and other protein cages. Our demonstration that synthesis of existing data can resolve long-standing mechanistic questions will encourage similar approaches throughout cell biology.

Enabling Future Research:

The integrated data resource and computational tools will enable numerous follow-on studies: testing specific mechanistic hypotheses through targeted simulations; designing synthetic selective barriers with tunable properties; developing therapeutic strategies targeting NPC dysfunction in disease; and generating experimentally testable predictions for validation. By providing validated models and curated data, we lower barriers for new researchers to enter this field.

Dissemination Plans:

Publications: We anticipate 4-6 peer-reviewed publications including: (1) a methods paper describing the data integration framework; (2) a research article on collective FG-nup states and transport mechanisms; (3) a comparative analysis across species; (4) a study of PTM regulation of barrier properties; and (5) tool/resource papers for the database and simulation models.

Workshops: We will organize two workshops at NCEMS facilities: (1) a training workshop for graduate students and postdocs on NPC simulation and analysis methods; and (2) a community workshop bringing together experimentalists and computational researchers to refine models and identify future directions.

Conference Presentations: Results will be presented at the ASCB Annual Meeting, Biophysical Society Meeting, and Gordon Research Conferences on Nuclear Organization and Function.

Long-Term Sustainability:

The integrated database will be deposited with NCEMS for long-term hosting and will be mirrored at participating institutions. We will establish a community curation model where researchers can contribute new data and annotations. Simulation models will be deposited in community repositories (Zenodo, Materials Cloud) with permanent DOIs. Analysis code will be maintained on GitHub with designated maintainers for at least five years post-project. We will engage with the nuclear transport community to identify champions for continued development and application of these resources.

[Budget and Resources]
We request a total budget of $750,000 over three years to support this synthesis research project. The budget is structured to maximize scientific productivity while ensuring broad participation and rigorous open science practices.

Personnel ($480,000 total; $160,000/year):

Postdoctoral Researcher - Computational Biology (100% effort, $65,000/year salary + benefits): This position will lead data integration, coarse-grained model development, and Markov state modeling. The postdoc will coordinate across team members and mentor graduate students. Justification: The scale of data integration and simulation exceeds what can be accomplished by existing lab members; dedicated effort is essential.

Postdoctoral Researcher - Machine Learning/Data Science (50% effort, $32,500/year salary + benefits): This position will develop ML pipelines for collective state identification and transport prediction. Justification: Specialized ML expertise is required for rigorous model development and validation.

Graduate Student Support (two students at 50% effort each, $30,000/year total including tuition): Students will contribute to specific project components (evolutionary analysis, PTM integration) while receiving training in synthesis research methods. Justification: Training the next generation is a core NCEMS mission; student involvement provides both workforce development and project capacity.

Software Developer (25% effort, $32,500/year): Professional software engineering support for database development, API implementation, and code maintenance. Justification: Sustainable, well-documented code requires professional development practices beyond typical academic standards.

Computing Resources ($120,000 total; $40,000/year):

Cloud Computing (AWS/Google Cloud): $25,000/year for scalable simulation and ML training workloads. Justification: Cloud resources provide flexibility for burst computing needs and ensure reproducibility across platforms.

High-Performance Computing Allocations: $10,000/year for HPC time at national facilities (XSEDE/ACCESS allocations supplemented by purchased time). Justification: Large-scale MD simulations require HPC resources beyond typical institutional allocations.

Data Storage and Hosting: $5,000/year for long-term data archiving and database hosting. Justification: Ensuring data availability beyond project duration requires dedicated resources.

Travel and Collaboration ($75,000 total; $25,000/year):

Working Group Meetings: $12,000/year for biannual in-person team meetings (travel for ~10 participants). Justification: Face-to-face collaboration is essential for synthesis research integrating diverse expertise.

Conference Travel: $8,000/year for team members to present results at national meetings. Justification: Dissemination and community feedback are critical for impact.

Collaborator Visits: $5,000/year for short-term visits between team members' institutions. Justification: Intensive collaborative work sessions accelerate progress on integration challenges.

Workshops and Training ($45,000 total; $15,000/year):

Training Workshop (Year 2): $20,000 for a 3-day workshop training 20 participants in NPC simulation and analysis methods. Justification: Workforce development and community capacity building.

Community Workshop (Year 3): $15,000 for a 2-day workshop bringing together experimentalists and computational researchers. Justification: Ensuring models address community needs and identifying future directions.

Online Training Materials: $10,000 for video production and hosting. Justification: Scalable training reaches broader audience than in-person events alone.

Open Science Infrastructure ($30,000 total; $10,000/year):

Repository Hosting and DOI Registration: $3,000/year for Zenodo Plus, GitHub organization, Docker Hub. Justification: Professional-grade infrastructure ensures long-term availability.

Documentation and Website: $4,000/year for ReadTheDocs hosting, domain registration, web development. Justification: Accessible documentation is essential for community adoption.

Reproducibility Testing: $3,000/year for cloud credits dedicated to reproducibility verification. Justification: Independent verification of reproducibility requires dedicated resources.

Budget Justification Summary:

This budget reflects the collaborative, synthesis-focused nature of the project. Personnel costs are the largest component because human expertise in data integration, modeling, and analysis is the primary requirement—we are not purchasing equipment or generating new data. Computing costs support the substantial simulation and ML workloads required. Travel and workshop costs enable the cross-institutional collaboration and community engagement that distinguish synthesis research from single-lab projects. Open science infrastructure investments ensure our deliverables remain accessible and useful to the community long after project completion.

abstract_original: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) exemplifies mesoscale emergence: ~500 intrinsically disordered FG-nucleoporins create a selective barrier with transport properties unpredictable from individual protein behaviors. This synthesis project will develop comprehensive models of emergent NPC gating by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB capturing NPC architecture, molecular dynamics trajectories from GPCRmd and similar repositories, single-molecule transport kinetics from published studies compiled in curated databases, FG-nup sequence data from UniProt, and nuclear proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas defining cargo flux. The fundamental question is: how do collective FG-nup dynamics create the emergent selective barrier that simultaneously enables rapid transport of specific cargoes while excluding others? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from mesoscale FG-nup network properties—including collective conformational states, transient crosslinks, and cargo-induced reorganization—rather than simple additive binding interactions. Our analytical approach employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics informed by structural data to simulate FG-nup meshwork behavior, network theory to model connectivity patterns, and machine learning to identify collective states from simulation ensembles. We will develop Markov state models capturing transitions between emergent barrier configurations, correlating these with experimental transport rates. Integration of phosphoproteomics data from PhosphoSitePlus will reveal how post-translational modifications tune emergent barrier properties. Cross-species comparative analysis using orthologous NPC data will identify conserved principles of emergent selectivity. This project requires collaboration between structural biologists interpreting NPC architecture, polymer physicists modeling FG-nup behavior, computational chemists running simulations, and cell biologists understanding transport regulation. The synthesis challenge—connecting angstrom-scale structural data to nanometer-scale meshwork organization to micron-scale transport phenotypes—exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models of emergent NPC selectivity, identification of collective FG-nup states governing transport, and principles applicable to designing synthetic selective barriers. All simulation protocols, analysis code, and model parameters will be openly shared, enabling community refinement of NPC models.
