full_text:
[Abstract]
Chromatin organization into A/B compartments, topologically associating domains (TADs), and nuclear bodies represents emergent mesoscale structure arising from DNA-protein interactions. This synthesis project will integrate multi-modal data to understand how molecular-level chromatin modifications create emergent nuclear compartmentalization with functional consequences. We will synthesize Hi-C contact maps from 4DN Data Portal and ENCODE, super-resolution imaging data from the Image Data Resource and Cell Image Library, ChIP-seq for histone modifications and chromatin proteins from ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics, ATAC-seq accessibility data, and single-cell multi-omics from the Human Cell Atlas. The central hypothesis is that emergent compartmentalization arises from phase separation driven by multivalent interactions among modified histones and reader proteins, creating mesoscale domains (100 nm - 1 μm) with distinct biochemical environments. We will develop integrative computational frameworks combining polymer physics models of chromatin, machine learning for predicting 3D organization from sequence and epigenetic features, and spatial statistics for analyzing imaging data. Novel algorithms will integrate contact frequencies with spatial positions, resolving the relationship between measured interactions and physical distances. Network analysis will identify emergent chromatin communities and their hierarchical organization. We will correlate compartmentalization patterns with transcriptional output using RNA-seq from matched samples, testing whether emergent nuclear organization causally influences gene expression or vice versa. Cross-cell-type analysis will reveal conserved versus cell-specific emergent organizational principles. This project demands expertise in chromosome biology, polymer physics, image analysis, machine learning, and genomics—requiring collaboration across traditionally separate fields. The data integration challenge spans contact maps, images, and sequencing data at different resolutions and from different experimental systems. Expected insights include quantitative models of compartmentalization emergence, identification of key molecular drivers of mesoscale organization, and understanding of how nuclear structure influences function. All analysis pipelines, trained models, and integrated datasets will be publicly released, establishing resources for the chromosome biology community.

[Background and Significance]
The eukaryotic nucleus represents one of biology's most sophisticated examples of emergent organization, where molecular-level interactions between DNA, histones, and chromatin-associated proteins give rise to mesoscale structures with profound functional consequences. This emergent nuclear architecture operates at scales between 100 nanometers and several micrometers—precisely the mesoscale regime where collective behaviors of molecular components produce organizational properties that cannot be predicted from individual molecular interactions alone.

Over the past decade, chromosome conformation capture technologies, particularly Hi-C, have revealed that genomes are organized into hierarchical structures including A/B compartments (megabase-scale regions of active versus inactive chromatin), topologically associating domains (TADs, typically 100 kb to 1 Mb), and chromatin loops connecting regulatory elements. The 4D Nucleome (4DN) Consortium and ENCODE Project have generated thousands of Hi-C datasets across diverse cell types and conditions, creating an unprecedented resource for understanding chromatin organization. Simultaneously, advances in super-resolution microscopy have enabled direct visualization of chromatin domains, with imaging datasets now available through the Image Data Resource (IDR) and Cell Image Library documenting nuclear organization at sub-diffraction resolution.

Despite this wealth of data, fundamental questions about the emergence of nuclear organization remain unanswered. Current understanding suggests that phase separation—driven by multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions of chromatin proteins and modified histone tails—underlies compartmentalization. Proteins such as HP1 (heterochromatin protein 1), Polycomb group proteins, and transcriptional coactivators form condensates that partition the nucleus into biochemically distinct environments. However, the quantitative rules governing how molecular-level modifications (histone acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation) translate into mesoscale compartments remain poorly defined.

Critically, existing studies have largely examined these data modalities in isolation. Hi-C provides contact frequencies but not absolute spatial positions. Imaging reveals spatial organization but typically for limited genomic loci. Epigenomic data (ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq) maps molecular features but not their three-dimensional context. The synthesis opportunity lies in integrating these complementary perspectives to build unified models of emergent chromatin organization.

Several specific gaps motivate this synthesis project. First, the relationship between Hi-C contact frequencies and physical distances measured by imaging remains incompletely resolved, with different studies reporting conflicting power-law relationships. Systematic integration of contact maps with imaging data across matched cell types can resolve these discrepancies. Second, while individual histone modifications correlate with compartmentalization, the combinatorial logic—how multiple modifications interact to drive phase separation—requires integrative analysis across epigenomic datasets. Third, single-cell data from the Human Cell Atlas reveals substantial cell-to-cell variability in both chromatin organization and gene expression, but whether this variability reflects stochastic fluctuations or functionally meaningful heterogeneity in emergent organization remains unclear.

The mesoscale nature of chromatin compartmentalization makes it an ideal target for NCEMS-supported synthesis research. Compartments and TADs occupy precisely the scale between individual nucleosomes (molecular) and the nucleus as a whole (organelle). Their emergence from molecular interactions exemplifies the type of multi-scale phenomenon that requires integrative approaches spanning polymer physics, genomics, and cell biology. Furthermore, the functional consequences of compartmentalization—including transcriptional regulation, DNA replication timing, and DNA repair—make understanding these emergent structures essential for molecular and cellular biology.

The publicly available data landscape has reached a critical mass enabling this synthesis. The 4DN Data Portal contains over 2,000 Hi-C datasets with standardized processing. ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics provide matched epigenomic profiles across hundreds of cell types. The Human Cell Atlas includes single-cell multi-omics data linking chromatin accessibility to transcription. Super-resolution imaging datasets in IDR document nuclear organization with unprecedented spatial resolution. No single laboratory possesses the expertise to integrate these diverse data types, making this project ideally suited for the collaborative, transdisciplinary approach that NCEMS promotes.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project addresses four interconnected research questions about the emergence of chromatin compartmentalization, each with specific testable hypotheses that can be validated using existing publicly available data.

**Research Question 1: What is the quantitative relationship between Hi-C contact frequencies and physical spatial distances in chromatin organization?**

Hypothesis 1a: The relationship between Hi-C contact frequencies and physical distances follows a cell-type-specific power law, with the exponent reflecting chromatin compaction state and compartmentalization strength.

Hypothesis 1b: Discrepancies between contact-based and imaging-based distance estimates are systematically explained by chromatin state (A versus B compartment), with heterochromatic regions showing greater deviation from contact-distance predictions.

These hypotheses will be tested by integrating Hi-C data from the 4DN Data Portal with matched super-resolution imaging data from IDR for cell types where both modalities are available (including IMR90 fibroblasts, HCT116 colon cancer cells, and K562 erythroleukemia cells). We will compute contact frequency-distance relationships for specific genomic loci visualized by DNA-FISH or oligopaint imaging, stratified by chromatin compartment identity. Measurable predictions include: (1) power-law exponents will differ by >0.2 between A and B compartments; (2) imaging-derived distances for heterochromatic loci will exceed Hi-C predictions by >30%.

**Research Question 2: Which combinations of histone modifications and chromatin proteins are necessary and sufficient to predict emergent compartmentalization?**

Hypothesis 2a: Emergent A/B compartmentalization can be predicted with >85% accuracy from a minimal set of histone modifications (H3K27ac, H3K4me3, H3K27me3, H3K9me3) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), reflecting the molecular grammar of phase separation.

Hypothesis 2b: The combinatorial logic of compartmentalization follows non-additive rules, where specific modification pairs (e.g., H3K27me3 + H3K9me3) show synergistic effects on compartment strength beyond individual contributions.

These hypotheses will be tested using machine learning models trained on matched Hi-C and epigenomic data from ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics. We will systematically evaluate feature importance and interaction terms, using cross-cell-type validation to assess generalizability. Measurable predictions include: (1) models using only 4-5 epigenomic features will achieve compartment prediction accuracy within 5% of models using all available features; (2) interaction terms between specific modification pairs will improve prediction accuracy by >10% compared to additive models.

**Research Question 3: How does cell-to-cell variability in chromatin organization relate to transcriptional heterogeneity?**

Hypothesis 3a: Single-cell variability in chromatin accessibility (measured by scATAC-seq) at compartment boundaries predicts transcriptional variability of genes near those boundaries, indicating that emergent organizational fluctuations have functional consequences.

Hypothesis 3b: Cells within a population occupy discrete organizational states corresponding to alternative compartmentalization patterns, rather than showing continuous variation around a mean configuration.

These hypotheses will be tested using single-cell multi-omics data from the Human Cell Atlas, particularly datasets with matched scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq from the same cells. We will correlate accessibility variability at computationally-defined compartment boundaries with expression variability of nearby genes. Clustering analysis will determine whether cells occupy discrete versus continuous organizational states. Measurable predictions include: (1) correlation coefficient >0.4 between accessibility variability and expression variability for boundary-proximal genes; (2) identification of 3-5 discrete organizational states per cell type based on accessibility patterns.

**Research Question 4: What are the conserved versus cell-type-specific principles governing emergent chromatin compartmentalization?**

Hypothesis 4a: Core organizational principles (TAD boundaries, compartment-defining modifications) are conserved across cell types, while compartment assignments for specific genomic regions show cell-type-specificity correlating with lineage-specific gene expression programs.

Hypothesis 4b: The hierarchical organization of chromatin—from loops to TADs to compartments—follows scale-invariant network properties that are conserved across cell types, even when specific domain boundaries differ.

These hypotheses will be tested through cross-cell-type meta-analysis of Hi-C and epigenomic data spanning >50 cell types from 4DN, ENCODE, and Roadmap Epigenomics. Network analysis will characterize hierarchical organization, and conservation metrics will quantify which features are invariant versus variable. Measurable predictions include: (1) >70% of TAD boundaries will be shared across >80% of cell types; (2) network modularity and hierarchical clustering coefficients will show <20% variation across cell types despite >50% variation in specific domain assignments.

**Mechanistic Insights Expected**

By addressing these questions, we expect to establish quantitative rules for how molecular-level chromatin features give rise to mesoscale organization. Specifically, we anticipate identifying: (1) the minimal molecular determinants of compartmentalization; (2) the biophysical parameters (interaction strengths, valencies) that polymer physics models require to recapitulate observed organization; (3) the functional consequences of organizational variability; and (4) the evolutionary constraints on nuclear architecture. These insights will transform chromatin biology from descriptive cataloging to predictive modeling of emergent nuclear organization.

[Methods and Approach]
**Data Sources and Acquisition**

This synthesis project will integrate data from six major publicly available repositories, totaling approximately 50 terabytes of processed data:

1. *4D Nucleome (4DN) Data Portal*: Hi-C contact maps from >500 experiments across human and mouse cell types, including high-resolution maps (1-5 kb) for key cell lines (IMR90, HCT116, K562, GM12878, H1-hESC). We will also access Micro-C data providing nucleosome-resolution contact information and DNA-FISH imaging datasets for specific loci.

2. *ENCODE Portal*: ChIP-seq data for >100 histone modifications and chromatin proteins across >200 cell types; ATAC-seq chromatin accessibility data; RNA-seq expression data matched to Hi-C samples; processed peak calls and signal tracks in standardized formats.

3. *Roadmap Epigenomics*: Comprehensive epigenomic profiles (ChIP-seq for 5 core histone modifications, DNase-seq, RNA-seq) across 127 human tissues and cell types, enabling broad cross-cell-type analysis.

4. *Human Cell Atlas (HCA)*: Single-cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data from >1 million cells across multiple tissues, including paired multi-omics datasets where both modalities are measured in the same cells.

5. *Image Data Resource (IDR)*: Super-resolution microscopy images of chromatin organization, including STORM/PALM imaging of nuclear structures, DNA-FISH for specific loci, and live-cell imaging of chromatin dynamics.

6. *Cell Image Library*: Additional nuclear organization images including electron microscopy of chromatin ultrastructure and conventional fluorescence microscopy of nuclear bodies.

**Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy**

Integrating heterogeneous data types represents the core methodological challenge. Our harmonization strategy proceeds in three phases:

*Phase 1 - Standardization (Months 1-6)*: All datasets will be mapped to common reference genomes (GRCh38 for human, GRCm39 for mouse) using established pipelines. Hi-C data will be processed using the 4DN-standard Juicer/cooler pipeline to generate multi-resolution contact matrices. ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data will be processed using ENCODE-standard pipelines (bowtie2 alignment, MACS2 peak calling). RNA-seq will be quantified using STAR/RSEM. Imaging data will be registered to genomic coordinates using probe sequences for DNA-FISH or protein identities for immunofluorescence.

*Phase 2 - Cross-modality alignment (Months 4-12)*: We will develop a unified coordinate system linking contact maps, epigenomic signals, and imaging data. For matched samples (same cell type, same laboratory), direct integration is straightforward. For unmatched samples, we will use transfer learning approaches to map between related cell types. Genomic bins (typically 10-100 kb) will serve as the fundamental unit of integration, with each bin annotated by contact frequencies, epigenomic features, and (where available) spatial positions.

*Phase 3 - Quality control and batch correction (Months 6-18)*: Systematic batch effects between laboratories, protocols, and sequencing depths will be addressed using established methods (ComBat for sequencing data, intensity normalization for imaging). We will maintain a comprehensive metadata database tracking experimental conditions, enabling sensitivity analyses.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Polymer Physics Modeling*: We will implement and extend block copolymer models of chromatin, where A and B compartments represent distinct polymer types with different self-interaction affinities. Using the Open Chromatin Collective (OpenMM) molecular dynamics framework, we will simulate chromatin organization under varying interaction parameters. Model parameters will be constrained by matching simulated contact maps to experimental Hi-C data using approximate Bayesian computation.

*Machine Learning for Compartment Prediction*: We will train gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost) and deep neural networks to predict compartment identity from epigenomic features. Input features will include ChIP-seq signal for histone modifications, ATAC-seq accessibility, and DNA sequence features (GC content, repeat density). Cross-validation will use held-out chromosomes and cell types. Feature importance analysis (SHAP values) will identify key molecular determinants.

*Spatial Statistics for Imaging Analysis*: Super-resolution imaging data will be analyzed using spatial point process methods to characterize chromatin domain organization. We will compute Ripley's K-function to quantify clustering at different scales, identify domain boundaries using change-point detection, and measure inter-domain distances. Custom algorithms will segment nuclear bodies and quantify their association with specific chromatin features.

*Contact-Distance Integration*: We will develop novel algorithms to jointly analyze Hi-C contact frequencies and imaging-derived distances. Using maximum entropy approaches, we will infer 3D chromatin structures consistent with both data types. This addresses a key gap where existing methods use either contacts or distances but not both.

*Network Analysis*: Chromatin organization will be analyzed as a network, with genomic bins as nodes and contact frequencies as edge weights. Community detection algorithms (Louvain, Infomap) will identify emergent chromatin communities. Hierarchical analysis will characterize multi-scale organization from loops to TADs to compartments.

**Validation Strategies**

All computational predictions will be validated using existing data, without generating new experiments:

1. *Cross-dataset validation*: Models trained on ENCODE data will be validated on 4DN data (and vice versa) to ensure generalizability.

2. *Cross-cell-type validation*: Compartment predictions will be tested on held-out cell types not used in training.

3. *Known positive controls*: Established compartment markers (H3K27me3 for B compartment, H3K27ac for A compartment) will serve as positive controls.

4. *Functional validation*: Predicted compartment changes will be correlated with expression changes in matched RNA-seq data.

5. *Literature benchmarking*: Our integrated models will be compared against published findings to ensure consistency with established knowledge.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1*: Data acquisition and harmonization (Q1-Q2); Polymer physics model development (Q2-Q3); Initial machine learning models (Q3-Q4); First cross-modality integration (Q4)

*Year 2*: Refined integration algorithms (Q1-Q2); Single-cell analysis (Q2-Q3); Cross-cell-type meta-analysis (Q3-Q4); Network analysis (Q4)

*Year 3*: Model validation and refinement (Q1-Q2); Tool development and documentation (Q2-Q3); Manuscript preparation and community release (Q3-Q4)

**Team Composition and Expertise**

This project requires collaboration across five distinct expertise areas:

1. *Chromosome Biology* (2 labs): Expertise in chromatin organization, Hi-C analysis, and nuclear structure
2. *Polymer Physics* (1 lab): Expertise in polymer simulations and theoretical modeling of chromatin
3. *Computational Image Analysis* (1 lab): Expertise in super-resolution microscopy analysis and spatial statistics
4. *Machine Learning/AI* (1 lab): Expertise in deep learning, feature engineering, and model interpretation
5. *Genomics/Bioinformatics* (1 lab): Expertise in epigenomic data analysis and multi-omics integration

No single laboratory possesses all required expertise, making this project ideally suited for NCEMS collaborative support.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
**Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce five categories of deliverables that will serve the chromosome biology community and advance understanding of emergent nuclear organization:

*Integrated Datasets*: We will generate harmonized, multi-modal datasets linking Hi-C contact maps, epigenomic profiles, and imaging data across >50 human cell types. These integrated datasets will be formatted for easy access and analysis, with standardized annotations including compartment assignments, TAD boundaries, and chromatin state classifications. The integrated resource will include: (1) a unified compartmentalization atlas across all cell types; (2) matched contact-epigenome-expression matrices for >200 cell type/condition combinations; (3) curated imaging-genomics linkages for >20 cell types with super-resolution data.

*Computational Tools*: We will develop and release a software suite for chromatin organization analysis, including: (1) ChromaSync—algorithms for integrating Hi-C contact frequencies with imaging-derived spatial positions; (2) CompartmentPredict—machine learning models for predicting compartmentalization from epigenomic features; (3) PolyChrom—parameterized polymer physics models for simulating chromatin organization; (4) NuclearNet—network analysis tools for characterizing hierarchical chromatin communities. All tools will be released as documented Python packages with tutorials and example workflows.

*Mechanistic Models*: We will deliver quantitative models describing: (1) the molecular determinants of A/B compartmentalization, including feature importance rankings and interaction rules; (2) biophysical parameters (interaction energies, valencies) governing phase separation-driven organization; (3) the relationship between organizational variability and transcriptional heterogeneity; (4) conserved versus cell-type-specific organizational principles.

*Trained Machine Learning Models*: Pre-trained models for compartment prediction, TAD boundary identification, and chromatin state classification will be released, enabling researchers to apply our methods to new datasets without extensive computational expertise.

*Comprehensive Documentation*: All methods, parameters, and analytical decisions will be documented in detailed protocols, enabling full reproducibility and extension by other researchers.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. Chromatin compartmentalization exemplifies emergence: the organizational patterns observed at 100 nm to 1 μm scales cannot be predicted from the properties of individual nucleosomes or DNA-protein interactions alone. Instead, compartments arise from collective behaviors—phase separation, multivalent interactions, and cooperative binding—that produce qualitatively new organizational states.

Our synthesis approach will establish quantitative rules for this emergence. By integrating molecular-level data (histone modifications, protein binding) with mesoscale observations (compartments, TADs), we will identify the minimal molecular features necessary for emergent organization. This addresses a fundamental question: what information at the molecular scale is sufficient to predict mesoscale structure? Our machine learning models will provide explicit answers, identifying which modifications matter and how they combine.

Furthermore, by linking organizational patterns to functional outcomes (gene expression), we will establish whether emergent nuclear structure causally influences cellular phenotypes. This addresses the broader question of why mesoscale organization exists—whether it serves functional purposes or emerges as a byproduct of molecular interactions without functional significance.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Beyond chromatin biology, this project will establish methodological paradigms for studying emergent phenomena in other cellular contexts. The computational frameworks for integrating contact maps, imaging data, and molecular profiles are generalizable to other mesoscale structures including: (1) membraneless organelles and biomolecular condensates; (2) cytoskeletal networks; (3) organelle contact sites; (4) signaling complexes. Our network analysis approaches for characterizing hierarchical organization apply broadly to multi-scale biological systems.

The project will also advance understanding of gene regulation. By establishing quantitative relationships between chromatin organization and transcription, we will provide insights relevant to developmental biology, cancer biology, and cellular reprogramming—all contexts where chromatin reorganization accompanies cell state changes.

**Enabling Future Research**

Our integrated datasets and computational tools will enable numerous follow-up studies:

1. *Disease applications*: Researchers can apply our compartment prediction models to cancer or developmental disorder samples to identify organizational disruptions.

2. *Evolutionary analysis*: Our cross-cell-type conservation analysis provides a framework for comparative studies across species.

3. *Perturbation prediction*: Polymer physics models parameterized by our data can predict organizational consequences of genetic or epigenetic perturbations.

4. *Single-cell extensions*: Our single-cell analysis framework enables future studies as additional single-cell chromatin organization data becomes available.

**Dissemination Plans**

*Publications*: We anticipate 4-6 peer-reviewed publications, including: (1) a flagship paper presenting the integrated framework and major findings; (2) methods papers for each major computational tool; (3) focused papers on specific biological insights (conservation, single-cell variability, structure-function relationships).

*Workshops*: We will organize two workshops during the project: (1) a mid-project workshop bringing together chromatin biology, physics, and computational communities to share preliminary findings and gather feedback; (2) an end-of-project workshop focused on training researchers to use our tools and datasets.

*Conference presentations*: Results will be presented at major meetings including the 4D Nucleome Annual Meeting, ASCB Cell Bio, and Biophysical Society Meeting.

*Online resources*: A dedicated project website will host documentation, tutorials, and links to all data and code repositories.

**Long-term Sustainability**

To ensure long-term impact, we will: (1) deposit integrated datasets in established repositories (4DN Data Portal, GEO) with permanent accession numbers; (2) release software through standard package managers (PyPI, Bioconda) with version control; (3) establish community governance for tool maintenance through GitHub organizations; (4) document all methods sufficiently for reproduction without our direct involvement. We will also engage with the 4DN Consortium and ENCODE to explore integration of our tools into their analysis pipelines, ensuring continued use and maintenance.

[Budget and Resources]
**Personnel (Total: $720,000 over 3 years)**

*Postdoctoral Researchers (3 positions, $180,000/year total)*: Three postdocs will lead major project components: (1) Data integration and harmonization specialist, responsible for building the unified multi-modal database; (2) Machine learning researcher, developing and validating predictive models; (3) Polymer physics/simulation specialist, implementing and parameterizing chromatin models. Postdocs are essential for the intellectual depth and sustained effort required for this synthesis project. ($540,000 total)

*Graduate Students (2 positions, $40,000/year total)*: Two PhD students will contribute to specific project aims while receiving training in synthesis research: (1) Student focusing on imaging data analysis and spatial statistics; (2) Student focusing on single-cell data integration. This directly addresses NCEMS's training mission. ($120,000 total)

*Research Software Engineer (0.5 FTE, $40,000/year)*: A dedicated software engineer will ensure code quality, documentation, and long-term maintainability of released tools. This investment is essential for the open science mission. ($60,000 total)

**Computing Resources (Total: $180,000 over 3 years)**

*Cloud Computing (AWS/Google Cloud, $40,000/year)*: Processing and integrating >50 TB of data requires substantial cloud computing resources. We will use cloud platforms for scalable data processing, machine learning model training, and hosting interactive resources. ($120,000 total)

*High-Performance Computing (HPC, $20,000/year)*: Polymer physics simulations require HPC resources. We will purchase allocations on XSEDE/ACCESS resources for molecular dynamics simulations. ($60,000 total)

**Travel for Collaboration and Dissemination (Total: $90,000 over 3 years)**

*Team Meetings ($15,000/year)*: Quarterly in-person meetings rotating among collaborating institutions are essential for integration across the distributed team. ($45,000 total)

*Conference Travel ($15,000/year)*: Presenting results at 4DN Annual Meeting, ASCB, Biophysical Society, and RECOMB to disseminate findings and engage the community. ($45,000 total)

**Workshops and Training Events (Total: $60,000 over 3 years)**

*Mid-project Workshop (Year 2, $25,000)*: Two-day workshop bringing together 30-40 researchers from chromatin biology, physics, and computation to review progress and gather community input.

*End-of-project Training Workshop (Year 3, $25,000)*: Three-day hands-on training workshop teaching researchers to use project tools and datasets.

*Virtual Training Materials ($10,000)*: Development of online tutorials, video documentation, and interactive learning resources.

**Open Science Infrastructure (Total: $30,000 over 3 years)**

*Data Storage and Hosting ($5,000/year)*: Long-term storage for integrated datasets and hosting for project website and interactive resources. ($15,000 total)

*DOI Registration and Repository Fees ($5,000/year)*: Costs for Zenodo, Figshare, and other repositories to ensure permanent data availability. ($15,000 total)

**Supplies and Other Costs (Total: $20,000 over 3 years)**

*Publication Costs ($15,000)*: Open-access publication fees for 4-6 anticipated papers.

*Miscellaneous ($5,000)*: Software licenses, minor equipment, and contingency.

**Total Budget: $1,100,000 over 3 years**

**Budget Justification**

This budget reflects the synthesis nature of the project. The majority (65%) supports personnel—the intellectual effort required to integrate heterogeneous data types and develop novel computational methods. Computing costs (16%) reflect the data-intensive nature of the work. Travel and workshops (14%) enable the collaboration and community engagement essential for synthesis science. Open science infrastructure (3%) ensures long-term availability of project outputs.

This project requires NCEMS support because: (1) the multi-disciplinary team spans 5+ laboratories that cannot be supported by single-PI grants; (2) the data integration challenge exceeds what any individual lab could accomplish; (3) the commitment to open science and community tools requires dedicated resources beyond typical research grants. The collaborative, synthesis-focused nature of this work aligns precisely with NCEMS's mission.

The analytical strategy relies on a secondary synthesis of public multimodal data to train computational models without new experiments. Key methods involve physics simulations of block copolymers via OpenMM and deep neural networks paired with transfer learning algorithms. This ambitious scope exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory and requires extensive cross disciplinary collaboration across multiple domains. abstract_original: Chromatin organization into A/B compartments, topologically associating domains (TADs), and nuclear bodies represents emergent mesoscale structure arising from DNA-protein interactions. This synthesis project will integrate multi-modal data to understand how molecular-level chromatin modifications create emergent nuclear compartmentalization with functional consequences. We will synthesize Hi-C contact maps from 4DN Data Portal and ENCODE, super-resolution imaging data from the Image Data Resource and Cell Image Library, ChIP-seq for histone modifications and chromatin proteins from ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics, ATAC-seq accessibility data, and single-cell multi-omics from the Human Cell Atlas. The central hypothesis is that emergent compartmentalization arises from phase separation driven by multivalent interactions among modified histones and reader proteins, creating mesoscale domains (100 nm - 1 μm) with distinct biochemical environments. We will develop integrative computational frameworks combining polymer physics models of chromatin, machine learning for predicting 3D organization from sequence and epigenetic features, and spatial statistics for analyzing imaging data. Novel algorithms will integrate contact frequencies with spatial positions, resolving the relationship between measured interactions and physical distances. Network analysis will identify emergent chromatin communities and their hierarchical organization. We will correlate compartmentalization patterns with transcriptional output using RNA-seq from matched samples, testing whether emergent nuclear organization causally influences gene expression or vice versa. Cross-cell-type analysis will reveal conserved versus cell-specific emergent organizational principles. This project demands expertise in chromosome biology, polymer physics, image analysis, machine learning, and genomics—requiring collaboration across traditionally separate fields. The data integration challenge spans contact maps, images, and sequencing data at different resolutions and from different experimental systems. Expected insights include quantitative models of compartmentalization emergence, identification of key molecular drivers of mesoscale organization, and understanding of how nuclear structure influences function. All analysis pipelines, trained models, and integrated datasets will be publicly released, establishing resources for the chromosome biology community.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Allosteric regulation in multi-subunit protein complexes represents emergent behavior where binding events at one site influence distant sites through collective conformational changes—properties absent in isolated subunits. This synthesis project will systematically discover and characterize emergent allosteric networks by mining structural databases. We will integrate the Protein Data Bank (>200,000 structures), molecular dynamics trajectories from MDAnalysis and related repositories, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) data from HDXsite, and mutational fitness landscapes from deep mutational scanning datasets in MaveDB. The central question is: what structural and dynamic features enable emergent long-range communication in protein complexes that individual subunits lack? We hypothesize that emergent allostery requires specific mesoscale organizational features—interface geometries, dynamic coupling patterns, and evolutionary constraints—that create communication pathways spanning 10-100 nm distances. Our computational approach combines graph-theoretical analysis of structure networks, normal mode analysis for collective motions, machine learning to predict allosteric sites from structural features, and evolutionary analysis to identify co-evolving residue networks. We will develop algorithms to automatically identify allosteric pathways by analyzing conformational ensembles across ligand-bound and apo states. Integration with disease mutation databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) will connect disrupted allosteric networks to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across protein families will reveal conserved principles of emergent allostery versus family-specific mechanisms. This project requires expertise spanning structural biology, protein dynamics, evolutionary biology, and machine learning—necessitating collaboration between computationally-focused and experimentally-informed laboratories. The synthesis of structural, dynamic, evolutionary, and phenotypic data across thousands of protein complexes exceeds any single lab's capacity. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive atlas of emergent allosteric networks, predictive models for allosteric site identification, and mechanistic principles governing long-range communication. All databases, analysis tools, and predictive models will be openly released, enabling rational design of allosteric modulators and understanding of how complex-level properties emerge from subunit assembly.

[Background and Significance]
Allostery—the phenomenon whereby ligand binding or modification at one site influences the activity at a distant site—represents one of the most fundamental regulatory mechanisms in biology. First described by Monod, Wyman, and Changeux in 1965, allosteric regulation enables cells to rapidly respond to environmental changes, integrate multiple signals, and achieve exquisite control over metabolic and signaling pathways. While classical allostery was initially understood through the lens of individual proteins like hemoglobin, contemporary research has revealed that the most sophisticated allosteric behaviors emerge specifically in multi-subunit protein complexes, where the assembly of individual subunits creates communication networks that no single subunit possesses in isolation.

This emergent property of allostery in protein complexes represents a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon. Individual protein subunits, typically spanning 2-10 nm, assemble into complexes that operate at the 10-100 nm scale—precisely the mesoscale regime between individual biomolecules and organelles that NCEMS prioritizes. At this scale, new properties arise that cannot be predicted from studying isolated components: cooperative binding emerges from subunit interactions, conformational changes propagate across interfaces spanning tens of nanometers, and information flows through dynamic networks that exist only in the assembled state. Understanding how these emergent allosteric properties arise from subunit assembly addresses fundamental questions about biological organization and function.

The past two decades have witnessed an explosion of publicly available structural and functional data that, when synthesized, can reveal principles of emergent allostery that no single dataset can illuminate. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) now contains over 200,000 experimentally determined structures, including thousands of multi-subunit complexes captured in multiple conformational states. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database provides predicted structures for virtually all known proteins, enabling comparative analysis across evolutionary scales. Critically, repositories such as MaveDB now house deep mutational scanning data for hundreds of proteins, providing residue-level fitness landscapes that reveal functional constraints. HDX-MS databases like HDXsite capture protein dynamics and conformational changes upon ligand binding. The Allosteric Database (ASD) catalogs known allosteric sites and modulators. Disease mutation databases including ClinVar and COSMIC connect structural features to pathological phenotypes.

Despite this wealth of data, fundamental gaps remain in our understanding of emergent allostery. First, we lack systematic knowledge of what structural features distinguish complexes with emergent allosteric properties from those without. Why do some protein assemblies exhibit exquisite long-range communication while others remain functionally independent? Second, the dynamic basis of allosteric communication—how conformational fluctuations propagate across subunit interfaces—remains poorly characterized at the proteome scale. Third, the evolutionary constraints that maintain allosteric networks are incompletely understood: which residues and interfaces are under selection to preserve communication pathways? Finally, we lack predictive models that can identify emergent allosteric sites in newly characterized complexes.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address these gaps. No single laboratory possesses the expertise or computational resources to integrate structural, dynamic, evolutionary, and phenotypic data across thousands of protein complexes. Individual studies typically focus on one protein family or one data type, missing the cross-cutting patterns that emerge from comprehensive analysis. By bringing together structural biologists who understand protein architecture, computational biophysicists who model protein dynamics, evolutionary biologists who analyze sequence conservation, and machine learning experts who can identify patterns across large datasets, this project will achieve insights impossible for any single research group.

The significance of understanding emergent allostery extends far beyond basic science. Allosteric drugs offer advantages over orthosteric modulators, including greater selectivity and the ability to fine-tune rather than completely block protein function. Yet rational design of allosteric modulators is hampered by our inability to predict allosteric sites and communication pathways. Disease mutations frequently disrupt allosteric networks, but connecting genotype to phenotype requires understanding how mutations affect long-range communication. By developing predictive models and mechanistic principles, this synthesis project will enable therapeutic development and illuminate disease mechanisms while advancing fundamental understanding of how complex-level properties emerge from molecular assembly.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project addresses four interconnected research questions that collectively aim to understand how emergent allosteric properties arise in multi-subunit protein complexes. Each question is accompanied by specific, testable hypotheses and clear predictions that can be validated using existing publicly available data.

**Research Question 1: What structural features distinguish protein complexes with emergent allosteric properties from those without?**

Not all multi-subunit protein complexes exhibit long-range allosteric communication. We seek to identify the structural determinants that enable emergent allostery by comparing complexes with documented allosteric behavior (from the Allosteric Database) to size-matched complexes without known allosteric regulation.

*Hypothesis 1a*: Emergent allostery requires specific interface geometries characterized by extensive buried surface area (>1500 Å²), high shape complementarity (Sc > 0.7), and the presence of interfacial salt bridges and hydrogen bond networks. We predict that allosteric complexes will show significantly different interface properties compared to non-allosteric assemblies of similar size.

*Hypothesis 1b*: Allosteric complexes exhibit characteristic network topologies when represented as residue interaction graphs. Specifically, we hypothesize that allosteric complexes will display higher betweenness centrality for interfacial residues and shorter path lengths between known allosteric and active sites compared to non-allosteric complexes.

These hypotheses will be tested by extracting interface properties from PDB structures using established tools (PISA, PDBePISA) and constructing residue interaction networks using distance cutoffs validated in the literature. Statistical comparison between allosteric and non-allosteric complex sets will quantify discriminative features.

**Research Question 2: How do conformational dynamics enable long-range communication in protein complexes?**

Allosteric communication requires the transmission of conformational changes across distances spanning 10-100 nm. We will characterize the dynamic basis of this communication by analyzing conformational ensembles from multiple sources.

*Hypothesis 2a*: Emergent allosteric communication is mediated by correlated motions that span subunit interfaces. We predict that residues along allosteric pathways will show significantly higher dynamic cross-correlation (|Cij| > 0.5) compared to residues not involved in communication, and that these correlations will be absent in isolated subunit simulations.

*Hypothesis 2b*: Allosteric complexes exhibit characteristic low-frequency normal modes that couple allosteric and active sites. We predict that the overlap between ligand-induced conformational changes (from comparing apo and holo structures in PDB) and the lowest-frequency normal modes will be significantly higher for allosteric complexes than for non-allosteric assemblies.

*Hypothesis 2c*: HDX-MS protection patterns will reveal allosteric communication pathways. Specifically, we predict that residues showing altered deuterium exchange upon allosteric modulator binding (data from HDXsite) will form contiguous pathways connecting allosteric and active sites, and that these pathways will correspond to regions of high dynamic correlation.

Validation will employ normal mode analysis using elastic network models (ANM, GNM), analysis of molecular dynamics trajectories from public repositories, and integration with HDX-MS data to identify regions of altered dynamics upon ligand binding.

**Research Question 3: What evolutionary constraints maintain emergent allosteric networks?**

If specific residues and interfaces are critical for allosteric communication, they should be under evolutionary selection. We will identify evolutionary signatures of allostery by analyzing sequence conservation and coevolution patterns.

*Hypothesis 3a*: Residues forming allosteric communication pathways show elevated evolutionary conservation compared to surface residues not involved in allostery. We predict conservation scores (from ConSurf analysis using UniRef90 alignments) for pathway residues will be significantly higher than for non-pathway surface residues.

*Hypothesis 3b*: Allosteric networks exhibit characteristic coevolutionary signatures. Specifically, we predict that residue pairs along allosteric pathways will show elevated coevolution scores (direct coupling analysis, mutual information) compared to non-pathway residue pairs at similar distances, indicating selection for coordinated function.

*Hypothesis 3c*: Deep mutational scanning fitness landscapes (from MaveDB) will reveal functional constraints on allosteric pathway residues. We predict that mutations at pathway residues will show fitness effects that correlate with disruption of allosteric communication, as measured by changes in cooperativity or allosteric response in functional assays reported in MaveDB.

These hypotheses will be tested by mapping conservation and coevolution scores onto identified allosteric pathways and comparing to null distributions from non-pathway residues.

**Research Question 4: Can we predict emergent allosteric sites and communication pathways from structural features alone?**

A key goal is developing predictive models that can identify potential allosteric sites in complexes without known allosteric behavior.

*Hypothesis 4a*: Machine learning models trained on structural, dynamic, and evolutionary features can predict known allosteric sites with high accuracy (AUROC > 0.85). We will validate predictions using held-out test sets from the Allosteric Database.

*Hypothesis 4b*: Predicted allosteric sites will be enriched for disease mutations (from ClinVar and COSMIC) compared to random surface sites, providing independent validation that our predictions identify functionally important regions.

*Hypothesis 4c*: Allosteric communication pathways predicted by our graph-theoretical algorithms will be validated by correspondence with HDX-MS protection patterns and enrichment for disease mutations that disrupt protein function.

These predictions enable validation using orthogonal data sources not used in model training, providing rigorous tests of predictive accuracy.

[Methods and Approach]
**Data Sources and Acquisition**

This synthesis project will integrate data from multiple publicly available repositories spanning structural, dynamic, evolutionary, and phenotypic information:

*Structural Data*: The Protein Data Bank (PDB; >200,000 structures) will provide experimentally determined structures of protein complexes. We will extract all multi-subunit assemblies (>2 chains) with resolution ≤3.0 Å, yielding approximately 45,000 complexes. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database will provide predicted structures for subunits lacking experimental structures, enabling comparative analysis of monomeric versus assembled states. The Biological Assemblies database within PDB will ensure we analyze biologically relevant oligomeric states.

*Allosteric Annotation*: The Allosteric Database (ASD; >65,000 allosteric modulators for >2,000 proteins) will provide positive examples of allosteric sites and modulators. CASBench and other benchmark datasets will provide curated sets for model training and validation.

*Dynamic Data*: MDAnalysis-compatible trajectory repositories including the MoDEL database, GPCRmd (GPCR dynamics), and COVID-19 Molecular Structure and Therapeutics Hub will provide molecular dynamics trajectories. HDXsite and the HDX Data Repository will provide hydrogen-deuterium exchange data capturing conformational dynamics. The Dynameomics database provides dynamics information for protein folds.

*Evolutionary Data*: UniRef90 and UniRef50 clusters will provide sequence alignments for conservation analysis. Pfam domain annotations will enable family-level comparisons. Pre-computed coevolution scores from EVcouplings and GREMLIN databases will supplement our direct coupling analysis.

*Mutational Fitness Data*: MaveDB (>1,000 datasets) will provide deep mutational scanning fitness landscapes. The Mutfunc database provides predicted functional effects of mutations.

*Disease Mutation Data*: ClinVar (>1.5 million variants) and COSMIC (>6 million coding mutations) will provide disease-associated variants for validation and biological interpretation.

**Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy**

Integrating heterogeneous data sources requires careful harmonization. We will establish a unified data model centered on protein complexes as the primary entity, with associated structural, dynamic, evolutionary, and phenotypic annotations.

*Structural Mapping*: All data will be mapped to PDB structures using UniProt accession numbers as the common identifier. For proteins with multiple PDB entries, we will select representative structures based on resolution, completeness, and ligand state. Structure alignments using TM-align will enable comparison across conformational states.

*Residue Numbering Harmonization*: We will adopt UniProt canonical sequence numbering as the reference, using SIFTS mappings to convert between PDB residue numbers and UniProt positions. This ensures consistent residue identification across datasets.

*Quality Control*: Automated pipelines will flag inconsistencies (missing residues, sequence mismatches, low-confidence regions in AlphaFold predictions). Human curation by domain experts will resolve ambiguous cases for benchmark datasets.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Graph-Theoretical Network Analysis*: Protein structures will be represented as residue interaction networks (RINs) where nodes are residues and edges connect residues within distance cutoffs (Cα-Cα < 8 Å or heavy atom contact < 4.5 Å). We will compute network metrics including betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, and community structure using NetworkX and graph-tool libraries. Allosteric pathways will be identified as shortest paths or maximum-flow paths between allosteric and active sites.

*Normal Mode Analysis*: Elastic network models (Anisotropic Network Model, Gaussian Network Model) implemented in ProDy will characterize collective motions. We will compute the overlap between low-frequency modes and ligand-induced conformational changes (comparing apo/holo structure pairs). Cross-correlation matrices will identify dynamically coupled residue pairs.

*Machine Learning for Allosteric Site Prediction*: We will develop ensemble classifiers (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Graph Neural Networks) trained on features including: local structural properties (secondary structure, solvent accessibility, B-factors), network metrics (centrality measures, community membership), evolutionary features (conservation scores, coevolution), and dynamic properties (flexibility, mode participation). Training will use known allosteric sites from ASD with 5-fold cross-validation and held-out test sets.

*Evolutionary Analysis*: Multiple sequence alignments from UniRef clusters will be analyzed using ConSurf for conservation scoring. Direct coupling analysis (DCA) using plmDCA and GREMLIN will identify coevolving residue pairs. Statistical coupling analysis (SCA) will identify sectors of coevolving residues potentially involved in allosteric communication.

*Pathway Identification Algorithms*: We will develop novel algorithms to automatically identify allosteric pathways by: (1) computing perturbation propagation through RINs using random walk approaches; (2) identifying residues with high mutual information between allosteric site occupancy and active site conformation in conformational ensembles; (3) mapping HDX-MS protection changes to identify residues with altered dynamics upon modulator binding.

**Validation Strategies**

*Cross-Dataset Validation*: Predictions from structural analysis will be validated against dynamic data (HDX-MS, MD trajectories). Evolutionary predictions will be validated against mutational fitness data.

*Known Positive Controls*: Well-characterized allosteric systems (hemoglobin, ATCase, GroEL, GPCRs) will serve as positive controls to validate our methods before proteome-wide application.

*Disease Mutation Enrichment*: Predicted allosteric sites and pathways should be enriched for disease mutations compared to random surface sites, providing independent functional validation.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1*: Data acquisition and harmonization (Months 1-4); Development of network analysis and normal mode pipelines (Months 3-8); Initial analysis of benchmark allosteric systems (Months 6-12); First working group meeting at NCEMS (Month 6).

*Year 2*: Machine learning model development and validation (Months 13-18); Proteome-wide pathway identification (Months 15-20); Integration with disease mutation data (Months 18-24); Second working group meeting (Month 18); Preprint of initial findings (Month 24).

*Year 3*: Comparative analysis across protein families (Months 25-30); Development of web-accessible atlas and tools (Months 27-33); Community workshops and training (Months 30-36); Final publications and database release (Months 33-36).

**Team Composition and Expertise**

This project requires expertise spanning: (1) Structural biology and protein biochemistry—for interpreting structural features and biological relevance; (2) Computational biophysics and molecular dynamics—for analyzing protein dynamics and normal modes; (3) Evolutionary biology and bioinformatics—for conservation and coevolution analysis; (4) Machine learning and data science—for predictive model development; (5) Biomedical informatics—for disease mutation interpretation. We will assemble a team of 4-5 PIs from distinct institutions representing these disciplines, with 3 postdoctoral researchers and 2 graduate students distributed across labs. A dedicated research software engineer will ensure code quality and reproducibility.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
**Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce four major categories of deliverables that collectively advance understanding of emergent allostery and enable future research:

*1. Comprehensive Atlas of Emergent Allosteric Networks (AlloAtlas)*: We will create a publicly accessible database cataloging allosteric sites, communication pathways, and network properties for all multi-subunit protein complexes in the PDB with sufficient structural data. AlloAtlas will include: (a) curated annotations of known allosteric sites integrated from ASD with standardized nomenclature; (b) predicted allosteric sites with confidence scores for complexes without known allosteric behavior; (c) identified communication pathways connecting allosteric and functional sites; (d) network metrics (centrality, community structure) for all residues; (e) evolutionary conservation and coevolution scores mapped to structures; (f) links to disease mutations affecting predicted allosteric residues. We anticipate cataloging allosteric properties for >10,000 protein complexes, representing a 5-fold expansion over current databases.

*2. Predictive Computational Tools*: We will release a suite of open-source tools including: (a) AlloPath—an algorithm for automated identification of allosteric communication pathways from structural data; (b) AlloPredict—machine learning models for predicting allosteric sites from structure, with web server implementation; (c) AlloNet—tools for constructing and analyzing residue interaction networks with allosteric-specific metrics; (d) AlloDyn—pipelines for integrating normal mode analysis and HDX-MS data to characterize dynamic communication. All tools will be distributed as Python packages with comprehensive documentation and tutorials.

*3. Mechanistic Principles of Emergent Allostery*: Beyond databases and tools, we will distill mechanistic insights into the principles governing emergent allostery. Expected findings include: (a) quantitative criteria for interface properties (buried surface area, shape complementarity, interaction density) that enable allosteric communication; (b) characteristic network topologies (motifs, community structures) associated with emergent allostery; (c) dynamic signatures (mode patterns, correlation structures) that distinguish allosteric from non-allosteric complexes; (d) evolutionary constraints (conservation patterns, coevolution signatures) that maintain allosteric networks. These principles will be published as a comprehensive review synthesizing our findings.

*4. Disease-Allostery Connection Maps*: By integrating predicted allosteric networks with disease mutation databases, we will identify: (a) disease mutations that likely disrupt allosteric communication rather than directly affecting active sites; (b) protein complexes where allosteric dysfunction may contribute to disease; (c) potential therapeutic targets where allosteric modulation could restore normal function. This disease-focused output will be of particular interest to the biomedical research community.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project directly addresses NCEMS's focus on emergent properties at the mesoscale. Allosteric communication in protein complexes exemplifies emergence: individual subunits lack the long-range communication capabilities that arise upon assembly. By systematically characterizing the structural, dynamic, and evolutionary basis of this emergence across thousands of complexes, we will establish general principles for how mesoscale organization enables new functional properties.

Our findings will illuminate several aspects of mesoscale emergence: (1) How interface properties create communication channels that span 10-100 nm distances; (2) How collective dynamics at the complex level enable information transmission impossible in isolated subunits; (3) How evolution shapes mesoscale organization to maintain emergent properties; (4) How disruption of mesoscale communication leads to disease. These insights extend beyond allostery to inform understanding of emergence in other mesoscale systems including phase-separated condensates, cytoskeletal assemblies, and signaling complexes.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

The tools and principles developed here will benefit multiple research communities:

*Drug Discovery*: Allosteric modulators offer advantages including greater selectivity and ability to fine-tune rather than abolish activity. Our predictive tools will enable identification of potential allosteric sites for therapeutic targeting, while mechanistic principles will guide modulator design.

*Protein Engineering*: Understanding allosteric communication enables rational engineering of proteins with designed regulatory properties. Our atlas will reveal design principles for creating synthetic allosteric switches.

*Disease Mechanism Understanding*: Many disease mutations have unclear mechanisms. By identifying mutations that disrupt allosteric networks, we provide mechanistic explanations for genotype-phenotype relationships.

*Evolutionary Biology*: Our analysis of evolutionary constraints on allosteric networks will reveal how selection maintains complex regulatory mechanisms and how allostery evolves across protein families.

**Enabling Future Research**

This synthesis project will enable numerous future studies by: (1) providing validated computational tools that individual labs can apply to their systems of interest; (2) generating hypotheses about specific protein complexes that can be tested with targeted experiments; (3) establishing benchmarks for evaluating new methods in allosteric site prediction; (4) creating training datasets for future machine learning applications.

**Dissemination Plans**

Findings will be disseminated through: (1) peer-reviewed publications in high-impact journals (target: 4-6 papers including methods papers, biological insights papers, and a comprehensive review); (2) preprints on bioRxiv to enable rapid community access; (3) presentations at major conferences (Biophysical Society, ISMB, Protein Society); (4) workshops at NCEMS for hands-on training with our tools; (5) webinars and video tutorials for remote users; (6) social media engagement to reach broader audiences.

**Long-Term Sustainability**

AlloAtlas will be hosted on stable infrastructure with commitment to 10+ year availability. We will engage with established resources (PDB, UniProt) to explore integration of our annotations into their platforms. Tools will be deposited in standard repositories (PyPI, Bioconda) with ongoing maintenance commitments. Documentation and tutorials will enable community contributions and extensions beyond the project period.

[Budget and Resources]
**Personnel (Total: $680,000 over 3 years)**

*Postdoctoral Researchers (3 positions, $180,000/year total including benefits)*: Three postdocs will form the core research team, each embedded in different PI laboratories to facilitate cross-disciplinary integration. Postdoc 1 (structural bioinformatics focus) will lead data integration and network analysis. Postdoc 2 (machine learning focus) will develop predictive models and validation frameworks. Postdoc 3 (evolutionary/dynamics focus) will conduct conservation analysis and dynamics integration. Postdocs will spend 2 weeks annually at NCEMS for intensive collaborative work. Total: $540,000.

*Graduate Students (2 positions, partial support $30,000/year each)*: Two PhD students will contribute to specific project components while receiving training in synthesis research. Student 1 will focus on disease mutation integration under supervision of the biomedical informatics PI. Student 2 will develop web interfaces and visualization tools. Total: $180,000.

*Research Software Engineer (0.5 FTE, $60,000/year)*: A dedicated software engineer will ensure code quality, maintain repositories, develop web infrastructure, and create documentation. This position is critical for long-term sustainability of tools. Total: $180,000.

**Computing Resources (Total: $120,000)**

*Cloud Computing (AWS/Google Cloud, $30,000/year)*: Large-scale analysis of >200,000 PDB structures and machine learning model training requires substantial computational resources beyond typical institutional allocations. Cloud computing enables elastic scaling for intensive computations. Total: $90,000.

*Data Storage ($10,000/year)*: Long-term storage of processed datasets, model checkpoints, and AlloAtlas database requires dedicated storage infrastructure. Total: $30,000.

**Travel and Collaboration (Total: $90,000)**

*Working Group Meetings at NCEMS ($15,000/year)*: Annual in-person meetings (5-day duration) for the full working group (approximately 15 participants including PIs, postdocs, students). Covers travel, lodging, and per diem. Total: $45,000.

*Conference Presentations ($10,000/year)*: Support for team members to present findings at major conferences (Biophysical Society, ISMB, Protein Society) and conduct workshops. Total: $30,000.

*PI Coordination Meetings ($5,000/year)*: Quarterly video conferences supplemented by annual PI-only coordination meeting. Total: $15,000.

**Workshops and Training (Total: $60,000)**

*Annual Community Workshops ($15,000/year)*: Two-day workshops at NCEMS for 20-30 participants including travel support for trainees from resource-limited institutions. Covers materials, catering, and participant support. Total: $45,000.

*Online Training Development ($5,000/year)*: Production of video tutorials, development of interactive training materials, and maintenance of documentation. Total: $15,000.

**Open Science Infrastructure (Total: $50,000)**

*Web Server Hosting ($10,000/year)*: Dedicated hosting for AlloAtlas database and web tools with appropriate bandwidth and reliability. Total: $30,000.

*DOI Registration and Data Archiving ($3,000/year)*: Costs for Zenodo Plus subscription, DOI registration, and long-term archiving. Total: $9,000.

*Software Licenses and Services ($4,000/year)*: GitHub organization, continuous integration services, code quality tools. Total: $11,000.

**Total Budget: $1,000,000 over 3 years**

**Budget Justification**

This budget reflects the collaborative, synthesis-focused nature of the project. Personnel costs (68%) are the largest category, appropriate for a project that synthesizes existing data rather than generating new data. The distributed postdoc model—with researchers embedded in different labs but working on integrated problems—is essential for genuine cross-disciplinary synthesis. Computing costs (12%) reflect the substantial computational demands of analyzing >200,000 structures and training machine learning models. Travel costs (9%) support the in-person collaboration that NCEMS emphasizes as critical for synthesis science. Workshop and training costs (6%) directly support NCEMS's mission of training the next generation. Open science infrastructure costs (5%) ensure long-term accessibility of project outputs. This budget is beyond the capacity of any single laboratory, justifying NCEMS support for this collaborative synthesis effort.

abstract_original: Allosteric regulation in multi-subunit protein complexes represents emergent behavior where binding events at one site influence distant sites through collective conformational changes—properties absent in isolated subunits. This synthesis project will systematically discover and characterize emergent allosteric networks by mining structural databases. We will integrate the Protein Data Bank (>200,000 structures), molecular dynamics trajectories from MDAnalysis and related repositories, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) data from HDXsite, and mutational fitness landscapes from deep mutational scanning datasets in MaveDB. The central question is: what structural and dynamic features enable emergent long-range communication in protein complexes that individual subunits lack? We hypothesize that emergent allostery requires specific mesoscale organizational features—interface geometries, dynamic coupling patterns, and evolutionary constraints—that create communication pathways spanning 10-100 nm distances. Our computational approach combines graph-theoretical analysis of structure networks, normal mode analysis for collective motions, machine learning to predict allosteric sites from structural features, and evolutionary analysis to identify co-evolving residue networks. We will develop algorithms to automatically identify allosteric pathways by analyzing conformational ensembles across ligand-bound and apo states. Integration with disease mutation databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) will connect disrupted allosteric networks to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across protein families will reveal conserved principles of emergent allostery versus family-specific mechanisms. This project requires expertise spanning structural biology, protein dynamics, evolutionary biology, and machine learning—necessitating collaboration between computationally-focused and experimentally-informed laboratories. The synthesis of structural, dynamic, evolutionary, and phenotypic data across thousands of protein complexes exceeds any single lab's capacity. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive atlas of emergent allosteric networks, predictive models for allosteric site identification, and mechanistic principles governing long-range communication. All databases, analysis tools, and predictive models will be openly released, enabling rational design of allosteric modulators and understanding of how complex-level properties emerge from subunit assembly.
