full_text:
[Abstract]
mRNA localization creates emergent spatial gene expression patterns through RNA-protein networks operating at the mesoscale—a phenomenon where RNA targeting achieves precision impossible from individual binding events. This synthesis project will decode emergent RNA localization by integrating spatial transcriptomics, structural biology, and RNA biology datasets. We will synthesize spatial transcriptomics from the Human Cell Atlas and published studies, RNA structure data from SHAPE-MaP experiments in public repositories, RNA-binding protein (RBP) interaction data from ENCODE eCLIP, and RBP localization from the Human Protein Atlas. The central question is: how do RBP networks create emergent mRNA targeting at the mesoscale (RNA granules of 100-1000 nm containing multiple mRNAs and RBPs) with subcellular precision? We hypothesize that emergent localization arises from combinatorial RBP binding, RNA secondary structure context, and phase separation into transport granules that integrate multiple weak targeting signals. Our computational approach combines machine learning to predict localization from sequence and structure features, network analysis of RBP-mRNA interactions, and spatial statistics to quantify localization precision. We will develop algorithms integrating RNA structure predictions with RBP binding sites to model targeting complexes. Integration with translation data will connect localization to local protein synthesis. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal conserved versus specialized emergent targeting mechanisms. This project demands expertise in RNA biology, spatial transcriptomics, structural biology, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of spatial, structural, and interaction data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent RNA localization, identification of key features determining targeting, and principles for engineering localized gene expression. Understanding emergent RNA targeting has implications for neurological diseases and mRNA therapeutics. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

[Background and Significance]
The spatial organization of mRNA within cells represents one of the most elegant examples of emergent biological phenomena, where the collective behavior of RNA-protein networks produces subcellular precision that cannot be predicted from individual molecular interactions alone. At the mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles spanning approximately 100-1000 nanometers—mRNA localization emerges through the coordinated action of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), RNA secondary structures, and phase-separated condensates known as RNA granules. This mesoscale organization is fundamental to cellular function, enabling local protein synthesis that underlies neuronal plasticity, embryonic axis formation, and cellular polarity.

Current understanding of mRNA localization has been built through decades of molecular studies identifying individual cis-acting localization elements (zipcodes) and trans-acting RBPs. Landmark work identified beta-actin mRNA localization signals and their recognition by ZBP1/IGF2BP1, while studies in Drosophila oocytes revealed the complexity of oskar and bicoid mRNA targeting. However, these reductionist approaches have revealed a paradox: individual RBP-RNA interactions are typically weak (micromolar affinity) and promiscuous, yet mRNA localization achieves remarkable specificity and precision. This gap between molecular properties and cellular outcomes exemplifies emergence—the appearance of system-level properties not predictable from component parts.

Recent technological advances have generated unprecedented publicly available datasets that, when synthesized, can address this emergence paradox. Spatial transcriptomics technologies, including MERFISH, seqFISH+, and Visium platforms, have mapped subcellular mRNA distributions across thousands of genes in multiple cell types. The Human Cell Atlas consortium has deposited extensive spatial transcriptomics data in the CZ CELLxGENE database, while individual studies have contributed datasets to the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress. Simultaneously, systematic mapping of RBP-RNA interactions through ENCODE's eCLIP experiments has catalogued binding sites for over 150 RBPs across multiple cell lines. RNA structure probing data from SHAPE-MaP and DMS-MaPseq experiments, deposited in the RNA Mapping Database (RMDB) and Structure Surfer, provide transcriptome-wide secondary structure information. The Human Protein Atlas has systematically imaged RBP subcellular localization, while proteomics studies have characterized RNA granule composition.

Despite this data wealth, critical gaps remain that synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address. First, no systematic integration exists between spatial transcriptomics data revealing where mRNAs localize and RBP interaction data explaining how they get there. Second, the role of RNA secondary structure in creating or masking localization signals has not been analyzed at transcriptome scale. Third, the combinatorial logic by which multiple RBPs cooperate to achieve emergent targeting precision remains undefined. Fourth, the relationship between mRNA localization and local translation has not been systematically examined across cell types.

Understanding emergent RNA localization at the mesoscale is significant for multiple reasons. Biologically, RNA granules represent a paradigmatic example of membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation, a fundamental organizational principle increasingly recognized across cell biology. Pathologically, mutations in RBPs including FUS, TDP-43, and hnRNPA1 cause neurodegenerative diseases through disrupted RNA granule dynamics. Therapeutically, mRNA-based medicines require understanding localization principles to optimize delivery and translation efficiency.

The synthesis approach proposed here will leverage the complementary strengths of existing datasets to decode emergent localization mechanisms. Spatial transcriptomics provides the phenotype—where mRNAs localize—while eCLIP data provides the molecular interactions, structure data provides the RNA context, and protein localization data provides the machinery distribution. No single dataset or laboratory possesses the expertise to integrate these diverse data types. By synthesizing across these domains, we can identify the emergent rules governing mesoscale RNA organization, transforming descriptive observations into predictive understanding. This synthesis is timely because sufficient data now exists across all required domains, computational methods for integration have matured, and the field recognizes that reductionist approaches alone cannot explain localization precision.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project addresses a central scientific question: How do RNA-binding protein networks create emergent mRNA targeting at the mesoscale with subcellular precision that exceeds the specificity of individual molecular interactions? This overarching question decomposes into four specific, testable research questions with associated hypotheses and validation strategies using existing data.

**Research Question 1: What is the combinatorial RBP binding code for mRNA localization?**

Individual RBP binding events show limited correlation with localization outcomes, suggesting that combinations of RBPs encode targeting information. We hypothesize that mRNA localization patterns are determined by specific combinations of RBP binding sites rather than individual RBP interactions, with emergent specificity arising from the co-occurrence of 3-5 RBP binding sites within defined spatial windows along the transcript.

Measurable predictions: (1) mRNAs with similar localization patterns will share RBP binding site combinations more than expected by chance; (2) the predictive power of machine learning models will increase substantially when incorporating combinatorial features versus single-RBP features; (3) specific RBP combinations will show statistically significant enrichment for particular subcellular compartments.

Validation approach: We will integrate ENCODE eCLIP data for 150+ RBPs with spatial transcriptomics localization annotations from CZ CELLxGENE. Using held-out test sets of mRNAs with known localization, we will compare predictive accuracy of single-RBP versus combinatorial models. Cross-validation across cell types (HepG2, K562, neurons) will test generalizability. Known localized mRNAs from the RNALocate database will serve as positive controls.

**Research Question 2: How does RNA secondary structure modulate RBP accessibility to create context-dependent localization signals?**

RBP binding motifs are short (4-8 nucleotides) and occur frequently throughout transcripts, yet only specific instances function as localization signals. We hypothesize that RNA secondary structure creates emergent localization specificity by controlling RBP accessibility, with functional binding sites occurring in single-stranded regions while non-functional motif occurrences are sequestered in base-paired structures.

Measurable predictions: (1) Functional RBP binding sites (from eCLIP peaks) will show significantly lower base-pairing probability than sequence-matched non-bound motifs; (2) mRNAs with similar sequences but different structures will show different localization patterns; (3) structure-aware binding predictions will outperform sequence-only predictions for localization modeling.

Validation approach: We will synthesize SHAPE-MaP reactivity data from RMDB and Structure Surfer with eCLIP binding peaks. For each RBP, we will compare structural context of bound versus unbound motif occurrences. Integration with spatial transcriptomics will test whether structure-modulated binding correlates with localization outcomes. The Rfam database of conserved RNA structures will provide evolutionary validation of functional structural elements.

**Research Question 3: How do RNA granule compositions emerge from individual RBP-mRNA interactions to create mesoscale targeting complexes?**

RNA granules (P-bodies, stress granules, neuronal transport granules) represent mesoscale assemblies where multiple mRNAs and RBPs co-localize through phase separation. We hypothesize that specific mRNA-RBP interaction networks predict RNA granule co-membership, with granule composition emerging from shared RBP binding profiles rather than direct mRNA-mRNA interactions.

Measurable predictions: (1) mRNAs sharing multiple RBP binders will co-localize in granules more frequently than mRNAs sharing few RBPs; (2) network analysis will identify RBP modules corresponding to distinct granule types; (3) mRNAs with high predicted phase separation propensity (based on RBP binding) will show punctate localization patterns in spatial transcriptomics.

Validation approach: We will construct bipartite RBP-mRNA networks from eCLIP data and apply community detection algorithms to identify co-regulated mRNA modules. These modules will be compared against published RNA granule proteomics and transcriptomics from GEO datasets characterizing stress granule and P-body contents. Spatial transcriptomics data will be analyzed for co-localization patterns matching predicted modules.

**Research Question 4: How does emergent mRNA localization couple to local translation to produce spatially organized protein synthesis?**

mRNA localization presumably functions to enable local protein synthesis, but the quantitative relationship between localization precision and translation efficiency remains unclear. We hypothesize that mRNA localization and local translation are coordinated through shared RBP regulators, with localized mRNAs showing translation signatures (ribosome occupancy, translation efficiency) that correlate with their subcellular position.

Measurable predictions: (1) Ribosome profiling data will show position-dependent translation efficiency for localized mRNAs; (2) RBPs controlling localization will overlap significantly with translation regulators; (3) spatial proteomics will show protein distributions matching mRNA localization patterns with predictable delays.

Validation approach: We will integrate ribosome profiling data from GWIPS-viz and Trips-Viz databases with spatial transcriptomics localization calls. The Human Protein Atlas subcellular proteomics will provide protein distribution data for comparison with mRNA localization. Published spatial proteomics datasets from GEO will enable direct mRNA-protein spatial correlation analysis.

**Expected Mechanistic Insights:**

Through systematic testing of these hypotheses, we expect to reveal the mechanistic principles underlying emergent RNA localization: (1) the combinatorial binding code specifying localization destinations; (2) the structural grammar controlling signal accessibility; (3) the network architecture enabling granule assembly; and (4) the regulatory coupling between localization and translation. These insights will transform understanding of mesoscale RNA organization from phenomenological description to predictive mechanistic models.

[Methods and Approach]
**Data Sources and Acquisition**

This synthesis project will integrate four major categories of publicly available data:

*Spatial Transcriptomics Data:* We will obtain subcellular mRNA localization data from multiple sources. The CZ CELLxGENE database contains Human Cell Atlas spatial transcriptomics datasets including MERFISH data from human brain (Fang et al., 2022), seqFISH+ data from mouse brain (Eng et al., 2019), and Visium data across multiple tissues. The Spatial Transcript Omics DataBase (STOmicsDB) provides additional curated spatial datasets. We will download raw and processed data from GEO (accessions GSE161918, GSE175692, GSE166852) covering neuronal, epithelial, and immune cell types. The Allen Brain Cell Atlas provides high-resolution spatial transcriptomics across brain regions. We estimate integration of 50+ spatial transcriptomics datasets covering >100,000 cells and >10,000 genes with subcellular resolution.

*RBP-RNA Interaction Data:* ENCODE eCLIP data provides genome-wide binding maps for 150 RBPs in HepG2 and K562 cells, available through the ENCODE portal (encodeproject.org). We will download processed peak calls and raw signal tracks. The POSTAR3 database aggregates CLIP-seq data across studies, providing additional RBP binding information. The ATtRACT database contains validated RBP binding motifs for computational prediction. oRNAment provides RBP binding site predictions across transcriptomes.

*RNA Structure Data:* The RNA Mapping Database (RMDB) contains SHAPE-MaP and DMS-MaPseq reactivity profiles for thousands of transcripts. Structure Surfer provides transcriptome-wide structure probing data. The RNAcentral database aggregates RNA structure information across databases. We will also utilize computational structure predictions from RNAfold and LinearFold for transcripts lacking experimental data, benchmarked against experimental structures.

*Protein Localization and Granule Composition:* The Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization data provides immunofluorescence-based RBP localization across cell lines. Published RNA granule proteomics (Jain et al., 2016; Markmiller et al., 2018) from GEO and PRIDE provide granule composition data. The RNALocate database contains curated mRNA localization annotations.

**Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy**

Integrating heterogeneous datasets requires careful harmonization. We will implement a multi-layer integration framework:

*Transcript-level harmonization:* All data will be mapped to GENCODE v38 transcript annotations using standardized identifiers. For spatial transcriptomics, we will aggregate isoform-level data to gene level where isoform resolution is unavailable, while preserving isoform information where possible.

*Coordinate system alignment:* RBP binding sites and structure data use transcript coordinates, while spatial data uses gene-level annotations. We will create unified coordinate mappings enabling feature extraction at consistent resolution.

*Cross-platform normalization:* Spatial transcriptomics platforms have different sensitivities and biases. We will apply platform-specific normalization (SCTransform for Visium, cell-level normalization for MERFISH) before integration, using mutual nearest neighbor batch correction for cross-dataset analysis.

*Quality control pipeline:* Automated QC will filter low-confidence binding peaks (IDR < 0.05), low-coverage structure probing regions, and spatial data with insufficient spot/cell density.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Machine Learning for Localization Prediction:* We will develop a multi-modal deep learning framework integrating sequence, structure, and RBP binding features. The architecture will use: (1) convolutional layers processing RNA sequence with attention mechanisms; (2) graph neural networks encoding RBP binding site configurations; (3) recurrent layers capturing structure context. Training will use spatial transcriptomics localization labels with 5-fold cross-validation. We will benchmark against existing tools (RNALocate, iLoc-mRNA) and ablation studies will quantify contribution of each feature type.

*Network Analysis:* RBP-mRNA bipartite networks will be constructed from eCLIP data. We will apply: (1) weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA) to identify co-regulated mRNA modules; (2) community detection (Louvain algorithm) to identify RBP functional groups; (3) network motif analysis to identify recurring regulatory patterns. Network statistics (degree distribution, clustering coefficient, modularity) will characterize emergent network properties.

*Spatial Statistics:* Subcellular localization patterns will be quantified using: (1) Ripley's K-function for clustering analysis; (2) spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I) for localization precision; (3) co-localization metrics (Pearson's correlation, Manders' coefficients) for mRNA-mRNA and mRNA-RBP spatial relationships. Null models based on random localization will establish statistical significance.

*Structure-Function Integration:* We will develop algorithms predicting RBP accessibility from structure probing data. SHAPE reactivity will be converted to base-pairing probabilities using established calibration curves. Accessibility scores will be computed for each RBP motif occurrence and integrated with binding data to identify structure-dependent regulation.

**Validation Strategies**

All validation uses existing data without new experiments:

*Cross-dataset validation:* Models trained on one spatial transcriptomics platform will be tested on held-out data from different platforms. Consistent predictions across platforms indicate robust biological signals.

*Known positive controls:* Well-characterized localized mRNAs (beta-actin, CaMKII, Arc in neurons; ASH1 in yeast) will serve as positive controls. Models must correctly predict these established cases.

*Evolutionary conservation:* Predicted localization signals will be tested for conservation across species using data from model organisms in GEO.

*Perturbation data:* Published RBP knockdown RNA-seq and localization studies will test whether predicted regulatory relationships match observed perturbation effects.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1:* Data acquisition and harmonization (months 1-4); QC pipeline development (months 3-6); initial network construction and exploratory analysis (months 5-9); machine learning framework development (months 7-12); first manuscript on RBP combinatorial code (month 12).

*Year 2:* Structure-function integration (months 13-18); granule composition modeling (months 16-21); translation coupling analysis (months 19-24); second manuscript on structure-dependent regulation (month 18); third manuscript on granule emergence (month 24).

*Year 3:* Model refinement and validation (months 25-30); tool development and documentation (months 28-33); synthesis manuscript and database release (months 31-36); workshops and training (months 33-36).

**Team Composition**

This project requires expertise spanning: (1) RNA biology and RBP biochemistry; (2) spatial transcriptomics analysis and single-cell genomics; (3) RNA structure prediction and analysis; (4) machine learning and network science; (5) statistical methods for spatial data. No single laboratory possesses this combination, necessitating transdisciplinary collaboration through NCEMS.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
**Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce four categories of tangible deliverables that advance understanding of emergent RNA localization at the mesoscale:

*Integrated Datasets:* We will create the first unified database linking mRNA subcellular localization patterns with RBP binding profiles, RNA secondary structure, and translation status. This resource, termed the RNA Localization Atlas (RLA), will contain: (1) harmonized localization annotations for >15,000 human genes across >20 cell types derived from spatial transcriptomics synthesis; (2) integrated RBP binding profiles linking each transcript to its complement of bound RBPs with positional information; (3) structure accessibility scores for all annotated RBP binding sites; (4) translation efficiency metrics linked to localization status. The RLA will be deposited in a sustainable repository (Zenodo with DOI) and made queryable through a web interface.

*Computational Tools:* We will release three software packages: (1) LocoPredict—a machine learning tool predicting mRNA subcellular localization from sequence, structure, and RBP binding features, benchmarked to exceed existing prediction accuracy by >15%; (2) GranuleNet—a network analysis toolkit for identifying mRNA co-localization modules and predicting RNA granule composition; (3) StructureBind—algorithms integrating RNA structure predictions with RBP binding site analysis to identify functional localization signals. All tools will be released as documented Python packages with tutorials and example workflows.

*Mechanistic Models:* We will develop quantitative models describing: (1) the combinatorial RBP binding code for major subcellular compartments (nucleus, cytoplasm, ER, mitochondria, neurites); (2) the structural grammar controlling localization signal accessibility; (3) the network architecture underlying RNA granule assembly; (4) the coupling between localization and local translation. These models will be formalized mathematically and validated against held-out data.

*Publications and Training Materials:* We anticipate 4-5 peer-reviewed publications: (1) a methods paper describing the data integration framework; (2) a research article on the combinatorial RBP code; (3) a research article on structure-dependent localization; (4) a synthesis paper presenting the unified model of emergent RNA localization; (5) a resource paper describing the RNA Localization Atlas. Additionally, we will produce comprehensive training materials including video tutorials, workshop curricula, and educational modules.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. RNA granules represent paradigmatic mesoscale structures—assemblies of 100-1000 nm containing dozens of RBPs and hundreds of mRNAs—that exhibit emergent properties not predictable from individual components. Our synthesis will reveal how weak, promiscuous molecular interactions (individual RBP-RNA binding events with micromolar affinity) collectively produce precise subcellular targeting (localization to specific compartments with submicron accuracy).

The emergent properties we will characterize include: (1) specificity amplification—how combinations of non-specific interactions produce specific outcomes; (2) robustness—how redundant targeting mechanisms ensure reliable localization despite molecular noise; (3) modularity—how the same RBPs participate in different localization programs across cell types; (4) phase behavior—how interaction networks drive phase separation into transport granules. These principles extend beyond RNA biology to inform understanding of mesoscale organization generally.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Our findings will impact multiple fields:

*RNA Biology:* The combinatorial binding code will transform understanding of how RBPs achieve specificity, resolving the long-standing paradox of how short, degenerate binding motifs encode precise regulatory information.

*Cell Biology:* Principles of RNA granule assembly will inform understanding of membraneless organelle formation more broadly, relevant to stress granules, P-bodies, and nuclear bodies.

*Neuroscience:* Local translation in neurons depends critically on mRNA localization. Our models will enable prediction of which mRNAs localize to dendrites and axons, informing understanding of synaptic plasticity.

*Disease Biology:* Mutations in RBPs (FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1) cause ALS and frontotemporal dementia through disrupted RNA granule dynamics. Our network models will identify which mRNAs are most affected by specific RBP mutations.

*Therapeutic Development:* mRNA therapeutics require understanding localization to optimize delivery and translation. Our predictive models will guide design of mRNA sequences with desired localization properties.

**Enabling Future Research**

This synthesis creates foundations for future investigations:

*Hypothesis Generation:* Predicted localization signals and regulatory relationships will generate testable hypotheses for experimental validation by the broader community.

*Tool Development:* Our computational frameworks will be extensible to new data types as spatial multi-omics technologies mature.

*Comparative Biology:* Methods developed here will enable analysis of RNA localization evolution across species as comparative spatial transcriptomics data accumulates.

*Clinical Translation:* Disease-associated variants can be analyzed for effects on predicted localization, prioritizing variants for functional follow-up.

**Dissemination Plans**

We will disseminate findings through multiple channels:

*Publications:* All manuscripts will be submitted to open-access journals (eLife, PLOS Biology, Nucleic Acids Research) or posted as preprints (bioRxiv) prior to peer review.

*Conferences:* We will present at RNA Society meetings, ASCB, and computational biology conferences (ISMB, RECOMB).

*Workshops:* Annual workshops at NCEMS will train researchers in using our tools and datasets, with materials made permanently available online.

*Database:* The RNA Localization Atlas will be maintained with a commitment to 10-year sustainability through institutional support and integration with established resources (RNAcentral).

**Long-term Sustainability**

Sustainability is ensured through: (1) deposition of all data in established repositories with permanent identifiers; (2) software release through Bioconductor/PyPI with community maintenance models; (3) documentation enabling independent use without developer support; (4) partnerships with database resources (ENCODE, Human Cell Atlas) for long-term hosting; (5) training of next-generation scientists who will maintain and extend the resources.

[Budget and Resources]
**Personnel (Total: $720,000 over 3 years)**

*Postdoctoral Researcher - Computational Biology ($180,000, 3 years at $60,000/year):* This position will lead machine learning model development, implementing deep learning architectures for localization prediction and conducting systematic benchmarking. Requires expertise in Python, PyTorch/TensorFlow, and biological sequence analysis. Essential for achieving core computational objectives.

*Postdoctoral Researcher - RNA Biology/Bioinformatics ($180,000, 3 years at $60,000/year):* This position will lead data integration efforts, harmonizing spatial transcriptomics and RBP binding datasets. Requires expertise in RNA biology, familiarity with ENCODE data, and experience with spatial transcriptomics analysis pipelines. Critical for biological interpretation and validation.

*Graduate Student - Network Analysis ($120,000, 3 years at $40,000/year including tuition):* This student will develop and apply network analysis methods to RBP-mRNA interaction data, identifying emergent network properties and co-localization modules. Provides training opportunity in synthesis research methods.

*Graduate Student - Structural Bioinformatics ($120,000, 3 years at $40,000/year including tuition):* This student will integrate RNA structure data with binding site analysis, developing structure-aware prediction algorithms. Provides training in interdisciplinary research.

*Research Software Engineer ($120,000, 2 years at $60,000/year):* This position will ensure code quality, documentation, and sustainability. Will implement continuous integration, containerization, and user interfaces. Essential for producing usable, maintainable tools meeting open science standards.

**Computing Resources (Total: $90,000)**

*Cloud Computing - AWS/Google Cloud ($60,000):* Machine learning model training requires GPU resources beyond typical institutional allocations. We budget for ~15,000 GPU-hours on A100 instances for model training and hyperparameter optimization. Cloud computing also enables reproducible analysis environments.

*Data Storage ($20,000):* Integrated datasets will require ~50TB storage for raw data, processed files, and model checkpoints. Cloud storage ensures accessibility and backup.

*HPC Allocation Supplement ($10,000):* Additional allocation on institutional HPC for CPU-intensive network analysis and spatial statistics computations.

**Travel for Collaboration and Dissemination (Total: $60,000)**

*Team Meetings ($24,000):* Quarterly in-person working group meetings at NCEMS or rotating institutions. Essential for synthesis projects requiring close collaboration across disciplines. Budget covers travel for 6 team members, 4 meetings/year, 3 years.

*Conference Presentations ($24,000):* Attendance at RNA Society, ASCB, ISMB, and RECOMB meetings to present findings and engage community. Budget covers 4 conferences/year for team members.

*Collaboration Visits ($12,000):* Short-term visits between labs for intensive collaborative work sessions, particularly for data integration requiring domain expertise.

**Workshops and Training Events (Total: $45,000)**

*Annual NCEMS Workshops ($30,000):* Three annual workshops training 20-30 participants each in project tools and methods. Covers participant travel support, materials, and catering. Critical for community adoption and training mission.

*Online Training Development ($15,000):* Professional video production for online tutorials, website hosting, and learning management system. Ensures broad accessibility of training materials.

**Open Science Infrastructure (Total: $25,000)**

*Repository and Database Hosting ($15,000):* Zenodo Plus subscription for large dataset hosting, domain registration, and web hosting for project portal and RNA Localization Atlas interface.

*Software Maintenance ($10,000):* Continuous integration services, code signing certificates, and package repository fees for sustainable software distribution.

**Supplies and Publication Costs (Total: $20,000)**

*Open Access Publication Fees ($15,000):* Covers APCs for 4-5 open access publications in journals like eLife, NAR, and PLOS Biology.

*Miscellaneous Supplies ($5,000):* Computing peripherals, reference materials, and incidentals.

**Total Budget: $960,000 over 3 years ($320,000/year)**

**Budget Justification Summary:**

This budget reflects the synthesis nature of the project—personnel-intensive rather than equipment-intensive. The majority (75%) supports personnel essential for data integration, computational analysis, and tool development that no single lab could accomplish alone. Computing resources (9%) enable the large-scale machine learning and data processing required. Travel and workshops (11%) support the collaborative, training-focused mission central to NCEMS goals. Open science infrastructure (3%) ensures sustainable, accessible outputs. This investment will produce lasting resources—integrated datasets, validated models, and trained scientists—that multiply the impact of existing public data investments.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) represent emergent metabolic organelles where protein shells encapsulate enzyme pathways, creating efficiency and selectivity impossible in the cytoplasm. This synthesis project will decode emergent BMC function by integrating structural biology, metabolomics, and systems biology datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of BMC shells and encapsulated enzymes, metabolomics from MetaboLights, enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, and genomic data on BMC operons from NCBI. The central question is: how does BMC shell architecture at the mesoscale (40-200 nm compartments) create emergent metabolic properties—enhanced pathway flux, toxic intermediate sequestration, and substrate selectivity—that free enzymes cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent efficiency arises from shell pore selectivity, enzyme co-localization effects, and internal environment optimization. Our computational approach combines finite element modeling of metabolite diffusion through BMC shells, kinetic modeling of encapsulated pathways, and machine learning to predict BMC function from shell composition. We will develop algorithms correlating shell protein properties with pore selectivity. Integration with fitness data from published studies will connect BMC organization to growth phenotypes. Comparative analysis across BMC types (carboxysomes, metabolosomes) will reveal shared principles of emergent encapsulated metabolism. This project requires expertise in BMC biology, structural biology, metabolic modeling, and biophysics—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, metabolic, and genomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent BMC efficiency, identification of key architectural features determining function, and principles for engineering synthetic compartments. Understanding emergent BMC function has implications for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

[Background and Significance]
Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) represent one of the most fascinating examples of emergent organization in prokaryotic cells. These proteinaceous organelles, ranging from 40 to 200 nanometers in diameter, encapsulate sequential metabolic enzymes within selectively permeable protein shells, creating distinct biochemical environments that fundamentally alter pathway behavior. BMCs occupy a critical position at the mesoscale—larger than individual protein complexes yet smaller than classical organelles—where emergent properties arise from the collective organization of molecular components in ways that cannot be predicted from studying individual parts in isolation.

The field has accumulated substantial structural and functional data on BMCs over the past two decades. Cryo-electron microscopy studies deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) have revealed the architecture of complete BMC shells, including carboxysomes from cyanobacteria and chemoautotrophs, and metabolosomes involved in propanediol and ethanolamine utilization. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) contains over 200 high-resolution structures of BMC shell proteins, revealing the hexameric (BMC-H), trimeric (BMC-T), and pentameric (BMC-P) building blocks that tile together to form icosahedral or elongated shells. These structures have identified central pores in shell proteins that serve as selective gates for metabolite transport, with pore diameters ranging from 4 to 14 Ångstroms and varying electrostatic properties.

Despite this wealth of structural information, fundamental questions about emergent BMC function remain unanswered. How does the specific arrangement of shell proteins create selective permeability that differs qualitatively from simple diffusion barriers? How does enzyme encapsulation within the confined BMC lumen alter kinetic parameters compared to the same enzymes operating freely in the cytoplasm? What organizational principles determine whether a BMC enhances pathway flux, sequesters toxic intermediates, or both? These questions cannot be answered by examining individual components; they require understanding how mesoscale organization creates system-level behaviors.

Existing data sources provide unprecedented opportunities for synthesis research to address these gaps. The BRENDA enzyme database contains kinetic parameters for many BMC-encapsulated enzymes measured both in isolation and in cellular contexts. MetaboLights and the Metabolomics Workbench house metabolomics datasets from organisms with and without functional BMCs, enabling comparative analysis of metabolic phenotypes. NCBI GenBank contains thousands of annotated BMC operons across diverse bacterial phyla, revealing the genomic organization and evolutionary relationships of these systems. Fitness data from high-throughput transposon mutagenesis studies, available through resources like FitnessBrowser, connect BMC gene disruptions to growth phenotypes under various conditions.

The significance of understanding emergent BMC function extends across multiple domains. From a fundamental biology perspective, BMCs represent a natural solution to the challenge of organizing metabolism at the mesoscale—a problem that eukaryotes solve with membrane-bound organelles. Understanding the principles by which protein shells create functional compartmentalization illuminates general mechanisms of cellular organization. From an applied perspective, BMCs are increasingly recognized as platforms for metabolic engineering, where encapsulating synthetic pathways could enhance production of valuable compounds. However, rational engineering requires quantitative understanding of how shell architecture determines function—precisely the knowledge gap this synthesis project addresses.

The mesoscale nature of BMCs makes them ideal subjects for NCEMS-supported research. At 40-200 nm, BMCs exist at the interface between molecular and cellular scales, where emergent properties arise from the collective behavior of hundreds of shell proteins and dozens of encapsulated enzymes. The internal environment of a BMC—with its altered pH, ionic strength, and molecular crowding—cannot be understood from molecular structures alone but requires modeling the integrated system. Similarly, the selective permeability of BMC shells emerges from the arrangement of multiple pore types across the shell surface, creating transport properties that depend on mesoscale organization.

Current understanding is fragmented across disciplines. Structural biologists have characterized shell protein architectures but rarely connect these to metabolic function. Metabolic modelers have simulated encapsulated pathways but often use simplified representations of shell permeability. Microbiologists have measured fitness effects of BMC mutations but lack mechanistic explanations linking genotype to phenotype. This synthesis project will bridge these disciplinary silos by integrating structural, metabolic, and genomic data into unified computational models that capture emergent BMC function. The collaborative, transdisciplinary approach required for this integration exemplifies the community-scale synthesis that NCEMS is uniquely positioned to support.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions about emergent properties of bacterial microcompartments at the mesoscale, each with specific hypotheses that can be tested using existing publicly available data.

**Research Question 1: How does BMC shell architecture create emergent selective permeability?**

BMC shells contain multiple pore types with different sizes and electrostatic properties, yet the collective transport behavior of assembled shells cannot be predicted from individual pore structures. We ask: what principles govern how the spatial arrangement and relative abundance of different pore types create shell-level permeability that selectively admits substrates while retaining intermediates?

*Hypothesis 1a*: Emergent shell selectivity arises from the ratio of different shell protein paralogs (BMC-H variants with different pore properties) rather than from any single pore type. We predict that organisms with BMCs handling charged intermediates will show enrichment of shell proteins with complementary electrostatic pore properties, creating electrostatic filtering at the shell level.

*Hypothesis 1b*: The spatial clustering of specific pore types on the shell surface creates local transport microdomains that enhance selectivity beyond what random pore distribution would achieve. We predict that structural data will reveal non-random arrangements of shell protein variants in assembled shells.

These hypotheses will be tested by synthesizing shell protein structures from PDB with genomic data on shell protein operon organization from NCBI. We will correlate shell protein composition (extracted from comparative genomics of BMC operons across >500 bacterial species) with the chemical properties of encapsulated pathway intermediates (from BRENDA and MetaboLights). Machine learning models will identify sequence features predictive of pore selectivity, validated against experimentally characterized pore properties in the literature.

**Research Question 2: How does enzyme co-localization within BMCs create emergent kinetic advantages?**

Encapsulated enzymes operate in a fundamentally different environment than cytoplasmic enzymes—confined within nanoscale volumes with altered crowding, potentially modified pH, and proximity to pathway partners. We ask: what quantitative kinetic advantages emerge from encapsulation, and which architectural features of BMCs determine the magnitude of these advantages?

*Hypothesis 2a*: Substrate channeling between co-localized enzymes creates emergent pathway flux enhancement that scales with the ratio of enzyme spacing to substrate diffusion length. We predict that BMCs with tightly packed enzymes (as determined from cryo-EM reconstructions) will show greater flux enhancement in kinetic models than those with dispersed enzyme arrangements.

*Hypothesis 2b*: The effective concentration of intermediates within BMC lumens exceeds cytoplasmic concentrations by 10-100 fold due to shell retention, creating emergent kinetic advantages even without direct enzyme-enzyme channeling. We predict that metabolomics data from BMC-disrupted strains will show accumulation of pathway intermediates in the cytoplasm, indicating loss of compartmental concentration.

*Hypothesis 2c*: Toxic intermediate sequestration provides fitness advantages that correlate with intermediate reactivity. We predict that fitness costs of BMC disruption (from transposon mutagenesis data) will correlate with the chemical reactivity of pathway aldehydes or other toxic intermediates.

These hypotheses will be tested by integrating enzyme kinetic parameters from BRENDA with structural data on enzyme arrangements within BMCs from EMDB. Finite element models of metabolite diffusion will simulate pathway flux under different organizational scenarios. Predictions will be validated against metabolomics data comparing wild-type and BMC-deficient strains, and against fitness data from systematic mutagenesis studies.

**Research Question 3: What universal principles govern emergent function across diverse BMC types?**

BMCs have evolved independently multiple times to encapsulate different metabolic pathways, from carbon fixation in carboxysomes to aldehyde-generating catabolic pathways in metabolosomes. We ask: do shared architectural principles underlie emergent function across BMC types, or has evolution found multiple solutions to the compartmentalization problem?

*Hypothesis 3a*: Despite sequence divergence, BMC shells converge on similar pore size distributions optimized for their encapsulated pathways. We predict that carboxysomes (handling CO2/HCO3-) and propanediol utilization compartments (handling propionaldehyde) will show distinct but internally consistent pore architectures matched to their substrates.

*Hypothesis 3b*: The ratio of shell volume to encapsulated enzyme content is optimized across BMC types to balance intermediate concentration against diffusion limitation. We predict a universal scaling relationship between BMC size and enzyme loading across diverse BMC types.

*Hypothesis 3c*: Emergent efficiency gains follow predictable relationships with pathway properties (number of steps, intermediate toxicity, substrate/product size differential) that can be captured in a general quantitative framework.

These hypotheses will be tested through comparative analysis synthesizing data across BMC types. We will compile a comprehensive database of BMC structural parameters, enzyme compositions, and pathway properties from PDB, EMDB, UniProt, BRENDA, and published literature. Statistical and machine learning approaches will identify conserved features and predictive relationships.

**Mechanistic Insights Expected**

By addressing these questions, we expect to develop mechanistic understanding of how mesoscale organization creates emergent metabolic properties. Specifically, we anticipate identifying: (1) quantitative relationships between shell protein composition and transport selectivity; (2) the relative contributions of substrate channeling, intermediate concentration, and toxic sequestration to overall pathway enhancement; (3) design principles that could guide engineering of synthetic compartments. These insights will transform BMCs from descriptively characterized structures to quantitatively understood systems, enabling predictive models of compartmentalized metabolism.

[Methods and Approach]
**Data Sources and Acquisition**

This synthesis project will integrate data from multiple publicly available repositories spanning structural biology, enzymology, metabolomics, and genomics. All data sources are established, well-curated repositories with programmatic access.

*Structural Data*: The Protein Data Bank (PDB; rcsb.org) contains >200 structures of BMC shell proteins, including hexameric BMC-H proteins (e.g., PDB: 3NGK, 5DIH), trimeric BMC-T proteins with gated pores (e.g., PDB: 4QIV), and pentameric vertex proteins (e.g., PDB: 3I96). The Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB; ebi.ac.uk/emdb) houses cryo-EM reconstructions of assembled BMC shells and encapsulated enzyme complexes, including carboxysome structures (e.g., EMD-0624) and metabolosome reconstructions. We will systematically retrieve all BMC-related entries using keyword searches and cross-references to UniProt identifiers.

*Enzyme Kinetics*: BRENDA (brenda-enzymes.org) provides kinetic parameters (Km, kcat, Ki) for enzymes encapsulated in BMCs, including RuBisCO, carbonic anhydrase, propanediol dehydratase, and aldehyde dehydrogenases. We will extract parameters measured under varying conditions (pH, temperature, ionic strength) to model how the BMC internal environment affects enzyme function.

*Metabolomics*: MetaboLights (ebi.ac.uk/metabolights) and the Metabolomics Workbench (metabolomicsworkbench.org) contain metabolomics datasets from bacteria with characterized BMC systems. We will identify studies comparing metabolite profiles in wild-type versus BMC-deficient strains, focusing on pathway intermediates and products.

*Genomics*: NCBI GenBank and RefSeq provide annotated genome sequences containing BMC operons. The IMG/M database (img.jgi.doe.gov) offers comparative genomics tools for analyzing BMC gene neighborhoods across thousands of bacterial genomes. We will extract BMC operon compositions, shell protein paralog distributions, and encapsulated enzyme complements.

*Fitness Data*: FitnessBrowser (fit.genomics.lbl.gov) contains genome-wide fitness data from transposon mutagenesis experiments, including studies in organisms with BMCs (e.g., Salmonella enterica). We will extract fitness scores for BMC genes under conditions where compartmentalized pathways are active.

**Data Integration and Harmonization**

Integrating heterogeneous data types requires careful harmonization. We will develop a unified data model centered on BMC systems, linking shell protein structures to their genomic contexts, encapsulated enzymes to their kinetic parameters, and pathway organization to metabolic phenotypes.

*Identifier Mapping*: We will use UniProt accession numbers as primary identifiers, mapping PDB structures, BRENDA entries, and genomic loci to unified protein identifiers. The UniProt ID mapping service and programmatic APIs will automate this process.

*Structural Standardization*: Shell protein structures will be processed using BioPython and MDAnalysis to extract consistent geometric parameters: pore diameters, electrostatic surface potentials (calculated using APBS), and oligomeric interfaces. Cryo-EM maps will be analyzed using UCSF ChimeraX to measure shell dimensions and enzyme positions.

*Kinetic Parameter Curation*: BRENDA entries will be filtered for data quality, retaining measurements with documented experimental conditions. Where multiple measurements exist, we will apply statistical methods to estimate consensus parameters with uncertainty bounds.

*Phylogenetic Framework*: BMC systems will be organized within a phylogenetic framework using 16S rRNA trees from the SILVA database, enabling evolutionary analysis of shell composition and function.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Finite Element Modeling of Shell Permeability*: We will construct 3D models of BMC shells by tiling shell protein structures according to icosahedral symmetry, using experimentally determined stoichiometries. Metabolite diffusion through shell pores will be simulated using COMSOL Multiphysics or the open-source FEniCS package, solving the Nernst-Planck equations for charged metabolites. Simulations will predict effective permeability coefficients for substrates, products, and intermediates as functions of shell composition.

*Kinetic Modeling of Encapsulated Pathways*: We will implement ordinary differential equation (ODE) models of BMC-encapsulated pathways using COPASI and custom Python code. Models will incorporate enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, metabolite transport rates from finite element simulations, and compartmental volumes from structural data. Sensitivity analysis will identify parameters most critical for emergent pathway properties.

*Machine Learning for Structure-Function Prediction*: We will train machine learning models to predict pore selectivity from shell protein sequences and structures. Features will include amino acid composition of pore-lining residues, electrostatic potential distributions, and pore geometry. Random forest and gradient boosting models will be implemented using scikit-learn; deep learning approaches using graph neural networks (PyTorch Geometric) will capture structural relationships. Models will be validated using cross-validation and held-out test sets of characterized pores.

*Comparative Genomics Analysis*: BMC operon compositions across bacterial genomes will be analyzed using custom Python pipelines. We will identify correlations between shell protein paralog distributions and encapsulated pathway properties using statistical methods (Spearman correlation, phylogenetically independent contrasts).

**Validation Strategies**

All computational predictions will be validated against existing data without generating new experiments.

*Cross-Dataset Validation*: Permeability predictions from structural models will be compared against published experimental measurements of BMC transport (from literature mining). Kinetic model predictions will be validated against metabolomics data showing intermediate accumulation in BMC mutants.

*Positive Controls*: Well-characterized BMC systems (alpha-carboxysomes, Pdu metabolosomes) will serve as positive controls, with model predictions compared against extensive published functional data.

*Phylogenetic Validation*: Predicted structure-function relationships will be tested for consistency across phylogenetically independent BMC origins, ensuring that correlations reflect functional constraints rather than shared ancestry.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1*:
- Months 1-4: Data acquisition and harmonization; construct unified BMC database
- Months 5-8: Develop finite element models of shell permeability; validate against known systems
- Months 9-12: Implement kinetic models of encapsulated pathways; initial comparative genomics analysis

*Year 2*:
- Months 13-16: Machine learning model development and training
- Months 17-20: Integration of permeability and kinetic models; cross-validation
- Months 21-24: Comparative analysis across BMC types; manuscript preparation

*Year 3*:
- Months 25-28: Model refinement based on community feedback; additional validation
- Months 29-32: Tool development and documentation; training workshops
- Months 33-36: Final publications; data and code release; sustainability planning

**Team Composition and Expertise**

This synthesis project requires expertise spanning multiple disciplines:

1. *BMC Biology* (PI 1): Deep knowledge of BMC systems, operon organization, and biological function
2. *Structural Bioinformatics* (PI 2): Expertise in analyzing protein structures, cryo-EM maps, and molecular modeling
3. *Metabolic Modeling* (PI 3): Experience with kinetic modeling, flux analysis, and systems biology
4. *Machine Learning/Data Science* (PI 4): Skills in predictive modeling, feature engineering, and large-scale data analysis
5. *Postdoctoral Researchers* (2): Dedicated effort for data integration, model development, and analysis
6. *Graduate Students* (2): Training opportunities in synthesis research methods
7. *Research Software Engineer* (1): Development of robust, documented, reproducible code

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
**Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce four categories of tangible deliverables that advance understanding of emergent BMC function and enable future research.

*Integrated BMC Database*: We will create a comprehensive, curated database linking BMC structural data, enzyme kinetics, genomic organization, and phenotypic information. This resource will include: (1) standardized structural parameters for >200 shell proteins; (2) curated kinetic parameters for >50 BMC-encapsulated enzymes; (3) annotated BMC operons from >500 bacterial genomes; (4) fitness data for BMC genes under relevant conditions. The database will be hosted on a sustainable platform with programmatic API access, enabling community use and extension.

*Computational Models of BMC Function*: We will deliver validated computational models at multiple scales: (1) Finite element models predicting shell permeability as a function of protein composition, available as parameterized simulation templates; (2) Kinetic models of major BMC-encapsulated pathways (carboxysome carbon fixation, Pdu propanediol utilization, Eut ethanolamine utilization) calibrated against experimental data; (3) Integrated multi-scale models connecting shell architecture to pathway flux and fitness. All models will be documented and released with example workflows.

*Machine Learning Tools*: We will develop and release trained machine learning models for: (1) predicting pore selectivity from shell protein sequences; (2) classifying BMC types from operon composition; (3) estimating pathway enhancement from BMC architectural features. These tools will be packaged as Python libraries with clear documentation and tutorials.

*Quantitative Principles of Emergent BMC Function*: Beyond tools and data, we will articulate general principles governing how mesoscale organization creates emergent metabolic properties. These principles will be formalized as quantitative relationships (e.g., scaling laws relating shell composition to selectivity) and qualitative design rules (e.g., conditions favoring channeling versus concentration mechanisms).

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. BMCs exemplify how organization at scales between molecules and organelles creates system-level behaviors unpredictable from component properties. Our synthesis will reveal:

*Emergent Selectivity*: How the collective arrangement of multiple pore types creates transport selectivity exceeding that of individual pores—a mesoscale property arising from spatial organization.

*Emergent Kinetic Enhancement*: How enzyme co-localization within confined volumes creates pathway flux and efficiency gains through mechanisms (channeling, concentration, sequestration) that require mesoscale organization.

*Emergent Robustness*: How BMC architecture buffers pathway function against perturbations, creating system-level robustness from component-level variability.

These insights will establish BMCs as a model system for mesoscale emergence, with lessons applicable to other compartmentalized biological systems including phase-separated condensates, viral capsids, and engineered protein cages.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Understanding emergent BMC function has implications extending beyond bacterial cell biology:

*Metabolic Engineering*: Quantitative models of BMC function will enable rational design of synthetic compartments for biotechnology applications. Our principles will guide selection of shell proteins, enzyme arrangements, and pathway designs for engineered BMCs producing valuable compounds.

*Evolutionary Biology*: Comparative analysis across BMC types will illuminate how evolution discovers solutions to the compartmentalization problem, revealing constraints and opportunities in the evolution of cellular organization.

*Synthetic Biology*: Design rules for emergent compartment function will inform broader efforts to engineer cellular organization, including protein-based organelles and membrane-less compartments.

*Education*: BMCs provide accessible examples of emergence for teaching systems biology concepts, and our curated resources will support educational use.

**Enabling Future Research**

Our synthesis will create foundations for future investigations:

*Hypothesis Generation*: Quantitative models will generate testable predictions about BMC function that can guide future experimental studies (by other groups generating new data).

*Comparative Framework*: The integrated database will enable systematic comparison of BMC systems, supporting discovery of novel BMC types and functions.

*Method Development*: Our computational approaches for modeling compartmentalized metabolism will be applicable to other systems, including eukaryotic organelles and synthetic compartments.

*Community Building*: By bringing together researchers from structural biology, metabolic modeling, and microbiology, this project will catalyze a community focused on quantitative understanding of bacterial compartmentalization.

**Dissemination Plans**

*Publications*: We anticipate 4-6 peer-reviewed publications: (1) database and resource paper; (2) finite element modeling of shell permeability; (3) kinetic modeling of encapsulated pathways; (4) machine learning for BMC function prediction; (5) comparative analysis and design principles; (6) review/perspective on emergent compartment function.

*Workshops*: We will organize two workshops during the project: (1) a methods workshop training researchers in BMC modeling approaches; (2) a synthesis workshop bringing together the BMC community to discuss findings and future directions.

*Conference Presentations*: Results will be presented at relevant meetings including the ASM Microbe meeting, Biophysical Society Annual Meeting, and ISCB conferences.

*Online Resources*: All tools, data, and documentation will be accessible through a project website with tutorials, example analyses, and community forums.

**Long-term Sustainability**

We will ensure lasting impact through:

*Repository Deposition*: Curated data will be deposited in established repositories (Zenodo for datasets, PyPI for Python packages) with persistent identifiers.

*Community Governance*: We will establish a community steering committee to guide database maintenance and extension beyond the funding period.

*Integration with Existing Resources*: Where possible, curated data will be contributed back to source databases (e.g., annotations to UniProt) ensuring long-term preservation.

*Documentation*: Comprehensive documentation will enable community members to maintain and extend tools independently.

[Budget and Resources]
**Personnel (Total: $720,000 over 3 years)**

*Postdoctoral Researchers (2 positions, $180,000/year total including benefits)*: Two postdocs will provide dedicated effort for data integration, model development, and analysis. Postdoc 1 will focus on structural analysis and finite element modeling, requiring expertise in structural bioinformatics and computational physics. Postdoc 2 will lead kinetic modeling and machine learning efforts, requiring expertise in systems biology and data science. Postdocs are essential for the intensive computational work required for synthesis across heterogeneous data types. Total: $540,000.

*Graduate Student Support (2 students, partial support, $60,000/year total)*: Two graduate students will participate in the project, gaining training in synthesis research methods. Students will contribute to specific analysis modules under postdoc mentorship, with thesis chapters derived from project work. This investment in training aligns with NCEMS's workforce development mission. Total: $180,000.

**Research Software Engineer ($150,000 over 3 years)**

A part-time research software engineer (0.5 FTE) will ensure code quality, documentation, and sustainability. The RSE will implement continuous integration, develop user interfaces, and maintain computational infrastructure. This investment is critical for producing tools that the community can actually use and maintain. Professional software engineering expertise is essential for open science goals.

**Computing Resources ($90,000 over 3 years)**

*Cloud Computing (AWS/Google Cloud, $50,000)*: Finite element simulations and machine learning training require substantial computational resources beyond typical lab allocations. Cloud computing provides flexible, scalable resources for computationally intensive analyses. Costs include GPU instances for deep learning and high-memory instances for large simulations.

*High-Performance Computing Allocation ($20,000)*: Supplementary HPC allocations through XSEDE/ACCESS will support large-scale parameter sweeps and ensemble simulations. Budget covers allocation purchase and data storage.

*Data Storage and Hosting ($20,000)*: Long-term storage for curated databases and simulation outputs, including Zenodo fees for large datasets and web hosting for project resources.

**Travel ($60,000 over 3 years)**

*Team Meetings ($30,000)*: Annual in-person meetings of the full working group are essential for synthesis research requiring deep collaboration across disciplines. Budget supports travel for 8-10 participants to two-day meetings at rotating locations.

*Conference Presentations ($20,000)*: Dissemination of results at scientific meetings (ASM Microbe, Biophysical Society, ISCB) ensures community engagement and feedback. Budget supports 4-6 conference trips per year across team members.

*Collaboration Visits ($10,000)*: Short visits between labs enable intensive collaborative work on specific project components.

**Workshops and Training ($40,000 over 3 years)**

*Methods Workshop (Year 2, $20,000)*: A two-day workshop training 20-30 researchers in BMC modeling approaches. Budget covers venue, participant support, and materials.

*Synthesis Workshop (Year 3, $20,000)*: A capstone workshop bringing together the BMC research community to discuss findings and future directions. Budget covers venue and participant support.

**Open Science Infrastructure ($15,000 over 3 years)**

*Repository and Hosting Fees ($5,000)*: Costs for GitHub organization, Docker Hub, and web hosting beyond free tiers.

*Documentation Tools ($5,000)*: Licenses and hosting for documentation platforms, tutorial hosting, and community forums.

*Publication Fees ($5,000)*: Open access publication fees for project papers, ensuring unrestricted access to findings.

**Supplies and Materials ($10,000 over 3 years)**

Miscellaneous supplies including computing peripherals, reference materials, and workshop supplies.

**Total Budget: $1,085,000 over 3 years**

**Budget Justification Summary**

This budget reflects the community-scale nature of the proposed synthesis. Personnel costs dominate because synthesis research is fundamentally a human intellectual endeavor requiring sustained effort to integrate heterogeneous data and develop sophisticated models. Computing costs are substantial but necessary for the finite element simulations and machine learning that enable quantitative modeling of emergent BMC function. Travel and workshop costs support the collaborative, transdisciplinary approach essential for synthesis research that no single lab could accomplish. Open science infrastructure costs ensure that project outputs are accessible, documented, and sustainable. This investment will produce lasting resources—databases, tools, and trained researchers—that benefit the molecular and cellular biology community far beyond the funding period.

abstract_original: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) represent emergent metabolic organelles where protein shells encapsulate enzyme pathways, creating efficiency and selectivity impossible in the cytoplasm. This synthesis project will decode emergent BMC function by integrating structural biology, metabolomics, and systems biology datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of BMC shells and encapsulated enzymes, metabolomics from MetaboLights, enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, and genomic data on BMC operons from NCBI. The central question is: how does BMC shell architecture at the mesoscale (40-200 nm compartments) create emergent metabolic properties—enhanced pathway flux, toxic intermediate sequestration, and substrate selectivity—that free enzymes cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent efficiency arises from shell pore selectivity, enzyme co-localization effects, and internal environment optimization. Our computational approach combines finite element modeling of metabolite diffusion through BMC shells, kinetic modeling of encapsulated pathways, and machine learning to predict BMC function from shell composition. We will develop algorithms correlating shell protein properties with pore selectivity. Integration with fitness data from published studies will connect BMC organization to growth phenotypes. Comparative analysis across BMC types (carboxysomes, metabolosomes) will reveal shared principles of emergent encapsulated metabolism. This project requires expertise in BMC biology, structural biology, metabolic modeling, and biophysics—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, metabolic, and genomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent BMC efficiency, identification of key architectural features determining function, and principles for engineering synthetic compartments. Understanding emergent BMC function has implications for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.
