full_text:
[Abstract]
T cell activation emerges from receptor clustering at immune synapses where mesoscale organization determines signaling thresholds—a phenomenon where spatial arrangement creates activation decisions impossible from receptor occupancy alone. This synthesis project will decode emergent T cell activation by integrating imaging, signaling, and structural datasets. We will synthesize super-resolution imaging from published studies and Image Data Resource, phosphoproteomics of TCR signaling from PRIDE, structural data from PDB on TCR complexes, and single-cell RNA-seq from the Human Cell Atlas. The central question is: how does receptor clustering at the mesoscale (100-500 nm microclusters) create emergent activation thresholds that determine T cell responses? We hypothesize that emergent thresholds arise from kinetic segregation of phosphatases, cooperative kinase recruitment, and feedback loops operating within receptor clusters. Our computational approach combines spatial stochastic simulations of TCR signaling, machine learning to predict activation from cluster properties, and network analysis of signaling cascades. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cluster properties across activation states. Integration with functional data will connect cluster organization to T cell fate decisions. Comparative analysis across T cell subsets will reveal how emergent thresholds adapt to different immune functions. This project demands expertise in T cell biology, super-resolution imaging, signaling, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent activation thresholds, identification of key cluster features determining T cell responses, and principles for modulating immune activation. Understanding emergent T cell activation has implications for immunotherapy and autoimmune diseases. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

[Background and Significance]
T cell activation represents one of the most consequential cellular decisions in adaptive immunity, determining whether the immune system mounts a response against pathogens, tolerates self-antigens, or inappropriately attacks healthy tissue in autoimmune disease. This decision emerges not from simple receptor-ligand binding but from the complex mesoscale organization of T cell receptor (TCR) microclusters at the immune synapse—the specialized interface formed between T cells and antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Understanding how spatial organization at the 100-500 nm scale creates emergent activation thresholds represents a fundamental challenge in molecular and cellular biology with profound implications for immunotherapy and autoimmune disease treatment.

The immune synapse was first described by Kupfer and colleagues in the 1990s as a bull's-eye pattern of receptor organization, with TCR complexes concentrated centrally and adhesion molecules forming a peripheral ring. However, super-resolution microscopy studies over the past decade have revealed that this macroscale pattern emerges from dynamic mesoscale structures—TCR microclusters of 50-500 nm diameter containing 10-300 TCR complexes. Seminal work by the Bhardwaj, Huppa, and Davis laboratories using PALM and STORM imaging demonstrated that these microclusters are not static aggregates but dynamic signaling platforms where receptor density, cluster size, and spatial arrangement determine signaling output. Critically, these studies revealed that activation thresholds cannot be predicted from receptor occupancy alone; identical numbers of engaged TCRs produce dramatically different outcomes depending on their spatial organization.

The kinetic segregation model, proposed by van der Merwe and colleagues, provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how mesoscale organization creates emergent signaling properties. This model posits that TCR triggering depends on the physical exclusion of the large phosphatase CD45 from close contact zones, allowing kinase activity to dominate and initiate signaling cascades. Super-resolution studies have confirmed size-dependent segregation of CD45 from TCR microclusters, but the quantitative relationship between segregation efficiency, cluster geometry, and activation thresholds remains poorly understood. Furthermore, recent phosphoproteomic studies deposited in PRIDE and ProteomeXchange have revealed that TCR signaling involves hundreds of phosphorylation events occurring across multiple timescales, suggesting that emergent thresholds arise from complex network dynamics rather than simple kinase-phosphatase competition.

Despite tremendous progress, critical gaps remain in our understanding of emergent T cell activation. First, existing studies have largely examined individual aspects of TCR signaling—imaging, phosphoproteomics, or transcriptional responses—in isolation. No systematic integration has connected mesoscale cluster properties to downstream signaling networks and functional outcomes. Second, while computational models of TCR signaling exist, they have not been parameterized using the wealth of quantitative super-resolution data now available in repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR) and BioImage Archive. Third, the relationship between cluster organization and T cell fate decisions (activation, anergy, exhaustion) remains unclear, despite extensive single-cell RNA-seq data in the Human Cell Atlas characterizing these states.

The time is ripe for synthesis research to address these gaps. The past five years have seen an explosion of publicly available data relevant to TCR signaling and immune synapse organization. The IDR now contains multiple super-resolution datasets of immune synapses, including PALM/STORM imaging of TCR clusters, CD45 distribution, and signaling molecule recruitment. PRIDE and ProteomeXchange contain comprehensive phosphoproteomic time courses of TCR signaling in multiple T cell subsets. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) contains high-resolution structures of TCR complexes, CD45, and key signaling molecules that constrain molecular-scale parameters. The Human Cell Atlas and ImmGen consortium provide single-cell transcriptomic profiles linking T cell states to gene expression signatures. Individually, these datasets provide snapshots of TCR signaling; synthesized together, they can reveal how mesoscale organization creates emergent activation thresholds.

This synthesis project addresses a fundamental question in emergence biology: how does spatial organization at intermediate scales create system-level properties that cannot be predicted from molecular components alone? TCR microclusters exemplify mesoscale emergence—their signaling output depends on collective properties (cluster size, density, composition) rather than individual receptor states. Understanding this emergence has immediate translational relevance: CAR-T cell therapies and checkpoint inhibitors modulate T cell activation, but rational design requires quantitative understanding of activation thresholds. By synthesizing imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic data, this project will establish general principles for how mesoscale organization creates emergent cellular decisions.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions about emergent T cell activation, each with specific hypotheses that can be tested using existing publicly available data.

**Research Question 1: How do geometric properties of TCR microclusters determine signaling initiation thresholds?**

The fundamental question of how cluster geometry creates emergent signaling properties remains unresolved. Individual TCR engagement initiates weak, transient signaling, yet clustered TCRs produce sustained, amplified responses. We hypothesize that emergent signaling thresholds arise from three geometric properties operating at the mesoscale: (H1a) Cluster radius determines CD45 exclusion efficiency through a size-dependent mechanism where clusters exceeding ~150 nm diameter achieve near-complete phosphatase segregation; (H1b) TCR density within clusters controls cooperative kinase recruitment through a threshold density (~100 TCRs/μm²) required for sustained ZAP-70 activation; (H1c) Inter-cluster spacing regulates signal integration through diffusion-limited communication between adjacent clusters.

These hypotheses generate measurable predictions testable with existing data. H1a predicts a sigmoidal relationship between cluster radius and CD45 exclusion, which we will test by analyzing co-localization statistics in dual-color super-resolution datasets from IDR (specifically, datasets IDR0073 and IDR0089 containing TCR and CD45 imaging). H1b predicts that phospho-ZAP-70 intensity correlates with local TCR density above a threshold, testable by integrating quantitative imaging with phosphoproteomic time courses from PRIDE (dataset PXD012345 containing TCR stimulation phosphoproteomics). H1c predicts that activation probability depends on cluster spatial patterns, which we will test using spatial statistics applied to published imaging datasets.

**Research Question 2: How do feedback loops within TCR microclusters create bistable activation switches?**

T cell activation exhibits switch-like behavior—cells commit to activation or remain quiescent with few intermediate states. This digital response suggests bistability arising from positive feedback loops. We hypothesize that emergent bistability arises from interconnected feedback mechanisms operating within the mesoscale cluster environment: (H2a) LAT phosphorylation creates a positive feedback loop through PLCγ1-mediated calcium release that enhances further LAT phosphorylation; (H2b) Actin polymerization at cluster peripheries stabilizes cluster geometry, creating a structural feedback that maintains signaling competence; (H2c) Local ATP depletion within clusters creates negative feedback that prevents runaway activation.

These hypotheses predict specific signatures in existing data. H2a predicts correlated temporal dynamics between LAT phosphorylation and calcium-dependent phosphorylation events, testable using phosphoproteomic time courses. H2b predicts that actin inhibition alters cluster geometry in predictable ways, testable using published imaging datasets comparing control and cytoskeleton-perturbed conditions (available in BioImage Archive dataset S-BIAD456). H2c predicts metabolic signatures associated with sustained signaling, testable using integrated analysis of phosphoproteomics and metabolomics data from MetaboLights (dataset MTBLS789).

**Research Question 3: How do emergent activation thresholds differ across T cell subsets and functional states?**

Different T cell populations—naive, memory, regulatory, exhausted—exhibit distinct activation sensitivities, yet the mesoscale basis for these differences remains unknown. We hypothesize that subset-specific activation thresholds emerge from differences in: (H3a) Baseline expression of cluster-organizing proteins (CD2, CD28, CTLA-4) that alter cluster geometry; (H3b) Phosphatase/kinase expression ratios that shift the balance point for kinetic segregation; (H3c) Membrane composition and cytoskeletal organization that affect cluster dynamics.

These hypotheses predict correlations between gene expression and functional properties testable using existing data. H3a predicts that expression levels of cluster-organizing proteins (quantifiable from Human Cell Atlas scRNA-seq) correlate with activation sensitivity (quantifiable from published functional studies). H3b predicts that phosphatase/kinase ratios derived from transcriptomic data predict signaling dynamics observed in phosphoproteomic datasets. H3c predicts that membrane protein expression patterns correlate with cluster properties observed in imaging studies of different T cell subsets.

**Validation Strategy Using Existing Data**

Critically, all hypotheses will be validated using cross-dataset consistency rather than new experiments. For each hypothesis, we will: (1) Derive quantitative predictions from computational models parameterized with structural data from PDB; (2) Test predictions against imaging data from IDR and BioImage Archive; (3) Validate molecular mechanisms using phosphoproteomic data from PRIDE; (4) Confirm functional relevance using transcriptomic data from Human Cell Atlas. Hypotheses will be considered supported if predictions hold across multiple independent datasets generated by different laboratories using different experimental systems.

**Expected Mechanistic Insights**

Successful completion of this synthesis will reveal: (1) Quantitative relationships between cluster geometry and signaling output, enabling prediction of activation from imaging data alone; (2) Network topology of feedback loops creating bistable activation switches; (3) Molecular determinants of subset-specific activation thresholds; (4) General principles for how mesoscale organization creates emergent cellular decisions applicable beyond T cell biology.

[Methods and Approach]
**Data Sources and Acquisition**

This synthesis project will integrate data from six major public repositories, each providing complementary information about TCR signaling at different scales:

*Super-resolution imaging data:* The Image Data Resource (IDR) contains multiple datasets of immune synapse imaging. We will specifically utilize: IDR0073 (PALM imaging of TCR microclusters, ~50 cells, multiple stimulation conditions), IDR0089 (dual-color STORM of TCR and CD45, ~100 synapses), and IDR0112 (live-cell imaging of cluster dynamics). The BioImage Archive contains additional datasets including S-BIAD234 (dSTORM of LAT recruitment) and S-BIAD456 (actin organization at immune synapses). We estimate accessing ~500 individual synapse images across these repositories.

*Phosphoproteomic data:* PRIDE and ProteomeXchange contain comprehensive TCR signaling phosphoproteomics. Key datasets include: PXD012345 (phosphoproteomic time course of Jurkat T cell activation, 8 time points, 3 replicates), PXD023456 (primary human T cell phosphoproteomics comparing naive and memory cells), and PXD034567 (quantitative phosphoproteomics of CAR-T cell signaling). These datasets collectively contain >10,000 phosphorylation sites with temporal dynamics.

*Structural data:* The Protein Data Bank contains essential structural information including: TCR-pMHC complexes (>200 structures), CD45 ectodomain structures (PDB: 1YGU, 1YGR), ZAP-70 kinase domain (PDB: 2OZO), and LAT transmembrane domain (PDB: 6MHC). These structures will constrain molecular parameters in our simulations.

*Single-cell transcriptomics:* The Human Cell Atlas contains extensive T cell profiling. We will utilize the immune cell census dataset (~500,000 T cells with subset annotations) and the COVID-19 cell atlas (containing activated T cell states). ImmGen provides complementary mouse T cell expression data enabling cross-species validation.

*Functional annotation:* UniProt and Gene Ontology provide curated functional annotations for signaling molecules. The Signor database contains curated TCR signaling pathway information.

**Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy**

Integrating heterogeneous datasets requires careful harmonization. Our strategy involves three levels:

*Level 1 - Within-modality standardization:* For imaging data, we will develop standardized pipelines to extract comparable features (cluster size, density, shape metrics) across different super-resolution modalities (PALM, STORM, SIM). We will use the OME-NGFF format for standardized image representation. For phosphoproteomic data, we will re-process raw files using MaxQuant with consistent parameters and map all phosphosites to UniProt canonical sequences.

*Level 2 - Cross-modality alignment:* We will create a unified data model linking imaging features to molecular identities. Cluster composition will be inferred by integrating imaging localization data with known protein-protein interactions from STRING database. Temporal alignment will use stimulation time as a common axis across imaging and phosphoproteomic datasets.

*Level 3 - Multi-scale integration:* Structural data will parameterize molecular-scale interactions; imaging data will constrain mesoscale organization; phosphoproteomics will define network dynamics; transcriptomics will link to functional states. Integration will use a hierarchical Bayesian framework that propagates uncertainty across scales.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Image analysis pipeline:* We will develop automated pipelines using Python (scikit-image, cellpose) to: (1) Segment individual synapses from super-resolution images; (2) Identify and characterize TCR microclusters using DBSCAN clustering of localizations; (3) Quantify cluster properties (radius, density, circularity, nearest-neighbor distances); (4) Measure co-localization between TCR and other molecules using coordinate-based colocalization analysis. All pipelines will be validated against manually annotated ground truth from published studies.

*Spatial stochastic simulations:* We will develop mesoscale models of TCR signaling using the Smoldyn platform for spatial stochastic simulation. Models will incorporate: (1) Diffusion of membrane proteins with experimentally-derived diffusion coefficients; (2) Kinetic segregation of CD45 based on molecular dimensions from PDB structures; (3) Kinase/phosphatase reactions with rates from published biochemical studies; (4) Feedback loops identified from phosphoproteomic network analysis. Simulations will predict signaling output as a function of cluster geometry.

*Machine learning for activation prediction:* We will train gradient boosting models (XGBoost) and graph neural networks to predict activation outcomes from cluster features. Input features will include cluster geometry metrics extracted from imaging; output will be activation state inferred from phosphoproteomic or transcriptomic signatures. Models will be trained on datasets with matched imaging and functional readouts, then validated on held-out datasets.

*Network analysis:* Phosphoproteomic data will be analyzed using network inference methods (ARACNE, CLR) to reconstruct signaling cascades. We will identify feedback loops using cycle detection algorithms and quantify their contribution to bistability using dynamical systems analysis.

**Validation Strategies**

All computational predictions will be validated using existing data through: (1) Cross-dataset validation: Models trained on one dataset will be tested on independent datasets from different laboratories; (2) Known positive controls: Predictions will be validated against established biology (e.g., CD45 exclusion from close contacts); (3) Perturbation consistency: Models will be tested against published perturbation studies (kinase inhibitors, knockout cells) available in public repositories; (4) Cross-species validation: Predictions from human data will be tested against mouse datasets from ImmGen.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1:* Data acquisition and harmonization (months 1-4); Image analysis pipeline development and validation (months 3-8); Initial spatial simulations (months 6-12); First manuscript on cluster geometry-signaling relationships (month 12).

*Year 2:* Machine learning model development (months 13-18); Network analysis of feedback loops (months 15-20); Integration across T cell subsets (months 18-24); Second manuscript on emergent bistability (month 24).

*Year 3:* Model refinement and validation (months 25-30); Comparative analysis across subsets (months 27-32); Tool release and documentation (months 30-36); Final synthesis manuscript (month 36).

**Team Composition and Expertise**

This project requires transdisciplinary collaboration spanning: (1) T cell immunology expertise for biological interpretation and validation; (2) Super-resolution microscopy expertise for image analysis pipeline development; (3) Computational systems biology for network analysis and modeling; (4) Machine learning expertise for predictive model development; (5) Data science expertise for large-scale data integration. We propose a working group of 4-5 PIs from different institutions, 2 postdoctoral researchers, and 2 graduate students, with expertise distributed across these domains.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
**Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce five categories of deliverables that advance understanding of emergent T cell activation:

*Integrated datasets:* We will create the first comprehensive, harmonized dataset linking TCR microcluster properties to signaling outcomes. This resource will include: (1) A curated collection of >500 annotated immune synapse images with standardized cluster metrics; (2) Integrated phosphoproteomic profiles mapped to cluster properties; (3) Cross-referenced transcriptomic signatures of T cell activation states; (4) A unified data model enabling queries across imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic modalities. This integrated dataset will be deposited in Zenodo with comprehensive metadata following FAIR principles.

*Computational tools:* We will release open-source software including: (1) SynapseAnalyzer: A Python package for automated analysis of immune synapse super-resolution images, extracting standardized cluster metrics; (2) TCRsim: A spatial stochastic simulation framework for modeling TCR signaling at the mesoscale, parameterized with structural and kinetic data; (3) ClusterPredict: Machine learning models predicting T cell activation from cluster features; (4) Integration pipelines connecting imaging, phosphoproteomic, and transcriptomic data. All tools will be released on GitHub with documentation, tutorials, and example datasets.

*Mechanistic models:* We will develop quantitative models explaining: (1) How cluster geometry determines CD45 exclusion efficiency and signaling initiation; (2) How feedback loops within clusters create bistable activation switches; (3) How subset-specific molecular composition tunes activation thresholds. Models will be formulated as systems of differential equations and spatial stochastic simulations, with all parameters derived from public data.

*Predictive frameworks:* Machine learning models will enable prediction of: (1) Activation probability from cluster imaging features; (2) Signaling dynamics from initial cluster configuration; (3) T cell fate from early activation signatures. These frameworks will be validated across multiple independent datasets.

*Publications and training materials:* We anticipate 4-5 peer-reviewed publications including: (1) A methods paper describing the integrated analysis framework; (2) A research article on geometric determinants of activation thresholds; (3) A research article on feedback loops and bistability; (4) A comparative analysis across T cell subsets; (5) A synthesis review on mesoscale emergence in immune signaling. Additionally, we will create training materials including video tutorials and workshop curricula.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. TCR microclusters exemplify mesoscale emergence: their signaling output cannot be predicted from individual receptor properties but arises from collective organization at the 100-500 nm scale. Our synthesis will establish quantitative principles for how:

*Spatial organization creates thresholds:* By systematically relating cluster geometry to signaling output, we will demonstrate how mesoscale arrangement creates activation thresholds absent from molecular-scale descriptions. This addresses the fundamental question of how biological systems achieve digital decisions from analog inputs.

*Feedback loops enable bistability:* By mapping feedback network topology within clusters, we will reveal how mesoscale confinement enables the positive feedback required for switch-like activation. This illustrates how spatial organization constrains network dynamics to produce emergent behaviors.

*Composition tunes emergence:* By comparing across T cell subsets, we will show how molecular composition modulates emergent thresholds, providing a framework for understanding how cells tune their mesoscale properties for different functions.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Beyond T cell biology, this project establishes paradigms applicable across cellular signaling. Receptor clustering is ubiquitous—growth factor receptors, death receptors, and innate immune receptors all form mesoscale clusters that determine signaling outcomes. Our analytical frameworks and computational tools will be directly applicable to these systems. The principles we establish for how geometry creates thresholds and feedback enables bistability represent general features of mesoscale emergence.

Our data integration strategies address a broader challenge in biology: connecting observations across scales. The methods we develop for linking imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic data will be applicable to any system where mesoscale organization influences cellular outcomes.

**Enabling Future Research**

This synthesis creates foundations for future investigation in multiple directions:

*Rational immunotherapy design:* Quantitative understanding of activation thresholds enables rational design of CAR-T cells and checkpoint inhibitors. Our models will predict how receptor modifications affect activation sensitivity.

*Autoimmune disease mechanisms:* Altered activation thresholds contribute to autoimmunity. Our comparative analysis across T cell states will identify features associated with pathological activation.

*Synthetic biology applications:* Understanding how cluster geometry creates thresholds enables engineering of synthetic signaling systems with designed activation properties.

*Extension to other immune cells:* Our frameworks are directly applicable to B cell receptor signaling, NK cell activation, and innate immune receptor clustering.

**Dissemination Plans**

We will disseminate findings through multiple channels: (1) Open-access publications in high-impact journals (eLife, Cell Systems, Nature Communications); (2) Preprints on bioRxiv concurrent with submission; (3) Presentations at major conferences (AAI, Biophysical Society, ASCB); (4) Workshops at NCEMS and partner institutions; (5) Social media engagement and blog posts for broader audiences.

**Long-term Sustainability**

To ensure lasting impact: (1) All code will be deposited on GitHub with open licenses (MIT/Apache 2.0) and archived on Zenodo with DOIs; (2) Integrated datasets will be deposited in established repositories (Zenodo, IDR) with long-term preservation; (3) Documentation will enable independent use without original team involvement; (4) We will engage the immunology community to establish ongoing curation and extension of resources.

[Budget and Resources]

Requires expertise in systems biology, mathematical modeling, and Python programming. Essential for translating biological hypotheses into quantitative models and integrating structural data with signaling dynamics.

*Postdoctoral Researcher 2 - Image Analysis/Machine Learning ($70,000 salary + $20,000 benefits):* This position will develop image analysis pipelines and machine learning models. Requires expertise in computer vision, deep learning, and super-resolution microscopy data. Essential for extracting quantitative features from imaging datasets and building predictive models.

*Graduate Student 1 ($35,000 stipend + $15,000 tuition/benefits):* Will focus on data integration and harmonization, working across all data modalities. Provides training opportunity in synthesis research methods.

*Graduate Student 2 ($35,000 stipend + $15,000 tuition/benefits):* Will focus on biological interpretation and validation, ensuring computational predictions align with immunological knowledge. Provides training in transdisciplinary research.

*Research Software Engineer (50% effort, $50,000 salary + $15,000 benefits):* Will ensure code quality, documentation, and long-term maintainability of software tools. Essential for producing robust, reusable tools meeting open science standards.

*PI effort (4 PIs at 5% effort each, cost-shared by institutions):* PIs will provide scientific direction, mentorship, and disciplinary expertise. Cost-sharing demonstrates institutional commitment.

**Computing Resources ($60,000/year)**

*Cloud computing - AWS/Google Cloud ($40,000/year):* Required for large-scale image processing, machine learning model training, and spatial simulations. Includes GPU instances for deep learning and high-memory instances for large dataset integration. Cloud computing enables scalable, reproducible analyses without local infrastructure limitations.

*High-performance computing allocation ($10,000/year):* Supplement to cloud computing for long-running simulations through XSEDE/ACCESS allocation. Provides access to specialized resources for parameter sweeps and sensitivity analyses.

*Data storage and transfer ($10,000/year):* Costs for storing intermediate results, transferring large imaging datasets, and maintaining public data repositories.

**Travel ($40,000/year)**

*Working group meetings ($20,000/year):* Quarterly in-person meetings rotating among PI institutions. Essential for transdisciplinary collaboration, enabling intensive working sessions that cannot be replicated virtually. Budget covers travel for all team members (8-10 people, 4 meetings/year).

**Workshops and Training ($25,000/year)**

*Annual synthesis workshop ($15,000/year):* One-week workshop at NCEMS teaching synthesis methods and tools developed in this project. Covers participant travel support (prioritizing trainees from underrepresented groups), materials, and logistics. Directly addresses NCEMS training mission.

*Webinar series ($5,000/year):* Monthly webinars on project progress and methods. Covers platform costs and speaker honoraria for external experts.

full_text:
[Abstract]
DNA repair pathway choice represents emergent decision-making where chromatin context, cell cycle stage, and damage characteristics collectively determine repair mechanism—a mesoscale phenomenon integrating multiple inputs into discrete outcomes. This synthesis project will decode emergent pathway choice by integrating damage proteomics, chromatin biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize DNA damage proteomics from PRIDE and published studies, ChIP-seq of repair factors from ENCODE, chromatin accessibility from ATAC-seq datasets, and cell cycle proteomics from published studies. The central question is: how do repair protein assemblies at damage sites (mesoscale foci of 100-1000 nm) create emergent pathway selection that individual protein-DNA interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent pathway choice arises from competitive recruitment kinetics, chromatin-mediated accessibility, and feedback loops that amplify initial pathway commitment. Our computational approach combines kinetic modeling of repair protein recruitment, machine learning to predict pathway choice from chromatin and damage features, and network analysis of repair factor interactions. We will develop algorithms integrating damage site proteomics with chromatin context to model pathway selection. Integration with mutation signature data from COSMIC will connect pathway choice to genomic outcomes. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal how emergent repair decisions adapt to different genomic contexts. This project requires expertise in DNA repair, chromatin biology, proteomics, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of damage, chromatin, and proteomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent pathway choice, identification of key features determining repair selection, and principles for modulating repair outcomes. Understanding emergent repair decisions has implications for cancer therapy and genome editing. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

[Background and Significance]
DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) represent one of the most dangerous forms of genomic damage, capable of triggering cell death, chromosomal rearrangements, and cancer when improperly repaired. Cells have evolved multiple repair pathways to address DSBs, including homologous recombination (HR), non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), alternative end joining (alt-EJ), and single-strand annealing (SSA). The selection among these pathways is not random but represents a sophisticated decision-making process that integrates multiple cellular inputs to produce discrete repair outcomes. This pathway choice phenomenon exemplifies emergent behavior at the mesoscale—the spatial and organizational level between individual biomolecules and organelles—where collective properties arise that cannot be predicted from individual molecular interactions alone.

At the molecular level, individual repair proteins have well-characterized biochemical activities: Ku70/80 binds DNA ends, BRCA1 promotes end resection, 53BP1 inhibits resection, and RAD51 catalyzes strand invasion. However, at DNA damage sites, these proteins assemble into mesoscale structures called repair foci, spanning 100-1000 nanometers and containing hundreds to thousands of protein molecules. Within these foci, emergent properties arise from the collective behavior of repair factors: competitive binding dynamics, phase separation phenomena, chromatin reorganization, and feedback amplification loops. The pathway choice that emerges from these foci cannot be explained by summing individual protein-DNA interactions; rather, it represents a higher-order property of the assembled repair machinery.

Substantial publicly available data now exists to address this emergent phenomenon through synthesis research. The PRIDE proteomics repository contains over 50 datasets examining DNA damage-induced protein recruitment, phosphorylation, and ubiquitination. ENCODE and 4D Nucleome projects have generated extensive ChIP-seq data for repair factors including 53BP1, BRCA1, γH2AX, and RAD51 across multiple cell types. ATAC-seq datasets from the ENCODE consortium and GEO repository provide chromatin accessibility maps that influence repair factor access. Cell cycle proteomics studies deposited in PRIDE and ProteomeXchange characterize the temporal dynamics of repair protein expression and modification. The COSMIC database contains mutation signatures that serve as genomic footprints of repair pathway activity. Despite this wealth of data, no systematic integration has been performed to model how mesoscale repair foci generate emergent pathway choice.

Critical gaps exist in our understanding that synthesis research can uniquely address. First, while individual datasets characterize specific aspects of repair (proteomics, chromatin state, or genomic outcomes), no integrated framework connects these scales. Second, the kinetic parameters governing competitive recruitment at damage sites remain poorly quantified across cellular contexts. Third, the chromatin features that bias pathway choice are incompletely catalogued and their predictive power untested. Fourth, how pathway choice varies across cell types and genomic locations—and whether universal principles exist—remains unknown.

Understanding emergent repair pathway choice has profound implications. In cancer therapy, many treatments induce DNA damage, and tumor cells often exhibit altered repair pathway usage. Predicting pathway choice could enable rational therapeutic combinations. In genome editing, CRISPR-induced breaks are repaired by cellular machinery, and controlling pathway choice is essential for precise editing outcomes. More fundamentally, DNA repair pathway choice represents a tractable model system for understanding how mesoscale biological assemblies generate emergent decision-making—a question central to NCEMS's scientific vision.

The synthesis approach proposed here is essential because the relevant data span multiple disciplines (proteomics, chromatin biology, genomics, cell biology) and exist in disparate repositories with different formats and standards. No single laboratory possesses the expertise to integrate damage proteomics, chromatin biology, and computational modeling required for this project. By bringing together specialists across these fields, we can achieve insights impossible for individual research groups, exemplifying the community-scale synthesis that NCEMS seeks to catalyze.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions that probe the emergent nature of DNA repair pathway choice at the mesoscale:

**Research Question 1: How do competitive recruitment kinetics at mesoscale repair foci generate emergent pathway commitment?**

At DNA damage sites, multiple repair pathways compete for access to broken DNA ends. The proteins 53BP1 and BRCA1 represent antagonistic factors promoting NHEJ and HR, respectively. However, the dynamics of their recruitment, accumulation, and displacement within mesoscale foci remain poorly understood. We hypothesize that pathway choice emerges from kinetic competition governed by three parameters: (1) initial recruitment rates determined by damage-induced chromatin modifications, (2) cooperative binding that amplifies initial pathway bias, and (3) feedback loops where early-arriving factors modify the chromatin environment to favor continued recruitment of pathway-specific proteins.

*Measurable Predictions:* By synthesizing time-resolved proteomics data from PRIDE with ChIP-seq binding profiles from ENCODE, we predict that the ratio of 53BP1 to BRCA1 recruitment within the first 30 minutes post-damage will predict ultimate pathway choice with >80% accuracy. We further predict that cooperative binding coefficients extracted from dose-response proteomics data will correlate with the sharpness of pathway commitment (switch-like versus graded responses).

*Validation Approach:* We will test these predictions by comparing our kinetic models against independent datasets not used in model training, and by examining whether predicted pathway choices match mutation signatures in COSMIC for the corresponding cell types and genomic contexts.

**Research Question 2: What chromatin features create emergent accessibility landscapes that bias pathway selection?**

Chromatin state profoundly influences repair pathway choice, with heterochromatin and euchromatin showing different repair pathway preferences. However, the specific chromatin features that determine pathway bias—and how they combine to create emergent accessibility landscapes—remain incompletely characterized. We hypothesize that pathway choice is determined by a chromatin accessibility code integrating histone modifications, nucleosome positioning, chromatin compaction, and three-dimensional genome organization. This code operates at the mesoscale, where the collective chromatin environment surrounding a break (spanning kilobases) matters more than local sequence features.

*Measurable Predictions:* By integrating ENCODE ChIP-seq for histone modifications, ATAC-seq for accessibility, and Hi-C data for 3D organization, we predict that a machine learning model incorporating features within 10 kb of damage sites will predict pathway choice with significantly higher accuracy than models using only local (<1 kb) features. We predict that specific chromatin feature combinations (e.g., H3K36me3 + high accessibility + A compartment) will show >90% HR usage, while alternative combinations (H3K9me3 + low accessibility + B compartment) will show >90% NHEJ usage.

*Validation Approach:* Predictions will be validated against mutation signature distributions across chromatin states in COSMIC, and against published repair pathway reporter assays mapped to genomic locations with known chromatin features.

**Research Question 3: How do cell type-specific contexts modulate emergent pathway choice rules?**

Different cell types show dramatically different repair pathway preferences—stem cells favor HR while differentiated cells often prefer NHEJ. We hypothesize that cell type-specific pathway choice emerges from the integration of three factors: (1) baseline expression levels of repair factors (setting the competitive landscape), (2) cell cycle distribution (determining HR competence), and (3) cell type-specific chromatin organization (creating distinct accessibility landscapes). Importantly, we hypothesize that universal pathway choice rules exist but are parameterized differently across cell types.

*Measurable Predictions:* By synthesizing cell type-specific proteomics from ProteomeXchange, cell cycle data from published studies, and chromatin profiles from ENCODE across multiple cell types, we predict that a unified pathway choice model with cell type-specific parameters will outperform cell type-specific models, indicating conserved underlying mechanisms. We predict that the ratio of 53BP1 to BRCA1 protein levels, combined with cell cycle phase distribution, will explain >60% of variance in pathway choice across cell types.

*Validation Approach:* We will perform leave-one-cell-type-out cross-validation, training models on data from multiple cell types and testing predictions on held-out cell types. Successful prediction of pathway choice in unseen cell types will validate the existence of universal rules.

**Mechanistic Insights Expected:**

Through addressing these questions, we expect to elucidate several mechanistic principles of mesoscale organization. First, we will quantify how competitive kinetics at repair foci create bistable pathway commitment—a hallmark of emergent decision-making systems. Second, we will identify the minimal set of chromatin features sufficient to predict pathway choice, revealing the information content of the chromatin accessibility code. Third, we will determine whether pathway choice represents a continuous spectrum or discrete states, informing whether repair foci function as analog sensors or digital switches. Fourth, we will map the parameter space of pathway choice, identifying conditions where small perturbations cause large outcome changes (sensitivity analysis) versus robust regions where pathway choice is buffered against variation. These insights will establish DNA repair pathway choice as a paradigm for understanding emergent decision-making at the mesoscale.

[Methods and Approach]
**Data Sources and Acquisition Strategy**

This synthesis project will integrate data from multiple publicly available repositories spanning proteomics, chromatin biology, genomics, and cell biology:

*Proteomics Data:* We will obtain DNA damage proteomics datasets from PRIDE (PRoteomics IDEntifications database) and ProteomeXchange, focusing on studies examining protein recruitment to damage sites, damage-induced post-translational modifications (phosphorylation, ubiquitination, SUMOylation), and temporal dynamics of repair factor accumulation. Specific datasets include: PXD004787 (quantitative proteomics of DNA damage response), PXD012345 (phosphoproteomics following ionizing radiation), PXD008934 (ubiquitin-modified proteome after DSB induction), and approximately 40 additional datasets identified through systematic repository searches. Cell cycle proteomics will be obtained from PXD006476 and related studies characterizing protein abundance across cell cycle phases.

*Chromatin Data:* ChIP-seq data for repair factors (53BP1, BRCA1, γH2AX, RAD51, Ku70, DNA-PKcs, MDC1) will be obtained from ENCODE (approximately 200 datasets across cell types), 4D Nucleome, and GEO. ATAC-seq data for chromatin accessibility will be sourced from ENCODE (>500 datasets) and published studies in GEO. Histone modification ChIP-seq (H3K4me3, H3K27me3, H3K36me3, H3K9me3, H3K27ac, H2AK119ub) will be obtained from ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics. Hi-C data for 3D genome organization will be sourced from 4D Nucleome and published studies.

*Genomic Outcome Data:* Mutation signatures will be obtained from COSMIC (Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer), which contains >40,000 whole-genome sequenced tumors with characterized mutation signatures. Signatures SBS3 (HR deficiency), ID6 and ID8 (NHEJ signatures), and others provide genomic footprints of repair pathway activity.

*Cell Type and Context Data:* Cell type-specific expression data will be obtained from the Human Protein Atlas, GTEx, and CCLE (Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia). Cell cycle phase markers and distributions will be extracted from published flow cytometry and single-cell studies deposited in GEO.

**Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy**

Integrating heterogeneous datasets requires systematic harmonization across multiple dimensions:

*Genomic Coordinate Harmonization:* All datasets will be mapped to GRCh38/hg38 coordinates using liftOver where necessary. ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq peaks will be processed through uniform pipelines (ENCODE standards) to ensure comparable peak calling and signal quantification.

*Protein Identifier Mapping:* Proteomics data use various identifier systems (UniProt, gene symbols, RefSeq). We will create a unified protein identifier mapping using UniProt ID mapping service, ensuring consistent protein identification across datasets.

*Cell Type Ontology:* Cell types will be mapped to Cell Ontology (CL) terms to enable systematic comparison across studies using different nomenclature.

*Batch Effect Correction:* For proteomics data, we will apply ComBat and related methods to correct batch effects while preserving biological variation. For ChIP-seq data, we will use quantile normalization and spike-in controls where available.

*Quality Control:* Each dataset will undergo quality assessment including: replicate correlation analysis, comparison to expected positive controls (e.g., γH2AX enrichment at known fragile sites), and outlier detection.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Kinetic Modeling of Repair Protein Recruitment:* We will develop ordinary differential equation (ODE) models describing competitive recruitment of repair factors to damage sites. Models will incorporate: (1) damage-induced chromatin modifications as initial signals, (2) protein-protein interactions enabling cooperative binding, (3) enzymatic activities that modify the chromatin environment, and (4) feedback loops where early factors influence subsequent recruitment. Parameters will be estimated from time-resolved proteomics data using Bayesian inference (PyMC3/Stan). Model selection will use information criteria (AIC/BIC) to identify minimal models capturing observed dynamics.

*Machine Learning for Pathway Choice Prediction:* We will train gradient boosting models (XGBoost, LightGBM) and neural networks to predict pathway choice from chromatin and damage features. Input features will include: local chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq signal), histone modifications (ChIP-seq signals for multiple marks), 3D genome compartment (A/B from Hi-C), replication timing, gene density, and sequence features (GC content, repetitive elements). Pathway choice labels will be derived from mutation signature enrichment in COSMIC. We will use nested cross-validation to prevent overfitting and SHAP values for feature importance interpretation.

*Network Analysis of Repair Factor Interactions:* Protein-protein interaction networks will be constructed from BioGRID and STRING databases, filtered for DNA repair-relevant interactions. We will apply network propagation algorithms to identify modules of co-recruited factors and community detection to identify pathway-specific subcomplexes. Dynamic network analysis will examine how interaction networks rewire across cell cycle phases.

*Integration Algorithm Development:* We will develop a novel Bayesian integration framework that combines: (1) prior probabilities from chromatin features, (2) likelihood functions from proteomics recruitment data, and (3) posterior pathway choice probabilities. This framework will explicitly model uncertainty from each data source and propagate it to final predictions.

**Validation Strategies**

*Cross-Dataset Validation:* Models trained on one set of cell types/conditions will be tested on held-out datasets. Successful generalization validates model robustness.

*Known Positive Controls:* We will verify that models correctly predict: (1) HR preference in S/G2 phases, (2) NHEJ preference in G1, (3) HR deficiency signatures in BRCA1/2-mutant samples from COSMIC, (4) increased NHEJ in heterochromatin.

*Mutation Signature Validation:* Predicted pathway choices will be compared against mutation signature distributions in COSMIC, providing independent validation from genomic outcomes.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1:*
- Months 1-4: Data acquisition, quality control, and harmonization
- Months 5-8: Kinetic model development and parameter estimation
- Months 9-12: Initial machine learning model training and validation

*Year 2:*
- Months 13-16: Integration framework development
- Months 17-20: Cross-cell type analysis and universal rule identification
- Months 21-24: Model refinement and comprehensive validation

*Year 3:*
- Months 25-28: Final model integration and testing
- Months 29-32: Tool development and documentation
- Months 33-36: Dissemination, publication, and community engagement

**Team Composition and Expertise Required**

*DNA Repair Biology:* Expert in repair pathway mechanisms, factor functions, and pathway choice regulation
*Chromatin Biology:* Specialist in chromatin modifications, accessibility, and 3D genome organization
*Proteomics/Mass Spectrometry:* Expert in proteomics data analysis, post-translational modifications
*Computational Biology/Machine Learning:* Specialist in predictive modeling, data integration, algorithm development
*Systems Biology/Mathematical Modeling:* Expert in kinetic modeling, dynamical systems, parameter estimation

This transdisciplinary team structure ensures that domain expertise guides data interpretation while computational specialists develop rigorous analytical frameworks.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
**Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce five major categories of deliverables that advance understanding of emergent DNA repair pathway choice:

*1. Integrated Multi-Omic Database of DNA Repair Pathway Choice (RepairChoiceDB):* We will create a comprehensive, harmonized database integrating damage proteomics, chromatin features, and pathway outcomes across cell types and conditions. This database will include: (a) curated proteomics data from >50 DNA damage studies with standardized protein identifiers and quantification, (b) processed ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data for repair factors and chromatin marks mapped to uniform coordinates, (c) cell type-specific pathway choice annotations derived from mutation signatures, and (d) metadata enabling filtering by cell type, damage type, and experimental conditions. RepairChoiceDB will be deposited in Zenodo with DOI assignment and maintained through a dedicated web interface.

*2. Kinetic Models of Competitive Repair Factor Recruitment:* We will deliver parameterized ODE models describing the dynamics of repair factor recruitment to damage sites. These models will include: (a) rate constants for initial recruitment of key factors (53BP1, BRCA1, Ku70/80, RAD51), (b) cooperativity coefficients quantifying positive feedback, (c) inhibition parameters describing antagonistic interactions, and (d) cell cycle-dependent parameter variations. Models will be implemented in Python (using scipy and PyMC3) and SBML format for compatibility with standard systems biology tools.

*3. Machine Learning Pathway Choice Predictor (PathwayPredict):* We will develop and release a trained machine learning model that predicts repair pathway choice from chromatin and damage features. The model will: (a) accept genomic coordinates and return predicted pathway probabilities (HR, NHEJ, alt-EJ), (b) provide confidence intervals on predictions, (c) output feature importance scores explaining predictions, and (d) include pre-computed predictions for the entire human genome at 1 kb resolution. PathwayPredict will be released as a Python package with command-line and API interfaces.

*4. Chromatin Feature Atlas for Pathway Choice:* We will produce a comprehensive atlas mapping chromatin features to pathway choice across the human genome. This atlas will include: (a) genome-wide maps of predicted pathway preference, (b) identification of genomic regions with strong pathway bias, (c) characterization of chromatin feature combinations associated with each pathway, and (d) cell type-specific pathway choice landscapes. The atlas will be available as genome browser tracks and downloadable files.

*5. Analysis Pipelines and Reproducible Workflows:* All computational methods will be released as documented, containerized pipelines including: (a) data harmonization workflows, (b) kinetic model fitting procedures, (c) machine learning training and evaluation scripts, and (d) visualization tools for exploring results.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project will establish DNA repair pathway choice as a paradigm for mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. Our work will demonstrate how collective behavior of repair proteins within mesoscale foci (100-1000 nm) generates pathway selection that cannot be predicted from individual protein properties. Specifically, we will:

*Quantify Emergent Decision-Making:* By parameterizing kinetic models, we will measure how competitive dynamics create bistable pathway commitment—a hallmark of emergent systems where collective behavior produces discrete outcomes from continuous inputs.

*Identify Information Integration Principles:* Our machine learning analysis will reveal how multiple chromatin features combine to determine pathway choice, establishing principles for how mesoscale assemblies integrate diverse inputs.

*Characterize Robustness and Sensitivity:* Parameter sensitivity analysis will identify conditions where pathway choice is robust versus sensitive to perturbation, informing how emergent systems maintain reliable function despite molecular noise.

*Establish Universal versus Context-Specific Rules:* Cross-cell type analysis will determine whether pathway choice follows universal principles with context-specific parameters, or whether fundamentally different mechanisms operate in different cellular contexts.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Beyond DNA repair, this project will impact multiple areas:

*Cancer Biology:* Understanding pathway choice has direct implications for cancer therapy. Many chemotherapeutics and radiation therapy induce DNA damage, and tumor cells often show altered repair pathway usage. Our predictive models could inform therapeutic strategies by identifying tumors likely to respond to specific treatments based on their pathway choice landscape.

*Genome Editing:* CRISPR-Cas9 and related technologies induce targeted DNA breaks that are repaired by cellular machinery. Controlling whether breaks are repaired by HR (enabling precise editing) or NHEJ (causing insertions/deletions) is a major challenge. Our chromatin-based pathway choice predictions could guide editing strategies and target site selection.

*Aging and Neurodegeneration:* DNA damage accumulation contributes to aging and neurodegenerative diseases. Understanding how pathway choice changes with age and in post-mitotic neurons could inform interventions to maintain genomic integrity.

*Methodology Transfer:* The computational frameworks we develop—integrating proteomics, chromatin data, and genomic outcomes to model emergent phenomena—will be applicable to other mesoscale processes including transcription factor hub formation, signaling complex assembly, and phase separation.

**Enabling Future Research**

Our deliverables will enable multiple future research directions:

*Hypothesis Generation:* PathwayPredict will identify genomic regions with unexpected pathway preferences, generating hypotheses for mechanistic investigation.

abstract_original: DNA repair pathway choice represents emergent decision-making where chromatin context, cell cycle stage, and damage characteristics collectively determine repair mechanism—a mesoscale phenomenon integrating multiple inputs into discrete outcomes. This synthesis project will decode emergent pathway choice by integrating damage proteomics, chromatin biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize DNA damage proteomics from PRIDE and published studies, ChIP-seq of repair factors from ENCODE, chromatin accessibility from ATAC-seq datasets, and cell cycle proteomics from published studies. The central question is: how do repair protein assemblies at damage sites (mesoscale foci of 100-1000 nm) create emergent pathway selection that individual protein-DNA interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent pathway choice arises from competitive recruitment kinetics, chromatin-mediated accessibility, and feedback loops that amplify initial pathway commitment. Our computational approach combines kinetic modeling of repair protein recruitment, machine learning to predict pathway choice from chromatin and damage features, and network analysis of repair factor interactions. We will develop algorithms integrating damage site proteomics with chromatin context to model pathway selection. Integration with mutation signature data from COSMIC will connect pathway choice to genomic outcomes. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal how emergent repair decisions adapt to different genomic contexts. This project requires expertise in DNA repair, chromatin biology, proteomics, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of damage, chromatin, and proteomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent pathway choice, identification of key features determining repair selection, and principles for modulating repair outcomes. Understanding emergent repair decisions has implications for cancer therapy and genome editing. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

Biomolecular condensates (10–500 nm substructures within micron-scale droplets) exhibit emergent material properties—viscosity, elasticity, percolation, and multiphase organization—that cannot be predicted from individual protein/RNA components. This project will test the hypothesis that condensate “material state” is a mesoscale emergent variable that systematically tunes transcriptional bursting and cell-to-cell gene expression noise across cell types and perturbations.

We will synthesize publicly available datasets that jointly report (i) condensate composition and disorder features (UniProt, Pfam, MobiDB, DisProt; LLPS/LLPT databases such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), (ii) condensate morphology and dynamics from imaging repositories (Image Data Resource/IDR, BioImage Archive, Cell Image Library; published FRAP time-series where available), (iii) subcellular localization and puncta statistics from the Human Protein Atlas (immunofluorescence), (iv) single-cell RNA-seq and multiome measurements capturing transcriptional variability (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, GEO; scATAC where available), and (v) perturbation signatures affecting phase behavior (LINCS L1000; CRISPR screens in DepMap where linked to condensate regulators).

Deep learning segmentation will standardize puncta calling across imaging sources; meta-analysis will harmonize batch effects and imaging modalities.

Expected insights include: (1) whether distinct condensate classes (nucleoli subcompartments, speckles, stress granules, P-bodies) occupy conserved regions of the material-state manifold across cell types; (2) which sequence grammars and interaction motifs predict transitions between liquid-like and gel-like substructures at 10–1000 nm; and (3) how these mesoscale states correlate with gene expression noise, enabling mechanistic hypotheses for robustness vs. plasticity.

This requires team science because it integrates polymer physics, image analysis, statistical genomics, and protein biophysics; no single lab typically spans high-throughput bioimage mining, scRNA noise modeling, and LLPS sequence/interaction theory. NCEMS support is essential for convening domain experts, creating open pipelines for condensate feature extraction, and producing a community resource: an open, reproducible atlas linking condensate mesoscale material states to emergent gene regulatory phenotypes.

[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates (10–500 nm substructures within micron-scale droplets) exhibit emergent material properties—viscosity, elasticity, percolation, and multiphase organization—that cannot be predicted from individual protein/RNA components.
