This requires team science because it integrates polymer physics, image analysis, statistical genomics, and protein biophysics; no single lab typically spans high-throughput bioimage mining, scRNA noise modeling, and LLPS sequence/interaction theory. NCEMS support is essential for convening domain experts, creating open pipelines for condensate feature extraction, and producing a community resource: an open, reproducible atlas linking condensate mesoscale material states to emergent gene regulatory phenotypes.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates organize cellular biochemistry through mesoscale assemblies that sit between molecular interactions and organelle-scale structures. At the mesoscale (roughly 10–1000 nm), condensates exhibit emergent behaviors—viscoelasticity, percolation, arrested coarsening, and multiphase organization—arising from collective interactions among proteins and RNAs. These properties are not predictable from individual components alone: the same set of proteins can form a fluid droplet in one context and a gel-like, dynamically arrested network in another, depending on concentration, multivalency, post-translational modifications, and the surrounding molecular milieu. The central challenge for molecular and cellular biosciences is to convert the descriptive catalog of condensate components into quantitative, predictive models of condensate material states and their downstream functional consequences.

A growing body of literature has established that many nuclear and cytoplasmic bodies—including nucleoli, nuclear speckles, Cajal bodies, stress granules, and P-bodies—share hallmarks of phase separation and dynamic exchange. Public databases now curate condensate-associated proteins and their biophysical features: UniProt provides canonical sequences and annotations; Pfam catalogs modular domains; MobiDB and DisProt provide intrinsic disorder annotations; and specialized LLPS resources such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, and DrLLPS compile experimentally supported condensate components and contexts. These resources collectively suggest that condensate proteins are enriched for intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), low-complexity sequences, RNA-binding domains, and multivalent interaction motifs. In parallel, imaging repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR), BioImage Archive, and the Cell Image Library host microscopy datasets that capture condensate morphology, puncta distributions, and in some cases time series. The Human Protein Atlas (HPA) provides immunofluorescence images across many cell lines, offering a systematic, albeit heterogeneous, view of subcellular localization and punctate patterns for thousands of proteins.

Despite this abundance, two gaps limit progress. First, most analyses treat condensates as categorical entities (e.g., “stress granule protein” vs. not) rather than as occupying a continuum of mesoscale material states. Yet mesoscale material state—capturing properties such as internal mobility, network connectivity, and substructure size distributions—is precisely where emergent behavior manifests. Second, functional consequences are often assessed qualitatively (e.g., “condensates regulate transcription”) without quantitative linkage to measurable cellular phenotypes. Gene expression noise—cell-to-cell variability driven by transcriptional bursting and regulatory fluctuations—is an especially relevant emergent phenotype because it integrates stochastic molecular events into population-level distributions. Single-cell transcriptomic resources such as the Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) provide extensive data on transcriptional variability across cell types and conditions, while multiome datasets (scRNA+scATAC) enable partial separation of transcriptional and chromatin contributions to variability.

The proposed synthesis addresses a long-standing puzzle: why do condensates sometimes buffer gene expression (reducing noise) while in other contexts they amplify variability (increasing noise and enabling plasticity)? Existing studies point to mechanisms including local concentration of transcription factors, sequestration, modulation of RNA processing, and changes in chromatin accessibility. However, these mechanisms are rarely unified under a mesoscale framework that treats condensate material state as a tunable variable. Polymer physics and soft-matter theory predict that transitions from liquid-like to gel-like states alter diffusion, reaction kinetics, and residence times—features expected to influence transcriptional bursting by changing the effective on/off rates of promoter-associated complexes. Yet no community-scale, cross-cell-type atlas currently links condensate material features to transcriptional noise in a standardized way.

Synthesis research is uniquely suited to close these gaps because the necessary evidence is distributed across disparate public resources: protein sequence and disorder annotations, curated LLPS membership lists, heterogeneous imaging datasets with puncta morphologies, and large-scale single-cell transcriptomes capturing variability. Integrating these data requires harmonization across modalities (sequence, images, expression), batch effects, and inconsistent metadata. It also requires methodological innovation: extracting mesoscale features from images at scale; learning low-dimensional representations (manifolds) that correspond to material states; and connecting those representations to cell-type-specific gene expression noise through probabilistic models.

Mesoscale emergent phenomena are important because they represent the level at which cells convert molecular interactions into robust, regulatable structures that impact phenotypes. Understanding condensate material states could explain context-dependent gene regulation, disease-associated aberrant phase transitions, and evolutionary design principles of IDR “sequence grammars.” Moreover, a cross-cell-type atlas would provide a reference for interpreting perturbation signatures from public resources such as LINCS L1000 (chemical/genetic perturbation transcriptional profiles) and DepMap CRISPR screens (gene essentiality and genetic dependencies), which include many regulators implicated in RNA granules and nuclear bodies. By leveraging the existing, rapidly expanding public data ecosystem, NCEMS can catalyze a community-scale synthesis that transforms fragmented observations into a coherent mesoscale theory linking condensate material state to emergent gene expression noise.

This project aligns directly with NCEMS’s mission: it targets emergent mesoscale properties; leverages AI and data science to synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and single-cell data; and requires a multidisciplinary working group spanning biophysics, polymer theory, bioimage analysis, and statistical genomics. The outcome will be a reusable, open, reproducible resource that enables the broader community to test mechanistic hypotheses without generating new experimental data, thereby accelerating discovery and training data-savvy scientists in best practices for synthesis research.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project centers on the idea that “condensate material state” is a latent mesoscale variable—emergent from collective molecular interactions—that can be inferred from heterogeneous public data and used to predict downstream gene regulatory phenotypes. We focus on transcriptional bursting and cell-to-cell gene expression noise as emergent cellular outcomes that integrate many molecular events. Our working group will address four tightly defined research questions (RQs) with testable hypotheses (Hs) and measurable predictions.

RQ1: Can condensate material states be represented as a low-dimensional manifold that is conserved across cell types and imaging modalities?
H1 (Material-state manifold): Imaging-derived mesoscale features (puncta size distributions, spatial clustering, texture metrics, coarsening proxies, and FRAP-derived recovery parameters where available) combined with composition/sequence features (IDR fraction, charge patterning, aromatic content, multivalency motifs, RNA-binding domains) will map onto a low-dimensional manifold (e.g., 2–6 latent dimensions) that captures continuous variation from liquid-like to gel-like/aged states and from single-phase to multiphase substructured states.
Predictions: (i) Canonical condensate classes (nucleolus, speckles, stress granules, P-bodies) will occupy partially separable regions of the manifold, but with overlaps reflecting context dependence. (ii) The same condensate class will shift position across cell types and perturbations in ways consistent with known regulators (e.g., chaperones, kinases, RNA abundance).
Validation using existing data: We will test manifold stability via cross-dataset validation (train on IDR/BioImage Archive subsets, evaluate on HPA images), and assess whether known FRAP-annotated proteins occupy expected manifold positions (liquid-like fast recovery vs. gel-like slow recovery).

RQ2: Which sequence grammars and interaction motifs predict mesoscale transitions between liquid-like and arrested/gel-like condensate substructures?
H2 (Grammar-to-state mapping): Specific “sequence grammar” features—e.g., sticker-spacer architectures, aromatic and arginine content, charge blockiness (kappa), prion-like low complexity, and modular RNA-binding domains—will predict manifold coordinates corresponding to material state, beyond what is explained by simple disorder fraction.
Predictions: (i) Proteins enriched in aromatic stickers and balanced charge patterning will associate with more liquid-like regions; (ii) proteins with high prion-like content, strong homotypic interaction propensity, or predicted beta-aggregation segments will associate with more arrested/gel-like regions; (iii) multiphase condensates (e.g., nucleolar subcompartments) will be associated with compositional heterogeneity and proteins with distinct grammar clusters.
Validation using existing data: Predictions will be tested by correlating sequence-derived features (from UniProt/Pfam/MobiDB/DisProt) with imaging-inferred manifold coordinates across proteins and cell types, controlling for expression level proxies (from scRNA-seq) and localization.

RQ3: Does condensate material state systematically tune transcriptional bursting parameters and gene expression noise across cell types?
H3 (State-to-noise coupling): Condensates in more liquid-like states will be associated with reduced extrinsic noise for target gene programs (buffering via rapid exchange and averaging), whereas more arrested/gel-like states will be associated with increased burst size variability and/or altered burst frequency (amplification via prolonged residence times and heterogeneous microenvironments). The direction and magnitude of effects will depend on condensate function (e.g., transcriptional hubs vs. RNA decay granules).
Predictions: (i) Cell types where nuclear speckle-associated factors map to more liquid-like manifold coordinates will show lower noise in splicing- and transcription-coupled gene sets; (ii) stress granule/P-body arrested states will correlate with increased noise in stress-response transcripts and altered mean–variance relationships; (iii) within a cell type, perturbations predicted to shift material state (from LINCS/DepMap) will correspond to predictable changes in inferred bursting parameters.
Validation using existing data: We will infer bursting parameters from scRNA-seq distributions using hierarchical Bayesian models (e.g., negative binomial/Poisson-beta frameworks) and quantify noise metrics (CV^2, Fano factor, residual variance after mean correction). We will link these to condensate state estimates at the level of (protein, cell type) and to gene programs using curated target sets (e.g., speckle-associated transcripts, stress granule-enriched mRNAs from published lists).

RQ4: Which regulators causally shift condensate material state and thereby modulate gene expression noise?
H4 (Regulatory control points): Perturbations affecting post-translational modification pathways (e.g., phosphorylation), RNA metabolism, chaperone systems, and chromatin regulators will emerge as causal drivers that move condensates along specific manifold directions and produce consistent changes in noise.
Predictions: (i) Perturbations in kinases/phosphatases implicated in LLPS will shift material state coordinates and yield coherent transcriptional variability signatures in LINCS L1000; (ii) CRISPR dependencies (DepMap) for condensate regulators will cluster by inferred material-state directionality; (iii) causal discovery will identify a small set of “state control nodes” whose perturbation effects generalize across cell contexts.
Validation using existing data: We will use causal inference and discovery on perturbation–expression datasets (LINCS L1000, GEO perturbation scRNA where available) and integrate with genetic dependency data (DepMap) to triangulate regulators. Validation will rely on replication across independent perturbation datasets and on known positive controls (e.g., stress granule regulators such as G3BP1/2; speckle factors such as SRRM2/SON) without performing any new experiments.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses are designed to yield mechanistic insights at the mesoscale: how collective material properties emerge from sequence and composition, how those properties vary across cellular contexts, and how they propagate upward to emergent gene expression variability. The emphasis is on measurable predictions that can be adjudicated using existing public data, enabling rigorous synthesis without new data generation.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
The project will create an integrated, cross-modal atlas that links (A) condensate composition and sequence-derived interaction grammars, (B) imaging-derived mesoscale morphology/dynamics, and (C) single-cell transcriptional variability and perturbation signatures. The core methodological idea is to infer a shared latent “material state manifold” from heterogeneous features and then test associations and putative causal relationships between manifold position and gene expression noise.

Specific data sources (publicly available)
1) Condensate membership and annotation
- PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS: curated condensate-associated proteins, condensate types, and experimental contexts.
- UniProt: protein sequences, isoforms, subcellular annotations.
- Pfam: domain architectures (RNA-binding, low complexity-associated domains).
- MobiDB and DisProt: intrinsic disorder annotations and curated disordered regions.
- Optional interaction resources for context: BioGRID and IntAct for protein–protein interactions; RNAcentral for RNA annotations.

2) Imaging repositories and localization
- Human Protein Atlas (HPA) Cell Atlas immunofluorescence images: puncta/localization across many cell lines.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated microscopy datasets with metadata.
- BioImage Archive: deposited microscopy datasets, including time series where available.
- Cell Image Library: additional microscopy datasets.
- Published FRAP time series and recovery curves available in supplementary materials or linked repositories (where explicitly public); we will only use datasets with clear reuse permissions.

3) Single-cell expression and multiome resources
- Human Cell Atlas (HCA) scRNA-seq: diverse tissues/cell types.
- Tabula Sapiens: human multi-tissue scRNA-seq.
- GEO and ArrayExpress: scRNA-seq datasets with perturbations or matched imaging contexts (when metadata permits).
- Public scRNA+scATAC multiome datasets (e.g., from GEO) to estimate chromatin accessibility variability when available.

4) Perturbation and dependency resources
- LINCS L1000: transcriptional signatures for chemical and genetic perturbations.
- DepMap (CRISPR screens): gene dependency profiles and co-dependency networks.

Data harmonization and entity resolution
- Protein identifiers: map across UniProt accessions, gene symbols, and database-specific IDs using UniProt mapping tables; maintain versioned mapping files.
- Condensate type ontology: build a controlled vocabulary aligning PhaSepDB/DrLLPS terms (e.g., “nuclear speckle” vs “speckles”) and map to Gene Ontology cellular component terms when possible.
- Cell-type harmonization: use Cell Ontology labels for scRNA-seq; map HPA cell lines to standardized identifiers (Cellosaurus).
- Metadata normalization: extract imaging modality, magnification, staining channel, and segmentation-relevant parameters from IDR/BioImage Archive metadata; record missingness explicitly.

Feature extraction
A) Sequence/composition features (per protein)
- Disorder metrics: fraction disordered, number/length of disordered segments (MobiDB/DisProt).
- Domain composition: counts of Pfam domains (RRM, KH, DEAD-box, etc.).
- Grammar features computed from UniProt sequences: amino-acid composition (aromatic, glycine, arginine), charge patterning (kappa), low complexity (SEG), prion-like propensity (PLAAC where permissible as an algorithm), predicted coiled-coils.
- Multivalency proxies: number of repeats, motif density (e.g., RG/RGG, SYGQ-rich segments).

B) Imaging-derived mesoscale features (per protein, cell line, dataset)
- Standardized puncta segmentation: train/finetune deep learning models (e.g., U-Net/Cellpose-style architectures) using weak supervision from existing annotations where available; otherwise apply self-supervised/transfer learning across datasets. Training uses only existing images.
- Puncta statistics: count per cell, size distribution, intensity distribution, spatial clustering (Ripley’s K), radial distribution relative to nucleus.
- Texture and morphology: Haralick features, fractal dimension proxies, shape descriptors.
- Dynamics proxies: where time series exist, compute coarsening proxies (change in size distribution over time), fusion/fission event rates via tracking.
- FRAP features: extract recovery half-time, mobile fraction, and fit parameters from published curves; where raw time series exist, re-fit using standardized models.

C) Single-cell noise and bursting inference (per gene program, cell type)
- Preprocessing: adopt standardized scRNA pipelines (e.g., Scanpy/Seurat equivalents) but implement in open workflows; apply ambient RNA correction when metadata supports it; rigorously document filtering.
- Noise metrics: mean–variance residuals, CV^2, Fano factor, and overdispersion parameters per gene, adjusted for mean expression and detection rate.
- Bursting models: hierarchical Bayesian models (Poisson-beta / negative binomial with latent transcription rate states) to infer burst frequency and burst size proxies; compare multiple models and use posterior predictive checks.
- Gene program mapping: define condensate-associated gene sets using curated lists (e.g., speckle-associated splicing factors’ targets; stress granule-enriched mRNAs from published compilations) and compute program-level noise.

Latent “material state manifold” modeling
- Multi-view representation learning: integrate sequence features and imaging features using methods such as variational autoencoders (multi-modal VAE), factor analysis with shared/private factors, or canonical correlation analysis variants. The output is a low-dimensional embedding with uncertainty.
- Interpretability: align latent axes with physical interpretations by regressing latent dimensions against FRAP parameters (where available) and against known liquid/gel annotations from LLPSDB contexts.
- Batch correction: use hierarchical modeling and domain-adversarial approaches to reduce modality-specific and dataset-specific artifacts while preserving biological variation.

Linking material state to gene expression noise
- Hierarchical association models: mixed-effects models linking manifold coordinates to noise metrics, with random effects for dataset/cell type and covariates (mean expression, cell cycle scores, technical factors).
- Mediation-style analyses: test whether perturbation-induced expression signatures (LINCS) associated with condensate regulators predict inferred state shifts and noise changes.
- Causal discovery: apply constraint-based and score-based methods (e.g., PC algorithm variants, NOTEARS-style continuous optimization) on perturbation graphs where interventions are known (LINCS perturbations), focusing on edges between regulator modules, material state coordinates, and noise outcomes. Emphasize robustness and sensitivity analyses rather than definitive causality claims.

Validation (no new experiments)
- Positive controls: known condensate markers (G3BP1/2 for stress granules; DCP1A for P-bodies; FBL for nucleolus; SON/SRRM2 for speckles) should map to expected manifold regions and show coherent imaging features.
- Cross-dataset replication: train embeddings on one repository (e.g., HPA+IDR) and test stability on another (BioImage Archive); replicate noise associations across HCA and Tabula Sapiens.
- Holdout strategies: cell-type holdouts, protein holdouts, and dataset holdouts; evaluate predictive performance for FRAP parameters (when available) and for noise outcomes.
- Sensitivity analyses: quantify dependence on segmentation choices, scRNA normalization, and cell-cycle correction.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6: Working group formation; ontology/ID mapping; assemble benchmark datasets; initial segmentation pipeline; initial sequence feature computation.
Months 7–12: Large-scale imaging feature extraction (HPA, IDR); compile FRAP-curated subset; first-generation manifold model; release v0.1 code and data schema.
Months 13–18: Integrate scRNA noise/bursting inference (HCA, Tabula Sapiens); link cell types and gene programs; preliminary state–noise models; internal replication.
Months 19–24: Perturbation integration (LINCS, DepMap); causal discovery analyses; refine manifold with multi-view learning; release atlas v1.0.
Months 25–30: Manuscripts and preprints; NCEMS-hosted training workshop; finalize open resource, documentation, and long-term hosting plan.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Polymer/soft-matter physicists: interpret manifold axes in terms of viscoelasticity, percolation, and coarsening; guide physically grounded feature design.
- Protein biophysicists/sequence analysts: implement sequence grammar metrics; connect motifs to interaction models.
- Bioimage analysts/computer vision experts: scalable segmentation, tracking, and harmonization across modalities.
- Statistical geneticists/single-cell methodologists: noise decomposition, bursting inference, covariate control, and replication.
- Causal inference/data science experts: perturbation graph modeling, robustness checks.
- Research software engineers: workflow automation, documentation, packaging, continuous integration.

All activities are strictly limited to synthesis of existing publicly available datasets and computational analyses; no new experimental data, imaging, sequencing, or sample generation is proposed.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) Cross-cell-type atlas of condensate material states
We will release an integrated atlas that assigns probabilistic “material state” coordinates (with uncertainty) to condensate-associated proteins across cell lines/cell types and condensate classes. The atlas will include: (i) standardized protein-level sequence/grammar features, (ii) imaging-derived puncta and morphology metrics with provenance to source images, (iii) FRAP-derived parameters where publicly available, and (iv) links to cell-type-specific gene expression noise summaries.

2) Open computational toolkit for condensate mesoscale feature extraction
A reusable software suite will implement standardized pipelines for puncta segmentation, feature extraction, and quality control across HPA, IDR, and BioImage Archive datasets. This toolkit will include model weights (where licensing permits), evaluation benchmarks, and guidance for applying the pipeline to new public imaging datasets.

3) Statistical models connecting mesoscale state to emergent transcriptional variability
We will provide validated hierarchical models that quantify how condensate material state coordinates associate with transcriptional noise and inferred bursting parameters across cell types. Outputs will include effect size estimates, credible intervals, and sensitivity analyses that explicitly account for technical confounders and dataset structure.

4) Candidate regulatory “state control nodes” from perturbation synthesis
By integrating LINCS L1000 perturbation signatures and DepMap co-dependency networks with the atlas, we will generate ranked lists of regulators predicted to shift condensate material state along specific manifold directions, together with predicted consequences for gene expression noise programs. These are not experimental claims but synthesis-derived hypotheses grounded in multiple independent public datasets.

5) Community benchmarks and ontologies
We will deliver a condensate-type controlled vocabulary mapping across LLPS databases and imaging resources, plus benchmark sets of proteins/images for evaluating segmentation and manifold inference methods. These benchmarks will lower barriers for future methodological development.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project advances a central NCEMS theme: understanding how new properties emerge at intermediate scales of organization. Condensate material state is inherently mesoscale—it reflects collective network connectivity, internal mobility, and substructure organization at tens to hundreds of nanometers. By learning a data-driven manifold of material states and anchoring it to physical proxies (FRAP, coarsening metrics), we will transform qualitative descriptions (“liquid-like”, “gel-like”) into quantitative, comparable coordinates across datasets.

The key conceptual advance is linking this mesoscale variable to an emergent cellular phenotype: gene expression noise. Noise is not a property of any single molecule; it emerges from stochastic processes distributed across promoters, chromatin, transcription machinery, RNA processing, and degradation. Condensates may modulate these processes by altering reaction-diffusion environments and residence times. Our synthesis will test whether a conserved relationship exists between condensate state and bursting parameters across cell types, providing a unifying framework for context-dependent condensate function.

Broader impacts
- Molecular and cellular biology: The atlas will help interpret why the same condensate-associated factor can have different regulatory outcomes in different contexts, supporting more accurate models of gene regulation.
- Disease relevance (via public data): Many neurodegenerative and cancer-related proteins are condensate-associated; our resource will enable hypothesis generation about how aberrant state shifts could influence transcriptional heterogeneity, a hallmark of tumor evolution and stress adaptation.
- Methodological innovation: Standardized, open pipelines for bioimage feature extraction and multi-modal manifold learning will be broadly applicable beyond condensates (e.g., cytoskeletal assemblies, endomembrane substructures).
- Workforce development: Trainees will gain cross-domain skills in reproducible bioimage analysis, single-cell statistics, and multi-modal integration—skills directly aligned with NCEMS’s training goals.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: At least two major manuscripts are anticipated: (i) the material-state manifold and imaging/sequence synthesis; (ii) the state–noise coupling and perturbation/causal synthesis.
- Preprints and open peer feedback: Preprints will be posted with open issue trackers for community input.
- Workshops: An NCEMS-hosted workshop will train participants to use the atlas and pipelines; tutorial notebooks will be published.
- Data deposition: The atlas (tables, embeddings, metadata, and links) will be deposited in long-term repositories (e.g., Zenodo and/or Figshare) with DOIs; code will be archived with releases.

Long-term sustainability
We will design the atlas as a versioned, modular resource: new imaging datasets, LLPS database updates, and scRNA compendia can be incorporated via reproducible workflows. Sustainability will be supported by (i) clear data schemas, (ii) containerized pipelines, (iii) continuous integration tests, and (iv) community governance practices (contribution guidelines, code of conduct, and an advisory group). By emphasizing interoperability with existing repositories (HPA, IDR, BioImage Archive, HCA), the resource will remain useful even as upstream datasets evolve.

Overall, the project will produce a durable community-scale synthesis that elevates condensate biology from component lists to predictive mesoscale theory and provides practical tools and training to accelerate future discovery—without generating any new experimental data.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy
Because this is a synthesis-only project, the budget prioritizes personnel time for data integration and method development, compute for large-scale image processing and model fitting, and NCEMS-centered collaboration/training activities. No funds are requested for experiments, reagents, sample collection, or instrument time.

Personnel (primary cost drivers)
1) Two postdoctoral researchers (2.0 FTE total)
- Postdoc A (bioimage/ML): develop and maintain segmentation, tracking, and feature extraction pipelines across HPA/IDR/BioImage Archive; implement QC and benchmarking.
- Postdoc B (statistical genomics/Bayesian modeling): implement scRNA noise and bursting inference, hierarchical association models, and replication analyses across HCA/Tabula Sapiens/GEO.
Justification: The project’s scale requires dedicated experts to ensure robust, validated pipelines across modalities.

2) One research software engineer / programmer analyst (1.0 FTE)
- Build workflow automation (Nextflow/Snakemake), containerization, CI testing, documentation, and release engineering for atlas versions.
Justification: Community-scale synthesis requires production-grade, reproducible software and data releases beyond typical single-lab capacity.

3) Graduate students (1–2 trainees, 0.5–1.0 FTE total)
- Projects include sequence grammar feature development, manifold learning experiments, and perturbation/causal discovery analyses.
Justification: Directly supports NCEMS training goals and expands capacity for exploratory analyses under mentorship.

4) Faculty/senior personnel (effort support as allowed)
- Modest support for coordination, supervision, and cross-disciplinary integration (biophysics, polymer theory, causal inference).
Justification: Ensures rigorous interpretation of mesoscale variables and alignment with emergence-focused aims.

Computing resources
- Cloud compute credits and/or HPC allocations for:
  - Large-scale image segmentation and feature extraction (GPU-intensive).
  - Multi-modal representation learning and Bayesian model fitting (CPU/GPU, memory-intensive).
- Storage for intermediate derived data (feature matrices, embeddings) and caching of permissible image subsets.
Justification: Processing thousands of microscopy images and fitting hierarchical models across large scRNA compendia exceeds typical lab compute; centralized resources enable standardized, reproducible runs.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings at NCEMS (e.g., 2–3 in-person meetings over 30 months) to integrate disciplines, conduct hackathons, and coordinate releases.
- Travel support for trainees and geographically distributed team members to ensure inclusive participation.
- Conference travel for dissemination (computational biology, cell biology, bioimage analysis), emphasizing presentations and workshops.
Justification: The project’s success depends on sustained cross-lab integration and community dissemination.

Workshops and training events
- Budget for an NCEMS-hosted training workshop (hybrid): venue costs, A/V, instructional materials, and participant support (especially trainees and underrepresented institutions).
Justification: Directly addresses NCEMS’s mandate to train the next-generation data-savvy workforce and to catalyze community uptake.

Open science infrastructure
- Costs for long-term archiving and dissemination: Zenodo (free) supplemented by optional paid storage or institutional repository fees if needed for large derived artifacts; domain/website hosting for documentation; DOI-enabled releases.
- Professional data curation support (if available through NCEMS) to ensure metadata quality and FAIR compliance.
Justification: Sustainability and reuse depend on well-curated, versioned releases with persistent identifiers.

Summary of resource necessity relative to synthesis goals
This budget is justified by the need to (i) harmonize and process heterogeneous public datasets at scale, (ii) develop and validate robust computational methods across modalities, (iii) maintain open, reproducible infrastructure suitable for community reuse, and (iv) convene a truly multidisciplinary team whose combined expertise and coordination requirements exceed what any single lab can provide.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates (10–500 nm substructures within micron-scale droplets) exhibit emergent material properties—viscosity, elasticity, percolation, and multiphase organization—that cannot be predicted from individual protein/RNA components. This project will test the hypothesis that condensate “material state” is a mesoscale emergent variable that systematically tunes transcriptional bursting and cell-to-cell gene expression noise across cell types and perturbations.

We will synthesize publicly available datasets that jointly report (i) condensate composition and disorder features (UniProt, Pfam, MobiDB, DisProt; LLPS/LLPT databases such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), (ii) condensate morphology and dynamics from imaging repositories (Image Data Resource/IDR, BioImage Archive, Cell Image Library; published FRAP time-series where available), (iii) subcellular localization and puncta statistics from the Human Protein Atlas (immunofluorescence), (iv) single-cell RNA-seq and multiome measurements capturing transcriptional variability (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, GEO; scATAC where available), and (v) perturbation signatures affecting phase behavior (LINCS L1000; CRISPR screens in DepMap where linked to condensate regulators).

Analytically, we will build a unified latent-variable model that maps composition/disorder/sequence grammars and imaging-derived mesoscale features (puncta size distributions, coarsening kinetics proxies, FRAP recovery parameters) onto a low-dimensional “material state manifold.” We will then connect that manifold to emergent transcriptional outcomes using hierarchical Bayesian models of bursting (inferring burst size/frequency from scRNA distributions), and causal discovery on perturbation datasets to identify regulators that shift condensates between states. Deep learning segmentation will standardize puncta calling across imaging sources; meta-analysis will harmonize batch effects and imaging modalities.

Expected insights include: (1) whether distinct condensate classes (nucleoli subcompartments, speckles, stress granules, P-bodies) occupy conserved regions of the material-state manifold across cell types; (2) which sequence grammars and interaction motifs predict transitions between liquid-like and gel-like substructures at 10–1000 nm; and (3) how these mesoscale states correlate with gene expression noise, enabling mechanistic hypotheses for robustness vs. plasticity.

This requires team science because it integrates polymer physics, image analysis, statistical genomics, and protein biophysics; no single lab typically spans high-throughput bioimage mining, scRNA noise modeling, and LLPS sequence/interaction theory. NCEMS support is essential for convening domain experts, creating open pipelines for condensate feature extraction, and producing a community resource: an open, reproducible atlas linking condensate mesoscale material states to emergent gene regulatory phenotypes.

title: Emergent Membrane Curvature Codes: Synthesizing Cryo-ET, Proteomics, and Lipidomics to Predict Organelle Contact Site Morphologies

abstract_text:
Membrane contact sites (MCS) between organelles are mesoscale structures (10–50 nm gaps; 50–500 nm lateral extents) whose emergent curvature, tether spacing, and protein crowding enable lipid exchange and signaling. The core emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of tethers, scaffolds, and lipids generates stable, functionally specific contact morphologies that are not inferable from single tether proteins.

We will synthesize existing public datasets spanning structure, composition, and function: (i) cryo-electron tomography subtomogram averages and annotations of ER–mitochondria, ER–PM, ER–endosome contacts (EMPIAR, EMDB; published tomograms with segmentation), (ii) proximity labeling and contact-site proteomes (BioID/APEX datasets in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) organelle-resolved lipidomics and membrane composition (LIPID MAPS, Metabolomics Workbench; published organelle fraction lipidomics), (iv) protein structures and predicted complexes for tethers and curvature generators (PDB, AlphaFold DB, EBI Complex Portal), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting contacts (DepMap CRISPR screens; SGD for yeast; MGI for mouse cell lines where applicable).

We will develop a multiscale inference framework that predicts mesoscale contact morphology from molecular components. First, we will extract quantitative geometry from cryo-ET (gap width distributions, curvature tensors, tether density estimates) using standardized segmentation and geometric morphometrics. Second, we will map proteome/lipidome composition to physical parameters (spontaneous curvature, bending rigidity proxies, crowding pressure) using coarse-grained biophysical models. Third, we will train graph neural networks that integrate tether interaction graphs (from structures/predicted interfaces) with lipid composition features to predict observed morphotypes. Finally, we will test whether specific “curvature codes” (combinations of lipid species and tether architectures) generalize across organisms and contact types.

Expected outcomes: (1) a taxonomy of MCS morphotypes grounded in quantitative geometry; (2) predictive rules linking lipid unsaturation, sterol content, and tether oligomerization to emergent curvature and spacing; (3) identification of minimal sets of components sufficient to produce particular morphologies; and (4) hypotheses for why some contacts are robust to perturbations while others switch states.

The work is inherently transdisciplinary: cryo-ET experts, lipidomics/proteomics analysts, structural biologists, and membrane physicists must align data standards and models. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation of heterogeneous datasets, shared open pipelines for geometry extraction and model fitting, and training for trainees in both quantitative imaging and biophysical machine learning. All code, derived features, and models will be released openly to seed community-scale predictive cell biology of mesoscale contact sites.

All code, derived features, and models will be released openly to seed community-scale predictive cell biology of mesoscale contact sites.

[Background and Significance]
Membrane contact sites (MCS) are regions where two organelles approach within ~10–50 nm without fusing, forming mesoscale platforms that coordinate lipid transfer, Ca2+ and metabolite exchange, organelle dynamics, and stress signaling. At this intermediate scale—larger than individual proteins but smaller than whole organelles—MCS exhibit emergent properties: stable gap widths, characteristic membrane curvatures, tether lattices, and protein crowding states that arise from collective organization rather than any single component. A central challenge in molecular and cellular biosciences is to connect molecular composition (tether identity, oligomerization, lipid species) to these mesoscale morphologies and, ultimately, to functional outcomes.

Existing work has established that MCS are assembled by diverse tethers and scaffolds (e.g., VAP-family adaptors, extended synaptotagmins, mitofusins, ERMES/EMC-associated factors, OSBP-related lipid transfer proteins) and that lipid composition differs between organelles and subdomains. Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) has revealed striking structural diversity: ER–mitochondria contacts can show relatively uniform gaps with discrete tether densities; ER–plasma membrane (ER–PM) contacts often present extended flat interfaces interspersed with curvature hotspots; and ER–endosome contacts can exhibit pronounced bending linked to tubulation and fission events. Yet, these observations are typically reported in individual studies using different segmentation conventions, different cell types, and different quantitative measures, making cross-study synthesis difficult.

Parallel advances have produced rich compositional datasets relevant to MCS. Proximity labeling (BioID, TurboID, APEX) has generated contact-enriched proteomes that identify candidate tethers, lipid transfer proteins, and regulatory factors, deposited in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange. Organelle-resolved lipidomics studies, accessible through LIPID MAPS and Metabolomics Workbench, quantify sterols, phosphoinositides, and acyl-chain unsaturation patterns that influence membrane mechanics and curvature propensity. Structural resources now include extensive experimentally determined structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and high-quality predicted structures and interfaces in AlphaFold DB, enabling inference of tether length, flexibility, oligomerization interfaces, and curvature-generating domains. Finally, functional and genetic perturbation resources—DepMap CRISPR screens for human cell lines, the Saccharomyces Genome Database (SGD) for yeast genetics, and the Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI) resource for mammalian phenotypes—encode how loss or modulation of specific proteins impacts organelle organization and viability.

Despite this abundance, key gaps remain that are uniquely addressable through community-scale synthesis rather than new experiments. First, there is no unified, quantitative taxonomy of MCS morphotypes grounded in geometry (curvature tensors, gap-width distributions, tether spacing statistics) across contact types, organisms, and physiological contexts. Second, existing compositional datasets are rarely integrated with structural and geometric measurements; consequently, we lack predictive rules—“curvature codes”—that map combinations of lipid species and tether architectures to emergent mesoscale morphology. Third, mechanistic models of membrane bending and crowding exist in biophysics, but they are seldom parameterized with real, heterogeneous cellular data at the scale of MCS. Fourth, the field lacks standardized, open pipelines that turn raw tomograms and proteome/lipidome tables into interoperable features suitable for cross-study inference and machine learning.

Mesoscale emergence at MCS matters because morphology is not a passive byproduct: curvature and spacing regulate which lipid transfer proteins can bridge the gap, how Ca2+ microdomains form, whether membranes are poised for fission or fusion, and how signaling complexes cluster. Small differences in gap width (e.g., 15 vs 30 nm) can change which tether architectures are feasible; changes in local curvature can bias recruitment of BAR-domain proteins or curvature-sensitive lipid transfer modules; and crowding can create entropic pressures that stabilize or destabilize contact interfaces. Understanding these emergent properties is therefore foundational to explaining how cells maintain organelle identity while enabling rapid exchange.

NCEMS is positioned to catalyze the needed synthesis because the project requires coordinated integration of imaging-derived geometry (EMPIAR/EMDB cryo-ET), compositional omics (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange; LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), structural data (PDB; AlphaFold DB; EBI Complex Portal), and perturbation phenotypes (DepMap; SGD; MGI). No single lab typically holds expertise across cryo-ET segmentation, lipidomics normalization, structural interface inference, and machine learning for multiscale prediction. Moreover, the heterogeneity of formats and annotations demands a working-group model to establish shared standards, curate interoperable datasets, and produce reusable open workflows. By synthesizing these resources, we can move from descriptive catalogs of MCS components to predictive, mechanistic understanding of how collective molecular organization yields stable, functionally specific mesoscale morphologies—an archetypal emergent phenomenon at the molecular-to-organelle interface.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how molecular composition and interaction architecture give rise to emergent mesoscale morphology at membrane contact sites (MCS). Our guiding premise is that contact morphology is an emergent “state” determined by the joint distribution of (i) tether geometry and oligomerization, (ii) lipid mechanical propensity (spontaneous curvature and bending rigidity proxies), and (iii) mesoscale crowding/packing constraints. We will test this premise with explicit, measurable questions using only existing publicly available datasets.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): What is the minimal set of quantitative geometric descriptors that robustly defines MCS morphotypes across cryo-ET studies?
Hypothesis 1 (H1): A low-dimensional morphospace defined by (a) gap-width distribution moments, (b) principal curvature statistics of each membrane leaflet (mean and Gaussian curvature), and (c) tether density/spacing metrics will cluster MCS into reproducible morphotypes that generalize across laboratories and organisms.
Measurable predictions: (1) Unsupervised clustering of these descriptors will yield stable clusters under cross-study resampling; (2) morphotypes will be conserved across related contact types (e.g., ER–PM vs ER–Golgi) but with systematic shifts in curvature and spacing.
Validation using existing data: We will compute descriptors from EMPIAR/EMDB tomograms with available segmentations and from published segmentations where permitted, then test cluster stability via bootstrapped consensus clustering and leave-one-study-out analyses.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): Do specific combinations of lipid composition features predict emergent curvature and gap width at MCS?
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Lipid “mechanical signatures”—including sterol fraction, phosphatidylethanolamine/phosphatidylcholine ratio, acyl-chain unsaturation index, and enrichment of cone-shaped lipids—predict higher absolute mean curvature and narrower effective gaps by modulating membrane bending propensity and packing stress.
Measurable predictions: (1) Contacts enriched in sterols and saturated chains will show reduced curvature variance and more planar interfaces; (2) contacts enriched in unsaturated and cone-shaped lipids will show increased curvature magnitude and heterogeneity; (3) lipid signatures will explain variance in geometry beyond what is explained by protein abundance alone.
Validation using existing data: We will map organelle-fraction lipidomics (Metabolomics Workbench; LIPID MAPS-linked studies) to contact types and cell contexts represented in cryo-ET where possible, using hierarchical models to account for study/cell-type effects. When direct matched datasets are unavailable, we will test predictions at the level of organelle pair identity (e.g., ER vs mitochondria) and organismal context, explicitly quantifying uncertainty.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): How does tether architecture (length, flexibility, oligomerization) constrain emergent gap width and curvature?
Hypothesis 3 (H3): The distribution of tether contour lengths and oligomerization interfaces inferred from PDB and AlphaFold DB, combined with interaction evidence from EBI Complex Portal, predicts the observed gap-width distribution and tether-spacing statistics in cryo-ET.
Measurable predictions: (1) Contact types dominated by extended, rigid tethers will exhibit narrower gap-width variance; (2) contact types dominated by flexible, multivalent tethers will exhibit broader gap distributions and higher curvature heterogeneity; (3) predicted oligomerization propensity will correlate with higher tether density and more uniform spacing.
Validation using existing data: We will construct tether feature vectors (domain composition, predicted coiled-coil length, interface area proxies, multivalency) and test associations with geometry via regularized regression and causal graphical models that include lipid features and study covariates.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Can an integrative model predict MCS morphotype from molecular composition and interaction graphs, and does it generalize across organisms and contact types?
Hypothesis 4 (H4): A graph neural network (GNN) that encodes (i) tether interaction graphs (nodes: proteins; edges: known/predicted interactions), (ii) protein structural features, and (iii) lipid mechanical signatures will predict morphotype labels and continuous geometry metrics with cross-contact generalization.
Measurable predictions: (1) Models trained on ER–mitochondria and ER–PM will predict ER–endosome morphotypes above baseline; (2) performance will degrade gracefully with missing modalities and improve with multimodal fusion; (3) interpretable attributions (e.g., integrated gradients) will recover known curvature drivers and propose new “codewords” (protein–lipid combinations).
Validation using existing data: We will use nested cross-validation stratified by study and organism, plus external validation on held-out datasets (e.g., tomograms from independent labs). Baselines will include linear models, random forests, and non-graph multimodal networks.

Research Question 5 (RQ5): Are there universal “curvature codes” and are there alternative, degenerate codes that yield similar mesoscale morphologies (robustness)?
Hypothesis 5 (H5): Multiple distinct molecular compositions can map to the same morphotype (degeneracy), but they share conserved latent physical parameters (effective spontaneous curvature, crowding pressure, tether rigidity) that constitute the true emergent code.
Measurable predictions: (1) Many-to-one mappings will be detectable as multimodal composition clusters converging on similar geometry; (2) latent-variable models will identify shared physical parameter regimes across these clusters; (3) perturbation phenotypes (DepMap/SGD/MGI) will show that morphotypes with higher degeneracy are more robust to single-gene loss.
Validation using existing data: We will quantify degeneracy via information-theoretic measures (mutual information between composition clusters and morphotypes) and test robustness associations using gene essentiality/phenotype scores and curated contact-related gene sets.

Collectively, these questions aim to produce mechanistic insight into how mesoscale morphology emerges from interacting molecular parts: not merely which proteins localize to MCS, but how ensembles of tethers and lipids encode curvature, spacing, and stability as predictable, generalizable properties.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will execute a 3-year, community-scale synthesis project that integrates five public data modalities—cryo-ET geometry, proximity proteomics, organelle lipidomics, structural/tether interaction information, and genetic perturbation phenotypes—into a unified multiscale inference framework for predicting membrane contact site (MCS) morphology. The core methodological goal is to harmonize heterogeneous datasets into interoperable “contact instances” (defined by organism, cell type, organelle pair, and condition) and to learn mappings from molecular composition/architecture to mesoscale geometry.

Specific public data sources
1) Cryo-ET and 3D structures of contacts:
- EMPIAR (Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive): raw tilt series/tomograms for published studies of ER–mitochondria, ER–PM, ER–endosome contacts.
- EMDB (Electron Microscopy Data Bank): subtomogram averages and associated maps.
- Where available, published segmentations/annotations deposited with EMPIAR/EMDB or in journal-associated repositories (e.g., Zenodo, Dryad) that are explicitly public.
2) Proteomics (contact-enriched proximity labeling and organelle proteomes):
- PRIDE / ProteomeXchange: BioID/APEX/TurboID datasets targeting MCS components (e.g., VAPs, ORPs, E-Syts, Mitofusins, ERMES-related factors), plus relevant organelle proteomes.
- UniProtKB for protein identifiers and isoform mapping.
3) Lipidomics:
- Metabolomics Workbench: organelle fraction lipidomics and comparative lipid profiles across conditions.
- LIPID MAPS (and linked datasets): lipid classifications, nomenclature, and reference properties.
4) Structural and interaction resources:
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): structures of tethers, lipid transfer proteins, curvature generators.
- AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (AlphaFold DB): predicted structures for missing components; pLDDT-based confidence filtering.
- EBI Complex Portal and IntAct: curated complexes and interactions.
- InterPro/Pfam for domain annotations.
5) Perturbation and phenotype resources:
- DepMap (Broad Institute): CRISPR gene effect scores and co-dependency networks in human cell lines.
- SGD (Saccharomyces Genome Database): genetic interaction and phenotype annotations for yeast contact-site genes.
- MGI (Mouse Genome Informatics): phenotype associations for orthologs where relevant.

Data harmonization and metadata model
We will build a contact-centric metadata schema that links each “contact instance” to: organelle pair, organism, cell type, condition, imaging dataset identifiers (EMPIAR/EMDB), omics dataset identifiers (PRIDE/Metabolomics Workbench), and gene/protein/lipid identifiers. Harmonization steps include:
- Identifier normalization: UniProt accessions for proteins; HGNC/SGD systematic names; orthology mapping via Ensembl Compara or OrthoDB (public) to enable cross-species comparisons.
- Lipid normalization: LIPID MAPS classification; conversion to common representations (sum composition where needed) and calculation of derived indices (unsaturation index, headgroup class fractions, sterol fraction).
- Batch/condition annotation: extraction of study-level covariates (instrument, labeling method, fractionation method) to be included as random effects.
All curated metadata and derived feature tables will be released as versioned artifacts.

Geometry extraction from cryo-ET (no new segmentation acquisition)
We will prioritize datasets with public segmentations; where raw tomograms are public but segmentations are not, we will restrict to studies that provide sufficient public annotations to compute geometry, or we will use only public, already-available segmentations. From segmentations, we will compute:
- Gap width: distance transform between opposing membranes, summarized as distributions (mean, variance, skewness) and spatial autocorrelation along the interface.
- Membrane curvature: estimation of principal curvatures from triangulated surfaces using discrete differential geometry; summary statistics and curvature maps.
- Contact extent: area/length measures of the interface and curvature heterogeneity metrics.
- Tether density proxies: counting filament-like densities where annotated; or using published subtomogram averages/particle picks when available.
We will standardize geometry computation in an open pipeline (Python, napari-compatible outputs) with unit tests and provenance.

Mapping composition to physical parameters
We will translate lipidomics and proteomics into physically interpretable features:
- Lipid-derived proxies: spontaneous curvature tendency scores per lipid class (from literature-informed priors), bending rigidity proxies based on sterol fraction and saturation, and packing parameter indices.
- Protein crowding proxies: surface density estimates derived from proximity proteomics enrichment scores combined with known organelle surface area scaling (from literature) and uncertainty propagation.
- Tether mechanical proxies: predicted coiled-coil length, flexibility (intrinsic disorder predictions from public tools where allowed, or domain-based heuristics), multivalency (number of binding domains), and oligomerization propensity (interface predictions from AlphaFold multimer where publicly available, otherwise from known complexes in EBI Complex Portal/PDB).
These features serve as bridges between molecular composition and mesoscale geometry.

Integrative modeling and AI/ML
We will implement two complementary modeling tracks.
Track A: Interpretable statistical models
- Hierarchical Bayesian models to relate geometry metrics (gap mean/variance, curvature stats) to lipid/protein/tether features with study and organism random effects.
- Sparse regression (elastic net) for feature selection and minimal component sets.
- Causal graphical modeling (structure learning with constraints) to distinguish direct vs mediated associations (e.g., lipids → curvature vs proteins → curvature).
Track B: Multimodal graph learning
- Construct protein interaction graphs per contact type using IntAct/Complex Portal edges; nodes annotated with structural features (PDB/AlphaFold) and proteomics abundance/enrichment.
- Fuse lipid features as global context vectors or as “membrane nodes” connected to proteins with known lipid-binding domains.
- Train graph neural networks (e.g., GraphSAGE/GAT) to predict morphotype labels and continuous geometry targets.
- Apply model interpretability (SHAP for tabular components; integrated gradients/attention analysis for GNNs) to extract candidate “curvature codewords.”

Synthesis and validation using existing data only
Validation will be entirely in silico and cross-dataset:
- Cross-study validation: leave-one-study-out tests on cryo-ET-derived geometry.
- Cross-contact validation: train on ER–mitochondria and ER–PM, test on ER–endosome.
- Cross-species validation: train on yeast datasets where available, test on mammalian (or vice versa) using orthology-mapped features.
- Positive controls: known curvature-associated proteins (e.g., BAR-domain proteins, reticulons) and known flat-interface tethers; check whether models recover expected directions.
- Negative controls: randomized lipid feature permutations within study; degree-preserving graph randomization to ensure GNN performance is not driven by trivial graph statistics.
- Phenotype triangulation: test whether predicted “essential codewords” correspond to higher DepMap dependency or enriched genetic interaction phenotypes in SGD.

Timeline and milestones (36 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize metadata schema; select initial dataset cohort (10–20 cryo-ET studies; 20–40 proteomics datasets; 10–20 lipidomics studies).
- Release v0 of curated dataset index and identifier mapping tables.
Months 6–12:
- Implement geometry extraction pipeline; compute initial morphometrics; draft morphotype clustering and stability analysis.
- Release open pipeline v1 (containers + notebooks) and first geometry feature tables.
Months 12–18:
- Build composition-to-physics feature layer; implement hierarchical models; quantify lipid/protein contributions.
- Submit methods preprint on standardized MCS morphometrics.
Months 18–24:
- Build interaction graphs and structural feature encoders; train first multimodal GNN models; perform cross-study and cross-contact validation.
- Release trained baseline models and benchmarking suite.
Months 24–30:
- Identify candidate curvature codes and degeneracy regimes; integrate perturbation/phenotype evidence.
- Draft synthesis manuscript on curvature codes and robustness.
Months 30–36:
- Finalize public resource: curated contact morphotype atlas, feature database, model zoo.
- Host NCEMS training workshop and publish final manuscripts.

Team composition and collaboration needs
This project requires expertise that exceeds any single lab:
- Cryo-ET and 3D morphometrics experts to interpret tomograms, curate segmentations, and ensure geometric validity.
- Proteomics analysts to standardize PRIDE/ProteomeXchange processing, handle labeling-method biases, and compute enrichment.
- Lipidomics experts to normalize lipid species, handle adduct/annotation differences, and derive mechanical indices.
- Structural biologists/computational structural experts to extract tether architecture features from PDB/AlphaFold DB and map complexes from EBI Complex Portal.
- Membrane physicists to parameterize coarse-grained physical proxies and interpret emergent curvature regimes.
- Machine learning/data integration scientists to build multimodal models, uncertainty quantification, and reproducible pipelines.
NCEMS support is essential to coordinate iterative, in-person and virtual synthesis meetings, shared curation standards, and cross-training of trainees working across modalities, while ensuring all outputs follow open and reproducible science practices.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) Quantitative MCS Morphotype Atlas (public resource):
We will produce a curated, versioned atlas of membrane contact site (MCS) morphotypes derived from cryo-ET datasets in EMPIAR/EMDB. The atlas will include standardized geometric descriptors (gap-width distributions, curvature statistics, interface extent metrics, and where available tether-density proxies), linked to dataset provenance and contact metadata (organelle pair, organism, cell type, condition). This will be released as a searchable table and interoperable files (CSV/Parquet + surface/mesh summaries) with clear licensing and citations.

2) Integrated Multimodal Feature Database:
We will release harmonized feature tables that connect (i) proximity proteomics from PRIDE/ProteomeXchange, (ii) organelle-resolved lipidomics from Metabolomics Workbench and LIPID MAPS-linked studies, (iii) structural/tether architecture features from PDB and AlphaFold DB, and (iv) interaction/complex evidence from EBI Complex Portal and IntAct, all mapped to the contact-centric metadata schema. This database will enable downstream community analyses beyond our initial modeling goals.

3) Open pipelines and benchmarking suite:
We will deliver robust, reusable software for (a) geometry extraction from public segmentations, (b) lipid/protein harmonization and derived physical proxy computation, and (c) model training/evaluation. A benchmarking suite will allow users to compare statistical models and graph neural networks (GNNs) on standardized prediction tasks (morphotype classification; curvature/gap regression) with cross-study splits.

4) Predictive models (“Curvature Code” model zoo):
We will release trained models that predict MCS morphotypes and continuous geometry metrics from molecular composition and interaction graphs. Models will include interpretable baselines (hierarchical regression) and multimodal GNNs, with documented performance, uncertainty estimates, and interpretability outputs (feature attributions and candidate codewords).

5) Mechanistic synthesis products (publications and hypotheses):
We anticipate at least two major synthesis manuscripts: (i) a methods/resource paper defining standardized MCS morphometrics and morphotype taxonomy; (ii) a mechanistic synthesis paper presenting curvature codes, degeneracy/robustness regimes, and cross-contact generalization. Importantly, hypotheses will be explicitly grounded in patterns supported by multiple public datasets (e.g., lipid signatures + tether architectures jointly predicting curvature regimes), enabling future experimentalists to test them—without our project generating new data.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project advances NCEMS’s mission by explaining an emergent mesoscale property—contact morphology—through synthesis across molecular composition, structural constraints, and physical principles. The central conceptual contribution is to formalize “curvature codes” as mappings from ensembles of lipids and tether architectures to stable mesoscale morphotypes. By quantifying degeneracy (multiple molecular solutions yielding similar morphology) and identifying latent physical parameters that unify these solutions, we will provide a general framework for emergence: robust mesoscale states can arise from diverse microscopic implementations.

The atlas and models will also clarify which geometric features are conserved across organisms and which are context-specific, addressing long-standing puzzles about why certain contact sites appear morphologically stereotyped while others are highly plastic. By integrating perturbation phenotypes (DepMap/SGD/MGI) as an orthogonal validation layer, we expect to identify which predicted codewords correspond to robust, essential contact architectures and which correspond to switch-like, regulatable states.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Predictive cell biology: The resulting models and datasets will enable researchers to infer likely MCS morphologies in contexts where only omics data exist, accelerating hypothesis generation.
- Data standards: Standardized morphometrics and contact-centric metadata will improve interoperability across imaging and omics communities.
- AI for biology: The multimodal integration approach (geometry + graphs + lipid/protein features) will provide a reusable blueprint for other mesoscale structures (e.g., endocytic pits, ER tubules, phase-separated condensates at membranes).
- Workforce development: Trainees will gain cross-disciplinary skills in cryo-ET computation, omics harmonization, and interpretable machine learning—aligned with NCEMS’s emphasis on training data-savvy scientists.

Dissemination and community engagement
We will disseminate results through:
- Preprints and peer-reviewed publications.
- An NCEMS-hosted working group website that links to datasets, code, and tutorials.
- Conference symposia and focused workshops (cryo-ET + omics integration; membrane biophysics + ML).
- Deposition of derived resources in stable repositories (Zenodo/OSF) with DOIs, alongside code in GitHub.

Long-term sustainability
Sustainability will be addressed by (i) versioned releases with semantic versioning, (ii) containerized workflows to minimize dependency rot, (iii) clear contribution guidelines enabling community pull requests, and (iv) alignment with existing community repositories (EMPIAR/EMDB, PRIDE, Metabolomics Workbench) by providing back-links and standardized derivative annotations. We will also provide lightweight “data packages” (e.g., Parquet + metadata JSON) so the atlas can be mirrored and reused without specialized infrastructure. By the end of the project, the community will have not only new biological insights but also durable, open synthesis infrastructure for mesoscale membrane contact biology.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget overview (2–3 year working group; synthesis-only)
The budget is designed to support community-scale data synthesis, integration, and training—activities that require coordination and technical capacity beyond a single lab. All items directly enable reuse and integration of existing public datasets (EMPIAR/EMDB, PRIDE/ProteomeXchange, Metabolomics Workbench/LIPID MAPS, PDB/AlphaFold DB, DepMap/SGD/MGI) and the creation of open, reproducible resources.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (computational):
  1) Cryo-ET morphometrics + geometry extraction lead (surface processing, curvature estimation, segmentation QC).
  2) Multimodal ML + graph learning lead (GNNs, benchmarking, interpretability, uncertainty quantification).
  Justification: Dedicated staff are required to build robust pipelines and models and to coordinate across modalities; this scope is not feasible as a side effort.
- 1 Graduate student (data integration/biophysics):
  Focus on mapping lipid/protein composition to physical proxies (spontaneous curvature indices, bending rigidity proxies) and hierarchical modeling.
  Justification: Provides cross-disciplinary training aligned with NCEMS workforce goals and supplies sustained effort on synthesis tasks.
- 1 Research software engineer / programmer analyst (0.5–1.0 FTE):
  Responsible for workflow engineering (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization (Docker/Apptainer), CI/testing, documentation, and release management.
  Justification: Ensures reproducibility, sustainability, and community usability of outputs.
- PI/co-PI effort (modest):
  Coordination, scientific oversight, and working group facilitation across participating labs.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations:
  Needed for processing large cryo-ET volumes (geometry computation on meshes), training ML models (GPU time), and running cross-validation at scale.
  Justification: Public datasets are large and heterogeneous; scalable compute is essential for timely synthesis and for reproducible reruns.
- Data storage and bandwidth:
  Funds for secure, redundant storage of downloaded public datasets and derived intermediate artifacts; use of institutional storage plus cloud object storage where appropriate.
  Justification: Enables shared access for distributed team members and supports reproducible builds.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2 in-person/year + regular virtual):
  Support travel for team members across institutions, prioritizing early-career researchers and participants from diverse geographic locations.
  Justification: In-person synthesis accelerates harmonization decisions (schemas, QC standards) and model interpretation across disciplines.
- Conference travel for dissemination:
  Present results at relevant venues (cell biology, cryo-EM, proteomics/lipidomics, computational biology).
  Justification: Maximizes community uptake and feedback.

Workshops and training events
- Two open workshops (materials + logistics):
  Costs include venue/virtual platform support, captioning/recording, and travel support for trainees.
  Justification: Directly addresses NCEMS training goals and broadens participation in synthesis methods.

Open science infrastructure
- Repository archiving and DOI minting:
  Zenodo archiving for code and derived datasets; OSF project hosting; potential costs for long-term hosting of documentation.
  Justification: Ensures persistent, citable outputs and compliance with open science requirements.

Budget justification relative to synthesis goals
This budget prioritizes personnel and infrastructure that enable (i) curation and harmonization of heterogeneous public datasets, (ii) rigorous cross-dataset validation and benchmarking, (iii) production of durable open pipelines and resources, and (iv) training and community engagement. No funds are allocated for wet-lab experiments, sample collection, or generation of new experimental data, consistent with NCEMS synthesis-only requirements.

abstract_original:
Membrane contact sites (MCS) between organelles are mesoscale structures (10–50 nm gaps; 50–500 nm lateral extents) whose emergent curvature, tether spacing, and protein crowding enable lipid exchange and signaling. The core emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of tethers, scaffolds, and lipids generates stable, functionally specific contact morphologies that are not inferable from single tether proteins.

We will synthesize existing public datasets spanning structure, composition, and function: (i) cryo-electron tomography subtomogram averages and annotations of ER–mitochondria, ER–PM, ER–endosome contacts (EMPIAR, EMDB; published tomograms with segmentation), (ii) proximity labeling and contact-site proteomes (BioID/APEX datasets in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) organelle-resolved lipidomics and membrane composition (LIPID MAPS, Metabolomics Workbench; published organelle fraction lipidomics), (iv) protein structures and predicted complexes for tethers and curvature generators (PDB, AlphaFold DB, EBI Complex Portal), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting contacts (DepMap CRISPR screens; SGD for yeast; MGI for mouse cell lines where applicable).

We will develop a multiscale inference framework that predicts mesoscale contact morphology from molecular components. First, we will extract quantitative geometry from cryo-ET (gap width distributions, curvature tensors, tether density estimates) using standardized segmentation and geometric morphometrics. Second, we will map proteome/lipidome composition to physical parameters (spontaneous curvature, bending rigidity proxies, crowding pressure) using coarse-grained biophysical models. Third, we will train graph neural networks that integrate tether interaction graphs (from structures/predicted interfaces) with lipid composition features to predict observed morphotypes. Finally, we will test whether specific “curvature codes” (combinations of lipid species and tether architectures) generalize across organisms and contact types.

Expected outcomes: (1) a taxonomy of MCS morphotypes grounded in quantitative geometry; (2) predictive rules linking lipid unsaturation, sterol content, and tether oligomerization to emergent curvature and spacing; (3) identification of minimal sets of components sufficient to produce particular morphologies; and (4) hypotheses for why some contacts are robust to perturbations while others switch states.

The work is inherently transdisciplinary: cryo-ET experts, lipidomics/proteomics analysts, structural biologists, and membrane physicists must align data standards and models. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation of heterogeneous datasets, shared open pipelines for geometry extraction and model fitting, and training for trainees in both quantitative imaging and biophysical machine learning. All code, derived features, and models will be released openly to seed community-scale predictive cell biology of mesoscale contact sites.

title: Mesoscale Cytoskeletal Percolation: A Synthesis of Actin/Microtubule Network Architecture and Emergent Intracellular Transport Efficiency

abstract_text:
Intracellular transport emerges from the collective mesoscale organization of actin and microtubule networks (10–1000 nm filament spacing, crosslinking, and branching) rather than from individual motors or filaments. The emergent phenomenon of interest is percolation-like connectivity and anisotropy in composite cytoskeletal networks that governs cargo routing, traffic jams, and robustness to perturbations.

We will synthesize public datasets across imaging, proteomics, and trafficking phenotypes: (i) super-resolution and expansion microscopy images of actin/microtubules and associated proteins (BioImage Archive, IDR; published STORM/SIM/ExM datasets), (ii) live-cell single-particle tracking of vesicles/organelles (Cell Tracking Challenge datasets; published tracking data in Zenodo/GEO supplements), (iii) proteomics of cytoskeletal fractions and crosslinkers (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) single-cell transcriptomics for cytoskeletal regulators across cell types (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens), and (v) perturbation screens affecting trafficking (DepMap CRISPR, genome-wide RNAi datasets; LINCS signatures for cytoskeletal drugs).

Computationally, we will build a standardized pipeline to reconstruct mesoscale network graphs from images: filament segmentation, orientation fields, junction detection, and estimation of mesh size and crosslink density. We will compute graph-theoretic and statistical physics descriptors (giant component size, betweenness centrality, anisotropy order parameters, percolation thresholds) and relate them to transport metrics derived from tracking (mean squared displacement regimes, directional persistence, stop-and-go statistics). A key methodological innovation is a multiscale “network-to-transport” emulator that predicts transport efficiency from network descriptors using physics-informed machine learning, enabling cross-dataset generalization.

The central hypothesis is that cells occupy constrained regions of a universal phase diagram for composite network organization, and that transitions between phases (e.g., isotropic mesh to aligned bundles; microtubule-dominant highways to actin-dominant cages) correspond to sharp changes in emergent transport behavior. We will test whether these phase boundaries are conserved across cell types and whether specific regulators (crosslinkers, severing enzymes, nucleators) move cells along predictable trajectories in this diagram.

Expected insights include mechanistic explanations for why certain cell types exhibit robust long-range transport despite noisy molecular composition, and how mesoscale architecture buffers or amplifies perturbations. The project requires team science: computer vision for filament reconstruction, statistical physics for percolation modeling, cell biology for interpretation, and data integration for harmonizing diverse imaging modalities. NCEMS support is needed to convene these communities, curate benchmark datasets, and deliver open, reproducible tools and an atlas linking cytoskeletal mesoscale states to emergent transport phenotypes.

[Abstract]

A key methodological innovation is a multiscale “network-to-transport” emulator that predicts transport efficiency from network descriptors using physics-informed machine learning, enabling cross-dataset generalization.
