The project requires team science: computer vision for filament reconstruction, statistical physics for percolation modeling, cell biology for interpretation, and data integration for harmonizing diverse imaging modalities. NCEMS support is needed to convene these communities, curate benchmark datasets, and deliver open, reproducible tools and an atlas linking cytoskeletal mesoscale states to emergent transport phenotypes.

[Background and Significance]
Intracellular transport is often described as the outcome of molecular-scale interactions—motor proteins stepping on filaments, adaptor complexes binding cargo, and regulatory enzymes tuning motor activity. Yet across cell types and physiological states, transport efficiency (e.g., long-range delivery, avoidance of congestion, and robustness to perturbations) varies in ways that cannot be explained by single-molecule parameters alone. A growing body of work points to the mesoscale organization of the cytoskeleton—filament spacing, crosslinking, branching, bundling, and alignment at ~10–1000 nm—as a key determinant of emergent transport behaviors. At this scale, actin and microtubules form composite networks whose connectivity and anisotropy constrain cargo trajectories and determine whether motion resembles free diffusion, intermittent trapping, guided runs, or jammed “stop-and-go” dynamics.

Conceptually, this mesoscale organization invites a statistical-physics framing. Percolation theory and network science formalize how global connectivity arises from local rules: below a threshold density of links/junctions, networks fragment into small components; above it, a “giant component” forms that supports long-range traversal. In cytoskeletal networks, analogous transitions may occur as crosslinker abundance, filament density, or alignment increases, yielding abrupt changes in the ability of cargos to find continuous routes. Similarly, anisotropy—alignment of filaments into preferred directions—can create “highways” that support persistent, directed transport but may also promote congestion if many cargos funnel into shared paths. These emergent properties are quintessential NCEMS targets: they arise from collective mesoscale organization rather than the properties of individual molecules.

Existing data already contain rich, underexploited information about mesoscale cytoskeletal architecture and transport phenotypes. Super-resolution microscopy (e.g., STORM, SIM) and expansion microscopy (ExM) have produced public image collections capturing actin and microtubule organization with sufficient resolution to quantify mesh size, junction density, and orientation fields. Repositories such as the BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI) and the Image Data Resource (IDR) host multi-condition, multi-cell-type imaging datasets, often with associated metadata and perturbations. In parallel, live-cell single-particle tracking datasets—curated in resources like the Cell Tracking Challenge and in community deposits on Zenodo and in supplementary materials linked to GEO records—provide trajectories of vesicles, endosomes, lysosomes, and other cargos across diverse conditions. These trajectories encode transport regimes (diffusive, subdiffusive, superdiffusive/ballistic), directional persistence, pauses, and heterogeneity.

Proteomics and transcriptomics further contextualize architecture. Cytoskeletal fraction proteomics and interactome studies deposited in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange quantify crosslinkers (e.g., α-actinin, filamin, spectraplakins), nucleators (e.g., Arp2/3 complex, formins), severing enzymes (e.g., cofilin, spastin), and microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) that plausibly tune connectivity and anisotropy. Single-cell atlases such as the Human Cell Atlas and Tabula Sapiens provide cell-type-resolved expression landscapes for these regulators, enabling synthesis across tissues and differentiation states. Finally, perturbation resources including DepMap CRISPR screens and LINCS (Library of Integrated Network-based Cellular Signatures) drug signatures provide systematic perturbation contexts that can be mapped onto predicted shifts in mesoscale network state and transport efficiency.

Despite these data riches, major gaps remain because the information is fragmented across modalities and because mesoscale descriptors are rarely standardized. First, imaging studies typically quantify local features (e.g., filament intensity, qualitative alignment) but do not reconstruct network graphs that permit percolation-style analyses. Second, tracking studies often report trajectory statistics without linking them to the underlying network architecture measured in the same or comparable cell types. Third, proteomics and scRNA-seq provide compositional snapshots but lack an explicit mapping from composition to mesoscale structural state. As a result, the field lacks a unifying “phase diagram” that connects molecular regulators to mesoscale architecture and, in turn, to emergent transport phenotypes.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to close these gaps. By integrating existing public imaging, tracking, and omics datasets, we can (i) derive comparable mesoscale network descriptors across many conditions and cell types, (ii) connect those descriptors to transport metrics across independent studies, and (iii) infer how regulatory programs shift cells through a constrained space of network organizations. This is beyond the capabilities of a single lab because it requires expertise in computer vision for filament reconstruction, statistical physics for percolation and phase transitions, machine learning for cross-dataset generalization, and cell biology for mechanistic interpretation. It also requires community-scale curation and harmonization of heterogeneous datasets—precisely the role of NCEMS.

Understanding emergent mesoscale control of transport has broad significance. Transport underlies secretion, endocytosis, signaling, organelle positioning, immune synapse formation, neuronal function, and cell polarity. Many diseases (neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathies, cancer metastasis) involve cytoskeletal dysregulation and trafficking defects, yet causal links are often unclear. A mesoscale phase-diagram framework would provide a mechanistic bridge from molecular perturbations to cellular phenotypes, enabling more predictive models of how cells maintain robust logistics in the face of noise and perturbation. The availability of vast public datasets spanning architecture, dynamics, and regulation makes this an ideal, timely target for NCEMS-supported synthesis to uncover fundamental principles of emergent intracellular transport.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group will pursue a set of precise, testable questions centered on the emergent mesoscale phenomenon of percolation-like connectivity and anisotropy in composite actin–microtubule networks, and how these properties govern intracellular transport efficiency. Each question is designed to be answerable using only existing publicly available datasets and to yield mechanistic, generalizable insights.

RQ1: Do composite cytoskeletal networks occupy a constrained, low-dimensional “phase space” of mesoscale organization across cell types and perturbations?
Hypothesis 1 (H1): Across diverse cell types and conditions, mesoscale descriptors of actin and microtubule organization (e.g., mesh size distributions, junction/crosslink density proxies, giant component fraction, orientation order parameters, and actin–microtubule co-alignment) lie on a small number of principal manifolds corresponding to distinct network phases (e.g., isotropic actin mesh, aligned actin bundles, radial microtubule arrays, mixed composite lattices).
Measurable predictions: (i) Dimensionality reduction (e.g., diffusion maps/UMAP on standardized descriptors) reveals clusters or continuous trajectories with reproducible boundaries across datasets; (ii) inferred phase regions are stable to imaging modality (STORM vs SIM vs ExM) after harmonization; (iii) phase membership correlates with cell functional categories (e.g., highly polarized vs non-polarized cells) more strongly than with single-gene expression alone.
Validation with existing data: Use multiple independent imaging datasets from BioImage Archive and IDR that label actin and microtubules, spanning different labs and modalities. Demonstrate reproducibility by training phase definitions on one subset and classifying held-out datasets.

RQ2: Are there percolation-like thresholds in mesoscale connectivity that produce sharp transitions in transport regimes?
Hypothesis 2 (H2): There exist critical ranges of network connectivity (quantified by graph giant component size, mean path length, and junction density) at which transport metrics transition nonlinearly from confined/subdiffusive to long-range superdiffusive/ballistic regimes.
Measurable predictions: (i) Piecewise or sigmoidal relationships between connectivity metrics and transport efficiency metrics (e.g., fraction of trajectories with sustained runs, effective diffusion coefficients at long lag times, directional persistence); (ii) increased variance near inferred thresholds (criticality-like fluctuations) across cells/fields of view; (iii) thresholds differ between actin-dominant and microtubule-dominant regimes but collapse under a composite connectivity index.
Validation with existing data: Pair imaging-derived descriptors with tracking-derived metrics through matched conditions when available (same cell line/perturbation across studies) and through meta-analytic alignment when not (e.g., mapping by cell line, drug, or genetic perturbation using LINCS/DepMap annotations). Use Cell Tracking Challenge datasets and published tracking deposits on Zenodo/GEO supplements as sources of trajectories.

RQ3: How does anisotropy (alignment) interact with connectivity to determine routing, congestion, and robustness?
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Transport efficiency is maximized in a “sweet spot” where connectivity is above percolation threshold but anisotropy is moderate—high enough to support directional routing yet low enough to prevent bottleneck-induced congestion.
Measurable predictions: (i) A non-monotonic dependence of congestion proxies (pause frequency, stop duration, trajectory crowding indices) on anisotropy at fixed connectivity; (ii) high anisotropy predicts increased betweenness centrality concentration in the reconstructed network graph, correlating with higher jam likelihood; (iii) robustness to perturbations (measured by transport metric degradation under cytoskeletal drugs or gene knockdowns) is greatest in intermediate anisotropy regimes.
Validation with existing data: Use perturbation datasets where cytoskeletal drugs (e.g., nocodazole, taxol, latrunculin, jasplakinolide) are present in public imaging/tracking studies and link to LINCS signatures to standardize perturbation identity and dose categories.

RQ4: Can molecular regulators be mapped onto predictable trajectories in mesoscale phase space?
Hypothesis 4 (H4): Variation in expression/abundance of specific regulator modules (crosslinkers, nucleators, severing enzymes, MAPs) predicts movement along interpretable axes of the phase diagram (e.g., “crosslinking/connectivity axis,” “alignment axis,” “actin–microtubule coupling axis”).
Measurable predictions: (i) Multivariate models using scRNA-seq (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens) and proteomics (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange) predict phase coordinates better than random gene sets; (ii) DepMap gene dependency patterns for trafficking-related phenotypes are enriched for regulators predicted to shift cells toward low-connectivity or high-congestion regimes; (iii) regulator modules are conserved across tissues, indicating general principles rather than idiosyncratic cell-line effects.
Validation with existing data: Build regulator scores from scRNA-seq and proteomics; test association with imaging-derived phase coordinates in matched cell types or cell lines; use cross-validation across datasets and labs.

RQ5 (Methodological): Can a physics-informed “network-to-transport” emulator generalize across datasets and predict transport from mesoscale descriptors?
Hypothesis 5 (H5): A model that combines percolation-inspired features (connectivity, path redundancy) with anisotropy and composite coupling will predict transport metrics across datasets more robustly than purely black-box models.
Measurable predictions: (i) Improved cross-dataset performance (train on one imaging/tracking source, test on another) relative to baseline regressors; (ii) calibrated uncertainty that increases near inferred phase boundaries; (iii) interpretable feature attributions consistent with percolation and congestion mechanisms.

Collectively, these questions move beyond cataloging cytoskeletal patterns to establishing causal-like, testable links between mesoscale emergent organization and transport behavior—using synthesis of existing public data as the sole evidentiary basis.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will conduct a community-scale synthesis that integrates five public data modalities—super-resolution/ExM imaging, live-cell tracking, proteomics, single-cell transcriptomics, and perturbation screens—into a unified mesoscale “network-to-transport” atlas. The core methodological contribution is a standardized, reproducible pipeline that converts heterogeneous cytoskeletal images into comparable network graphs and links graph-level descriptors to transport phenotypes via meta-analytic alignment and physics-informed machine learning. No new experimental data will be generated.

1) Data sources (public repositories)
Imaging (actin/microtubules and associated proteins):
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI): super-resolution and ExM datasets with raw and processed images.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated multi-condition imaging studies with metadata.
- Additional published STORM/SIM/ExM datasets deposited on Zenodo, Figshare, or journal-associated repositories (ingested via DOI-based harvesting).

Tracking (cargo trajectories):
- Cell Tracking Challenge (CTC): benchmark tracking datasets with ground truth for some tasks.
- Zenodo/Figshare deposits associated with trafficking and organelle motility papers.
- GEO supplementary files when trajectory tables are linked to imaging studies (used only when trajectories are already extracted and public).

Proteomics:
- PRIDE / ProteomeXchange: cytoskeletal fraction proteomics, interactomes, and whole-proteome studies with quantification of cytoskeletal regulators.

Single-cell transcriptomics:
- Human Cell Atlas (HCA): scRNA-seq across tissues/cell types.
- Tabula Sapiens: cross-tissue human scRNA-seq atlas.

Perturbation and functional screens:
- DepMap (Broad): CRISPR knockout dependency screens; used to connect regulator essentiality to trafficking/cytoskeletal gene modules.
- LINCS L1000 (clue.io data portal): drug and genetic perturbation signatures to harmonize perturbation identities and infer pathway-level effects.
- Public genome-wide RNAi/CRISPR screen datasets deposited in GEO/ArrayExpress where trafficking phenotypes are quantified (used for synthesis, not for new screening).

2) Data ingestion, curation, and harmonization
- Metadata normalization: build a unified schema (cell type/line, species, imaging modality, labeling, pixel size, z-stack info, perturbation identity/dose/time, cargo type for tracking). Use controlled vocabularies (Cellosaurus for cell lines; ChEBI/DrugBank identifiers for compounds; HGNC gene symbols).
- File standardization: convert images to OME-NGFF (OME-Zarr) when permitted; store derived masks/graphs as OME-compatible labels.
- Batch and modality correction: harmonize descriptor distributions across modalities using calibration on shared reference datasets and domain adaptation techniques (e.g., CORAL, adversarial domain adaptation) applied to descriptor space rather than raw images to avoid overfitting.

3) Image-to-network reconstruction pipeline (mesoscale focus)
Goal: extract mesoscale graph representations capturing connectivity and anisotropy in 10–1000 nm organization.
- Preprocessing: denoising (Noise2Void-style self-supervised denoisers applied only as a transformation on existing data), deconvolution if PSF metadata exists, intensity normalization.
- Filament segmentation: combine classical and deep learning approaches depending on dataset:
  - Classical: ridge filters (Frangi/Steger), steerable filters for filament enhancement.
  - Deep learning: U-Net/Cellpose-style models fine-tuned via transfer learning using publicly available annotated filament datasets where licensing permits; otherwise use weak supervision (synthetic filaments) for initialization.
- Skeletonization and junction detection: convert filament probability maps to skeleton graphs; detect branch points and crossings; estimate local filament density.
- Orientation fields and anisotropy: compute structure tensor-based orientation maps; derive nematic order parameter S, alignment coherence length, and radial/tangential alignment relative to cell centroid when cell masks exist.
- Mesh size and spacing: estimate actin mesh size distributions via distance transforms and pore-size statistics; for microtubules estimate inter-filament spacing and bundle thickness proxies.
- Composite coupling metrics: quantify actin–microtubule co-localization and co-alignment at mesoscale (e.g., mutual information of orientation fields, cross-correlation lengths).
- Graph construction: nodes = junctions/crossings/endpoints; edges = filament segments with weights (length, orientation, intensity proxy). Compute connected components and spatially embedded graph measures.

4) Transport phenotype extraction from trajectories
- Standardize trajectory formats (x,y,t; optionally z) and units.
- Compute transport metrics: mean squared displacement (MSD) with regime classification (subdiffusive, diffusive, superdiffusive), velocity distributions, run-lengths, directional persistence, pausing statistics, turning angles, confinement ratios, and intermittent “stop-and-go” models (hidden Markov models / switching diffusion models).
- Congestion proxies: local trajectory density, encounter rates, and pause clustering; when multiple cargos are tracked, compute spatiotemporal crowding indices.

5) Synthesis: linking network descriptors to transport across datasets
Because many datasets will not have paired imaging and tracking in the same cells, we will use a tiered linkage strategy:
- Tier A (paired): datasets where cytoskeleton imaging and cargo tracking are available under the same conditions/cell line/perturbation. Directly regress transport metrics on network descriptors.
- Tier B (matched condition): separate studies sharing cell line and perturbation (drug or gene). Link via standardized perturbation identifiers (LINCS) and cell line IDs (Cellosaurus).
- Tier C (meta-analytic): link by cell type/state using scRNA-seq-derived regulator module scores and proteomics profiles; infer likely phase coordinates and compare to transport distributions reported in tracking datasets.
Statistical approach: hierarchical Bayesian models to account for study-level effects (lab, modality, analysis pipeline) and to propagate uncertainty from segmentation and tracking.

6) Physics-informed “network-to-transport” emulator
- Model classes: (i) generalized additive models and gradient-boosted trees as interpretable baselines; (ii) graph neural networks (GNNs) on embedded cytoskeletal graphs; (iii) physics-informed neural networks/regularized models where loss functions include penalties enforcing monotonicity with connectivity above threshold and capturing nonlinearity near critical points.
- Domain generalization: train with leave-one-dataset-out evaluation; incorporate study embeddings to separate biological signal from batch effects.
- Interpretability: SHAP/feature attribution; partial dependence to identify thresholds and non-monotonic regions.

7) Validation using existing data (no experiments)
- Cross-dataset validation: hold out entire repositories/studies; test generalization.
- Positive controls: known perturbations with established effects (e.g., nocodazole disrupting microtubules; latrunculin affecting actin mesh) should shift descriptors and transport in expected directions.
- Internal consistency: replicate descriptor extraction on repeated acquisitions within IDR studies; quantify technical variance.
- Sensitivity analyses: vary segmentation thresholds/models; propagate uncertainty into phase boundary estimates.

8) Timeline and milestones (30 months; adaptable to 24–36)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble Working Group; finalize metadata schema; ingest initial benchmark datasets from BioImage Archive/IDR/CTC.
- Release v0.1 of image-to-descriptor pipeline and curated benchmark list.

Months 7–12:
- Complete robust filament segmentation and graph construction across modalities.
- Release v0.5: standardized mesoscale descriptor tables and QC reports.

Months 13–18:
- Integrate tracking metrics; implement hierarchical linkage (Tier A/B).
- First phase diagram draft; preprint on descriptor standardization.

Months 19–24:
- Train and evaluate network-to-transport emulator with leave-one-dataset-out tests.
- Release v1.0 open-source toolkit + example notebooks.

Months 25–30:
- Integrate omics and perturbation screens; map regulator modules to phase coordinates.
- Release public atlas (interactive site + downloadable data) and final synthesis manuscripts.

9) Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Computer vision/imaging informatics lab: segmentation, OME-NGFF conversion, QC.
- Statistical physics/network science lab: percolation modeling, phase boundary inference.
- ML/data integration lab: emulator development, domain adaptation, hierarchical modeling.
- Cell biology/cytoskeleton lab: biological interpretation, regulator module definition, curation of known perturbation expectations.
- Trainee cohort (grad students/postdocs) embedded across labs; an RSE (research software engineer) to ensure robust tooling.
NCEMS support is essential to coordinate cross-lab standards, host working sessions for dataset curation and model comparison, and produce community-facing deliverables that exceed what any single lab could sustain.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables (concrete products)
1) A curated, citation-ready benchmark collection of public cytoskeletal imaging and transport datasets.
We will publish a living registry (with DOIs/links, licenses, and standardized metadata) pointing to BioImage Archive, IDR, Cell Tracking Challenge, Zenodo/Figshare, PRIDE/ProteomeXchange, HCA, Tabula Sapiens, DepMap, and LINCS records used in the synthesis. The registry will include inclusion criteria, QC summaries, and recommended train/test splits for algorithm development.

2) Open, standardized mesoscale cytoskeletal descriptors and graph representations.
For each imaging dataset, we will release derived products (where licensing permits): filament probability maps, skeletons, spatial graph files, and descriptor tables capturing connectivity (giant component fraction, component size distributions, redundancy), anisotropy (nematic order, coherence length), mesh size distributions, and actin–microtubule coupling metrics. These descriptors will be modality-harmonized and accompanied by uncertainty estimates.

3) A “phase diagram” atlas of composite actin–microtubule network organization.
A central outcome is an empirically derived, cross-cell-type map of mesoscale network states. The atlas will identify conserved regions (phases) and transitional boundaries, quantify how frequently different cell types occupy each region, and provide interpretable axes (e.g., connectivity, anisotropy, composite coupling). Where data permit, we will annotate trajectories through phase space under perturbations (drug treatments, genetic perturbations inferred from DepMap/LINCS-linked contexts).

4) A network-to-transport emulator with cross-dataset generalization.
We will deliver a validated predictive model that maps mesoscale descriptors to transport outcomes (MSD regime probabilities, directional persistence, pausing/jam indices). The emulator will include uncertainty quantification and be benchmarked against baseline models. Importantly, it will be designed for reuse: users can input their own (public) cytoskeletal images or descriptor tables and obtain predicted transport phenotypes, enabling hypothesis generation without new experiments.

5) Mechanistic synthesis linking regulators to mesoscale states and transport phenotypes.
By integrating PRIDE/ProteomeXchange proteomics and HCA/Tabula Sapiens scRNA-seq, we will identify regulator modules (crosslinkers, nucleators, severing enzymes, MAPs, actin–microtubule crosslinkers such as spectraplakins) that statistically associate with specific phase regions and with predicted transport efficiency. DepMap dependencies and LINCS perturbation signatures will provide orthogonal evidence for which modules are functionally important for maintaining high-connectivity/low-congestion regimes.

Scientific impact: advancing understanding of emergent mesoscale phenomena
This project will provide a principled, quantitative bridge from molecular composition to mesoscale architecture to emergent intracellular logistics. The percolation/anisotropy framing offers a mechanistic explanation for nonlinear phenotype shifts: small changes in crosslinking or alignment can induce abrupt transitions in long-range traversability and congestion, consistent with phase-transition behavior. Demonstrating conserved phase boundaries across cell types would elevate cytoskeletal organization from a descriptive catalog to a predictive theory of mesoscale emergence.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Generalizable mesoscale metrics: The descriptor standards and graph representations can be applied to other filamentous systems (intermediate filaments, extracellular matrices) and to other emergent behaviors (mechanotransduction, organelle positioning).
- Reproducibility and benchmarking: By delivering benchmark splits and gold-standard workflows, we reduce duplication and enable fair comparison of filament reconstruction and tracking analyses.
- Enabling future research: The atlas will highlight underexplored network regimes and suggest which existing perturbations (from LINCS) are likely to move cells across critical boundaries—supporting future experimental work by the community (outside this project).
- Workforce development: Trainees will gain cross-cutting skills in bioimage informatics, network science, and open, reproducible data synthesis.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: (i) Methods paper on image-to-graph mesoscale reconstruction and harmonization; (ii) synthesis paper presenting the phase diagram and network-to-transport mapping; (iii) resource paper describing the benchmark registry and atlas.
- Community events: NCEMS-hosted working group meetings, hackathons focused on filament graphs and transport metrics, and tutorials at relevant conferences (e.g., ASCB, ISBI) emphasizing reuse of public data.
- Databases/tools: Release an interactive web portal (static site + API) to browse phase regions by cell type/perturbation and download descriptors.

Long-term sustainability
We will design outputs to be maintainable beyond the award: (i) deposit derived artifacts in stable repositories (Zenodo with versioned DOIs; BioImage Archive/IDR for image-derived labels when allowed); (ii) modular, well-tested codebase with community governance; (iii) clear contribution guidelines and issue templates to encourage external extensions. By aligning with OME standards (OME-Zarr) and common bioinformatics practices, the atlas and tools will remain interoperable as new public datasets appear.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy
This project is a synthesis-only, community-scale integration effort. The budget prioritizes personnel time for curation, harmonization, and robust software/model development; computing resources for large-scale image processing and model training; and NCEMS-enabled collaboration and training events. No funds are allocated to experimental data generation.

Personnel (largest cost; essential for synthesis)
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (2–3 years):
  1) Bioimage informatics postdoc to lead filament segmentation, OME-NGFF conversions, QC, and graph extraction across BioImage Archive/IDR datasets.
  2) Computational modeling postdoc to lead percolation/phase diagram inference, hierarchical meta-analysis, and integration with transport metrics.
- 1 Research Software Engineer (RSE) / programmer (full-time): responsible for pipeline engineering (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, testing/CI, documentation, and release management. This role is critical for producing reusable community tools and ensuring reproducibility.
- 1 Graduate student (part-time across years): focuses on trajectory analytics, congestion metrics, and benchmarking with Cell Tracking Challenge and Zenodo trajectory datasets; participates in cross-lab integration.
- Faculty/PI effort (modest, distributed across participating labs): coordination, scientific oversight, and Working Group leadership; ensures multidisciplinary integration and trainee mentoring.
Justification: Community-scale synthesis requires sustained, dedicated effort for data wrangling and robust tooling that cannot be accomplished through PI time alone.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations for:
  - Large-scale image preprocessing and segmentation across multi-terabyte public datasets.
  - Graph feature computation and hierarchical Bayesian modeling.
  - Training and evaluation of the network-to-transport emulator (including leave-one-dataset-out experiments).
- Storage and data management:
  - Versioned storage for derived artifacts (graphs, descriptor tables, QC outputs) and intermediate files.
Justification: Processing high-resolution microscopy at scale and running cross-dataset model comparisons exceed typical single-lab compute budgets.

Travel and collaboration
- Working Group meetings hosted/organized through NCEMS (in-person when feasible, otherwise hybrid):
  - 2–3 meetings/year to align standards, conduct hands-on integration sprints, and coordinate cross-validation benchmarks.
- Travel support for trainees and early-career participants to attend meetings and present results at conferences (e.g., ASCB, ISBI, or relevant network science venues).
Justification: The project’s success depends on tight coordination among imaging, physics, ML, and cell biology experts, and on training a distributed cohort in shared practices.

Workshops and training events
- Annual open workshop/hackathon (NCEMS-facilitated):
  - Day 1: tutorials on OME-Zarr, filament graphs, and trajectory metrics.
  - Day 2: community challenge on phase diagram inference or emulator generalization.
- Materials and support: captioning/recording for accessibility; small participant support for trainees from under-resourced institutions.
Justification: Aligns with NCEMS goals to recruit diverse talent and train a data-savvy workforce using public data.

Open science infrastructure
- Costs for persistent archiving and dissemination:
  - Zenodo community deposits (free but includes personnel time for curation), potential fees for web hosting of the atlas portal, DOI-backed releases, and optional use of services for dataset indexing.
- Accessibility and documentation:
  - Professional technical editing for documentation and tutorials (optional, if allowed) to maximize usability.
Justification: High-quality, maintained open resources are central deliverables of a synthesis center project.

Overall resource justification relative to NCEMS requirements
The budget directly supports (i) integration of heterogeneous public datasets, (ii) development of innovative analytical strategies (image-to-graph + percolation + physics-informed ML), (iii) cross-disciplinary collaboration beyond a single lab, and (iv) open, reproducible products and training activities that amplify community impact.

abstract_original:
Intracellular transport emerges from the collective mesoscale organization of actin and microtubule networks (10–1000 nm filament spacing, crosslinking, and branching) rather than from individual motors or filaments. The emergent phenomenon of interest is percolation-like connectivity and anisotropy in composite cytoskeletal networks that governs cargo routing, traffic jams, and robustness to perturbations.

We will synthesize public datasets across imaging, proteomics, and trafficking phenotypes: (i) super-resolution and expansion microscopy images of actin/microtubules and associated proteins (BioImage Archive, IDR; published STORM/SIM/ExM datasets), (ii) live-cell single-particle tracking of vesicles/organelles (Cell Tracking Challenge datasets; published tracking data in Zenodo/GEO supplements), (iii) proteomics of cytoskeletal fractions and crosslinkers (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) single-cell transcriptomics for cytoskeletal regulators across cell types (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens), and (v) perturbation screens affecting trafficking (DepMap CRISPR, genome-wide RNAi datasets; LINCS signatures for cytoskeletal drugs).

Computationally, we will build a standardized pipeline to reconstruct mesoscale network graphs from images: filament segmentation, orientation fields, junction detection, and estimation of mesh size and crosslink density. We will compute graph-theoretic and statistical physics descriptors (giant component size, betweenness centrality, anisotropy order parameters, percolation thresholds) and relate them to transport metrics derived from tracking (mean squared displacement regimes, directional persistence, stop-and-go statistics). A key methodological innovation is a multiscale “network-to-transport” emulator that predicts transport efficiency from network descriptors using physics-informed machine learning, enabling cross-dataset generalization.

The central hypothesis is that cells occupy constrained regions of a universal phase diagram for composite network organization, and that transitions between phases (e.g., isotropic mesh to aligned bundles; microtubule-dominant highways to actin-dominant cages) correspond to sharp changes in emergent transport behavior. We will test whether these phase boundaries are conserved across cell types and whether specific regulators (crosslinkers, severing enzymes, nucleators) move cells along predictable trajectories in this diagram.

Expected insights include mechanistic explanations for why certain cell types exhibit robust long-range transport despite noisy molecular composition, and how mesoscale architecture buffers or amplifies perturbations. The project requires team science: computer vision for filament reconstruction, statistical physics for percolation modeling, cell biology for interpretation, and data integration for harmonizing diverse imaging modalities. NCEMS support is needed to convene these communities, curate benchmark datasets, and deliver open, reproducible tools and an atlas linking cytoskeletal mesoscale states to emergent transport phenotypes.

title: Emergent Chromatin Nanodomain Topology: Integrating Hi-C, Super-Resolution Imaging, and Epigenomics to Explain Cell-Type-Specific Gene Regulation

abstract_text:
Chromatin forms mesoscale nanodomains (50–300 nm) whose collective folding and compartmentalization produce emergent regulatory behaviors—enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting—that cannot be inferred from individual nucleosome modifications. This project will synthesize 3D genome conformation and imaging data to test whether a small set of mesoscale topological motifs explains cell-type-specific gene regulation across mammals.

We will integrate publicly available datasets: (i) population and single-cell Hi-C / Micro-C maps (4D Nucleome, GEO, ENCODE), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed DNA FISH imaging of chromatin domains (4DN data portal, BioImage Archive; Oligopaint datasets), (iii) epigenomic marks and accessibility (ENCODE ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq; Roadmap Epigenomics), (iv) transcriptional outputs (single-cell RNA-seq from Human Cell Atlas; nascent transcription where available), and (v) structural constraints from nucleosome and chromatin fiber models (PDB where relevant; polymer simulation benchmarks).

Methodologically, we will create a joint inference framework that maps between contact matrices and physical 3D domain geometries. We will (1) infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction strengths from Hi-C/Micro-C using multi-resolution community detection; (2) calibrate polymer models with imaging-derived distance distributions to resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions; (3) learn a “motif dictionary” of recurrent mesoscale folding patterns (e.g., loop clusters, rosettes, compartment microdomains) using unsupervised representation learning that ingests both contact and imaging features; and (4) link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes—bursting parameters, enhancer responsiveness, and lineage stability—using hierarchical models across cell types.

The hypothesis is that despite molecular diversity, chromatin nanodomain topology falls into a limited set of mesoscale motifs whose combinations predict regulatory capacity and noise. We will test whether developmental transitions correspond to motif switching, and whether disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially disrupt specific motifs rather than individual loops.

Expected outputs include: a cross-cell-type atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs, quantitative relationships between motif composition and transcriptional variability, and open tools for jointly analyzing Hi-C and imaging. This synthesis requires collaboration among genome informaticians, polymer physicists, microscopy experts, and statistical modelers; no single lab typically has access to and expertise across these modalities. NCEMS working group support is essential for harmonizing standards, building reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to bridge 3D genomics and quantitative imaging under open-science practices.

[Abstract]

The hypothesis is that despite molecular diversity, chromatin nanodomain topology falls into a limited set of mesoscale motifs whose combinations predict regulatory capacity and noise. Expected outputs include: a cross-cell-type atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs, quantitative relationships between motif composition and transcriptional variability, and open tools for jointly analyzing Hi-C and imaging. This synthesis requires collaboration among genome informaticians, polymer physicists, microscopy experts, and statistical modelers; no single lab typically has access to and expertise across these modalities. NCEMS working group support is essential for harmonizing standards, building reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to bridge 3D genomics and quantitative imaging under open-science practices.

[Background and Significance]
Chromatin organization is a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon: it emerges from molecular interactions among nucleosomes, DNA-binding proteins, and transcriptional machinery, yet manifests as higher-order spatial domains that are tens to hundreds of nanometers in size—larger than single nucleosomes but smaller than whole chromosomes or nuclei. At this mesoscale (roughly 50–300 nm), chromatin exhibits “nanodomains” and microcompartments whose collective topology influences gene regulation in ways not reducible to any single molecular mark. These emergent behaviors include probabilistic enhancer–promoter communication, insulation between regulatory neighborhoods, and transcriptional bursting kinetics. Understanding how such behaviors arise requires synthesis across modalities that each capture only partial projections of the underlying 3D polymer state.

Over the past decade, chromosome conformation capture assays (Hi-C, Micro-C, and related methods) have produced extensive public maps of genome-wide contact frequencies across cell types and species. The 4D Nucleome (4DN) Data Portal, Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), ENCODE, and other repositories host hundreds of high-depth bulk Hi-C maps and growing collections of single-cell Hi-C and Micro-C datasets. These data revealed canonical organizational features—A/B compartments, topologically associating domains (TADs), and loops—while also highlighting that fine-scale contact patterns vary strongly by cell type, differentiation state, and perturbations. Micro-C, with nucleosome-scale resolution, further suggests that contact maps contain rich mesoscale structure beyond classical TAD boundaries, including nested communities and microcompartmentalization.

In parallel, advances in super-resolution and multiplexed imaging have made it possible to directly measure spatial distances and domain shapes in single cells. Public resources such as the 4DN Data Portal, the BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI), and community-shared Oligopaint and multiplexed DNA FISH datasets provide imaging of chromatin loci, domain boundaries, and nuclear landmarks at tens-of-nanometers precision. Unlike contact maps, which are ensemble-averaged and indirect, imaging provides geometric constraints (distance distributions, radius of gyration, anisotropy, and spatial co-localization) that can disambiguate multiple 3D conformations consistent with the same contact matrix.

Epigenomic maps add a third key axis. ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics provide thousands of ChIP-seq profiles for histone modifications and architectural proteins, along with ATAC-seq and DNase-seq accessibility maps. These data connect chromatin state to physical organization: active and inactive marks correlate with compartment identity; CTCF/cohesin occupancy correlates with loop anchors; and enhancer states correlate with dynamic regulatory potential. Finally, transcriptional outputs are richly represented in the Human Cell Atlas and other single-cell RNA-seq collections, as well as publicly available nascent transcription datasets (e.g., GRO-seq/PRO-seq in GEO/ENCODE for select cell types). Together, these resources enable a synthesis-driven approach to link mesoscale topology to emergent gene expression phenotypes such as cell-type-specific expression programs and transcriptional noise.

Despite this abundance, a major gap remains: we lack a unified, quantitative mapping between (i) contact-based representations of chromatin organization and (ii) physical, nanoscale domain geometries observed by imaging, and we do not know whether diverse cell types share a limited “vocabulary” of mesoscale topological motifs. Current analyses often focus on individual features (e.g., a specific loop, a single TAD boundary, or a single histone mark) and then infer regulatory outcomes. Yet emergent regulatory behavior likely depends on combinations of mesoscale structures: clustered loops may create rosette-like hubs, microcompartments may generate local phase-separated neighborhoods, and boundary strength may modulate enhancer reach and bursting probability. These multi-feature combinations are difficult to infer from any single data type.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to resolve this gap by integrating heterogeneous public datasets at scale and extracting generalizable motifs across cell types and mammals. First, contact maps alone are degenerate: many 3D polymer conformations can produce similar contact frequencies. Imaging-derived distance distributions can serve as orthogonal constraints to calibrate and select among candidate polymer models, thereby converting ambiguous contact patterns into interpretable 3D nanodomain geometries. Second, epigenomic annotations can be used to interpret motif composition (e.g., whether a motif preferentially occurs in H3K27ac-rich regions or Polycomb-associated domains) and to test whether motif boundaries align with chromatin state transitions. Third, transcriptional data allow evaluation of emergent outcomes: if mesoscale motifs are mechanistically meaningful, their occupancy should predict not only mean expression but also variability and bursting-related proxies across cell types.

The mesoscale focus aligns with NCEMS’s vision: nanodomain topology sits between molecular interactions (nucleosome modifications, binding factors) and higher-order cellular outcomes (lineage commitment, disease states). Emergence is central here: regulatory behaviors arise from collective folding patterns, not from any single molecular component. By synthesizing publicly available Hi-C/Micro-C, super-resolution imaging, epigenomics, and transcriptomics—without generating new data—this project aims to identify a compact set of mesoscale topological motifs and quantify how motif combinations produce cell-type-specific gene regulation. The availability of community-scale datasets across multiple repositories now makes it feasible to test these ideas rigorously and comparatively across mammals, developmental transitions, and disease-associated variant contexts, but doing so requires coordinated, transdisciplinary expertise and shared standards that exceed the capabilities of any single laboratory.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address a central question in mesoscale genome biology: do chromatin nanodomains organize into a limited set of recurrent topological motifs whose combinations generate emergent, cell-type-specific regulatory behaviors? We focus on motifs at the 50–300 nm scale—larger than nucleosome-level features but smaller than whole-chromosome compartments—because this is the scale at which enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting are thought to be tuned by collective folding.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): What is the minimal “motif dictionary” of chromatin nanodomain topologies that recurs across mammalian cell types?
Hypothesis 1 (H1): Across diverse mammalian cell types and tissues, mesoscale chromatin can be represented by a small number of motifs (e.g., loop clusters/rosettes, boundary-insulated domains, microcompartment patches, and hub-like interaction communities) that recur with conserved geometric signatures.
Measurable predictions: (i) Unsupervised joint embeddings of contact-map features (from Hi-C/Micro-C) and imaging-derived geometric features will cluster into a limited number of stable motif classes; (ii) motif classes will be reproducible across independent datasets and platforms (e.g., different Hi-C protocols, different imaging studies) after harmonization; (iii) motif frequency distributions will differ by cell type, but motif definitions (feature centroids) will remain conserved.
Validation using existing data: We will test motif stability via cross-study replication (train motif models on 4DN Hi-C + BioImage Archive imaging from one set of cell types, validate on ENCODE/GEO and independent imaging datasets). We will quantify reproducibility using adjusted mutual information between motif assignments and evaluate whether motifs persist under downsampling of contact depth and imaging cell counts.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): How do motif combinations and transitions relate to emergent regulatory phenotypes such as transcriptional variability and enhancer responsiveness?
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Motif composition at gene regulatory neighborhoods predicts emergent transcriptional outcomes—particularly variability proxies—better than individual molecular marks or single loops.
Measurable predictions: (i) For matched cell types, motif occupancy around genes (e.g., within 1–2 Mb windows or within inferred nanodomains) will explain significant variance in gene expression dispersion (from Human Cell Atlas scRNA-seq) beyond what is explained by promoter accessibility and histone marks alone; (ii) genes in motifs characterized by strong insulation and limited cross-boundary contacts will show reduced enhancer-linked coexpression and lower expression noise; (iii) motifs with clustered enhancer–promoter contacts (hub/rosette-like) will associate with higher burst frequency proxies and stronger enhancer-dependent expression.
Validation using existing data: We will use hierarchical models that incorporate covariates from ENCODE/Roadmap (ATAC-seq, H3K27ac, H3K4me3, CTCF/cohesin where available) and compare predictive performance with and without motif features using cross-validation across cell types and donors. Where nascent transcription datasets exist in GEO/ENCODE for specific cell lines, we will test whether motif classes correlate with polymerase density and transcriptional initiation proxies.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): Can imaging constraints resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions sufficiently to infer physically meaningful nanodomain geometries?
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Joint inference that explicitly fits both contact frequencies and imaging distance distributions will produce a constrained ensemble of 3D conformations whose inferred geometric parameters (domain radius, compaction, inter-domain separation) are consistent across datasets and predictive of regulatory outcomes.
Measurable predictions: (i) Polymer model ensembles calibrated with imaging will show reduced uncertainty (narrower posterior distributions) in geometric parameters compared with contact-only models; (ii) calibrated models will better reproduce independent imaging metrics not used in fitting (e.g., distance quantiles for held-out locus pairs); (iii) geometric parameters derived from calibrated ensembles will correlate with motif classes and explain additional variance in transcriptional outcomes.
Validation using existing data: We will perform hold-out tests where imaging distance distributions from a subset of locus pairs are withheld during calibration and then predicted. We will also compare calibrated polymer ensembles to existing published polymer simulation benchmarks and constraints (e.g., nucleosome/chromatin fiber parameters drawn from literature and structural models in the Protein Data Bank when relevant to coarse-graining).

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Do developmental transitions and disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially correspond to motif switching rather than isolated loop disruptions?
Hypothesis 4 (H4): Changes in cell identity and regulatory dysfunction are often mediated by shifts among mesoscale motifs (e.g., from insulated to hub-like motifs or from active microcompartments to repressed compact domains), and disease-associated noncoding variants are enriched in genomic contexts where motif switching occurs.
Measurable predictions: (i) Across developmental trajectories represented in public scRNA-seq atlases and matched epigenomes, motif transitions inferred from available Hi-C/Micro-C datasets will align with lineage bifurcations and changes in expression variance; (ii) GWAS Catalog variants and ClinVar noncoding variants will be enriched at motif boundaries or within motifs characterized by high regulatory sensitivity (e.g., hub-like motifs), compared with matched control variants.
Validation using existing data: We will perform enrichment analyses using GWAS Catalog and ClinVar coordinates, controlling for mappability, GC content, and chromatin accessibility. For developmental contexts, we will leverage publicly available multi-omic references where cell types overlap across 4DN/ENCODE and Human Cell Atlas, and use statistical matching rather than new data generation.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses aim to deliver mechanistic insight into how mesoscale chromatin topology—captured as a small motif vocabulary and its combinations—produces emergent regulatory behaviors across mammalian cell types. The emphasis is on testable, quantitative predictions validated entirely through synthesis of existing public datasets, with rigorous cross-dataset replication as the primary standard of evidence.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
This project is a community-scale synthesis effort integrating orthogonal public data modalities to infer mesoscale chromatin nanodomain motifs and link them to emergent regulatory phenotypes. We will not generate any new experimental data. Instead, we will build harmonized, reproducible pipelines to (i) extract nanodomain-scale features from Hi-C/Micro-C, (ii) extract geometric constraints from super-resolution/multiplexed DNA FISH imaging, (iii) align these with epigenomic annotations and transcriptional outputs, and (iv) jointly infer a motif dictionary and motif–phenotype relationships.

Specific data sources (public repositories)
1) 3D genome contact maps:
- 4D Nucleome (4DN) Data Portal: bulk Hi-C, single-cell Hi-C, Micro-C for key human and mouse cell lines and primary cells.
- ENCODE Portal: Hi-C/Micro-C where available, plus extensive metadata and processing standards.
- NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) / SRA: additional Hi-C/Micro-C datasets, including developmental and disease contexts.
2) Imaging of chromatin organization:
- 4DN Data Portal imaging datasets (DNA FISH, multiplexed FISH, super-resolution imaging where deposited).
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI): curated raw and processed microscopy datasets.
- Public Oligopaint/multiplexed DNA FISH datasets released with publications (accessed via linked repositories such as Zenodo/Figshare when applicable and permissive).
3) Epigenomics and accessibility:
- ENCODE: ChIP-seq (H3K27ac, H3K4me3, H3K27me3, CTCF, RAD21/SMC1A where available), ATAC-seq/DNase-seq.
- Roadmap Epigenomics: reference histone marks and chromatin state segmentations for primary tissues.
4) Transcriptional outputs:
- Human Cell Atlas (HCA) scRNA-seq: cell-type-resolved expression distributions.
- GEO/ENCODE: scRNA-seq for specific cell lines/tissues; GRO-seq/PRO-seq/NET-seq where available for nascent transcription proxies.
5) Structural constraints and benchmarks:
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): structural information relevant to nucleosome and chromatin fiber coarse-graining (used as literature-constrained priors, not for new modeling beyond synthesis).
- Published polymer simulation benchmarks and open datasets (e.g., from prior 4DN challenges) to compare reconstruction performance.

Data harmonization and linkage across modalities
- Genome builds and coordinates: standardize to hg38 (human) and mm10 (mouse), with liftOver where needed; store all intervals in BED format with provenance.
- Cell type matching: define a “cell-type concordance table” using ontology terms (Cell Ontology IDs) and repository metadata; prioritize cell types with at least two modalities available (contacts + epigenomics; contacts + imaging; ideally all three plus scRNA-seq).
- Resolution harmonization: represent contact maps at multiple resolutions (e.g., 1 kb–100 kb) and focus motif inference on scales corresponding to 50–300 nm, operationalized via genomic scales inferred from imaging distance–genomic distance calibration and polymer scaling (e.g., tens to hundreds of kb depending on compaction).
- Batch effects: apply modality-specific normalization (ICE/KR balancing for Hi-C; intensity/segmentation QC for imaging; standard ENCODE processing for ChIP/ATAC) and then use cross-study calibration (ComBat-like adjustments for derived features; domain-adversarial learning for embeddings where appropriate).

Aim 1: Infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction communities from Hi-C/Micro-C
- Feature extraction: compute insulation score, directionality index, and multi-scale contact decay features; detect loops (e.g., HiCCUPS-like peaks where available from processed calls) but treat loops as features rather than primary units.
- Multi-resolution community detection: apply graph-based community detection on contact graphs (nodes=bins; edges=normalized contacts) using multi-resolution modularity optimization and/or stochastic block models to identify nested domains and microcommunities.
- Single-cell integration: for scHi-C, use latent embedding methods (e.g., topic models or variational autoencoders designed for sparse contact matrices) to infer cell-to-cell variability in motif occupancy and to estimate uncertainty.
Deliverable: a standardized “nanodomain feature table” per cell type with boundaries, community assignments, and uncertainty estimates.

Aim 2: Extract geometric constraints from imaging and calibrate polymer models
- Imaging processing (existing images only): use published segmentations when available; otherwise apply reproducible, containerized pipelines for spot calling and distance extraction (for FISH) or domain segmentation (for labeled chromatin regions) using established open-source tools.
- Geometric summaries: distance distributions for locus pairs; radius of gyration for labeled regions; domain volume/compactness proxies; spatial co-localization frequencies.
- Polymer modeling: use coarse-grained polymer simulations (e.g., strings-and-binders or loop-extrusion-informed polymer priors) to generate ensembles consistent with contact features. Calibration will be performed by Bayesian or approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) approaches that fit both contact-derived constraints and imaging distance distributions.
- Degeneracy reduction: compare posterior uncertainty for geometric parameters in contact-only vs joint (contact+imaging) inference; quantify improvement via held-out imaging prediction.
Deliverable: calibrated mapping functions between contact features and physical geometry, plus a library of inferred geometric parameters per nanodomain.

Aim 3: Learn a joint motif dictionary from contacts + imaging + epigenomic features
- Representation learning: construct a multimodal feature vector per genomic region/nanodomain including contact-community metrics, imaging-derived geometry, and epigenomic state summaries (e.g., ChromHMM states from Roadmap/ENCODE where available).
- Unsupervised motif discovery: apply mixture models and deep clustering (e.g., variational mixture of autoencoders) to learn discrete motif classes with interpretable feature loadings. Motif number will be selected by stability criteria (bootstrapped clustering stability, held-out likelihood) rather than arbitrary choice.
- Cross-species mapping: map syntenic regions (human–mouse) using chain files and test whether motif classes transfer, allowing for species-specific frequency shifts.
Deliverable: an “Atlas of Chromatin Nanodomain Motifs” with motif definitions, representative examples, and per-cell-type motif occupancy tracks.

Aim 4: Link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes
- Outcome variables: gene expression mean and dispersion (from HCA scRNA-seq), coexpression modules, and where available nascent transcription proxies.
- Modeling: hierarchical Bayesian regression or generalized linear mixed models with random effects for cell type/study; predictors include motif occupancy near genes, motif transition scores across regions, and covariates (promoter accessibility, enhancer marks, gene length, GC content).
- Variant enrichment: test enrichment of GWAS Catalog and ClinVar noncoding variants in motif boundaries and motif classes, using matched controls and logistic regression controlling for confounders.
- Positive controls: known locus archetypes (e.g., Hox clusters, globin loci, immunoglobulin loci) with extensive public 3D genome and epigenomic characterization will be used as interpretability anchors; we will also validate that known compartment shifts correspond to motif composition changes.
Deliverable: quantitative motif–phenotype maps and statistical evidence for emergent regulatory roles.

Validation (no experiments)
- Cross-dataset replication: train motif models on one subset of studies and test on independent studies within 4DN/ENCODE/GEO.
- Cross-modality prediction: predict imaging distances from contact-derived motifs and evaluate against held-out imaging datasets; predict transcriptional dispersion from motifs and evaluate against held-out cell types.
- Sensitivity analyses: downsample contacts and imaging to assess robustness; evaluate alternative normalizations and domain-calling methods.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6: Working group kickoff; finalize cell-type concordance table; build ingestion pipelines; release v0 data inventory and metadata schema.
Months 7–12: Generate nanodomain feature tables from Hi-C/Micro-C; implement imaging distance extraction; first joint calibration prototypes; release v1 reproducible pipelines.
Months 13–18: Complete joint contact+imaging calibration; perform motif discovery; release v1 motif dictionary and initial atlas tracks.
Months 19–24: Motif–phenotype modeling with scRNA-seq/epigenomics; variant enrichment analyses; cross-study replication; preprint 1.
Months 25–30: Final atlas and software release; documentation and tutorials; working group synthesis paper; capstone training workshop; long-term hosting plan.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- 3D genomics informatics (Hi-C/Micro-C processing, domain calling, single-cell contact modeling).
- Quantitative imaging/microscopy experts (FISH/super-resolution data interpretation, segmentation QC, imaging-derived metrics).
- Polymer physics/modeling (coarse-grained polymer priors, simulation, ABC/Bayesian calibration).
- Statistical modeling/causal inference (hierarchical models, uncertainty quantification, enrichment analyses).
- Machine learning (multimodal representation learning, clustering stability, domain adaptation).
- Research software engineering (workflow automation, containers, documentation, CI/CD).
This breadth is essential: no single lab typically has deep expertise across Hi-C, super-resolution imaging, polymer physics, and hierarchical statistical modeling, and the synthesis requires coordinated standards and shared tooling consistent with NCEMS working group goals.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) Atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs across mammalian cell types: A public, versioned resource that defines a motif dictionary (discrete motif classes with interpretable feature signatures) and provides genome-wide motif occupancy tracks for prioritized human and mouse cell types. Outputs will include BED/BigWig tracks, per-region motif probabilities, and uncertainty estimates.

2) Joint inference toolkit for contacts + imaging: Open-source software implementing pipelines to (i) extract nanodomain-scale features from Hi-C/Micro-C, (ii) extract imaging-derived geometric constraints (distance distributions and domain geometry summaries), and (iii) perform joint calibration of polymer-based reconstructions. The toolkit will emphasize modularity so users can swap in alternative normalizations, domain callers, or polymer priors.

3) Quantitative motif–phenotype models: Statistical models linking motif composition to emergent regulatory phenotypes, including gene expression dispersion (as a proxy for transcriptional noise/bursting), enhancer responsiveness proxies (e.g., association with enhancer marks and coexpression), and lineage-associated expression stability. Results will be released as model objects, summary tables, and reproducible notebooks.

4) Variant-context synthesis: A resource quantifying enrichment of GWAS Catalog and ClinVar noncoding variants in specific motif classes and motif boundaries, with matched-control analyses. This will provide a mesoscale organizational lens for interpreting noncoding variation beyond single-loop narratives.

Mechanistic advances in mesoscale emergence
This project’s core impact is to move from descriptive catalogs of loops/TADs/compartments to a mesoscale theory of emergent regulation grounded in a compact motif vocabulary. By explicitly integrating imaging geometry with contact maps, we will clarify which contact-derived patterns correspond to physically distinct nanodomain shapes and separations, addressing a major ambiguity in 3D genome inference. The motif dictionary will provide a mesoscale “state space” in which chromatin organization can be compared across cell types, species, and conditions.

We expect to establish quantitative relationships between motif composition and emergent transcriptional behaviors. If motifs explain expression dispersion beyond molecular covariates, it would support the idea that mesoscale topology is not merely a reflection of epigenomic state but an organizing principle that shapes regulatory noise and responsiveness. Such findings would contribute to a mechanistic understanding of how stable cell identities arise from fluctuating molecular interactions: cell-type-specific combinations of mesoscale motifs could buffer or amplify transcriptional variability, thereby influencing lineage stability.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- A unifying framework across modalities: The field currently has parallel literatures—Hi-C-centric and imaging-centric—that often disagree in interpretation. A joint inference framework will provide a common language, enabling more rigorous cross-validation and improving confidence in structural conclusions.
- Improved interpretability for AI in genomics: Rather than black-box predictors, motif classes offer interpretable mesoscale units that can be used as features in downstream predictive models of gene regulation, differentiation, and disease.
- Comparative and evolutionary insights: Cross-species motif transfer analyses can reveal which mesoscale organizational principles are conserved and which are lineage-specific, informing how genome regulation evolves.
- Disease relevance without new experiments: By synthesizing variant catalogs with motif contexts, we can generate testable mechanistic hypotheses for why certain noncoding variants have outsized regulatory effects (e.g., by destabilizing hub-like motifs or weakening insulation), guiding future experimental work by the community.

Enabling future research
The atlas and tools will enable investigators to (i) annotate any region of interest with motif probabilities, (ii) compare motif composition across cell types, and (iii) integrate new public datasets as they appear. Because the project focuses on synthesis and standards, it will lower barriers for labs to incorporate imaging constraints into 3D genome analyses and to interpret contact maps at the nanodomain scale.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: At least two major manuscripts are anticipated: (1) methods paper describing joint inference and motif discovery; (2) synthesis paper reporting the motif atlas and motif–phenotype relationships.
- NCEMS-style workshops: Annual working group meetings and a capstone training workshop focused on multimodal 3D genome synthesis (contacts + imaging + epigenomics), with hands-on tutorials.
- Public resources: Deposited motif tracks and metadata schema in community repositories (e.g., Zenodo for versioned releases; GitHub for code; links and descriptors suitable for indexing by 4DN/ENCODE portals where permitted).

Long-term sustainability
We will design the resource as a lightweight, versioned data product with clear provenance and automated rebuilds. Continuous integration will re-run key pipelines when upstream references change (e.g., genome build patches, updated annotations). We will provide a governance document for community contributions, including how new datasets can be added, how motif dictionary updates are versioned, and how to cite releases via DOIs (Zenodo). The emphasis on open formats, containerized workflows, and thorough documentation will allow the atlas and tools to persist beyond the funding period and be extended by the broader community.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy and alignment with NCEMS
This project is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring substantial coordination, shared computational infrastructure, and dedicated personnel for data engineering, multimodal modeling, and open-science productization. Funds are requested to support a distributed working group spanning multiple labs and disciplines; no funds are requested for experimental data generation.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (2–3 years):
  1) Multimodal 3D genomics postdoc (Hi-C/Micro-C feature extraction, motif discovery, cross-dataset replication).
  2) Quantitative modeling postdoc (hierarchical models linking motifs to scRNA-seq phenotypes; variant enrichment analyses).
- 1 Research software engineer / scientific programmer (2–3 years): workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, CI/CD, documentation, and packaging of tools for community use.
- 1 Graduate student (2–3 years, partial support): imaging-derived feature extraction pipelines, QC metrics, and integration with contact-derived features under mentorship from imaging and genomics leads.
- Trainee support (supplemental): short-term support for additional graduate students/postdocs participating in working group sprints, ensuring training and broad participation.
Justification: Synthesis at this scale requires sustained engineering and statistical capacity beyond typical single-lab staffing, especially for reproducible workflows and multimodal harmonization.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations: required for processing large Hi-C/Micro-C matrices, running polymer simulations/ABC calibration, and training multimodal representation learning models.
- Storage: budget for secure, redundant storage of downloaded public datasets (where permitted) and large intermediate files; emphasis on storing derived features rather than duplicating raw archives.
Justification: Joint inference and cross-validation across many cell types requires repeated model fitting and simulation; shared compute prevents bottlenecks and enables reproducibility.

Working group meetings and travel
- Annual in-person working group meetings (2–3 meetings total): support travel for PIs, postdocs, graduate students, and key collaborators across institutions to conduct intensive synthesis, align standards, and accelerate integration across modalities.
- Targeted travel to disseminate outcomes: conference travel for trainees and key personnel to present the atlas/toolkit and recruit adopters.
Justification: NCEMS’s value is catalyzing transdisciplinary integration; in-person meetings materially improve coordination between genomics, imaging, polymer physics, and statistics teams.

Workshops and training events
- Capstone training workshop (in-person, final year): venue costs, training materials, and travel support for trainees from diverse institutions (including those with fewer resources) to broaden participation.
- Quarterly virtual tutorial series: minimal costs for webinar hosting, captioning, and archiving.
Justification: Training the next-generation data-savvy workforce is a core NCEMS goal; workshops ensure broad, lasting impact beyond publications.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo DOI-backed releases for data products; costs for curation time and preparation.
- Web hosting for documentation (e.g., GitHub Pages) and optional lightweight registry site for atlas browsing.
- Professional support for accessibility (captioning tutorials, documentation QA) where feasible.
Justification: Open, reproducible science requires time and infrastructure to make resources discoverable and usable.

Overall resource justification
Each budget category directly enables synthesis: personnel build and validate integrated pipelines; compute supports large-scale multimodal inference and replication; travel and meetings create the cross-disciplinary cohesion that no single lab can achieve; and open-science infrastructure ensures that the community can reuse, audit, and extend the resulting atlas and tools.

Chromatin forms mesoscale nanodomains (50–300 nm) whose collective folding and compartmentalization produce emergent regulatory behaviors—enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting—that cannot be inferred from individual nucleosome modifications. This project will synthesize 3D genome conformation and imaging data to test whether a small set of mesoscale topological motifs explains cell-type-specific gene regulation across mammals.

We will integrate publicly available datasets: (i) population and single-cell Hi-C / Micro-C maps (4D Nucleome, GEO, ENCODE), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed DNA FISH imaging of chromatin domains (4DN data portal, BioImage Archive; Oligopaint datasets), (iii) epigenomic marks and accessibility (ENCODE ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq; Roadmap Epigenomics), (iv) transcriptional outputs (single-cell RNA-seq from Human Cell Atlas; nascent transcription where available), and (v) structural constraints from nucleosome and chromatin fiber models (PDB where relevant; polymer simulation benchmarks).

Methodologically, we will create a joint inference framework that maps between contact matrices and physical 3D domain geometries. We will (1) infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction strengths from Hi-C/Micro-C using multi-resolution community detection; (2) calibrate polymer models with imaging-derived distance distributions to resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions; (3) learn a “motif dictionary” of recurrent mesoscale folding patterns (e.g., loop clusters, rosettes, compartment microdomains) using unsupervised representation learning that ingests both contact and imaging features; and (4) link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes—bursting parameters, enhancer responsiveness, and lineage stability—using hierarchical models across cell types.

The hypothesis is that despite molecular diversity, chromatin nanodomain topology falls into a limited set of mesoscale motifs whose combinations predict regulatory capacity and noise. We will test whether developmental transitions correspond to motif switching, and whether disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially disrupt specific motifs rather than individual loops.

Expected outputs include: a cross-cell-type atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs, quantitative relationships between motif composition and transcriptional variability, and open tools for jointly analyzing Hi-C and imaging. This synthesis requires collaboration among genome informaticians, polymer physicists, microscopy experts, and statistical modelers; no single lab typically has access to and expertise across these modalities. NCEMS working group support is essential for harmonizing standards, building reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to bridge 3D genomics and quantitative imaging under open-science practices.

title: Protein Crowding as an Emergent Mesoscale Regulator: A Pan-Proteome Synthesis of Cytoplasmic Viscosity, Diffusion, and Reaction Rates

abstract_text:
Cells exhibit emergent mesoscale physical properties—effective viscosity, anomalous diffusion, and spatially heterogeneous crowding—arising from collective protein/RNA concentrations at 10–1000 nm scales. These properties shape signaling and metabolism but are not predictable from individual macromolecules. This project will test whether crowding-related emergent parameters can be predicted from proteome composition and subcellular organization across organisms and conditions.

We will synthesize: (i) quantitative proteomics and absolute protein copy numbers (ProteomeXchange, PaxDB), (ii) subcellular localization and abundance maps (Human Protein Atlas; spatial proteomics datasets such as hyperLOPIT in PRIDE), (iii) measurements of diffusion and viscosity from fluorescence correlation spectroscopy, single-particle tracking, and FRAP compiled from public repositories and literature supplements (IDR/BioImage Archive; curated datasets), (iv) metabolomics that influences osmotic/crowding states (Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) structural/biophysical properties of proteins (PDB, AlphaFold DB; predicted disorder from MobiDB; oligomerization from Complex Portal).

We will construct mesoscale “crowding fields” by combining spatial proteomics with protein size/shape estimates (from structures/predictions) to estimate excluded volume and soft interaction potentials in different compartments. We will fit these fields to observed diffusion/viscosity measurements using Bayesian calibration and coarse-grained physical models (e.g., obstruction scaling, fractional Brownian motion). Machine learning models will predict diffusion regimes for probe classes (enzymes, ribosomes, signaling proteins) given local proteome composition and interaction propensity.

Key questions: Do cells maintain conserved crowding setpoints in specific compartments (nucleoplasm vs cytosol) despite large proteome changes? Which protein classes (ribosomal proteins, chaperones, intrinsically disordered proteins) disproportionately control emergent viscosity? Can we predict condition-dependent shifts (stress, cell cycle, differentiation) in mesoscale diffusion landscapes from omics alone?

Expected insights include a quantitative, cross-species map linking proteome composition to emergent physical states, and identification of “crowding hubs” whose abundance changes re-tune global reaction kinetics. The project enables reinterpretation of many phenotypes (e.g., slowed signaling under stress) as consequences of mesoscale physical state changes.

This requires team science integrating quantitative proteomics, soft-matter physics, microscopy-based biophysics, and statistical learning, plus substantial data curation across heterogeneous measurement types. NCEMS support is needed to coordinate community standards for reporting diffusion/viscosity, build open databases of calibrated measurements, and deliver reproducible pipelines and training modules for a new generation of data-savvy biophysical cell biologists.
