[Background and Significance]
Mesoscale cell biology (approximately 10–1000 nm) is where molecular composition becomes collective material state. In this regime, the cytoplasm and nucleoplasm behave neither like dilute solution nor like a simple polymer melt; instead they exhibit emergent properties—effective viscosity, viscoelasticity, anomalous diffusion, and spatially heterogeneous crowding—that arise from the combined concentrations, sizes, shapes, interactions, and organization of proteins, RNAs, and macromolecular assemblies. These emergent physical states influence reaction kinetics, encounter rates, phase behavior, and spatial signaling, yet remain difficult to predict from the properties of individual molecules. Understanding how mesoscale material properties emerge from proteome composition is a fundamental challenge aligned with NCEMS’s vision: to explain how new system properties appear across scales, especially at the mesoscale where biomolecules give rise to organelle-level behaviors.

A large body of work has established that intracellular diffusion deviates from Brownian motion for many probes, showing subdiffusion or heterogeneous dynamics depending on probe size and binding (e.g., fractional Brownian motion or continuous-time random walk phenomenology). Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS), and single-particle tracking (SPT) studies have repeatedly demonstrated that diffusion coefficients can vary by orders of magnitude across compartments, cell types, and conditions, and that stress responses can globally slow diffusion. Parallel research in soft-matter and polymer physics provides mechanistic frameworks—obstruction models, effective medium theories, and viscoelastic models—that connect excluded volume and interaction potentials to transport. In vitro reconstitutions and simulations further show that mixtures of globular proteins, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), and ribonucleoprotein complexes can generate nontrivial rheology and anomalous diffusion. However, most quantitative links between composition and transport remain qualitative or system-specific.

At the same time, the data landscape has changed dramatically. Quantitative proteomics repositories such as ProteomeXchange (including PRIDE) and abundance compendia such as PaxDB provide organism- and condition-specific protein abundance estimates, including absolute copy numbers for many systems. Subcellular localization resources (Human Protein Atlas) and spatial proteomics datasets (e.g., hyperLOPIT and related fractionation-based localization maps deposited in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange) make it possible to estimate compartment-specific proteome composition rather than whole-cell averages. Structural databases (Protein Data Bank) and large-scale structure predictions (AlphaFold DB) enable estimation of protein size/shape descriptors relevant to excluded volume, while MobiDB provides disorder annotations that relate to soft interactions, entanglement-like effects, and binding promiscuity. Complex Portal and related resources curate stable assemblies and stoichiometries that influence mesoscale packing. Metabolomics resources such as Metabolomics Workbench provide measurements of osmolytes and metabolites that modulate hydration and macromolecular crowding.

Despite these advances, major gaps remain that are uniquely addressable by synthesis research. First, diffusion/viscosity measurements are scattered across publications, supplementary tables, and imaging repositories (e.g., Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive), with heterogeneous reporting standards (probe identity, size, temperature, cell cycle stage, analysis model, photophysics). This fragmentation prevents the community from building predictive models across systems. Second, proteome abundance and localization data are typically analyzed for pathways, not for their collective physical consequences. Third, existing models often treat crowding as a single scalar (e.g., volume fraction) and do not incorporate spatial heterogeneity and composition-dependent soft interactions (e.g., charge patterning, disorder content, oligomerization) that can create compartment-specific “crowding fields.” Finally, it is unclear whether cells maintain conserved “crowding setpoints” in specific compartments (cytosol vs nucleoplasm) across evolution and perturbation, or whether they tune material state as a regulatory layer.

This proposal addresses these gaps by synthesizing publicly available proteomics, spatial localization, structural/biophysical annotations, metabolomics, and imaging-derived transport measurements into a unified, open, community-scale resource and modeling framework. The significance is twofold. Conceptually, it reframes intracellular transport and reaction kinetics as emergent mesoscale outcomes of proteome organization, enabling mechanistic hypotheses about how cells regulate physical state to control biochemical networks. Practically, it provides predictive tools that allow researchers to infer diffusion regimes and effective viscosity landscapes from omics and localization data, supporting reinterpretation of phenotypes (e.g., slowed signaling under stress, altered metabolic flux) as consequences of mesoscale state shifts.

The project requires NCEMS-scale coordination because no single lab typically has (i) deep expertise in quantitative proteomics and spatial proteome mapping, (ii) biophysical microscopy and transport modeling, (iii) soft-matter theory for crowded heterogeneous media, and (iv) modern Bayesian/ML methods for calibration across heterogeneous datasets—nor the capacity to curate and harmonize the dispersed diffusion/viscosity literature into a reusable database with community standards. NCEMS support will enable working-group meetings, shared infrastructure, and open-science governance to produce durable, reusable synthesis products. By leveraging existing data only, the project turns the community’s accumulated measurements into a coherent framework for understanding how mesoscale crowding emerges and how it regulates cellular function.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address the overarching question: Can emergent mesoscale transport properties (effective viscosity, diffusion coefficients, and anomalous diffusion exponents) be predicted from compartment-specific proteome composition and organization across organisms and conditions using only existing public data? We decompose this into precise, testable research questions with measurable predictions.

RQ1: Are there conserved compartment-specific “crowding setpoints” across cell types and organisms? Here, a “setpoint” refers to a constrained range of inferred excluded-volume fraction and/or calibrated effective viscosity in a given compartment (e.g., cytosol, nucleoplasm, mitochondrial matrix) despite large variation in proteome identity and abundance. 
H1: For major compartments, inferred crowding metrics (e.g., effective volume fraction, calibrated obstruction parameter, or Bayesian posterior mean viscosity) fall within a narrow, conserved range across diverse eukaryotes under baseline conditions, even when total protein concentration differs. 
Predictions: (i) After harmonization for temperature and probe class, diffusion coefficients for standardized probe categories (e.g., GFP-like proteins, ribosomes, endogenous enzymes) will cluster by compartment more strongly than by species; (ii) inferred crowding-field parameters will show lower variance within compartments across species than across compartments within a species. 
Validation using existing data: We will test clustering and variance partitioning using diffusion/FRAP/FCS/SPT datasets from IDR/BioImage Archive and literature, aligned with compartment proteome estimates derived from Human Protein Atlas and spatial proteomics (hyperLOPIT) plus abundance from PaxDB/ProteomeXchange.

RQ2: Which proteome features disproportionately control emergent viscosity and anomalous diffusion? 
H2: A small number of “crowding hubs”—protein classes with high abundance and strong soft interactions—dominate mesoscale transport outcomes. Candidate classes include ribosomal proteins/ribosomes, chaperones, cytoskeletal polymers, and IDP-rich proteins. 
Predictions: (i) Models that include features capturing IDP content (MobiDB), multivalency/oligomerization (Complex Portal), and assembly size (PDB/AlphaFold-derived hydrodynamic radius proxies) will outperform models based on total protein concentration alone in predicting diffusion and anomalous exponents; (ii) Shapley-value or posterior inclusion analyses will identify consistent high-impact features across datasets (e.g., fraction of mass in large complexes; fraction of residues disordered; abundance of ribosome-associated proteins). 
Validation: We will evaluate predictive performance via cross-dataset validation (train on one organism/condition set, test on another) and compare nested models (total concentration only vs concentration + composition + interaction proxies).

RQ3: Can condition-dependent shifts in mesoscale diffusion landscapes be inferred from omics and metabolomics without direct transport measurements? 
H3: Stress, cell cycle, and differentiation shift mesoscale transport primarily through coordinated changes in (i) proteome mass reallocation to large assemblies and (ii) osmolyte/metabolite profiles that modulate hydration and effective interactions. 
Predictions: (i) In conditions with known global slowing of diffusion (e.g., osmotic stress, heat shock), proteomics will show increased abundance of chaperones and/or stress granule-associated proteins and increased predicted disorder/multivalency; (ii) metabolomics will show shifts in osmolytes (e.g., trehalose in yeast; amino acid/osmolyte changes in mammalian cells) that correlate with inferred viscosity parameters. 
Validation: We will link condition-labeled proteomics (ProteomeXchange) and metabolomics (Metabolomics Workbench) to transport measurements where available; where transport measurements are absent, we will test whether the inferred crowding-field shifts align with known qualitative phenotypes reported in literature (e.g., slowed cytosolic diffusion under hyperosmotic shock) and with independent proxies such as measured cell volume changes or macromolecular concentration estimates when reported.

RQ4: Do mesoscale “crowding fields” exhibit spatial heterogeneity that is predictable from spatial proteomics and compartment architecture? 
H4: Spatial proteomics supports the inference of heterogeneous crowding fields within broad compartments (e.g., perinuclear vs peripheral cytosol; nucleolus vs nucleoplasm), and these fields predict spatially varying diffusion regimes observed by SPT/FRAP. 
Predictions: (i) Where spatial proteomics provides multi-localization probabilities or gradient-like distributions, inferred local excluded volume will correlate with spatially resolved diffusion maps in imaging datasets; (ii) compartments enriched for large complexes and RNA-binding proteins will show stronger subdiffusion (lower anomalous exponent) than compartments dominated by small globular enzymes at similar total concentration. 
Validation: We will use imaging datasets with spatially resolved transport (IDR/BioImage Archive) and align them to compartment/subcompartment annotations; model fit will be assessed by posterior predictive checks and spatial correlation metrics.

Mechanistically, these hypotheses aim to establish that mesoscale transport is not merely a byproduct of “how much protein is present” but an emergent state governed by compositional allocation to assemblies, disorder-mediated soft interactions, and spatial organization. The synthesis will yield quantitative, falsifiable relationships between proteome organization and transport parameters, enabling a predictive mesoscale biophysics layer that can be integrated with signaling and metabolic models without generating any new experimental data.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy. The project will build an integrated, analysis-ready knowledge base linking compartment-specific proteome composition to measured transport/viscosity outcomes, then fit mechanistic and data-driven models that map composition to emergent mesoscale parameters. All activities are synthesis: we will only download, curate, standardize, and analyze existing publicly available datasets and literature supplements; no new experiments, samples, or data generation will be performed.

1) Data sources (public repositories and curated literature)
A. Quantitative proteomics and absolute abundance
- ProteomeXchange Consortium datasets, primarily via PRIDE (mass spectrometry raw/processed files and sample metadata).
- PaxDB (integrated protein abundance and copy-number estimates across organisms and tissues).
- Where available, organism-specific absolute proteome resources linked from PaxDB and ProteomeXchange metadata (e.g., yeast and bacterial absolute proteomes deposited publicly).
B. Spatial localization and compartment abundance
- Human Protein Atlas (subcellular localization annotations; where quantitative, use intensity/abundance proxies).
- Spatial proteomics datasets such as hyperLOPIT and related subcellular fractionation maps deposited in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange (multi-compartment probability assignments).
- UniProt subcellular location annotations (as a harmonization layer for non-human organisms).
C. Transport/viscosity and anomalous diffusion measurements
- Image Data Resource (IDR) and BioImage Archive for deposited FRAP/SPT/FCS imaging datasets and derived measurements when provided.
- Published datasets with diffusion coefficients/anomalous exponents in supplementary tables; we will curate these into a structured database with explicit provenance (DOI, figure/table, analysis method).
- When repositories provide raw trajectories or time series, we will reanalyze using standardized, published algorithms (analysis of existing data is permitted; no new data collection).
D. Metabolomics and osmolytes
- Metabolomics Workbench (condition-labeled metabolite profiles; osmolytes and metabolites affecting hydration and crowding).
E. Structural and biophysical annotations
- Protein Data Bank (PDB) for experimentally determined structures and complex assemblies.
- AlphaFold Protein Structure Database for predicted structures to estimate size/shape proxies broadly.
- MobiDB for intrinsic disorder annotations and disorder content.
- Complex Portal for curated macromolecular complexes and stoichiometries.
- Optional supporting resources: BioGRID/IntAct for interaction degree (as a proxy for binding propensity), used cautiously to avoid confounding by study bias.

2) Harmonization and integration
A. Entity resolution
- Map proteins across datasets using UniProt accessions and gene identifiers; maintain organism-specific namespaces.
- Standardize compartments using Gene Ontology Cellular Component (GO-CC) terms; build a compartment ontology mapping (e.g., “cytosol” vs “cytoplasm” vs “cytoplasmic matrix”) with explicit rules.
B. Condition and metadata normalization
- Create a controlled vocabulary for conditions (stress type, osmolarity, temperature, cell cycle stage, differentiation state) using existing ontologies where possible (e.g., EFO terms in sample metadata).
- Standardize units: diffusion coefficients (µm^2/s), viscosity (Pa·s or cP), temperature (K), probe size (nm), timescales, and analysis model used.
C. Measurement-model harmonization
- For FRAP, record fitting model (single exponential, diffusion model, reaction-diffusion) and extract comparable summary parameters (effective diffusion, mobile fraction) with uncertainty.
- For SPT, standardize MSD computation windows and fit anomalous diffusion MSD ~ t^α to obtain α and generalized diffusion coefficient; apply published localization-error corrections when raw trajectories are available.
- For FCS, record model (1- vs 2-component, anomalous exponent) and extract comparable parameters.
D. Data quality scoring
- Assign quality flags based on metadata completeness, probe identity, calibration reporting, and replicate availability. Analyses will be repeated under “strict” and “broad” inclusion criteria to assess robustness.

3) Constructing mesoscale “crowding fields” from composition
A. Compartment proteome composition
- For each organism/condition/compartment, estimate protein concentration distributions using absolute abundance (PaxDB/ProteomeXchange) combined with compartment assignment probabilities (hyperLOPIT/HPA/UniProt).
B. Size/shape and excluded-volume proxies
- Estimate hydrodynamic radius proxies from PDB/AlphaFold structures using computational geometry (e.g., radius of gyration, solvent-excluded volume) and sequence-based predictors when structures are missing.
- Incorporate oligomerization/complex membership (Complex Portal) to adjust effective particle sizes and volume occupancy.
C. Soft interaction and viscoelasticity proxies
- Disorder fraction and low-complexity regions (MobiDB) as predictors of soft interactions and transient binding.
- Interaction propensity proxies (Complex membership counts; curated interactions) to represent transient sticking that can induce subdiffusion.
D. Field representation
- Define a compartment-level crowding state vector: total macromolecular volume fraction estimate, fraction in large complexes, mean/variance of size distribution, disorder-weighted concentration, and an interaction “stickiness” index.
- Where spatial proteomics supports subcompartment gradients, represent the crowding field as a coarse spatial mixture (e.g., two- or three-zone model) rather than a single scalar.

4) Modeling and inference
A. Mechanistic coarse-grained models
- Obstruction/effective-medium models: relate excluded volume to effective diffusion (e.g., D/D0 as a function of volume fraction and size ratio).
- Viscoelastic/anomalous diffusion models: fractional Brownian motion (FBM) and generalized Langevin approaches to connect α to viscoelastic parameters; treat α as an emergent parameter influenced by disorder-weighted concentration and interaction proxies.
B. Bayesian calibration
- Use hierarchical Bayesian models to calibrate mapping from composition features to observed diffusion/viscosity, with random effects for lab/assay/probe and explicit temperature correction.
- Output posterior distributions for crowding parameters and quantify uncertainty propagation from proteomics and localization uncertainty.
C. Machine learning for prediction and feature attribution
- Train supervised models (e.g., gradient-boosted trees, elastic net, and Bayesian additive regression trees) to predict (D, α, viscosity) from crowding state vectors.
- Use cross-validation stratified by dataset/lab to avoid leakage; evaluate generalization across organisms and compartments.
- Interpretability: SHAP values and Bayesian variable inclusion to identify “crowding hubs” and key compositional drivers.

5) Validation without new experiments
- Cross-dataset validation: train on one repository/literature subset and test on independent subsets.
- Positive controls: known trends such as slower diffusion for larger probes, and reported diffusion slowdowns under osmotic stress; verify that models recover these directions.
- Consistency checks: compare inferred viscosity against independent published viscosity estimates (where available) and against metabolomics-predicted osmotic shifts.
- Posterior predictive checks: simulate expected diffusion distributions from inferred crowding fields and compare to observed distributions.

6) Timeline and milestones (30 months; adaptable to 24–36 months)
Months 0–6: Working group kickoff; finalize metadata standards; build ingestion pipelines; initial curation of diffusion/viscosity literature; release v0 schema and minimal dataset.
Months 7–12: Integrate proteomics + localization + structural annotations; compute compartment crowding state vectors; release v1 integrated dataset and documentation.
Months 13–18: Implement mechanistic and Bayesian calibration models; perform cross-dataset validation; preprint on harmonized database and baseline models.
Months 19–24: ML prediction models; feature attribution and “crowding hub” identification; cross-species/condition analyses; release v2 tools and notebooks.
Months 25–30: Community workshop; finalize manuscripts; harden software (containers/workflows); deposit final database snapshots; sustainability handoff plan.

7) Team composition and roles (multidisciplinary, multi-lab)
- Quantitative proteomics experts: curate ProteomeXchange/PaxDB mappings, normalization, batch effects.
- Spatial proteomics/localization experts: interpret hyperLOPIT/HPA, compartment ontology mapping.
- Biophysical microscopy and transport analysts: standardize FRAP/FCS/SPT parameter extraction and error models.
- Soft-matter/biophysical theorists: guide obstruction/viscoelastic modeling and interpretation.
- Statistical learning/Bayesian modelers: hierarchical calibration, uncertainty quantification, ML generalization tests.
- Research software engineers/data curators: build pipelines, database, APIs, documentation, and reproducible workflows.
- Trainees (graduate students/postdocs): lead curation sprints, model development, and open training materials.

NCEMS support is essential to convene these perspectives, support sustained curation and standard setting, and produce community-scale synthesis products that exceed the capacity of any single laboratory.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will deliver a set of durable, open resources and mechanistic insights that collectively advance understanding of emergent mesoscale physical regulation in cells.

1) Primary deliverables
A. An open, curated database of intracellular transport and material-state measurements
- A structured “Cellular Transport & Crowding” database containing diffusion coefficients, anomalous exponents, FRAP recovery parameters, and viscosity estimates extracted from Image Data Resource (IDR), BioImage Archive, and published supplements.
- Rich metadata: probe identity and size class, compartment, organism/cell type, condition, temperature, acquisition modality (FRAP/FCS/SPT), analysis model used, uncertainty/replicates, and provenance.
- A community reporting template (machine-readable) for future deposition of diffusion/viscosity results, aligned with existing imaging metadata standards where possible.
B. An integrated multi-omics “crowding state” atlas
- For each organism/condition/compartment represented, a derived crowding state vector combining: absolute abundance (PaxDB/ProteomeXchange), compartment allocation (Human Protein Atlas/hyperLOPIT), structural size proxies (PDB/AlphaFold DB), disorder content (MobiDB), and complex membership (Complex Portal), with metabolomics covariates (Metabolomics Workbench) when available.
- Versioned snapshots deposited in long-term repositories with clear licensing and citations.
C. Reproducible modeling toolkit
- Open-source pipelines to (i) ingest and harmonize datasets, (ii) compute crowding fields/state vectors, (iii) fit mechanistic and Bayesian calibration models, and (iv) train ML predictors with robust cross-dataset validation.
- Prebuilt notebooks demonstrating key analyses, including uncertainty-aware predictions and feature attribution.

2) Scientific outcomes: mechanistic insights into emergent mesoscale regulation
A. Evidence for (or against) conserved crowding setpoints
- Quantitative assessment of whether cytosol, nucleoplasm, and other compartments maintain constrained ranges of inferred crowding/viscosity across species and baseline conditions.
- If supported, this would suggest that maintaining mesoscale material state is a conserved cellular objective, akin to homeostasis of pH or ion concentration.
B. Identification of “crowding hubs” and compositional control knobs
- A ranked set of protein classes and compositional features that disproportionately influence emergent viscosity and anomalous diffusion (e.g., allocation to ribosomes/large complexes, disorder-weighted concentration, chaperone abundance).
- Mechanistic interpretation linking these hubs to soft interactions and viscoelasticity, providing a physical layer to complement genetic/pathway-centric views.
C. Predictive links from omics to transport landscapes
- Validated models that predict diffusion regimes (D and α) for probe classes given compartment composition, enabling inference in systems where transport has not been directly measured.
- Condition-dependent predictions (stress, cell cycle, differentiation) that connect proteome/metabolome shifts to mesoscale physical consequences, reframing diverse phenotypes as material-state transitions.

3) Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Integrative understanding: The project will connect proteome allocation and organization to emergent transport constraints that shape signaling, metabolism, and assembly dynamics.
- Reinterpretation of phenotypes: Many reported changes in pathway activity under stress may be partially explained by altered encounter rates and diffusion-limited kinetics; our atlas will help researchers test these ideas quantitatively.
- Methodological advancement: By combining hierarchical Bayesian calibration with mechanistic crowding models and interpretable ML, the project will provide a general blueprint for synthesizing heterogeneous biophysical measurements.

4) Enabling future research (without committing to new experiments)
- The database and standards will lower the barrier for the community to reuse existing imaging datasets and to deposit future measurements in interoperable form.
- The crowding state atlas can be integrated downstream with existing systems biology models (e.g., metabolic network simulations) to incorporate diffusion/viscosity constraints.
- The identified “crowding hubs” will generate testable hypotheses for future experimentalists, but this project itself will not perform experimental validation.

5) Dissemination and sustainability
- Publications: at least two major manuscripts (database/standards paper; cross-species mechanistic/predictive modeling paper) plus method notes.
- Workshops: an NCEMS-hosted training workshop on “Synthesis biophysics of intracellular transport,” including hands-on sessions using the released pipelines.
- Persistent hosting: database snapshots and DOIs via Zenodo; code on GitHub/GitLab; container images on public registries; documentation site (e.g., ReadTheDocs).
- Sustainability plan: governance for community contributions (issue trackers, contribution guidelines, schema versioning), and coordination with existing repository communities (IDR/BioImage Archive, ProteomeXchange) to align metadata fields and reduce duplication.

Collectively, these outcomes will establish protein crowding as a quantitatively predictable, emergent mesoscale regulator and provide the community-scale synthesis infrastructure needed to make intracellular material-state biology a routine, data-driven component of molecular and cellular science.

[Budget and Resources]
This project is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring sustained curation, multi-repository integration, and advanced modeling. The budget emphasizes personnel time for data harmonization and research software engineering, computational resources for large-scale reanalysis and model fitting, and NCEMS-facilitated collaboration and training.

1) Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (2.0 FTE total across participating labs): One focused on biophysical transport modeling (FRAP/FCS/SPT harmonization; mechanistic and Bayesian models) and one focused on proteome/spatial proteomics integration (ProteomeXchange/PaxDB normalization; localization mapping; feature engineering). Postdocs are essential because the project requires deep cross-domain synthesis rather than narrow single-dataset analysis.
- 1 Research software engineer / data curator (1.0 FTE): Builds and maintains ingestion pipelines, database schema, APIs/exports, workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), CI/testing, and documentation. This role is critical for producing reusable community infrastructure.
- 1 Graduate student (0.5–1.0 FTE equivalent): Supports literature curation, quality scoring, and development of training notebooks; gains workforce training in data-centric biophysical cell biology.
- Part-time PI/co-PI effort across multiple institutions: Provides domain oversight (proteomics, spatial proteomics, soft-matter physics, statistical learning), ensures cross-lab integration, and mentors trainees. The multi-PI structure reflects the transdisciplinary nature of the work.

2) Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or institutional HPC allocations: Needed for (i) downloading and processing large imaging datasets from IDR/BioImage Archive, (ii) structural feature computation at scale from AlphaFold DB/PDB, and (iii) Bayesian hierarchical model fitting and cross-validation.
- Data storage: Budget for secure, backed-up storage of intermediate processed files and cache layers (while respecting that authoritative raw data remain in source repositories). Emphasis is on storing derived, analysis-ready representations and provenance.

3) Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venues): Funds for travel and lodging for diverse participants (multiple institutions, career stages, and geographic locations). In-person synthesis meetings accelerate agreement on standards, resolve integration bottlenecks, and support trainee networking.
- Conference dissemination: Targeted travel for presenting results and standards at relevant meetings (computational biology, proteomics, biophysics), maximizing adoption.

4) Workshops and training events
- Budget for at least one hands-on training workshop (hybrid when possible): venue/AV support (if needed), training materials preparation, and trainee participation support.
- Curation sprints and hackathons: modest support for coordination, facilitation, and participant access (e.g., temporary compute accounts) to broaden community contribution.

5) Open science infrastructure
- DOI and archival costs are minimized by using Zenodo and existing repositories, but budget supports: documentation hosting (if needed), automated testing infrastructure, and maintenance time to ensure long-term usability.
- Accessibility and interoperability: resources for implementing standard exports (CSV/Parquet), lightweight APIs, and metadata validation tools.

6) Justification relative to synthesis goals and NCEMS need
The requested resources are necessary because the core challenge is not a single analysis but the creation of a reusable, community-scale synthesis product: a harmonized transport/viscosity database linked to multi-omics and structural annotations, with validated models and reproducible pipelines. This scope exceeds a typical single-lab effort due to heterogeneous data types (omics, imaging, structure, metabolomics), the need for standard setting and provenance-aware curation, and the requirement to produce open, maintained infrastructure and training materials. NCEMS support uniquely enables the coordination, convening power, and open-science scaffolding required to deliver these outcomes without generating any new experimental data.

Cells exhibit emergent mesoscale physical properties—effective viscosity, anomalous diffusion, and spatially heterogeneous crowding—arising from collective protein/RNA concentrations at 10–1000 nm scales. These properties shape signaling and metabolism but are not predictable from individual macromolecules. This project will test whether crowding-related emergent parameters can be predicted from proteome composition and subcellular organization across organisms and conditions.

We will synthesize: (i) quantitative proteomics and absolute protein copy numbers (ProteomeXchange, PaxDB), (ii) subcellular localization and abundance maps (Human Protein Atlas; spatial proteomics datasets such as hyperLOPIT in PRIDE), (iii) measurements of diffusion and viscosity from fluorescence correlation spectroscopy, single-particle tracking, and FRAP compiled from public repositories and literature supplements (IDR/BioImage Archive; curated datasets), (iv) metabolomics that influences osmotic/crowding states (Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) structural/biophysical properties of proteins (PDB, AlphaFold DB; predicted disorder from MobiDB; oligomerization from Complex Portal).

We will fit these fields to observed diffusion/viscosity measurements using Bayesian calibration and coarse-grained physical models (e.g., obstruction scaling, fractional Brownian motion). Machine learning models will predict diffusion regimes for probe classes (enzymes, ribosomes, signaling proteins) given local proteome composition and interaction propensity.

Key questions: Do cells maintain conserved crowding setpoints in specific compartments (nucleoplasm vs cytosol) despite large proteome changes? Which protein classes (ribosomal proteins, chaperones, intrinsically disordered proteins) disproportionately control emergent viscosity? Can we predict condition-dependent shifts (stress, cell cycle, differentiation) in mesoscale diffusion landscapes from omics alone?

Expected insights include a quantitative, cross-species map linking proteome composition to emergent physical states, and identification of “crowding hubs” whose abundance changes re-tune global reaction kinetics. The project enables reinterpretation of many phenotypes (e.g., slowed signaling under stress) as consequences of mesoscale physical state changes.

This requires team science integrating quantitative proteomics, soft-matter physics, microscopy-based biophysics, and statistical learning, plus substantial data curation across heterogeneous measurement types. NCEMS support is needed to coordinate community standards for reporting diffusion/viscosity, build open databases of calibrated measurements, and deliver reproducible pipelines and training modules for a new generation of data-savvy biophysical cell biologists.

title: Emergent Ribosome Assembly Landscapes: Integrating Cryo-EM Intermediates, rRNA Processing Maps, and Proteomics to Explain Assembly Robustness
title_norm: emergent ribosome assembly landscapes integrating cryoem intermediates rrna processing maps and proteomics to explain assembly robustness
abstract_text:
Ribosome biogenesis involves mesoscale ribonucleoprotein intermediates (20–30 nm) that undergo coordinated folding, processing, and factor exchange. The emergent phenomenon is robust, directional assembly arising from collective interactions among rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and dozens of assembly factors—behavior not deducible from any single component. This project will synthesize structural and functional datasets to infer universal principles governing assembly pathway robustness and failure modes.

We will integrate: (i) cryo-EM structures of ribosome assembly intermediates and associated factors (EMDB, PDB), (ii) time-resolved rRNA processing and modification maps (RNA-seq and specialized datasets in GEO/SRA; MODOMICS for modifications), (iii) quantitative proteomics of assembly factors and ribosomal proteins under perturbations (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) genetic interaction and essentiality data for assembly factors (BioGRID, DepMap; yeast genetic interaction networks), and (v) subcellular localization/imaging of nucleolar subcompartments (Human Protein Atlas; IDR datasets).

We will build a unified “assembly state graph” where nodes are structural intermediates (from cryo-EM) and edges represent transitions constrained by rRNA processing events and factor binding/unbinding. Using probabilistic graphical models and energy landscape concepts, we will infer transition probabilities and identify bottlenecks. Comparative analysis across bacteria, yeast, and human will reveal conserved vs lineage-specific modules. We will also apply network controllability analysis to identify minimal sets of factors that steer assembly away from dead-end states.

Hypotheses: (1) assembly robustness emerges from redundant, partially ordered modules that buffer factor loss; (2) specific mesoscale nucleolar subcompartments correspond to distinct regions of the assembly state graph; and (3) disease mutations in ribosomopathies disproportionately affect transitions with low redundancy, explaining tissue-specific vulnerability.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of assembly intermediates aligned to processing timelines, quantitative identification of fragile transitions, and mechanistic explanations for why some perturbations cause global collapse while others are compensated. Methodological advances include pipelines to harmonize heterogeneous cryo-EM intermediate annotations and to integrate structural states with sequencing-based processing data.

This project requires collaboration among cryo-EM structural biologists, RNA processing experts, network scientists, and disease geneticists, and it depends entirely on integrating numerous public datasets beyond any single lab’s scope. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open workflows, and trainee-led hackathons to produce reusable resources for understanding emergent mesoscale assembly in RNP machines.

Ribosome biogenesis is among the most complex and consequential self-assembly processes in cells. It transforms long precursor rRNAs and dozens of ribosomal proteins into a functional ribonucleoprotein (RNP) machine through a coordinated sequence of rRNA folding, chemical modification, endo/exonucleolytic processing, and exchange of transient assembly factors. The key mesoscale entities in this process are pre-ribosomal particles—20–30 nm RNP intermediates—whose composition and structure evolve over time and space. At this scale, emergent properties arise: directionality (net forward progress despite reversibility of individual steps), robustness (successful assembly under genetic and environmental variability), and quality control (selective degradation or recycling of aberrant intermediates). These behaviors cannot be inferred from any single molecule (an rRNA helix, a ribosomal protein, or an assembly factor) because they result from collective interactions among many components and from the coupling of molecular events to subcellular organization.

Over the last decade, cryo-electron microscopy has produced a rich structural catalog of assembly intermediates in bacteria, yeast, and human. Deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and Protein Data Bank (PDB), these structures reveal transient factor binding, rRNA domain docking order, and large-scale conformational checkpoints. In parallel, high-throughput sequencing has generated maps of rRNA processing and modification. Public repositories such as NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA) contain RNA-seq, NET-seq, and specialized rRNA-focused datasets (including pulse-chase and time-course experiments) that quantify precursor rRNA species and processing kinetics under perturbations. MODOMICS and related resources compile known rRNA modifications and the enzymes that install them, providing an additional functional layer that influences folding and factor recruitment.

Quantitative proteomics has further expanded what is known. PRIDE/ProteomeXchange hosts datasets measuring the abundance of ribosomal proteins and assembly factors across conditions, including depletion of specific factors, stress responses, and disease contexts. These data provide system-level readouts of how perturbations redistribute factors, stall intermediates, or trigger compensatory pathways. Genetic interaction resources (BioGRID for curated interactions; comprehensive yeast genetic interaction networks from large-scale screens; and human essentiality/fitness screens such as DepMap) add a complementary view of functional redundancy and pathway buffering. Finally, imaging and localization data—e.g., the Human Protein Atlas and imaging datasets in the Image Data Resource (IDR)—provide spatial context, including nucleolar subcompartment localization and dynamic relocalization of assembly factors.

Despite the abundance of public data, key gaps remain because these datasets are rarely integrated. First, structural intermediates are often annotated inconsistently across studies, species, and labs (e.g., naming of states, factor occupancy, rRNA processing stage). Second, structural snapshots are difficult to align to processing timelines: an intermediate resolved by cryo-EM is not automatically linked to a specific rRNA cleavage or modification state measured by sequencing. Third, robustness and failure modes are not directly visible in any one dataset. A proteomics dataset may show accumulation of factors, but without structural and processing alignment it is hard to interpret which transition failed. Conversely, a structural intermediate may suggest a checkpoint, but without genetic interaction and perturbation data it is unclear whether that checkpoint is buffered by redundancy.

This proposal addresses these gaps through synthesis research: building a unified, cross-species “assembly state graph” that integrates structural states (EMDB/PDB), rRNA processing/modification trajectories (GEO/SRA, MODOMICS), proteomic perturbation responses (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), genetic buffering (BioGRID, DepMap, yeast interaction networks), and mesoscale spatial organization (Human Protein Atlas, IDR). The central significance is that ribosome assembly is a canonical mesoscale emergence problem: a large RNP transitions through a landscape of partially ordered states, where local molecular interactions are shaped by global constraints (particle topology, factor availability, nucleolar organization) and where robustness emerges from modularity and redundancy.

Understanding these emergent principles has broad implications. Ribosome biogenesis defects underlie ribosomopathies and cancer-associated nucleolar stress, yet tissue-specific vulnerability remains puzzling. A synthesis framework can identify which transitions are fragile (low redundancy) and therefore more likely to produce disease phenotypes. More generally, ribosome assembly provides a tractable testbed for mesoscale emergence in RNP machines, with parallels to spliceosome assembly, ribonucleoprotein granules, and viral capsid maturation.

Existing public data now make this synthesis feasible at community scale. The breadth of cryo-EM intermediate structures, the depth of sequencing-based processing maps, and the diversity of perturbation proteomics and genetic interaction datasets collectively enable inference of transition structure, directionality constraints, and buffering mechanisms. However, harmonizing these heterogeneous resources requires coordinated expertise (structural biology, RNA biology, proteomics, network science, statistical modeling, and disease genetics) and substantial curation and computational infrastructure—well beyond a single lab. NCEMS support is essential to convene a multidisciplinary working group, build reusable open workflows, and produce a community resource that converts disparate public datasets into mechanistic insight about emergent mesoscale assembly robustness.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around precise questions about how robust, directional ribosome assembly emerges from the collective behavior of mesoscale pre-ribosomal particles. We focus on inference and prediction using only publicly available data, with validation performed by cross-dataset consistency checks, held-out datasets, and benchmarking against well-established checkpoints described in the literature.

Research Question 1: What is the minimal set of mesoscale assembly states and transitions that explains the diversity of observed cryo-EM intermediates across studies and species?
Hypothesis 1A (state modularity): Cryo-EM intermediates can be represented as combinations of a limited number of conserved structural modules (e.g., rRNA domain docking modules, factor-binding modules) that recur across datasets, generating apparent diversity by recombination.
Measurable predictions: (i) clustering intermediates by factor occupancy and rRNA conformational descriptors will yield a small set of reproducible “module signatures” shared across independent studies; (ii) module presence will correlate with specific rRNA processing/modification milestones.
Validation using existing data: We will test reproducibility by training module definitions on a subset of EMDB/PDB entries and evaluating whether held-out intermediates from different labs/species map to the same module signatures with high confidence.

Research Question 2: How are structural intermediates coupled to rRNA processing and modification timelines to produce directionality?
Hypothesis 2A (processing-gated transitions): Directionality emerges because certain structural transitions are conditionally permitted only after specific rRNA cleavage or modification events, effectively gating transitions and preventing backtracking.
Measurable predictions: (i) inferred transition probabilities in the assembly state graph will increase sharply after specific processing events (e.g., cleavage at defined sites in pre-rRNA); (ii) perturbations that slow a processing step (as observed in GEO/SRA time courses) will shift occupancy toward pre-gated structural states (as observed in cryo-EM and proteomics).
Validation using existing data: We will align rRNA processing kinetics from published time courses with structural state occupancy inferred from cryo-EM and proteomics perturbation datasets; consistency will be assessed via likelihood-based model comparison (gated vs ungated models).

Research Question 3: What network features explain robustness to loss or fluctuation of assembly factors?
Hypothesis 3A (redundant, partially ordered pathways): Robustness arises from redundant alternative routes through the state graph, enabled by partially ordered modules and compensatory factor exchange.
Measurable predictions: (i) factors with many synthetic genetic interactions (yeast networks in BioGRID and large-scale screens) will correspond to nodes/edges with high alternative-path counts; (ii) proteomics under perturbation will show compensatory upregulation/relocalization of factors predicted to provide alternative routes.
Validation using existing data: We will compute redundancy metrics (k-shortest paths, edge-disjoint paths) and test correlation with genetic interaction degree and with proteomic compensation signatures across PRIDE datasets.

Research Question 4: How does mesoscale spatial organization in the nucleolus map onto the assembly state graph?
Hypothesis 4A (spatial compartmentalization of graph regions): Distinct nucleolar subcompartments correspond to contiguous regions of the state graph (sets of states/transitions) characterized by shared factor localization and processing events.
Measurable predictions: (i) factors localized to fibrillar center/dense fibrillar component/granular component (from Human Protein Atlas and IDR) will preferentially associate with early/mid/late graph regions; (ii) transitions that cross these regions will coincide with known trafficking or maturation steps.
Validation using existing data: We will integrate localization annotations with factor occupancy in structural states and test for enrichment of subcompartment labels along inferred pseudotime ordering of states.

Research Question 5: Why do disease-associated mutations produce tissue-specific vulnerability despite ubiquitous ribosome biogenesis?
Hypothesis 5A (fragile transitions drive vulnerability): Ribosomopathy-associated genes disproportionately affect low-redundancy transitions (bottlenecks) in the state graph, leading to context-dependent failure when factor supply or stress differs by tissue.
Measurable predictions: (i) genes implicated in ribosomopathies (curated from OMIM/ClinVar and literature) will be enriched among controllability-critical nodes/edges (network controllability and betweenness); (ii) DepMap dependency patterns will align with predicted bottlenecks, with cell lines exhibiting high dependency on bottleneck factors showing expression/proteomic signatures consistent with limited buffering.
Validation using existing data: Enrichment tests (permutation-based) will quantify whether disease genes map to fragile transitions more than expected by chance, controlling for annotation bias and gene essentiality.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses aim to produce mechanistic insight into mesoscale emergence: how a large RNP navigates an energy- and information-constrained landscape, how gating and modularity produce directionality, how network redundancy yields robustness, how spatial compartmentalization organizes the landscape, and how fragility explains pathological failure modes—all inferred and tested through synthesis of existing public structural, sequencing, proteomic, genetic, and imaging data.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and guiding principle (synthesis-only): All analyses will use publicly available datasets; no new experiments, samples, or data collection will be performed. The working group will focus on harmonization, integration, and modeling to infer an emergent assembly landscape across bacteria, yeast, and human.

1) Data sources (specific repositories)
Structural intermediates:
- Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB): density maps and metadata for pre-ribosomal particles.
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): atomic models and factor annotations for intermediates.
- UniProt: protein identifiers, domains, isoforms, and cross-references.
- Pfam/InterPro: domain architecture for assembly factors.

rRNA processing and modification:
- NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA): RNA-seq and specialized datasets reporting pre-rRNA intermediates, processing defects, and time courses.
- ENA (European Nucleotide Archive) as mirrored access where relevant.
- MODOMICS: curated rRNA modification types, positions, and enzymes.
- RiboMethSeq and related published datasets (as deposited in GEO/SRA) for 2’-O-methylation profiles.

Proteomics:
- PRIDE / ProteomeXchange: quantitative proteomics of ribosome biogenesis factors and ribosomal proteins under perturbations.

Genetic interactions and essentiality:
- BioGRID: physical and genetic interactions for assembly factors.
- DepMap (Cancer Dependency Map): CRISPR/RNAi gene dependency scores and expression for human cell lines.
- Published yeast genetic interaction matrices (available via repositories and supplementary data; indexed through BioGRID where possible).

Subcellular localization and imaging:
- Human Protein Atlas (HPA): subcellular localization annotations and images.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated microscopy datasets including nucleolar markers and protein localization.

Disease variant resources (for mapping, not experimentation):
- ClinVar and OMIM (where accessible) and curated literature lists of ribosomopathy genes.

2) Data ingestion, identifier harmonization, and curation
- Establish a unified identifier mapping layer across species using UniProt accessions, Ensembl gene IDs, and NCBI Gene IDs; orthology mapping via eggNOG or OrthoDB.
- Create controlled vocabularies for assembly factors, ribosomal proteins, and processing steps (cleavage sites, ITS/ETS regions) and map synonyms from EMDB/PDB metadata and publications.
- Structural metadata standardization: parse EMDB/PDB entries to extract factor occupancy, rRNA segments present, resolution, organism, and assigned maturation stage (when provided). Where stage labels are inconsistent, derive standardized labels via computed descriptors (below).

3) Feature extraction from cryo-EM intermediates
- Represent each structural intermediate as a feature vector capturing:
  a) Factor occupancy (binary/probabilistic from model annotations).
  b) rRNA conformational descriptors: presence/absence of major rRNA domains, inter-domain contacts, and global compaction metrics derived from atomic coordinates (PDB) or segmented maps (EMDB).
  c) Ribosomal protein incorporation status.
- Compute similarity between intermediates using mixed-type distance metrics (e.g., Jaccard for occupancy + continuous distances for geometric descriptors).
- Cluster intermediates using consensus clustering (e.g., hierarchical + Leiden on similarity graphs) to define reproducible state families. Stability assessed by bootstrap resampling across entries.

4) Aligning structural states to rRNA processing/modification timelines
- For each organism, curate processing events (cleavage sites, trimming steps, modification installation) from GEO/SRA datasets and literature-linked metadata.
- Where time-course data exist, infer processing pseudotime using probabilistic models (e.g., hidden Markov models on precursor abundance trajectories).
- Link structural states to processing stages by probabilistic matching: states with factor signatures known to associate with certain processing steps serve as priors; posterior assignments refined by maximizing agreement with perturbation datasets (below).

5) Integrating proteomics perturbations to estimate state occupancies
- From PRIDE/ProteomeXchange, select datasets with perturbations to assembly factors (knockdown/knockout/degradation systems already performed by original authors) and quantify differential abundance of relevant factors and ribosomal proteins.
- Use a deconvolution approach: treat observed proteomic changes as mixtures of underlying state occupancy shifts, where each state has an expected factor composition. Fit mixture weights via constrained regression (nonnegative least squares / Bayesian deconvolution) with uncertainty estimates.

6) Building the “assembly state graph” and inferring transitions
- Nodes: harmonized structural state families.
- Directed edges: candidate transitions constrained by (i) monotonicity of processing events (cleavage/modification order) and (ii) feasible factor exchange (gain/loss patterns).
- Infer edge weights (transition probabilities) using probabilistic graphical models:
  - Dynamic Bayesian networks / hidden Markov models where latent states are structural nodes and emissions are processing/proteomics observables.
  - Regularization to favor sparse, interpretable graphs.
- Energy landscape interpretation: define an effective potential over states derived from negative log stationary probabilities and transition asymmetries; identify barriers and metastable basins.

7) Robustness, redundancy, and controllability analyses
- Redundancy metrics: number of alternative paths between early and late states; edge-disjoint path counts; sensitivity of reachability to edge removal.
- Bottleneck detection: betweenness centrality, minimum cut sets, and transition entropy.
- Network controllability: apply structural controllability frameworks to identify minimal driver nodes/factors whose modulation (inferred from perturbation datasets) can steer the system away from dead-end basins.
- Map genetic interaction data (BioGRID, yeast matrices) onto graph features: test whether synthetic sick/lethal interactions concentrate around predicted bottlenecks or low-redundancy modules.

8) Spatial mapping to nucleolar subcompartments
- Use HPA/IDR localization annotations to label factors by nucleolar subcompartment when available.
- Compute enrichment of localization labels across graph regions (early/mid/late) and across modules; test compartment boundaries against predicted high-barrier transitions.

9) Disease mapping and cross-species comparison
- Map ribosomopathy genes/variants (ClinVar/OMIM/literature) onto factors and graph positions.
- Compare bacteria/yeast/human graphs via orthology-mapped modules; identify conserved cores vs lineage-specific branches.
- Use DepMap dependencies to test whether bottleneck factors show higher essentiality and context dependence.

10) Validation (no experiments)
- Cross-dataset validation: hold out subsets of cryo-EM intermediates or proteomics datasets and test predictive likelihood of the inferred graph.
- Positive controls: known checkpoints (e.g., established factor dependencies) should appear as high-barrier transitions or strong gating constraints.
- Negative controls: randomized identifier mappings and permuted interaction networks to ensure signals exceed null expectations.

11) Timeline and milestones (30 months; adaptable to NCEMS cycle)
Months 0–6: Working group kickoff; ontology/identifier layer; initial EMDB/PDB ingestion; first reproducible pipeline release.
Months 6–12: Structural feature extraction; consensus state families; first cross-species mapping draft; trainee-led hackathon on curation.
Months 12–18: Processing timeline inference from GEO/SRA; probabilistic alignment of states to processing; first assembly state graph per organism.
Months 18–24: Proteomics deconvolution; transition inference with graphical models; robustness and controllability analyses.
Months 24–30: Spatial compartment mapping; disease and DepMap integration; finalize atlas, manuscripts, and public resource portal.

12) Team composition (multilab, transdisciplinary)
- Cryo-EM structural biologists (annotation standards, structural descriptors).
- RNA processing/modification experts (processing event curation, interpretation).
- Proteomics specialists (dataset selection, normalization, batch correction).
- Network scientists/statisticians (graph inference, controllability, uncertainty quantification).
- Computational biologists/software engineers (workflow infrastructure, packaging).
- Disease geneticists/clinician-scientists (variant curation, ribosomopathy interpretation).
- Trainees (graduate students/postdocs) embedded across tasks, leading reproducible notebooks and hackathon modules.

NCEMS support is essential for convening these perspectives, sustaining community-scale curation, and providing neutral infrastructure for open, reproducible synthesis products that no single lab can produce alone.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables (concrete, reusable products)
1) Cross-species Ribosome Assembly Atlas (public resource):
- A harmonized catalog of cryo-EM pre-ribosomal intermediates from EMDB/PDB, standardized with consistent factor occupancy, rRNA domain descriptors, and mapped organism/stage metadata.
- A curated library of rRNA processing and modification events linked to GEO/SRA accessions and MODOMICS entries, with standardized cleavage/modification nomenclature.
- Integrated perturbation summaries from PRIDE/ProteomeXchange that quantify how factor/ribosomal protein abundances shift across conditions.

2) Assembly State Graphs and inferred landscapes:
- For bacteria, yeast, and human: directed assembly state graphs with estimated transition probabilities, uncertainty intervals, and inferred gating constraints tied to processing events.
- Identification of metastable basins (stall states), high-barrier transitions, and alternative routes that contribute to robustness.

3) Robustness and controllability toolkit:
- Open-source software implementing redundancy metrics, bottleneck identification, and network controllability analyses tailored to assembly graphs.
- A standardized reporting format (“assembly graph schema”) enabling other groups to add additional RNP machines or new public datasets without reengineering.

4) Mechanistic synthesis insights (testable, literature-grounded explanations)
- A quantitative explanation of how partially ordered modules and redundant routes generate robust directionality at the mesoscale, even when individual steps are reversible.
- A map of which processing events act as gates and which factor exchanges are most predictive of forward progression.
- A spatially informed model linking nucleolar subcompartments to contiguous regions of the assembly landscape, providing a mesoscale bridge between molecular events and organelle-scale organization.

5) Disease-relevant interpretations without new experiments
- A ranked list of “fragile transitions” disproportionately impacted by ribosomopathy genes/variants, with mechanistic rationales grounded in graph redundancy and controllability.
- Integration with DepMap to contextualize which bottleneck factors show cell-type-dependent essentiality, offering a synthesis-based explanation for variable vulnerability.

Impact on understanding mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project directly advances NCEMS’s mission by explaining an emergent mesoscale phenomenon—robust, directional RNP assembly—through community-scale synthesis of heterogeneous public data. Rather than treating ribosome biogenesis as a linear pathway, we will formalize it as a landscape of states and transitions whose global properties (robustness, fragility, compartmentalization) emerge from network structure and gating constraints. The resulting framework will clarify how mesoscale particles navigate competing interactions, how redundancy is distributed across the landscape, and how the nucleolus organizes and constrains assembly.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Generalizable methodology: The assembly graph schema and inference pipeline will be transferable to other mesoscale assembly systems (spliceosome, proteasome assembly, viral capsid maturation, mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis), enabling broader synthesis efforts.
- Improved interpretability of perturbation datasets: By providing a state-based model, the project will help researchers interpret existing proteomics and transcriptomics perturbations in terms of which assembly transitions are affected.
- Training and workforce development: Trainees will gain experience in integrative analysis across structural biology, omics, and network science, aligned with NCEMS’s goal of training data-savvy scientists.

Enabling future research
While this project will not generate new data, it will substantially increase the value of existing datasets by making them interoperable and mechanistically interpretable. The atlas and tools will allow future investigators to:
- Rapidly map new public cryo-EM intermediates into a shared state space.
- Predict which processing steps or factors are likely to be compensable vs catastrophic when perturbed.
- Formulate targeted hypotheses for future experimental work (outside the scope of this proposal) based on identified bottlenecks and gates.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least two major manuscripts (methods/resource paper; biological synthesis insights across species and disease mapping), plus organism-specific or module-focused collaborative papers.
- Workshops: NCEMS-hosted working group meetings and open tutorials on using the atlas and pipelines.
- Public portal: a lightweight web interface (e.g., static site + downloadable artifacts) to browse state graphs, modules, and linked datasets, with programmatic access via APIs.

Long-term sustainability
- Persistent archiving: versioned releases deposited in Zenodo with DOIs; container images archived in public registries.
- Community governance: a contributor guide and curation policy enabling ongoing additions, with issue tracking for annotation disputes.
- Interoperability: adoption of standard identifiers (UniProt/Ensembl) and export formats (JSON schema, TSV, GraphML) to ensure the atlas remains usable as repositories evolve.

Overall, the project will produce a durable, open, community resource that transforms fragmented public data into a coherent mechanistic understanding of emergent mesoscale ribosome assembly landscapes and their robustness and failure modes.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy and NCEMS fit
This is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring coordinated curation, integration, and modeling across multiple public repositories. Funds are requested to support personnel time for data engineering and analysis, compute for large-scale integration (cryo-EM feature extraction and multi-omics modeling), and working-group activities that enable cross-disciplinary collaboration and trainee training. No funds are allocated for experiments, sample acquisition, or new data generation.

Personnel (primary cost driver)
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (computational focus; 2–3 years):
  1) Structural/graph modeling postdoc to lead cryo-EM feature extraction, state clustering, and graph inference.
  2) Multi-omics integration postdoc to lead processing timeline inference, proteomics deconvolution, and cross-dataset validation.
- 2 Graduate research assistants (part-time over 2–3 years):
  Support curation (ontology, identifier mapping), documentation, and notebook-based reproducibility; trainees will lead hackathon modules and tutorials.
- 1 Research software engineer / programmer analyst (50–100% FTE depending on award size):
  Build and maintain ETL pipelines, workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, CI testing, and the public portal.
- PI/Co-PI effort (modest, distributed across participating labs):
  Coordination, scientific oversight, and integration across disciplines; emphasis on enabling team science rather than duplicative analysis.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations:
  Needed for batch downloading and parsing EMDB/PDB, computing structural descriptors at scale, running Bayesian/graphical models with resampling, and generating reproducible containers.
- Data storage and backup:
  Storage for derived feature matrices, intermediate files, and cached public datasets (within repository terms). Costs include secure backups and long-term archiving of releases.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2 in-person meetings per year, plus virtual meetings):
  Travel support for geographically distributed participants, with priority for trainees and early-career researchers and for inclusion of investigators from primarily undergraduate institutions and under-resourced institutions.
- Conference dissemination:
  Limited travel for presenting synthesis outputs at relevant meetings (e.g., ASCB, RNA Society, Gordon Conferences on Ribosome Biogenesis, cryo-EM meetings), emphasizing outreach and recruitment of contributors.

Workshops and training events
- Annual open workshop hosted through NCEMS:
  Hands-on training in using the atlas, running workflows, and contributing annotations; includes support for instructional materials, venue/virtual platform costs, and trainee participation.
- Trainee-led hackathons (1–2/year):
  Microgrants for trainee participation, facilitation, and compute to run reproducibility checks and curation sprints.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo archiving (no direct cost, but effort allocated):
  Personnel time to prepare versioned releases, metadata, and DOIs.
- Web dissemination:
  Minimal hosting costs for a static documentation/portal site (e.g., GitHub Pages) plus optional lightweight server costs if interactive graph browsing is implemented.

Justification relative to synthesis goals
Personnel support enables the intensive, expert curation and integration required to harmonize heterogeneous datasets and build validated assembly graphs—work that cannot be accomplished by a single lab. Compute resources are essential for scalable structural feature extraction and probabilistic modeling. Travel and workshops are integral to NCEMS’s working-group model, ensuring diverse expertise, training the next generation, and producing community-adopted standards. All budget categories directly support synthesis, integration, open dissemination, and workforce development, fully aligned with NCEMS funding requirements and the constraint of no new data generation.

Comparative analysis across bacteria, yeast, and human will reveal conserved vs lineage-specific modules. We will also apply network controllability analysis to identify minimal sets of factors that steer assembly away from dead-end states.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of assembly intermediates aligned to processing timelines, quantitative identification of fragile transitions, and mechanistic explanations for why some perturbations cause global collapse while others are compensated. Methodological advances include pipelines to harmonize heterogeneous cryo-EM intermediate annotations and to integrate structural states with sequencing-based processing data.

This project requires collaboration among cryo-EM structural biologists, RNA processing experts, network scientists, and disease geneticists, and it depends entirely on integrating numerous public datasets beyond any single lab’s scope. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open workflows, and trainee-led hackathons to produce reusable resources for understanding emergent mesoscale assembly in RNP machines.

title: Mesoscale Signaling Microclusters as Emergent Computation: A Synthesis of Immune Receptor Imaging, Phosphoproteomics, and Single-Cell Responses

abstract_text:
Immune receptors form mesoscale microclusters (50–300 nm) at the plasma membrane that act as emergent computational units, integrating ligand binding, mechanical forces, and feedback to produce switch-like or graded activation. The emergent phenomenon is that collective receptor organization and kinase/phosphatase partitioning yields signaling behaviors not predictable from receptor–ligand affinity alone.

We will synthesize: (i) TCR/BCR and Fc receptor super-resolution and TIRF imaging datasets with cluster statistics (IDR, BioImage Archive; published single-molecule localization microscopy datasets), (ii) phosphoproteomics time courses following receptor stimulation (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) single-cell functional readouts (CyTOF and flow cytometry in ImmPort; scRNA-seq activation time courses in GEO), (iv) ligand affinity/kinetics and epitope data (IEDB; structural complexes in PDB), and (v) perturbation datasets for kinases, phosphatases, and cytoskeletal regulators (DepMap; LINCS small-molecule perturbations).

Analytically, we will develop a multiscale model linking microcluster architecture to downstream phosphorylation and transcription. Computer vision and point-process statistics will quantify cluster size distributions, lifetimes, and nanoscale colocalization of signaling proteins. We will integrate these features with phosphoproteomic trajectories via dynamical systems identification (sparse regression / SINDy) and with single-cell outcomes using mixture models to capture heterogeneous activation states. A key goal is to infer whether there exist universal “microcluster motifs” (e.g., kinase-rich cores with phosphatase-exclusion shells) that correspond to distinct emergent response modes.

Hypotheses: (1) microcluster morphology encodes a mesoscale “gain control” that determines sensitivity vs specificity; (2) cytoskeletal coupling shifts microcluster systems between excitable and bistable regimes; and (3) disease-associated variants in signaling proteins act by altering partitioning into clusters rather than changing catalytic rates.

Expected insights include predictive relationships between nanoscale organization and functional immune outcomes, a cross-study standardized microcluster feature set, and mechanistic explanations for disparate experimental results in the literature. This requires team science spanning immunology, quantitative imaging, proteomics, and dynamical modeling, plus significant synthesis to harmonize stimulation protocols and imaging modalities.

NCEMS support is essential to convene communities, build open pipelines for microcluster quantification, and create an openly accessible benchmark dataset and modeling toolkit. Trainees will gain cross-disciplinary training in image analysis, omics integration, and reproducible computational immunology.
