We will integrate these features with phosphoproteomic trajectories via dynamical systems identification (sparse regression / SINDy) and with single-cell outcomes using mixture models to capture heterogeneous activation states. A key goal is to infer whether there exist universal “microcluster motifs” (e.g., kinase-rich cores with phosphatase-exclusion shells) that correspond to distinct emergent response modes.

Hypotheses: (1) microcluster morphology encodes a mesoscale “gain control” that determines sensitivity vs specificity; (2) cytoskeletal coupling shifts microcluster systems between excitable and bistable regimes; and (3) disease-associated variants in signaling proteins act by altering partitioning into clusters rather than changing catalytic rates.

Expected insights include predictive relationships between nanoscale organization and functional immune outcomes, a cross-study standardized microcluster feature set, and mechanistic explanations for disparate experimental results in the literature. This requires team science spanning immunology, quantitative imaging, proteomics, and dynamical modeling, plus significant synthesis to harmonize stimulation protocols and imaging modalities.

NCEMS support is essential to convene communities, build open pipelines for microcluster quantification, and create an openly accessible benchmark dataset and modeling toolkit. Trainees will gain cross-disciplinary training in image analysis, omics integration, and reproducible computational immunology.

[Background and Significance]
Immune receptor signaling is frequently portrayed as a molecular cascade initiated by ligand binding and propagated through kinase/phosphatase reactions. Yet decades of imaging and biochemical work indicate that the relevant “unit” of signaling is often mesoscale: receptor and adaptor proteins assemble into microclusters and higher-order patterns at the plasma membrane, typically tens to hundreds of nanometers in size. In T cells, T cell receptor (TCR) microclusters form within seconds of engagement, recruit ZAP70 and LAT-associated complexes, and can mature into larger supramolecular assemblies. In B cells, B cell receptor (BCR) clustering and antigen extraction are tightly coupled to actin dynamics and mechanical forces. Fc receptors (FcRs) similarly signal through spatially organized assemblies that depend on receptor crosslinking and cytoskeletal coupling. Across these systems, the mesoscale arrangement of receptors and signaling regulators is increasingly recognized as a primary determinant of downstream outcomes such as digital vs graded activation, adaptation, and heterogeneous single-cell responses.

The central emergent phenomenon motivating this proposal is that collective organization at the mesoscale produces computation-like behaviors—thresholding, gain control, bistability/excitability, and noise filtering—that are not predictable from receptor–ligand affinity or single-molecule kinetics alone. Microclusters can enrich kinases (e.g., Lck, ZAP70, Syk) while excluding or segregating phosphatases (e.g., CD45, SHP-1/2), creating local reaction environments that reshape effective rates and feedback structure. Mechanical coupling to actin retrograde flow and membrane tension can further bias cluster growth, lifetime, and transport, introducing time-dependent forcing that changes the dynamical regime of signaling. These are quintessential mesoscale effects: they emerge from spatial partitioning, collective interactions, and multicomponent feedback at length scales between individual proteins and whole organelles.

A large body of publicly available data exists, but it is fragmented across modalities and experimental communities. Imaging repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the BioImage Archive host TIRF, confocal, and super-resolution datasets, including single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) and structured illumination microscopy, that capture receptor and adaptor distributions. Many published studies also provide localization tables or processed images as supplementary data, enabling re-analysis of cluster statistics. In parallel, time-resolved phosphoproteomics datasets deposited in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange quantify thousands of phosphorylation events following immune receptor stimulation, offering a systems-level readout of kinase/phosphatase activity over time. Single-cell outcome measurements are likewise abundant: ImmPort contains flow cytometry and CyTOF immune monitoring studies, while the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress host scRNA-seq activation time courses and perturbation studies that reveal heterogeneous transcriptional states.

Despite this wealth, key gaps persist that are ideally suited to synthesis research. First, there is no cross-study, standardized feature representation of microclusters (size distributions, lifetimes, spatial point patterns, colocalization metrics, and motif descriptors). As a result, imaging-derived conclusions are difficult to compare across receptors, cell types, ligands, and microscopy modalities. Second, mesoscale organization is rarely quantitatively linked to downstream phosphoproteomic trajectories or single-cell functional states in a unified framework; most studies analyze one modality at a time. Third, the field lacks generalizable, testable mechanistic models that map microcluster architecture to emergent response modes (digital vs analog, adaptive vs sustained, excitable vs bistable). Finally, disease-associated variants and pharmacologic perturbations are often interpreted through changes in catalytic activity, yet public datasets (e.g., DepMap genetic dependency screens and LINCS perturbational signatures) suggest many regulators act through network- and context-dependent mechanisms that could plausibly operate via altered spatial partitioning.

NCEMS’s emphasis on emergence at the mesoscale aligns directly with these needs. The mesoscale is where spatial organization, mechanical coupling, and multivalent interactions conspire to generate new system properties. Importantly, the availability of large, heterogeneous public datasets now makes it feasible to infer cross-system “microcluster motifs” and to test whether such motifs correspond to conserved dynamical regimes and cellular outcomes. Achieving this requires coordinated integration: harmonizing metadata about stimulation conditions, ligand properties, imaging resolution, and time axes; extracting comparable quantitative features from images; linking those features to phosphoproteomic and single-cell trajectories; and building interpretable dynamical models that can be validated across independent datasets. No single laboratory typically has the breadth of expertise or the time to curate and integrate these modalities at community scale.

This working group will therefore address a foundational question in molecular and cellular immunology: how mesoscale microclusters implement emergent computation to control immune activation. By synthesizing imaging, phosphoproteomics, ligand/structure resources, single-cell outcomes, and perturbation compendia, we will produce a principled, open, and reusable framework that moves the field beyond qualitative cartoons toward predictive, cross-study generalization. The proposal leverages existing data to resolve long-standing puzzles—why similar affinities can yield different activation thresholds, why some perturbations produce paradoxical signaling, and why responses are heterogeneous even in clonal populations—by placing mesoscale organization at the center of explanation.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project is organized around precise research questions about how mesoscale microclusters (50–300 nm) generate emergent signaling behaviors across immune receptor systems. Each question is designed to be testable using only existing, publicly available datasets spanning imaging, phosphoproteomics, single-cell readouts, ligand properties, and perturbations.

RQ1: Are there universal microcluster “motifs” that recur across receptor classes (TCR, BCR, FcR) and experimental contexts, and do these motifs map to distinct emergent response modes?
Motivation: The literature describes qualitative patterns—central kinase enrichment, peripheral phosphatase exclusion, actin-associated transport, and coalescence into larger assemblies—but it is unknown whether these can be formalized into motif classes that generalize across studies.
Hypothesis 1 (H1): Microcluster architectures fall into a small number of conserved motif families (e.g., kinase-rich cores with phosphatase-exclusion shells; mixed kinase/phosphatase puncta; transient nanoclusters coupled to actin flow), and motif membership predicts downstream signaling regime (digital vs graded, adaptive vs sustained).
Measurable predictions: (i) Unsupervised clustering of standardized image-derived features will yield stable motif classes reproducible across independent datasets and modalities; (ii) motif classes will correlate with phosphoproteomic trajectory shapes (e.g., transient vs sustained phosphorylation modules) and with single-cell activation state mixtures.
Validation using existing data: Motif stability will be assessed by training on one set of imaging datasets (e.g., TCR SMLM) and testing classification on another (e.g., BCR TIRF). Downstream mapping will be validated by linking motif prevalence (or inferred motif parameters) to matched stimulation conditions represented in phosphoproteomics and single-cell datasets.

RQ2: How does microcluster morphology implement mesoscale “gain control” that tunes sensitivity vs specificity beyond receptor–ligand affinity?
Motivation: Immune receptors discriminate ligands with subtle kinetic differences, and affinity alone often fails to predict activation thresholds. Spatial organization may implement a gain mechanism by modulating local kinase/phosphatase balance and effective dwell times.
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Microcluster morphology (size distribution, density, lifetime, and nanoscale colocalization) encodes a gain-control variable that scales the effective coupling between ligand engagement and phosphorylation flux.
Measurable predictions: (i) For a given ligand affinity/kinetic class (from IEDB and PDB-linked studies), datasets exhibiting larger/longer-lived clusters or stronger kinase enrichment will show higher early phosphorylation flux (phosphoproteomics) and higher probability of crossing activation thresholds (single-cell functional markers or transcriptomic activation signatures); (ii) the relationship between affinity and outcome will be significantly improved by including microcluster features as covariates.
Validation using existing data: We will meta-analyze studies that report or enable inference of ligand potency/kinetics and imaging under comparable stimulation paradigms. Predictive models will be evaluated via cross-study validation, quantifying improvement in explained variance or classification accuracy when microcluster features are included.

RQ3: Does cytoskeletal coupling shift microcluster systems between excitable and bistable dynamical regimes?
Motivation: Actin dynamics and mechanical forces are repeatedly implicated in receptor clustering and signaling, yet the dynamical consequences (excitability vs bistability vs linear amplification) remain disputed.
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Perturbations affecting actin regulators and membrane-cortex coupling (inferred from perturbation datasets and from imaging studies with reported inhibitors) systematically move the inferred signaling dynamics between excitable (pulse-like, threshold-triggered) and bistable (hysteretic, sustained) regimes.
Measurable predictions: (i) Dynamical systems identification applied to phosphoproteomic time courses will reveal regime shifts (e.g., presence/absence of positive feedback terms, changes in effective nonlinearities) associated with conditions known to alter cytoskeletal coupling; (ii) single-cell outcome distributions will shift from unimodal graded to bimodal digital mixtures when bistability is inferred.
Validation using existing data: We will use published time-course phosphoproteomics under cytoskeletal perturbations where available, and complement with LINCS transcriptional perturbation signatures for actin regulators to infer consistent downstream state shifts. Agreement between inferred regimes and observed single-cell heterogeneity will serve as a cross-modality validation.

RQ4: Do disease-associated variants and oncogenic alterations primarily act by changing partitioning into microclusters rather than changing catalytic rates?
Motivation: Many immune dysregulation and hematologic malignancy phenotypes involve signaling proteins (kinases, adaptors, phosphatases). Public resources contain variant annotations and dependencies, but mechanistic interpretation is often limited.
Hypothesis 4 (H4): Variants and context-dependent dependencies alter emergent signaling by changing microcluster recruitment/segregation propensity (effective partition coefficients) more than intrinsic enzymatic activity.
Measurable predictions: (i) Proteins with strong immune-cell-line dependencies in DepMap and strong perturbational signatures in LINCS will be enriched among microcluster-localized components; (ii) variant-implicated proteins will occupy network positions that disproportionately affect motif classification and inferred partition parameters in the multiscale model.
Validation using existing data: We will integrate protein localization/interaction knowledge (e.g., UniProt annotations and curated interaction databases) with cluster colocalization evidence from imaging datasets and with dependency/perturbation signals. Mechanistic plausibility will be assessed by whether model fits improve when variant effects are modeled as partition changes.

Collectively, these questions aim to produce mechanistic insight into how mesoscale organization generates emergent computation: microclusters as tunable reaction compartments whose geometry and composition determine network dynamics and single-cell fate distributions. The hypotheses are deliberately framed to yield measurable, falsifiable predictions using only existing public data and to be testable across receptors, cell types, and perturbation contexts through cross-dataset synthesis.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
This project will build an end-to-end synthesis pipeline that (1) curates and harmonizes public datasets spanning immune receptor imaging, phosphoproteomics, single-cell outcomes, ligand/structure resources, and perturbation compendia; (2) extracts standardized mesoscale microcluster features from images; (3) links those features to time-resolved phosphorylation and single-cell state outcomes through aligned metadata and latent-variable mapping; and (4) infers interpretable multiscale dynamical models that can be validated across independent datasets. No new experimental data will be generated; all analyses use publicly available data.

Specific data sources (public repositories)
Imaging (microcluster architecture):
- Image Data Resource (IDR): immune signaling imaging studies with accessible metadata and image files.
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI): raw and processed microscopy datasets including TIRF and super-resolution.
- Published SMLM datasets provided via journal repositories/supplementary materials (e.g., localization tables in CSV) and Zenodo where available.

Phosphoproteomics (signaling trajectories):
- PRIDE Archive / ProteomeXchange: time-course phosphoproteomics following TCR/BCR/FcR stimulation, including inhibitor/perturbation conditions when available.

Single-cell functional outcomes:
- ImmPort: flow cytometry and CyTOF immune monitoring datasets capturing activation markers, cytokines, and signaling readouts.
- Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress: scRNA-seq activation time courses and perturbation studies in immune cells.

Ligand affinity/kinetics, epitope, and structure:
- Immune Epitope Database (IEDB): epitope annotations, assay outcomes, and where available, potency/kinetic descriptors.
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): receptor–ligand structural complexes enabling structural class annotation and interface features.

Perturbation/genetic dependency:
- DepMap (Broad): CRISPR gene dependency and expression data in immune-relevant cell lines.
- LINCS L1000 (CLUE): small-molecule and genetic perturbation transcriptional signatures for kinases, phosphatases, and cytoskeletal regulators.

Data harmonization and metadata alignment
A central challenge is aligning heterogeneous experiments without new data collection. We will create a unified metadata schema capturing: receptor type, cell type/species, stimulation modality (soluble vs surface-bound, crosslinking, APC), ligand identity and potency class, time points, imaging modality/resolution, measured markers, and perturbations (drug, knockdown/knockout). We will:
- Use controlled vocabularies/ontologies where possible (e.g., Cell Ontology for cell types; UniProt IDs for proteins; PSI-MS terms for proteomics; OBI terms for assays).
- Normalize time axes by mapping reported time points to a common scale and, where necessary, using interpolation only within existing sampled times (no extrapolative “new data”).
- Harmonize stimulation categories using rule-based mapping from methods text and repository metadata (e.g., “anti-CD3/anti-CD28 on coverslip” vs “pMHC on supported lipid bilayer”).
- Track provenance rigorously: every derived feature will be linked to source accession IDs (IDR/BioImage Archive/PRIDE/GEO/ImmPort) and processing parameters.

Microcluster feature extraction from imaging
We will develop open computer-vision pipelines to quantify mesoscale features from TIRF and super-resolution images.
Key steps:
1) Preprocessing: illumination correction, denoising (non-learning or self-supervised methods where appropriate), drift correction for SMLM localization tables when metadata allow.
2) Segmentation/detection: spot detection via Laplacian-of-Gaussian and/or wavelet methods for diffraction-limited data; density-based clustering (DBSCAN/HDBSCAN) or Bayesian clustering for SMLM point clouds.
3) Feature computation:
- Size/shape: cluster area, radius of gyration, eccentricity, fractal dimension proxies.
- Density/spacing: Ripley’s K/L functions, pair-correlation functions, nearest-neighbor distributions.
- Dynamics (when time-lapse available): lifetime distributions, fission/fusion events, tracking via probabilistic data association.
- Composition/colocalization: Manders coefficients (for pixel-based), coordinate-based colocalization for SMLM, radial intensity profiles to detect core–shell patterns.
4) Motif representation: we will encode clusters into a standardized “microcluster feature vector” plus optional graph representations (clusters as nodes with edges for proximity/interaction) enabling motif discovery.

Integrating microcluster features with phosphoproteomics
Phosphoproteomics time courses provide a high-dimensional but indirect readout of microcluster function. We will:
- Map phosphosites to proteins and pathways using UniProt and curated pathway resources (e.g., Reactome) for module-level summaries.
- Perform trajectory alignment and smoothing using methods appropriate for sparse time courses (Gaussian process regression with uncertainty, constrained to observed time windows).
- Apply dynamical systems identification (SINDy / sparse regression) to infer low-dimensional ODE models for key signaling modules (e.g., proximal phosphorylation, MAPK, NF-κB proxies) using phosphoproteomic module scores as observables.
- Link image-derived features to inferred dynamical parameters using hierarchical models: dataset-level covariates (imaging features) predicting dynamical coefficients (feedback strengths, nonlinearities), with random effects capturing study-specific biases.

Linking to single-cell outcomes and heterogeneity
Single-cell datasets (CyTOF/flow/scRNA-seq) will be used to quantify emergent outcome distributions.
- For CyTOF/flow (ImmPort), we will standardize marker panels where possible and compute activation state mixtures using mixture models and latent variable models (Gaussian mixture models; Dirichlet process mixtures when appropriate).
- For scRNA-seq (GEO/ArrayExpress), we will use established pipelines (Scanpy/Seurat) for normalization and batch correction, then derive activation programs (gene set scores for immediate early genes, cytokine programs, exhaustion markers). Time-resolved state transitions will be summarized via RNA velocity where available, or via pseudotime constrained by known sampling times.
- We will connect these outcomes to microcluster motifs through a mediation-style framework: motif class (or continuous motif scores) → inferred phosphorylation dynamics → probability of single-cell activation states. This explicitly tests whether mesoscale organization explains outcome heterogeneity.

Cross-dataset validation and positive controls (no experiments)
Validation will rely on independent datasets and known qualitative expectations:
- Cross-study motif reproducibility: train motif classifier on one repository subset (e.g., IDR TCR datasets) and test on BioImage Archive BCR/FcR datasets.
- Known perturbation controls: conditions with documented effects on clustering (e.g., actin disruption or phosphatase exclusion contexts when present in public datasets) should shift extracted features in expected directions.
- Predictive validation: models trained to predict phosphoproteomic trajectory classes from microcluster features will be evaluated on held-out studies; similarly, prediction of single-cell activation mixture weights will be tested across cohorts.
- Sensitivity analyses: quantify robustness to imaging resolution differences by downsampling/blur transforms applied to existing images (a computational control, not new data) and re-extracting features.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize metadata schema; curate initial dataset inventory with accession lists.
- Build v1 imaging feature extraction pipeline; release as open repository with example notebooks.

Months 7–12:
- Complete first harmonized imaging feature table across TCR/BCR/FcR datasets.
- Curate and process initial PRIDE phosphoproteomics time courses; compute module trajectories.
- First motif discovery analysis; internal benchmark report.

Months 13–18:
- Integrate imaging motifs with phosphoproteomic dynamics (SINDy + hierarchical linking).
- Curate ImmPort CyTOF/flow and GEO scRNA-seq activation time courses; derive outcome mixtures.
- Release v1 “Microcluster Motif Atlas” (features + provenance + documentation).

Months 19–24:
- Full multiscale model linking motifs → phosphorylation dynamics → single-cell outcomes.
- Integrate ligand/epitope/structure metadata (IEDB/PDB) and perturbation compendia (DepMap/LINCS) for hypothesis tests H2–H4.
- Cross-dataset validation and robustness analyses.

Months 25–30:
- Finalize software toolkit, benchmark datasets, and manuscript preprints.
- Host NCEMS workshop/tutorial; publish living documentation and training materials.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
This effort requires expertise rarely housed in one lab:
- Quantitative immunology (TCR/BCR/FcR signaling biology; interpretation of stimulation paradigms).
- Computational imaging and computer vision (SMLM/TIRF processing; point-process statistics).
- Proteomics bioinformatics (phosphosite mapping, batch effects, time-course modeling).
- Single-cell genomics and cytometry analysis (state mixtures, batch correction, trajectory inference).
- Dynamical systems and statistical modeling (SINDy, hierarchical Bayesian modeling, causal/mediation-style integration).
- Research software engineering (workflow automation, packaging, documentation, CI/CD).
NCEMS support is essential to convene these contributors, coordinate standards, and deliver community-grade, reusable synthesis products that exceed what an individual lab could sustain.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) Microcluster Feature Standard (MFS) and ontology-aligned metadata schema: A community-usable specification for describing immune receptor microclusters, including core quantitative features (size, density, lifetime, colocalization, point-pattern statistics), motif labels/scores, and required provenance fields. This will be released as a versioned standard with examples and validation tests.

2) Microcluster Motif Atlas (open benchmark dataset): A harmonized, cross-study table linking imaging-derived microcluster features to experimental context (receptor, cell type, ligand class, perturbations) with direct pointers to source accessions in the Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive. Where licensing permits, we will provide curated subsets of images or localization tables; otherwise, we will provide reproducible scripts that re-download from primary repositories.

3) Open pipelines for microcluster quantification: Reusable, documented software implementing the image processing, segmentation/clustering, and feature extraction steps for both pixel images and SMLM point clouds. The pipeline will include unit tests, example notebooks, and containerized execution.

4) Multiscale dynamical modeling toolkit: An interpretable modeling framework that links mesoscale microcluster motif parameters to phosphoproteomic dynamics (via sparse dynamical identification) and to single-cell outcome distributions (via mixture/latent state models). Outputs will include fitted model parameters for each dataset, uncertainty estimates, and predictive evaluation on held-out studies.

5) Synthesis manuscripts and review resources: At least two major publications/preprints are anticipated: (i) a methods/benchmark paper introducing the Microcluster Feature Standard and Atlas; (ii) a biological synthesis paper establishing motif-to-dynamics-to-outcome relationships and testing the core hypotheses about gain control, cytoskeletal regime shifts, and variant/perturbation mechanisms.

Mechanistic advances in mesoscale emergence
This project will advance understanding of emergent phenomena at the mesoscale by converting qualitative concepts (microclusters as “signaling hubs”) into quantitative, testable principles:
- Motif-level organization: identifying whether a limited set of mesoscale architectures recur across immune receptors and contexts, implying conserved design principles.
- Emergent computation: demonstrating how microcluster geometry and composition implement gain control and thresholding, thereby explaining why ligand affinity alone is insufficient.
- Dynamical regimes: connecting cytoskeletal coupling and spatial partitioning to excitable vs bistable signaling behaviors, providing a unifying explanation for disparate reports of digital vs graded activation.
- Mechanisms of perturbations and disease: offering a spatially grounded interpretation of why certain genetic dependencies or pharmacologic perturbations have context-specific or paradoxical effects—because they reshape partitioning and motif prevalence rather than simply scaling catalytic rates.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
Although focused on immune receptors, the outputs will be broadly applicable to other mesoscale signaling systems (e.g., RTK nanoclusters, integrin adhesions, synaptic receptor nanodomains) because the methods—point-pattern statistics, motif discovery, and multiscale dynamical linking—generalize to any membrane-associated signaling microdomain. The Microcluster Feature Standard can serve as a template for community standards in mesoscale cell biology, enabling meta-analyses that are currently infeasible.

Enabling future research (without generating new data here)
By producing benchmark datasets and validated pipelines, this project lowers barriers for future experimental and computational work. Experimentalists will be able to compute standardized features from their own images and compare them to the Atlas. Modelers will be able to test new hypotheses against curated, multi-modal benchmarks. Importantly, the synthesis will identify which existing datasets are most informative and where public data are sparse, guiding future data deposition practices.

Dissemination plan
- Publications in open-access venues when possible; preprints released upon submission.
- A project website hosted through NCEMS-linked infrastructure with living documentation.
- Workshops/tutorials: at least one NCEMS-hosted training workshop and one virtual mini-symposium to engage imaging, proteomics, and immunology communities.
- Deposition of derived resources: feature tables and metadata to Zenodo (DOI), code to GitHub, containers to Docker Hub/GitHub Container Registry, and (where appropriate) workflows to WorkflowHub.

Long-term sustainability
We will design the pipelines as modular packages with clear APIs, enabling community contributions beyond the award period. Sustainability will be supported by: (i) semantic versioning and changelogs; (ii) continuous integration testing; (iii) clear governance for accepting pull requests and issues; (iv) archiving major releases on Zenodo for citability. By anchoring all derived products to stable accession IDs in IDR/BioImage Archive/PRIDE/GEO/ImmPort, the resources remain re-runnable as repositories evolve.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy and alignment with NCEMS synthesis goals
The budget prioritizes personnel and infrastructure needed for community-scale data synthesis, harmonization, and open, reusable tooling—activities that exceed the capacity of a single laboratory. Funds support cross-disciplinary coordination, trainee development, compute for large-scale reprocessing of public imaging/omics datasets, and dissemination through workshops and open releases. No funds are requested for experiments, sample collection, or new data generation.

Personnel (primary cost drivers)
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (computational):
  1) Imaging/vision postdoc to lead microcluster quantification, point-process statistics, and motif discovery across IDR/BioImage Archive/SMLM datasets.
  2) Multi-omics/dynamical modeling postdoc to lead phosphoproteomics processing (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), SINDy-based model identification, and integration with single-cell outcomes.
- 1 Graduate student (or equivalent trainee support): focused on single-cell (ImmPort CyTOF/flow; GEO scRNA-seq) state mixture modeling and outcome mapping.
- 1 Research software engineer / programmer analyst (0.5–1.0 FTE): to productionize pipelines (Snakemake/Nextflow), implement CI/CD, manage containers, documentation, and releases.
- PI and co-PI effort (modest): coordination of working group meetings, scientific integration, mentoring, and dissemination.
Justification: The diversity of modalities (imaging, proteomics, single-cell, dynamical systems) requires dedicated experts; robust open-source deliverables require professional software engineering support.

Computing resources
- Cloud compute credits and storage for scalable reprocessing of large imaging datasets and proteomics matrices (burst capacity for feature extraction and model fitting).
- Access to institutional HPC where available, with budget for additional allocations if needed.
- Data storage for intermediate products and public release packaging (with redundancy and backup).
Justification: Recomputing standardized features across many imaging studies and running cross-validation/model selection at scale is compute-intensive; centralized, reproducible environments reduce barriers for community reuse.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (in-person, 1–2 per year): travel support for geographically distributed team members, with priority for trainees and participants from institutions with fewer resources.
- Conference travel for dissemination (targeted): presenting the Microcluster Feature Standard/Atlas and modeling results at relevant meetings (computational biology, quantitative cell biology, immunology).
Justification: NCEMS’s mission emphasizes catalyzing multidisciplinary teams; in-person synthesis meetings accelerate harmonization decisions, standard development, and cross-training.

Workshops and training events
- NCEMS-hosted workshop (hybrid): venue/AV support (if applicable), training materials development, and limited participant travel support.
- Virtual tutorial series: platform support and captioning/accessibility services.
Justification: Training a data-savvy workforce and community uptake of standards/tools requires structured instruction and accessible materials.

Open science infrastructure costs
- Zenodo archiving (no cost) supplemented by budget for data curation labor and, if needed, paid long-term hosting for a lightweight project site.
- DOI-backed releases of code and derived datasets; preparation of extensive documentation and example datasets.
Justification: High-quality, reusable synthesis products require sustained curation, documentation, and release engineering.

Overall feasibility within 2–3 years
The personnel mix, compute resources, and meeting/workshop support are calibrated to deliver: (i) a curated cross-modality benchmark; (ii) robust pipelines; and (iii) validated multiscale models—without generating new data. Each budget element directly supports NCEMS priorities: multidisciplinary synthesis, open/reproducible science, community-scale integration, and trainee development.

abstract_text:
Mitochondrial cristae are mesoscale membrane folds (20–100 nm curvature radii; 10–30 nm junctions) whose collective organization determines respiratory efficiency and signaling. The emergent phenomenon is that cristae architecture—junction density, lamellar vs tubular balance, and local protein crowding—produces nonlinear changes in bioenergetic output not predictable from individual OXPHOS complexes.

NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, open workflows, and trainee training in quantitative 3D ultrastructure analysis and integrative modeling.

[Background and Significance]
Mitochondria adapt their energy-conversion capacity across tissues and environmental conditions, yet the mechanistic “control knobs” that enable this plasticity remain incompletely defined. A central mesoscale feature of mitochondria is the crista: invaginated folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) that create a highly structured, nanometer-to-submicron labyrinth. Cristae are neither purely molecular assemblies nor organelles themselves; they occupy the mesoscale where geometry, topology, and molecular crowding jointly determine emergent properties. At this scale, the spatial arrangement of respiratory chain complexes, ATP synthase oligomers, and membrane-shaping proteins (e.g., MICOS, OPA1, and associated factors) can generate nonlinear changes in proton-motive force distribution, diffusion constraints, local curvature energy, and protein–lipid phase behavior. These collective effects are not predictable by summing properties of individual complexes in isolation.

Current understanding supports several key principles. First, crista junctions (CJs)—narrow necks connecting cristae to the inner boundary membrane—act as diffusion barriers and structural gatekeepers, influencing metabolite exchange and potentially compartmentalizing electrochemical gradients. Second, ATP synthase forms dimers and higher-order rows that impose and stabilize high curvature at crista ridges, while MICOS complexes organize CJs and crista attachment sites. Third, OPA1 processing and oligomerization modulate IMM fusion, crista remodeling, and CJ stability, linking signaling (e.g., apoptosis) to crista architecture. Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) has provided exquisite 3D snapshots of crista morphologies across organisms and perturbations, and has revealed the spatial organization of ATP synthase rows, MICOS-associated junctional structures, and distinct lamellar versus tubular crista forms. Parallel advances in quantitative fluorescence microscopy and live-cell imaging have characterized mitochondrial network dynamics, fission–fusion cycles, and stress responses that correlate with crista remodeling. Meanwhile, proteomics and phosphoproteomics have quantified variation in abundance and post-translational regulation of IMM shaping components across tissues, cell lines, and perturbations.

Despite this rich empirical base, three synthesis gaps persist. (1) There is no standardized, cross-study “morphometric language” for cristae that connects cryo-ET reconstructions to quantitative descriptors (curvature distributions, junction graphs, topological invariants) in a way that is comparable across datasets, organisms, and sample preparation pipelines. Many cryo-ET studies provide qualitative or semi-quantitative summaries that are not directly interoperable. (2) Links between mesoscale geometry and functional output remain fragmented. Respiration measurements (e.g., oxygen consumption rates, coupling efficiency) are widely available in public repositories and literature, but they are rarely integrated with matched structural descriptors; as a result, the field lacks a predictive mapping from “architecture” to “bioenergetics.” (3) Molecular drivers of architectural state transitions are known in parts (MICOS, ATP synthase dimerization, OPA1), but how combinations of these factors produce distinct stable crista states—and why similar molecular changes yield different functional consequences across tissues—remains unresolved. These are quintessential emergence questions: system-level properties (bioenergetic plasticity, resilience to perturbation) arise from collective spatial organization and constraints.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that resolves these gaps using only existing public data. Structural data are abundant and growing: EMPIAR hosts raw cryo-ET tilt series; EMDB provides reconstructed volumes and annotations; and a subset of studies provide segmentations or can be re-segmented from public reconstructions. Image repositories such as the BioImage Archive and the Image Data Resource (IDR) include mitochondrial reporters and time-lapse imaging that capture network-level dynamics related to crista remodeling. Proteomics repositories (PRIDE, ProteomeXchange) contain mitochondrial fraction proteomes, complexome profiling, and phosphoproteomics capturing MICOS/OPA1 regulation and ATP synthase assembly states. Genomics resources (GTEx for tissue expression; ENCODE for regulatory context) and single-cell atlases (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, Mouse Cell Atlas) provide cell-type-resolved expression of shaping genes, enabling inference about tissue-specific constraints. Functional datasets exist in DepMap (CRISPR dependency and some perturbation phenotypes) and in public respiratory phenotyping datasets and literature compilations, including Seahorse XF measurements deposited as supplementary data or in repositories.

The significance of synthesizing these resources is twofold. Scientifically, it will enable a mesoscale theory of crista architecture as a set of conserved “architectural states” with quantifiable transitions driven by protein stoichiometry and regulation, explaining emergent bioenergetic regimes. Practically, it will provide a reusable atlas and open computational infrastructure for extracting and integrating crista geometry from tomograms—an enabling capability for the broader community studying mitochondrial disease, aging, immune metabolism, and neurodegeneration where morphology–function decoupling is often observed. Because the necessary integration spans cryo-ET, quantitative imaging, proteogenomics, membrane physics, and machine learning, it is beyond the scope of any single lab and fits NCEMS’s mission to drive multidisciplinary synthesis around mesoscale emergence.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project targets emergent mesoscale phenomena in which crista geometry and topology act as collective variables that constrain and enable bioenergetic function. We will address four tightly defined research questions (RQs), each paired with testable hypotheses (Hs) and measurable predictions derived exclusively from public datasets.

RQ1: Do mitochondria occupy a finite set of conserved crista “architectural states” across species, cell types, and perturbations?
H1 (state discreteness and partial conservation): Cristae morphologies cluster into a small number of recurrent architectural states characterized by (i) CJ density and connectivity, (ii) lamellar-to-tubular ratio, (iii) ridge curvature and ATP synthase row organization proxies, and (iv) topological measures (e.g., surface genus, compartment connectivity). These states will be partially conserved across organisms (e.g., yeast, mammals) but with tissue-specific occupancy frequencies.
Predictions and validation: Using standardized geometric descriptors extracted from EMDB/EMPIAR reconstructions, unsupervised models (mixture models, spectral clustering, or variational autoencoders constrained to interpretable latent factors) will identify stable clusters with high silhouette scores and reproducibility under bootstrapping and cross-dataset splits. Conservation will be supported if cluster definitions remain stable when trained on one organism and projected to another, and if state assignments correlate with known qualitative categories reported in source publications (positive controls).

RQ2: How do MICOS composition, ATP synthase oligomerization, and OPA1 processing jointly determine transitions between architectural states?
H2 (combinatorial control with nonlinear interactions): Transitions between states are governed by a low-dimensional set of molecular control axes: MICOS subunit stoichiometry (e.g., MIC60/MIC19 balance), ATP synthase dimer/oligomer propensity, and OPA1 long/short form balance (or phosphorylation proxies). The effect of any single axis depends on the others (interaction terms), producing nonlinear state boundaries.
Predictions and validation: Integrated models linking proteomics (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange) and transcriptomics (GTEx; single-cell atlases) to state assignments will show that multivariate models with interactions outperform additive models in predicting architectural state (evaluated by cross-validated accuracy/AUROC for classification or explained variance for continuous state coordinates). Evidence for OPA1 processing effects will come from datasets with quantified OPA1 isoforms/processing enzymes (e.g., OMA1, YME1L) and phosphoproteomics signatures; MICOS/ATP synthase axes will be supported by complexome profiling and abundance correlations.

RQ3: Can mesoscale crista geometry explain why similar proteomic changes yield different respiratory outcomes across tissues and contexts?
H3 (geometry as a context-dependent mediator): The mapping from molecular composition to respiration is mediated by geometry; tissue-specific baseline geometry and physical constraints (membrane tension, lipid composition proxies, mitochondrial size) modulate the functional consequences of similar molecular perturbations. Thus, geometry will statistically mediate a significant fraction of the association between shaping-protein abundance and respiratory phenotypes.
Predictions and validation: In datasets where functional readouts (OCR, coupling efficiency, spare respiratory capacity) can be matched to molecular profiles and/or perturbations (public Seahorse datasets, literature-curated values, DepMap perturbation phenotypes), mediation/causal inference analyses will show that including geometric state variables reduces direct molecular-to-function effect sizes while improving prediction of function. Multi-task models trained across tissues/cell lines will reveal shared molecular drivers but tissue-specific geometry–function transfer functions.

RQ4: What physical principles (membrane elasticity, curvature generation, crowding) are sufficient to reproduce observed state distributions and transition pathways?
H4 (physics-informed sufficiency with data-calibrated parameters): A physics-informed generative model combining Helfrich-like membrane bending energy, constraints from CJ stabilization, and protein-induced curvature fields (ATP synthase rows; MICOS junction scaffolding) can reproduce the empirical distribution of curvature and topology descriptors across states. Transition pathways correspond to shifts in a small number of effective parameters (e.g., spontaneous curvature magnitude, junction line tension, protein crowding pressure).
Predictions and validation: Calibrated models will generate synthetic descriptor distributions that match observed ones (e.g., via maximum mean discrepancy or likelihood-based fit) and will correctly predict directionality of changes under known perturbations captured in public data (e.g., MICOS depletion associated with CJ loss and altered connectivity; ATP synthase dimerization changes associated with ridge curvature alterations) without fitting to those specific perturbation labels (held-out validation).

Across all RQs, hypotheses are validated through cross-dataset replication: a finding must hold across multiple independent cryo-ET studies and be consistent when integrating orthogonal evidence streams (structural descriptors, omics profiles, and functional phenotypes). The mechanistic insight sought is a unified, quantitative explanation of bioenergetic plasticity as an emergent property of mesoscale crista organization—where architecture is treated as a measurable, predictive state variable shaped by molecular composition and constrained by physical laws.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will conduct a community-scale synthesis integrating 3D ultrastructure, live-cell imaging, proteogenomics, and functional phenotypes to build an atlas of crista architectural states and models linking these states to molecular drivers and respiration. No new experiments or data generation will be performed; all analyses will use publicly available datasets and published supplementary data.

1) Data sources (specific repositories)
A. Cryo-ET / 3D EM structure
- EMPIAR (raw tilt series; associated metadata on organism, cell type, perturbation)
- EMDB (reconstructed tomograms/volumes; some segmentations)
- Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) linked segmentations when available; additionally, public segmentations from GitHub/Zenodo accompanying papers
- Optional cross-reference: Cell Image Library for legacy EM datasets when relevant

B. Light microscopy / live imaging
- BioImage Archive (time-lapse datasets of mitochondrial dynamics; reporter-based imaging)
- Image Data Resource (IDR) (high-content screens and curated imaging studies with mitochondrial markers)
- Allen Cell Explorer / Allen Institute for Cell Science (public 3D fluorescence datasets and cell models with mitochondrial labels where available)

C. Proteomics / phosphoproteomics / complexome
- PRIDE Archive via ProteomeXchange (mitochondrial fraction proteomes; phosphoproteomics; complexome profiling)
- CPTAC (Cancer Proteome Atlas) for tissue/cell-line proteomes including mitochondrial proteins (where licensing permits open reuse)

D. Genomics / transcriptomics / regulation
- GTEx (tissue-level expression of mitochondrial shaping genes)
- ENCODE (regulatory context for shaping genes; transcription factor binding and chromatin states as covariates)
- Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, Mouse Cell Atlas (single-cell RNA-seq atlases to infer cell-type-specific expression programs)

E. Functional phenotypes
- DepMap (CRISPR gene effect scores; co-dependency networks; selected phenotype datasets)
- Public Seahorse XF datasets deposited as supplementary tables, Figshare, Zenodo, or institutional repositories; additionally, curated OCR/ECAR values from meta-analysis of published studies with accessible underlying data
- MitoCarta 3.0 (as a reference annotation set for mitochondrial proteins)

2) Data ingestion, harmonization, and metadata standardization
- Create a unified metadata schema (JSON/CSV) capturing: organism, tissue/cell type, perturbation (genetic/chemical), growth condition, imaging modality, resolution, segmentation availability, and links to omics/functional datasets.
- Use controlled vocabularies: NCBI Taxonomy for species, UBERON/Cell Ontology for tissues/cell types, PSI-MS terms for proteomics, and OBI terms for assays.
- Map gene/protein identifiers across datasets (Ensembl, UniProt, HGNC/MGI) and harmonize mitochondrial-shaping gene sets (MICOS subunits, OPA1 pathway genes, ATP synthase assembly/dimerization factors).

3) Quantifying crista mesoscale geometry from cryo-ET
3.1 Segmentation reuse and standardization
- Prefer author-provided segmentations; when absent but reconstructions are public, apply reproducible, open segmentation workflows using pre-trained models (no new training data required) such as nnU-Net models released with open weights for membrane segmentation, or classical tools (ilastik pixel classification with published models where available). Any applied model weights and parameters will be versioned and cited; outputs will be deposited openly as derived data.
3.2 Geometric descriptors
- Surface reconstruction of IMM and crista membranes (marching cubes + smoothing with topology-preserving constraints).
- Curvature analysis: mean and Gaussian curvature distributions; ridge curvature signatures.
- Crista junction detection: identify neck-like constrictions via medial axis/skeletonization and local radius minima; represent as a junction graph (nodes = junctions, edges = crista sheets/tubules).
- Topology measures: connected components, genus estimates, Betti numbers (persistent homology) to quantify connectivity and compartmentalization.
- Morphotype summary metrics: lamellar-to-tubular ratio (via local sheetness/tubeness measures), junction density per mitochondrial volume, crista surface area-to-volume ratio.

4) Integrating live imaging with ultrastructure
- Extract mitochondrial network descriptors from BioImage Archive/IDR/Allen datasets: branch length distributions, fission/fusion event rates (where annotated), motility proxies, and network fragmentation indices.
- Link to crista states via shared perturbations/cell types and by constructing a hierarchical model: network-level dynamics (microscale–cellular) as covariates that modulate probability of occupying certain crista states (mesoscale).
- Use domain adaptation techniques to reconcile modality differences (e.g., contrastive learning on summary statistics rather than raw pixels) while maintaining interpretability.

5) Proteogenomic integration and driver inference
- Build a “shaping complex stoichiometry” feature set from proteomics: MICOS subunit ratios, ATP synthase subunit abundance and assembly factor proxies, OPA1 and processing enzyme abundances; include phosphosite intensities for regulatory sites when available.
- Integrate transcriptomics (GTEx and scRNA-seq atlases) to estimate baseline expression programs and tissue composition; use scRNA-seq to generate cell-type-weighted expression priors for tissues.
- Statistical modeling:
  - Multi-task learning (e.g., elastic net multi-task regression, gradient-boosted trees with shared structure, or Bayesian hierarchical models) predicting geometric state coordinates from proteogenomic features across tissues/cell lines.
  - Causal inference: use causal graphs informed by biology (genes → protein complexes → geometry → respiration) and apply methods such as double machine learning / orthogonalized regression for mediation; sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.
  - Network analysis: integrate DepMap co-dependency networks to identify modules that co-vary with shaping genes and test enrichment for predicted geometry drivers.

6) Linking geometry to respiration and emergent bioenergetic regimes
- Curate functional respiration endpoints (OCR, coupling efficiency, spare capacity) from public Seahorse datasets and accessible supplementary tables; harmonize units and assay conditions.
- Fit predictive models mapping geometry descriptors/state assignments to respiration endpoints, controlling for tissue/cell type and mitochondrial content proxies when available.
- Identify nonlinearities (emergence) by testing for threshold effects and interactions among geometry variables (e.g., CJ density × lamellar fraction) using generalized additive models and interpretable ML (SHAP on tree models) with strict cross-validation.

7) Physics-informed modeling of state distributions and transitions
- Implement a reduced generative model of crista membranes:
  - Energy terms: bending energy (Helfrich), junction line tension, protein-induced spontaneous curvature fields (ATP synthase rows), and crowding pressure.
  - Fit effective parameters to match empirical descriptor distributions via approximate Bayesian computation or likelihood-free inference.
- Predict transition pathways by varying parameters along inferred molecular axes (e.g., decreasing MICOS junction stabilization) and compare predicted descriptor shifts to held-out perturbation datasets.

8) Validation using existing data (no experiments)
- Cross-dataset replication: train on one subset of studies and validate on independent studies (different labs/sample prep).
- Positive controls: known perturbations with established morphological effects (e.g., MICOS disruption associated with CJ loss; ATP synthase dimerization perturbations affecting ridge curvature) used only as evaluation benchmarks.
- Robustness checks: batch-effect assessment (ComBat/limma for omics; study-level random effects for imaging) and sensitivity to segmentation uncertainty (Monte Carlo perturbations of surfaces).

9) Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize metadata schema and governance.
- Inventory and ingest priority datasets from EMPIAR/EMDB/PRIDE/GTEx/DepMap.
- Release v0 “CristaeDescriptor” pipeline prototype and example notebooks.

Months 7–12:
- Complete descriptor extraction for initial benchmark set of tomograms (multi-organism).
- First unsupervised state model; internal cross-validation.
- Public release of curated metadata index (Zenodo) and code (GitHub).

Months 13–18:
- Integrate proteomics and transcriptomics; build stoichiometry features.
- Driver inference models (multi-task + interaction testing).
- Workshop 1 at NCEMS: training on 3D ultrastructure quantification.

Months 19–24:
- Curate respiration phenotypes; fit geometry→function models; mediation analyses.
- Physics-informed generative model calibration; held-out perturbation validation.
- Release v1 atlas of architectural states with interactive visualization.

Months 25–30:
- Cross-modal synthesis (live imaging covariates); finalize mechanistic narratives.
- Manuscripts (methods + biology), Workshop 2 (integrative modeling), sustainability plan.

10) Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Cryo-ET/3D EM experts: data selection, segmentation standards, interpretation of ultrastructure.
- Mitochondrial biologists: curation of perturbations, shaping pathways, functional interpretation.
- Membrane physicists: formulation and calibration of elasticity/curvature models.
- ML/data scientists: representation learning, causal inference, multi-task modeling, uncertainty quantification.
- Bioinformaticians/omics specialists: proteomics processing, phosphosite mapping, transcriptomic integration.
- Research software engineers: pipeline engineering, packaging, documentation, reproducibility.
- Trainees (grad students/postdocs): cross-training through paired mentorship across modalities.

NCEMS support is essential for coordinating data governance, hosting working sessions, providing synthesis-focused computing and staff expertise, and enabling sustained cross-lab integration beyond any single group’s capacity.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) An open, curated “Cristae Architectural State Atlas”
- A harmonized index of cryo-ET crista datasets (EMPIAR/EMDB accessions) with standardized metadata, including organism, cell type/tissue, perturbation, and imaging/processing parameters.
- For each tomogram (where permitted by licenses), derived quantitative descriptors: curvature distributions, junction graphs, lamellar/tubular metrics, topology/persistent homology summaries, and uncertainty estimates.
- A state model assigning each sample to one or more architectural states (hard and probabilistic assignments), with state definitions grounded in interpretable geometric features.

2) Open-source computational tools
- “CristaeDescriptor”: a reproducible software package (Python + optional C++/CUDA acceleration) implementing segmentation ingestion, surface reconstruction, curvature estimation, junction detection, and topological analysis.
- “CristaeGraph”: utilities for building and analyzing CJ graphs, including graph kernels and summary measures.
- Visualization modules: interactive dashboards (e.g., Plotly/Dash) to explore state distributions across organisms, tissues, and perturbations.

3) Integrated molecular drivers and predictive models
- A harmonized feature set of mitochondrial shaping complex stoichiometry and regulatory proxies derived from PRIDE/ProteomeXchange proteomics and phosphoproteomics, linked to state occupancy.
- Multi-task predictive models that map proteogenomic features to architectural states and to geometry descriptors, with quantified cross-tissue generalization.
- A ranked list of candidate driver combinations (MICOS subunit ratios, ATP synthase oligomerization proxies, OPA1 processing signatures) that best explain state transitions, including interaction effects.

4) Geometry–function synthesis and emergence quantification
- A curated compendium of respiration phenotypes (OCR, coupling efficiency, spare capacity) extracted from public Seahorse datasets and accessible supplementary materials, with standardized units and covariates.
- Statistical evidence for emergent nonlinearities: identification of geometric thresholds or combinations that produce disproportionate changes in predicted respiration.
- Mediation/causal analyses demonstrating when and how geometry mediates molecular-to-function relationships, clarifying why similar proteomic shifts can yield divergent outcomes across tissues.

5) Physics-informed mechanistic models
- A reduced generative model of crista morphodynamics (in the sense of state distributions and transitions, not time-resolved new measurements) calibrated to empirical geometry descriptors.
- Mechanistic interpretations in terms of effective parameters (spontaneous curvature, junction stabilization/line tension, crowding) that correspond to molecular axes and explain observed morphotypes.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergence
This synthesis will advance a central NCEMS theme: emergent properties at the mesoscale that influence higher-order cellular outcomes. By treating crista architecture as a measurable state variable—rather than a qualitative phenotype—we will establish a quantitative bridge from molecules (complex stoichiometry and regulation) to mesoscale organization (geometry/topology) to function (respiration). The key conceptual advance is explaining bioenergetic plasticity as an emergent consequence of collective membrane organization and constraints, not simply as changes in abundance or activity of individual OXPHOS components.

Broader impacts for molecular and cellular biology
- Mitochondrial disease and aging: Many disorders show discordance between respiratory complex abundance and functional output. Our atlas and models will generate testable mechanistic hypotheses (for future studies by the community) about geometry-mediated dysfunction and compensatory regimes.
- Cell type specificity: Linking GTEx and single-cell atlases to crista states will illuminate how tissue-specific expression programs constrain feasible architectures, informing studies of immunometabolism, neuroenergetics, and muscle physiology.
- Methodological generalization: The geometric/topological toolchain will be reusable for other mesoscale membrane systems (ER sheets/tubules, Golgi cisternae, thylakoids), aligning with NCEMS’s broader emergence mission.

Dissemination
- Publications: at least two major manuscripts (methods/software; integrative biology/physics of crista states) plus a data descriptor paper for the atlas.
- Community resources: deposition of derived datasets and metadata on Zenodo with DOIs; code on GitHub; optional mirroring of key derived image products to BioImage Archive when compatible.
- Training and workshops: two NCEMS-hosted workshops (3D ultrastructure quantification; integrative modeling and causal inference) with hands-on notebooks.

Long-term sustainability
- Governance: establish a lightweight community steering subgroup to maintain metadata standards and accept contributions.
- Maintenance plan: semantic versioning, automated CI tests, and containerized releases to ensure reproducibility over time.
- Interoperability: export formats compatible with OME-NGFF for imaging metadata and PSI standards for proteomics, enabling reuse by other synthesis centers and community databases.

By delivering an atlas, tools, and mechanistic models grounded in public data, the project will create durable infrastructure for mesoscale mitochondrial research and provide a blueprint for how multidisciplinary synthesis can uncover emergent principles in molecular and cellular systems.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget overview (2.5–3 years; synthesis-only)
The budget is designed to support a distributed, multi-lab working group whose primary outputs are integrated datasets, open software, and reproducible models. No funds are requested for experimental reagents, sample preparation, or data generation.

Personnel
1) Lead research software engineer / scientific programmer (1.0 FTE)
- Role: build and maintain the CristaeDescriptor pipeline, implement workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), manage containers/CI, package releases, and support community contributions.
- Justification: robust, reusable tooling is essential for cross-lab synthesis and cannot be sustained by short-term trainee effort alone.

2) Postdoctoral fellow in integrative modeling (1.0 FTE)
- Role: develop state models, multi-task learning, mediation/causal inference analyses, and coordinate cross-dataset validation.
- Justification: central to linking structure→omics→function and ensuring statistical rigor.

3) Postdoctoral fellow or senior graduate researcher in membrane physics (0.5–1.0 FTE)
- Role: implement and calibrate physics-informed generative models; translate fitted parameters into mechanistic interpretations.
- Justification: required to connect emergent geometry patterns to physical principles.

4) Graduate students (2 trainees at ~0.5 FTE each) and/or rotating trainees across participating labs
- Roles: dataset curation, benchmark case studies, documentation and tutorial notebooks, and specific sub-analyses (e.g., persistent homology, live-imaging feature extraction).
- Justification: aligns with NCEMS training mission and distributes effort across modalities.

5) Part-time data curator/biocurator (0.2–0.3 FTE)
- Role: metadata harmonization, ontology mapping (Cell Ontology/UBERON/PSI), accession tracking, and data dictionary maintenance.
- Justification: interoperability and reuse depend on high-quality curation.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or NCEMS-supported HPC allocations for:
  - processing large cryo-ET volumes (surface extraction, curvature computation),
  - running cross-validated ML models, and
  - storing intermediate derived artifacts.
- Budget includes object storage for derived datasets (meshes, graphs, descriptor tables) and compute for container builds and CI.
- Justification: cryo-ET volumes are large and heterogeneous; scalable compute is required for community-scale synthesis.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings: 2 in-person synthesis meetings per year at NCEMS (or rotating hubs) to coordinate standards, resolve integration challenges, and conduct hands-on hack sessions.
- Conference dissemination: support for trainees and key personnel to present at meetings (e.g., ASCB, Biophysical Society, Gordon Conferences on mitochondria/EM) emphasizing open resources.
- Justification: team science and cross-disciplinary integration require sustained coordination beyond virtual meetings.

Workshops and training events
- Two NCEMS-hosted workshops (hands-on):
  1) Quantitative 3D ultrastructure analysis from public cryo-ET data.
  2) Integrative modeling and causal inference for mesoscale emergence.
- Budget covers venue costs, training materials, and limited travel support for trainees from under-resourced institutions.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo deposition (free) supplemented by budget for:
  - domain/hosting for documentation site (if needed),
  - long-term archival of larger derived datasets via institutional repositories or negotiated storage,
  - accessibility services for workshop materials (captioning).
- Justification: ensures broad reuse and longevity of outputs.

Why NCEMS resources are required
This project depends on coordinated synthesis across multiple labs and data modalities, requiring shared standards, dedicated engineering, and convening power. NCEMS support enables (i) structured working group meetings, (ii) shared compute and data management practices, (iii) trainee-focused training, and (iv) dissemination of community resources—capabilities that exceed what a single lab or pre-existing collaboration can provide.

Mitochondrial cristae are mesoscale membrane folds (20–100 nm curvature radii; 10–30 nm junctions) whose collective organization determines respiratory efficiency and signaling. The emergent phenomenon is that cristae architecture—junction density, lamellar vs tubular balance, and local protein crowding—produces nonlinear changes in bioenergetic output not predictable from individual OXPHOS complexes.

We will synthesize public datasets: (i) cryo-ET reconstructions and segmentations of cristae across conditions and organisms (EMPIAR, EMDB), (ii) live-cell imaging of mitochondrial dynamics and cristae reporters where available (IDR/BioImage Archive; Mitochondria Dynamics datasets), (iii) proteomics/phosphoproteomics of mitochondrial fractions and MICOS/OPA1/ATP synthase oligomers (PRIDE), (iv) genomics and transcriptomics for mitochondrial-shaping genes (GTEx, ENCODE; scRNA-seq atlases), and (v) functional readouts of respiration (public Seahorse datasets and compiled literature values; gene perturbation phenotypes in DepMap).

We will quantify mesoscale cristae geometry from cryo-ET via curvature analysis, junction graph extraction, and topology measures (surface genus, connectivity). We will integrate these with proteomic abundance of shaping complexes and with genetic perturbation effects using causal inference and multi-task learning. Physics-informed models of membrane elasticity and protein-induced curvature will be calibrated to explain observed morphotypes and predict transitions.

Central questions: Are there conserved cristae “architectural states” across cell types that correspond to distinct metabolic regimes? Which combinations of MICOS components, ATP synthase dimerization, and OPA1 processing drive state transitions? Can we explain why similar proteomic changes yield different functional outcomes in different tissues as a consequence of mesoscale geometry constraints?

Expected insights include an atlas of cristae architectural states, quantitative links between shaping complex stoichiometry and emergent cristae topology, and mechanistic hypotheses for mitochondrial diseases where morphology and function decouple. Methodological advances will include open-source tools for extracting standardized geometric descriptors from tomograms.

The project demands collaboration between cryo-ET experts, mitochondrial biologists, membrane physicists, and machine learning scientists, and requires extensive synthesis of heterogeneous structural and omics data beyond a single lab’s capability. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, open workflows, and trainee training in quantitative 3D ultrastructure analysis and integrative modeling.

title: Mesoscale Assembly of Viral Replication Compartments: A Cross-Virus Synthesis of Host Factor Recruitment and Emergent Replication Efficiency

abstract_text:
Many viruses create mesoscale replication compartments (100–1000 nm membraneless inclusions or membrane-bound organelles) that concentrate viral and host factors. The emergent phenomenon is that collective compartment organization yields replication efficiencies and immune evasion strategies not predictable from individual viral proteins. This project will ask whether replication compartments share universal mesoscale design principles across unrelated viruses.

We will synthesize: (i) viral replication compartment imaging datasets (electron microscopy and fluorescence) from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR, spanning RNA viruses (coronaviruses, flaviviruses) and DNA viruses (herpesviruses), (ii) host–virus protein interaction networks (IntAct, BioGRID, VirHostNet), (iii) CRISPR and RNAi screens for host dependency factors (DepMap viral screens; published screens in GEO/SRA), (iv) viral and host transcriptomic responses (GEO; single-cell infection atlases where available), and (v) structural data for viral scaffold proteins and host recruited complexes (PDB, AlphaFold DB).

We will develop a comparative mesoscale compartment feature framework: size distributions, internal subcompartmentalization, proximity to organelles, and dynamics proxies. Using network embedding and community detection on host–virus interactomes, we will identify recurrent host modules (e.g., RNA metabolism, membrane trafficking, stress granule components) recruited into compartments. We will then relate these modules to compartment morphotypes and to replication phenotypes (viral titers/replication markers from public datasets) using multi-level regression and causal graph methods.

Hypotheses: (1) replication compartments implement convergent mesoscale strategies—phase separation, membrane curvature scaffolding, or hybrid forms—to optimize reaction kinetics and shield nucleic acids; (2) the emergent efficiency depends on a small number of host module recruitments that act as “mesoscale organizers”; and (3) antiviral perturbations that disrupt mesoscale organization (rather than single enzymes) provide broad-spectrum leverage.

Expected insights include a cross-virus taxonomy of replication compartment architectures, identification of conserved host mesoscale organizers, and predictive models linking host factor modules to compartment type and replication success. Deliverables will include open compartment feature datasets and interoperable pipelines for image and network integration.

This requires team science across virology, quantitative imaging, network biology, and statistical modeling, and it relies entirely on integrating diverse public datasets. NCEMS support is crucial to coordinate cross-virus data harmonization, establish open standards for compartment annotation, and train trainees in integrative, reproducible computational virology focused on emergent mesoscale organization.
