[Background and Significance]
Viruses remodel host cells to create replication compartments (RCs)—mesoscale structures typically ~100–1000 nm that concentrate viral genomes, polymerases, and recruited host factors while excluding or modulating antiviral sensors. Across virus families, RCs appear as membraneless inclusions (often described as liquid-like or gel-like condensates), membrane-bound organelles (e.g., double-membrane vesicles and spherules), or hybrid assemblies combining scaffolded membranes with phase-separated interiors. The mesoscale is central: it is the scale at which many weak molecular interactions, crowding, and transport constraints collectively produce new system properties (reaction acceleration, shielding, spatial segregation) that cannot be inferred from any one protein’s biochemistry. In this sense, viral RCs are a tractable and data-rich model for emergent mesoscale organization in cells.

Current understanding is fragmented across virology subfields. For positive-strand RNA viruses, electron microscopy (EM) studies have documented membrane curvature and invagination to generate spherules, convoluted membranes, or double-membrane vesicles, while fluorescence microscopy has revealed dynamic viral protein foci that coalesce and mature over time. For negative-strand RNA viruses and many DNA viruses, large cytoplasmic or nuclear inclusions assemble, often in association with stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins, chaperones, and cytoskeletal or trafficking machinery. A growing literature suggests that some RCs exhibit hallmarks of biomolecular condensation (concentration-dependent assembly, spherical morphology, fusion events), whereas others are clearly constrained by membrane geometry and organelle contact sites. Yet, a unified framework to compare RC architectures across unrelated viruses is lacking, in part because evidence is distributed across imaging modalities, cell types, and annotation practices.

Public data resources now make cross-virus synthesis feasible at community scale. Imaging data relevant to RC morphology and substructure are increasingly deposited in the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource (IDR), and EMPIAR, including correlative light and electron microscopy in some systems. Host–virus protein interaction (HV-PPI) data are curated in IntAct, BioGRID, and VirHostNet, enabling cross-study integration of physical and functional interactions. Functional genomics screens for host dependency factors—CRISPR knockout, CRISPRi, and RNAi—are available in repositories such as GEO and SRA, and in aggregated resources including DepMap’s viral perturbation collections where available, as well as numerous published screens with accessible count matrices and hit lists. Transcriptomic responses to infection (bulk RNA-seq, microarray, and in some cases single-cell atlases) are also available in GEO and ArrayExpress, and increasingly in cell atlas initiatives that include infection perturbations or time courses. Finally, structural information about viral scaffolds and host complexes has expanded via the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold DB, enabling mechanistic interpretation of interaction modules and potential multivalency that drives mesoscale assembly.

Despite this abundance, key gaps persist that synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address. First, RC morphology is typically described qualitatively and within a single virus system; quantitative, standardized feature extraction across viruses is rare. Second, HV-PPI networks and genetic dependency screens are usually analyzed separately, leading to inconsistent conclusions about which host processes are central versus context-dependent. Third, replication phenotypes (e.g., viral titers, reporter expression, replication markers) are often reported in heterogeneous units and experimental contexts, limiting cross-study comparability. Fourth, the emergent link between mesoscale organization and replication efficiency—how compartment architecture and host module recruitment jointly produce system-level outcomes—has not been tested systematically across viruses.

NCEMS’s emphasis on mesoscale emergence and synthesis makes RCs an ideal target. RCs sit between molecules and organelles, precisely the mesoscale where emergent behaviors arise from collective interactions, crowding, and geometry. A cross-virus synthesis can reveal whether seemingly different RCs implement convergent “design principles” (e.g., selective permeability, spatial segregation of replication/transcription/assembly, organelle tethering) and whether a small set of host modules repeatedly acts as mesoscale organizers. Importantly, these questions are beyond a single lab: they require harmonizing imaging, interaction, genetic, transcriptomic, and structural datasets across many viruses and laboratories, and developing shared standards for RC annotation.

This proposal leverages existing publicly available datasets to build a comparative, mechanistic understanding of RC emergence. By integrating quantitative imaging-derived morphotypes with network modules and functional dependencies, we will move from virus-specific narratives to generalizable mesoscale principles. The payoff is twofold: fundamental insight into how mesoscale cellular organization emerges under viral perturbation, and practical identification of conserved host “organizer modules” whose disruption may broadly impair RC formation and replication. This synthesis will also produce reusable datasets and workflows for the broader community studying mesoscale compartments, condensates, and organelle remodeling in diverse biological contexts.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address the overarching question: do viral replication compartments (RCs) share universal mesoscale design principles across unrelated viruses, and can those principles be expressed as measurable, predictive relationships between (i) RC morphotype features, (ii) recruited host factor modules, and (iii) replication efficiency phenotypes? We focus on emergent mesoscale properties—organization, permeability proxies, spatial coupling to organelles, and dynamic assembly—rather than on single-protein enzymology.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): Can RC architectures across diverse viruses be represented in a common quantitative feature space that yields a robust, cross-virus taxonomy of morphotypes?
Prediction 1A: When EM and fluorescence datasets are mapped into standardized features (size distributions, shape descriptors, internal texture/subcompartmentalization, membrane association, proximity to organelles, and time-resolved assembly proxies), RCs will cluster into a small number of recurrent morphotypes (e.g., membrane-invaginated spherules; double-membrane vesicle networks; membraneless inclusion bodies; hybrid membrane/condensate assemblies) that transcend viral phylogeny.
Prediction 1B: Morphotype clusters will be stable across imaging modalities and laboratories after harmonization and batch correction, with uncertainty quantifiable via bootstrap resampling and leave-one-study-out validation.
Validation using existing data: We will test clustering robustness using independent imaging datasets from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR, applying modality-specific feature extraction and then aligning features via domain adaptation and batch-effect models. Known exemplar systems (e.g., well-characterized spherules vs double-membrane vesicles) serve as positive controls for separability.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): Are there conserved host “mesoscale organizer” modules that are preferentially recruited into RCs and that predict RC morphotype?
Hypothesis 2: Across viruses, RC assembly depends on a limited set of host modules that repeatedly appear as highly central, enriched, and functionally required—such as RNA metabolism/RNP granule proteins, membrane trafficking and curvature machinery, lipid remodeling pathways, chaperones/proteostasis, and cytoskeletal transport.
Measurable predictions:
- 2A: Community detection on integrated HV-PPI networks will identify recurrent host modules whose membership is conserved across multiple viruses more than expected by degree-preserving randomization.
- 2B: These modules will be significantly enriched among hits from CRISPR/RNAi dependency screens (GEO/SRA; DepMap viral screens where available), after harmonizing gene identifiers and applying meta-analysis across studies.
- 2C: Module activity inferred from transcriptomic signatures (bulk and single-cell where available) will correlate with RC morphotype and/or replication outcomes, consistent with module recruitment and functional engagement.
Validation using existing data: We will validate module recurrence by comparing results across interaction databases (IntAct vs BioGRID vs VirHostNet) and across screen types (CRISPR vs RNAi). We will also use curated host complexes (CORUM) and pathways (Reactome, KEGG) as external references to test biological coherence.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): How do RC morphotype and host module recruitment jointly determine emergent replication efficiency across viruses?
Hypothesis 3: Replication efficiency is an emergent outcome determined by a small number of mesoscale variables—compartment capacity (size/volume proxies), organization (subcompartmentalization/texture), coupling to organelles (e.g., ER, mitochondria, Golgi proximity), and selective recruitment of organizer modules—rather than by any single interaction.
Measurable predictions:
- 3A: Multilevel models incorporating morphotype features plus module-level predictors will explain replication phenotypes (viral titers, reporter readouts, replication marker expression) better than models using only viral taxonomy or only single-gene effects.
- 3B: Causal graph analyses will support directed relationships consistent with “module recruitment → morphotype stabilization → replication efficiency,” with alternative explanations (e.g., replication level driving apparent compartment size) evaluated via time-course ordering and sensitivity analyses.
- 3C: The same organizer modules will predict replication outcomes across multiple viruses, indicating broad-spectrum leverage points.
Validation using existing data: We will assemble replication phenotype measures from published datasets (often in GEO/SRA-linked studies) and standardize them to comparable effect sizes within study, then meta-analyze across studies. Time-course transcriptomics and imaging timepoints (when available) will support temporal constraints in causal modeling.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Do structural features of viral scaffold proteins and recruited host complexes explain convergent mesoscale assembly strategies?
Hypothesis 4: Viral proteins that nucleate RCs exhibit convergent structural properties—multivalency, intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), modular interaction motifs, and/or membrane-binding/curvature-inducing domains—that align with the inferred assembly strategy (phase separation, membrane scaffolding, or hybrid).
Predictions:
- 4A: Structural annotations from PDB and AlphaFold DB (disorder propensity, predicted interaction interfaces, oligomerization likelihood, membrane association motifs) will associate with morphotype cluster membership.
- 4B: Host complexes recruited as organizer modules will show compatible structural/biophysical features (e.g., RNA-binding multivalency; coatomer/ESCRT architecture; lipid-modifying enzyme complexes) consistent with mesoscale assembly.
Validation using existing data: We will quantify structural features using established predictors and curated annotations, then test associations with morphotypes and network modules using permutation tests and hierarchical models.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses yield a rigorous, testable synthesis agenda: define a cross-virus mesoscale feature language; identify conserved organizer modules; and build predictive, mechanistic models linking mesoscale organization to emergent replication efficiency—entirely through integration and reanalysis of publicly available datasets.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and scope (synthesis-only): We will conduct a community-scale synthesis integrating five public data modalities—imaging, host–virus interactions, functional genetic screens, transcriptomics, and structural models—across multiple viruses (initial focus: coronaviruses, flaviviruses, and herpesviruses; expandable to additional families as data density permits). No new experiments, samples, or data generation will occur. All analyses will use existing publicly available datasets and metadata.

A. Specific data sources (by modality)
1) Imaging (RC morphology and spatial context)
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI): infection imaging datasets with fluorescence microscopy and metadata.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated multi-dimensional microscopy studies, including infection-related datasets.
- EMPIAR: raw EM datasets, including virus-induced membrane remodeling and replication organelles.
- Supplementary imaging from published studies when deposited in the above archives; we will only use data that are publicly accessible.
2) Host–virus protein interactions (HV-PPI)
- IntAct (EMBL-EBI): curated molecular interactions, including virus–host.
- BioGRID: host–pathogen interaction datasets.
- VirHostNet: integrated virus–host interaction knowledgebase.
- Optional cross-references: STRING (for host-only network context; used cautiously with confidence thresholds).
3) Functional screens (host dependency)
- NCBI GEO and SRA: CRISPR knockout/CRISPRi and RNAi screens with available count matrices or hit lists.
- DepMap (Broad Institute): where viral perturbation screens or relevant host essentiality context can be leveraged for interpretation and priors.
- PubChem BioAssay / ChEMBL (optional): for reported antiviral perturbations with mechanistic annotations, used only as existing data to contextualize “mesoscale disruptors.”
4) Transcriptomics
- NCBI GEO and ArrayExpress: bulk RNA-seq/microarray infection time courses.
- Single-cell infection atlases where public (e.g., COVID-19 Cell Atlas and other scRNA-seq infection datasets deposited in GEO/ArrayExpress); also Human Cell Atlas where infection perturbation datasets are available.
5) Structural data
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): experimentally determined structures of viral scaffolds and host complexes.
- AlphaFold DB: predicted structures for viral and host proteins lacking PDB coverage.
- UniProt: domain annotations, subcellular localization, and sequence features.

B. Data harmonization and governance
- Entity normalization: unify virus names/strains, host species/cell lines, gene/protein identifiers (HGNC/Ensembl/UniProt), and experimental conditions using controlled vocabularies.
- Metadata schema: develop an RC-centric metadata model extending existing standards (OME for imaging; PSI-MI for interactions), capturing virus, time post-infection, cell type, imaging modality, markers, and reported replication readouts.
- Batch and study effects: record study-level covariates and implement hierarchical models and ComBat-like adjustments where appropriate; for imaging, use domain adaptation to reduce modality/lab differences.
- Provenance: every derived dataset will include provenance links (accession IDs, versioned downloads, checksums) and transformation logs.

C. Imaging feature extraction and RC morphotyping
Goal: produce a standardized mesoscale feature framework.
1) Preprocessing
- Convert microscopy formats using Bio-Formats/OME tools; standardize voxel sizes and intensity scaling when metadata permit.
- For EMPIAR volumes/micrographs, apply established denoising and contrast normalization pipelines (parameterized and documented).
2) Segmentation and compartment detection (existing images)
- Use a combination of classical and ML-assisted segmentation, relying on pretrained models where available (e.g., Cellpose/StarDist for fluorescence; EM segmentation via ilastik or pretrained U-Net models). We will not train on new labeled data; if labels exist publicly within IDR studies, they may be used.
- Generate uncertainty estimates by ensembling methods and quantifying agreement.
3) Feature computation (mesoscale descriptors)
- Size/shape: area/volume proxies, equivalent diameter, eccentricity, surface roughness.
- Internal organization: texture features (Haralick), radial intensity profiles, subcompartment counts via watershed/peak detection.
- Spatial context: distances to organelle markers (ER, Golgi, mitochondria, nucleus) when channels exist; proximity to membranes in EM via boundary detection.
- Dynamics proxies: when time-lapse exists, track RCs to estimate fusion frequency, growth rates, and mobility; otherwise infer “assembly stage” from timepoint metadata.
4) Morphotype taxonomy
- Build a joint embedding of features using variational autoencoders or contrastive learning with modality labels as nuisance variables; assess stability with repeated subsampling.
- Cluster using HDBSCAN or Gaussian mixture models; select cluster number via stability metrics.
- Output: a probabilistic morphotype assignment per dataset/timepoint with confidence intervals.

D. Network synthesis: HV-PPI integration and module discovery
1) Construct virus-specific bipartite networks (virus proteins ↔ host proteins) from IntAct/BioGRID/VirHostNet; retain evidence codes and publication provenance.
2) Harmonize interaction confidence: map database-specific scores to a unified scale using calibration against replicated interactions.
3) Embed and detect modules
- Compute host-side embeddings using node2vec/DeepWalk on projected host networks, and/or graph neural network embeddings with virus identity as feature.
- Identify host modules via Leiden/Louvain community detection and overlapping community methods (e.g., link communities) to capture multifunctional proteins.
4) Module interpretation
- Enrich modules for Reactome/KEGG pathways, Gene Ontology, and CORUM complexes.
- Define “recurrent organizer modules” as modules that (i) appear across multiple viruses, (ii) are enriched for screen hits, and (iii) show consistent association with morphotypes.

E. Functional screen meta-analysis (CRISPR/RNAi)
1) Curate screens from GEO/SRA and published supplementary tables; include only those with sufficient metadata and accessible results.
2) Standardize effect sizes
- For CRISPR: use MAGeCK-style summary statistics when available; otherwise compute log-fold changes and robust z-scores.
- For RNAi: harmonize to gene-level scores and account for off-target propensity using published correction methods.
3) Meta-analysis
- Combine across studies using random-effects models; stratify by virus family, cell type, and assay.
- Map hits to network modules and test module-level enrichment via permutation tests.

F. Transcriptomic integration (bulk and single-cell)
1) Bulk: compute differential expression signatures per condition/timepoint; infer pathway activity (GSVA) and regulator activity (DoRothEA/PROGENy where applicable).
2) Single-cell (where public): harmonize cell annotations; infer infection state; compute module activity scores and heterogeneity metrics.
3) Link to RC features: align transcriptomic timepoints with imaging timepoints when possible; otherwise use coarse staging (early/mid/late) based on reported hours post-infection.

G. Multimodal modeling: linking morphotypes, modules, and replication phenotypes
1) Outcome harmonization: within each study, convert replication readouts (titer, qPCR, reporter) to standardized effect sizes relative to controls; retain units for transparency.
2) Multilevel regression
- Fit hierarchical models with random effects for study and virus, predictors including morphotype probabilities, module enrichment scores, and transcriptomic module activities.
- Evaluate predictive performance with leave-one-virus-out and leave-one-study-out cross-validation.
3) Causal inference (observational)
- Construct causal graphs with constraints from time ordering; apply methods such as invariant causal prediction and sensitivity analyses to unmeasured confounding.
- Compare alternative models (e.g., replication drives size vs size enables replication) using time-course evidence.

H. Validation without new experiments
- Cross-database replication: confirm organizer modules across IntAct/BioGRID/VirHostNet.
- Cross-modality coherence: test whether morphotype-associated modules also show consistent transcriptomic activation.
- Known positive controls: benchmark morphotype assignments against canonical RC descriptions from the literature for selected viruses.
- Negative controls: randomized networks (degree-preserving), permuted gene labels, and shuffled timepoints to assess false discovery.

I. Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize metadata schema; curate initial virus set and datasets; implement reproducible data ingestion.
- Milestone: public registry of included datasets with accession IDs and harmonized metadata v1.
Months 7–12:
- Imaging pipelines operational; first-pass feature extraction; preliminary morphotype clustering.
- Milestone: RC feature dataset v1 and morphotype taxonomy draft.
Months 13–18:
- HV-PPI integration; module discovery; screen meta-analysis; initial module recurrence results.
- Milestone: organizer module catalog v1 with provenance and enrichment analyses.
Months 19–24:
- Multimodal modeling linking morphotypes/modules to replication phenotypes; causal graph analyses; robustness checks.
- Milestone: predictive models v1 and cross-validation reports.
Months 25–30:
- Final synthesis, manuscripts, and community resources; NCEMS workshop; finalize open pipelines and documentation.
- Milestone: public release of datasets/tools v2; preprints and submission-ready manuscripts.

J. Team composition (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Virology experts (RNA and DNA viruses) to ensure biological interpretation and correct mapping of viral life cycle stages.
- Quantitative imaging scientists to lead feature extraction, morphometrics, and modality harmonization.
- Network biologists to integrate HV-PPI, perform module detection, and interpret pathway/complex enrichment.
- Statistical modelers/causal inference experts to build multilevel and causal models with rigorous uncertainty quantification.
- Structural bioinformaticians to quantify scaffold multivalency, disorder, and interaction interface features from PDB/AlphaFold DB.
- Research software engineers to build reproducible pipelines, data packaging, and documentation.
- Trainees (graduate students/postdocs) embedded across tasks, receiving cross-training in imaging, networks, and reproducible computational science.

This integrated approach directly addresses NCEMS priorities: mesoscale emergence, synthesis of existing public data, cross-disciplinary collaboration beyond a single lab, and production of open, reusable resources for the community.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverable 1: A cross-virus replication compartment (RC) feature atlas and morphotype taxonomy. We will release a standardized, quantitative feature dataset describing RCs across viruses, imaging modalities, and timepoints, with probabilistic morphotype assignments and uncertainty estimates. This atlas will include harmonized metadata (virus, strain where available, host cell type, time post-infection, imaging modality, markers) and will be linked to the original BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR accession identifiers. The taxonomy will provide a shared language for describing RC mesoscale organization—moving beyond qualitative labels to measurable, comparable descriptors.

Deliverable 2: An integrated catalog of conserved host “mesoscale organizer” modules. By synthesizing IntAct, BioGRID, and VirHostNet interactions with CRISPR/RNAi screen meta-analyses (GEO/SRA; DepMap context where relevant) and transcriptomic module activity (GEO/ArrayExpress; public single-cell infection datasets), we will produce a ranked set of host modules recurrently recruited and required across viruses. Each module will be accompanied by evidence provenance (interaction sources, screen studies, enrichment statistics), functional annotations (Reactome/KEGG/GO, CORUM complexes), and network centrality measures. This catalog will help the field distinguish broadly conserved organizers from virus- or context-specific factors.

Deliverable 3: Predictive, interpretable models linking mesoscale organization to replication efficiency. We will deliver multilevel predictive models that estimate replication outcomes (standardized within-study effect sizes derived from public replication readouts) from RC morphotype features and module-level predictors. Importantly, these models will be interpretable: we will report which mesoscale features (e.g., size distribution shifts, increased internal subcompartmentalization, organelle proximity signatures) and which host modules contribute most strongly, with uncertainty and cross-validation results. Where time-course data permit, causal graph analyses will propose directional relationships (e.g., organizer module engagement preceding morphotype stabilization) and quantify robustness to confounding.

Deliverable 4: Mechanistic synthesis of convergent assembly strategies across viruses. Integrating structural annotations (PDB, AlphaFold DB, UniProt) with the morphotype and module results, we will generate mechanistic hypotheses about convergent mesoscale assembly strategies: (i) phase-separation–dominated RCs driven by multivalent RNA-binding and disordered viral scaffolds; (ii) membrane-curvature–scaffolded RCs driven by viral membrane proteins and host trafficking/curvature modules; and (iii) hybrid RCs combining membrane topology with condensate-like interiors. The impact is a generalizable conceptual framework for how mesoscale organization emerges from ensembles of weak interactions, geometry, and cellular resource allocation.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergent phenomena. This project advances NCEMS’s mission by providing a concrete, quantitative example of emergence at the mesoscale: RCs exhibit system-level properties—selective concentration, shielding, kinetic enhancement, spatial segregation—that arise from collective organization rather than from single molecules. By comparing across unrelated viruses, we can separate universal mesoscale principles (e.g., modular recruitment, permeability proxies, organelle coupling) from lineage-specific implementations. The resulting framework can inform broader cell biology questions about condensates, organelle contact sites, and mesoscale reaction engineering in living cells.

Broader impacts and downstream utility. The outputs will enable multiple future research directions without requiring new data generation by this project: (i) hypothesis generation for antiviral strategies targeting organizer modules or mesoscale assembly processes; (ii) improved annotation standards for infection imaging datasets; (iii) transfer of methods to other mesoscale compartments (stress granules, P bodies, autophagosomes, centrosomal material); and (iv) benchmarking datasets for AI methods in multimodal biological synthesis. By providing standardized feature sets and module definitions, we lower barriers for diverse researchers—including those outside virology—to contribute to mesoscale emergence science.

Dissemination plan. We will produce at least two major manuscripts: (1) the RC morphotype atlas and feature framework; (2) the multimodal organizer-module and replication-efficiency synthesis with predictive/causal models. We will release preprints and submit to open-access journals when possible. We will host an NCEMS-aligned workshop (virtual + in-person) to train participants in using the pipelines and interpreting the atlas, and we will present at cross-disciplinary venues spanning virology, quantitative cell biology, and network science.

Long-term sustainability. All datasets will be packaged with stable identifiers and deposited in long-lived repositories (e.g., Zenodo for derived datasets and code releases; links back to BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR for primary imaging; interaction and transcriptomic resources referenced by accession). We will design the atlas as an extensible resource: new viruses and datasets can be incorporated by running the same containerized workflows and adding metadata-compliant entries. Sustainability will be reinforced through community engagement—inviting external groups to contribute additional public datasets and annotations via documented contribution guidelines and periodic “data sprints.”

[Budget and Resources]
Budget rationale (2.5–3 years; synthesis-only). The proposed work is computationally intensive and coordination-heavy, requiring personnel across multiple disciplines, robust computing, and dedicated resources for open science dissemination and training. All items below are justified by the need to integrate and harmonize heterogeneous public datasets at community scale—beyond the capacity of a single lab.

Personnel
1) Two postdoctoral researchers (computational synthesis focus).
- Postdoc A (quantitative imaging + morphometrics): leads imaging ingestion from BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR, feature extraction, morphotype taxonomy, and uncertainty quantification.
- Postdoc B (network biology + multimodal modeling): leads HV-PPI integration (IntAct/BioGRID/VirHostNet), screen meta-analysis (GEO/SRA), and multilevel/causal models linking modules and morphotypes to replication phenotypes.
Justification: The project’s core deliverables require sustained, expert-level integration across modalities; two postdocs provide parallel progress and cross-validation.

2) One graduate student (integrative analysis + training pipeline).
- Focus on transcriptomic integration (GEO/ArrayExpress; public single-cell infection datasets), module activity inference, and contribution to causal/time-course analyses.
Justification: Provides structured training in data synthesis and contributes to deliverables; aligns with NCEMS workforce goals.

3) Research software engineer/programmer (0.5–1.0 FTE depending on award size).
- Builds and maintains Snakemake/Nextflow pipelines, containers (Docker/Singularity), CI, documentation, and data packaging for Zenodo releases.
Justification: Reproducibility and sustainability require professional engineering support; essential for open workflows usable by the community.

4) PI/co-PI effort (fractional) across participating labs.
- Supports coordination, scientific integration, mentoring, and dissemination.
Justification: Multi-lab synthesis demands active leadership, consensus building on standards, and oversight of open science practices.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or institutional HPC allocations for:
  (i) large-scale image processing (segmentation, feature extraction) from EMPIAR and high-content fluorescence datasets;

Travel and collaboration

rephrased_abstract: Virology and cellular mesoscale organization investigate viral replication compartments, which comprise membrane bound organelles or membraneless inclusions whose formation mechanisms hold crucial importance for understanding diverse RNA and DNA viruses. Currently, knowledge remains fragmented across subfields, and researchers do not understand whether compartment architecture and recruited host protein modules share universal design principles that determine viral replication efficiency. This project will establish predictive relationships between compartment features and host modules by applying deep learning image processing, network analysis algorithms, and causal modeling to synthesize public data and determine universal design principles. The study will integrate diverse repositories including BioImage Archive, BioGRID, and AlphaFold DB by utilizing controlled vocabularies, unified metadata schemas, and joint feature embeddings to align imaging datasets and transcriptomic profiles. abstract_original:
Many viruses create mesoscale replication compartments (100–1000 nm membraneless inclusions or membrane-bound organelles) that concentrate viral and host factors. The emergent phenomenon is that collective compartment organization yields replication efficiencies and immune evasion strategies not predictable from individual viral proteins. This project will ask whether replication compartments share universal mesoscale design principles across unrelated viruses.

We will synthesize: (i) viral replication compartment imaging datasets (electron microscopy and fluorescence) from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR, spanning RNA viruses (coronaviruses, flaviviruses) and DNA viruses (herpesviruses), (ii) host–virus protein interaction networks (IntAct, BioGRID, VirHostNet), (iii) CRISPR and RNAi screens for host dependency factors (DepMap viral screens; published screens in GEO/SRA), (iv) viral and host transcriptomic responses (GEO; single-cell infection atlases where available), and (v) structural data for viral scaffold proteins and host recruited complexes (PDB, AlphaFold DB).

We will develop a comparative mesoscale compartment feature framework: size distributions, internal subcompartmentalization, proximity to organelles, and dynamics proxies. Using network embedding and community detection on host–virus interactomes, we will identify recurrent host modules (e.g., RNA metabolism, membrane trafficking, stress granule components) recruited into compartments. We will then relate these modules to compartment morphotypes and to replication phenotypes (viral titers/replication markers from public datasets) using multi-level regression and causal graph methods.

Hypotheses: (1) replication compartments implement convergent mesoscale strategies—phase separation, membrane curvature scaffolding, or hybrid forms—to optimize reaction kinetics and shield nucleic acids; (2) the emergent efficiency depends on a small number of host module recruitments that act as “mesoscale organizers”; and (3) antiviral perturbations that disrupt mesoscale organization (rather than single enzymes) provide broad-spectrum leverage.

Expected insights include a cross-virus taxonomy of replication compartment architectures, identification of conserved host mesoscale organizers, and predictive models linking host factor modules to compartment type and replication success. Deliverables will include open compartment feature datasets and interoperable pipelines for image and network integration.

This requires team science across virology, quantitative imaging, network biology, and statistical modeling, and it relies entirely on integrating diverse public datasets. NCEMS support is crucial to coordinate cross-virus data harmonization, establish open standards for compartment annotation, and train trainees in integrative, reproducible computational virology focused on emergent mesoscale organization.

abstract_text:
Cell walls are mesoscale composite materials (10–500 nm fibril bundles, crosslinks, and pores) whose emergent mechanical properties enable growth, morphogenesis, and stress resistance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polysaccharide architecture produces nonlinear stiffness, anisotropy, and fracture behavior not predictable from monomer composition. This project will synthesize multi-omics and imaging data to uncover universal principles of cell wall nanocomposite design in plants and fungi.

We will integrate: (i) cell wall compositional datasets (glycomics and carbohydrate-active enzyme annotations from CAZy; polysaccharide composition in Metabolomics Workbench and literature-derived datasets), (ii) solid-state NMR and scattering data where publicly available (BMRB; published SAXS/WAXS datasets), (iii) AFM nanomechanics maps and electron microscopy of wall ultrastructure (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (iv) transcriptomics of wall biosynthesis during growth and stress (GEO; Arabidopsis eFP, fungal expression atlases), and (v) mutant/perturbation phenotypes affecting morphology (TAIR, SGD, FungiDB; high-content imaging screens).

Analytically, we will build a mesoscale structure–property model linking polymer composition and enzyme expression to ultrastructural descriptors (fibril orientation, bundling, pore size distributions) and to mechanical outputs (Young’s modulus maps, viscoelastic parameters). We will use Bayesian meta-analysis to harmonize AFM protocols and machine learning to infer ultrastructure from indirect measurements (NMR/scattering) when imaging is absent. Network models of CAZyme co-expression will be linked to predicted architectural states.

Key questions: Do plant and fungal walls occupy shared regions of a mesoscale “design space” balancing stiffness and extensibility? Which crosslink motifs (e.g., lignin–cellulose coupling vs chitin–glucan branching) create emergent anisotropic growth? Can we predict growth patterns and failure modes under stress from mesoscale architecture rather than gene lists?

Expected insights include a cross-kingdom atlas of wall mesoscale architectures, identification of convergent nanocomposite strategies, and mechanistic hypotheses for how cells tune growth directionality by reorganizing nanoscale fibrils. The project will generate open tools for quantifying wall ultrastructure and mechanical heterogeneity.

This synthesis requires plant biologists, mycologists, polymer physicists, and computational image analysts, and depends on integrating heterogeneous public datasets beyond any single lab. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation, shared modeling infrastructure, and trainee training in quantitative biomaterials analysis under open science principles.

We will use Bayesian meta-analysis to harmonize AFM protocols and machine learning to infer ultrastructure from indirect measurements (NMR/scattering) when imaging is absent. Network models of CAZyme co-expression will be linked to predicted architectural states.

Key questions: Do plant and fungal walls occupy shared regions of a mesoscale “design space” balancing stiffness and extensibility? Can we predict growth patterns and failure modes under stress from mesoscale architecture rather than gene lists?

Expected insights include a cross-kingdom atlas of wall mesoscale architectures, identification of convergent nanocomposite strategies, and mechanistic hypotheses for how cells tune growth directionality by reorganizing nanoscale fibrils. The project will generate open tools for quantifying wall ultrastructure and mechanical heterogeneity.

This synthesis requires plant biologists, mycologists, polymer physicists, and computational image analysts, and depends on integrating heterogeneous public datasets beyond any single lab. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation, shared modeling infrastructure, and trainee training in quantitative biomaterials analysis under open science principles.

[Background and Significance]
Cell walls are defining features of plants and fungi and exemplary mesoscale biological materials. At the mesoscale (roughly 10–500 nm), walls comprise oriented fibril bundles (cellulose microfibrils in plants; chitin microfibrils in fungi), matrix polysaccharides (hemicelluloses, pectins; β-glucans, mannans), covalent and noncovalent crosslinks, and water-filled pores. These components self-organize into heterogeneous networks whose collective behavior yields emergent properties—nonlinear elasticity, viscoelastic relaxation, strain stiffening/softening, anisotropy, and fracture resistance—that cannot be inferred by summing monomer composition alone. These emergent mechanical properties are central to cell growth, morphogenesis, and stress resistance: cells expand under turgor, remodel walls to direct growth, and withstand environmental challenges (osmotic shock, pathogens, desiccation) while maintaining integrity.

Current understanding is fragmented across scales and disciplines. Plant cell wall biology has detailed catalogs of biosynthetic enzymes and polymers, and fungal biology has deep knowledge of chitin and glucan synthesis and remodeling. In parallel, polymer physics and soft-matter mechanics provide theoretical frameworks for fiber-reinforced composites, percolation, and network elasticity. However, the key mesoscale mapping—from biochemical composition and enzyme activity to ultrastructural organization, and from ultrastructure to mechanical response—remains incomplete, especially across kingdoms. Many studies focus on single species, a limited set of mutants, or one measurement modality (e.g., composition assays, AFM indentation, or electron microscopy). As a result, the field lacks generalizable principles that explain how diverse organisms tune wall nanostructure to achieve specific mechanical and growth phenotypes.

Public data now make synthesis research feasible at a community scale. Composition and enzyme repertoires are increasingly accessible through carbohydrate-active enzyme annotations in CAZy and organismal genome resources (FungiDB, SGD, TAIR). Metabolomics Workbench and published glycomics datasets provide quantitative polysaccharide and monosaccharide composition measurements across tissues, developmental stages, and perturbations. Transcriptomic compendia in NCBI GEO, Expression Atlas, and curated resources such as Arabidopsis eFP Browser and fungal expression atlases capture coordinated regulation of wall biosynthesis and remodeling during growth and stress.

Critically, imaging and biophysical datasets that directly probe mesoscale organization and mechanics are also becoming available. The BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource (IDR) host microscopy datasets, including cell wall-related fluorescence imaging and high-content screens with morphological phenotypes. EMPIAR provides raw electron microscopy datasets, enabling reanalysis for fibril alignment, layering, and pore architecture. For structure at intermediate length scales, solid-state NMR data deposited in the Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank (BMRB) and scattering datasets (SAXS/WAXS) in general-purpose repositories (e.g., Zenodo, Figshare, institutional repositories linked from publications) contain constraints on polymer packing, crystallinity, and fibril spacing. AFM nanomechanics maps and indentation datasets are often shared as supplementary data or deposited in open repositories; while heterogeneous, they can be harmonized through careful metadata extraction and statistical modeling.

Despite this abundance, major gaps persist that are well-suited to synthesis. First, there is no cross-kingdom, mesoscale “design space” that jointly represents composition, ultrastructure, and mechanics, making it difficult to identify convergent strategies (e.g., different chemistries producing similar anisotropy). Second, measurements are siloed: mechanical maps are rarely integrated with ultrastructural descriptors extracted from EM, with NMR/scattering constraints, or with transcriptional programs controlling CAZymes. Third, protocol heterogeneity (AFM tip geometry, indentation depth, sample preparation; EM staining and sectioning; NMR sample state) obstructs meta-analysis and prevents robust cross-study comparisons. Fourth, the field lacks predictive models that connect enzyme co-regulation and polymer composition to emergent mechanical phenotypes such as directional growth or stress-induced failure.

Emergent mesoscale phenomena matter because they mediate how molecular-level changes scale up to cellular outcomes. Gene lists alone do not predict growth directionality, wall yielding, or fracture; instead, these behaviors arise from collective architecture—fibril orientation distributions, bundling, matrix crosslink density, and porosity. Understanding these emergent principles has broad implications: it can explain how pathogens breach walls, how crops resist lodging and drought, how fungi maintain hyphal tip growth, and how evolution discovers different biochemical routes to similar mechanical functions. Moreover, cell walls are paradigms for biological nanocomposites, providing generalizable insights into mesoscale emergence relevant to other systems (extracellular matrices, biofilms, cytoskeletal composites).

This proposal leverages NCEMS’s mission by synthesizing existing, publicly available multi-omics, imaging, and biophysical data to infer universal mesoscale structure–property relationships. The work is beyond any single lab because it requires coordinated curation across databases, standardized extraction of quantitative descriptors from raw images and spectra, and integrative modeling that spans plant and fungal biology, polymer physics, and machine learning. By integrating distinct datasets into a shared analytical framework, we will transform dispersed observations into mechanistic, testable principles of emergent cell wall nanomechanics.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how mesoscale architecture gives rise to emergent mechanical behavior in plant and fungal cell walls, and whether universal design principles span kingdoms despite distinct chemistries. We focus on questions that are precise, testable with existing data, and explicitly tied to mesoscale emergence (10–500 nm organization) rather than purely molecular composition or macroscopic tissue mechanics.

RQ1: Do plant and fungal cell walls occupy shared regions of a mesoscale mechanical “design space” defined by architecture-dependent tradeoffs between stiffness, extensibility, and toughness?
Hypothesis 1A (convergence): Across kingdoms, walls cluster into a limited number of mesoscale architectural states (e.g., highly aligned fibril-reinforced networks vs isotropic, highly crosslinked gels) that map to similar mechanical signatures (anisotropy ratio, strain-stiffening exponent, viscoelastic relaxation times), even when polymer chemistries differ.
Measurable predictions: (i) Dimensionality reduction on integrated descriptors (fibril alignment, bundling, pore size distribution, crystallinity proxies) will yield recurring clusters containing both plant and fungal samples; (ii) these clusters will show conserved mechanical patterns in AFM-derived modulus distributions and relaxation parameters after protocol harmonization.
Validation with existing data: Use AFM datasets (published maps), EMPIAR ultrastructure, and NMR/scattering constraints where available; evaluate whether cross-kingdom samples co-occupy clusters more than expected by chance using permutation tests controlling for measurement modality.

RQ2: Which mesoscale crosslinking motifs and network topologies generate emergent anisotropic growth, and can they be inferred from integrated omics and structural proxies?
Hypothesis 2A (distinct routes to anisotropy): Plant anisotropy is primarily achieved by cellulose microfibril alignment and lignin/hemicellulose-mediated coupling that increases load transfer along preferred directions, whereas fungal anisotropy is achieved by chitin–β-glucan branching and spatially localized remodeling that creates a circumferential reinforcement pattern; both routes produce similar emergent anisotropy metrics but differ in predicted pore anisotropy and relaxation behavior.
Measurable predictions: (i) Samples with high growth anisotropy (from morphological phenotypes and imaging) will exhibit high fibril orientation order parameters (from EM/image analysis) and/or high inferred crosslink density proxies (from CAZyme expression modules and NMR/scattering features); (ii) plant vs fungal anisotropic states will separate along secondary axes corresponding to pore anisotropy and viscoelastic signatures.
Validation with existing data: Link mutant/perturbation phenotypes (TAIR, SGD, FungiDB; high-content screens in IDR) to transcriptomic modules (GEO, Expression Atlas) and to ultrastructure/mechanics descriptors, testing mediation models in which architecture mediates gene-to-phenotype relationships.

RQ3: Can mesoscale architecture predict failure modes under stress (cracking, delamination, tip bursting, swelling) better than gene-centric predictors?
Hypothesis 3A (architecture-first prediction): Models using mesoscale descriptors (alignment, bundling, porosity, inferred crosslink topology) will outperform models using gene expression alone in predicting stress phenotypes (osmotic shock sensitivity, mechanical rupture, pathogen susceptibility) recorded in curated phenotype databases and imaging screens.
Measurable predictions: (i) Cross-validated AUC/accuracy will be significantly higher for architecture-based predictors; (ii) adding gene expression to architecture will yield smaller incremental gains than adding architecture to gene expression, indicating that architecture captures emergent integration of molecular processes.
Validation with existing data: Use stress phenotype annotations from TAIR and SGD, fungal phenotype data from FungiDB, and quantitative morphological readouts from IDR datasets; evaluate predictive performance via nested cross-validation with organism-stratified splits to test generalization.

RQ4: When direct imaging is absent, can we infer key mesoscale ultrastructural descriptors from indirect measurements (solid-state NMR, SAXS/WAXS, composition) and transcriptional programs?
Hypothesis 4A (latent architecture inference): A latent-variable model trained on samples with paired imaging and indirect data can infer fibril spacing, crystallinity-related features, and pore-size distributions from NMR/scattering features and composition/CAZyme modules with quantified uncertainty.
Measurable predictions: (i) Posterior predictive checks will show calibrated uncertainty; (ii) inferred descriptors will recover known relationships (e.g., increased crystallinity proxies associated with higher modulus) in held-out datasets.
Validation with existing data: Train on subsets with paired modalities; test on independent studies and organisms; compare inferred descriptors to any available ultrastructure annotations in the literature.

Mechanistic insight expected: Collectively, these questions and hypotheses aim to reveal how cells tune emergent mechanical behavior by navigating a constrained mesoscale design space. We expect to identify a small set of architectural “control knobs” (alignment, bundling, crosslink topology, porosity) that integrate diverse molecular pathways into reproducible mechanical outcomes, and to articulate cross-kingdom parallels and differences in how these knobs are implemented biochemically.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will conduct a community-scale synthesis that (1) curates and harmonizes public datasets spanning composition, enzyme repertoires and expression, ultrastructure, and mechanics; (2) extracts standardized mesoscale descriptors from raw images and spectra; and (3) builds integrative, uncertainty-aware models linking molecular inputs to emergent mesoscale mechanical outputs and growth phenotypes. No new experimental data will be generated; all analyses will use existing publicly available data and metadata.

Specific data sources (public repositories)
1) Composition and enzyme annotations
- CAZy (Carbohydrate-Active enZymes database): CAZyme family assignments for plant and fungal genomes; used to define biosynthetic/remodeling capacity.
- UniProtKB and Ensembl Plants / Ensembl Fungi: protein annotations and cross-references for mapping CAZy families to genes.
- Metabolomics Workbench: datasets containing monosaccharide composition, cell wall sugar profiles, and related metabolite measurements.
- Literature-derived glycomics/cell wall composition tables: extracted from supplementary materials and deposited to Zenodo as a curated, citation-linked compilation (derived data only, with original sources cited).

2) Transcriptomics and expression compendia
- NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO): RNA-seq and microarray datasets for wall biosynthesis during development and stress.
- EMBL-EBI Expression Atlas: standardized reprocessed expression where available.
- Arabidopsis eFP Browser (BAR): curated expression patterns for key wall genes.
- Fungal expression atlases (species-specific portals where public, plus GEO/Expression Atlas entries) to assemble comparable growth/stress conditions.

3) Imaging and ultrastructure
- EMPIAR: raw electron microscopy datasets (TEM, cryo-EM/ET where available) containing wall ultrastructure.
- BioImage Archive: microscopy datasets relevant to wall organization and growth.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): high-content imaging screens and phenotype datasets (including fungal/plant cell morphology screens when available).

4) Biophysical structure constraints and mechanics
- Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank (BMRB): solid-state NMR datasets and assignments relevant to cell wall polymers.
- Small-angle and wide-angle X-ray scattering datasets (SAXS/WAXS): obtained from open repositories linked to publications (Zenodo, Figshare, institutional repositories) and from supplementary data.
- AFM nanomechanics: publicly shared datasets from publications (supplementary files, Zenodo/Figshare/GitHub data releases) containing force curves, modulus maps, and metadata.

5) Genotype/phenotype resources
- TAIR (The Arabidopsis Information Resource): mutant phenotypes, gene function, and trait annotations.
- SGD (Saccharomyces Genome Database): phenotype annotations for wall genes and stress sensitivities.
- FungiDB: phenotype and functional annotations across fungal species, including pathogens and model fungi.

Data harmonization and knowledge graph
We will create a unified “WallMesoscale” data model with a minimal required metadata schema: organism/strain, cell type/tissue, growth condition, perturbation (mutant/drug/stress), measurement modality, sample preparation notes, and quantitative outputs. Entities (genes, CAZy families, polymers, imaging samples, AFM maps, NMR spectra, scattering profiles, phenotypes) will be linked in a knowledge graph (RDF/JSON-LD) to preserve provenance and enable queries. Identifier mapping will use standard cross-references (UniProt accessions, Ensembl IDs, TAIR locus IDs, SGD systematic names) with explicit versioning.

Quantitative descriptor extraction (mesoscale features)
Imaging (EM and fluorescence where relevant)
- Fibril orientation and anisotropy: structure tensor analysis and Fourier-domain methods to compute orientation distribution functions and an order parameter.
- Bundling and spacing: filament segmentation (classical + deep learning where appropriate) to estimate bundle thickness distributions and nearest-neighbor spacing.
- Porosity and pore-size distributions: thresholding/segmentation with uncertainty quantification; compute pore size via distance transforms and Minkowski functionals.
- Layering and delamination signatures: texture metrics and lamellar periodicity where present.
All pipelines will be benchmarked on publicly available annotated subsets and will output standardized feature tables with units and confidence metrics.

AFM nanomechanics
- Protocol harmonization: extract metadata (tip radius, indentation model used, loading rate, indentation depth, sample hydration) and reanalyze force curves when raw data are available.
- Bayesian meta-analysis: hierarchical models to estimate comparable mechanical parameters (effective Young’s modulus, viscoelastic relaxation times) while accounting for study-level protocol effects.
- Spatial heterogeneity metrics: compute modulus distribution moments, spatial autocorrelation, and anisotropy of mechanical maps.

NMR and scattering
- Feature engineering: derive spectral/scattering descriptors (peak positions, widths, intensity ratios; Porod exponents; correlation lengths) that proxy packing, crystallinity, and characteristic spacings.
- Cross-modal alignment: map indirect features to imaging-derived structural descriptors using latent-variable models (below).

Integrative modeling (linking molecular inputs → architecture → mechanics → phenotype)
1) CAZyme co-expression networks
- Build condition-specific co-expression networks from GEO/Expression Atlas compendia; infer modules enriched for CAZy families and wall pathways.
- Use graph community detection (e.g., Leiden) and module eigengenes as predictors of architectural states.

2) Mesoscale structure–property models
- Multilevel Bayesian models to relate composition (sugar fractions), CAZyme modules, and indirect structural proxies to imaging-derived architecture and AFM mechanics.
- Causal/mediation-inspired analyses (within observational limits): test whether architectural descriptors statistically mediate relationships between gene modules and growth/stress phenotypes.

3) Machine learning for prediction and inference
- Supervised prediction: gradient-boosted trees and regularized regression for phenotype prediction; organism-stratified cross-validation to test generalization.
- Multimodal representation learning: variational approaches to infer latent “architectural states” from partial modalities (e.g., NMR+composition without EM), with uncertainty estimates.
- Model interpretability: SHAP/feature importance and posterior summaries to identify key architectural control knobs.

Validation strategies (no new experiments)
- Cross-dataset replication: train models on one set of studies/species and test on independent datasets/species.
- Positive controls: known wall mutants with established mechanical/structural effects (e.g., cellulose synthase mutants in Arabidopsis; chitin synthase/glucan synthase mutants in fungi) used to verify directionality of inferred changes.
- Protocol sensitivity analyses: evaluate robustness of AFM harmonization by leaving out studies and checking stability of pooled estimates.
- Posterior predictive checks and calibration curves for uncertainty-aware models.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6: Team onboarding; finalize metadata schema; initial curation of representative plant and fungal datasets; set up knowledge graph; pilot EM and AFM pipelines on 2–3 benchmark datasets.
Months 7–12: Scale curation across repositories; release v0.1 WallMesoscale dataset; implement Bayesian AFM harmonization; extract imaging descriptors from EMPIAR/BioImage Archive datasets.
Months 13–18: Integrative modeling phase I: define latent architectural states; build CAZyme co-expression modules; initial cross-kingdom design-space maps.
Months 19–24: Integrative modeling phase II: phenotype prediction and stress/failure mode analyses; cross-dataset validation; refine inference from NMR/scattering.
Months 25–30: Final atlas and tool release (v1.0); manuscripts; NCEMS-hosted training workshop; sustainability plan and handoff to community repositories.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Plant cell wall biologists: curate plant-specific datasets, interpret polymer biology, phenotype mapping.
- Mycologists/fungal cell wall experts: curate fungal datasets, interpret chitin/glucan remodeling and phenotypes.
- Polymer physicists/biomechanics experts: guide mesoscale mechanics interpretation, composite theory, and model formulation.
- Computational image analysts: develop and validate EM/AFM image processing pipelines.
- Statistical data scientists: Bayesian harmonization, meta-analysis, uncertainty quantification.
- Research software engineers: workflow engineering, knowledge graph implementation, packaging tools for reuse.
This breadth is essential to integrate heterogeneous modalities and to ensure biological and physical interpretability—precisely the kind of team science NCEMS is designed to enable.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) Cross-kingdom mesoscale atlas (WallMesoscale Atlas)
We will produce an open, queryable atlas that maps plant and fungal cell wall samples into a common mesoscale design space. Each entry will include: (i) curated provenance-linked metadata; (ii) standardized composition features (sugar fractions, polymer proxies when available); (iii) CAZyme repertoire and co-expression module scores; (iv) ultrastructural descriptors (fibril orientation order, bundling metrics, pore-size distributions, layering indices) extracted from EMPIAR/BioImage Archive/IDR datasets; and (v) harmonized AFM mechanical parameters with uncertainty estimates. The atlas will support cross-kingdom comparisons and enable downstream hypothesis generation without requiring new data collection.

2) Harmonization and analysis toolkit
We will release a modular, open-source toolkit for:
- AFM nanomechanics meta-analysis: hierarchical Bayesian harmonization of modulus and viscoelastic parameters across protocols, with standardized reporting and uncertainty.
- Cell wall ultrastructure quantification: reproducible pipelines to extract fibril orientation, bundling, and porosity descriptors from EM images, with quality control and confidence metrics.
- Multimodal inference: models that infer likely architectural descriptors from indirect NMR/scattering/composition data when imaging is absent, producing posterior distributions rather than point estimates.

3) Mechanistic models of emergent structure–property relationships
We will deliver interpretable models linking molecular programs (CAZyme modules and composition) to emergent mesoscale architecture and mechanical outputs. Key expected products include:
- Identification of a small set of latent architectural states that recur across species and conditions, serving as “mesoscale phenotypes.”
- Quantified tradeoffs (Pareto fronts) between stiffness, extensibility, anisotropy, and heterogeneity, revealing constraints that shape wall evolution and function.
- Evidence-based hypotheses for how specific crosslinking strategies (e.g., lignin/hemicellulose coupling vs chitin–glucan branching) realize similar emergent mechanical goals via distinct mesoscale implementations.

4) Predictive framework for growth and stress phenotypes
A central impact will be demonstrating whether mesoscale descriptors predict growth patterns and stress/failure phenotypes better than gene-centric signatures. Deliverables include validated predictive models and a set of “architectural biomarkers” (e.g., orientation order thresholds, porosity regimes, heterogeneity signatures) associated with bursting, cracking, swelling sensitivity, or altered morphogenesis.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergence
This project directly advances understanding of emergent phenomena at the mesoscale by showing how collective organization—rather than component identity alone—determines mechanical behavior. By integrating multiple measurement modalities, we will move the field from qualitative narratives (“more cellulose increases stiffness”) to quantitative, cross-validated principles (“a shift from isotropic to aligned fibril states increases anisotropy ratio and reduces relaxation time in a predictable manner, conditional on porosity and crosslink proxies”). The cross-kingdom scope is essential: convergence would indicate universal mesoscale laws of biological composites, while divergence would identify kingdom-specific constraints and evolutionary solutions.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Generalizable synthesis framework: The knowledge-graph-based integration, protocol harmonization, and multimodal inference approaches will be transferable to other mesoscale systems (e.g., extracellular matrix networks, biofilm matrices, cytoskeletal composites).
- Accelerating discovery without new experiments: By unlocking value from existing datasets, the project lowers barriers for labs lacking specialized instrumentation (AFM, EM, NMR) to engage in mechanistic wall research.
- Enabling rational engineering: Insights into architectural control knobs can inform future work on crop resilience, fungal biotechnology, and antifungal strategies by targeting emergent mechanical vulnerabilities.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least three manuscripts (atlas/resource paper; AFM harmonization methodology; cross-kingdom design principles and phenotype prediction).
- NCEMS working group meetings and an open training workshop focused on reproducible biomaterials data synthesis.
- Community resources: deposition of curated tables and derived descriptors to Zenodo with DOIs; code and workflows publicly released; atlas hosted with a lightweight web interface and downloadable snapshots.

Long-term sustainability
We will design outputs for longevity: (i) stable, versioned releases (semantic versioning) with DOIs; (ii) use of community standards for metadata and identifiers; (iii) containerized workflows to ensure future executability; and (iv) alignment with existing repositories (BioImage Archive/EMPIAR links preserved; derived datasets mirrored on Zenodo). We will also cultivate community maintainers by onboarding trainees and external contributors through documented contribution guidelines and periodic virtual “data sprints.”

[Budget and Resources]
Budget overview (2.5–3 years; synthesis-only)
The budget is designed to support intensive data curation, harmonization, and integrative modeling across multiple labs and modalities, with strong emphasis on research software engineering, trainee training, and open science infrastructure. No funds are allocated for experiments, sample collection, or new data generation.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (one plant-focused, one fungal/mechanics-focused; 2.0 FTE total across institutions): lead dataset curation, biological interpretation, and integrative modeling; coordinate cross-kingdom comparisons and manuscript preparation.
- 1 Research software engineer / programmer-analyst (1.0 FTE): build and maintain data ingestion pipelines, knowledge graph infrastructure, containerized workflows, CI/testing, and the public-facing atlas interface.
- 1 Graduate student (0.5–1.0 FTE depending on institutional norms): develop imaging descriptor extraction pipelines and benchmarking; contribute to training materials and reproducibility audits.
- Part-time statistical consultant or senior personnel effort (0.1–0.2 FTE across PIs): guide Bayesian meta-analysis, uncertainty quantification, and validation design.
Justification: The heterogeneity of AFM, EM, NMR/scattering, and omics datasets makes software and statistical rigor essential. Dedicated engineering effort is required to ensure reusable, reproducible synthesis products beyond what typical single-lab staffing can sustain.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and storage (e.g., AWS/GCP or NSF-supported cloud allocations): for scalable image processing (EMPIAR volumes), model training, and hosting reproducible workflow runs.
- HPC time (institutional clusters and/or national allocations): for computationally intensive Bayesian inference and multimodal representation learning.
- Persistent storage and backup: to maintain cached copies of publicly available datasets (where permitted) and derived feature tables; includes costs for object storage and snapshotting.
Justification: Reprocessing raw EM datasets and harmonizing AFM force-curve analyses require substantial compute and I/O, and reproducibility requires stable, versioned computational environments.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2 in-person meetings per year, supplemented by monthly virtual meetings): support travel for cross-disciplinary team members, including trainees, to co-develop standards, resolve integration issues, and accelerate synthesis.
- Conference dissemination travel: limited support for presenting resource/tool outputs at relevant meetings (cell wall biology, fungal biology, biophysics, computational biology) and for recruiting external adopters.
Justification: The project’s success depends on sustained, structured collaboration across disciplines and institutions; in-person synthesis meetings are a core NCEMS mechanism for catalyzing integration beyond existing collaborations.

Workshops and training events
- One NCEMS-hosted open workshop (hybrid) on reproducible mesoscale biomaterials synthesis: instructor time, materials preparation, and participant support (with priority for trainees and underrepresented institutions).
- Two virtual tutorial series: minimal platform costs, captioning/transcription for accessibility.
Justification: Training is a core NCEMS goal; these events create a pipeline of data-savvy scientists and broaden participation.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo DOI archiving for releases (no direct cost, but staff time allocated for curation and documentation).
- Web hosting and maintenance for the atlas interface (lightweight static hosting plus optional backend for search; domain/SSL if needed).
- Data curation tools: modest funds for software subscriptions only if required for parsing proprietary formats; preference given to open-source tooling.
Justification: Sustained usability and discoverability of synthesis outputs require professional-grade documentation, versioning, and accessible interfaces.

Overall justification relative to synthesis goals
Every budget category directly supports (i) integration of heterogeneous public datasets at scale, (ii) robust statistical harmonization and cross-validation without new experiments, (iii) production of reusable community resources, and (iv) training and dissemination consistent with NCEMS’s open, team-based synthesis mission.
standardized_text: This project investigates mesoscale architecture in plant and fungal cell walls to build missing cross kingdom predictive models. Extensive catalogs of biosynthetic enzymes exist but heterogeneous experimental protocols keep structural data isolated and prevent direct comparisons. The study asks if these walls share universal design principles to mechanistically explain crop resilience and pathogen infection. This secondary data synthesis extracts architectural descriptors from public datasets to build models of molecular inputs and outputs. Methods include structure tensor analysis and gradient boosted trees alongside multilevel Bayesian models to evaluate the curated data. The team validates results through nested cross validation and posterior predictive checks alongside positive controls using known mutants. Data sources include genetic databases (UniProtKB) and structural repositories (BioImage Archive) alongside public files from Zenodo and Figshare. The project integrates these datasets into a knowledge graph by using explicit versioning and schemas for identifier mapping. The team will address missing imaging data and protocol heterogeneity by deploying hierarchical Bayesian harmonization and latent variable models. The thirty month timeline progresses from initial data curation and pipeline development to final predictive modeling and atlas releases. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating biology with machine learning exceeds the capacity of one laboratory. The team will release an open source public atlas alongside containerized analytical workflows and complete data depositions on Zenodo. The diverse team includes physicists and early career biologists who will receive collaborative training through virtual tutorial series.
rephrased_abstract: The mesoscale organization of plant and fungal cell walls dictates emergent mechanical properties such as stiffness and fracture behavior, but isolated data and protocol heterogeneity prevent unified synthesis across these biological domains. A significant gap remains in developing cross kingdom predictive models and generalizable principles that connect biochemical composition and enzyme activity to ultrastructural organization and mechanical responses. This project will synthesize multi omics and imaging data using Bayesian meta analysis, Fourier domain methods, and gradient boosted trees to determine universal mesoscale design principles and build integrative models linking molecular inputs to mechanical outputs. Information from databases including CAZy, FungiDB, EMPIAR, and the BioImage Archive will be integrated into a unified semantic knowledge graph using standard cross reference identifier mapping and explicit versioning. This research will establish quantitative relationships linking molecular changes to cellular outcomes, providing mechanistic explanations for crop resilience, pathogen infection, and biological nanocomposite behavior independent of simple gene lists.
abstract_original:
Cell walls are mesoscale composite materials (10–500 nm fibril bundles, crosslinks, and pores) whose emergent mechanical properties enable growth, morphogenesis, and stress resistance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polysaccharide architecture produces nonlinear stiffness, anisotropy, and fracture behavior not predictable from monomer composition. This project will synthesize multi-omics and imaging data to uncover universal principles of cell wall nanocomposite design in plants and fungi.

We will integrate: (i) cell wall compositional datasets (glycomics and carbohydrate-active enzyme annotations from CAZy; polysaccharide composition in Metabolomics Workbench and literature-derived datasets), (ii) solid-state NMR and scattering data where publicly available (BMRB; published SAXS/WAXS datasets), (iii) AFM nanomechanics maps and electron microscopy of wall ultrastructure (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (iv) transcriptomics of wall biosynthesis during growth and stress (GEO; Arabidopsis eFP, fungal expression atlases), and (v) mutant/perturbation phenotypes affecting morphology (TAIR, SGD, FungiDB; high-content imaging screens).

Analytically, we will build a mesoscale structure–property model linking polymer composition and enzyme expression to ultrastructural descriptors (fibril orientation, bundling, pore size distributions) and to mechanical outputs (Young’s modulus maps, viscoelastic parameters). We will use Bayesian meta-analysis to harmonize AFM protocols and machine learning to infer ultrastructure from indirect measurements (NMR/scattering) when imaging is absent. Network models of CAZyme co-expression will be linked to predicted architectural states.

Key questions: Do plant and fungal walls occupy shared regions of a mesoscale “design space” balancing stiffness and extensibility? Which crosslink motifs (e.g., lignin–cellulose coupling vs chitin–glucan branching) create emergent anisotropic growth? Can we predict growth patterns and failure modes under stress from mesoscale architecture rather than gene lists?

Expected insights include a cross-kingdom atlas of wall mesoscale architectures, identification of convergent nanocomposite strategies, and mechanistic hypotheses for how cells tune growth directionality by reorganizing nanoscale fibrils. The project will generate open tools for quantifying wall ultrastructure and mechanical heterogeneity.

This synthesis requires plant biologists, mycologists, polymer physicists, and computational image analysts, and depends on integrating heterogeneous public datasets beyond any single lab. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation, shared modeling infrastructure, and trainee training in quantitative biomaterials analysis under open science principles.

title: Mesoscale Proteasome and Autophagy Hub Organization: Integrating Spatial Proteomics, Imaging, and Ubiquitinome Data to Explain Proteostasis Emergence
title_norm: mesoscale proteasome and autophagy hub organization integrating spatial proteomics imaging and ubiquitinome data to explain proteostasis emergence
abstract_text:
Proteostasis emerges from mesoscale organization of degradation hubs—proteasome-rich microdomains, aggresomes, and autophagy initiation sites (50–1000 nm)—that coordinate substrate selection, sequestration, and clearance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective spatial organization and phase-like sequestration yields system-level robustness to misfolded proteins, not predictable from individual E3 ligases or proteases.

We will synthesize: (i) spatial proteomics identifying proteasome/autophagy component localization (Human Protein Atlas; hyperLOPIT and proximity labeling datasets in PRIDE), (ii) ubiquitinomics and proteome turnover datasets (PRIDE; ubiquitin linkage-specific studies), (iii) bioimaging of aggresomes, p62 bodies, autophagosome markers, and proteasome foci (IDR/BioImage Archive), (iv) genetic perturbation screens for proteostasis regulators (DepMap; CRISPR screens for aggregation/toxicity), and (v) disease datasets with proteostasis failure signatures (AMP-AD proteomics; ALS/FTD proteomics and transcriptomics in GEO).

We will quantify mesoscale hub features from images (number, size, spatial distribution relative to organelles) using standardized segmentation and spatial statistics. We will integrate these with ubiquitinome features (linkage composition, substrate networks) and with turnover rates to infer how hub organization modulates degradation flux. Dynamical modeling will connect hub formation kinetics to emergent outcomes such as threshold-like aggregation onset. Multi-omic factor analysis will identify latent “proteostasis states” shared across stresses and diseases.

Hypotheses: (1) cells switch between distinct mesoscale proteostasis strategies—distributed microdomains vs centralized aggresome routing—depending on crowding and ubiquitin network topology; (2) specific ubiquitin linkage patterns bias substrates toward particular hubs; and (3) neurodegenerative disease signatures reflect a shift in mesoscale hub organization rather than solely changes in expression.

Expected insights include a unified atlas of proteostasis hub architectures across cell types and stresses, mechanistic links between ubiquitin network structure and mesoscale sequestration, and candidate mesoscale biomarkers of early proteostasis collapse.

This requires team science across imaging, ubiquitin biochemistry, systems biology, and neurodegeneration, with heavy emphasis on data harmonization and reproducible pipelines. NCEMS support is needed to curate dispersed datasets, develop open standards for hub annotation, and train trainees in integrative analysis of spatial proteomics and bioimage-derived mesoscale features.

[Abstract]
