We will quantify mesoscale hub features from images (number, size, spatial distribution relative to organelles) using standardized segmentation and spatial statistics. We will integrate these with ubiquitinome features (linkage composition, substrate networks) and with turnover rates to infer how hub organization modulates degradation flux. Dynamical modeling will connect hub formation kinetics to emergent outcomes such as threshold-like aggregation onset. Multi-omic factor analysis will identify latent “proteostasis states” shared across stresses and diseases.

Hypotheses: (1) cells switch between distinct mesoscale proteostasis strategies—distributed microdomains vs centralized aggresome routing—depending on crowding and ubiquitin network topology; (2) specific ubiquitin linkage patterns bias substrates toward particular hubs; and (3) neurodegenerative disease signatures reflect a shift in mesoscale hub organization rather than solely changes in expression.

Expected insights include a unified atlas of proteostasis hub architectures across cell types and stresses, mechanistic links between ubiquitin network structure and mesoscale sequestration, and candidate mesoscale biomarkers of early proteostasis collapse.

This requires team science across imaging, ubiquitin biochemistry, systems biology, and neurodegeneration, with heavy emphasis on data harmonization and reproducible pipelines. NCEMS support is needed to curate dispersed datasets, develop open standards for hub annotation, and train trainees in integrative analysis of spatial proteomics and bioimage-derived mesoscale features.

[Background and Significance]
Proteostasis—the ability of cells to maintain a functional proteome despite continual synthesis, folding errors, damage, and stress—has long been described in terms of molecular components: chaperones, E3 ligases, the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS), and autophagy. Yet a central empirical observation across organisms is that proteostasis is not simply the sum of these parts. Cells often show threshold-like transitions between manageable misfolding and catastrophic aggregation, maintain robustness despite large variation in expression of individual factors, and exhibit stress-specific routing of substrates to distinct degradation pathways. These behaviors are hallmarks of emergence: system-level properties that arise from collective organization and interactions and are not predictable from single-molecule functions.

A growing body of work points to mesoscale organization—tens to hundreds of nanometers up to ~1 µm—as a key explanatory layer. At this scale, proteasomes form enriched microdomains and foci; misfolded proteins are sequestered into p62/SQSTM1-positive condensates; aggresomes concentrate ubiquitinated substrates near the microtubule-organizing center; and autophagy initiation occurs at spatially defined sites that interface with organelles such as ER, mitochondria, and endosomes. These hubs act as “reaction environments” that regulate encounter rates, substrate selection, and pathway choice. Mesoscale sequestration can buffer cells by isolating toxic species, concentrating degradation machinery, and enabling coordinated handoffs between the UPS and autophagy.

Despite this conceptual shift, current understanding remains fragmented because relevant evidence is distributed across modalities and communities. Imaging studies richly describe spatial phenotypes (e.g., number and size of p62 bodies, proteasome foci, aggresome formation), but are often not quantitatively linked to ubiquitin linkage chemistry, substrate networks, or turnover flux. Conversely, ubiquitinomics and proteome turnover studies quantify ubiquitin linkage composition (e.g., K48 vs K63 chains), identify ubiquitinated substrates, and estimate degradation rates, but typically lack spatial context. Spatial proteomics—via subcellular fractionation (e.g., hyperLOPIT) or proximity labeling—bridges molecules to compartments, yet has rarely been integrated with imaging-derived mesoscale features. Disease proteomics and transcriptomics (e.g., Alzheimer’s and ALS/FTD datasets) show signatures of proteostasis failure, but it remains unclear whether these reflect altered expression of components, altered ubiquitin network topology, or a deeper shift in mesoscale organization and routing.

The NCEMS mission—to catalyze community-scale synthesis of publicly available molecular and cellular data to understand emergence, especially at the mesoscale—makes proteostasis hub organization an ideal target. The phenomenon is explicitly mesoscale: hubs typically span 50–1000 nm and interact with organelles without being reducible to a single organelle identity. It is also inherently emergent: the same set of UPS and autophagy components can yield qualitatively different outcomes depending on whether they are spatially distributed, clustered into multiple microdomains, or centralized into an aggresome-like structure.

Existing public data now enable a rigorous synthesis that was previously infeasible. The Human Protein Atlas (HPA) provides immunofluorescence-based localization for thousands of proteins, including proteasome subunits, autophagy factors (LC3 family, ATG proteins), and adaptors (p62, NBR1), across cell lines with standardized imaging. The Image Data Resource (IDR) and BioImage Archive host raw and processed microscopy datasets for stress responses, autophagy markers, and protein aggregation phenotypes, often with perturbations and time series. Proteomics repositories such as PRIDE contain large-scale ubiquitinomics (including linkage-specific enrichment), proteome turnover datasets (e.g., pulse SILAC-based half-lives), and proximity labeling studies (BioID/APEX) that define local protein neighborhoods. DepMap and associated CRISPR screen portals provide genetic dependency and perturbation phenotypes, including screens for proteotoxic stress sensitivity, aggregation, and viability. Finally, disease-focused resources like AMP-AD Knowledge Portal, GEO, and ProteomeXchange-linked studies provide multi-omic signatures of neurodegeneration where proteostasis collapse is central.

Key gaps that synthesis research can address include: (1) lack of a cross-study, quantitative “atlas” of proteostasis hub architectures defined by measurable mesoscale features; (2) missing links between ubiquitin chain topology/substrate networks and spatial routing to specific hubs; (3) absence of integrative models that connect hub formation dynamics to emergent outcomes such as sharp aggregation thresholds and robustness; and (4) limited frameworks to interpret disease omics as shifts in mesoscale organization rather than only expression changes.

A community-scale synthesis effort is required because the data are heterogeneous (imaging, spatial proteomics, ubiquitinomics, turnover, genetic screens, disease omics), dispersed across repositories, and encoded with inconsistent metadata and annotations. Integrating them demands expertise in quantitative bioimage analysis, ubiquitin biology, spatial proteomics, statistical multi-omics integration, and disease biology—well beyond a single lab. By unifying these public resources into a coherent mesoscale framework, we will advance fundamental understanding of how proteostasis emerges from spatial organization and provide generalizable methods for mesoscale synthesis in molecular and cellular science.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how mesoscale organization of proteasome- and autophagy-associated hubs generates emergent proteostasis behaviors. Our questions are designed to be testable using only existing public datasets and to yield mechanistic insight that is not accessible from any single modality.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): What are the dominant mesoscale “hub architectures” of proteostasis across cell types, stresses, and genetic contexts?
Proteostasis hubs include proteasome-enriched microdomains, p62/SQSTM1 bodies, ubiquitin-positive inclusions, aggresomes, and autophagy initiation/engulfment structures (LC3 puncta, WIPI/ATG puncta). We will define hub architectures by quantitative features: hub count per cell, size distribution, intensity/contrast relative to cytosol, spatial clustering metrics, proximity to organelle markers (ER, mitochondria, centrosome), and co-localization between UPS and autophagy markers.
Hypothesis H1: Cells occupy a small number of recurrent mesoscale proteostasis states (e.g., distributed microdomains vs centralized routing/aggresome) that recur across datasets and are conserved across stresses.
Predictions: (i) unsupervised embedding of image-derived hub features will reveal discrete clusters with reproducible centroids across independent imaging datasets (HPA, IDR, BioImage Archive); (ii) these clusters will align with known biological contexts (e.g., proteasome inhibition, mitochondrial stress, heat shock) but will also reveal unrecognized states shared across contexts.
Validation using existing data: replicate detection of the same state structure across repositories and across cell lines; concordance with published qualitative annotations (e.g., “aggresome formation”) where available.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): How does ubiquitin linkage composition and ubiquitinated substrate network topology bias routing to distinct mesoscale hubs?
Ubiquitin chains encode routing information: K48-linked chains typically signal proteasomal degradation, while K63 and mixed/branched chains can favor signaling, trafficking, or autophagy-related handling. Yet the mapping from linkage patterns to mesoscale routing is not established.
Hypothesis H2: Ubiquitin linkage composition and network topology predict hub architecture and pathway choice.
Predictions: (i) datasets with higher relative K63 (and/or specific mixed/branched chain signatures where measured) will associate with increased p62-body/LC3 puncta features and increased hub–organelle proximity consistent with autophagy initiation sites; (ii) higher K48 dominance will associate with more proteasome microdomain enrichment and fewer large centralized inclusions; (iii) substrate networks enriched for intrinsically disordered, phase-separating, or RNA-binding proteins will associate with condensate-like hub states.
Validation using existing data: linkage-specific ubiquitinomics in PRIDE will be mapped to conditions/cell lines that overlap with imaging datasets; where direct overlap is limited, we will use meta-analytic association across matched perturbations (e.g., proteasome inhibition, autophagy inhibition, oxidative stress) and compare predicted routing with turnover datasets (see RQ3).

Research Question 3 (RQ3): How does mesoscale hub organization modulate degradation flux and produce emergent threshold behaviors?
A key emergent phenomenon is the sharp onset of aggregation and loss of viability beyond a stress threshold, despite gradual changes in molecular parameters. We propose that mesoscale hub formation creates nonlinearities by altering effective concentrations, encounter rates, and saturation of clearance pathways.
Hypothesis H3: Hub architecture is a principal determinant of effective degradation flux and explains threshold-like aggregation onset.
Predictions: (i) conditions/cell lines exhibiting centralized hubs (aggresome-like) will show bimodal or heavy-tailed distributions of turnover/half-life changes (some proteins stabilized dramatically) compared with distributed microdomain states; (ii) hub size and clustering will correlate with saturation signatures in turnover data (global half-life increases for specific substrate classes) and with genetic screen sensitivity to proteotoxic stress.
Validation using existing data: proteome turnover datasets in PRIDE will be integrated with hub states inferred from imaging; DepMap/CRISPR screens will provide independent phenotypic readouts (viability under stress, aggregation reporters in published screens) to test whether hub states predict functional outcomes.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Do neurodegenerative disease omics signatures reflect a shift in mesoscale hub organization rather than only altered expression?
Neurodegeneration features ubiquitin-positive inclusions and disrupted autophagy/UPS, but causal interpretation is difficult from bulk omics.
Hypothesis H4: Disease-associated proteostasis signatures correspond to a specific mesoscale hub state characterized by altered routing and reduced flux robustness.
Predictions: (i) latent factors learned from integrated multi-omics (ubiquitinome/proteome/turnover) will map disease samples (AMP-AD, ALS/FTD in GEO/ProteomeXchange-linked studies) to hub states that resemble stress-induced centralized routing; (ii) genetic dependencies from DepMap for disease-relevant genes (e.g., SQSTM1, VCP, UBQLN2 pathways) will align with the inferred hub-state vulnerabilities.
Validation using existing data: cross-cohort replication across independent disease datasets; consistency with published neuropathology annotations (ubiquitin/p62 inclusion burden) when available.

Collectively, these hypotheses make measurable predictions linking mesoscale spatial features to ubiquitin chemistry, network structure, and functional flux proxies. The outcome will be mechanistic understanding of how spatial organization at the mesoscale creates emergent robustness—and how its reconfiguration drives collapse.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will conduct a community-scale synthesis integrating five public data streams into a unified, analyzable framework that links mesoscale hub architecture (from images and spatial proteomics) to ubiquitin network structure and degradation flux (from ubiquitinomics and turnover), and to functional phenotypes (from genetic screens and disease omics). No new experimental data will be generated; all analyses will use publicly available datasets and metadata.

Data sources (specific repositories)
1) Spatial proteomics and localization
- Human Protein Atlas (HPA) Cell Atlas immunofluorescence images and localization calls for proteasome subunits (PSMA/PSMB/PSMC/PSMD), autophagy machinery (ATG proteins, LC3/GABARAP family), and adaptors (SQSTM1/p62, NBR1).
- PRIDE Archive (ProteomeXchange) for hyperLOPIT/subcellular fractionation datasets and proximity labeling datasets (BioID/APEX) that capture local neighborhoods of proteasome/autophagy components.
2) Ubiquitinomics and proteome turnover
- PRIDE Archive for ubiquitin remnant (diGly) datasets, linkage-specific enrichment datasets (K48, K63, and others where available), and quantitative proteomics.
- PRIDE Archive for proteome turnover/half-life datasets (e.g., pulse SILAC, dynamic SILAC, TMT-based time courses) that provide degradation flux proxies.
3) Bioimaging datasets
- Image Data Resource (IDR) for high-content imaging screens and curated studies involving autophagy markers (LC3, WIPI), proteasome reporters, p62 bodies, and aggregation phenotypes.
- BioImage Archive for raw microscopy datasets including stress responses and inclusion formation.
4) Genetic perturbation and dependency
- DepMap (Broad Institute) CRISPR knockout screens and gene effect scores; ancillary portals/datasets linked to DepMap for stress-specific screens when publicly released.
- Public CRISPR screen datasets deposited in GEO/SRA/ArrayExpress that assay aggregation/toxicity phenotypes (where available) will be included as synthesis inputs.
5) Disease datasets
- AMP-AD Knowledge Portal for Alzheimer’s disease proteomics/transcriptomics and associated metadata.
- Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) for ALS/FTD transcriptomics and proteomics-linked studies; ProteomeXchange/PRIDE accessions referenced by GEO where applicable.

Data harmonization and metadata alignment
A central challenge is aligning conditions across modalities. We will build a “Proteostasis Hub Synthesis Index” (PHSI): a standardized metadata schema capturing cell line/tissue, perturbation (drug/genetic/stress), time point, imaging markers, proteomics platform, and repository identifiers. We will:
- Normalize identifiers: map proteins to UniProt accessions; genes to HGNC/Ensembl; cell lines to Cellosaurus; diseases to DOID/MeSH.
- Standardize perturbations: map compounds to ChEMBL/PubChem; stresses to controlled vocabulary.
- Create crosswalk tables linking imaging studies to proteomics studies via shared cell line + perturbation + time window, and via higher-level matching when exact overlap is absent (meta-analytic matching).
All harmonized tables and provenance will be versioned and released.

Quantifying mesoscale hub features from images
We will develop reproducible pipelines for segmentation and feature extraction from immunofluorescence and high-content microscopy:
- Preprocessing: illumination correction, deconvolution when PSF is provided/appropriate, channel alignment, and intensity normalization.
- Segmentation: Cellpose and/or StarDist for nuclei/cell boundaries; marker-specific puncta/aggregate segmentation using a hybrid approach (LoG/DoG filtering + adaptive thresholding + watershed) and deep-learning refinement when ground-truth annotations exist in public sets.
- Feature extraction: per-cell hub count, area/volume proxies, eccentricity, radial distribution relative to nucleus/centrosome, Ripley’s K / pair-correlation for clustering, nearest-neighbor distances to organelle markers when present, and co-localization metrics (Manders, Li’s ICQ) for UPS–autophagy marker overlap.
- Mesoscale definition: features will be calibrated to pixel size metadata to ensure hubs in the 50–1000 nm regime are quantified consistently; analyses will include sensitivity checks to resolution limits.

Spatial proteomics integration
From hyperLOPIT and proximity labeling datasets (PRIDE), we will:
- Reprocess quantitative tables to consistent normalization (e.g., median normalization, batch correction with ComBat/limma where appropriate).
- Infer subcellular/mesoscale neighborhood association scores for proteasome/autophagy components and candidate substrates.
- Derive “hub membership likelihoods” for proteins: probability of association with proteasome microdomains vs autophagy initiation/engulfment neighborhoods.
These scores provide a molecular bridge between imaging-derived hub states and ubiquitin/turnover features.

Ubiquitin network and linkage feature engineering
For ubiquitinomics datasets (PRIDE):
- Extract ubiquitinated sites and quantitative changes by condition.
- Compute linkage composition vectors when linkage-enriched measurements exist; otherwise infer pathway bias using curated knowledge (e.g., known K48/K63 site contexts) with uncertainty explicitly modeled.
- Build substrate networks: integrate ubiquitinated proteins with protein–protein interaction priors from STRING, BioGRID, and CORUM complexes; compute network metrics (degree, modularity, community structure) and enrichment for disorder/phase-separation propensity using public annotations (e.g., DisProt, PhaSePro) where available.

Multi-omic integration and latent state discovery
We will integrate imaging features, spatial proteomics neighborhood scores, ubiquitin/linkage features, turnover changes, and genetic screen phenotypes using:
- MOFA+ (Multi-Omics Factor Analysis) to learn latent “proteostasis state” factors across modalities.
- Similarity network fusion (SNF) as an alternative integration method robust to missing blocks.
- Hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis to combine partially matched studies while accounting for study-specific effects.
Outputs will include interpretable factors linked to hub architectures and quantitative predictions of flux robustness.

Dynamical and mechanistic modeling (computational, no new experiments)
To connect hub formation to emergent thresholds, we will build coarse-grained dynamical models:
- ODE/Markov models describing misfolded protein production, ubiquitination, sequestration into hubs, and clearance via UPS/autophagy with saturable kinetics.
- Parameter estimation constrained by turnover data and by time-resolved imaging datasets in IDR/BioImage Archive when available.
- Bifurcation/threshold analysis to identify regimes producing abrupt aggregation onset; compare inferred regimes across hub states.

Validation using existing data (no experimental validation)
- Cross-dataset replication: hub-state clustering must reproduce across independent imaging repositories and across cell lines.
- Positive controls: known perturbations (e.g., proteasome inhibition, autophagy inhibition, microtubule disruption) present in public datasets should map to expected hub-state shifts.
- Predictive validation: train models on a subset of studies to predict hub state or flux proxies in held-out studies (cross-study generalization).
- Concordance checks: hub-state assignments should correlate with independent phenotypes (DepMap dependencies; disease severity strata in AMP-AD when available).

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize PHSI metadata schema; ingest initial cohorts from HPA, IDR, PRIDE; release v0.1 harmonized index.
- Prototype image segmentation/feature pipeline; benchmark on 2–3 representative studies.
Months 7–12:
- Scale image feature extraction across prioritized datasets; release hub-feature tables v1.
- Reprocess key ubiquitinomics and turnover datasets; compute linkage/network features.
Months 13–18:
- Perform multi-omic integration (MOFA+/SNF); define initial proteostasis state taxonomy; cross-dataset replication.
- Begin dynamical modeling constrained by turnover and time-series imaging.
Months 19–24:
- Integrate DepMap/CRISPR phenotypes; test predictions linking hub states to vulnerabilities.
- Map disease datasets (AMP-AD, ALS/FTD GEO) onto latent state space; replication across cohorts.
Months 25–30:
- Finalize atlas, models, and software; submit manuscripts; host training workshop; release v2.0 datasets, containers, and documentation.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Quantitative bioimage analysis lab: segmentation, mesoscale feature engineering, spatial statistics.
- Ubiquitin/proteostasis biology lab (computationally oriented): interpretation of linkage patterns, substrate routing logic, curation of pathway priors.
- Spatial proteomics/data integration lab: hyperLOPIT/proximity labeling processing, neighborhood inference, batch correction.
- Systems biology/modeling lab: latent factor modeling, Bayesian meta-analysis, dynamical threshold modeling.
- Neurodegeneration informatics lab: AMP-AD/GEO harmonization, disease stratification, interpretation.
- Research software engineer: workflow engineering, packaging, documentation, CI/CD.
Trainees (graduate students/postdocs) will rotate across modalities through structured hackweeks and code sprints, ensuring workforce development aligned with NCEMS goals.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) Proteostasis Hub Atlas (PHA): a public, versioned atlas of mesoscale proteostasis hub architectures across cell types, perturbations, and disease contexts. The atlas will include:
- Per-cell and per-condition quantitative hub features derived from HPA, IDR, and BioImage Archive studies.
- Harmonized annotations linking hub features to imaging markers, cell lines, perturbations, and time points via the Proteostasis Hub Synthesis Index (PHSI).
- A taxonomy of recurrent “proteostasis states” (distributed microdomain, mixed, centralized/aggresome-like, autophagy-dominant, etc.) with uncertainty estimates.

2) Integrated multi-omic resource linking space, ubiquitin chemistry, and flux
We will release curated, analysis-ready matrices that connect:
- Spatial proteomics neighborhood association scores (from hyperLOPIT and BioID/APEX datasets in PRIDE),
- Ubiquitin linkage/substrate network features (from PRIDE ubiquitinomics),
- Proteome turnover/half-life changes (from PRIDE turnover datasets), and
- Genetic vulnerability signatures (from DepMap and public CRISPR screens).
This resource will enable researchers to query, for example, which ubiquitin network properties predict a shift toward centralized routing, or which hub states correspond to selective stabilization of substrate classes.

3) Open-source software toolkit for mesoscale hub synthesis
We will deliver a modular toolkit (Python-first, with R interfaces where appropriate) that implements:
- Reproducible image segmentation and hub feature extraction,
- Metadata harmonization utilities (PHSI builders and validators),
- Multi-omic integration workflows (MOFA+/SNF wrappers, cross-study validation), and
- Visualization dashboards for exploring hub states and associated molecular features.
The toolkit will be designed for reuse beyond proteostasis (e.g., other mesoscale condensates and organelle contact sites).

4) Mechanistic, testable models of emergent proteostasis
A core scientific product will be mechanistic models connecting mesoscale organization to emergent behaviors:
- Quantitative relationships between hub architecture and effective degradation flux (inferred from turnover data),
- Dynamical models showing how saturable sequestration/clearance and spatial concentration can produce threshold-like aggregation onset,
- Hypothesis-driven predictions about which ubiquitin linkage patterns and substrate network topologies bias routing to specific hubs.
Although we will not perform new experiments, these models will generate falsifiable predictions that the community can test in future work.

Scientific impact on emergence at the mesoscale
This project will advance a general principle: mesoscale organization acts as an intermediate “computational layer” that transforms molecular-level rules (ubiquitin chain building, E3 specificity, proteasome/autophagy capacity) into cell-level outcomes (robustness vs collapse). By explicitly quantifying hub architectures and integrating them with ubiquitin chemistry and flux proxies, we will provide a mechanistic account of how collective spatial organization yields emergent robustness.

Broader impacts for molecular and cellular biology
- Unification across fields: The atlas and state taxonomy will provide a shared quantitative language for imaging scientists, proteomics researchers, and disease biologists.
- Data reuse and efficiency: By synthesizing existing datasets, we increase the value of public investments in imaging and omics repositories.
- Methodological advances: Our harmonization schema and cross-modal integration approach can be applied to other mesoscale phenomena (stress granules, signaling clusters, membrane-less organelles, organelle contact sites).

Enabling future research
The outputs will enable:
- Prioritization of candidate mesoscale biomarkers: hub-state scores that can be computed from existing images/omics and potentially used for early detection of proteostasis collapse.
- Better interpretation of disease omics: mapping disease samples into a mesoscale state space to distinguish expression-driven changes from organizational shifts.
- Benchmark datasets for AI: standardized, annotated hub features and images suitable for training and evaluating models of mesoscale organization.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least two primary manuscripts (Proteostasis Hub Atlas; integrative mechanistic modeling) plus methods/software notes.
- Community workshops: an NCEMS-hosted hackweek on “Mesoscale image-to-omics synthesis” and a focused tutorial on reproducible bioimage feature extraction.
- Web presence: a lightweight, open web portal (static + queryable downloads) for atlas browsing; all data mirrored in established repositories.

Long-term sustainability
We will ensure sustainability by:
- Depositing derived datasets in stable archives (Zenodo with DOIs; BioImage Archive/IDR links where appropriate; PRIDE re-uploads only when permitted, otherwise cross-referenced),
- Maintaining semantic versioning and clear provenance,
- Designing the toolkit as a community-maintained package with automated tests and continuous integration,
- Engaging external users through issues, contributions, and periodic community calls, aligning with NCEMS’s role as a synthesis catalyst.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy and alignment with synthesis goals
This is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring intensive data harmonization, software engineering, and cross-disciplinary coordination rather than laboratory experimentation. The budget prioritizes personnel time for integration and reproducibility, computing for large-scale image processing and multi-omic modeling, and travel/workshops to catalyze collaboration and train trainees.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (2.0 FTE total):
  1) Quantitative bioimage analysis + spatial statistics lead (segmentation pipelines, mesoscale feature engineering).
  2) Multi-omics integration/modeling lead (MOFA+/SNF integration, Bayesian meta-analysis, dynamical modeling).
  Justification: These roles drive the core synthesis tasks and ensure methodological rigor across modalities.
- 1 Graduate student (0.5–1.0 FTE): supports metadata harmonization (PHSI), dataset curation, and contributes to analysis modules; gains cross-training in imaging and omics.
- 1 Research software engineer/programmer analyst (0.5–1.0 FTE): workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, continuous integration, documentation, and release management.
  Justification: Community adoption depends on robust, reusable software and reproducible pipelines—work that typically exceeds what trainees can sustainably provide.
- PI/co-PI effort (collective): modest support for coordination, supervision, and NCEMS working group leadership; emphasis on team science rather than single-lab execution.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations for:
  - Large-scale image processing (HPA/IDR/BioImage Archive volumes), including GPU time for segmentation (Cellpose/StarDist).
  - Storage for intermediate derived products (feature tables, embeddings) and caching of open-access images as permitted.
  - Multi-omic integration and Bayesian modeling (CPU-intensive, memory-demanding).
Justification: Processing multi-terabyte imaging collections and running cross-study integration is beyond typical single-lab capacity.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2–3 in-person meetings over 2–3 years) plus support for trainees to attend.
- Targeted travel to disseminate results at relevant conferences (e.g., ASCB, HUPO, bioimage analysis meetings) and to coordinate with repository/community stakeholders.
Justification: NCEMS goals emphasize catalyzing multidisciplinary teams; in-person synthesis meetings accelerate consensus on standards and integration decisions.

Workshops and training events
- Budget for one public hackweek/training workshop hosted through NCEMS: venue/AV (if applicable), trainee travel scholarships, and instructional support.
- Development of training materials (tutorial notebooks, recorded lectures) and maintenance.
Justification: Training the next-generation data-savvy workforce is a core requirement; workshops also broaden community engagement and adoption.

Open science infrastructure
- Costs for persistent archiving and dissemination:
  - Zenodo deposition (free) supplemented by funds for data preparation, curation labor, and optional mirrored hosting if needed.
  - Domain/hosting for a lightweight atlas portal (static site + download index), and monitoring/maintenance.
- Support for DOI-minted releases, documentation, and long-term repository stewardship.
Justification: The value of synthesis hinges on durable, accessible outputs with clear provenance.

Overall justification relative to NCEMS need
No single lab typically possesses the expertise and resources to (i) reprocess heterogeneous proteomics and ubiquitinomics, (ii) extract standardized mesoscale features from large imaging repositories, (iii) harmonize metadata across repositories, (iv) integrate modalities with rigorous cross-study validation, and (v) package outputs into reusable, open workflows. NCEMS support enables the coordination, computing, and training infrastructure necessary to deliver community-scale, reproducible synthesis products.

abstract_original:
Proteostasis emerges from mesoscale organization of degradation hubs—proteasome-rich microdomains, aggresomes, and autophagy initiation sites (50–1000 nm)—that coordinate substrate selection, sequestration, and clearance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective spatial organization and phase-like sequestration yields system-level robustness to misfolded proteins, not predictable from individual E3 ligases or proteases.

We will synthesize: (i) spatial proteomics identifying proteasome/autophagy component localization (Human Protein Atlas; hyperLOPIT and proximity labeling datasets in PRIDE), (ii) ubiquitinomics and proteome turnover datasets (PRIDE; ubiquitin linkage-specific studies), (iii) bioimaging of aggresomes, p62 bodies, autophagosome markers, and proteasome foci (IDR/BioImage Archive), (iv) genetic perturbation screens for proteostasis regulators (DepMap; CRISPR screens for aggregation/toxicity), and (v) disease datasets with proteostasis failure signatures (AMP-AD proteomics; ALS/FTD proteomics and transcriptomics in GEO).

We will quantify mesoscale hub features from images (number, size, spatial distribution relative to organelles) using standardized segmentation and spatial statistics. We will integrate these with ubiquitinome features (linkage composition, substrate networks) and with turnover rates to infer how hub organization modulates degradation flux. Dynamical modeling will connect hub formation kinetics to emergent outcomes such as threshold-like aggregation onset. Multi-omic factor analysis will identify latent “proteostasis states” shared across stresses and diseases.

Hypotheses: (1) cells switch between distinct mesoscale proteostasis strategies—distributed microdomains vs centralized aggresome routing—depending on crowding and ubiquitin network topology; (2) specific ubiquitin linkage patterns bias substrates toward particular hubs; and (3) neurodegenerative disease signatures reflect a shift in mesoscale hub organization rather than solely changes in expression.

Expected insights include a unified atlas of proteostasis hub architectures across cell types and stresses, mechanistic links between ubiquitin network structure and mesoscale sequestration, and candidate mesoscale biomarkers of early proteostasis collapse.

This requires team science across imaging, ubiquitin biochemistry, systems biology, and neurodegeneration, with heavy emphasis on data harmonization and reproducible pipelines. NCEMS support is needed to curate dispersed datasets, develop open standards for hub annotation, and train trainees in integrative analysis of spatial proteomics and bioimage-derived mesoscale features.

abstract_text:
Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are proteinaceous organelles (50–300 nm) whose emergent permeability and enzyme colocalization enable metabolic pathways that would be inefficient or toxic in the cytosol. The emergent phenomenon is that shell protein assembly and pore organization generate selective transport and reaction microenvironments not predictable from individual enzymes.

We will synthesize: (i) BMC gene clusters across bacterial genomes (NCBI RefSeq, IMG; curated BMC databases), (ii) shell protein and encapsulated enzyme structures (PDB, AlphaFold DB), (iii) metabolomics and flux measurements for BMC-associated pathways (Metabolomics Workbench; published 13C flux studies), (iv) cryo-EM structures of intact BMCs and shells (EMDB/EMPIAR), and (v) environmental metadata and phenotypes for host organisms (GOLD database; literature-derived growth phenotypes).

We will build a comparative framework linking genetic composition to mesoscale shell architecture and emergent function. First, we will annotate shell protein families and predict pore properties (charge, diameter, gating motifs) from structures. Second, we will infer likely shell stoichiometries and tessellation patterns using assembly modeling and constraints from cryo-EM. Third, we will integrate pathway enzyme kinetics (from BRENDA) with predicted permeability to simulate emergent metabolite gradients and flux enhancement using reaction–diffusion models. Machine learning will map gene cluster features to predicted organelle performance metrics (toxicity mitigation, flux gain).

Key questions: Are there universal shell “permeability motifs” that recur across unrelated BMC types? How do small changes in pore composition produce emergent switches between retention vs throughput regimes? Can we predict ecological niches where particular BMC designs confer advantage?

Expected insights include design rules for emergent mesoscale selectivity, a taxonomy of BMC architectures linked to metabolic outcomes, and open tools for predicting BMC function from genomes. While synthetic biology implications exist, the project itself uses only public data and focuses on fundamental principles of mesoscale emergence.

This effort requires collaboration among microbiologists, structural biologists, metabolic modelers, and evolutionary bioinformaticians, and depends on integrating large-scale genomic data with structural and metabolic measurements. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open pipelines, and trainee training in multiscale modeling of protein-based organelles.

While synthetic biology implications exist, the project itself uses only public data and focuses on fundamental principles of mesoscale emergence.

This effort requires collaboration among microbiologists, structural biologists, metabolic modelers, and evolutionary bioinformaticians, and depends on integrating large-scale genomic data with structural and metabolic measurements. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open pipelines, and trainee training in multiscale modeling of protein-based organelles.

[Background and Significance]
Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are widespread protein-based organelles that package enzymes within polyhedral shells assembled from thousands of small proteins. At 50–300 nm, BMCs occupy the mesoscale—larger than individual macromolecular complexes yet smaller than many membrane-bound organelles—and they exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences: collective shell assembly, pore organization, and enzyme colocalization generate selective chemical microenvironments that cannot be predicted from the properties of isolated enzymes or shell proteins alone. In canonical BMC systems (e.g., carboxysomes for CO2 fixation; metabolosomes for catabolism of 1,2-propanediol or ethanolamine), encapsulation can increase pathway flux, prevent loss of volatile intermediates, and mitigate toxicity from reactive aldehydes. These are emergent functional outcomes that arise from mesoscale organization: (i) spatial confinement, (ii) selective permeability, (iii) altered effective concentrations, and (iv) coupled transport–reaction dynamics.

Current understanding has advanced through decades of genetics, biochemistry, and structural biology. Comparative genomics has revealed that BMCs are encoded by operon-like gene clusters containing shell proteins (hexamers/pseudohexamers, pentamers, and specialized vertices) and encapsulated enzymes; curated resources such as the Bacterial Microcompartment Database and annotations in NCBI RefSeq and the Integrated Microbial Genomes & Microbiomes (IMG/M) system provide starting points for cataloging BMC diversity. Structural biology has uncovered conserved shell protein folds and pores, with high-resolution structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and, more recently, predicted structures for many shell proteins and enzymes in AlphaFold DB. Cryo-electron microscopy has provided intact-shell and intact-organelle reconstructions for select systems in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and raw data in EMPIAR, enabling inference of shell curvature, facet organization, and in some cases pore densities.

Despite these advances, major gaps remain in linking genotype and molecular structure to emergent mesoscale function. First, permeability is often treated qualitatively (“selective pores”), but the field lacks a comparative, quantitative map of pore physicochemical properties (diameter distributions, electrostatics, gating motifs) across the full diversity of BMC shell protein families. Second, shell architecture is typically described for a handful of model organisms; we do not yet know how gene cluster composition and shell protein paralog diversity constrain mesoscale tessellation patterns, stoichiometry, and pore spatial arrangement. Third, mechanistic models of BMC function are fragmented: some models treat diffusion barriers abstractly, whereas others focus on enzyme kinetics without integrating shell transport. The emergent regimes—where slight changes in pore properties shift the system from retention to throughput, or from detoxification to leakage—are therefore not systematically characterized across BMC types.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address these gaps because the necessary evidence is distributed across heterogeneous, publicly available datasets that no single laboratory typically integrates: (i) large-scale genome catalogs (NCBI RefSeq; IMG/M), (ii) structural repositories (PDB; AlphaFold DB), (iii) enzyme kinetic databases (BRENDA; SABIO-RK where available), (iv) metabolomics repositories (Metabolomics Workbench; selected studies in GNPS/MassIVE for relevant metabolites), (v) published 13C metabolic flux analysis datasets and reconstructions, and (vi) environmental and phenotype metadata (GOLD; BioSample/BioProject metadata; literature-derived growth phenotypes and substrate utilization). NCEMS’s mission—community-scale synthesis of public data to discover emergent principles at the mesoscale—aligns precisely with the need to integrate these resources into a unified framework.

The significance of focusing on BMCs extends beyond cataloging a bacterial curiosity. BMCs are a tractable, naturally occurring “design space” for mesoscale compartments built without membranes. Their shells are modular and evolvable, and their functions span carbon fixation, redox metabolism, and degradation of diverse substrates. Understanding the emergent design rules that connect shell pores, shell geometry, and enzyme packing to metabolic outcomes will illuminate general principles of how cells engineer microenvironments using protein assemblies—principles relevant to other mesoscale phenomena such as phase-separated condensates, viral capsids, and cytoskeletal scaffolds. Moreover, BMCs offer an opportunity to connect mesoscale architecture to ecology: if shell permeability and architecture predict which metabolites are retained or excluded, then BMC design should correlate with environmental niches and metabolic strategies.

This proposal leverages the unprecedented growth of public data to move the field from descriptive to predictive. Genomes provide the “parts list,” structures provide the “physical constraints,” and metabolomics/flux datasets provide functional readouts. By synthesizing these data at scale, we can identify universal motifs and emergent regimes that are invisible when studying single systems. The project is explicitly designed as a community working group effort: it requires expertise spanning microbial genomics, structural bioinformatics, cryo-EM interpretation, metabolic flux analysis, reaction–diffusion modeling, and machine learning. NCEMS support is essential to coordinate cross-lab curation, develop shared open workflows, and train trainees in multiscale synthesis approaches that connect molecules to mesoscale organelles and cellular outcomes.

Ultimately, the project will deliver a rigorous, open, and reusable framework for predicting organelle-like function from genomes by explicitly modeling the emergent mesoscale properties of BMC shells. This will address a long-standing puzzle—how protein shells achieve selective transport and flux enhancement—using only existing publicly available data, fulfilling NCEMS’s core synthesis mission.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address fundamental, testable questions about how mesoscale organization in bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) gives rise to emergent metabolic function. Our central premise is that BMC performance is not determined solely by the catalytic properties of encapsulated enzymes, but by the coupled system of (i) shell pore physicochemistry, (ii) shell geometry and pore spatial distribution, and (iii) pathway kinetics operating under confinement. We will formalize this premise into specific research questions and hypotheses with measurable predictions that can be evaluated using existing public datasets.

RQ1: Do universal “permeability motifs” exist across unrelated BMC types, and do they define discrete transport regimes?
H1.1: Shell protein pores cluster into a small number of conserved physicochemical motif classes (e.g., positively charged narrow pores favoring anionic metabolites; hydrophobic constrictions favoring neutral volatile intermediates; gated pores with conformational switches) that recur across phylogenetically distant BMCs.
Prediction: When pore properties are computed from PDB and AlphaFold DB structures (pore radius profiles, electrostatic potential, residue composition at constrictions), unsupervised clustering will recover a limited set of motif classes that are enriched in specific functional BMC categories inferred from gene cluster content (e.g., aldehyde-generating metabolosomes vs carboxysomes).
Validation using existing data: motif enrichment will be tested against curated BMC annotations from public BMC databases and RefSeq/IMG functional gene cluster labels; robustness will be assessed by comparing results from experimentally solved structures (PDB) vs predicted structures (AlphaFold DB) and by bootstrapping across paralogs.

RQ2: How does gene cluster composition constrain mesoscale shell architecture (stoichiometry, tessellation, and pore spatial arrangement)?
H2.1: The diversity and copy number of shell protein paralogs within a BMC locus predict mesoscale architectural parameters, including facet composition and effective pore density.
Prediction: BMC loci with multiple BMC-H paralogs and specialized “BMC-T” proteins will correspond to higher predicted pore density and/or heterogeneous pore types across facets, whereas loci with fewer paralogs will yield more uniform pore landscapes.
H2.2: Shell geometry (approximated by polyhedral models) is constrained by the ratio of pentameric vertex proteins (BMC-P) to hexameric shell proteins (BMC-H/T), leading to predictable size classes.
Prediction: Integrating gene cluster stoichiometry priors with cryo-EM–derived size distributions from EMDB/EMPIAR will reveal that certain gene cluster architectures map to distinct BMC diameter ranges and curvature regimes.
Validation using existing data: for BMCs with intact reconstructions in EMDB, we will compare predicted size/stoichiometry to reported capsid-like geometry parameters; for systems without intact reconstructions, we will validate indirectly using known BMC type size ranges reported in literature and by internal consistency across phylogenetically related loci.

RQ3: Can coupled transport–reaction modeling explain emergent switches between retention (detoxification/containment) and throughput (flux maximization) regimes?
H3.1: Small changes in pore charge or radius can induce nonlinear transitions in internal metabolite gradients, shifting the dominant function from intermediate sequestration to rapid exchange.
Prediction: Reaction–diffusion simulations parameterized by enzyme kinetics (BRENDA/SABIO-RK) and pore permeability estimates will show bifurcation-like behavior in internal intermediate concentration and leakage rate when permeability crosses a threshold.
H3.2: BMCs processing toxic aldehydes exhibit stronger selection for low-permeability shells to aldehydes but permissive permeability to cofactors/substrates, yielding a characteristic “selectivity vector.”
Prediction: In aldehyde-associated metabolosomes (identified by signature enzymes in gene clusters), modeled aldehyde leakage will be minimized relative to alternative pore motifs; the inferred selectivity vector will correlate with host tolerance phenotypes and growth on relevant substrates reported in the literature.
Validation using existing data: model outputs (e.g., predicted leakage rates, flux gains) will be compared to published metabolomics profiles and 13C flux estimates for organisms/pathways where available, and to qualitative phenotypes (growth/no growth; sensitivity) extracted from publications and linked via GOLD/BioProject metadata.

RQ4: Can we predict ecological niches and evolutionary drivers of BMC design from integrated genotype–structure–function signatures?
H4.1: Environmental metadata (habitat, oxygen availability, host association) predicts BMC pore motif class and modeled transport regime, reflecting adaptation to substrate availability and stressors.
Prediction: Multivariate models trained on gene cluster features plus environmental metadata from GOLD will predict pore motif classes and emergent performance metrics better than phylogeny alone.
H4.2: Convergent evolution produces similar permeability motifs in distinct lineages when they face similar metabolic constraints.
Prediction: After controlling for phylogenetic relatedness, motif similarity will correlate with pathway type and ecological context, indicating convergence.
Validation using existing data: phylogenetically informed regression and comparative methods will test for convergence; performance will be evaluated via cross-validation across taxonomic clades.

Across these questions, the mechanistic insight sought is explicit: emergent function arises from mesoscale coupling between shell architecture (pore distribution and permeability) and encapsulated pathway kinetics under confinement. By translating diverse public data into quantitative, testable models, we will move from “BMCs are selective” to predictive statements about which shell designs produce which emergent metabolic outcomes, and why.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will execute a community-scale synthesis pipeline that integrates genomic “parts lists,” structural pore and assembly features, mesoscale architectural constraints from cryo-EM, and functional readouts from metabolomics/flux and enzyme kinetics. The core product will be a harmonized, versioned “BMC Design Space Atlas” linking BMC loci → shell protein structures/pore metrics → inferred shell architecture → reaction–diffusion performance metrics → ecological/phenotype context. No new experimental data will be generated; all analyses will use publicly available datasets.

1) Data sources (public repositories)
Genomes and gene clusters:
- NCBI RefSeq (complete and draft bacterial genomes; protein annotations)
- NCBI GenBank for additional assemblies where needed
- IMG/M (Integrated Microbial Genomes & Microbiomes; locus context, functional annotations)
- Curated BMC resources (e.g., Bacterial Microcompartment Database; published locus catalogs)
Structures:
- Protein Data Bank (PDB) for experimentally solved shell proteins and encapsulated enzymes
- AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (AlphaFold DB) for predicted structures of shell proteins/enzymes lacking PDB entries
- UniProt for sequence cross-references and functional annotations
Cryo-EM mesoscale structures:
- EMDB for reconstructed BMC shells/organelles
- EMPIAR for raw cryo-EM datasets enabling re-analysis of particle size distributions and symmetry where feasible
Metabolomics and flux:
- Metabolomics Workbench (targeted/untargeted metabolomics datasets; metadata)
- GNPS/MassIVE for relevant public MS datasets when annotated
- Published 13C metabolic flux analysis datasets (supplementary tables; repositories when available)
Enzyme kinetics and pathways:
- BRENDA for kinetic parameters (kcat, Km) and conditions
- SABIO-RK for curated kinetic entries and reaction context
- KEGG and MetaCyc for pathway definitions and metabolite identities (IDs, stoichiometry)
Environment and phenotypes:
- GOLD (Genomes OnLine Database) for habitat and metadata
- NCBI BioSample/BioProject for sample context
- Literature-derived growth phenotypes and substrate utilization (systematic text-mined plus manual curation)

2) Harmonization and entity resolution
We will build an ID mapping layer:
- Genome/strain identifiers: RefSeq/GenBank assembly accessions ↔ IMG genome IDs ↔ GOLD IDs ↔ BioSample.
- Gene/protein identifiers: locus tags ↔ protein accessions ↔ UniProt IDs.
- Metabolites: KEGG Compound ↔ MetaCyc ↔ HMDB (when present in metabolomics) using standardized InChIKeys.
All mappings, provenance, and confidence scores will be stored in a relational schema (PostgreSQL) with a companion graph representation (e.g., Neo4j) to support flexible queries.

3) BMC locus detection, classification, and feature extraction
- Identify candidate BMC loci using HMM profiles for shell proteins (BMC-H, BMC-T, BMC-P) and signature enzymes; HMMs will be built/curated from PFAM/TIGRFAM families and published shell protein sets.
- Classify loci into BMC functional types using gene neighborhood signatures (e.g., presence of aldehyde dehydrogenase, diol dehydratase, carbonic anhydrase, RuBisCO) and existing curated labels.
- Extract quantitative locus features: shell paralog counts, predicted encapsulation peptides, enzyme complements, operon organization metrics, GC content and mobility indicators.

4) Structural pore analytics (molecular to mesoscale interface)
For each shell protein family member with a PDB or AlphaFold structure:
- Identify pore axes and compute pore radius profiles using tools such as HOLE or equivalent geometry algorithms.
- Compute electrostatic potential and charge distribution at constriction sites (APBS or fast approximations) and summarize as “pore selectivity descriptors.”
- Detect gating motifs and flexible loops via structural alignment and AlphaFold confidence (pLDDT) patterns; annotate candidate conformationally variable regions.
- Cluster pores into motif classes using unsupervised learning (Gaussian mixture models, spectral clustering) on standardized descriptors; assess stability across methods.
Known positive controls: carboxysome shell proteins with characterized pores and metabolosome pores with known selectivity will be used to sanity-check descriptor behavior.

5) Inferring shell architecture and pore spatial distribution
We will infer mesoscale shell parameters by combining gene cluster–derived priors with cryo-EM constraints:
- For BMCs with EMDB reconstructions: extract reported symmetry, diameter, and shell thickness; where available, re-analyze EMPIAR data to estimate particle size distributions.
- Use polyhedral shell models (icosahedral-like approximations adapted for BMCs) to translate size and symmetry into approximate counts of hexamers/pentamers.
- Infer plausible stoichiometries by solving constrained optimization problems: minimize deviation from gene-paralog priors while matching EM-derived size constraints.
- Generate “pore landscape” models: assign pore motif classes to facets based on paralog composition, yielding an effective pore density and heterogeneity index.
Cross-dataset validation: compare inferred stoichiometries for systems with multiple independent EM entries; test sensitivity to uncertainty in size and symmetry.

6) Reaction–diffusion and kinetic modeling of emergent function
We will build compartment models that couple transport across the shell with internal reactions:
- Define pathway modules per BMC type using KEGG/MetaCyc stoichiometries.
- Parameterize enzyme kinetics from BRENDA/SABIO-RK; where multiple values exist, use hierarchical priors and propagate uncertainty.
- Convert pore descriptors to permeability estimates using calibrated relationships (e.g., size/charge-based hindrance models); treat unknowns with Bayesian inference.
- Simulate steady-state and dynamic regimes using reaction–diffusion or well-mixed-with-permeability ODE approximations depending on data support.
Performance metrics (emergent): predicted internal intermediate concentration, leakage rate, flux gain relative to no-compartment baseline, and toxicity mitigation proxy.
Validation using existing data:
- Compare predicted metabolite accumulation/leakage patterns to metabolomics datasets (Metabolomics Workbench) for organisms with annotated BMC activity.
- Compare predicted flux gains to published 13C flux estimates where available.
- Use leave-one-system-out validation: fit permeability mapping on a subset of BMC types with richer data and test on held-out types.

7) Machine learning synthesis: mapping genotype to emergent performance
We will train interpretable ML models to predict pore motif class and performance metrics from genomic locus features:
- Models: gradient-boosted trees and sparse generalized additive models; incorporate phylogeny-aware features and regularization.
- Evaluation: nested cross-validation stratified by taxonomic clade to avoid overfitting to lineage.
- Interpretation: SHAP values and partial dependence to identify “design rules” (e.g., which paralog patterns predict retention regimes).

8) Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6: Team onboarding; finalize data schema; assemble genome/locus catalog; release v0.1 of BMC locus atlas.
Months 6–12: Structural pore pipeline; release pore descriptor library and motif clustering v0.1; initial EMDB-linked architecture inference for known systems.
Months 12–18: Reaction–diffusion model framework; parameter compilation from BRENDA/SABIO-RK; benchmark on 2–3 well-studied BMC types.
Months 18–24: Scale modeling across BMC diversity; integrate metabolomics/flux validations; ML genotype→function models v0.1.
Months 24–30: Final synthesis: BMC Design Space Atlas v1.0; manuscripts; community workshop; long-term hosting plan.

9) Team composition and collaboration structure
This working group requires:
- Microbial genomics/evolution: locus detection, phylogeny-aware analyses.
- Structural biology/bioinformatics: pore analytics, structural clustering, AlphaFold-based modeling.
- Cryo-EM expertise: interpretation of EMDB/EMPIAR metadata, mesoscale geometry constraints.
- Metabolic modeling/flux analysis: pathway module definition, flux dataset interpretation.
- Applied math/biophysics: reaction–diffusion modeling, uncertainty quantification.
- Data engineering/research software: pipelines, databases, reproducibility infrastructure.
NCEMS support is essential to coordinate iterative cross-disciplinary integration, convene working sessions, and maintain shared open infrastructure beyond any single lab’s capacity.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables (concrete, open, and reusable)
1) BMC Design Space Atlas (integrated dataset): A versioned, queryable resource linking (i) BMC loci and gene cluster features from NCBI RefSeq/IMG, (ii) shell protein and enzyme structures from PDB and AlphaFold DB, (iii) pore descriptors and motif class assignments, (iv) inferred shell architecture parameters constrained by EMDB/EMPIAR, (v) pathway modules and kinetic parameter sets from KEGG/MetaCyc and BRENDA/SABIO-RK, and (vi) associated metabolomics/flux references and environmental metadata from Metabolomics Workbench and GOLD. The atlas will include explicit provenance and confidence scores for each link.

2) Open software toolkit for BMC pore and architecture analysis:
- A reproducible pipeline to compute pore radius/electrostatics descriptors from PDB/AlphaFold structures.
- A motif clustering and annotation module producing standardized “permeability motif” labels.
- A shell architecture inference module translating gene cluster composition plus EM constraints into mesoscale pore landscape models.

3) Mechanistic models of emergent BMC function:
- Reaction–diffusion (or permeability-coupled kinetic) models for major BMC pathway classes, with uncertainty propagation.
- A library of emergent performance metrics (flux gain, intermediate retention, leakage risk) computed across BMC diversity.

4) Predictive genotype→function models:
- Interpretable ML models that predict pore motif class and emergent performance metrics from gene cluster features, with phylogeny-aware evaluation.
- A “design rule” summary describing which locus configurations are associated with retention vs throughput regimes.

5) Community outputs:
- At least two synthesis manuscripts: (i) a comparative pore motif taxonomy across BMCs; (ii) a genotype–architecture–function synthesis establishing emergent regime transitions.
- A public tutorial series (notebooks + recorded sessions) on multiscale synthesis for mesoscale organelles.

Scientific impact: advancing understanding of mesoscale emergence
This project will deliver mechanistic insight into how emergent properties arise at the mesoscale in protein-based organelles. Specifically, it will:
- Quantify how collective pore properties (distribution, heterogeneity, charge) produce selective transport regimes that cannot be inferred from single protein structures.
- Establish how gene cluster composition constrains mesoscale architecture (stoichiometry and pore landscapes), providing a predictive bridge from genomes to organelle geometry.
- Demonstrate, via coupled transport–reaction modeling, that small molecular-scale changes in pore constrictions can yield nonlinear, system-level switches in function (retention vs throughput), a hallmark of emergent behavior.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biosciences
- Generalizable principles: Protein shells are one class of mesoscale compartments. The analytical framework—integrating structural pores, assembly constraints, and reaction–diffusion—will generalize to other mesoscale systems where selective exchange and confinement matter (e.g., viral capsids, enzyme scaffolds, and potentially biomolecular condensates where permeability analogs exist).
- Data-centric workforce training: Trainees will gain hands-on experience in open, reproducible synthesis research spanning genomics, structural bioinformatics, and systems modeling—skills aligned with NCEMS’s training mission.
- Enabling future research: By identifying high-confidence design rules and gaps in current public data coverage, the atlas will guide future experimental work by the broader community without proposing or requiring new data generation within this project.

Dissemination plan
- Publications in open-access venues when possible; preprints posted upon submission.
- A dedicated project website hosted via GitHub Pages or NCEMS infrastructure, providing documentation, data access instructions, and interactive summaries.
- Two community workshops (virtual + hybrid if feasible): one focused on pore/structure analytics and one on multiscale modeling and atlas usage.
- Deposition of derived datasets to long-term repositories (Zenodo with DOIs; potential mirroring to Figshare) and code to GitHub with archival releases.

Long-term sustainability
Sustainability will be achieved through:
- Modular, well-tested open-source code with continuous integration.
- Versioned data releases with stable identifiers and clear provenance.
- Community governance: a lightweight steering group and contribution guidelines to enable external pull requests and new BMC type additions.
- Interoperability: export formats compatible with common bioinformatics tooling (FAIR tables, JSON-LD metadata, SBML for models).

By integrating distributed public data into a coherent, predictive framework, the project will transform BMC research from case studies into a quantitative science of mesoscale emergence, aligned with NCEMS’s goal of uncovering unexpected system properties across scales.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy
The budget prioritizes personnel and shared computational infrastructure needed to integrate, curate, and model large, heterogeneous public datasets—work that exceeds the capacity of a single lab and directly supports NCEMS’s synthesis, training, and open-science goals. All items are justified for computational synthesis and community coordination; no funds are allocated for experiments, sample collection, or new data generation.

Personnel (major cost drivers)
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (24–30 months each):
  1) Structural/biophysical postdoc to lead pore descriptor computation, motif taxonomy, and structure-to-permeability mapping.
  2) Systems/modeling postdoc to lead reaction–diffusion modeling, uncertainty quantification, and integration with metabolomics/flux datasets.
- 2 Graduate research assistants (part-time across 2–3 years):
  - One focused on comparative genomics and locus classification; one on phylogeny-aware ML and ecological metadata integration.
- 1 Research software engineer / data engineer (50–100% FTE depending on NCEMS norms):
  - Responsible for database schema, ETL pipelines, workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), CI, packaging, and documentation.
- Undergraduate/rotation student support (hourly):
  - Targeted tasks (literature phenotype curation, testing, documentation), providing early-stage training in data-centric biology.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits (AWS/GCP/Azure or NSF-supported clouds): needed for scalable structure processing (AlphaFold DB downloads, pore calculations), large-scale genome HMM scans, and ML training with repeated cross-validation.
- HPC allocations (institutional clusters or national resources): for parallelized simulation sweeps in reaction–diffusion models and for processing EM-derived constraints.
- Storage and data management: object storage for cached public inputs and versioned derived outputs; database hosting for the atlas (PostgreSQL) with routine backups.
Justification: The project’s synthesis scope (thousands of loci, many structures, repeated simulations) requires compute and storage beyond typical lab desktops.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (annual in-person or hybrid, aligned with NCEMS practices): support for PI/co-PI and trainee travel to enable intensive cross-disciplinary integration sprints.
- Conference dissemination: limited travel for trainees to present synthesis results at relevant meetings (microbiology, structural biology, systems biology), maximizing workforce development.
Justification: Cross-lab integration and consensus curation are central to community-scale synthesis and benefit from structured, face-to-face collaboration.

Workshops and training events
- Two open workshops (virtual-first with optional hybrid): costs for event hosting platforms, captioning/accessibility, and small participant support (e.g., trainee travel scholarships if in-person).
- Training materials production: support for recording, editing, and maintaining tutorial content.
Justification: Directly advances NCEMS’s training mission and broadens participation.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo archival (no direct cost) plus optional domain/website hosting and minimal funds for long-term maintenance of documentation sites.
- DOI-backed releases and metadata curation time (personnel effort) to ensure FAIR compliance.
Justification: Sustains reuse of synthesis products and ensures reproducibility.

Overall, the requested resources are tightly aligned with the core synthesis activities: integrating public data across scales, building reproducible computational pipelines, convening a diverse team to produce consensus design rules, and training trainees in open, data-intensive mesoscale biology.
standardized_text: This project explores the mesoscale organization of bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) to resolve missing maps for properties of pores and shells. These polyhedral organelles encapsulate enzymes to alter metabolic flux but mechanisms connecting clusters of genes to structural geometry remain unclear. The primary question asks how genetic composition determines the architecture of shells to provide predictive models for other biological structures. The study design features a computational synthesis of public datasets to predict properties of pores and simulate gradients of metabolites. The analytical approach applies hidden Markov models for the detection of loci and gradient boosted trees to evaluate genomic features. Results will be validated by comparing predictions of motifs against established structures and benchmarking models against published data from metabolomics. The project will utilize databases of sequences including UniProt and repositories of structures such as the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Distinct datasets will be integrated through a mapping layer of identifiers stored within a relational database and graph database. Known uncertainties of predictions for structures will be mitigated by filtering data with confidence scores and utilizing Bayesian inference. The project spans thirty months and includes milestones for releasing an atlas of loci and developing computational pipelines. This extensive scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to successfully integrate specialized expertise in microbial genomics and machine learning. The researchers will share findings through open access manuscripts and release open source code and data on public repositories. The team incorporates principal investigators and graduate students to offer computational training opportunities across multiple distinct career stages.
