The study will integrate diverse structural and metabolic datasets from Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold DB, and KEGG by building a standardized identifier mapping layer stored across relational and graph database architectures. This research will deliver a predictive framework establishing general principles of chemical microenvironment construction, generating structural and functional insights broadly applicable to other mesoscale biological assemblies like viral capsids.
abstract_original:
Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are proteinaceous organelles (50–300 nm) whose emergent permeability and enzyme colocalization enable metabolic pathways that would be inefficient or toxic in the cytosol. The emergent phenomenon is that shell protein assembly and pore organization generate selective transport and reaction microenvironments not predictable from individual enzymes.

We will synthesize: (i) BMC gene clusters across bacterial genomes (NCBI RefSeq, IMG; curated BMC databases), (ii) shell protein and encapsulated enzyme structures (PDB, AlphaFold DB), (iii) metabolomics and flux measurements for BMC-associated pathways (Metabolomics Workbench; published 13C flux studies), (iv) cryo-EM structures of intact BMCs and shells (EMDB/EMPIAR), and (v) environmental metadata and phenotypes for host organisms (GOLD database; literature-derived growth phenotypes).

We will build a comparative framework linking genetic composition to mesoscale shell architecture and emergent function. First, we will annotate shell protein families and predict pore properties (charge, diameter, gating motifs) from structures. Second, we will infer likely shell stoichiometries and tessellation patterns using assembly modeling and constraints from cryo-EM. Third, we will integrate pathway enzyme kinetics (from BRENDA) with predicted permeability to simulate emergent metabolite gradients and flux enhancement using reaction–diffusion models. Machine learning will map gene cluster features to predicted organelle performance metrics (toxicity mitigation, flux gain).

Key questions: Are there universal shell “permeability motifs” that recur across unrelated BMC types? How do small changes in pore composition produce emergent switches between retention vs throughput regimes? Can we predict ecological niches where particular BMC designs confer advantage?

Expected insights include design rules for emergent mesoscale selectivity, a taxonomy of BMC architectures linked to metabolic outcomes, and open tools for predicting BMC function from genomes. While synthetic biology implications exist, the project itself uses only public data and focuses on fundamental principles of mesoscale emergence.

This effort requires collaboration among microbiologists, structural biologists, metabolic modelers, and evolutionary bioinformaticians, and depends on integrating large-scale genomic data with structural and metabolic measurements. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open pipelines, and trainee training in multiscale modeling of protein-based organelles.

title: Mesoscale Vesicle Coat Self-Organization: Integrating Structural Proteomics and Imaging to Explain Cargo Selectivity Emergence
title_norm: mesoscale vesicle coat selforganization integrating structural proteomics and imaging to explain cargo selectivity emergence
abstract_text:
Vesicle coats (clathrin, COPI, COPII) assemble into mesoscale lattices (50–150 nm vesicles; ~10–20 nm lattice spacing) that generate curvature and select cargo. The emergent phenomenon is that collective lattice geometry and adaptor clustering yields cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual coat subunits.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of coat assemblies and adaptor complexes (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proteomics of coated vesicles and adaptor interactomes (PRIDE; BioGRID/IntAct interactions), (iii) high-content imaging of trafficking markers and coat puncta (IDR; Cell Painting datasets where relevant), (iv) cargo proteomes and sorting signal annotations (UniProt; curated motif databases), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes for coat/adaptor genes (DepMap; yeast deletion phenotypes in SGD).

We will quantify coat puncta and vesicle size proxies from imaging, and integrate with structural parameters (lattice curvature preferences, binding site densities). Graph-based models will represent adaptor–cargo networks, while physics-informed simulations will connect adaptor clustering to emergent cargo enrichment under constraints of lattice geometry. We will use probabilistic models to infer how adaptor competition and cooperative binding produce sharp cargo sorting thresholds.

Hypotheses: (1) vesicle coats operate near geometric frustration points where small changes in adaptor composition shift vesicle size and cargo repertoire; (2) emergent cargo selectivity is driven by mesoscale clustering of adaptors into subdomains within the coat; and (3) disease mutations in trafficking genes often act by altering mesoscale lattice parameters rather than abolishing binding.

Expected insights include a unified model connecting coat architecture to cargo selection across pathways, identification of conserved mesoscale adaptor subdomain motifs, and open resources linking structural and imaging-derived coat features.

This synthesis requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, trafficking cell biology, and computational modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize disparate datasets, build open analysis pipelines, and train trainees to integrate structure, networks, and bioimage-derived mesoscale phenotypes under reproducible open science.
full_text:
[Abstract]
Vesicle coats (clathrin, COPI, COPII) assemble into mesoscale lattices (50–150 nm vesicles; ~10–20 nm lattice spacing) that generate curvature and select cargo. The emergent phenomenon is that collective lattice geometry and adaptor clustering yields cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual coat subunits.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of coat assemblies and adaptor complexes (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proteomics of coated vesicles and adaptor interactomes (PRIDE; BioGRID/IntAct interactions), (iii) high-content imaging of trafficking markers and coat puncta (IDR; Cell Painting datasets where relevant), (iv) cargo proteomes and sorting signal annotations (UniProt; curated motif databases), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes for coat/adaptor genes (DepMap; yeast deletion phenotypes in SGD).

We will quantify coat puncta and vesicle size proxies from imaging, and integrate with structural parameters (lattice curvature preferences, binding site densities). Graph-based models will represent adaptor–cargo networks, while physics-informed simulations will connect adaptor clustering to emergent cargo enrichment under constraints of lattice geometry. We will use probabilistic models to infer how adaptor competition and cooperative binding produce sharp cargo sorting thresholds.

Hypotheses: (1) vesicle coats operate near geometric frustration points where small changes in adaptor composition shift vesicle size and cargo repertoire; (2) emergent cargo selectivity is driven by mesoscale clustering of adaptors into subdomains within the coat; and (3) disease mutations in trafficking genes often act by altering mesoscale lattice parameters rather than abolishing binding.

Expected insights include a unified model connecting coat architecture to cargo selection across pathways, identification of conserved mesoscale adaptor subdomain motifs, and open resources linking structural and imaging-derived coat features.

This synthesis requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, trafficking cell biology, and computational modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize disparate datasets, build open analysis pipelines, and train trainees to integrate structure, networks, and bioimage-derived mesoscale phenotypes under reproducible open science.

[Background and Significance]
Vesicular trafficking depends on coat proteins that assemble into curved lattices to deform membranes and concentrate specific cargo. Canonical coats—clathrin/AP complexes at the plasma membrane and trans-Golgi network, COPII at ER exit sites, and COPI at Golgi/retrograde routes—are built from modular subunits that bind membranes, recruit adaptors, and capture cargo. While the molecular interactions of individual subunits and sorting motifs are well characterized, the key biological output—robust cargo selectivity coupled to characteristic vesicle size distributions—emerges at the mesoscale: tens to hundreds of nanometers, where hundreds to thousands of protein copies organize into a lattice with local defects, variable curvature, and heterogeneous adaptor composition.

At this mesoscale, collective phenomena dominate. Lattice geometry constrains which adaptor complexes can pack, how many cargo binding sites are presented per unit area, and what membrane curvature is energetically favorable. Conversely, adaptor and cargo clustering can bias lattice assembly pathways, stabilize particular curvature states, and create subdomains with distinct binding-site densities. The result is an emergent “sorting function” that is not a simple sum of pairwise interactions: small changes in adaptor composition, cargo abundance, or binding affinity can yield disproportionate shifts in what is packaged and in vesicle size. Such nonlinear behavior is consistent with cooperative binding, competition among adaptors, and geometric frustration—situations where local preferred curvature or lattice spacing cannot be simultaneously satisfied everywhere, leading to defects and heterogeneous microenvironments.

Existing public datasets already capture many facets of this system, but they remain siloed by modality. Structural biology has produced a large body of cryo-EM maps and atomic models for coat components and partial assemblies, deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB). These resources provide quantitative parameters directly relevant to mesoscale behavior: lattice spacing, preferred curvature, triskelion or cage angles, and adaptor binding-site locations and stoichiometries. In parallel, proteomics studies of purified coated vesicles and adaptor complexes, deposited in PRIDE (Proteomics Identifications Database), report cargo repertoires and coat/adaptor compositions across cell types, perturbations, and conditions. Protein–protein interaction resources such as BioGRID and IntAct curate adaptor–cargo and adaptor–coat interactions, offering a network-level view of potential recruitment pathways.

Imaging datasets provide a complementary mesoscale readout in intact cells. The Image Data Resource (IDR) hosts high-content microscopy datasets, including trafficking marker localization, coat puncta patterns, and perturbation phenotypes. Cell Painting resources (e.g., Broad Institute Cell Painting datasets) can be leveraged when perturbations of trafficking genes are present, providing morphological signatures that can be linked to coat organization and cargo flux. Finally, functional genetics datasets quantify phenotypic consequences of perturbing coat and adaptor genes: DepMap (Cancer Dependency Map) provides CRISPR loss-of-function effects across many human cell lines, while Saccharomyces Genome Database (SGD) aggregates yeast deletion phenotypes and genetic interaction information for conserved trafficking machinery.

Despite this wealth of public data, three gaps limit mechanistic understanding of emergent cargo selectivity. First, there is no unified quantitative framework linking structural parameters of coat lattices (curvature, lattice spacing, binding-site density) to proteomics-derived cargo enrichment. Many studies interpret cargo selection in terms of motif recognition by adaptors, but do not incorporate the physical constraints of lattice assembly and membrane curvature that can amplify or suppress recruitment. Second, mesoscale heterogeneity—subdomains of adaptor clustering, lattice defects, and curvature gradients—is rarely integrated with cargo selection models. Imaging suggests puncta heterogeneity and variable coat sizes, yet these observations are not systematically mapped onto structural and network features. Third, disease-associated mutations in trafficking genes are often interpreted as “loss of binding” or “loss of function,” but public variant annotations and structural data suggest many mutations may instead tune mesoscale parameters (e.g., altering lattice flexibility or adaptor clustering propensity), producing subtle but system-level shifts in cargo thresholds.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address these gaps because the decisive evidence is distributed across modalities and organisms. No single laboratory can reasonably harmonize cryo-EM structural measurements, large-scale vesicle proteomes, interaction networks, imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes, and genetic dependency profiles, nor develop integrative models that respect both physical constraints and network complexity. By integrating these public datasets, we can test whether common mesoscale principles govern cargo selectivity across clathrin, COPI, and COPII systems, identify conserved adaptor subdomain motifs, and explain how small molecular changes yield emergent sorting outcomes.

Understanding emergence at this mesoscale matters broadly. Vesicle trafficking underlies secretion, receptor signaling, organelle homeostasis, and neuronal function; defects contribute to neurodegeneration, immunodeficiency, and developmental disorders. Mechanistically, vesicle coats are an archetype of mesoscale self-organization: a molecularly specified parts list that produces higher-order geometry, spatial heterogeneity, and nonlinear functional thresholds. NCEMS’s emphasis on mesoscale emergence aligns directly with the opportunity here: publicly available structural, proteomic, imaging, and genetic datasets are now sufficiently rich to enable community-scale synthesis that can move the field from descriptive catalogs toward predictive, cross-system principles of coat-driven cargo selection.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how mesoscale self-organization of vesicle coats produces emergent cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions. We focus on testable questions that can be answered exclusively through synthesis of publicly available structural, proteomic, imaging, interaction, and genetic datasets.

Research Question 1: How do coat lattice geometry and adaptor binding-site density jointly determine cargo enrichment profiles?
Hypothesis 1 (Geometry–density coupling): Cargo enrichment in coated vesicles is best predicted not by adaptor–motif affinity alone, but by an effective “mesoscale recruitment capacity” determined by (i) lattice curvature and spacing (from PDB/EMDB structures) and (ii) adaptor binding-site density and stoichiometry (from structures and interaction annotations). Prediction 1a: Across datasets in PRIDE, vesicle proteomes with higher inferred adaptor site density per membrane area will show steeper enrichment of motif-bearing cargo (e.g., YxxΦ, dileucine, DxE) relative to background membrane proteomes. Prediction 1b: Structural classes of cages/assemblies with different curvature regimes will correspond to distinct cargo size/length distributions (e.g., luminal domain size proxies, cytosolic tail lengths) because curvature imposes packing constraints.
Validation using existing data: We will compute structural metrics (curvature, lattice spacing, site density) from PDB/EMDB assemblies and map them to proteomics-derived cargo enrichment statistics from PRIDE studies annotated for coat type and preparation. We will test predictive models that include geometry terms versus motif-only baselines, using cross-study validation.

Research Question 2: Do adaptor subdomains and cooperative clustering create sharp cargo sorting thresholds (switch-like behavior) at the mesoscale?
Hypothesis 2 (Subdomain cooperativity): Adaptors self-organize into mesoscale subdomains within coats, producing local cooperative binding that generates threshold-like cargo selection: below a cargo abundance/affinity threshold, cargo is excluded; above it, cargo is strongly enriched. Prediction 2a: Imaging datasets in IDR will show multimodal distributions of coat puncta intensity/size proxies consistent with heterogeneous adaptor occupancy states, rather than a single continuous distribution. Prediction 2b: In proteomics datasets, cargo enrichment will show nonlinear dependence on adaptor abundance (when adaptor levels are reported) or on adaptor gene dependency/essentiality (from DepMap/SGD), consistent with cooperative recruitment.
Validation using existing data: We will quantify puncta features (size proxies, intensity, spatial clustering) from IDR datasets with labeled coat/adaptor markers and perturbations. We will link these features to network-derived adaptor centrality (BioGRID/IntAct) and to cargo enrichment profiles (PRIDE). We will fit probabilistic mixture models and Hill-type cooperative models to identify thresholds and compare to null models with independent binding.

Research Question 3: Is coat assembly poised near geometric frustration points where small compositional changes shift vesicle size and cargo repertoire?
Hypothesis 3 (Frustration proximity): Coats operate near parameter regimes where preferred curvature of coat subunits and membrane constraints cannot be simultaneously satisfied, making vesicle size distributions highly sensitive to adaptor composition and cargo load. Prediction 3a: Structural assemblies will show signatures of frustration—variable angles, defects, or multiple curvature states—correlated with broader vesicle size proxies in imaging datasets (IDR) and broader cargo diversity in proteomics (PRIDE). Prediction 3b: Genetic perturbation effects (DepMap dependencies; SGD phenotypes/genetic interactions) will be enriched for epistatic relationships among genes predicted to tune curvature (coat scaffold) and genes predicted to tune clustering (adaptors/accessory factors), consistent with a system near a critical regime.
Validation using existing data: We will extract variability measures from structural ensembles (multiple EMDB maps/structures for a coat) and relate them to imaging-derived heterogeneity metrics. We will test whether predicted “curvature-tuning” genes and “clustering-tuning” genes form interaction modules in SGD genetic interaction networks and whether these modules align with strong dependencies in DepMap.

Research Question 4: Do disease-associated variants act by tuning mesoscale lattice parameters rather than abolishing binding?
Hypothesis 4 (Mesoscale tuning by variants): Many pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in coat/adaptor genes shift mesoscale parameters (flexibility, oligomerization interfaces, lattice packing) leading to altered cargo thresholds and vesicle size distributions, even when core binding motifs remain intact. Prediction 4a: Variants mapped onto structures (PDB) will be enriched at interfaces controlling lattice angles/hinges rather than at canonical cargo-binding pockets. Prediction 4b: Cell-line-specific dependencies (DepMap) for genes with interface-enriched variants will correlate with trafficking-related morphological signatures in Cell Painting perturbation datasets (where available) more strongly than variants in binding pockets.
Validation using existing data: We will use public variant resources (e.g., ClinVar for clinical variants; gnomAD for population variation) and map variants onto PDB structures to classify structural context. We will relate variant context to gene dependency patterns in DepMap and to imaging phenotypes in public high-content datasets.

Across questions, the unifying mechanistic insight sought is a quantitative, cross-coat model in which mesoscale lattice geometry, adaptor clustering, and network competition collectively generate emergent cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions. The hypotheses are designed to be falsifiable with existing data: each yields quantitative predictions about enrichment slopes, heterogeneity distributions, network epistasis, and structural localization of impactful variants.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will build an integrative, open, multi-modal atlas and modeling pipeline that links (1) structural parameters of coat lattices and adaptor complexes, (2) proteomics-derived coat/cargo compositions, (3) imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes (puncta/vesicle proxies), (4) interaction networks connecting adaptors and cargo, and (5) genetic perturbation phenotypes. The core methodological principle is “triangulation”: each mechanistic claim must be supported by concordant evidence from at least two independent public modalities (e.g., structure + proteomics; imaging + genetics), avoiding reliance on any single dataset.

Specific public data sources
Structural data:
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): atomic models for clathrin, AP complexes, COPI/COPII subunits, adaptors/accessory proteins.
- Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB): cryo-EM maps of coat assemblies/cages and partial lattices.
- UniProt: domain boundaries, isoforms, subcellular localization annotations.
Proteomics and interactions:
- PRIDE: coated vesicle proteomes, adaptor immunoprecipitation proteomes, quantitative comparisons.
- BioGRID and IntAct: curated protein–protein interactions (adaptor–cargo, adaptor–coat, accessory factors).
- Complex Portal (EMBL-EBI): curated complexes and subunit compositions (where available).
Imaging:
- Image Data Resource (IDR): high-content imaging datasets with trafficking markers, coat components, perturbations.
- Broad Institute Cell Painting resources (public releases): morphological profiles for gene perturbations, including trafficking genes.
Genetics/phenotypes:
- DepMap: genome-wide CRISPR dependency scores across human cell lines.
- Saccharomyces Genome Database (SGD): deletion phenotypes, genetic interactions for conserved trafficking genes.
Variants (for hypothesis 4):
- ClinVar: clinically interpreted variants.
- gnomAD: population variation for constraint/context.

Data harmonization and knowledge graph
We will implement a harmonized identifier and metadata layer:
- Map all proteins to UniProt accessions; crosswalk to gene symbols, Ensembl IDs, and yeast orthologs (via resources such as OrthoDB or Ensembl Compara, used only for mapping).
- Standardize experimental context metadata: organism, cell type, coat system (clathrin/COPI/COPII), compartment, perturbation type, and assay modality.
- Create a “Coat Emergence Knowledge Graph” integrating: nodes (proteins, complexes, cargo motifs, datasets) and edges (structural contacts, PPIs, co-enrichment, co-localization, genetic interactions).
Storage and access:
- Use a graph database representation (e.g., Neo4j exportable format) plus flat, analysis-ready tables (Parquet) for reproducible analytics.

Feature extraction
Structural features (PDB/EMDB):
- Lattice geometry: estimate curvature radius, lattice spacing, and angular distributions from fitted assemblies or published symmetry parameters; where multiple structures exist, compute ensemble variability.
- Binding-site density: count adaptor/cargo-binding sites per coat unit and infer areal density given lattice geometry.
- Interface classification: annotate residues at lattice interfaces/hinges vs cargo-binding pockets for variant mapping.
Proteomics features (PRIDE):
- Compute cargo enrichment scores (e.g., log2 fold-change vs controls when available; spectral count normalization or intensity-based measures depending on dataset).
- Infer coat/adaptor stoichiometry proxies from relative abundances.
- Annotate cargo sorting motifs using UniProt sequences plus curated motif resources (e.g., ELM—Eukaryotic Linear Motif; Prosite for relevant patterns), focusing on cytosolic tail motifs.
Imaging features (IDR/Cell Painting):
- Use reproducible segmentation and feature extraction pipelines (e.g., CellProfiler workflows when applicable; or deep-learning-based segmentation with pre-trained models) to quantify puncta number, size proxies, intensity, spatial clustering (Ripley’s K / pair-correlation), and cell-to-cell heterogeneity.
- For Cell Painting, use published feature sets and embeddings to connect trafficking gene perturbations to morphological signatures.
Genetic features (DepMap/SGD):
- DepMap: dependency scores, co-dependency networks, context specificity.
- SGD: phenotype categories and genetic interaction scores; build curvature-tuning vs clustering-tuning modules.

Integrative modeling
1) Graph-based adaptor–cargo competition models:
- Construct bipartite graphs between adaptors and cargo proteins weighted by motif presence, interaction evidence (BioGRID/IntAct), and co-enrichment (PRIDE).
- Apply community detection (Leiden/Louvain) to identify adaptor subdomain modules; quantify module conservation across coat systems.
- Use probabilistic graphical models (e.g., Bayesian networks) to infer conditional dependencies of cargo enrichment on adaptor abundance and structural capacity.
2) Physics-informed mesoscale simulations:
- Implement coarse-grained, physics-informed models linking lattice geometry to recruitment capacity. Parameters include curvature preference, lattice spacing, adaptor site density, and cooperative clustering terms.
- Use approximate Bayesian computation or likelihood-free inference to fit model parameters to observed distributions (imaging heterogeneity + proteomics enrichment).
- Identify “frustration proximity” by locating parameter regimes where small changes induce large shifts in predicted vesicle size/cargo composition.
3) Statistical tests and ML:
- Compare motif-only predictors vs integrated predictors (motif + geometry + network + clustering) using regularized regression (elastic net), gradient-boosted trees, and calibrated probabilistic models.
- Use nested cross-validation across datasets (train on subset of PRIDE/IDR studies; test on held-out studies) to ensure generalization.
- Positive controls: well-established cargo classes (e.g., COPII DxE exporters; clathrin/AP2 YxxΦ cargo) should be recovered as enriched under appropriate contexts.

Cross-dataset validation and robustness
- Replication across independent studies: require that key findings (e.g., threshold behavior, module composition) replicate in at least two independent PRIDE datasets and one imaging dataset when available.
- Sensitivity analyses: test robustness to motif annotation uncertainty, proteomics normalization choices, and imaging segmentation parameters.
- Null models: randomized networks preserving degree distributions; shuffled motif labels; permuted structural parameters within coat class.

Timeline and milestones (30 months; adaptable to 24–36 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize data inclusion criteria; build identifier mapping and metadata schema.
- Curate initial corpus from PDB/EMDB, PRIDE, BioGRID/IntAct, IDR, DepMap, SGD.
Deliverables: v0 knowledge graph; reproducible ingestion pipelines.
Months 7–12:
- Structural feature extraction and motif annotation; initial proteomics harmonization.
- Imaging pipeline deployment on selected IDR datasets; define puncta/heterogeneity metrics.
Deliverables: v1 integrated tables; baseline motif-only models.
Months 13–18:
- Integrative modeling: graph modules, cooperative/threshold inference; cross-validation across datasets.
- Begin variant-to-structure mapping and dependency/morphology associations.
Deliverables: preprint-level results for Questions 1–2; open software release.
Months 19–24:
- Physics-informed simulation fitting; frustration proximity analyses; genetic interaction module integration.
Deliverables: mechanistic model paper draft; interactive atlas prototype.
Months 25–30:
- Consolidation, replication, and documentation; workshops and training; final atlas and pipelines.
Deliverables: public data portal release (static + repositories), manuscripts, training materials.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Structural biology experts: curate coat assemblies; define geometry metrics; interpret interface/hinge features.
- Quantitative trafficking cell biologists: curate biological context, coat pathway distinctions, cargo classes; define positive controls.
- Proteomics specialists: harmonize PRIDE datasets; normalization strategies; interpret vesicle purification biases.
- Bioimage analysts: implement IDR/Cell Painting feature extraction; heterogeneity quantification.
- Network scientists/statisticians: knowledge graph, community detection, causal/probabilistic modeling.
- Physics/biophysics modelers: coarse-grained lattice/adaptor clustering models; frustration analysis.
- Research software engineers: reproducible pipelines, packaging, documentation, CI.
- Trainees (graduate students/postdocs): cross-training rotations across modalities.

All validation and inference will use only existing publicly available data; no new experiments, sample generation, or data collection are proposed.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) Coat Emergence Atlas (open, integrated resource):
- Harmonized, analysis-ready datasets linking coat structural parameters (curvature, lattice spacing, binding-site density), adaptor–cargo networks, vesicle/cargo proteomes, imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes, and genetic perturbation profiles.
- A knowledge graph export (open format) plus curated tables (Parquet/CSV) with provenance and standardized metadata.
2) Open-source software toolkit:
- Reproducible pipelines for ingesting PDB/EMDB, PRIDE, BioGRID/IntAct, IDR, DepMap, and SGD data.
- Modules for motif annotation (ELM/UniProt-based), structural feature extraction, imaging feature extraction, and integrative modeling.
- Benchmark suite implementing motif-only baselines and integrated predictors for cargo enrichment.
3) Mechanistic, testable models of mesoscale emergence:
- Quantitative models explaining when and why cargo sorting becomes threshold-like, identifying parameters governing cooperativity (adaptor clustering) and capacity (geometry/site density).
- A “frustration proximity” framework that predicts sensitivity of vesicle size and cargo repertoire to small compositional changes.
4) Cross-system principles and conserved motifs:
- Identification of adaptor subdomain modules conserved (or distinctly specialized) across clathrin, COPI, and COPII systems.
- Catalog of predicted mesoscale “subdomain motifs” (combinations of adaptors/accessory factors and cargo classes) supported by network + proteomics + imaging concordance.
5) Variant interpretation resource (optional but high-value extension within synthesis scope):
- Structural-context annotation of ClinVar variants in coat/adaptor genes (interface/hinge vs binding pocket) and associations with dependency/morphology signals from DepMap/Cell Painting.

Scientific impact: advancing understanding of mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project directly addresses NCEMS’s mission by explaining how emergent properties arise at the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles. Vesicle coats are an ideal exemplar: individual binding interactions are known, yet system-level outputs—cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions—require collective organization. By integrating structural, proteomic, imaging, network, and genetic evidence, we will move from qualitative narratives (“adaptors bind motifs”) to quantitative, predictive principles (“given lattice geometry and adaptor clustering propensity, cargo selection exhibits a threshold at X and vesicle size shifts by Y”).

We expect to establish:
- Geometry–selectivity coupling: explicit links between lattice parameters and cargo enrichment slopes.
- Subdomain-driven cooperativity: evidence that adaptor clustering into mesoscale subdomains produces switch-like sorting.
- Critical-regime behavior: identification of parameter regimes consistent with geometric frustration, explaining sensitivity and heterogeneity.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Generalizable framework: The methods (knowledge graph integration, physics-informed inference, cross-modality validation) will be applicable to other mesoscale assemblies (e.g., phase-separated condensates, cytoskeletal networks, nuclear pore organization).
- Improved interpretation of perturbation phenotypes: Integrating DepMap/SGD with mesoscale models can help interpret why certain trafficking genes show context-specific essentiality.
- Disease relevance: A mesoscale-tuning perspective on variants can inform mechanistic hypotheses for trafficking-related disorders without requiring new experiments.

Enabling future research
Because all outputs are open and modular, future investigators can:
- Add additional public datasets (new cryo-EM maps, proteomes, imaging screens) via standardized ingestion.
- Use the atlas to select candidate adaptor modules or cargo classes for targeted experimental follow-up (outside the scope of this proposal).
- Apply the modeling framework to compare trafficking systems across organisms or cell types.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least two major manuscripts (integrated atlas + mechanistic modeling) and one methods/software paper.
- NCEMS-style working group meetings and hackathons: focused sprints on data harmonization, imaging quantification, and modeling.
- Community resources: a public website (static, low-maintenance) linking datasets, documentation, and tutorials; deposition of derived datasets in appropriate repositories (e.g., Zenodo for versioned releases; PRIDE/IDR links for provenance).

Long-term sustainability
- Versioned releases with DOIs (Zenodo) and semantic versioning for the atlas and software.
- Containerized workflows to ensure executability over time.
- Governance: a lightweight maintainer model (RSE + rotating community contributors) and contribution guidelines.
- Interoperability: adoption of common identifiers (UniProt), standard metadata fields, and open formats to facilitate reuse by the trafficking, structural biology, and bioimaging communities.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget overview and justification (2.5–3 years)
This project is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring coordinated expertise, substantial computing for multi-modal processing (cryo-EM feature extraction, proteomics harmonization, large-scale imaging quantification), and dedicated research software engineering to ensure open, reproducible outputs. The budget is structured to support personnel time for integration and modeling, shared computational resources, and the NCEMS-style working group activities that make the collaboration more than the sum of individual labs.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (computational/quantitative focus; 100% each):
  - Postdoc A: integrative modeling (probabilistic models, network inference), cross-validation, mechanistic synthesis writing.
  - Postdoc B: physics-informed mesoscale simulations, structural feature extraction, frustration analyses.
  Justification: the modeling and synthesis tasks require full-time effort beyond typical single-lab capacity.
- 1 Graduate student (50–100%):
  - Focus on imaging feature extraction from IDR/Cell Painting and linking phenotypes to model parameters.
  Justification: provides training of next-generation data-savvy workforce and sustained development of imaging pipelines.
- 1 Research Software Engineer / Programmer (50–100%):
  - Builds and maintains ingestion pipelines, workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), containers, documentation, CI, and release management.
  Justification: essential for reproducibility, open science deliverables, and long-term sustainability.
- Faculty/PI and co-PI effort (modest, as allowed by program norms):
  - Coordination, domain expertise, working group facilitation, and supervision.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations:
  - Imaging quantification at scale (IDR datasets can be terabytes; feature extraction requires parallel compute).
  - Model fitting and simulation (ABC/likelihood-free inference, cross-validation).
  Justification: synthesis across modalities demands compute beyond standard lab workstations; scalable compute ensures timely milestones.
- Storage and data management:
  - Versioned storage for derived datasets, intermediate artifacts, and container images.
  Justification: reproducibility requires retaining intermediate processed forms and provenance.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2–3 in-person meetings over project):
  - Support travel for geographically distributed participants, including trainees and investigators from diverse institution types.
  Justification: NCEMS goals emphasize catalyzing multidisciplinary teams; in-person synthesis accelerates integration, resolves conceptual mismatches, and enables cross-training.
- Conference dissemination:
  - Travel for trainees and key personnel to present at relevant meetings (cell biology, structural biology, bioinformatics).
  Justification: ensures broad adoption and feedback from multiple communities.

Workshops and training events
- 2 virtual workshops + 1 hybrid/in-person hackathon:
  - Costs include platform support, captioning/accessibility services, and limited participant support.
  Justification: aligns with NCEMS training mission and expands the user base of the open tools.

Open science infrastructure
- DOI archiving and data release costs:
  - Zenodo is free, but budget includes contingency for institutional repository fees or web hosting for a lightweight portal.
- Documentation and website:
  - Hosting for documentation site and atlas landing page; optional interactive visualization hosting.
  Justification: dissemination and sustainability require accessible, well-documented resources.

Why NCEMS support is required
The project’s value depends on coordinated synthesis across structural, proteomic, imaging, genetic, and modeling domains—work that exceeds a single lab’s expertise and bandwidth. NCEMS resources enable: (i) convening and sustaining the multidisciplinary team, (ii) dedicated engineering for reproducible pipelines and open releases, (iii) compute and storage for large-scale integration, and (iv) training activities that build a broader community of mesoscale data-synthesis scientists.

All requested resources directly support synthesis using existing public data; no funds are allocated for experimental reagents, sample preparation, or new data generation.

abstract_original:
Vesicle coats (clathrin, COPI, COPII) assemble into mesoscale lattices (50–150 nm vesicles; ~10–20 nm lattice spacing) that generate curvature and select cargo. The emergent phenomenon is that collective lattice geometry and adaptor clustering yields cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual coat subunits.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of coat assemblies and adaptor complexes (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proteomics of coated vesicles and adaptor interactomes (PRIDE; BioGRID/IntAct interactions), (iii) high-content imaging of trafficking markers and coat puncta (IDR; Cell Painting datasets where relevant), (iv) cargo proteomes and sorting signal annotations (UniProt; curated motif databases), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes for coat/adaptor genes (DepMap; yeast deletion phenotypes in SGD).

We will quantify coat puncta and vesicle size proxies from imaging, and integrate with structural parameters (lattice curvature preferences, binding site densities). Graph-based models will represent adaptor–cargo networks, while physics-informed simulations will connect adaptor clustering to emergent cargo enrichment under constraints of lattice geometry. We will use probabilistic models to infer how adaptor competition and cooperative binding produce sharp cargo sorting thresholds.

Hypotheses: (1) vesicle coats operate near geometric frustration points where small changes in adaptor composition shift vesicle size and cargo repertoire; (2) emergent cargo selectivity is driven by mesoscale clustering of adaptors into subdomains within the coat; and (3) disease mutations in trafficking genes often act by altering mesoscale lattice parameters rather than abolishing binding.

Expected insights include a unified model connecting coat architecture to cargo selection across pathways, identification of conserved mesoscale adaptor subdomain motifs, and open resources linking structural and imaging-derived coat features.

This synthesis requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, trafficking cell biology, and computational modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize disparate datasets, build open analysis pipelines, and train trainees to integrate structure, networks, and bioimage-derived mesoscale phenotypes under reproducible open science.

abstract_text:
Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) are ~100 nm assemblies whose central FG-nucleoporin (FG-Nup) network forms a selective permeability barrier—an emergent property arising from collective polymer behavior rather than any single FG repeat. This project will synthesize structural, sequence, and transport datasets to test how mesoscale organization of FG-Nups encodes selectivity and transport modes across species and cell states.

We will integrate: (i) NPC structural data from cryo-ET and cryo-EM (EMDB/EMPIAR; PDB for scaffold subcomplexes), (ii) FG-Nup sequences, disorder annotations, and repeat grammars (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt), (iii) quantitative transport kinetics measurements (single-molecule transport, FRAP, import/export rates) from published datasets and supplements, (iv) proteomics of NPC composition and post-translational modifications (PRIDE), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting transport (SGD; DepMap; disease variant databases for nucleoporins).

We will build a multiscale model linking FG-Nup polymer physics to observed transport selectivity. Sequence-derived features (FG motif spacing, charge patterning) will parameterize coarse-grained polymer simulations and analytical theories (brush/gels). Structural constraints from NPC ultrastructure will define boundary conditions. We will then fit model predictions to transport kinetics via Bayesian inference, enabling estimation of emergent parameters such as mesh size, cohesive interaction strength, and heterogeneity across the pore.

Key questions: Do different cell types or organisms achieve similar selectivity via distinct FG-Nup sequence grammars (many-to-one mapping)? Are there discrete “barrier states” corresponding to transport regimes (fast/slow, size cutoff shifts) modulated by phosphorylation or composition changes? Can disease-associated mutations be explained as shifts in emergent barrier parameters rather than loss of specific interactions?

Expected insights include a comparative atlas of FG-Nup grammars mapped to inferred barrier states, quantitative links between ultrastructure and transport, and open tools for fitting polymer-based NPC models to data.

This effort requires collaboration among polymer physicists, structural biologists, quantitative microscopists, and computational biologists, and hinges on synthesizing diverse public datasets. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, reproducible modeling workflows, and trainee training at the interface of disordered protein science and mesoscale transport phenomena.

[Abstract]
Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) are ~100 nm assemblies whose central FG-nucleoporin (FG-Nup) network forms a selective permeability barrier—an emergent property arising from collective polymer behavior rather than any single FG repeat. This project will synthesize structural, sequence, and transport datasets to test how mesoscale organization of FG-Nups encodes selectivity and transport modes across species and cell states.

We will integrate: (i) NPC structural data from cryo-ET and cryo-EM (EMDB/EMPIAR; PDB for scaffold subcomplexes), (ii) FG-Nup sequences, disorder annotations, and repeat grammars (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt), (iii) quantitative transport kinetics measurements (single-molecule transport, FRAP, import/export rates) from published datasets and supplements, (iv) proteomics of NPC composition and post-translational modifications (PRIDE), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting transport (SGD; DepMap; disease variant databases for nucleoporins).

We will build a multiscale model linking FG-Nup polymer physics to observed transport selectivity. Sequence-derived features (FG motif spacing, charge patterning) will parameterize coarse-grained polymer simulations and analytical theories (brush/gels). Structural constraints from NPC ultrastructure will define boundary conditions. We will then fit model predictions to transport kinetics via Bayesian inference, enabling estimation of emergent parameters such as mesh size, cohesive interaction strength, and heterogeneity across the pore.

Key questions: Do different cell types or organisms achieve similar selectivity via distinct FG-Nup sequence grammars (many-to-one mapping)? Are there discrete “barrier states” corresponding to transport regimes (fast/slow, size cutoff shifts) modulated by phosphorylation or composition changes? Can disease-associated mutations be explained as shifts in emergent barrier parameters rather than loss of specific interactions?

Expected insights include a comparative atlas of FG-Nup grammars mapped to inferred barrier states, quantitative links between ultrastructure and transport, and open tools for fitting polymer-based NPC models to data.

This effort requires collaboration among polymer physicists, structural biologists, quantitative microscopists, and computational biologists, and hinges on synthesizing diverse public datasets. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, reproducible modeling workflows, and trainee training at the interface of disordered protein science and mesoscale transport phenomena.

[Background and Significance]
Selective nucleocytoplasmic transport is a defining eukaryotic cellular function that couples gene regulation, signaling, and stress responses to spatial compartmentalization. The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is the sole gateway across the nuclear envelope and operates at the mesoscale: a ~100 nm, multi-megadalton assembly whose transport barrier emerges from the collective organization of intrinsically disordered FG-nucleoporins (FG-Nups) within a confined channel. This barrier is not a property of any single FG repeat or single FG-Nup. Instead, it arises from polymeric crowding, cohesion, and dynamic binding to transport receptors (karyopherins), producing a selective permeability that allows rapid passage of receptor-bound cargo while restricting passive diffusion of most macromolecules.

Over the past decade, major advances have produced rich, but fragmented, public datasets relevant to NPC emergence. First, structural biology has delivered increasingly complete maps of scaffold architecture and pore geometry across species and states. Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) and subtomogram averaging deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and raw data in EMPIAR provide mesoscale constraints on channel diameter, spoke-ring arrangement, and overall NPC dimensions. Atomic and near-atomic structures of scaffold subcomplexes and nucleoporin domains in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) constrain anchoring sites and the spatial distribution of FG-Nup attachment points. Second, sequence resources such as UniProt provide curated FG-Nup sequences across taxa, while MobiDB and DisProt offer disorder annotations and experimentally supported intrinsically disordered region (IDR) boundaries. These data enable quantitative descriptions of “FG grammar”: motif types (FG, FxFG, GLFG), spacing distributions, charge patterning, and low-complexity composition.

Third, quantitative transport measurements—single-molecule tracking, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), import/export kinetics, and size-selectivity assays—are widely reported in the literature, often with numerical data embedded in supplementary tables or source-data files. These measurements provide functional readouts of emergent barrier behavior: dwell times, flux, selectivity ratios, and effective permeability for different cargo sizes and receptor states. Fourth, proteomics repositories such as PRIDE contain NPC-enriched proteomes, stoichiometry estimates, and post-translational modification (PTM) datasets (notably phosphorylation) that can alter FG-Nup cohesion and charge. Finally, genetics and functional genomics resources provide perturbational context. The Saccharomyces Genome Database (SGD) curates phenotypes for nucleoporin mutants and transport factors in yeast, while DepMap provides CRISPR dependency and coessentiality patterns in human cell lines that implicate nucleoporins and transport factors in proliferation and stress pathways. Human disease variant resources (e.g., ClinVar, gnomAD, OMIM where available, and locus-specific databases) catalog nucleoporin mutations linked to developmental disorders, neurodegeneration, and cancer.

Despite this abundance, fundamental gaps remain because the key phenomenon—selectivity—emerges from mesoscale collective behavior that spans sequence, structure, composition, and dynamics. Existing studies often focus on one axis at a time: polymer theory without direct fitting to diverse kinetic datasets; structural snapshots without quantitative mapping to barrier parameters; or disease variants interpreted as localized defects rather than shifts in collective material properties. Moreover, comparisons across species and cell states remain qualitative, leaving unresolved whether NPCs implement a conserved “design principle” (similar emergent barrier parameters) using divergent FG grammars, or whether distinct grammars correspond to distinct barrier regimes.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address these gaps because it can integrate heterogeneous public datasets into a coherent, testable multiscale framework. By combining (i) geometry and anchoring constraints from EMDB/EMPIAR/PDB, (ii) sequence- and disorder-derived polymer descriptors from UniProt/MobiDB/DisProt, (iii) functional kinetic readouts from published transport datasets, and (iv) compositional/PTM and perturbation context from PRIDE/SGD/DepMap/variant databases, we can infer latent mesoscale parameters—mesh size, cohesion strength, heterogeneity, and effective binding site density—that govern emergent selectivity.

Understanding emergent NPC selectivity at the mesoscale is important beyond nuclear transport. The FG-Nup barrier is a canonical example of a confined, multicomponent IDR-based material whose function derives from dynamic, collective organization rather than stable structure. Principles learned here can generalize to other mesoscale emergent systems (e.g., phase-separated condensates at organelle interfaces, selective barriers in cilia, and crowded polymer brushes at membranes). Additionally, a quantitative synthesis connecting FG grammar and ultrastructure to transport outcomes would reframe how mutations and regulatory PTMs affect function: not merely as “broken interactions,” but as shifts in emergent material-state parameters. Public data are now sufficiently mature and plentiful to enable this synthesis, but only if curated, harmonized, and modeled by a coordinated, multidisciplinary working group—precisely the niche NCEMS is designed to support.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how NPC selectivity emerges from mesoscale organization of FG-Nups under geometric confinement, and how this emergent behavior varies across species, cell states, and perturbations. We focus on questions that are (i) mechanistically precise, (ii) testable using existing public data, and (iii) aimed at inferring latent mesoscale parameters rather than cataloging observations.

RQ1: Is there a many-to-one mapping between FG-Nup “sequence grammar” and emergent barrier state?
Hypothesis H1 (degeneracy of design): Distinct FG grammars (motif types and spacing, charge patterning, IDR length distributions) can yield similar inferred barrier parameters (e.g., effective mesh size and cohesion) when constrained by NPC geometry, implying multiple molecular implementations of a conserved mesoscale material state.
Measurable predictions: (1) Across species (e.g., yeast, vertebrates, plants where data exist), inferred barrier parameters fitted to transport kinetics will cluster more tightly than raw sequence features do. (2) Within a species, paralogous FG-Nups with divergent motif grammar will map to similar contributions to effective cohesion/binding density once compositional stoichiometry is accounted for.
Validation using existing data: We will extract FG grammar features from UniProt sequences with disorder boundaries from MobiDB/DisProt, combine with species-specific geometry from EMDB/EMPIAR, and fit polymer-model parameters to compiled transport kinetics (published FRAP, single-molecule dwell times, permeability vs size). We will quantify “many-to-one” mapping via information-theoretic measures (mutual information between grammar features and inferred parameters) and clustering consistency across datasets.

RQ2: Are there discrete, recurrent “barrier states” corresponding to distinct transport regimes, and are these states modulated by PTMs and composition?
Hypothesis H2 (state space is low-dimensional): NPC selectivity occupies a small number of mesoscale regimes (e.g., more brush-like vs more gel-like; more homogeneous vs heterogeneous), and transitions between regimes can be explained by changes in phosphorylation level and/or FG-Nup stoichiometry rather than wholesale architectural remodeling.
Measurable predictions: (1) When we fit a unified model across many kinetic datasets, posterior distributions of key parameters (cohesion strength, effective mesh size, receptor-binding site density) will be multimodal, indicating discrete regimes. (2) Datasets annotated with high phosphorylation of specific FG-Nups (from PRIDE phosphoproteomics) will preferentially occupy parameter modes consistent with reduced cohesion and increased effective mesh size. (3) Datasets with altered NPC composition (from proteomics or curated literature) will show systematic shifts along the same low-dimensional axes.
Validation using existing data: We will link kinetic datasets to matched or proximate proteomics/PTM datasets when available (same organism/cell line/condition) and otherwise use curated condition annotations. We will test multimodality with Bayesian model comparison (mixture models vs unimodal priors) and evaluate whether PTM/composition covariates predict regime membership using hierarchical Bayesian regression.

RQ3: How does NPC ultrastructure constrain emergent selectivity, and can structural variation explain kinetic differences without invoking new molecular interactions?
Hypothesis H3 (geometry as a control parameter): Variation in pore geometry (channel radius, FG-anchor distribution, central channel volume) measurably shifts emergent barrier parameters and transport outcomes, even if FG grammars are held constant.
Measurable predictions: (1) Across cryo-ET reconstructions, differences in effective channel dimensions will correlate with inferred mesh size and passive permeability cutoffs derived from kinetics. (2) Models that incorporate structure-derived boundary conditions (anchor positions and confinement dimensions) will fit kinetics with fewer free parameters than models lacking structural constraints.
Validation using existing data: We will extract geometric descriptors from EMDB/EMPIAR reconstructions and PDB-based scaffold models. We will compare fits of constrained vs unconstrained models using predictive criteria (WAIC/LOO-CV) on held-out kinetic datasets.

RQ4: Can disease-associated nucleoporin mutations and essentiality patterns be explained as shifts in emergent barrier parameters rather than single-point failures?
Hypothesis H4 (emergent-parameter pathology): Many pathogenic variants in FG-Nups or NPC-associated factors primarily perturb collective parameters (cohesion, charge balance, effective binding density) and thereby shift the NPC into a maladaptive barrier state; similarly, DepMap coessentiality modules will align with inferred barrier-state axes.
Measurable predictions: (1) Variants that alter FG motif density/spacing or charge patterning will be predicted to shift inferred cohesion/mesh parameters in a direction consistent with reported transport defects. (2) Human cell lines with dependencies on specific nucleoporins/transport factors (DepMap) will show transcriptomic or proteomic signatures (from public resources where linkable) consistent with particular barrier regimes (e.g., stress-adapted transport).
Validation using existing data: We will annotate variants from ClinVar/gnomAD/OMIM-linked reports and map them to sequence-derived features; we will integrate curated phenotype readouts from literature and SGD for yeast. For human cell lines, we will use DepMap dependency matrices and coessentiality networks to test alignment between genetic modules and model-inferred parameter axes (e.g., via canonical correlation analysis).

Collectively, these questions target mechanistic understanding of mesoscale emergence: how confined, heterogeneous IDR polymers and receptor-binding interactions produce robust selectivity, how that selectivity is tuned, and how diverse molecular implementations converge on shared mesoscale states. All hypotheses are testable through synthesis, integration, and modeling of existing public datasets without generating new experimental data.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will build an integrated, multiscale inference pipeline that links (1) NPC geometry/anchoring constraints, (2) FG-Nup sequence/disorder-derived polymer descriptors, (3) composition and PTM context, and (4) quantitative transport kinetics. The core methodological goal is to infer latent mesoscale “barrier parameters” that explain diverse functional readouts and to test whether these parameters form discrete regimes and/or conserved targets across divergent FG grammars.

Data sources (public repositories)
1) Structural/ultrastructure constraints
- Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB): cryo-ET and cryo-EM reconstructions of NPCs across species and conditions.
- Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR): raw tomograms/micrographs enabling re-processing where necessary for consistent geometric measurements.
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): atomic structures of NPC scaffold subcomplexes (e.g., Y-complex components) and nucleoporin domains that define FG-Nup attachment sites.

2) Sequences, disorder, and IDR annotations
- UniProt: canonical sequences for nucleoporins across species; isoform information where available.
- MobiDB: consensus disorder predictions and curated IDR regions.
- DisProt: experimentally supported disorder annotations for relevant proteins where available.

3) Proteomics, stoichiometry, and PTMs
- PRIDE Archive: NPC proteome datasets, enrichment studies, and phosphoproteomics identifying modified residues and condition-specific changes.
- (Where available as public resources) ProteomeXchange metadata harmonization to link PRIDE datasets to conditions and cell types.

4) Transport kinetics and functional readouts
- Published source data and supplementary tables from peer-reviewed studies reporting: FRAP recovery curves for nuclear import/export reporters; single-molecule tracking dwell times and trajectories; passive permeability vs cargo size; receptor concentration dependence; and perturbation effects.
- Where datasets are deposited: Zenodo, Dryad, Figshare, and journal-linked source-data repositories.

5) Genetics, perturbations, and disease variants
- Saccharomyces Genome Database (SGD): curated phenotypes for nucleoporin and transport-factor mutants; genetic interactions.
- DepMap (Broad Institute): CRISPR gene effect scores, coessentiality networks, and cell line metadata.
- ClinVar and gnomAD: human variant annotations and population frequencies; OMIM-linked disease associations where publicly accessible.

Data harmonization and knowledge graph
We will create an “NPC Synthesis Knowledge Graph” that unifies identifiers and metadata across sources:
- Entity resolution: map proteins across UniProt accessions, gene symbols, and organism-specific IDs (SGD systematic names; HGNC symbols).
- Condition ontology: normalize cell type, organism strain, perturbation, and treatment using controlled vocabularies (NCBI Taxonomy; Cell Ontology; PSI-MI terms where relevant).
- Structural mapping: link EMDB entries to organism and subcomplex models; map PDB subunits to UniProt sequences; annotate FG-anchor positions using known scaffold contacts from structures and curated literature.
- Kinetics normalization: standardize units (s, µm^2/s, molecules/s), temperature, reporter size, receptor identity, and measurement modality; capture uncertainty (SE/CI) when reported.
All harmonization code will be scripted and versioned; intermediate tables will be stored as machine-readable parquet/CSV with provenance fields.

Modeling framework: from FG grammar to emergent barrier parameters
We will implement a family of mechanistic, coarse-grained models that are complex enough to connect to data but simple enough to be identifiable from heterogeneous measurements.
1) Sequence-to-parameter mapping
- Compute FG grammar features: motif density, motif type fractions (FG/FxFG/GLFG), inter-motif spacing distributions, low-complexity composition, net charge per residue, charge patterning metrics (e.g., kappa), and predicted sticker-spacer architecture.
- Use disorder boundaries from MobiDB/DisProt to restrict feature calculation to FG-rich IDRs.
- Translate features into priors for polymer parameters (e.g., sticker density, effective interaction strength, persistence length proxies).

2) Geometry and boundary conditions
- From EMDB/EMPIAR: extract pore radius/length, channel volume, and (where resolvable) density distributions consistent with FG mass.
- From PDB/scaffold models: infer approximate FG-anchor radial/axial distributions; represent as boundary conditions for polymer brush/gels in confinement.

3) Emergent barrier models
We will use complementary approaches:
- Analytical polymer theory: brush and gel/mesh models in cylindrical confinement to relate sticker density/cohesion to mesh size and permeability.
- Coarse-grained simulations: minimal bead-spring or sticker-spacer polymer models parameterized by grammar-derived priors and constrained by geometry; compute density profiles, mesh statistics, and receptor-mediated transport proxies.
- Transport mapping: connect barrier parameters to observables (passive permeability vs size, receptor-dependent flux, dwell-time distributions) using established kinetic formalisms (e.g., diffusion in a potential of mean force; facilitated diffusion with transient binding).

Inference and statistical integration
We will fit model parameters to kinetic datasets using Bayesian inference:
- Hierarchical models to share information across studies while accounting for modality-specific noise and batch effects.
- Likelihood functions tailored to data type: FRAP curves (time-series), dwell-time distributions (survival models), permeability vs size (nonlinear regression).
- Priors informed by sequence and proteomics (e.g., phosphorylation as covariate shifting cohesion priors).
- Computation: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan) for tractable models; simulation-based inference (e.g., neural posterior estimation) for models requiring expensive simulations.
We will evaluate identifiability and sensitivity with posterior predictive checks and global sensitivity analysis.

Cross-dataset validation and positive controls (no new experiments)
- Hold-out validation: fit parameters on a subset of studies and predict kinetics in held-out datasets matched by organism/condition.
- Internal consistency checks: compare inferred mesh sizes to independent structural constraints (e.g., channel dimensions) and to reported passive size cutoffs.
- Positive controls: well-characterized perturbations from literature (e.g., specific FG-Nup deletions in yeast with known transport phenotypes curated in SGD) should produce directionally consistent parameter shifts.
- Negative controls: random reassignment of sequence features to kinetics across species should destroy predictive performance, supporting meaningful mapping.

AI/ML components (used for synthesis, not discovery-by-black-box)
- Document/data mining: semi-automated extraction of numeric kinetics from supplements and source-data files using reproducible parsers; LLM-assisted triage will be used only to suggest candidate tables/figures, with human verification and scripted extraction.
- Representation learning: embed FG grammar features and PTM profiles to detect clusters; compare to Bayesian-inferred barrier states.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Phase 1 (Months 0–6): Team onboarding; define data standards; build identifier mapping; initial corpus of EMDB/PDB/UniProt FG-Nups; pilot extraction of 10–15 kinetics datasets; release v0.1 knowledge graph schema and curation guide.
Milestone: Public repository with schema, curation scripts, and first harmonized dataset bundle.

Phase 2 (Months 7–14): Expand kinetics corpus (target 50+ datasets across modalities); integrate PRIDE PTM/composition datasets; implement baseline analytical models; initial Bayesian fits for 2–3 organisms.
Milestone: Preprint-level results on cross-species parameter inference; release v1.0 harmonized dataset.

Phase 3 (Months 15–22): Add coarse-grained simulations; implement simulation-based inference; test multimodality (barrier states) and PTM/composition covariates; integrate variant annotations and SGD phenotypes.
Milestone: “Barrier state atlas” draft; open-source inference toolkit beta.

Phase 4 (Months 23–30): Full cross-validation; finalize many-to-one mapping analyses; DepMap module alignment; polishing of tools and documentation; dissemination workshop.
Milestone: Final publications; stable tool release; long-term hosting plan.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab necessity)
- Polymer physicists: develop/validate analytical and simulation models of confined sticker-spacer polymers.
- Structural biologists/EM experts: interpret EMDB/EMPIAR data; extract geometric constraints; map scaffold structures to anchor distributions.
- Quantitative cell biologists/microscopists: interpret transport assay modalities; standardize kinetic observables and uncertainty.
- Computational biologists/data scientists: build knowledge graph, harmonization pipelines, Bayesian inference, and reproducible workflows.
- Trainees (grad students/postdocs): lead curation sprints, implement modules, and co-develop training materials.
This scope exceeds a single lab because it requires deep expertise across EM structure processing, IDR sequence biophysics, transport kinetics interpretation, and scalable inference—plus sustained community-grade curation and open tool development, which NCEMS support is designed to enable.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) NPC Synthesis Knowledge Graph and harmonized datasets
- A versioned, citation-ready knowledge graph linking EMDB/EMPIAR structures, PDB scaffold models, UniProt/MobiDB/DisProt FG-Nup annotations, PRIDE proteomics/PTMs, curated transport kinetics datasets, and perturbation/variant metadata (SGD, DepMap, ClinVar/gnomAD).
- Curated “transport kinetics compendium” with standardized metadata, units, uncertainty fields, and modality descriptors, distributed as open tables and as an API-ready bundle.

2) Open inference toolkit for emergent barrier parameters
- A modular software package that takes (i) FG-Nup sequences and disorder boundaries, (ii) NPC geometry constraints, and (iii) transport kinetic datasets, and returns posterior distributions over emergent barrier parameters (mesh size, cohesion strength, heterogeneity, receptor-binding site density).
- Reference implementations of analytical models (brush/gel/mesh) and coarse-grained simulation wrappers, with consistent interfaces for fitting and prediction.

3) Comparative “Barrier State Atlas”
- A cross-species and cross-condition atlas mapping FG grammar features and PTM/composition context to inferred barrier-state parameters.
- Identification and quantitative definition of candidate discrete barrier regimes (if supported), including uncertainty and conditions associated with each regime.

4) Mechanistic synthesis of structure–sequence–function relationships
- Quantitative links between ultrastructure (geometry and anchor distributions) and transport outcomes, clarifying when geometry alone can explain kinetic differences and when changes in FG grammar/PTMs are required.
- A principled assessment of many-to-one mapping: whether distinct FG grammars converge on conserved emergent parameter targets.

5) Variant and perturbation interpretation framework
- A public annotation resource that maps disease-associated variants and curated genetic perturbations to predicted shifts in emergent barrier parameters, offering a mesoscale “material-state” interpretation layer.

Scientific impact: advancing mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular science
This project directly addresses NCEMS’s emphasis on emergent mesoscale phenomena by treating NPC selectivity as a collective material property arising from confined, heterogeneous IDR polymers coupled to receptor binding. The core advance is not another catalog of NPC components, but a unifying parameterization that explains diverse functional measurements across organisms and contexts. If successful, the work will:
- Provide the first community-scale quantitative synthesis that connects FG-Nup disorder grammar and PTM/composition changes to emergent selectivity parameters constrained by ultrastructure.
- Resolve long-standing conceptual disagreements (e.g., brush vs gel vs mixed regimes) by reframing them as points in an inferred barrier-state space, evaluated against many independent datasets rather than single-study interpretations.
- Establish whether NPCs exhibit design degeneracy: multiple molecular grammars achieving similar mesoscale barrier states, a hallmark of robust emergent systems.

Broader impacts on molecular/cellular biology
- Generalizable principles for IDR-based selective barriers: The modeling and inference methods will transfer to other systems where disordered polymers under confinement create emergent function (e.g., ciliary transition zone barriers, pericentriolar material, and condensate–membrane interfaces).
- Improved interpretability of perturbations and variants: By emphasizing emergent parameters, the project enables a mechanistic vocabulary for how mutations/PTMs shift system-level behavior, complementing residue-level narratives.
- Data reuse and workforce training: The curated compendium and tools lower barriers for experimentalists and theorists to test new hypotheses using existing data.

Enabling future research
The outputs will enable downstream studies without requiring new data generation by this project. Examples include:
- Predicting transport outcomes for unmeasured FG-Nup compositions using inferred parameter mappings.
- Designing targeted re-analyses of existing EMPIAR datasets to test geometric hypotheses.
- Meta-analyses of how stress, differentiation, or disease contexts shift barrier states using already deposited proteomics and functional data.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least two major manuscripts (methods/toolkit; biological synthesis/atlas) plus focused analyses (variants; geometry constraints).
- NCEMS-hosted working group meetings and an open workshop focused on “Mesoscale inference for IDR-based barriers,” including hands-on tutorials.
- Deposition of curated datasets to Zenodo (DOIs) and/or Dryad; code release with archival snapshots.

Long-term sustainability
- Maintain the knowledge graph and toolkit under a permissive license with community governance (issue templates, contribution guidelines, code owners).
- Provide stable, versioned releases and archived containers to ensure reproducibility.
- Coordinate with existing community resources (e.g., UniProt cross-references; PRIDE dataset identifiers) to minimize duplication and maximize interoperability.
By delivering reusable datasets, open tools, and a mechanistic atlas, the project will create durable infrastructure for mesoscale synthesis and strengthen the community’s capacity to study emergence in molecular and cellular systems using publicly available data.

[Budget and Resources]
This working group is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring sustained coordination, curation labor, and computational modeling capacity. The budget prioritizes personnel time for integration and reproducible tool development, plus resources for collaboration, training, and compute. Exact dollar amounts will be tailored to NCEMS guidelines; below we justify cost categories relative to synthesis goals.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (24–30 months each):
  1) “Synthesis modeler” (polymer physics + Bayesian inference) to implement analytical/simulation models, inference pipelines (Stan/simulation-based inference), and cross-validation.
  2) “Data synthesis lead” (computational biology) to build the knowledge graph, harmonization pipelines, and curated kinetics compendium, including provenance and metadata standards.
- 1 Research software engineer / programmer analyst (50–100% FTE): to productionize code, implement workflow orchestration (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, CI testing, and documentation.
- Graduate student support (1–2 trainees across participating labs): to lead focused modules (e.g., PTM integration, variant mapping, DepMap analyses) and develop training materials.
- Faculty/PI effort (modest): coordination, mentoring, and integration across disciplines.
Justification: Synthesis requires extensive curation and engineering beyond typical single-lab projects; dedicated software and data personnel are essential to produce reusable community infrastructure.

Computing resources
- HPC allocations (university clusters and/or national resources where available) for coarse-grained simulations and Bayesian sampling.
- Cloud computing credits for scalable, reproducible runs and to support workshop participants (temporary compute environments).
- Data storage for intermediate harmonized datasets, cached EMDB/EMPIAR-derived geometry descriptors, and container registries.
Justification: Parameter inference across many datasets and simulation-based inference can be compute-intensive; reproducibility requires pinned environments and accessible compute for collaborators.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2 in-person meetings over the project, supplemented by monthly virtual meetings): travel support for geographically distributed participants, with priority for trainees and under-resourced institutions.
- Conference travel for dissemination (e.g., ASCB, Biophysical Society, Gordon Conferences on Nucleocytoplasmic Transport/IDRs), contingent on NCEMS rules.
Justification: Cross-disciplinary synthesis depends on structured, face-to-face integration of domain knowledge (EM, polymer physics, transport kinetics) and on training outcomes.

Workshops and training events
- One NCEMS-hosted open workshop (hybrid) on “Mesoscale inference for NPC selectivity,” including hands-on sessions using the released datasets and containers.
- Two smaller virtual curation sprints with trainee breakout groups.
Budget items include venue/AV (if in-person), accessibility services (captioning), and participant support.
Justification: Training and community uptake are explicit NCEMS goals; workshops convert synthesis products into broadly usable infrastructure.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo archiving (no direct cost) plus budget for optional mirrored hosting (institutional repositories) and a small web presence for documentation.
- DOI-backed releases, long-term container storage (e.g., GitHub Container Registry), and automated documentation hosting.
Justification: Sustained accessibility and reproducibility require maintained documentation, archived releases, and stable hosting.

Why NCEMS support is required
No single lab typically combines (i) EM-derived mesoscale geometry extraction, (ii) IDR grammar quantification, (iii) transport kinetics meta-analysis, and (iv) mechanistic Bayesian inference with simulation-based components—while also producing community-grade curated datasets and training materials. NCEMS resources enable the necessary coordination, cross-lab participation, trainee involvement, and open-science infrastructure to deliver durable synthesis outcomes that extend beyond existing collaborations.
