abstract_original:
Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) are ~100 nm assemblies whose central FG-nucleoporin (FG-Nup) network forms a selective permeability barrier—an emergent property arising from collective polymer behavior rather than any single FG repeat. This project will synthesize structural, sequence, and transport datasets to test how mesoscale organization of FG-Nups encodes selectivity and transport modes across species and cell states.

We will integrate: (i) NPC structural data from cryo-ET and cryo-EM (EMDB/EMPIAR; PDB for scaffold subcomplexes), (ii) FG-Nup sequences, disorder annotations, and repeat grammars (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt), (iii) quantitative transport kinetics measurements (single-molecule transport, FRAP, import/export rates) from published datasets and supplements, (iv) proteomics of NPC composition and post-translational modifications (PRIDE), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting transport (SGD; DepMap; disease variant databases for nucleoporins).

We will build a multiscale model linking FG-Nup polymer physics to observed transport selectivity. Sequence-derived features (FG motif spacing, charge patterning) will parameterize coarse-grained polymer simulations and analytical theories (brush/gels). Structural constraints from NPC ultrastructure will define boundary conditions. We will then fit model predictions to transport kinetics via Bayesian inference, enabling estimation of emergent parameters such as mesh size, cohesive interaction strength, and heterogeneity across the pore.

Key questions: Do different cell types or organisms achieve similar selectivity via distinct FG-Nup sequence grammars (many-to-one mapping)? Are there discrete “barrier states” corresponding to transport regimes (fast/slow, size cutoff shifts) modulated by phosphorylation or composition changes? Can disease-associated mutations be explained as shifts in emergent barrier parameters rather than loss of specific interactions?

Expected insights include a comparative atlas of FG-Nup grammars mapped to inferred barrier states, quantitative links between ultrastructure and transport, and open tools for fitting polymer-based NPC models to data.

This effort requires collaboration among polymer physicists, structural biologists, quantitative microscopists, and computational biologists, and hinges on synthesizing diverse public datasets. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, reproducible modeling workflows, and trainee training at the interface of disordered protein science and mesoscale transport phenomena.

title: Mesoscale Emergence in Bacterial Biofilm Matrix Nanostructure: Integrating Omics, Imaging, and Rheology to Predict Community Robustness

abstract_text:
Biofilms are stabilized by extracellular matrix (ECM) nanostructures (10–500 nm fibers, pores, and crosslinked networks) whose emergent viscoelasticity and diffusional barriers create antibiotic tolerance and spatial metabolic stratification. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polymer and protein assembly yields community-level robustness not predictable from individual ECM components.

We will synthesize: (i) biofilm imaging datasets including confocal, super-resolution, and electron microscopy of ECM architectures (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) metagenomic and transcriptomic profiles of biofilm communities (NCBI SRA; MG-RAST), (iii) proteomics of ECM and secretomes (PRIDE), (iv) publicly available rheology/viscoelastic measurements and diffusion assays (compiled from literature with open data), and (v) antibiotic susceptibility and perturbation datasets (PATRIC; published screens).

We will extract mesoscale structural descriptors from images (fiber thickness distributions, pore size, network connectivity) using segmentation and graph reconstruction. We will integrate these with ECM composition inferred from omics (polysaccharide synthesis genes, amyloid proteins, eDNA abundance proxies) to build predictive models of emergent rheology and diffusional barrier properties. Reaction–diffusion modeling will connect matrix structure to nutrient/antibiotic penetration and to spatial gene expression patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) diverse biofilms converge on a small set of mesoscale ECM architectures that define mechanical and barrier “states”; (2) community composition influences architecture through modular ECM programs; and (3) transitions between ECM states under stress explain abrupt changes in tolerance.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of ECM mesoscale architectures, mechanistic links between matrix nanostructure and emergent tolerance, and open tools for standardized ECM quantification. The work is purely synthesis-based, leveraging existing datasets to unify previously disconnected measurements.

Team science is required across microbiology, materials science, image analysis, and ecological modeling. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous datasets, establish open standards for ECM feature reporting, and train trainees in integrative analysis of microbial communities and mesoscale biomaterials under open science practices.

[Abstract]
Biofilms are stabilized by extracellular matrix (ECM) nanostructures (10–500 nm fibers, pores, and crosslinked networks) whose emergent viscoelasticity and diffusional barriers create antibiotic tolerance and spatial metabolic stratification. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polymer and protein assembly yields community-level robustness not predictable from individual ECM components.

Reaction–diffusion modeling will connect matrix structure to nutrient/antibiotic penetration and to spatial gene expression patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) diverse biofilms converge on a small set of mesoscale ECM architectures that define mechanical and barrier “states”; (2) community composition influences architecture through modular ECM programs; and (3) transitions between ECM states under stress explain abrupt changes in tolerance.

The work is purely synthesis-based, leveraging existing datasets to unify previously disconnected measurements.

Team science is required across microbiology, materials science, image analysis, and ecological modeling. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous datasets, establish open standards for ECM feature reporting, and train trainees in integrative analysis of microbial communities and mesoscale biomaterials under open science practices.

[Background and Significance]
Biofilms are multicellular microbial communities embedded in a self-produced extracellular matrix (ECM) composed of polysaccharides, proteins (including amyloid fibers), extracellular DNA (eDNA), lipids, and assorted small molecules. While the molecular identities of many ECM components are known, the key protective and organizational functions of biofilms—mechanical stability, resistance to shear, retention of enzymes and metabolites, and slowed penetration of antibiotics and nutrients—arise from mesoscale ECM nanostructure. At the 10–500 nm scale, ECM polymers assemble into fibers, bundles, and crosslinked networks that generate pores, channels, and heterogeneous microdomains. These mesoscale features underpin emergent material properties (viscoelasticity, yield stress, poroelasticity) and emergent transport properties (effective diffusion, tortuosity, binding/retardation), which in turn shape higher-level outcomes such as antibiotic tolerance, metabolic stratification, and spatial gene expression.

Current understanding is fragmented across disciplines. Microbiology has identified genetic programs for matrix production (e.g., polysaccharide synthesis loci, adhesins, amyloidogenic proteins, autolysis and eDNA release pathways) and has connected these programs to phenotypes like pellicle formation and colony morphology. Biophysics and soft-matter approaches have measured bulk viscoelasticity of biofilms and extracted effective diffusion coefficients for antibiotics, dyes, and nutrients, often under controlled laboratory conditions. Imaging communities have revealed striking ECM architectures via confocal microscopy, super-resolution methods, and electron microscopy, including fibrous scaffolds, meshworks, and pore networks. However, these bodies of work are rarely integrated: images are often qualitative; rheology is rarely paired with detailed structural quantification; and omics profiles are seldom linked to mesoscale descriptors that could mechanistically explain robustness.

The central scientific challenge is that emergent biofilm robustness is not predictable from the presence/absence of individual ECM components. For example, similar polysaccharide biosynthesis genes can yield distinct mechanical phenotypes depending on co-produced proteins, crosslinking, and spatial organization. Conversely, different taxa can display convergent mechanical behavior despite divergent molecular compositions. This mismatch suggests that mesoscale architecture functions as an intermediate “state variable” that mediates between molecular composition and community-level outcomes. Yet we lack a cross-species, cross-condition synthesis that quantifies ECM nanostructure in a standardized way and connects it to both composition and function.

The opportunity for synthesis is unusually strong because large volumes of relevant data already exist and are publicly accessible, but remain disconnected. Imaging datasets of microbial biofilms and matrices are deposited in the BioImage Archive and the Image Data Resource (IDR), including confocal time series and multi-channel fluorescence images that label polysaccharides, proteins, and eDNA. Electron microscopy datasets, including cryo-EM and tomography of biofilm matrices and extracellular fibers, are available through EMPIAR. In parallel, metagenomic and transcriptomic datasets from biofilms in clinical, environmental, and engineered contexts are available via the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) and MG-RAST, enabling inference of ECM-related gene content and expression. Proteomics datasets in PRIDE contain ECM-enriched fractions, secretomes, and extracellular vesicle proteomes that report on matrix proteins and enzymes. Finally, rheology and diffusion measurements are scattered across the literature, with an increasing fraction accompanied by open supplementary tables or deposited datasets; antibiotic susceptibility and perturbation screens are available through PATRIC and linked publications.

Despite this richness, major gaps persist that only a community-scale synthesis effort can address. First, there is no standardized atlas of mesoscale ECM architectures across taxa and environments, nor a common feature vocabulary (e.g., fiber thickness distributions, pore size spectra, connectivity metrics) that would allow quantitative comparison. Second, the mapping from composition (genes, transcripts, proteins) to architecture is poorly understood: which combinations of ECM modules reliably produce specific network topologies and pore structures? Third, the mapping from architecture to emergent function is incomplete: can we predict viscoelasticity and diffusional barrier properties from image-derived descriptors, and can these predictions explain abrupt shifts in tolerance under stress?

Mesoscale emergence is important because it represents the scale at which collective polymer physics meets cellular physiology. At this scale, small molecular changes can be amplified into large changes in transport and mechanics, producing nonlinear transitions in community robustness (e.g., sudden increases in tolerance when a network percolates or crosslink density passes a threshold). Understanding these transitions is fundamental to explaining why biofilms are resilient and why interventions often fail. It is also broadly relevant beyond microbiology: ECM-like mesoscale networks are a recurring motif in biology, and principled approaches for linking composition–structure–function can generalize to other emergent biomaterials.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze this synthesis. The project requires coordinated expertise in microbial genomics, proteomics, quantitative imaging, soft-matter rheology, and mechanistic modeling, plus sustained effort in data harmonization and open standards. No single lab can curate heterogeneous imaging and omics repositories, extract comparable mesoscale descriptors across modalities, and integrate them with transport and mechanical measurements to build predictive, interpretable models. By leveraging existing public datasets and combining AI-enabled image analysis with statistical and mechanistic modeling, this working group will transform disconnected observations into a cohesive, testable framework for mesoscale emergence in biofilm matrices.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how mesoscale ECM nanostructure emerges from molecular composition and, in turn, governs community robustness. We focus on quantitative, testable questions that can be answered entirely through synthesis of existing public data and reanalysis with standardized pipelines.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): Do diverse bacterial biofilms converge onto a limited set of mesoscale ECM “architecture states”?
Biofilms are often described as idiosyncratic, yet many exhibit similar functional outcomes (e.g., slowed diffusion, high elasticity). We will test whether quantitative structural descriptors extracted from imaging cluster into a small number of recurring mesoscale states (e.g., fiber-dominated meshworks, granular/particulate gels, pore-rich channel networks, dense crosslinked mats).
Hypothesis 1 (H1): Across taxa and environments, ECM nanostructure occupies a low-dimensional manifold with a small number of stable architecture states.
Predictions: (i) Unsupervised clustering of standardized image-derived descriptors (fiber thickness distributions, pore size spectra, network connectivity, fractal dimension, anisotropy) will yield a small set of clusters that are robust to imaging modality and lab-of-origin; (ii) these clusters will correspond to distinct distributions of rheological properties (storage modulus, loss modulus, yield stress) and effective diffusion metrics.
Validation using existing data: We will quantify architecture features from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR datasets, then test cluster stability via bootstrapping and cross-dataset replication (training on one repository subset, testing on another). We will link clusters to rheology/diffusion measurements curated from open literature tables and to antibiotic tolerance phenotypes from PATRIC-linked studies.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): Which compositional “ECM programs” (gene/protein modules) drive specific mesoscale architectures?
We define ECM programs as modular sets of biosynthetic and assembly functions (e.g., polysaccharide synthesis/export, amyloid fiber formation, adhesins, eDNA release and binding, crosslinking enzymes). The key is to move beyond single genes to multi-omic modules that can be inferred across species.
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Mesoscale architecture states are determined by combinations of conserved ECM programs rather than by individual components.
Predictions: (i) Multivariate models using module-level features derived from metagenomes/transcriptomes (SRA, MG-RAST) and proteomes (PRIDE) will predict architecture state membership better than any single marker; (ii) different taxa will achieve the same architecture state via functionally analogous modules (convergent solutions), detectable through pathway-level annotations (e.g., KEGG orthologs, eggNOG groups) and protein family mapping.
Validation using existing data: For datasets where imaging and omics are linked by study accession or sample metadata, we will directly model architecture from omics. Where direct linkage is absent, we will use hierarchical meta-analysis at the study/strain/condition level, integrating reported genotypes and conditions with image-derived features and reported matrix components.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): How does mesoscale architecture control emergent transport and tolerance, and can we predict abrupt transitions under stress?
Biofilm tolerance often shows threshold-like behavior: small perturbations (nutrient shifts, antibiotics, chelators, enzymatic treatments reported in prior studies) can trigger large changes in penetration and survival. We will test whether these shifts correspond to transitions between architecture states and to measurable changes in network topology (e.g., percolation of pores, increased connectivity).
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Abrupt changes in tolerance arise from architecture state transitions that alter effective diffusion and binding/retardation, not merely from changes in expression of resistance genes.
Predictions: (i) Reaction–diffusion models parameterized by image-derived pore size/connectivity will predict penetration profiles and spatial gradients consistent with published diffusion assays; (ii) tolerance phenotypes (MIC shifts, killing curves, survival fractions) will be better explained by architecture-derived transport parameters than by taxonomic composition alone; (iii) stress conditions (antibiotic exposure, oxidative stress, osmotic stress) will be associated with increased probability of switching between architecture states.
Validation using existing data: We will use published diffusion/penetration datasets (e.g., FRAP-based diffusion, fluorescent antibiotic analog penetration, microelectrode gradients) and pair them with imaging-derived structure from the same studies when available. For tolerance, we will integrate PATRIC-linked susceptibility data and published perturbation screens that report matrix-disrupting treatments and outcomes.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Can we construct an interpretable composition–structure–function model that generalizes across species and modalities?
Hypothesis 4 (H4): A hybrid modeling framework combining (i) interpretable machine learning for mapping omics → structure and structure → function with (ii) mechanistic transport models will generalize across datasets and reveal causal constraints.
Predictions: (i) Models trained on a subset of species/conditions will predict architecture and functional properties in held-out species; (ii) feature attribution will identify a small set of module interactions and structural descriptors that act as “control knobs” for robustness.
Validation using existing data: We will perform strict cross-study and cross-species validation, using domain adaptation methods to handle modality differences and using known positive controls (e.g., well-characterized amyloid-forming matrices) to ensure biological plausibility.

Collectively, these questions target mesoscale emergence directly: how nanostructure states arise, how they mediate between molecules and community phenotypes, and how state transitions generate nonlinear robustness. The hypotheses are designed to be falsifiable with measurable predictions, using only existing public data and rigorous cross-dataset validation.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis design
We will conduct a community-scale synthesis that integrates five data types—imaging, omics (meta/genomics and transcriptomics), proteomics, rheology/diffusion, and tolerance/perturbation phenotypes—into a unified composition–structure–function framework. The work is explicitly non-experimental: all analyses will use publicly available datasets and literature-derived open tables. The core methodological product will be an “ECM mesoscale feature store” that links standardized image-derived descriptors to matched or meta-linked omics and phenotype measurements.

1) Specific data sources (public repositories)
Imaging:
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI): biofilm and ECM microscopy datasets.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated multi-dimensional biofilm imaging studies.
- EMPIAR: electron microscopy image datasets, including tomography where available.
- Zenodo/Figshare/Dryad: imaging datasets released with publications (filtered for open licenses).

Metagenomics/transcriptomics:
- NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA): bulk RNA-seq, metatranscriptomics, metagenomes from biofilms.
- MG-RAST: annotated metagenomes/metatranscriptomes with environmental metadata.
- NCBI GenBank/RefSeq: reference genomes for mapping ECM programs across taxa.

Proteomics:
- PRIDE (ProteomeXchange): ECM-enriched proteomes, secretomes, extracellular fractions.

Phenotypes and perturbations:
- PATRIC/BV-BRC: antimicrobial susceptibility metadata and linked isolate/genome context where available.
- Published screens with open supplementary tables (e.g., matrix-degrading enzyme treatments, chelation, dispersal agents) deposited in Dryad/Zenodo/Figshare.

Rheology/diffusion:
- Open data tables from publications (supplements) and generalist repositories (Dryad/Zenodo/Figshare).
- Where only plots are available but underlying data are not open, we will exclude those measurements to comply with public-data-only constraints.

2) Data ingestion, harmonization, and metadata standardization
- Create a registry of studies with persistent identifiers (accessions/DOIs), organism(s), growth context (flow cell, colony, pellicle), matrix labels (e.g., lectins, DNA dyes), imaging modality, and perturbations.
- Map organisms to NCBI Taxonomy IDs; map genes/proteins to KEGG Orthologs, eggNOG orthogroups, Pfam domains.
- Standardize units for rheology (Pa, Pa·s) and diffusion (µm^2/s), and capture assay type (FRAP, penetration depth, tracer size/charge).
- Develop a minimal “ECM feature reporting schema” (JSON/YAML) aligned with existing community standards where possible (OME-NGFF for imaging metadata; MIxS for metagenome metadata), enabling reproducible linking.

3) Image analysis: extracting mesoscale structural descriptors
Goal: convert heterogeneous images into comparable mesoscale descriptors.
- Preprocessing: rescaling to physical units (nm/µm), illumination correction, denoising (non-local means), and channel registration.
- Segmentation:
  - Classical + ML hybrid: adaptive thresholding and filament enhancement (Frangi filters) combined with deep learning segmentation (U-Net/Cellpose-like architectures adapted for ECM fibers) trained using transfer learning on publicly labeled datasets when available. If no labels exist, we will use weak supervision (self-training) strictly within existing images.
- Feature extraction:
  - Fiber statistics: thickness distribution (via skeleton + distance transform), length, curvature, orientation anisotropy.
  - Pore space: pore size distribution (maximal inscribed spheres), porosity, tortuosity proxies.
  - Network topology: graph reconstruction from skeletons; compute degree distribution, betweenness, clustering coefficient, connected component sizes, percolation-related metrics.
  - Texture and multiscale descriptors: power spectral density, wavelet features, fractal dimension.
- Modality alignment: use domain adaptation (e.g., CORAL, adversarial feature alignment) to reduce confocal vs EM feature shifts; include modality as a covariate in downstream models.

4) Omics and proteomics processing: inferring ECM programs
- Metagenomes: quality-filtered reads (existing), taxonomic profiling (Kraken2/Bracken using public databases), functional profiling (HUMAnN or equivalent) to obtain pathway/module abundances.
- Transcriptomes: quantify expression using reference-based or pseudoalignment approaches (e.g., Salmon) when reference genomes exist; otherwise use functional annotation of assembled contigs if provided by MG-RAST.
- Proteomics: reanalyze PRIDE identifications where possible using standardized protein family mapping; extract extracellular/matrix-associated proteins and enzymes.
- ECM program definitions: curate module sets (polysaccharide biosynthesis/export, amyloidogenesis, adhesins, autolysis/eDNA release, DNABII proteins, crosslinking enzymes) as gene/protein family collections; compute module scores per sample/study.

5) Integrative modeling: composition → structure → function
A) Discovering architecture states (RQ1)
- Dimensionality reduction (UMAP/PHATE) on standardized structural features.
- Clustering (Gaussian mixture models, HDBSCAN) with stability analysis.
- Define “architecture states” with interpretable centroids and feature ranges.

B) Mapping omics programs to architecture (RQ2)
- Supervised learning: multinomial logistic regression with elastic net, random forests, and gradient-boosted trees; emphasize interpretability (SHAP) and robustness.
- Multi-view learning: canonical correlation analysis (CCA) and multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) to identify shared latent factors across omics and structure.
- Cross-species generalization: leave-one-taxon-out validation; hierarchical models with taxon as random effect.

C) Structure to rheology/diffusion and tolerance (RQ3)
- Regression models predicting rheological parameters and diffusion metrics from structural descriptors.
- Mechanistic transport modeling:
  - Reaction–diffusion with binding/retardation terms; parameterize effective diffusivity as a function of porosity/tortuosity and tracer size.
  - Where spatial gene expression is available (e.g., transcriptomic gradients reported in studies), compare predicted nutrient/antibiotic gradients to reported stratification markers.
- Tolerance modeling: meta-analytic models linking predicted penetration/transport to survival outcomes; control for antibiotic class, dose, and exposure time.

D) Hybrid, interpretable framework (RQ4)
- Construct a directed acyclic model: ECM programs → architecture state → transport/mechanics → tolerance.
- Use causal discovery cautiously (constraint-based methods) only where metadata supports temporal/perturbation interpretation; otherwise present associations with clear limitations.

6) Validation using only existing data
- Cross-dataset validation: train on one subset of studies and test on independent studies.
- Positive controls: well-studied matrices (e.g., amyloid-rich vs polysaccharide-dominant) expected to differ in fiber metrics and viscoelasticity.
- Negative controls: shuffled metadata links; modality-only predictors to quantify confounding.
- Sensitivity analyses: robustness to segmentation parameters, resolution differences, and missing metadata.

7) Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize data inclusion criteria; build study registry.
- Implement ingestion pipelines; pilot image feature extraction on 10–15 representative studies.
Milestones: registry v1; feature schema v1; pilot feature store.

Months 7–12:
- Scale image processing across repositories; implement omics module scoring pipelines.
- Begin rheology/diffusion/tolerance table curation with provenance.
Milestones: feature store v2 with ≥100 image samples; ECM program library v1.

Months 13–18:
- Architecture state discovery; cross-modality alignment; initial composition→structure models.
Milestones: architecture atlas preprint draft; validated clustering.

Months 19–24:
- Structure→function models; reaction–diffusion modeling; tolerance integration.
Milestones: predictive benchmarks; mechanistic modeling report.

Months 25–30:
- Final integrated framework; tool packaging; community documentation and workshops.
Milestones: public release v1.0 (data + code + containers); manuscripts submitted.

8) Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Microbial biofilm biologists: interpret ECM programs, curate biological metadata, define positive controls.
- Quantitative imaging scientists: OME metadata, segmentation, network reconstruction.
- Soft-matter/materials scientists: rheology interpretation, mapping structure to viscoelastic parameters.
- Computational biologists: omics processing, module definition, cross-species functional mapping.
- Statistical/ML experts: multi-view learning, domain adaptation, uncertainty quantification.
- Mechanistic modelers: reaction–diffusion and poroelastic/transport modeling.
- Research software engineer: pipelines, containers, workflow automation, documentation.

NCEMS support is essential for sustained coordination, shared compute/workflow infrastructure, and convening iterative working sessions to harmonize standards and integrate perspectives—tasks that exceed a single lab’s scope and are central to community-scale synthesis.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables (concrete, public, reusable)
1) Cross-species ECM Mesoscale Atlas
- A curated, indexed atlas of biofilm ECM architectures spanning taxa, environments, and growth contexts, derived from BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR and linked open repositories.
- Each entry will include standardized mesoscale descriptors (fiber/pore/network metrics), modality metadata, and provenance.
- Output format: OME-compatible metadata plus a feature-table “ECM feature store” (parquet/CSV + JSON schema) enabling downstream analysis.

2) Standardized open-source toolkit for ECM quantification
- A reproducible software package (Python) implementing:
  - Image preprocessing and segmentation workflows adaptable to confocal and EM.
  - Graph-based network reconstruction and pore/fiber quantification.
  - Quality-control reports and uncertainty estimates.
- The toolkit will include reference notebooks demonstrating analyses on exemplar public datasets and will be designed to run on HPC/cloud.

3) ECM program library and multi-omic module scores
- Curated definitions of ECM functional modules (gene/protein families and pathways) with mapping to KEGG Orthologs, eggNOG orthogroups, and Pfam.
- Computed module scores for public metagenome/metatranscriptome/proteome samples included in the synthesis, with clear links to accessions and processing parameters.

4) Predictive, interpretable models linking composition–structure–function
- Architecture state model: a low-dimensional representation and clustering that defines recurring mesoscale “states” of ECM organization.
- Composition→structure predictors: models that infer likely architecture states from omics-derived ECM programs, including cross-species generalization benchmarks.
- Structure→function predictors: models that predict rheological parameters and diffusion/penetration metrics from structural descriptors.
- Tolerance linkage: meta-analytic models connecting predicted transport/mechanical properties to antibiotic susceptibility and perturbation outcomes.

5) Mechanistic synthesis: reaction–diffusion framework grounded in measured structure
- A set of mechanistic models parameterized by image-derived porosity/tortuosity/connectivity that reproduce published diffusion/penetration profiles.
- A “state transition” analysis identifying conditions associated with shifts between architecture states and corresponding nonlinear changes in predicted penetration and tolerance.

Scientific impact: advancing mesoscale emergence
The project will provide a principled explanation for how emergent robustness arises at the mesoscale: not as a direct sum of molecular components, but as a consequence of self-organized ECM architectures that act as intermediate state variables. By demonstrating convergence onto a small set of architecture states (if supported) and by quantifying how these states control transport and mechanics, we will move the field from qualitative descriptions (“dense matrix,” “fibrous scaffold”) to quantitative, predictive science.

This synthesis directly addresses fundamental emergence questions central to NCEMS: how new properties appear when molecules assemble into mesoscale structures and how those structures shape higher-level cellular/community outcomes. The work also establishes a generalizable template for linking composition–structure–function in other biological mesoscale networks (e.g., intracellular condensates, cytoskeletal meshes, extracellular matrices in multicellular organisms), thereby broadening NCEMS’s influence.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biosciences
- Antibiotic tolerance and infection control: Even without generating new experiments, improved predictive understanding can help prioritize intervention strategies by identifying structural “control knobs” (e.g., connectivity thresholds, pore percolation) that correlate with tolerance transitions.
- Environmental and industrial microbiology: Predicting robustness of biofilms in bioreactors, wastewater systems, and biofouling contexts.
- Data science for biology: Establishing interoperable standards and reusable pipelines for quantitative ECM analysis from public images.

Enabling future research
Because all outputs are open and standardized, future experimentalists can:
- Design targeted perturbations to shift architecture states.
- Compare new biofilm images to the atlas to infer likely transport/mechanical behavior.
- Use module-to-architecture mappings to interpret omics from complex communities.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least three manuscripts (atlas + architecture states; composition→structure models; structure→function/tolerance synthesis).
- NCEMS-hosted working group workshops: (i) “Quantifying ECM mesoscale features from public images” and (ii) “Integrative modeling of biofilm robustness.”
- Community resources: deposition of the atlas/feature store in long-term repositories (e.g., Zenodo with DOI; links back to BioImage Archive/EMPIAR accessions) and a dedicated documentation site.

Long-term sustainability
- Versioned releases of code and datasets with semantic versioning.
- Containerized workflows to ensure longevity.
- Governance: lightweight community contribution guidelines, issue tracking, and an advisory panel drawn from working group members to maintain the feature schema and accept pull requests after the award period.
- Integration readiness: alignment with OME/OME-NGFF and use of widely adopted bioinformatics identifiers ensures the outputs remain interoperable as repositories evolve.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy
This is a synthesis-only, working-group-driven project. Budget requests prioritize (i) personnel time for curation, software engineering, and integrative analysis; (ii) compute for large-scale image processing and multi-omic reanalysis; and (iii) convening and training to enable true cross-disciplinary integration. No funds are requested for wet-lab experiments, sample collection, or new data generation.

Personnel (primary cost driver)
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (24–30 months each):
  - Postdoc A (quantitative imaging/ML): leads segmentation, feature extraction, domain adaptation, QC.
  - Postdoc B (multi-omics/statistical modeling): leads ECM program definitions, module scoring, integrative modeling, meta-analysis.
- 1 Research software engineer / scientific programmer (30 months):
  - Builds and maintains reproducible pipelines (Snakemake/Nextflow), containers, documentation site, CI, and data releases.
- 2 Graduate students (part-time effort, 24–30 months):
  - Student A: graph/network reconstruction and topology metrics; contributes to atlas.
  - Student B: mechanistic reaction–diffusion modeling and benchmarking against published diffusion assays.
- Faculty/senior personnel (modest percent effort across multiple institutions):
  - Microbiology, materials/rheology, computational modeling, and statistics leads provide oversight, ensure biological/physical interpretability, and coordinate working group outputs.
Justification: The breadth of repositories and modalities requires dedicated staff to curate, process, and maintain reproducible infrastructure; these tasks exceed what distributed faculty effort alone can accomplish.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or NCEMS/HPC allocations for:
  - Bulk image processing (3D stacks, EM volumes) including GPU acceleration for segmentation.
  - Multi-omic reanalysis (read mapping/profiling) and model training/validation.
- Storage for intermediate derived products (feature tables, embeddings, model artifacts) and caching of public-access subsets where repository terms allow.
Justification: Scaling feature extraction across hundreds of large imaging datasets and running repeated cross-validation/domain adaptation requires resources beyond typical single-lab capacity.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2 in-person meetings per year + virtual sprints):
  - Travel support for diverse participants across geography and institution type, including trainees.
  - Funds for an annual NCEMS-hosted synthesis summit session to share interim results and solicit community feedback.
Justification: Emergence-focused synthesis depends on iterative alignment of concepts and standards across disciplines; in-person time accelerates consensus on schemas, controls, and interpretation.

Workshops and training events
- Two open training workshops (hybrid):
  - Venue/AV support, materials, and limited travel scholarships for trainees from underrepresented institutions.
- Mini-grants for trainee-led “analysis sprints” (e.g., short visits or dedicated weeks) to complete well-scoped integration tasks.
Justification: Workforce training is a core NCEMS goal; workshops convert project methods into transferable skills in reproducible data synthesis.

Open science infrastructure
- Costs for persistent hosting and dissemination:
  - DOI-based dataset releases (Zenodo primarily; optional Dryad fees if needed for larger curated packages).
  - Documentation hosting (e.g., ReadTheDocs) and long-term archival of containers and workflow snapshots.
Justification: Sustained usability of synthesis products requires stable, citable releases and well-maintained documentation.

Overall resource need beyond a single lab
The project’s success depends on coordinated multi-institution expertise (imaging, omics, rheology, modeling) and on shared, production-grade computational infrastructure for harmonizing and analyzing heterogeneous public data. NCEMS support enables the convening power, staffing continuity, and open-science scaffolding necessary to produce community-scale, reusable synthesis outputs.

abstract_original:
Biofilms are stabilized by extracellular matrix (ECM) nanostructures (10–500 nm fibers, pores, and crosslinked networks) whose emergent viscoelasticity and diffusional barriers create antibiotic tolerance and spatial metabolic stratification. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polymer and protein assembly yields community-level robustness not predictable from individual ECM components.

We will synthesize: (i) biofilm imaging datasets including confocal, super-resolution, and electron microscopy of ECM architectures (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) metagenomic and transcriptomic profiles of biofilm communities (NCBI SRA; MG-RAST), (iii) proteomics of ECM and secretomes (PRIDE), (iv) publicly available rheology/viscoelastic measurements and diffusion assays (compiled from literature with open data), and (v) antibiotic susceptibility and perturbation datasets (PATRIC; published screens).

We will extract mesoscale structural descriptors from images (fiber thickness distributions, pore size, network connectivity) using segmentation and graph reconstruction. We will integrate these with ECM composition inferred from omics (polysaccharide synthesis genes, amyloid proteins, eDNA abundance proxies) to build predictive models of emergent rheology and diffusional barrier properties. Reaction–diffusion modeling will connect matrix structure to nutrient/antibiotic penetration and to spatial gene expression patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) diverse biofilms converge on a small set of mesoscale ECM architectures that define mechanical and barrier “states”; (2) community composition influences architecture through modular ECM programs; and (3) transitions between ECM states under stress explain abrupt changes in tolerance.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of ECM mesoscale architectures, mechanistic links between matrix nanostructure and emergent tolerance, and open tools for standardized ECM quantification. The work is purely synthesis-based, leveraging existing datasets to unify previously disconnected measurements.

Team science is required across microbiology, materials science, image analysis, and ecological modeling. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous datasets, establish open standards for ECM feature reporting, and train trainees in integrative analysis of microbial communities and mesoscale biomaterials under open science practices.

abstract_text:
Pre-mRNA splicing is executed by spliceosomes and associated nuclear speckle substructures at mesoscale dimensions (20–200 nm RNP assemblies; 100–500 nm speckle subdomains). The emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of splicing factors into dynamic assemblies produces cell-type-specific isoform distributions and noise, beyond what individual RNA-binding proteins predict.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of spliceosome intermediates (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proximity labeling proteomics of speckles and splicing assemblies (PRIDE), (iii) super-resolution imaging of speckle organization and splicing factor puncta (BioImage Archive/IDR), (iv) long-read and single-cell RNA-seq isoform datasets (ENCODE long-read; GEO; Human Cell Atlas where isoform-resolved methods exist), and (v) perturbation screens of splicing factors (DepMap; CRISPR screens; ClinVar variants for splicing genes).

We will build a multiscale model connecting structural intermediate occupancy and speckle mesoscale organization to isoform outcomes. Image-derived features will quantify speckle subdomain size, factor partitioning, and dynamics proxies. Structural states will be represented as a Markov model of assembly intermediates, parameterized by factor availability from proteomics. We will relate these latent variables to isoform variability using hierarchical models and information-theoretic measures of splicing entropy.

Hypotheses: (1) cells regulate splicing by shifting mesoscale partitioning of factors between speckles and nucleoplasm, altering effective assembly kinetics; (2) specific speckle organizational states correspond to low-entropy (deterministic) vs high-entropy (diverse) isoform programs; and (3) disease mutations increase isoform noise by destabilizing particular intermediate transitions.

Expected insights include an atlas linking speckle mesoscale states to isoform variability across cell types, identification of key factors controlling emergent splicing entropy, and open pipelines for integrating imaging with isoform-resolved transcriptomics.

This requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, transcriptomics, and statistical modeling. NCEMS support is essential for harmonizing disparate data modalities and producing reproducible workflows and training materials enabling trainees to operate across RNP structural biology and single-cell genomics.

[Abstract]
Pre-mRNA splicing is executed by spliceosomes and associated nuclear speckle substructures at mesoscale dimensions (20–200 nm RNP assemblies; 100–500 nm speckle subdomains). The emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of splicing factors into dynamic assemblies produces cell-type-specific isoform distributions and noise, beyond what individual RNA-binding proteins predict.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of spliceosome intermediates (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proximity labeling proteomics of speckles and splicing assemblies (PRIDE), (iii) super-resolution imaging of speckle organization and splicing factor puncta (BioImage Archive/IDR), (iv) long-read and single-cell RNA-seq isoform datasets (ENCODE long-read; GEO; Human Cell Atlas where isoform-resolved methods exist), and (v) perturbation screens of splicing factors (DepMap; CRISPR screens; ClinVar variants for splicing genes).

We will build a multiscale model connecting structural intermediate occupancy and speckle mesoscale organization to isoform outcomes. Image-derived features will quantify speckle subdomain size, factor partitioning, and dynamics proxies. Structural states will be represented as a Markov model of assembly intermediates, parameterized by factor availability from proteomics. We will relate these latent variables to isoform variability using hierarchical models and information-theoretic measures of splicing entropy.

Hypotheses: (1) cells regulate splicing by shifting mesoscale partitioning of factors between speckles and nucleoplasm, altering effective assembly kinetics; (2) specific speckle organizational states correspond to low-entropy (deterministic) vs high-entropy (diverse) isoform programs; and (3) disease mutations increase isoform noise by destabilizing particular intermediate transitions.

Expected insights include an atlas linking speckle mesoscale states to isoform variability across cell types, identification of key factors controlling emergent splicing entropy, and open pipelines for integrating imaging with isoform-resolved transcriptomics.

This requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, transcriptomics, and statistical modeling. NCEMS support is essential for harmonizing disparate data modalities and producing reproducible workflows and training materials enabling trainees to operate across RNP structural biology and single-cell genomics.

[Background and Significance]
Pre-mRNA splicing is a foundational information-processing step in eukaryotic gene expression, producing mature mRNAs and shaping proteome diversity. While the chemistry of intron removal is executed by the spliceosome, a large ribonucleoprotein (RNP) machine, the cellular context in which splicing factors are organized is increasingly recognized as central to splicing outcomes. At the mesoscale—between individual macromolecules and organelles—splicing factors assemble into dynamic RNP complexes (tens to hundreds of nanometers) and partition into nuclear speckles and related substructures (roughly 100–500 nm subdomains within speckles; micrometer-scale speckle bodies). The emergent phenomenon motivating this proposal is that collective nano-organization of splicing factors into mesoscale assemblies yields cell-type-specific isoform distributions and stochastic variability (“isoform noise”) that cannot be predicted from the abundance or binding preferences of individual RNA-binding proteins alone.

A rich literature has established that spliceosomes proceed through ordered assembly and catalytic intermediates (e.g., A, B, Bact, C, P, ILS), with cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and integrative structural biology providing near-atomic models for many states. These structures, deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB), reveal extensive remodeling and transient interactions that are sensitive to factor availability and post-translational modifications. In parallel, proximity labeling proteomics (e.g., APEX, BioID/TurboID) has enabled mapping of protein neighborhoods in nuclear speckles and around splicing factors, with datasets deposited in PRIDE and related ProteomeXchange resources. These studies suggest that speckles are not homogeneous storage depots but contain subdomains with distinct compositions and exchange dynamics, implying that local concentrations and interaction networks could modulate spliceosome assembly kinetics.

Imaging advances further support this view. Super-resolution microscopy and quantitative image analysis have shown that speckles are structured, dynamic, and heterogeneous, with splicing factors forming puncta and showing regulated partitioning between speckles and nucleoplasm. Public repositories such as the BioImage Archive and the Image Data Resource (IDR) now host curated microscopy datasets, including many with immunofluorescence markers for speckle components (e.g., SON, SC35/SRSF2) and splicing factors. Together, these data suggest that mesoscale spatial organization is a controllable variable in gene regulation.

Despite these advances, a major gap remains: we lack a coherent, multiscale synthesis that connects (i) structural occupancy of spliceosome intermediates, (ii) mesoscale speckle organization and factor partitioning, and (iii) cell-type-specific isoform outcomes and their variability. Transcriptomic datasets have matured to the point where isoform-resolved quantification is increasingly feasible. ENCODE has released long-read transcriptome datasets, and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) contains numerous long-read (PacBio Iso-Seq, Oxford Nanopore) and single-cell RNA-seq datasets, including emerging single-cell long-read and isoform-aware protocols. The Human Cell Atlas (HCA) provides broad cell-type coverage, and while many HCA datasets are short-read, isoform inference and targeted isoform-resolved datasets exist for subsets of tissues and technologies. These resources enable comparative analysis across cell types and conditions without generating new data.

Another critical gap concerns mechanistic interpretation of isoform variability. Many studies characterize differential splicing using percent-spliced-in (PSI) or isoform abundance, but fewer quantify “splicing entropy” or other information-theoretic measures capturing how deterministically a gene’s isoform choice is executed within and across cells. At the same time, disease genetics underscores the importance of splicing regulation: ClinVar catalogs pathogenic variants in core spliceosomal proteins and regulators, and large-scale CRISPR screens and dependency maps (DepMap) provide functional constraints and context-specific essentiality for splicing factors. Yet, these functional and genetic data are rarely integrated with mesoscale organization or structural intermediate models.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that bridges these levels. The project is inherently beyond a single laboratory: it requires structural biologists to interpret and parameterize intermediate-state models from PDB/EMDB; proteomics experts to normalize proximity labeling data from PRIDE across protocols; quantitative imaging scientists to extract robust speckle and puncta features from BioImage Archive/IDR; and computational biologists/statisticians to integrate transcriptome-wide isoform data from ENCODE, GEO, and HCA into hierarchical, multiscale models. The emergent mesoscale focus aligns directly with NCEMS’s emphasis on properties arising between biomolecules and organelles—here, the nano-organization of RNP assemblies and speckle subdomains and their system-level consequences for isoform programs.

The significance is threefold. First, it addresses a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how spatial organization and dynamic assembly at the mesoscale regulate information flow from DNA to functional mRNAs. Second, it provides a mechanistic framework for interpreting cell-type-specific splicing programs and their stochasticity, a key determinant of phenotypic heterogeneity. Third, it offers translational relevance by explaining how disease-associated perturbations may increase isoform noise or shift isoform distributions by destabilizing specific intermediate transitions or mesoscale organizational states.

Crucially, the public data landscape is now sufficiently rich to enable this synthesis. Cryo-EM structures provide discrete intermediate states; proximity proteomics provides local neighborhood and relative availability constraints; imaging provides mesoscale organization readouts; and isoform-resolved transcriptomics provides functional outputs. The opportunity—and the need—is to integrate these heterogeneous data into a unified, open, reproducible framework that reveals emergent principles of spliceosome nano-organization and speckle-mediated regulation across cell types and perturbation contexts.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how mesoscale organization of splicing factors—specifically, nano-scale RNP assemblies and nuclear speckle subdomains—gives rise to emergent, cell-type-specific isoform distributions and variability. Our central premise is that splicing outcomes are governed not only by sequence and factor identity, but also by collective organization that modulates effective reaction kinetics, interaction networks, and buffering of fluctuations. We define three tightly linked research questions (RQs) with testable hypotheses (Hs), each grounded in measurable quantities from existing public datasets.

RQ1: How does mesoscale partitioning of splicing factors between speckles and nucleoplasm modulate effective spliceosome assembly kinetics and intermediate-state occupancy?
H1 (Partitioning–Kinetics Hypothesis): Cell types regulate splicing by shifting the partition coefficient of key factors (e.g., U2AF, SF3B, PRPFs, helicases) between speckles and nucleoplasm, thereby changing effective concentrations at sites of co-transcriptional splicing and altering the relative occupancy of spliceosome assembly intermediates.
Measurable predictions: (i) Imaging-derived features indicating increased speckle enrichment (e.g., higher speckle-to-nucleoplasm intensity ratios; increased puncta density near speckles) will correlate with proteomics-derived enrichment of the same factors in speckle proximity labeling datasets. (ii) Across cell types, inferred intermediate-state transition rates in a Markov model (parameterized by factor availability) will predict shifts in isoform usage for genes sensitive to kinetic competition (e.g., alternative 3’ splice sites, exon skipping). (iii) Cell types with higher speckle enrichment of late-acting factors will show transcriptome-wide signatures consistent with altered catalytic step efficiency (e.g., changes in intron retention vs exon skipping patterns).
Validation using existing data: Partitioning metrics will be extracted from BioImage Archive/IDR images annotated with speckle markers; factor availability proxies will come from PRIDE proximity labeling datasets; intermediate states will be defined from PDB/EMDB structures; and isoform outcomes will be quantified from ENCODE/GEO/HCA isoform-resolved RNA-seq.

RQ2: Do distinct mesoscale speckle organizational states correspond to low-entropy (deterministic) versus high-entropy (diverse/noisy) isoform programs?
H2 (Speckle-State–Entropy Hypothesis): Speckles occupy a limited set of organizational “states” (defined by subdomain size distributions, compositional gradients, and factor co-partitioning patterns) that act as mesoscale regulators of splicing determinism. Certain states buffer fluctuations and yield low splicing entropy, while others amplify variability and yield high splicing entropy.
Measurable predictions: (i) Unsupervised clustering of imaging-derived speckle features (e.g., subdomain size, circularity, texture, spatial autocorrelation, puncta co-localization) will reveal recurring states across datasets and labs, despite differences in staining or imaging modality. (ii) These speckle states will associate with transcriptome-wide distributions of gene-level splicing entropy (e.g., Shannon entropy over isoform proportions per gene; cell-to-cell entropy where single-cell isoform calls exist). (iii) Speckle states characterized by higher compositional segregation (stronger subdomain partitioning) will correspond to more deterministic isoform selection for a subset of regulated genes, whereas more dispersed states will correspond to broader isoform repertoires.
Validation using existing data: Speckle states will be learned from BioImage Archive/IDR datasets; isoform entropy will be computed from long-read bulk RNA-seq and from single-cell isoform-resolved datasets in GEO and emerging HCA subsets; robustness will be tested across independent datasets and cell types.

RQ3: How do genetic and functional perturbations of splicing factors reshape mesoscale organization and increase isoform noise, and can these effects be mapped to specific structural intermediate transitions?
H3 (Perturbation–Transition Hypothesis): Disease-associated variants and functional dependencies in splicing factors increase isoform noise by selectively destabilizing specific spliceosome intermediate transitions (e.g., B to Bact activation, catalytic step transitions), which in turn manifests as altered speckle partitioning signatures and increased splicing entropy.
Measurable predictions: (i) Factors with high essentiality or context-specific dependency in DepMap will occupy central positions in proximity proteomics interaction neighborhoods and correspond to high-impact nodes in the structural intermediate transition graph. (ii) ClinVar pathogenic variants in core spliceosomal proteins will be enriched at interfaces that are remodeled between specific intermediates (as annotated from PDB/EMDB structures), predicting which transitions are most vulnerable. (iii) Transcriptomic datasets in GEO/ENCODE with perturbations of splicing factors (e.g., knockdowns, CRISPR perturbations) will show increased splicing entropy and characteristic isoform signatures consistent with the predicted vulnerable transitions.
Validation using existing data: Variant mapping will use ClinVar plus structural interface annotation; functional constraints will use DepMap and published CRISPR screen results; perturbation transcriptomes will be mined from GEO/ENCODE; and imaging/proteomics perturbation datasets (where available publicly) will provide mesoscale readouts.

Across all RQs, we will explicitly test emergent behavior: whether mesoscale organizational variables explain isoform outcomes beyond what is predicted by factor expression alone. The key mechanistic insight sought is a quantitative mapping from (a) structural intermediate landscape and (b) mesoscale speckle organization to (c) isoform distributions and variability. Success will be measured by predictive models that generalize across independent datasets and by identification of a small set of mesoscale features and intermediate transitions that act as control knobs for splicing determinism.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
This project is a community-scale synthesis integrating five public data modalities into a single multiscale framework: (1) spliceosome structural intermediates, (2) proximity proteomics of speckles/splicing assemblies, (3) super-resolution and quantitative imaging of speckle organization, (4) isoform-resolved transcriptomics (bulk long-read and single-cell where available), and (5) perturbation/constraint data from functional screens and clinical genetics. No new data will be generated; all analyses will use publicly available datasets and will be designed to be reproducible and extensible.

Specific data sources (repositories)
1) Structural data: Protein Data Bank (PDB) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) entries for human and model-organism spliceosome intermediates (A, pre-B, B, Bact, C, C*, P, ILS) and related complexes (U1, U2 snRNP components). Where needed, UniProt and Pfam will provide domain annotations.
2) Proteomics: PRIDE Archive (via ProteomeXchange) proximity labeling datasets targeting nuclear speckles (e.g., SON, SR proteins) and splicing factors (e.g., SF3B1, PRPFs), plus relevant affinity purification mass spectrometry datasets. Protein identifiers will be harmonized via UniProt.
3) Imaging: BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource (IDR) datasets containing nuclear speckle markers (SON, SRSF2/SC35) and splicing factors, including super-resolution modalities (SIM, STED, PALM/STORM) and high-content imaging where available. Metadata will be parsed from OME-NGFF/OME-TIFF and associated annotations.
4) Transcriptomics: ENCODE long-read RNA-seq (where available), GEO long-read datasets (PacBio Iso-Seq, Oxford Nanopore cDNA/direct RNA), and isoform-aware single-cell datasets in GEO and Human Cell Atlas releases that include long-read or validated isoform calling. For broader coverage, short-read scRNA-seq from HCA may be used for expression covariates and cell-type mapping, while isoform quantification will be restricted to datasets where isoform resolution is supported.
5) Perturbation/constraint: DepMap (CRISPR gene effect, expression, co-dependency), published CRISPR screens deposited in GEO/SRA with splicing-focused perturbations, and ClinVar for pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in splicing genes. Additional variant annotations will use gnomAD (population frequencies) and Ensembl VEP consequences (public resources).

Data harmonization and metadata integration
We will build a harmonized “Spliceosome Mesoscale Synthesis Index” (SMSI) that links datasets through shared identifiers and standardized metadata:
- Genes/proteins: map all proteomics and perturbation entities to HGNC symbols and UniProt accessions; structural chains mapped to UniProt using SIFTS.
- Cell types/lines: standardize to Cell Ontology terms where possible; map cell lines to Cellosaurus.
- Imaging conditions: standardize speckle markers, fixation/live imaging status, modality, resolution, and segmentation parameters.
- Transcriptome conditions: standardize library type, read length, platform, and isoform-calling pipeline versions.
All harmonization steps will be captured in versioned configuration files and provenance logs.

Analytical methods
Aim 1: Structural intermediate state graph and transition features
- Construct a spliceosome intermediate “state graph” from curated PDB/EMDB entries. For each intermediate, compute features: presence/absence of factors, interface areas, predicted interaction networks, and conformational changes (e.g., RMSD of core components where comparable).
- Map ClinVar variants onto structures: annotate whether variants fall in interfaces unique to specific transitions (e.g., factors gained/lost between B and Bact). Use structural bioinformatics tools (interface annotation, solvent accessibility) and curated mapping.
- Build a Markov state model (MSM) at the level of intermediates, where transition propensities are parameterized by factor availability proxies from proteomics and expression covariates from transcriptomics. This is not a molecular dynamics MSM; it is a discrete kinetic model whose parameters are inferred statistically.

Aim 2: Mesoscale speckle organization feature extraction and state discovery
- Image preprocessing: use Bio-Formats/OME tools to standardize formats; apply illumination correction where metadata permits; enforce quality control filters (signal-to-noise, saturation).
- Segmentation: use reproducible, pretrained or classical pipelines (e.g., Cellpose/StarDist for nuclei; marker-based segmentation for speckles using SON/SRSF2 channels). Parameters will be dataset-specific but recorded.
- Feature extraction: compute speckle number, size distributions, subdomain texture (Haralick features), radial intensity profiles, speckle-to-nucleoplasm partition coefficients for each factor channel, puncta density and co-localization metrics, and spatial statistics (Ripley’s K, pair correlation) to quantify clustering at 20–200 nm scales where resolution supports it.
- State discovery: apply unsupervised learning (Gaussian mixture models, hierarchical clustering, and variational autoencoders where appropriate) to define recurring “speckle organizational states.” Batch effects across labs/modalities will be addressed using domain adaptation strategies (e.g., ComBat for features; adversarial alignment for embeddings) with explicit diagnostics.

Aim 3: Isoform quantification and splicing entropy modeling
- Isoform calling (long-read): use established open-source tools (e.g., TALON/FLAIR/StringTie2 long-read modes) depending on dataset type; quantify isoform abundances per gene.
- Single-cell isoform datasets: where full-length single-cell protocols exist, use published pipelines consistent with each dataset; otherwise, restrict to robustly supported isoform events.
- Splicing entropy: compute gene-level entropy over isoform proportions (Shannon entropy), event-level entropy (e.g., for exon skipping), and cell-to-cell variability measures (e.g., entropy across cells, Fano factor of isoform ratios) where single-cell isoform data allow.
- Covariates: incorporate gene expression, sequencing depth, and cell cycle signatures (derived from existing transcriptome data) as confounders.

Aim 4: Multiscale integration and causal-inference-inspired validation
- Latent variable model: build a hierarchical Bayesian model linking (i) speckle state (latent categorical/continuous), (ii) factor partitioning and proximity proteomics enrichment (continuous), and (iii) spliceosome intermediate occupancy parameters (latent kinetic parameters) to (iv) isoform entropy/outcomes.
- Integration strategy: use multi-view learning (e.g., MOFA-style factor models) to learn shared latent dimensions across imaging, proteomics, and transcriptomics, with interpretability constraints tied to structural state features.
- Cross-dataset validation: train models on subsets of cell types/datasets and test on held-out datasets from different repositories/labs. Evaluate predictive accuracy for isoform entropy and specific splicing outcomes.
- Positive controls: use known speckle-associated regulators (e.g., SON, SR proteins) and known splicing-factor perturbation signatures from GEO as benchmarks. Confirm that models recover established relationships (e.g., speckle disruption associated with splicing changes) without relying on new experiments.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6: Working group kickoff; finalize dataset inclusion criteria; build SMSI index; curate PDB/EMDB spliceosome state graph; initial proteomics harmonization.
Months 6–12: Imaging pipelines finalized and benchmarked across IDR/BioImage Archive datasets; initial speckle state clustering; long-read isoform quantification pipelines established; first entropy atlas draft.
Months 12–18: Integrative modeling v1 linking speckle features to isoform entropy; incorporate proximity proteomics; begin structural MSM parameter inference; release open dataset descriptors and pipelines.
Months 18–24: Add perturbation/ClinVar/DepMap constraints; map variants to transitions; cross-dataset generalization tests; refine models and interpretability.
Months 24–30: Final atlas and model release; manuscripts; community workshop; training modules; sustainability plan and handoff to public repositories.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab)
- Structural biology group: curate spliceosome intermediates; interface/variant mapping; define structural features.
- Proteomics group: normalize PRIDE proximity labeling datasets; define enrichment and uncertainty models.
- Quantitative imaging group: build segmentation/feature pipelines; define speckle state representations; batch correction.
- Transcriptomics group: isoform quantification; entropy metrics; cell-type harmonization with HCA.
- Statistics/ML group: hierarchical modeling, multi-view integration, validation design, uncertainty quantification.
- Research software engineer (cross-cutting): workflow automation, containers, documentation, testing.
NCEMS support is required to coordinate these disciplines, host intensive synthesis meetings, and provide shared computational and open-science infrastructure that enables consistent harmonization and reproducible integration across modalities.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) A public “Speckle–Spliceosome–Isoform Atlas” (SSIA): an integrated, queryable resource linking (a) speckle organizational states derived from BioImage Archive/IDR imaging, (b) factor neighborhood and enrichment signatures from PRIDE proximity proteomics, (c) spliceosome intermediate state features from PDB/EMDB, and (d) isoform distributions and splicing entropy metrics from ENCODE/GEO/HCA isoform-resolved datasets. The atlas will include standardized metadata, harmonized identifiers, and uncertainty estimates.

2) Open computational tools and workflows:
- An imaging analysis pipeline for speckle segmentation, feature extraction, and state discovery that is robust across modalities and archived with reproducible environments.
- An isoform/entropy pipeline for long-read and isoform-resolved datasets with standardized outputs.
- A structural intermediate curation and feature extraction toolkit that outputs a state graph suitable for statistical modeling.
- A multiscale integration package implementing the hierarchical models and multi-view latent factor approaches used in the project.

3) Mechanistic models of emergent mesoscale regulation:
- A quantitative mapping from mesoscale speckle states and factor partitioning to predicted spliceosome intermediate transition propensities and to isoform entropy.
- Identification of a small set of “control nodes” (factors and transitions) whose mesoscale organization most strongly predicts deterministic versus noisy isoform programs.

4) Disease and perturbation interpretation framework:
- A catalog of ClinVar splicing-gene variants mapped to structural interfaces and predicted vulnerable intermediate transitions.
- Integration with DepMap dependencies to prioritize factors whose perturbation is expected to increase isoform noise in specific cellular contexts.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project advances understanding of emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences by explicitly connecting nanoscale RNP assemblies and mesoscale speckle subdomains to transcriptome-scale functional outputs. The key conceptual advance is to treat speckles and spliceosome assembly not as separate topics—one “cell biology,” one “structural biology”—but as coupled layers of a multiscale system. Emergent behavior will be demonstrated if mesoscale organizational variables (speckle state, partitioning, neighborhood composition) explain isoform entropy and cell-type-specific isoform programs beyond what can be explained by factor expression alone.

We expect to uncover general principles such as:
- Buffering versus amplification regimes: organizational states that reduce stochastic fluctuations in isoform choice versus those that permit broader isoform exploration.
- Kinetic gating at the mesoscale: how spatial partitioning effectively gates access to particular assembly intermediates, shifting the balance among alternative splicing outcomes.
- Vulnerable transitions: specific intermediate steps disproportionately sensitive to factor availability and disease-associated variants, providing a mechanistic basis for increased isoform noise.

Broader impacts
- Molecular and cellular biology: The atlas and models will provide a new lens for interpreting splicing regulation across cell types, developmental contexts, and disease states, enabling researchers to generate testable mechanistic hypotheses without additional data generation.
- Data science and AI/ML: The project will produce reusable methods for integrating imaging, proteomics, structural states, and transcriptomics—an exemplar of mesoscale synthesis that can be generalized to other nuclear bodies and RNP assemblies.
- Training: Trainees will gain cross-disciplinary skills in reproducible image analysis, proteomics normalization, isoform quantification, and statistical modeling—exactly the “data-savvy workforce” NCEMS aims to cultivate.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least two major manuscripts are anticipated: (i) the atlas and speckle-state framework; (ii) the multiscale mechanistic model linking speckle organization to intermediate transitions and isoform entropy, including disease/perturbation interpretation.
- Community resources: SSIA will be released as a browsable website and downloadable tables, with deposition of derived datasets in appropriate repositories (e.g., Zenodo for derived features and model outputs; links back to original IDR/BioImage Archive/PRIDE/ENCODE/GEO accessions).
- Workshops: an NCEMS-hosted workshop will train participants in running the pipelines and in principles of multimodal synthesis for mesoscale biology.

Long-term sustainability
Sustainability will be achieved by (i) using stable community repositories (Zenodo with DOIs; GitHub/GitLab; container registries), (ii) adopting widely used standards (OME for imaging, UniProt/HGNC for proteins/genes, common transcriptome formats), (iii) modular pipeline design so individual components can be maintained independently, and (iv) recruiting community contributors through clear governance, contribution guidelines, and issue tracking. The SSIA will be designed to accept new public datasets over time via automated ingestion scripts and documented metadata schemas, enabling continued growth beyond the award period.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget overview (2.5–3 years; synthesis-only)
The budget prioritizes personnel and shared computational infrastructure needed to harmonize and integrate heterogeneous public datasets, plus travel and training activities essential for a distributed, multi-lab working group. No funds are requested for experiments, sample collection, or new data generation.

Personnel
1) Lead postdoctoral researcher (1.0 FTE, 30–36 months): responsible for end-to-end integration, coordinating across modalities, and leading manuscript preparation. This role is essential to maintain continuity across structural, imaging, proteomics, and transcriptomics components.
2) Research software engineer / scientific programmer (1.0 FTE, 24–30 months): builds and maintains reproducible pipelines (Snakemake/Nextflow), containers, CI/testing, data ingestion scripts, and the atlas packaging. This is critical for NCEMS-grade reproducibility and for making outputs usable by the community.
3) Graduate students (2 trainees, 0.5 FTE each, 24–36 months): one focused on quantitative imaging feature extraction and speckle-state modeling; one focused on isoform quantification and entropy metrics. Trainees will rotate through cross-disciplinary tasks as part of workforce training.
4) Part-time statistician/ML scientist (0.2–0.3 FTE, 18–24 months): supports hierarchical modeling, uncertainty quantification, and cross-dataset validation design.
5) PI/co-PI effort (modest, e.g., 0.1–0.2 FTE each): oversight, working group leadership, mentoring, and dissemination.
Justification: The integration challenge (multiple repositories, formats, and batch effects) requires dedicated staff beyond typical single-lab capacity; personnel are the primary drivers of synthesis productivity.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or NCEMS/HPC allocations for: (i) downloading and processing large imaging datasets (IDR/BioImage Archive), (ii) running segmentation and feature extraction at scale, (iii) long-read isoform calling on multiple datasets, and (iv) model training (multi-view factor models, Bayesian inference). Budget includes storage for intermediate artifacts and caching to avoid repeated downloads.
- Compute for container builds, CI, and automated testing.
Justification: Imaging and long-read processing are computationally intensive; centralized, reproducible compute environments are necessary for consistent synthesis.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (in-person, 1–2 per year) to accelerate cross-disciplinary integration, resolve metadata/ontology decisions, and conduct code/data sprints.
- Conference travel for dissemination (e.g., ASCB, RNA Society, ISMB) with a focus on presenting open resources and recruiting community users.
Justification: The project’s defining feature is team science across disciplines and institutions; in-person synthesis meetings materially increase integration speed and quality.

Workshops and training events
- NCEMS-hosted training workshop (1 major event) plus 2–3 virtual mini-workshops focused on: reproducible imaging analysis, isoform/entropy computation, and multimodal integration.
- Support for trainee participation (travel scholarships where allowable) to broaden access and recruit diverse talent.
Justification: Training is a core NCEMS goal; workshops ensure outputs are adopted and that trainees gain cross-domain skills.

Open science infrastructure
- Costs for persistent archiving and dissemination: Zenodo releases (free, but budget for curation time), domain/hosting for an atlas landing page, and optional lightweight cloud hosting for interactive browsing.
- Professional data curation support (fractional effort) to ensure metadata quality, documentation, and long-term usability.
Justification: Open deliverables must be maintained, documented, and accessible; curation is essential to community-scale impact.

Overall justification relative to synthesis goals
Every budget item supports the central synthesis mission: integrating existing public structural, proteomic, imaging, transcriptomic, and perturbation datasets into reusable resources and models. The requested resources enable coordination across multiple labs, scalable computation for large public datasets, rigorous reproducibility, and training/dissemination consistent with NCEMS funding requirements.

abstract_original:
Pre-mRNA splicing is executed by spliceosomes and associated nuclear speckle substructures at mesoscale dimensions (20–200 nm RNP assemblies; 100–500 nm speckle subdomains). The emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of splicing factors into dynamic assemblies produces cell-type-specific isoform distributions and noise, beyond what individual RNA-binding proteins predict.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of spliceosome intermediates (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proximity labeling proteomics of speckles and splicing assemblies (PRIDE), (iii) super-resolution imaging of speckle organization and splicing factor puncta (BioImage Archive/IDR), (iv) long-read and single-cell RNA-seq isoform datasets (ENCODE long-read; GEO; Human Cell Atlas where isoform-resolved methods exist), and (v) perturbation screens of splicing factors (DepMap; CRISPR screens; ClinVar variants for splicing genes).

We will build a multiscale model connecting structural intermediate occupancy and speckle mesoscale organization to isoform outcomes. Image-derived features will quantify speckle subdomain size, factor partitioning, and dynamics proxies. Structural states will be represented as a Markov model of assembly intermediates, parameterized by factor availability from proteomics. We will relate these latent variables to isoform variability using hierarchical models and information-theoretic measures of splicing entropy.

Hypotheses: (1) cells regulate splicing by shifting mesoscale partitioning of factors between speckles and nucleoplasm, altering effective assembly kinetics; (2) specific speckle organizational states correspond to low-entropy (deterministic) vs high-entropy (diverse) isoform programs; and (3) disease mutations increase isoform noise by destabilizing particular intermediate transitions.

Expected insights include an atlas linking speckle mesoscale states to isoform variability across cell types, identification of key factors controlling emergent splicing entropy, and open pipelines for integrating imaging with isoform-resolved transcriptomics.

This requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, transcriptomics, and statistical modeling. NCEMS support is essential for harmonizing disparate data modalities and producing reproducible workflows and training materials enabling trainees to operate across RNP structural biology and single-cell genomics.
