abstract_text:
Many metabolic enzymes assemble into mesoscale filaments and bundles (50–1000 nm), such as CTP synthase cytoophidia and IMPDH filaments. The emergent phenomenon is that polymerization changes enzyme kinetics, sequestration, and pathway flux in a nonlinear manner not predictable from monomeric enzyme properties. This project will synthesize imaging, structural, and metabolomic data to uncover universal principles of enzyme filament-based regulation.

We will integrate: (i) fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets showing enzyme filaments across organisms and conditions (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) enzyme structures and filament models (PDB; AlphaFold DB; published helical reconstructions), (iii) metabolomics profiling nucleotide pools and related pathways (Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) transcriptomics and proteomics for enzyme abundance and PTMs (GEO; PRIDE), and (v) perturbation datasets (LINCS for metabolic inhibitors; genetic screens affecting filament formation).

We will quantify filament morphology (length distributions, bundling, subcellular localization) and link these to metabolic state variables (nucleotide ratios, energy stress markers). Using mechanistic modeling, we will compare alternative hypotheses: polymerization as inhibition, activation, or buffering reservoir, and determine which best explains cross-study correlations. We will use phylogenetic comparative methods to test whether filament regulation evolved convergently and whether specific sequence motifs predict polymerization propensity.

Key questions: Are there discrete mesoscale filament “states” corresponding to metabolic regimes (growth, stress, differentiation)? Do filaments act as emergent metabolic capacitors that reduce noise in metabolite levels? Can we predict when filamentation will stabilize vs destabilize pathway flux?

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of enzyme filament states, quantitative links between filament morphology and metabolite homeostasis, and open tools for filament detection and meta-analysis. This synthesis will unify scattered observations into a coherent framework for mesoscale metabolic regulation.

Team science is required across metabolism, structural biology, imaging analysis, and evolutionary genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation of diverse datasets, development of open pipelines, and trainee training in integrative analysis of mesoscale enzyme assemblies and metabolic phenotypes.

[Abstract]
Many metabolic enzymes assemble into mesoscale filaments and bundles (50–1000 nm), such as CTP synthase cytoophidia and IMPDH filaments. The emergent phenomenon is that polymerization changes enzyme kinetics, sequestration, and pathway flux in a nonlinear manner not predictable from monomeric enzyme properties. This project will synthesize imaging, structural, and metabolomic data to uncover universal principles of enzyme filament-based regulation.

We will integrate: (i) fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets showing enzyme filaments across organisms and conditions (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) enzyme structures and filament models (PDB; AlphaFold DB; published helical reconstructions), (iii) metabolomics profiling nucleotide pools and related pathways (Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) transcriptomics and proteomics for enzyme abundance and PTMs (GEO; PRIDE), and (v) perturbation datasets (LINCS for metabolic inhibitors; genetic screens affecting filament formation).

We will quantify filament morphology (length distributions, bundling, subcellular localization) and link these to metabolic state variables (nucleotide ratios, energy stress markers). Using mechanistic modeling, we will compare alternative hypotheses: polymerization as inhibition, activation, or buffering reservoir, and determine which best explains cross-study correlations. We will use phylogenetic comparative methods to test whether filament regulation evolved convergently and whether specific sequence motifs predict polymerization propensity.

Key questions: Are there discrete mesoscale filament “states” corresponding to metabolic regimes (growth, stress, differentiation)? Do filaments act as emergent metabolic capacitors that reduce noise in metabolite levels? Can we predict when filamentation will stabilize vs destabilize pathway flux?

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of enzyme filament states, quantitative links between filament morphology and metabolite homeostasis, and open tools for filament detection and meta-analysis. This synthesis will unify scattered observations into a coherent framework for mesoscale metabolic regulation.

Team science is required across metabolism, structural biology, imaging analysis, and evolutionary genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation of diverse datasets, development of open pipelines, and trainee training in integrative analysis of mesoscale enzyme assemblies and metabolic phenotypes.

[Background and Significance]
Metabolic enzymes are traditionally modeled as freely diffusing molecules whose activity is regulated by allostery, covalent modification, and expression level. Over the last decade, however, a growing body of microscopy and structural work has revealed that many enzymes can reversibly self-assemble into mesoscale polymers, filaments, and bundles on the order of ~50–1000 nm. Prominent examples include CTP synthase (CTPS) cytoophidia observed in bacteria, yeast, plants, Drosophila, and mammalian cells, and inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) filaments in mammalian cells and other taxa. Additional enzymes reported to polymerize include asparagine synthetase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, glutamine synthetase, and others, suggesting filamentation may be a widespread, underappreciated regulatory layer.

The key emergent phenomenon motivating this proposal is that polymerization changes system-level metabolic behavior in ways that cannot be predicted from monomeric enzyme properties alone. Filamentation can alter catalytic activity, substrate channeling, cooperative effects, and spatial sequestration; it can also create switch-like or hysteretic responses to metabolites or stress. At the mesoscale, enzyme polymers can concentrate or exclude metabolites, interact with organelles and cytoskeletal elements, and couple to phase-separated compartments. These behaviors are inherently nonlinear: small changes in metabolite levels or post-translational modifications (PTMs) can trigger large changes in filament abundance or morphology, which in turn feed back on pathway flux and metabolite pools. Understanding such mesoscale emergence is central to NCEMS’ vision because it links molecular-scale interactions (polymer interfaces, allostery) to cellular outcomes (growth, stress tolerance, differentiation) via intermediate-scale organization.

Despite abundant observations, current understanding remains fragmented across organisms, imaging modalities, and experimental contexts. For CTPS, cytoophidia have been associated with nutrient limitation, nucleotide imbalance, developmental programs, and disease states, yet whether filaments represent an inhibited storage form, an activated form, or a buffering reservoir appears context-dependent. For IMPDH, filaments correlate with proliferative signals and nucleotide demand, but reported functional consequences range from altered sensitivity to inhibitors to changes in guanine nucleotide homeostasis. Structural studies (including cryo-EM helical reconstructions deposited in the Protein Data Bank) show multiple filament architectures and interface modes, implying that “filamentation” is not a single state but a family of mesoscale assemblies whose functional roles may differ.

Synthesis research can resolve long-standing puzzles that single-lab studies cannot. First, the field lacks a cross-species, cross-condition atlas that quantifies filament morphology (length, bundling, curvature, localization) using consistent metrics. Published images and deposited microscopy datasets contain rich information, but differences in acquisition settings, cell types, and annotation practices hinder comparison. Second, there is no integrated framework linking filament morphology to metabolic state variables such as nucleotide ratios (ATP/ADP/AMP, GTP/GDP, CTP/UTP), energy stress markers, or pathway flux proxies. Metabolomics profiles exist in repositories such as the Metabolomics Workbench, yet they are rarely analyzed jointly with imaging-derived filament phenotypes. Third, mechanistic interpretations are often inferred from limited perturbations; a synthesis across inhibitor perturbations (e.g., LINCS L1000 signatures), genetic screens, and omics readouts could distinguish whether polymerization is best explained as inhibition, activation, or buffering under different regimes.

Existing public data now make these integrative analyses feasible. The BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource (IDR) host fluorescence microscopy datasets, often with rich metadata; EMPIAR provides raw electron microscopy data enabling reprocessing and standardized morphometrics. Structural information is available via the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, enabling mapping of polymerization interfaces and motif conservation. Transcriptomics and epigenomic context from GEO and ArrayExpress, and proteomics/PTM datasets from PRIDE, provide quantitative measures of enzyme abundance and modification states that may gate filament formation. Perturbation-response data from LINCS and curated genetic interaction resources (e.g., BioGRID, DepMap for human cell viability screens where relevant) provide orthogonal evidence for functional coupling between filamentation and metabolic homeostasis.

A community-scale synthesis is essential because the required expertise spans imaging informatics, cryo-EM/structural biology, metabolic network modeling, evolutionary genomics, and causal inference across heterogeneous datasets. No single lab typically has the capacity to curate dozens to hundreds of imaging studies, reanalyze raw EM datasets, harmonize metabolomics across platforms, and build mechanistic models with phylogenetic comparative controls. NCEMS support is specifically needed to convene a working group that can (i) establish shared standards for filament annotation and morphology quantification, (ii) build reproducible pipelines that connect mesoscale filament states to multi-omics and perturbation signatures, and (iii) train trainees in transdisciplinary synthesis approaches.

By focusing on enzyme filaments as mesoscale regulatory devices, this project targets an emergent layer of cellular organization that sits between molecular interactions and organelle-scale compartmentalization. The payoff is a unifying, predictive framework for when and why filamentation stabilizes versus destabilizes metabolic flux, how distinct filament states correspond to metabolic regimes, and whether convergent evolution has repeatedly discovered filament-based regulation as a robust solution to controlling nucleotide metabolism and related pathways.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address four tightly defined, testable questions about mesoscale emergence in metabolic enzyme filamentation. Each question is paired with hypotheses that yield measurable predictions using only existing public datasets.

RQ1: Do metabolic enzyme filaments occupy discrete mesoscale “states” that correspond to reproducible metabolic regimes across species and cell types?

H1.1 (Discrete-state hypothesis): Filament phenotypes cluster into a small number of reproducible states (e.g., diffuse, short punctate polymers, long filaments, bundled cytoophidia, perinuclear/organellar-associated) that recur across datasets and organisms. Prediction: Unsupervised clustering of standardized morphometrics from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR will reveal stable clusters that are robust to imaging modality and lab-of-origin after harmonization.

H1.2 (Regime mapping hypothesis): These filament states map onto metabolic regimes characterized by nucleotide imbalance or energetic stress. Prediction: Datasets with matched or comparable conditions will show consistent associations between filament states and metabolite ratios (e.g., CTP/UTP for CTPS, GTP/GDP for IMPDH), AMPK activation signatures, or transcriptomic stress programs.

Validation using existing data: We will test cluster stability via cross-dataset replication (train on one subset of studies, predict states in held-out studies) and evaluate associations using metabolomics from Metabolomics Workbench and transcriptomic signatures from GEO/LINCS.

RQ2: What is the dominant functional role of filamentation— inhibition, activation, or buffering— and does this role switch across contexts?

H2.1 (Inhibition/storage hypothesis): Polymerization sequesters enzyme into a low-activity state, reducing effective catalytic capacity. Prediction: Filament-promoting conditions correlate with decreased pathway product pools (e.g., reduced CTP for CTPS) or compensatory upregulation of salvage pathways in transcriptomics/proteomics.

H2.2 (Activation/demand hypothesis): Polymerization increases activity or stabilizes an active conformation under high demand. Prediction: Filament-promoting conditions correlate with increased product pools or increased flux proxy signals (e.g., proliferation signatures, ribosome biogenesis programs) and reduced sensitivity to certain inhibitors.

H2.3 (Buffering/capacitor hypothesis): Filaments act as a reservoir that buffers fluctuations, reducing variance (noise) in metabolite pools across time or across cells/replicates. Prediction: Across comparable conditions, filament-positive states associate with lower coefficient of variation (CV) in nucleotide measurements (metabolomics replicates) and dampened transcriptional stress responses to perturbations.

Validation using existing data: We will fit alternative mechanistic models (see Methods) to integrated morphology–omics datasets and compare them using information criteria and out-of-sample predictive performance. Perturbation datasets (LINCS signatures for metabolic inhibitors; published genetic screens) will be used to test whether filamentation predicts direction and magnitude of metabolic response.

RQ3: Which molecular features predict polymerization propensity and filament architecture across evolution?

H3.1 (Interface motif hypothesis): Specific sequence motifs and structural interface residues predict polymerization propensity and filament architecture (e.g., helical pitch, bundle formation). Prediction: Conservation or convergent emergence of interface residues identified from PDB filament structures will correlate with reported filamentation across taxa; AlphaFold models will show compatible surface features in filament-forming homologs.

H3.2 (PTM gating hypothesis): PTMs modulate transitions between filament states. Prediction: PRIDE phosphoproteomics/acetylomics datasets will show enrichment of PTMs on interface-adjacent regions under filament-forming conditions; PTM abundance will correlate with filament state probabilities inferred from imaging.

Validation using existing data: We will map PTM sites onto structures (PDB/AlphaFold) and test enrichment near interfaces using permutation tests. Phylogenetic comparative methods will assess whether filamentation traits exhibit convergent evolution beyond expectations from shared ancestry.

RQ4: Can we predict when filamentation stabilizes versus destabilizes pathway flux at the mesoscale?

H4.1 (Stabilizing negative feedback): Filamentation introduces negative feedback that stabilizes metabolite pools (homeostasis), especially under fluctuating nutrient supply. Prediction: Conditions associated with filamentation show reduced variability in nucleotide pools and reduced sensitivity of downstream gene expression to perturbations.

H4.2 (Destabilizing positive feedback / bistability): Filamentation can create bistable switches that amplify perturbations, leading to sharp transitions (e.g., stress-induced collapse of nucleotide pools). Prediction: Across studies with graded perturbations (dose series in LINCS or published inhibitor titrations with imaging), filament state transitions will be abrupt and associated with nonlinear changes in omics signatures.

Validation using existing data: We will exploit dose-response and time-series datasets already available in GEO, Metabolomics Workbench, and LINCS to test for hysteresis/bistability signatures (e.g., different state probabilities at the same metabolite proxy under different histories) using model selection and change-point analysis.

Collectively, these questions target mesoscale emergence: how nanometer-scale polymer interfaces yield 50–1000 nm assemblies with system-level consequences. The hypotheses are designed to be adjudicated by synthesis across modalities rather than by new experiments, aligning tightly with NCEMS’ mission and constraints.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
This project will build a cross-species, multimodal synthesis pipeline that links mesoscale filament phenotypes to metabolic state and evolutionary determinants. The core deliverable is an integrated “Filamentome” knowledge graph and analysis suite connecting (i) imaging-derived filament states, (ii) structural determinants and interface annotations, (iii) metabolite pool measurements, (iv) expression/protein/PTM context, and (v) perturbation-response signatures. All analyses will use only publicly available datasets; no new experiments or data generation will be conducted.

1) Data sources (public repositories)
Imaging (filament phenotypes):
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI): fluorescence microscopy datasets with raw and processed images.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated imaging studies with metadata and phenotypic annotations.
- EMPIAR: raw cryo-EM and EM tomography datasets enabling reprocessing and measurement of filament ultrastructure.
- Supplemental image sets linked to publications where images are deposited in public repositories or journal-associated archives; only those with public access will be included.

Structural data (interfaces and architectures):
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): monomeric and filamentous structures; cryo-EM helical reconstructions for CTPS/IMPDH where available.
- AlphaFold Protein Structure Database: predicted structures for homologs lacking experimental structures.
- UniProt: sequence features, isoforms, and curated annotations.

Metabolomics (nucleotide pools and related pathways):
- Metabolomics Workbench: targeted and untargeted metabolomics, including nucleotide measurements where available.
- GNPS/MassIVE (when nucleotide-relevant datasets are public and appropriately annotated).

Transcriptomics and proteomics/PTMs:
- NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress: bulk RNA-seq/microarray time series and perturbation studies.
- PRIDE: proteomics and phosphoproteomics/acetylomics datasets for abundance and PTM mapping.

Perturbation and genetic interaction context:
- LINCS (L1000 and associated perturbation metadata): small molecule and genetic perturbation signatures relevant to nucleotide metabolism.
- BioGRID (and other public interaction resources as needed): genetic and physical interaction evidence linked to filament-forming enzymes.
- DepMap (public CRISPR screens): for human cell contexts to associate essentiality/fitness with expression of filament-forming enzymes and pathway partners.

2) Data ingestion, curation, and harmonization
Metadata normalization: We will create a controlled vocabulary for organism, cell type, perturbation (drug, nutrient, stress), imaging modality, and time/dose. Where metadata are incomplete, we will use publication text-mining (on open abstracts/full text where available) to extract condition labels, with manual verification by the working group.

Identifier harmonization: Proteins will be mapped across UniProt accessions, gene symbols, and orthology groups (OrthoDB/eggNOG mappings where publicly available). Metabolites will be standardized using HMDB/ChEBI identifiers.

Batch and platform correction: For metabolomics, we will apply robust scaling and, when possible, harmonize by using within-study ratios (e.g., CTP/UTP, ATP/ADP) to reduce platform effects. For transcriptomics/proteomics, we will use standard normalization (e.g., DESeq2-style size factors for RNA-seq when counts available; quantile normalization for arrays; median normalization for proteomics) and include study as a random effect in downstream models.

3) Quantifying mesoscale filament morphology from images
Filament detection and morphometrics: We will develop and benchmark open pipelines using:
- Classical image analysis: ridge/line enhancement (Frangi/Sato filters), adaptive thresholding, skeletonization, and connected-component analysis to quantify length distributions, branching, bundling proxies (thickness), and spatial localization.
- Deep learning segmentation: fine-tuning of publicly available models (e.g., U-Net variants) using existing annotated datasets from IDR where available; if annotations are insufficient, we will use weak supervision from classical pipelines and transfer learning across studies. This does not generate new biological data; it produces derived labels from public images.

State inference: For each enzyme/condition, we will compute a feature vector (e.g., filament count per cell, mean/median length, Gini coefficient of length distribution, bundling index, subcellular localization descriptors). We will infer discrete filament states using mixture models (Gaussian mixture models, Dirichlet process mixtures) and validate with silhouette stability and cross-study prediction.

EM-derived ultrastructure: From EMPIAR datasets, we will extract filament diameter, packing, and helical parameters where reconstructions exist, and compute comparable morphometrics to bridge fluorescence and EM scales.

4) Structural synthesis: mapping interfaces to evolution and PTMs
Interface annotation: Using PDB filament structures, we will identify interface residues (e.g., via PISA or contact-based definitions) and map them to UniProt sequences. For homologs without structures, we will use AlphaFold models and structural alignment to project interface regions.

Evolutionary analysis: We will build phylogenies for CTPS and IMPDH families (and selected additional filament-forming enzymes where data permit) and apply phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) and discrete trait models to test for convergent evolution of predicted interface motifs and reported filamentation.

PTM integration: PTM sites from PRIDE will be mapped onto structures and tested for enrichment near interfaces and allosteric sites. We will model PTM presence/abundance as predictors of filament state probabilities.

5) Linking filament states to metabolic state and perturbations
Multi-omic association modeling: We will relate filament state probabilities to metabolite ratios and expression/protein/PTM covariates using hierarchical Bayesian models with study-level random effects and organism/cell-type covariates.

Mechanistic modeling and hypothesis adjudication:
- Enzyme-polymerization models: We will implement mechanistic models in which monomer–polymer equilibria couple to catalytic rates (inhibition, activation, or buffering reservoir). Parameters will be constrained using literature-reported kinetics and fitted to cross-study associations.
- Flux proxies: Where direct flux is unavailable, we will use metabolite ratios, pathway gene expression signatures, and proliferation/stress programs as proxies. Competing models will be compared via WAIC/LOO-CV and predictive checks.
- Nonlinearity and bistability: We will apply change-point detection and generalized additive models to dose/time series to test for abrupt transitions and hysteresis-like patterns.

Validation (no new experiments)
- Cross-dataset validation: Train models on a subset of studies and test predictions on held-out studies from different labs/modalities.
- Positive controls: Use well-characterized filament-forming conditions reported across multiple organisms (e.g., known CTPS cytoophidia-inducing stresses) as benchmarks for detection and state inference.
- Negative controls: Use enzymes/conditions in the same datasets where filamentation is not reported, and randomized label permutations to assess false discovery.

6) Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6: Working group kickoff; finalize controlled vocabulary; ingest initial imaging datasets (IDR/BioImage Archive) and structural sets (PDB/AlphaFold); prototype filament morphometrics pipeline; release v0 schema and repository.
Months 7–12: Scale imaging analysis across studies; build first cross-species atlas for CTPS and IMPDH; ingest metabolomics and transcriptomics/proteomics for matched conditions; release v1 atlas and notebooks.
Months 13–18: Integrate perturbation signatures (LINCS) and genetic interaction context; implement hierarchical association models; begin mechanistic model comparison; mid-project workshop and trainee hackathon.
Months 19–24: Evolutionary/interface motif analyses; PTM-interface enrichment tests; finalize model adjudication (inhibition vs activation vs buffering); release v2 knowledge graph and pipelines.
Months 25–30: Manuscripts and preprints; public training materials; final NCEMS synthesis meeting; sustainability plan and handoff to community repositories.

7) Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Imaging informatics lab: segmentation, morphometrics, cross-modality harmonization.
- Structural biology/cryo-EM lab: interface annotation, helical architecture interpretation, structure-function mapping.
- Metabolism systems biology lab: mechanistic modeling, metabolomics harmonization, pathway interpretation.
- Evolutionary genomics lab: phylogenetic comparative methods, motif evolution, orthology mapping.
- Data engineering/open science specialist: knowledge graph construction, workflow automation, packaging.
- Trainees (grad students/postdocs): cross-cutting analyses with mentored rotations across subprojects.

NCEMS support is essential to coordinate these components into a single synthesis framework, run in-person working sessions, and maintain shared infrastructure for reproducible, open, community-scale integration.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) Cross-species atlas of enzyme filament states (“Filamentome Atlas”): A curated, searchable catalog of mesoscale filament phenotypes for CTPS and IMPDH (and additional enzymes where sufficient data exist), including standardized morphometrics (length distributions, bundling indices, localization descriptors), inferred discrete states, and links to original datasets in BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR. The atlas will include explicit provenance and quality metrics.

2) Integrated multimodal knowledge graph: A public knowledge graph connecting imaging-derived filament states to (i) structural interfaces (PDB/AlphaFold annotations), (ii) sequence motifs and orthology, (iii) metabolite pool measurements and ratios (Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) expression/protein/PTM context (GEO/PRIDE), and (v) perturbation-response signatures (LINCS) and interaction evidence (BioGRID/DepMap where applicable). This will enable complex queries such as “which PTMs near the CTPS interface co-occur with bundled cytoophidia under low CTP/UTP conditions?”

3) Open computational tools: Reusable pipelines for filament detection and morphometrics, cross-study harmonization, and model fitting. Tools will be designed to generalize beyond CTPS/IMPDH to other mesoscale assemblies (e.g., cytoskeletal-like enzyme polymers) and will include benchmarking on public datasets.

4) Mechanistic model comparison results: A set of rigorously evaluated mechanistic models that adjudicate when polymerization is best described as inhibition, activation, or buffering reservoir. Outputs will include parameter posteriors, predictive checks, and clear, testable predictions for future experimental work (without conducting experiments in this project).

5) Evolutionary insights and motif maps: Phylogenetically informed analyses identifying conserved or convergently evolved interface features associated with filamentation, and maps of PTM hotspots near polymer interfaces that correlate with filament state transitions.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergence
This project will advance understanding of emergent properties at the mesoscale by converting scattered qualitative observations (“filaments appear under stress”) into quantitative, generalizable principles. Specifically, it will:
- Define discrete mesoscale filament states and show whether these states are universal across taxa or context-specific.
- Establish quantitative links between mesoscale organization and metabolic homeostasis, clarifying whether filaments act as capacitors that buffer metabolite fluctuations or as switches that enforce metabolic transitions.
- Provide a framework for how molecular-scale interface changes (sequence motifs, PTMs) scale up to mesoscale architectures and then to cellular-scale phenotypes.

Broader impacts for molecular and cellular biology
Enzyme filamentation intersects with cancer metabolism, immune activation, microbial stress tolerance, and developmental programs. By synthesizing public data, the project will produce a resource that (i) helps interpret phenotypes from genetic screens and perturbation studies, (ii) informs drug targeting strategies where polymerization alters inhibitor sensitivity, and (iii) provides new conceptual models for intracellular metabolic regulation beyond classical allostery.

Enabling future research
The atlas and tools will allow researchers to rapidly place new observations into a comparative framework: if a lab observes CTPS filaments in a new organism, they can map morphology to known states and infer likely metabolic regimes and regulatory mechanisms. The mechanistic models will generate prioritized hypotheses (e.g., which PTMs are candidate switches) that others can test experimentally. Importantly, the outputs will also generalize to other mesoscale assemblies (RNA granules, metabolic condensates) by providing reusable methods for state inference and multimodal integration.

Dissemination plan
- Publications and preprints: At least two major synthesis manuscripts are planned: (1) the Filamentome Atlas and state taxonomy; (2) mechanistic and evolutionary principles of filament-based regulation.
- Community workshops: NCEMS-hosted workshops will train participants in image-based morphometrics, knowledge-graph querying, and mechanistic modeling using the project’s datasets.
- Public portal and deposition: Derived datasets and metadata tables will be deposited in appropriate repositories (e.g., Zenodo for versioned releases; links back to BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR, Metabolomics Workbench, GEO, PRIDE).

Long-term sustainability
We will design outputs to be maintainable beyond the award period by:
- Versioning releases with DOIs (Zenodo) and clear schemas.
- Using community standards for metadata and identifiers.
- Providing modular pipelines that can be run on new datasets with minimal configuration.
- Engaging the community through documentation, issues, and contribution guidelines so that the atlas can evolve as additional public datasets become available.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy and fit to NCEMS synthesis requirements
This project is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring coordinated curation, integration, and analysis of large, heterogeneous public datasets. The budget prioritizes personnel for data engineering and cross-disciplinary analysis, computing for large-scale image processing, and travel/workshops to enable intensive working-group collaboration. No funds are requested for wet-lab experiments, sample collection, or new data generation.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (2.0 FTE total):
  - Postdoc A (imaging + ML): leads filament detection, morphometrics, and cross-modality harmonization across BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR.
  - Postdoc B (systems metabolism + modeling): leads metabolomics integration, hierarchical modeling, and mechanistic model comparison.
- 1 Research software engineer / programmer-analyst (1.0 FTE): builds and maintains workflows (Snakemake/Nextflow), knowledge graph infrastructure, containerization, CI, and public releases.
- 2 Graduate research assistants (0.5–1.0 FTE total depending on institutional norms):
  - Focus on evolutionary/interface analyses (phylogenetics, motif mapping) and PTM integration, plus contributions to documentation and tutorials.
- Undergraduate/rotation trainees (hourly, as allowed): support metadata curation and benchmarking under supervision; this also advances workforce training goals.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations for:
  - Large-scale image processing (batch segmentation, feature extraction) across many TB-scale imaging datasets.
  - Model training/fine-tuning for segmentation (GPU time) and Bayesian model fitting (CPU time).
- Data storage for derived products and intermediate caches (not duplicating raw repository holdings): secure object storage with lifecycle policies.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings: support for 2–3 in-person synthesis meetings hosted/organized through NCEMS to enable rapid integration across disciplines (imaging, structural biology, metabolomics, evolution).
- Conference travel: limited, targeted travel for presenting synthesis outputs at meetings spanning cell biology, metabolism, and bioimage analysis, maximizing dissemination and community uptake.

Workshops and training events
- Budget for two hands-on training events (venue/AV if needed, materials, and trainee travel support), aligned with NCEMS’ goal to train a data-savvy workforce.
- Instructor time is covered by personnel lines; events will produce openly licensed training modules.

Open science infrastructure
- Costs associated with maintaining public repositories, documentation hosting, and persistent identifiers:
  - Zenodo DOI releases (no direct cost) but includes staff time for curation.
  - Optional lightweight web portal hosting for atlas browsing and knowledge-graph query endpoints.
- Accessibility and reproducibility investments: CI runners, automated notebook execution, and container registry usage.

Justification relative to synthesis goals
Personnel and compute are essential because synthesis at this scale involves reprocessing and quantifying filaments across many independent imaging datasets, harmonizing metabolomics across platforms, and integrating structures, PTMs, and perturbation signatures into a single analyzable framework. Travel and workshops are essential for NCEMS-style working-group productivity: the integration challenges (ontology alignment, model assumptions, validation standards) require sustained, in-person team science that exceeds what a single lab or a small existing collaboration can accomplish. All budget categories directly support the creation of open, reusable synthesis products and trainee training, consistent with NCEMS funding requirements.

abstract_original:
Many metabolic enzymes assemble into mesoscale filaments and bundles (50–1000 nm), such as CTP synthase cytoophidia and IMPDH filaments. The emergent phenomenon is that polymerization changes enzyme kinetics, sequestration, and pathway flux in a nonlinear manner not predictable from monomeric enzyme properties. This project will synthesize imaging, structural, and metabolomic data to uncover universal principles of enzyme filament-based regulation.

We will integrate: (i) fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets showing enzyme filaments across organisms and conditions (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) enzyme structures and filament models (PDB; AlphaFold DB; published helical reconstructions), (iii) metabolomics profiling nucleotide pools and related pathways (Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) transcriptomics and proteomics for enzyme abundance and PTMs (GEO; PRIDE), and (v) perturbation datasets (LINCS for metabolic inhibitors; genetic screens affecting filament formation).

We will quantify filament morphology (length distributions, bundling, subcellular localization) and link these to metabolic state variables (nucleotide ratios, energy stress markers). Using mechanistic modeling, we will compare alternative hypotheses: polymerization as inhibition, activation, or buffering reservoir, and determine which best explains cross-study correlations. We will use phylogenetic comparative methods to test whether filament regulation evolved convergently and whether specific sequence motifs predict polymerization propensity.

Key questions: Are there discrete mesoscale filament “states” corresponding to metabolic regimes (growth, stress, differentiation)? Do filaments act as emergent metabolic capacitors that reduce noise in metabolite levels? Can we predict when filamentation will stabilize vs destabilize pathway flux?

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of enzyme filament states, quantitative links between filament morphology and metabolite homeostasis, and open tools for filament detection and meta-analysis. This synthesis will unify scattered observations into a coherent framework for mesoscale metabolic regulation.

Team science is required across metabolism, structural biology, imaging analysis, and evolutionary genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation of diverse datasets, development of open pipelines, and trainee training in integrative analysis of mesoscale enzyme assemblies and metabolic phenotypes.

title: Emergent Endocytic Pit Nanoscale Heterogeneity: Integrating Single-Molecule Imaging and Proteomics to Explain Uptake Variability

abstract_text:
Clathrin-mediated endocytosis produces ~100 nm pits whose emergent behavior—variable lifetimes, abortive events, and cargo-dependent maturation—arises from collective assembly of many proteins and membrane mechanics. The emergent phenomenon is nanoscale heterogeneity in pit trajectories that creates cell-to-cell and site-to-site variability in uptake.

We will synthesize: (i) single-molecule and live-cell imaging datasets tracking endocytic proteins and pit lifetimes (IDR/BioImage Archive; published tracking datasets), (ii) proteomics of endocytic complexes and phosphorylation dynamics (PRIDE), (iii) cargo-specific uptake assays and receptor datasets (GEO; literature datasets with quantitative uptake), (iv) membrane lipid composition datasets relevant to endocytosis (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) perturbation screens for endocytosis regulators (DepMap; yeast endocytosis screens).

We will standardize pit trajectory extraction and build a probabilistic “pit state machine” model capturing transitions among assembly, maturation, scission, and abortive states. We will link state transition probabilities to protein abundance/PTMs and lipid composition using hierarchical Bayesian inference. Unsupervised clustering will identify recurrent mesoscale pit “phenotypes” and relate them to cargo classes.

Hypotheses: (1) emergent uptake variability is governed by a small number of mesoscale control parameters (effective adaptor cooperativity, actin coupling strength, membrane tension proxies) that can be inferred from omics and imaging; (2) different cargos shift pits into distinct dynamical regimes; and (3) cells tune variability (noise) as a functional feature for receptor signaling.

Expected insights include a unified dynamical model explaining why pits with similar molecular parts produce divergent outcomes, and an open atlas of pit phenotypes across conditions. Methodological deliverables will include reproducible pipelines for cross-study trajectory harmonization.

This project requires collaboration among quantitative microscopists, trafficking biologists, proteomics experts, and statisticians. NCEMS support is needed for data curation, development of open standards for reporting trajectories and pit features, and training trainees in integrative modeling of mesoscale membrane remodeling.

[Abstract]
Clathrin-mediated endocytosis produces ~100 nm pits whose emergent behavior—variable lifetimes, abortive events, and cargo-dependent maturation—arises from collective assembly of many proteins and membrane mechanics. The emergent phenomenon is nanoscale heterogeneity in pit trajectories that creates cell-to-cell and site-to-site variability in uptake.

We will synthesize: (i) single-molecule and live-cell imaging datasets tracking endocytic proteins and pit lifetimes (IDR/BioImage Archive; published tracking datasets), (ii) proteomics of endocytic complexes and phosphorylation dynamics (PRIDE), (iii) cargo-specific uptake assays and receptor datasets (GEO; literature datasets with quantitative uptake), (iv) membrane lipid composition datasets relevant to endocytosis (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) perturbation screens for endocytosis regulators (DepMap; yeast endocytosis screens).

We will standardize pit trajectory extraction and build a probabilistic “pit state machine” model capturing transitions among assembly, maturation, scission, and abortive states. We will link state transition probabilities to protein abundance/PTMs and lipid composition using hierarchical Bayesian inference. Unsupervised clustering will identify recurrent mesoscale pit “phenotypes” and relate them to cargo classes.

Hypotheses: (1) emergent uptake variability is governed by a small number of mesoscale control parameters (effective adaptor cooperativity, actin coupling strength, membrane tension proxies) that can be inferred from omics and imaging; (2) different cargos shift pits into distinct dynamical regimes; and (3) cells tune variability (noise) as a functional feature for receptor signaling.

Expected insights include a unified dynamical model explaining why pits with similar molecular parts produce divergent outcomes, and an open atlas of pit phenotypes across conditions. Methodological deliverables will include reproducible pipelines for cross-study trajectory harmonization.

This project requires collaboration among quantitative microscopists, trafficking biologists, proteomics experts, and statisticians. NCEMS support is needed for data curation, development of open standards for reporting trajectories and pit features, and training trainees in integrative modeling of mesoscale membrane remodeling.

[Background and Significance]
Clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) is a canonical membrane remodeling pathway that internalizes receptors, nutrients, and signaling molecules through the formation of ~80–150 nm clathrin-coated pits (CCPs) that mature into clathrin-coated vesicles. Although the molecular parts list of CME is extensive—clathrin, AP2, cargo adaptors, BAR-domain proteins, actin regulators, and dynamin among many others—the pathway’s most striking feature is its emergent heterogeneity at the mesoscale: within a single cell, CCPs at similar locations and with similar core components can exhibit widely varying lifetimes, assembly rates, curvature trajectories, and outcomes (productive scission versus abortive disassembly). This nanoscale-to-mesoscale variability is not merely noise; it shapes uptake flux, receptor signaling duration, and spatial patterning of internalization.

At the mesoscale—between individual molecular interactions and organelle-scale trafficking—CME is governed by collective behaviors: cooperative lattice assembly, recruitment waves, curvature generation by ensembles, and feedback between membrane mechanics and protein networks. Existing studies using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRF), lattice light-sheet microscopy, and single-particle tracking have shown that CCP lifetimes are broadly distributed, often multimodal, and sensitive to cargo identity and cellular context. Imaging-based “pit cohorts” reveal that pits can stall, oscillate in intensity, or abort early, while a subset proceeds through a stereotyped maturation sequence. Meanwhile, proteomics has cataloged dynamic endocytic assemblies and post-translational modifications (PTMs), including phosphorylation cycles that modulate adaptor interactions, actin engagement, and scission timing. Lipidomics and membrane composition studies implicate PI(4,5)P2 abundance, cholesterol content, and acyl chain saturation in tuning curvature energetics and adaptor recruitment. Genetic and CRISPR screens identify regulators spanning cytoskeletal organization, lipid metabolism, ubiquitin pathways, and signaling.

Despite this wealth of public data, the field lacks an integrative, quantitative explanation for why ostensibly similar pits diverge into distinct dynamical fates. Most analyses are constrained to single laboratories, specific cell lines, and limited perturbations, making it difficult to disentangle universal mesoscale control parameters from context-specific effects. Moreover, imaging-derived pit trajectories are rarely harmonized across studies: differences in frame rate, labeling strategy, tracking algorithms, and feature definitions impede synthesis. Proteomics and PTM datasets are rich but often disconnected from dynamic phenotypes; lipid composition is measured in different experimental regimes; and uptake assays quantify cargo internalization without mapping to pit-state dynamics.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to close these gaps. First, publicly available imaging repositories now contain large volumes of raw and processed CME movies and particle tracks. The Image Data Resource (IDR) and the BioImage Archive host datasets with endocytic protein markers and time series suitable for re-analysis, while many publications provide supplementary tracking tables. Second, proteomics repositories such as PRIDE contain affinity-purification mass spectrometry (AP-MS), proximity labeling, and phosphoproteomics datasets relevant to CME components and their regulatory modifications. Third, functional readouts of cargo uptake and receptor trafficking are available in transcriptomic and perturbation datasets deposited in GEO and ArrayExpress, and in structured data extracted from literature. Fourth, lipid databases (LIPID MAPS) and metabolomics repositories (Metabolomics Workbench) provide standardized lipid identities and quantitative profiles that can be mapped to membrane mechanical proxies. Fifth, perturbation screens from DepMap (CRISPR dependency/fitness and expression context) and organismal genetic screens (e.g., yeast endocytosis regulators) offer orthogonal constraints on causal regulators.

The central significance of this proposal is to explain a fundamental emergent phenomenon: how mesoscale assemblies convert the same molecular toolkit into multiple dynamical regimes that collectively determine uptake variability. Understanding this phenomenon will clarify how cells balance robustness (reliable internalization) with flexibility (cargo- and context-tuned responses). It will also provide a quantitative bridge between molecular composition (proteins, PTMs, lipids) and mesoscale behavior (state transitions, maturation probability), enabling predictive models of endocytic outcomes under perturbations. Beyond CME, the conceptual framework—inferring low-dimensional control parameters from heterogeneous data and mapping them to mesoscale state machines—will generalize to other membrane remodeling systems such as caveolar dynamics, COPI/COPII budding, and autophagosome initiation.

NCEMS is essential because this work requires community-scale synthesis: cross-repository data curation, consensus standards for trajectory features, and integrated modeling spanning imaging, proteomics, lipidomics, and functional screens—well beyond a single laboratory’s scope. The project will deliver an open, reusable atlas of pit phenotypes and a rigorous probabilistic modeling toolkit, advancing mesoscale emergence science by transforming fragmented public datasets into a unified mechanistic understanding of endocytic heterogeneity.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how mesoscale endocytic assemblies generate heterogeneous outcomes and how that heterogeneity is tuned by cargo, molecular composition, and membrane context. The overarching goal is to move from descriptive distributions of pit lifetimes to a mechanistic, predictive model linking pit state transitions to measurable molecular and biophysical correlates derived from existing public datasets.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): What are the recurrent mesoscale “pit phenotypes” that appear across cell types, cargos, and perturbations, and how many are needed to explain observed variability?

Hypothesis 1 (H1): A small number of conserved dynamical phenotypes (e.g., rapid productive, slow productive, stalled/actin-assisted, early abortive, late abortive) recur across datasets, and most observed lifetime variability can be explained as mixtures of these phenotypes rather than a continuum.

Measurable predictions: (i) Unsupervised models applied to harmonized trajectory features will yield a stable, low-cardinality clustering with high cross-dataset reproducibility; (ii) phenotype mixtures will differ systematically by cargo class and perturbation; (iii) phenotype definitions will transfer between studies when expressed in standardized, dimensionless features (e.g., normalized intensity growth rate, curvature proxy trajectories, dwell-time distributions).

Validation using existing data: We will perform cross-study replication by training clustering models on one subset of IDR/BioImage Archive datasets and testing assignment stability on held-out datasets with different microscopes/labels. Known positive controls include conditions reported to increase abortive events (e.g., adaptor perturbations) or prolong lifetimes (e.g., actin coupling changes) in published datasets.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): Can pit maturation be represented as a probabilistic state machine with transition rates that are predictable from molecular composition and membrane context?

Hypothesis 2 (H2): CCP trajectories can be mapped onto a Markovian (or semi-Markov) state machine with a limited set of states—assembly, curvature/maturation, scission-competent, abortive disassembly—and the transition probabilities are governed by a low-dimensional set of latent “control parameters.”

Measurable predictions: (i) Hidden Markov models (HMMs) or switching state-space models fitted to trajectories will identify consistent state sequences; (ii) inferred transition rates will correlate with proteomic abundance of specific modules (AP2/adaptors, actin regulators, scission factors) and with PTM signatures from PRIDE phosphoproteomics; (iii) lipid composition proxies (PI(4,5)P2-related species, cholesterol/sphingolipid abundance, saturation indices) will explain additional variance in transitions associated with curvature generation and maturation.

Validation using existing data: We will compare inferred state occupancies and transitions to published annotations where available (e.g., dynamin bursts near scission, actin recruitment timing). We will also test predictive performance: models trained on combined omics-imaging covariates should predict state transition distributions in independent datasets better than imaging-only baselines.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): How does cargo identity reshape the dynamical landscape of pits, and are cargo-specific effects mediated by distinct molecular modules?

Hypothesis 3 (H3): Cargo classes (e.g., transferrin receptor-like constitutive cargo, GPCRs, ubiquitinated receptors, signaling receptors) shift pits into distinct dynamical regimes by modulating adaptor cooperativity and checkpoint stringency rather than by altering the existence of states.

Measurable predictions: (i) Cargo-specific uptake datasets (from GEO and curated literature) will associate with shifts in phenotype mixture weights and with specific transition-rate changes (e.g., increased probability of abort after assembly for certain cargos); (ii) cargo-associated expression or phosphorylation of adaptors (e.g., epsin, CALM/AP180, arrestins) will mediate these shifts; (iii) cargo effects will be partially predictable from receptor cytosolic motif content and ubiquitination-related pathways using existing annotations.

Validation using existing data: We will connect cargo uptake phenotypes to pit dynamics in datasets where both are available, and otherwise use hierarchical modeling to integrate cargo class as a covariate. Known cases (e.g., ligand-stimulated GPCR internalization) provide benchmarks for model directionality.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Is uptake variability (noise) itself a tunable functional output, and does it correlate with signaling-related constraints?

Hypothesis 4 (H4): Cells tune the variance-to-mean relationship of pit outcomes (productive fraction, lifetime dispersion) in ways that correlate with signaling pathway activity and receptor fate decisions, implying that heterogeneity is an adaptive mesoscale feature.

Measurable predictions: (i) Across contexts, increased signaling receptor internalization will correlate with increased heterogeneity (broader lifetime distributions and higher abortive fractions) consistent with regulated checkpointing; (ii) perturbations affecting actin coupling or membrane tension proxies will modulate not only mean uptake but also dispersion in a predictable manner; (iii) variability metrics will align with transcriptomic signatures of signaling and cytoskeletal state in public datasets.

Validation using existing data: We will compute standardized variability metrics (e.g., Fano factor of productive events, coefficient of variation of lifetimes) and relate them to expression/phosphorylation modules and to pathway activity scores derived from GEO expression profiles. The emphasis is on inference and prediction from existing data rather than experimental manipulation.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses aim to produce mechanistic insight into mesoscale organization: the emergence of discrete dynamical regimes from many-component assemblies, and the mapping from molecular composition and membrane state to probabilistic fate decisions at the ~100 nm scale.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will conduct a community-scale synthesis that integrates five public data modalities—live-cell imaging trajectories, proteomics/PTMs, cargo uptake functional datasets, lipidomics, and perturbation screens—into a unified probabilistic modeling framework of CCP state transitions. The methodological core is (i) harmonization of heterogeneous imaging-derived trajectories into a common feature schema, (ii) construction of a “pit state machine” via HMM/semi-Markov models, and (iii) hierarchical Bayesian linking of state transition parameters to omics- and lipid-derived covariates, with cross-dataset validation and open, reproducible workflows.

Specific data sources (public repositories)
1) Imaging (raw movies and/or processed tracks):
- Image Data Resource (IDR; https://idr.openmicroscopy.org) for published CME imaging studies with particle tracks or raw time series.
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/bioimage-archive/) for deposited microscopy datasets.
- Supplemental datasets from peer-reviewed publications providing CCP tracks/features (curated with DOIs and licenses).
- Where available, EMPIAR entries containing related correlative or high-resolution imaging of coated structures (used for contextual priors, not new data generation).

2) Proteomics and PTMs:
- PRIDE (Proteomics Identifications Database; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/) for AP-MS/proximity labeling of endocytic complexes and phosphoproteomics under perturbations.
- PhosphoSitePlus (for curated PTM sites and regulatory annotations) and UniProt (for protein features/motifs) as annotation layers.

3) Cargo uptake and receptor datasets:
- NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress for quantitative uptake-related assays, receptor trafficking time courses, and perturbation transcriptomics.
- Curated quantitative uptake measurements from literature (extracted into machine-readable tables with provenance).

4) Lipid composition:
- Metabolomics Workbench (https://www.metabolomicsworkbench.org) for lipidomics studies relevant to membrane composition changes.
- LIPID MAPS (https://www.lipidmaps.org) for standardized lipid identifiers, pathways, and mapping tools.

5) Perturbation screens and context:
- DepMap (Broad Institute; https://depmap.org) for CRISPR gene effect, expression, and co-dependency networks to prioritize conserved regulators and modules.
- Public yeast endocytosis genetic screens (e.g., Saccharomyces Genome Database-linked datasets; curated from publications) to identify conserved functional modules.

Data curation and harmonization
Imaging harmonization will proceed in three layers:
(1) Metadata standardization: cell type, temperature, imaging modality, frame rate, pixel size, labels (e.g., clathrin light chain, AP2), perturbations, cargo condition. We will adopt OME-NGFF/OME metadata conventions and extend with CME-specific fields.
(2) Trajectory reprocessing when needed: when raw movies are available, we will re-run particle detection/tracking using a consistent pipeline (e.g., TrackMate via scripting, u-track equivalents, or deep-learning detectors where appropriate). When only tracks are available, we will map provided columns to a common schema.
(3) Feature schema: per-pit time series features (intensity, growth rate, lifetime, disappearance mode), event-aligned features (putative scission time from dynamin bursts when present), and derived dimensionless features (normalized intensity curves, time-warped profiles). We will include quality control metrics (SNR, track gaps) and propagate uncertainty.

Proteomics/PTM harmonization:
- Map protein IDs to UniProt accessions; normalize abundances within-study (e.g., median normalization) and compute module scores (adaptor module, actin module, scission module) via curated gene sets.
- For phosphoproteomics, compute site-level and protein-level phosphorylation scores; annotate known regulatory sites (PhosphoSitePlus) and kinase motifs.

Lipidomics harmonization:
- Map lipid species to LIPID MAPS identifiers; compute summary indices relevant to mechanics (cholesterol fraction proxies, saturation index, headgroup distributions, PI species abundance proxies).

Cargo/uptake harmonization:
- Standardize uptake measures to comparable effect sizes (e.g., log fold-change relative to control, time-to-half-uptake where available). Annotate cargo classes and receptor motifs/ubiquitination propensity using UniProt features and curated motif databases.

Modeling: pit state machine and integrative inference
1) State discovery and segmentation:
- Fit HMMs and switching linear dynamical systems to per-pit time series (intensity and other markers when available). For datasets with multiple fluorescent channels (e.g., clathrin + AP2 + dynamin), we will use multivariate HMMs.
- Use semi-Markov variants to better capture dwell-time distributions.
- Select state number via Bayesian model comparison (WAIC/LOO-CV) and stability analysis across datasets.

2) Phenotype clustering:
- After state inference, represent each pit by a compact embedding: state occupancy vector, transition counts, dwell-time moments, and aligned intensity trajectory coefficients.
- Apply unsupervised clustering (Gaussian mixture models, Dirichlet process mixtures, spectral clustering) to identify recurrent phenotypes; evaluate with adjusted mutual information across datasets and bootstrap stability.

3) Linking transitions to molecular and membrane covariates:
- Hierarchical Bayesian regression where per-condition transition rates depend on covariates from proteomics/PTMs/lipidomics and context variables (cell type, cargo class).
- Regularization via sparsity priors to identify a small set of predictive control parameters.
- Where direct matching between imaging and omics is imperfect, use multilevel partial pooling and latent variable models to integrate at the level of shared conditions (cell line/perturbation) and to propagate uncertainty.

4) Causal structure and module discovery:
- Use DepMap co-dependency networks and yeast genetic interaction data to define conserved modules; incorporate as priors on regression coefficients.
- Use mediation-style analyses (within observational constraints) to test whether cargo effects on transitions are mediated by adaptor/PTM module scores.

Validation (no new experiments)
- Cross-dataset validation: train models on a subset of imaging datasets and predict phenotype mixtures/transition distributions in held-out datasets.
- Positive controls: replicate known qualitative effects reported in publications (e.g., perturbations that increase abortive pits, dynamin-related changes to scission timing).
- Negative controls: shuffled covariate assignments and label-permutation tests to ensure associations are not driven by batch structure.
- Sensitivity analyses: assess robustness to tracking algorithm choice, frame-rate downsampling, and feature definitions.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6: Working group kickoff; finalize metadata/feature standards; curate initial dataset inventory across IDR/BioImage Archive/PRIDE/GEO/Metabolomics Workbench; build first reproducible pipelines.
Months 7–12: Harmonize and QC imaging trajectories for initial core datasets; implement baseline HMM/semi-Markov state models; release v0 “trajectory schema” and example notebooks.
Months 13–18: Integrate proteomics/PTM and lipidomics covariates; implement hierarchical Bayesian linking; produce first cross-dataset validated state machine; preprint on standards + baseline atlas.
Months 19–24: Cargo-class integration and variability/noise analyses; finalize phenotype atlas v1; release open software package and containerized workflows.
Months 25–30: Synthesis manuscript(s) on mesoscale control parameters and cargo-specific regimes; host training workshop; deposit final curated datasets and models; sustainability plan and community handoff.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Quantitative microscopists/computational image analysts: trajectory reprocessing, feature engineering, state modeling.
- Cell biologists/trafficking experts: biological interpretation, curation of perturbations/cargo classes, module definitions.
- Proteomics experts: PRIDE dataset selection, normalization, PTM interpretation.
- Lipidomics/membrane biophysics experts: lipid feature mapping to mechanical proxies and interpretation.
- Statisticians/ML researchers: hierarchical Bayesian inference, model selection, uncertainty quantification.
- Research software engineer/data curator: pipeline engineering, metadata standards, packaging, documentation.
NCEMS support is required to convene these experts, coordinate data governance and standards, and provide the collaborative synthesis environment and training structure that exceeds any single lab’s capacity.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) An open “Endocytic Pit Phenotype Atlas” (EPPA): a curated, harmonized collection of CCP trajectories and derived features spanning multiple labs, cell types, cargos, and perturbations. The atlas will include standardized metadata, QC flags, and per-pit embeddings (state occupancies, transition statistics), enabling reuse by the community.

2) A probabilistic pit state machine model: a rigorously validated HMM/semi-Markov framework that defines a small set of mesoscale states (assembly, maturation, scission-competent, abortive) and quantifies transition probabilities and dwell-time distributions across conditions. The model will be distributed as executable code plus frozen parameter sets for key datasets.

3) Low-dimensional mesoscale control parameters: a set of inferred latent parameters (e.g., effective adaptor cooperativity, actin coupling strength, membrane composition/tension proxies) that explain a large fraction of variability in pit outcomes. These parameters will be quantitatively linked to proteomic abundance, phosphorylation module scores, and lipidomic indices.

4) Cross-modal integrative analysis tools: reproducible pipelines for (i) trajectory harmonization from raw movies or track tables, (ii) state inference and phenotype clustering, and (iii) hierarchical Bayesian integration with omics and lipidomics. Tools will be released as a versioned Python package with documented APIs and example notebooks.

5) Community standards and reporting templates: a CME trajectory feature schema and minimal metadata standard compatible with OME practices, enabling future studies to deposit tracks in a synthesis-ready form. This will include recommended units, frame-rate normalization practices, and uncertainty reporting.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergence
The central advance will be a mechanistic explanation for how nanoscale assemblies produce heterogeneous mesoscale trajectories and fate decisions. Instead of treating lifetime distributions as descriptive endpoints, we will identify discrete dynamical regimes and quantify how cells move probability mass between them. By linking transition rates to molecular modules and membrane composition, the project will clarify how collective assembly and mechanics jointly create emergent variability.

A key conceptual outcome is the demonstration that uptake variability can be decomposed into (i) state structure (which states exist), (ii) transition kinetics (how quickly and how often pits progress), and (iii) mixture weights (how frequently each phenotype is instantiated). This decomposition provides a general template for studying emergent behavior in other mesoscale systems where many components yield multiple dynamical outcomes.

Broader impacts for molecular and cellular biology
- Predictive framework for interpreting perturbations: Researchers can map genetic or pharmacological perturbations (already represented in public datasets) to specific changes in state transitions, enabling more precise mechanistic hypotheses without new experiments.
- Cargo-specific trafficking logic: By associating cargo classes with dynamical regimes and molecular mediators, the atlas will help interpret receptor-specific signaling and downregulation behaviors.
- Method transferability: The state-machine-plus-hierarchical-inference approach applies to other punctate cellular processes (stress granule nucleation, focal adhesion maturation, mitochondrial fission events), promoting cross-domain synthesis.

Dissemination
- Publications: at least two major outputs are planned—(1) a methods/standards paper describing harmonization and state modeling, and (2) a biology-focused synthesis paper identifying control parameters and cargo-specific regimes.
- NCEMS-hosted workshops: annual working group meetings plus a hands-on training workshop on trajectory synthesis and Bayesian integration.
- Public resources: deposition of curated data products to appropriate repositories (BioImage Archive/IDR for derived track tables where permitted; Zenodo for versioned releases; PRIDE/GEO links and processed tables with provenance).

Long-term sustainability
We will design the atlas and software to be maintainable beyond the award period: modular pipelines, continuous integration tests, semantic versioning, and community contribution guidelines. We will coordinate with repository best practices (OME-NGFF metadata, FAIR principles) and provide a governance model for schema evolution. The end state is a living, citable resource that lowers the barrier for new labs and trainees to perform synthesis analyses of mesoscale membrane remodeling using only public data, aligning tightly with NCEMS goals of catalyzing community-scale, open, data-driven discovery.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget overview (2.5–3 years; illustrative categories aligned to synthesis goals)
This working group budget is designed to support community-scale data synthesis and integrative modeling without any new experimental data generation. Costs prioritize personnel for curation and analysis, compute for large-scale reprocessing of public imaging, and collaboration/training activities essential to NCEMS’s mission.

Personnel
- 1 full-time Research Software Engineer/Data Curator (multi-year): builds and maintains harmonization pipelines; implements schema; manages dataset registry, provenance, and releases; ensures CI/testing and containerization.
- 1 postdoctoral researcher (computational microscopy/statistical modeling): leads trajectory reprocessing, state-space/HMM modeling, and cross-dataset validation; coordinates with imaging contributors.
- 1 postdoctoral researcher (integrative omics/modeling): leads PRIDE phosphoproteomics integration, module scoring, and hierarchical Bayesian linking to imaging-derived parameters.
- 1 graduate student (or equivalent trainee appointment): develops cargo-class annotations, variability metrics, and documentation/training materials; participates in cross-lab code reviews and reproducibility checks.
Personnel effort is justified because synthesis requires sustained, expert-level integration and software engineering beyond typical single-lab capacity.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations for:
  (i) downloading and storing large public imaging datasets,
  (ii) re-running standardized tracking on raw movies,
  (iii) fitting Bayesian hierarchical models (MCMC/variational inference) across many conditions.
- Storage for intermediate derived products and public releases (with mirrored backups).
These resources are essential for harmonizing heterogeneous imaging at scale and for computationally intensive inference.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2 per year): support travel for cross-disciplinary participants (imaging, trafficking biology, proteomics, lipidomics, statistics) from multiple institutions and career stages.
- Conference travel for dissemination (selected members/trainees): present atlas and methods at relevant meetings (cell biology, bioimage analysis, proteomics/data science).
Travel is justified because NCEMS emphasizes catalyzing new collaborations and community-scale synthesis that benefits from in-person coordination and training.

Workshops and training events
- Annual hands-on workshop hosted through NCEMS: training trainees and community members in reproducible trajectory synthesis, Bayesian modeling, and open-science practices.
- Hackathon-style events to expand dataset coverage and refine standards.
Funds cover venue/virtual platform costs, training materials, and limited participant support (especially for trainees and underrepresented institutions).

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo DOI releases (no direct cost) supplemented by budget for:
  (i) professional documentation support (technical writing time embedded in personnel),
  (ii) long-term archival storage solutions as needed,
  (iii) domain registration/website hosting for a lightweight project portal that points to repositories, schema docs, and tutorials.

Justification relative to synthesis goals
Every budget item directly enables synthesis: personnel to curate and integrate public data, compute to reprocess and model at scale, and meetings/workshops to coordinate a multidisciplinary team and train the next generation in data-savvy, reproducible mesoscale emergence science—without generating any new experimental data.

Current research catalogs pathway components but isolated datasets lack quantitative links to the dynamic trajectories of clathrin coated pits. This project asks how state transitions link to molecular variables to establish a novel framework for membrane remodeling systems. The study design is a secondary analysis that integrates five public data modalities into a probabilistic model of transitions. The analytical approach applies hierarchical Bayesian regression alongside unsupervised clustering algorithms and specific variants of discrete Markov models. Results will undergo validation through label permutation tests and sensitivity analyses of algorithms alongside replication of established biological effects. This project utilizes databases including the Image Data Resource and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) alongside the BioImage Archive. The team will integrate these resources by harmonizing trajectories from imaging and applying latent variable models to connect covariates. The study mitigates heterogeneous imaging parameters by reprocessing raw movies with standardized pipelines to extract dimensionless metrics for analysis. The proposed project spans thirty months to harmonize data before integrating variables and releasing a comprehensive atlas of phenotypes. This extensive scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise across cell biology and statistics alongside data standardization. rephrased_abstract: The research domain of clathrin mediated endocytosis features mesoscale heterogeneity in the trajectories, lifetimes, and outcomes of clathrin coated pits, which are broadly distributed and sensitive to cargo and cellular context. This secondary analysis will build a predictive model linking pit state transitions and recurrent dynamical phenotypes to molecular variables by applying Hidden Markov models, hierarchical Bayesian regression, and unsupervised clustering algorithms to public data. Databases including Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive, and PRIDE will be integrated by harmonizing imaging trajectories into a common schema and applying latent variable models to connect transition rates to omics covariates. This predictive model will quantitatively connect molecular composition to mesoscale behavior, explain endocytosis regulation, and provide a data integration framework applicable to other membrane remodeling systems.
abstract_original:
Clathrin-mediated endocytosis produces ~100 nm pits whose emergent behavior—variable lifetimes, abortive events, and cargo-dependent maturation—arises from collective assembly of many proteins and membrane mechanics. The emergent phenomenon is nanoscale heterogeneity in pit trajectories that creates cell-to-cell and site-to-site variability in uptake.

We will synthesize: (i) single-molecule and live-cell imaging datasets tracking endocytic proteins and pit lifetimes (IDR/BioImage Archive; published tracking datasets), (ii) proteomics of endocytic complexes and phosphorylation dynamics (PRIDE), (iii) cargo-specific uptake assays and receptor datasets (GEO; literature datasets with quantitative uptake), (iv) membrane lipid composition datasets relevant to endocytosis (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) perturbation screens for endocytosis regulators (DepMap; yeast endocytosis screens).

We will standardize pit trajectory extraction and build a probabilistic “pit state machine” model capturing transitions among assembly, maturation, scission, and abortive states. We will link state transition probabilities to protein abundance/PTMs and lipid composition using hierarchical Bayesian inference. Unsupervised clustering will identify recurrent mesoscale pit “phenotypes” and relate them to cargo classes.

Hypotheses: (1) emergent uptake variability is governed by a small number of mesoscale control parameters (effective adaptor cooperativity, actin coupling strength, membrane tension proxies) that can be inferred from omics and imaging; (2) different cargos shift pits into distinct dynamical regimes; and (3) cells tune variability (noise) as a functional feature for receptor signaling.

Expected insights include a unified dynamical model explaining why pits with similar molecular parts produce divergent outcomes, and an open atlas of pit phenotypes across conditions. Methodological deliverables will include reproducible pipelines for cross-study trajectory harmonization.

This project requires collaboration among quantitative microscopists, trafficking biologists, proteomics experts, and statisticians. NCEMS support is needed for data curation, development of open standards for reporting trajectories and pit features, and training trainees in integrative modeling of mesoscale membrane remodeling.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of Synaptic Active Zone Nanoclusters: A Synthesis of Proteomics, Super-Resolution Maps, and Functional Plasticity
title_norm: mesoscale emergence of synaptic active zone nanoclusters a synthesis of proteomics superresolution maps and functional plasticity
abstract_text:
Synaptic active zones contain nanoscale protein nanoclusters (20–200 nm) whose collective arrangement controls neurotransmitter release probability and plasticity. The emergent phenomenon is that mesoscale spatial patterning of channels, scaffolds, and vesicle docking sites produces nonlinear release dynamics not predictable from single protein abundances.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution maps of active zone proteins (STED/PALM datasets in BioImage Archive/IDR), (ii) synaptosome and active zone proteomics across brain regions and conditions (PRIDE; SynProt resources), (iii) electrophysiological and imaging-derived functional measures (paired-pulse ratios, release probability proxies) from public repositories and literature open data, (iv) genetic variant and perturbation data for synaptic proteins (SFARI, ClinVar; mouse phenotyping databases), and (v) developmental single-cell transcriptomics of neuronal types (Allen Brain Atlas; scRNA-seq datasets).

We will quantify nanocluster geometry (cluster size, spacing, co-localization networks) and build spatial point-process models linking organization to release probability. Integrative modeling will connect proteomic stoichiometry to predicted nanoscale architectures using constraints from known structural interactions (PDB/AlphaFold). We will test whether synapses occupy discrete “organizational states” corresponding to functional plasticity modes.

Hypotheses: (1) active zones implement a small set of mesoscale architectures that tune reliability vs flexibility; (2) plasticity involves transitions between these architectures mediated by scaffold phosphorylation and remodeling; and (3) neurodevelopmental disorder variants shift synapses into maladaptive organizational states.

Expected insights include a cross-region atlas of active zone nanoscale architectures, mechanistic links between organization and emergent release dynamics, and open analysis tools for nanocluster quantification and integration with proteomics.

This requires team science across neuroscience, proteomics, quantitative imaging, and spatial statistics, with extensive synthesis across disparate datasets. NCEMS support will enable harmonization, open workflows, and trainee training bridging nanoscale organization and systems-level synaptic function.
