[Abstract]
Synaptic active zones contain nanoscale protein nanoclusters (20–200 nm) whose collective arrangement controls neurotransmitter release probability and plasticity. The emergent phenomenon is that mesoscale spatial patterning of channels, scaffolds, and vesicle docking sites produces nonlinear release dynamics not predictable from single protein abundances.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution maps of active zone proteins (STED/PALM datasets in BioImage Archive/IDR), (ii) synaptosome and active zone proteomics across brain regions and conditions (PRIDE; SynProt resources), (iii) electrophysiological and imaging-derived functional measures (paired-pulse ratios, release probability proxies) from public repositories and literature open data, (iv) genetic variant and perturbation data for synaptic proteins (SFARI, ClinVar; mouse phenotyping databases), and (v) developmental single-cell transcriptomics of neuronal types (Allen Brain Atlas; scRNA-seq datasets).

We will quantify nanocluster geometry (cluster size, spacing, co-localization networks) and build spatial point-process models linking organization to release probability. Integrative modeling will connect proteomic stoichiometry to predicted nanoscale architectures using constraints from known structural interactions (PDB/AlphaFold). We will test whether synapses occupy discrete “organizational states” corresponding to functional plasticity modes.

Hypotheses: (1) active zones implement a small set of mesoscale architectures that tune reliability vs flexibility; (2) plasticity involves transitions between these architectures mediated by scaffold phosphorylation and remodeling; and (3) neurodevelopmental disorder variants shift synapses into maladaptive organizational states.

Expected insights include a cross-region atlas of active zone nanoscale architectures, mechanistic links between organization and emergent release dynamics, and open analysis tools for nanocluster quantification and integration with proteomics.

This requires team science across neuroscience, proteomics, quantitative imaging, and spatial statistics, with extensive synthesis across disparate datasets. NCEMS support will enable harmonization, open workflows, and trainee training bridging nanoscale organization and systems-level synaptic function.

[Background and Significance]
Chemical synapses transform electrical activity into quantal neurotransmitter release through a specialized presynaptic mesoscale structure: the active zone (AZ). The AZ is neither a single macromolecular complex nor an organelle; it is a mesoscale assembly (tens to hundreds of nanometers) composed of scaffold proteins (e.g., RIM/UNC13/ELKS/Bassoon/Piccolo), voltage-gated calcium channels, vesicle-tethering and priming machinery, and cytomatrix components that position release-ready vesicles near calcium sources. A central and increasingly data-supported idea is that AZ proteins are not uniformly distributed; instead, they form nanoclusters and subdomains whose geometry (cluster size, density, relative spacing, and co-alignment) constrains calcium microdomains, vesicle docking probability, and short-term plasticity. The emergent phenomenon is that collective spatial patterning at the AZ mesoscale produces nonlinear release dynamics—such as steep dependence of release probability on calcium channel–vesicle distance, and state-dependent facilitation/depression—that cannot be predicted from bulk protein abundance or single-molecule properties alone.

Over the past decade, super-resolution microscopy (STED, PALM/STORM, DNA-PAINT) has provided compelling snapshots of AZ nanoscale organization. Studies have reported modular AZ architectures (“nanomodules” or “release sites”) and protein-specific clustering behaviors, including sub-100 nm clusters of RIM, Munc13, and calcium channels, and heterogeneous alignment with postsynaptic nanodomains. These imaging results, however, are distributed across laboratories, species, brain regions, developmental stages, and sample preparations, with inconsistent segmentation and quantification pipelines. Meanwhile, proteomics of synaptosomes and isolated presynaptic fractions has matured, with large-scale mass spectrometry datasets deposited in PRIDE and curated resources such as SynProt. These datasets quantify stoichiometric shifts across brain regions, development, activity manipulations, and disease contexts. Yet proteomics alone lacks spatial information; it cannot distinguish whether a twofold change in an AZ scaffold is realized as increased cluster number, altered cluster size, or redistributed co-localization.

Functional measures of presynaptic output—release probability (Pr), paired-pulse ratio (PPR), short-term facilitation/depression, and optical proxies (e.g., synapto-pHluorin, iGluSnFR-based presynaptic release readouts)—are available in public electrophysiology repositories, open-data supplements, and structured metadata in some imaging archives. However, these functional datasets are rarely integrated quantitatively with nanoscale organization, and they are almost never linked to proteomic stoichiometry or genetic variation. In parallel, human genetic resources (SFARI Gene, ClinVar, gnomAD) and mouse phenotype repositories (Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI), International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium (IMPC), Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) for perturbation transcriptomics) implicate AZ proteins in neurodevelopmental disorders and synaptopathies. These data suggest that subtle perturbations in scaffold interactions or phosphorylation sites may shift AZ organization, but the field lacks a synthesis framework to connect variants to mesoscale organizational states and then to functional consequences.

NCEMS’s focus on emergent mesoscale properties is well matched to the AZ problem. The AZ is a canonical mesoscale system: it is built from molecular interactions, but its function arises from spatial organization across 20–200 nm and from collective behavior across multiple release sites. Key gaps that synthesis research can address include: (1) whether there exist conserved, discrete AZ “organizational states” across synapse types and brain regions; (2) which geometric features (e.g., channel–vesicle distance distributions, cluster co-alignment, anisotropy) best predict Pr and plasticity; (3) how proteomic stoichiometry constrains feasible spatial architectures; and (4) how genetic variants and perturbations map onto predicted architectural shifts.

The time is ripe because the necessary public data streams now exist at scale. Imaging datasets are increasingly deposited in the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource (IDR), and EMPIAR, often with multi-channel super-resolution images suitable for re-analysis. Proteomics in PRIDE provides raw and processed spectra enabling re-quantification and cross-study normalization. Structural interaction constraints can be drawn from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, enabling physically informed network priors for scaffold assembly. Developmental and cell-type context is available through the Allen Brain Atlas (cell types database), the Human Cell Atlas and related scRNA-seq studies in GEO/SRA, allowing us to relate AZ organization to neuronal identity and maturation. Finally, literature-derived functional measures can be systematically harvested from open supplements and repositories, enabling meta-analytic linking of organization to physiology.

A community-scale synthesis is required because no single lab spans super-resolution reprocessing, spatial statistics, proteomics reanalysis, structural modeling, and synaptic physiology meta-analysis, and because harmonizing across heterogeneous datasets demands coordinated standards, shared workflows, and iterative cross-validation. By integrating these public resources into a unified mesoscale atlas and modeling framework, this working group will transform scattered observations into mechanistic, testable principles of emergent AZ function.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project targets a fundamental mesoscale question: how does nanoscale-to-mesoscale spatial organization of active zone proteins give rise to emergent presynaptic output and plasticity? We frame this as a synthesis problem: existing datasets already contain the necessary evidence, but only an integrative, cross-modal analysis can reveal latent organizational states and their mechanistic links to function.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): Do synaptic active zones occupy a small number of reproducible mesoscale “organizational states” that are conserved across brain regions, neuronal types, and developmental stages?
Hypothesis 1 (H1): AZs cluster into a limited set of organizational states defined by joint geometry of scaffold and channel nanoclusters (e.g., number of release modules, cluster compactness, inter-cluster spacing, and co-localization topology). These states are not continuous but appear as discrete modes when measured across datasets and laboratories.
Measurable predictions: (i) Unsupervised models applied to standardized feature vectors from super-resolution datasets will reveal stable clusters (high silhouette/consensus stability) that replicate across independent datasets (different labs/species) after harmonization; (ii) state membership will correlate with synapse class (excitatory vs inhibitory), brain region, and developmental time in scRNA-seq-derived cell-type context.
Validation using existing data: replicate state discovery across multiple imaging repositories (BioImage Archive/IDR) and validate robustness via leave-one-dataset-out analyses and batch-correction sensitivity tests.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): Which mesoscale geometric features best predict presynaptic release probability and short-term plasticity across conditions?
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Functional output is determined primarily by a small set of mesoscale parameters—especially the distribution of calcium channel–release site distances and the modularity of scaffold co-localization networks—leading to nonlinear mapping from organization to Pr/PPR.
Measurable predictions: (i) Spatial point-process and marked point-process models will show that Pr proxies are best predicted by parameters capturing nearest-neighbor distances between channel clusters and priming machinery clusters (e.g., RIM/Munc13) rather than by total protein abundance; (ii) models incorporating cooperative calcium effects (Hill-like nonlinearity) will outperform linear models linking abundance to function; (iii) AZs in “high reliability” states will show tighter channel–priming co-alignment and smaller distance variance, whereas “high flexibility” states will show larger variance and higher sensitivity to facilitation.
Validation using existing data: link imaging-derived organization features to functional measures extracted from public electrophysiology datasets and open supplementary tables; use meta-analytic hierarchical models to account for study-level differences and quantify predictive generalization.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): How do proteomic stoichiometry constraints shape the feasible space of mesoscale AZ architectures?
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Proteomics-derived stoichiometries constrain organizational states by limiting the number and composition of nanomodules; certain states require specific scaffold ratios (e.g., RIM:UNC13:ELKS) and are therefore enriched in regions/conditions with matching proteomic profiles.
Measurable predictions: (i) Integrative models that combine proteomic abundance vectors (from PRIDE/SynProt) with known interaction networks (PDB/AlphaFold-informed) will predict a bounded set of feasible cluster compositions; (ii) predicted module counts from stoichiometry will correlate with imaging-inferred module counts across matched brain regions/species; (iii) deviations between stoichiometry-predicted and imaging-observed architectures will identify candidate regulatory mechanisms (e.g., phosphorylation-driven relocalization) reflected in phosphoproteomics datasets when available in PRIDE.
Validation using existing data: cross-study proteomic normalization and comparison to imaging features at the level of region/species/condition; sensitivity analyses to peptide detectability and batch effects.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Do neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and synaptopathy-associated variants shift AZs into maladaptive organizational states?
Hypothesis 4 (H4): Variants in AZ scaffolds and regulators (e.g., RIMS1, UNC13A/B, CACNA1A family, SYT1 regulators) bias synapses toward organizational states characterized by increased heterogeneity, reduced channel–priming co-alignment, or altered module spacing, consistent with reduced reliability or aberrant plasticity.
Measurable predictions: (i) Genes enriched for pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in ClinVar and high-confidence SFARI categories will be overrepresented among proteins that define state boundaries (high feature importance) in imaging-derived state classifiers; (ii) mouse perturbation phenotypes (MGI/IMPC) for these genes will align with predicted functional consequences (e.g., altered PPR, seizure phenotypes) via literature and repository metadata; (iii) cell-type expression patterns from Allen Brain Atlas scRNA-seq will identify neuronal populations where variant effects are most likely to manifest, predicting state shifts in those populations.
Validation using existing data: enrichment analyses, cross-resource triangulation (variant databases + phenotype repositories + expression atlases), and comparison to any publicly available imaging/proteomics datasets from relevant genetic models deposited in archives.

Collectively, these questions test a mechanistic chain from molecular composition → mesoscale organization → emergent function, entirely through synthesis of existing public data. The outcome will be a quantitative, generalizable theory of AZ organizational states and their transitions, grounded in reproducible measurements and cross-modal validation.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and guiding principle (synthesis-only): We will not generate any new experimental data. All analyses will be performed on publicly available datasets, reprocessed with shared, open workflows. The core methodological advance is a harmonized representation of AZ organization that can be linked to proteomic stoichiometry, structural interaction priors, functional physiology, and genetic perturbation evidence.

1) Data sources (named repositories)
A. Super-resolution and ultrastructural imaging
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI) and Image Data Resource (IDR): STED/PALM/STORM datasets containing presynaptic AZ markers (e.g., RIM, Bassoon, Piccolo, Munc13, Cav2.1/2.2).
- EMPIAR (Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive): where available, correlated EM or high-resolution EM datasets relevant to AZ ultrastructure.
- Selected datasets with accessible raw or minimally processed localization tables (for SMLM), plus associated metadata.
B. Proteomics and phosphoproteomics
- PRIDE Archive: synaptosome, synaptic fraction, and AZ-enriched proteomics datasets (raw MS files where possible for re-quantification).
- SynProt and related curated synaptic proteome resources for cross-references and region annotations.
C. Functional measures (electrophysiology and optical proxies)
- Open physiology datasets where available (e.g., DANDI for neurophysiology datasets with appropriate metadata; CRCNS where relevant), plus systematic extraction from open supplementary materials accompanying publications.
- Public imaging datasets containing functional readouts (e.g., synapto-pHluorin-based release, calcium imaging proxies) in BioImage Archive/IDR.
D. Genetic variation and perturbation/phenotypes
- SFARI Gene; ClinVar; gnomAD (constraint metrics); OMIM (for gene-disease mapping where licensing allows; otherwise use open summaries).
- MGI and IMPC for mouse knockout/allele phenotypes; GEO/SRA for perturbation transcriptomics relevant to AZ genes.
E. Developmental and cell-type context
- Allen Brain Atlas (Cell Types Database; developmental transcriptomic resources).
- Human Cell Atlas / related scRNA-seq datasets in GEO/SRA for developmental trajectories and neuronal subclass mapping.
F. Structural priors
- Protein Data Bank (PDB) for known complexes and interaction interfaces.
- AlphaFold Protein Structure Database for predicted structures enabling interface plausibility scoring.
- Interaction databases (e.g., BioGRID, IntAct) as supporting evidence for network edges.

2) Harmonization and metadata standardization
- Imaging metadata: map dataset annotations to a controlled vocabulary (species, brain region, synapse type, developmental stage, labeling targets, imaging modality, resolution, fixation/prep). Use OME-NGFF where possible for standardized image access.
- Proteomics metadata: standardize sample descriptors (region, age, condition, fractionation method), re-map protein identifiers to UniProt accessions, and harmonize quantification units (iBAQ/LFQ where available) with batch-aware normalization.
- Functional metadata: encode assay type (PPR, Pr estimate, EPSC amplitude distributions), temperature, extracellular calcium, stimulation protocol, and synapse identity.
- Genetic metadata: unify gene identifiers (HGNC/MGI), variant consequence categories, and evidence tiers.

3) Imaging re-analysis and nanocluster quantification
- For SMLM localization tables: apply consistent filtering (localization precision thresholds), drift correction if needed (using published fiducial-based or cross-correlation approaches when raw data permit), and density-based clustering.
- Cluster detection: compare DBSCAN/HDBSCAN, Ripley’s K/L functions, and Bayesian clustering; choose method per modality with benchmarking on shared reference datasets.
- Feature extraction (per AZ): cluster size distributions, cluster density, inter-cluster distances, anisotropy, radial distribution functions, pair cross-correlation between channels and scaffolds, and graph representations of co-localization (nodes=clusters; edges=proximity/co-association).
- Spatial statistics: fit (marked) Gibbs/Poisson cluster processes and compute summary statistics enabling cross-dataset comparability.

4) Integrative modeling from organization to function
- Build hierarchical Bayesian models linking organizational features to functional outcomes (Pr proxies, PPR, facilitation/depression indices), with study-level random effects to address heterogeneity.
- Nonlinear mapping: incorporate cooperative calcium dependence via mechanistic-inspired link functions (e.g., Hill exponents) and compare to flexible ML models (gradient-boosted trees, Gaussian processes) with strict cross-validation.
- Causal-inference-informed synthesis (observational): use propensity-score-like covariate adjustment at the dataset level (e.g., extracellular calcium, temperature) and sensitivity analyses to confounding.

5) Stoichiometry-to-architecture constraints
- Proteomics reprocessing: where raw MS data available, re-quantify using open pipelines (e.g., MSFragger/FragPipe or MaxQuant outputs when provided) and normalize across studies using ComBat/limma-style batch correction and internal reference scaling.
- Map abundance vectors to predicted module counts: develop a constrained optimization model in which modules are composed of interacting proteins with stoichiometric ratios bounded by structural/interaction priors (PDB/AlphaFold/BioGRID). Output: feasible architectures (module number, composition) consistent with abundance.
- Compare predicted architectures to imaging-derived module counts and co-localization topology at matched resolution (region/species/condition).

6) Organizational state discovery and transition analysis
- State discovery: perform unsupervised learning on standardized AZ feature vectors (mixture models, spectral clustering, topic-model-like approaches on graph motifs). Use consensus clustering and stability selection.
- State annotation: associate states with region, cell type (via scRNA-seq expression signatures), development, and condition.
- Transitions (plasticity): infer likely transitions using datasets with activity manipulations or developmental series; model as state-space or Markov transition networks, recognizing observational limitations.

7) Variant and phenotype integration
- Gene prioritization: compute enrichment of NDD-associated genes among state-defining proteins and among proteins whose spatial relationships most strongly predict function.
- Variant-to-organization mapping: score variants by predicted disruption of interfaces (AlphaFold/PDB-informed) and regulatory sites (phosphosite annotations when available in PRIDE phosphoproteomics). Link to predicted state shifts using the stoichiometry/architecture model.
- Cross-validation: triangulate with mouse phenotypes (MGI/IMPC) and reported synaptic physiology changes in open literature datasets.

8) Validation (no experiments)
- Cross-dataset replication: train organizational state models on one set of imaging datasets and test on independent datasets (different labs/modality).
- Positive controls: known relationships such as tighter channel–release coupling correlating with higher Pr in specific synapse classes; known scaffold dependencies (e.g., RIM/Munc13 co-localization).
- Negative controls: randomized label permutations within AZs; spatial jittering to test whether observed correlations exceed what is expected from density alone.

9) Timeline and milestones (30 months)
- Months 0–6: dataset inventory; metadata schema; initial imaging and proteomics pipeline containerization; pilot re-analysis of 3–5 imaging datasets.
- Months 7–12: full imaging feature extraction across prioritized datasets; initial state discovery; release v0 “AZ-Features” dataset and code.
- Months 13–18: proteomics harmonization and stoichiometry-to-architecture modeling; first cross-modal linkage to imaging states.
- Months 19–24: organization-to-function hierarchical modeling; meta-analysis of functional measures; state-function atlas release.
- Months 25–30: variant/phenotype integration; final synthesis manuscripts; community workshop; release v1 integrated atlas, notebooks, and reproducible workflows.

10) Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Quantitative imaging experts (super-resolution reprocessing; OME/IDR standards).
- Spatial statisticians (point processes, marked processes, Bayesian hierarchical models).
- Proteomics computational analysts (MS reanalysis, batch correction, stoichiometry modeling).
- Structural bioinformaticians (PDB/AlphaFold priors; interface disruption scoring).
- Synaptic physiologists/neuroscientists (functional metric interpretation; confounder encoding; domain validation).
- Data engineers/research software engineers (pipeline automation, containers, data packaging).
- Trainees (grad students/postdocs) embedded across subteams with cross-training rotations.

NCEMS support is essential to convene and coordinate these expertise areas, maintain shared infrastructure, and deliver community-grade synthesis products that exceed what any single lab can produce.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables (concrete, open, synthesis-focused)
1) A cross-region, cross-condition atlas of active zone mesoscale organizational states
- A curated, harmonized dataset of AZ nanocluster features derived from publicly available super-resolution datasets (BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR where applicable), including standardized metadata and per-AZ feature vectors.
- A state taxonomy: discrete organizational states with quantitative definitions (centroids, uncertainty, decision boundaries) and annotations by species, brain region, synapse class, and developmental stage.

2) Open computational tools for nanocluster quantification and spatial modeling
- A reproducible software toolkit (“AZ-Synth”) implementing: localization-table ingestion, clustering/feature extraction, spatial point-process summaries, co-localization graph construction, and state inference.
- Benchmark reports comparing clustering/statistics choices across modalities and datasets, enabling best-practice recommendations.

3) Integrative models linking mesoscale organization to emergent function
- Hierarchical Bayesian and/or ML models that predict functional measures (Pr proxies, PPR, short-term plasticity indices) from organizational features, with quantified uncertainty and cross-dataset generalization metrics.
- Identification of the minimal set of mesoscale parameters that explain the largest fraction of functional variance, thereby distilling mechanistic principles from heterogeneous studies.

4) Stoichiometry-constrained architecture inference bridging proteomics and imaging
- A harmonized synaptic/AZ proteomics compendium from PRIDE and SynProt-linked studies, normalized for cross-study comparison.
- A constrained architecture inference framework that maps abundance vectors and structural/interaction priors (PDB/AlphaFold/BioGRID/IntAct) to feasible module compositions and counts, enabling mechanistic interpretation of proteomic shifts.

5) Variant-to-architecture-to-phenotype synthesis for synaptopathies
- A ranked set of AZ genes/variants (SFARI, ClinVar, gnomAD constraint) predicted to shift organizational state occupancy, with supporting evidence from mouse phenotypes (MGI/IMPC) and expression context (Allen Brain Atlas, HCA/GEO scRNA-seq).
- A set of testable, community-use hypotheses (without performing experiments in this project) specifying which organizational features are likely disrupted in particular genetic contexts.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project will provide a rigorous, data-driven account of how mesoscale patterning at the AZ generates emergent presynaptic behaviors. By moving beyond single-study qualitative descriptions, we will quantify whether AZs implement a small number of architectural “solutions” (organizational states) and how transitions among these solutions relate to plasticity modes (reliability vs flexibility). The key conceptual advance is treating the AZ as a mesoscale phase space: protein composition constrains possible organizations, and organization nonlinearly determines functional output. Establishing this chain with publicly available data will advance general principles of emergence: how collective spatial arrangements of molecules produce new system-level properties.

Broader impacts for molecular and cellular biosciences
- Generalizable synthesis framework: The methods (spatial statistics + stoichiometry constraints + state discovery) will be transferable to other mesoscale assemblies (e.g., focal adhesions, endocytic pits, nuclear bodies).
- Data reuse and standardization: By reprocessing and harmonizing existing imaging and proteomics data, we increase the value and interpretability of community datasets and encourage deposition of analysis-ready formats.
- Training the data-savvy workforce: Trainees will gain cross-domain skills spanning imaging informatics, proteomics, statistical modeling, and open science engineering.

How results enable future research (without proposing new data here)
The atlas and models will generate prioritized predictions for the community: which geometric parameters are most functionally consequential; which synapse types occupy which organizational states; and which genetic perturbations are most likely to shift state occupancy. These outputs will guide future experimentalists in designing targeted tests, but the NCEMS-funded work itself remains purely synthesis and computational.

Dissemination and community engagement
- Publications: at least two major synthesis manuscripts (organizational state atlas; organization-to-function modeling) plus a methods/software paper.
- Workshops: an NCEMS-hosted working group workshop on “Mesoscale spatial statistics for cell biology imaging” with hands-on tutorials using our open datasets.
- Data deposition: processed feature datasets and metadata tables deposited in Zenodo with DOIs; imaging-derived annotations and links returned to BioImage Archive/IDR records where feasible.

Long-term sustainability
- Maintain software as an open-source project with continuous integration, versioned releases, and archived containers.
- Provide a lightweight “data package” format (e.g., parquet + JSON schema) enabling others to add new public datasets as they appear, extending the atlas beyond the award period.
- Establish governance for community contributions (code of conduct, contribution guidelines, issue templates) to support ongoing adoption and reuse.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy: The budget prioritizes personnel time for cross-dataset harmonization and method development, shared computing for large-scale reprocessing, and NCEMS-enabled collaboration/training. No funds are allocated to experiments, sample acquisition, or new data generation.

Personnel (major cost driver)
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (2.0 FTE total):
  - Postdoc A (quantitative imaging + spatial statistics): leads super-resolution reprocessing, feature extraction, and point-process modeling.
  - Postdoc B (proteomics + integrative modeling): leads PRIDE reanalysis/harmonization and stoichiometry-to-architecture inference.
- 1 Research Software Engineer / Programmer (0.75–1.0 FTE): builds and maintains reproducible pipelines (Snakemake/Nextflow), containers, CI testing, data packaging, and documentation.
- 2 Graduate students (0.5 FTE each, or equivalent support):
  - Student 1 focuses on organizational state discovery and validation.
  - Student 2 focuses on variant/phenotype integration and scRNA-seq contextualization.
- Partial PI support (as allowed/needed): coordination, supervision, and synthesis writing; emphasis on working group leadership rather than lab-specific aims.

Computing resources
- Cloud compute and storage credits (or direct costs) for:
  - Large imaging dataset reprocessing (SMLM localization tables and multi-channel images), including intermediate storage.
  - Proteomics reanalysis from PRIDE raw files where feasible.
  - Model training (Bayesian inference, cross-validation) using scalable CPU/GPU resources as appropriate.
- Access to institutional HPC where available, supplemented by NCEMS-supported shared compute to ensure equitable participation across institutions with different resource levels.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings: 2 in-person meetings per year (or as aligned with NCEMS policies), enabling intensive cross-disciplinary integration (imaging/proteomics/physiology/structure/statistics).
- Targeted travel for trainees to attend NCEMS workshops and to present synthesis outputs at relevant conferences (e.g., Society for Neuroscience, HUPO for proteomics, image analysis meetings), emphasizing dissemination of open tools and datasets.

Workshops and training events
- Budget for one NCEMS-hosted community workshop (hybrid format): venue/AV (if in person), instructional support, and participant travel scholarships prioritizing trainees and underrepresented institutions.
- Support for hackathons (virtual infrastructure, small participant support) to expand the contributor base and train users on pipelines.

Open science infrastructure
- DOI and archiving costs are typically minimal (Zenodo free), but we include support for:
  - Long-term storage of derived datasets (mirrors on OSF/institutional repositories if needed).
  - Domain registration or minimal web hosting for documentation portals.
  - Professional-quality documentation and tutorials (time allocated primarily via RSE and trainee effort).

Justification relative to synthesis goals
- Personnel are essential because synthesis requires labor-intensive harmonization, reprocessing, and iterative cross-validation across modalities; this cannot be automated without dedicated engineering.
- Computing is required to reanalyze large public imaging and proteomics datasets consistently, ensuring that conclusions are not artifacts of heterogeneous processing.
- Travel and workshops are integral to NCEMS’s mission of catalyzing multidisciplinary teams and training the next-generation workforce; they directly enable integration across labs and broad dissemination of reusable synthesis products.

Overall, the requested resources are tightly coupled to producing community-grade, open, reproducible synthesis deliverables that exceed the capacity of any single laboratory.

abstract_original:
Synaptic active zones contain nanoscale protein nanoclusters (20–200 nm) whose collective arrangement controls neurotransmitter release probability and plasticity. The emergent phenomenon is that mesoscale spatial patterning of channels, scaffolds, and vesicle docking sites produces nonlinear release dynamics not predictable from single protein abundances.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution maps of active zone proteins (STED/PALM datasets in BioImage Archive/IDR), (ii) synaptosome and active zone proteomics across brain regions and conditions (PRIDE; SynProt resources), (iii) electrophysiological and imaging-derived functional measures (paired-pulse ratios, release probability proxies) from public repositories and literature open data, (iv) genetic variant and perturbation data for synaptic proteins (SFARI, ClinVar; mouse phenotyping databases), and (v) developmental single-cell transcriptomics of neuronal types (Allen Brain Atlas; scRNA-seq datasets).

We will quantify nanocluster geometry (cluster size, spacing, co-localization networks) and build spatial point-process models linking organization to release probability. Integrative modeling will connect proteomic stoichiometry to predicted nanoscale architectures using constraints from known structural interactions (PDB/AlphaFold). We will test whether synapses occupy discrete “organizational states” corresponding to functional plasticity modes.

Hypotheses: (1) active zones implement a small set of mesoscale architectures that tune reliability vs flexibility; (2) plasticity involves transitions between these architectures mediated by scaffold phosphorylation and remodeling; and (3) neurodevelopmental disorder variants shift synapses into maladaptive organizational states.

Expected insights include a cross-region atlas of active zone nanoscale architectures, mechanistic links between organization and emergent release dynamics, and open analysis tools for nanocluster quantification and integration with proteomics.

This requires team science across neuroscience, proteomics, quantitative imaging, and spatial statistics, with extensive synthesis across disparate datasets. NCEMS support will enable harmonization, open workflows, and trainee training bridging nanoscale organization and systems-level synaptic function.

title: Emergent Organelle Size Control via Mesoscale Substructure: Integrating Imaging Atlases and Omics to Explain Scaling Laws

abstract_text:
Organelle size (nucleoli, centrosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes) is governed by mesoscale substructures—subcompartments, scaffolds, and assembly intermediates (10–1000 nm)—that create emergent scaling laws with cell size and growth state. The emergent phenomenon is that collective assembly dynamics yield robust organelle size distributions across noisy molecular environments.

We will synthesize: (i) large-scale cell imaging atlases with organelle segmentation (Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas; IDR high-content datasets; Cell Painting), (ii) single-cell transcriptomics and proteomics capturing cell state (Human Cell Atlas; CITE-seq datasets; PRIDE single-cell proteomics where available), (iii) known organelle biogenesis pathways and interaction networks (Reactome, BioGRID), (iv) perturbation datasets affecting organelle size (DepMap; LINCS), and (v) ultrastructural datasets for organelle subcompartments (EMPIAR for selected organelles).

We will extract organelle size distributions and mesoscale texture/substructure features from images (granularity, internal puncta, boundary roughness) and relate them to molecular composition and cell size using scaling analysis and stochastic assembly models (nucleation–growth, coalescence, fragmentation). We will test competing mechanistic models (limiting pool, feedback control, coarsening-limited growth) across organelles and cell types.

Key questions: Are there universal mesoscale control motifs that recur across organelles (e.g., scaffold-limited nucleation, fragmentation-mediated size homeostasis)? Which molecular regulators tune variance vs mean size? Do disease states reflect altered control motifs leading to broader distributions (loss of homeostasis) rather than simple size shifts?

Expected insights include generalized principles of organelle size control grounded in measurable mesoscale features, and open tools for extracting substructure descriptors from public imaging. The project will yield a comparative “organelle scaling atlas” linking size control regimes to molecular networks.

This requires team science across quantitative cell imaging, stochastic modeling, and omics integration. NCEMS support is essential for large-scale data harmonization, development of reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to connect mesoscale organization to emergent cellular-scale phenotypes under open science.

[Abstract]
Organelle size (nucleoli, centrosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes) is governed by mesoscale substructures—subcompartments, scaffolds, and assembly intermediates (10–1000 nm)—that create emergent scaling laws with cell size and growth state. The emergent phenomenon is that collective assembly dynamics yield robust organelle size distributions across noisy molecular environments.

We will synthesize: (i) large-scale cell imaging atlases with organelle segmentation (Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas; IDR high-content datasets; Cell Painting), (ii) single-cell transcriptomics and proteomics capturing cell state (Human Cell Atlas; CITE-seq datasets; PRIDE single-cell proteomics where available), (iii) known organelle biogenesis pathways and interaction networks (Reactome, BioGRID), (iv) perturbation datasets affecting organelle size (DepMap; LINCS), and (v) ultrastructural datasets for organelle subcompartments (EMPIAR for selected organelles).

We will extract organelle size distributions and mesoscale texture/substructure features from images (granularity, internal puncta, boundary roughness) and relate them to molecular composition and cell size using scaling analysis and stochastic assembly models (nucleation–growth, coalescence, fragmentation). We will test competing mechanistic models (limiting pool, feedback control, coarsening-limited growth) across organelles and cell types.

Key questions: Are there universal mesoscale control motifs that recur across organelles (e.g., scaffold-limited nucleation, fragmentation-mediated size homeostasis)? Which molecular regulators tune variance vs mean size? Do disease states reflect altered control motifs leading to broader distributions (loss of homeostasis) rather than simple size shifts?

Expected insights include generalized principles of organelle size control grounded in measurable mesoscale features, and open tools for extracting substructure descriptors from public imaging. The project will yield a comparative “organelle scaling atlas” linking size control regimes to molecular networks.

This requires team science across quantitative cell imaging, stochastic modeling, and omics integration. NCEMS support is essential for large-scale data harmonization, development of reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to connect mesoscale organization to emergent cellular-scale phenotypes under open science.

[Background and Significance]
Organelle size is a canonical example of biological robustness: despite noisy gene expression, fluctuating nutrient conditions, and heterogeneous cell-cycle states, many organelles exhibit reproducible size distributions and characteristic scaling with cell size. This robustness is an emergent property: it cannot be explained by any single molecule, but instead arises from collective mesoscale organization—subcompartments, scaffolds, phase-separated domains, membrane microdomains, and assembly intermediates spanning ~10–1000 nm—that mediate assembly, disassembly, transport, and feedback. At this mesoscale, local interactions (binding, nucleation, coalescence, fragmentation, membrane remodeling) produce global outcomes (mean size, variance, number of organelles per cell, and scaling exponents with cell size). Understanding how mesoscale substructure governs organelle size is a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology with implications for growth control, proteostasis, innate immunity, neurodegeneration, and cancer.

Several conceptual models have been proposed for organelle size control. “Limiting pool” ideas posit that a finite supply of building blocks sets size; “self-limiting” or feedback control models posit that growth slows with increasing size via inhibitory signals, geometric constraints, or depletion zones; and “coarsening-limited” or “active fragmentation” models suggest that dynamic breakup counteracts coalescence to maintain a stable size distribution. For nucleoli, evidence supports roles for liquid–liquid phase separation, internal subcompartments (FC/DFC/GC), and ribosomal biogenesis flux in setting size and number. Centrosome size and pericentriolar material organization have been linked to scaffold proteins, phosphorylation-driven assembly, and cell-cycle cues. Lysosome size and abundance depend on membrane trafficking, fusion–fission balance, and transcriptional programs (e.g., TFEB-related networks). Peroxisome size and number depend on biogenesis factors, lipid metabolism, and division machinery. While these literatures provide mechanistic candidates, they are often organelle-specific, derived from limited cell types, and measured with different assays, making it difficult to identify general principles.

Public data resources have changed the landscape. Large imaging atlases now capture organelle morphology at scale across cell types and perturbations. The Human Protein Atlas (HPA) Cell Atlas provides immunofluorescence localization patterns for thousands of proteins in standardized cell lines, including organelle markers and rich variation in subcellular patterns. The Image Data Resource (IDR) aggregates high-content microscopy studies with curated metadata, including phenotypic screens that affect organelle morphology. The Cell Painting assay (e.g., Broad Institute’s Cell Painting datasets) provides multiplexed morphological profiles across many perturbations, enabling systematic quantification of organelle-related texture and size proxies. In parallel, single-cell omics resources such as the Human Cell Atlas (HCA) scRNA-seq, many CITE-seq datasets (paired RNA and surface proteins), and proteomics repositories like PRIDE (including emerging single-cell or low-input proteomics) provide cell-state context—growth, stress, differentiation, and cell cycle—that is essential for interpreting size scaling laws. Molecular interaction and pathway knowledge bases (Reactome, BioGRID, STRING) encode organelle biogenesis pathways and regulatory networks that can link morphological phenotypes to molecular mechanisms. Finally, ultrastructural repositories like EMPIAR provide electron microscopy volumes and images that can reveal sub-organelle architecture and mesoscale features (e.g., nucleolar subcompartments, centrosomal material organization, lysosomal internal structures) that are not visible in light microscopy.

Despite these resources, major gaps remain. First, organelle “size” is measured inconsistently across studies (area, volume proxies, intensity, number), and mesoscale substructure is rarely quantified systematically. Second, existing analyses often treat organelles as homogeneous objects, ignoring internal texture, punctation, boundary roughness, and subcompartment organization—features that may encode the control regime (e.g., coalescence vs fragmentation). Third, cross-organelle comparisons are rare: we do not know whether different organelles share universal control motifs or whether each organelle is governed by idiosyncratic mechanisms. Fourth, the relationship between mean size and variance (homeostasis) is poorly understood. Many diseases may reflect altered variance (loss of control) rather than a simple shift in mean size, but this has not been tested systematically across datasets. Finally, integrating morphology with molecular networks and perturbation responses remains challenging due to heterogeneous metadata, batch effects, and mismatched identifiers.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address these gaps because it can integrate imaging, omics, perturbational, and ultrastructural data at community scale without generating new experiments. By extracting comparable organelle size distributions and mesoscale texture descriptors across multiple imaging repositories, aligning them with cell-state features from single-cell omics, and embedding them in known regulatory networks, we can test mechanistic models across organelles, cell types, and perturbations. This integration can reveal emergent scaling laws—relationships between organelle size distributions and cell size/growth state—that are not apparent within any single dataset.

Focusing on mesoscale emergent phenomena is important because this is the scale at which molecular interactions are organized into functional assemblies that determine organelle architecture and dynamics. Mesoscale substructures act as “control knobs” that can tune assembly kinetics and stability, shaping size distributions. Identifying universal mesoscale control motifs would provide a unifying framework for organelle biology and a predictive basis for interpreting morphological phenotypes in genetic screens and disease contexts.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires (i) harmonization of heterogeneous public datasets across imaging modalities, cell types, and perturbation platforms; (ii) development of robust, open, reproducible pipelines for mesoscale feature extraction and scaling analysis; and (iii) a coordinated, multidisciplinary team spanning quantitative imaging, stochastic modeling, network biology, and single-cell data integration. This scope exceeds the capacity of a single lab and aligns directly with NCEMS’s mission to catalyze community-scale synthesis to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project centers on the emergent phenomenon that organelles maintain robust size distributions and scaling relationships with cell size and growth state, despite molecular noise. We posit that this robustness is encoded in mesoscale substructure—internal compartmentalization, scaffold organization, and dynamic assembly intermediates—that constrains stochastic growth processes. Our synthesis will test whether shared mesoscale “control motifs” explain scaling laws across distinct organelles.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): Do different organelles share universal scaling forms between organelle size distributions and cell size/growth state?
Hypothesis 1 (H1): Across organelles, size distributions follow a small number of parametric families (e.g., lognormal/gamma) whose parameters scale with cell size and cell-cycle state via conserved exponents, but with organelle-specific offsets.
Measurable predictions: (i) For each organelle, the relationship between mean size (or volume proxy) and cell size will be well described by a power law, mean(organelle) ~ cell_size^α, with α clustering into a small number of regimes across organelles and datasets. (ii) Variance-to-mean relationships (e.g., Fano factor, coefficient of variation) will collapse onto shared curves when conditioned on cell state (cell cycle, growth programs).
Validation using existing data: We will estimate distributions and scaling exponents in multiple independent imaging sources (HPA Cell Atlas, IDR studies, Cell Painting) and test reproducibility via cross-dataset meta-analysis. Cell size proxies (cell area, nuclear area) are available in segmentation outputs or can be computed from images.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): Which mesoscale substructure descriptors predict size-control regimes (limiting pool, feedback, coarsening/fragmentation) across organelles?
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Mesoscale texture features—granularity spectra, internal puncta statistics, boundary roughness/fractality, and multi-scale intensity heterogeneity—are sufficient to classify organelles into mechanistic regimes that correspond to distinct stochastic assembly models.
Measurable predictions: (i) Organelles dominated by coalescence-limited growth will show increasing boundary roughness and reduced internal puncta counts with increasing size, consistent with coarsening. (ii) Organelles under fragmentation-mediated homeostasis will exhibit size distributions with stable mean but constrained variance and a characteristic relationship between number and size (many small vs few large) across perturbations. (iii) Feedback-controlled organelles will show signatures of size-dependent growth inhibition, inferred from perturbation response curves: perturbations that increase building blocks will increase number more than size, or vice versa, depending on feedback topology.
Validation using existing data: We will fit alternative stochastic models to observed size distributions and perturbation response profiles from LINCS (morphological/perturbational signatures where available) and DepMap (gene dependency patterns linked to expression). Model selection will be performed using information criteria and posterior predictive checks; classification performance will be tested across datasets.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): Which molecular regulators tune mean size versus variance (homeostasis) and how do they map onto interaction networks?
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Distinct network modules regulate mean size (biosynthetic/biogenesis capacity) versus variance (stabilization, fragmentation/fission, quality control), and these modules are conserved across organelles.
Measurable predictions: (i) Genes/proteins in assembly scaffolds, nucleators, and biogenesis pathways (Reactome annotations) will associate with shifts in mean size across perturbations and cell states. (ii) Genes/proteins involved in fission–fusion balance, chaperones, and turnover pathways will preferentially associate with changes in variance (broader or narrower distributions) at similar means. (iii) Network centrality and module membership in BioGRID/STRING interaction networks will predict the magnitude and direction of morphological effects.
Validation using existing data: We will link perturbational signatures from LINCS (and Cell Painting perturbation datasets) to gene targets/pathways, and integrate with expression/protein abundance from HCA and PRIDE where matched cell types exist. We will test enrichment of identified regulators in curated organelle biogenesis pathways (Reactome) and evaluate replicability across independent perturbation datasets.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Do disease-associated states preferentially manifest as altered control motifs (loss of homeostasis) rather than simple size shifts?
Hypothesis 4 (H4): Disease-related transcriptional programs (stress, oncogenic signaling, lysosomal storage-like programs) are associated with increased organelle size variance and altered mesoscale texture indicative of disrupted fragmentation/quality control.
Measurable predictions: (i) In cell lines or perturbations modeling disease pathways (e.g., mTOR/TFEB axis, proteostasis stress), organelle size distributions will broaden (increased CV/Fano factor) even when mean size changes modestly. (ii) Texture features will shift toward signatures predicted by coarsening-dominated growth (e.g., smoother interiors, larger contiguous regions) or defective subcompartmentalization.
Validation using existing data: We will use disease-relevant perturbations in LINCS and IDR screens, and cell-state programs inferred from HCA scRNA-seq (stress, proliferation). Where possible, we will incorporate public imaging datasets from disease-model cell lines included in IDR or other repositories.

Collectively, these hypotheses yield mechanistic insight into how mesoscale organization constrains stochastic assembly to produce emergent size scaling laws. The key advance is not identifying single “size genes,” but rather mapping measurable mesoscale phenotypes to model classes and network modules that generalize across organelles and datasets.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will perform a community-scale synthesis that integrates (1) high-content fluorescence imaging atlases for organelle morphology, (2) single-cell omics for cell-state context, (3) curated pathways and interaction networks for mechanistic anchoring, (4) perturbation resources for causal inference via existing interventions, and (5) ultrastructural EM datasets for mesoscale subcompartment ground truth. No new experiments or data generation will be performed; all analyses use publicly available datasets.

Data sources (named repositories)
1) Imaging atlases and high-content screens
- Human Protein Atlas (HPA) Cell Atlas / Subcellular section: immunofluorescence images and protein localization annotations.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated high-content microscopy datasets, including phenotypic screens with metadata.
- Cell Painting datasets from the Broad Institute (e.g., JUMP Cell Painting consortium releases where publicly available; Broad’s Cell Painting data portal): multiplexed morphological profiles and, in many cases, images.
- Additional public segmentation benchmarks as needed (e.g., Broad Bioimage Benchmark Collection, where relevant for method calibration).
2) Single-cell transcriptomics/proteomics
- Human Cell Atlas (HCA) scRNA-seq: cell-type and state programs across tissues.
- CITE-seq datasets deposited in GEO/SRA: paired RNA and surface protein measurements for state inference.
- PRIDE (Proteomics Identifications Database): proteomics datasets including low-input and single-cell where available; complemented by ProteomeXchange identifiers.
3) Pathways and interaction networks
- Reactome: curated pathways for organelle biogenesis, trafficking, and metabolism.
- BioGRID: physical and genetic interactions.
- STRING (as an auxiliary network resource for confidence-weighted associations).
4) Perturbation and dependency resources
- LINCS (Library of Integrated Network-based Cellular Signatures): perturbational signatures; where morphological components exist, integrate; otherwise use transcriptomic signatures to infer pathway activation states linked to morphology datasets.
- DepMap (Cancer Dependency Map): CRISPR gene dependency, expression, and copy-number context across cell lines.
5) Ultrastructure
- EMPIAR: electron microscopy image/volume archives for selected organelles (nucleolus, centrosome, lysosome-related structures) to derive mesoscale subcompartment descriptors and validate light-microscopy texture proxies.

Data harmonization and metadata alignment
- Identifier standardization: map genes/proteins using HGNC/Ensembl/UniProt cross-references; map compounds/perturbations via LINCS IDs and PubChem/ChEMBL where applicable.
- Cell line and cell type mapping: harmonize cell line names (Cellosaurus) and annotate lineage/tissue.
- Imaging metadata normalization: unify pixel sizes, channels, staining/marker identities, and segmentation conventions; record provenance in a data catalog.
- Batch correction: for morphological features, apply ComBat/empirical Bayes and/or domain-adversarial approaches to reduce dataset-specific effects while preserving biological variance; evaluate with replicate concordance.

Image analysis: organelle size and mesoscale substructure features
- Segmentation: use existing segmentation masks when provided (common in Cell Painting pipelines) and apply standardized, open segmentation methods when only raw images are available (e.g., Cellpose or Stardist models used as off-the-shelf tools, not retrained on new labeled data unless labels already exist publicly). We will document parameters and evaluate against available ground-truth masks in public benchmarks.
- Organelle-specific marker selection: define marker panels for nucleoli (e.g., fibrillarin/NPM1), centrosomes (pericentrin/γ-tubulin), lysosomes (LAMP1/2), peroxisomes (PEX14/catalase) based on HPA annotations and literature.
- Size metrics: area/volume proxies (2D area; 3D where z-stacks exist), integrated intensity, number per cell, and normalized size (organelle size relative to cell size).
- Mesoscale descriptors (10–1000 nm proxies from diffraction-limited images):
  - Multi-scale texture: Haralick features, local binary patterns, wavelet energy across scales.
  - Granularity spectra: size distribution of bright structures via morphological opening at multiple radii.
  - Internal puncta: spot detection (LoG/DoG filters) to quantify substructures and their spatial dispersion.
  - Boundary roughness: perimeter-to-area ratios, Fourier descriptors, fractal dimension estimates.
  - Spatial organization: radial distribution relative to nucleus/cell boundary; nearest-neighbor distances among organelles.
- EM-derived features (from EMPIAR): quantify subcompartment sizes, surface roughness, and internal density heterogeneity; use these to calibrate which light-microscopy texture features best correlate with true mesoscale architecture.

Scaling analysis and statistical modeling
- Distribution fitting: fit lognormal, gamma, Weibull, and mixture models to organelle size distributions per condition; compare via AIC/BIC and posterior predictive checks.
- Scaling laws: estimate power-law relationships between organelle size moments (mean, variance) and cell size proxies; use hierarchical Bayesian models to share information across datasets while allowing dataset-specific offsets.
- Variance control: analyze mean–variance relationships (Taylor’s law), CV dependence on cell size/state, and number–size tradeoffs.

Mechanistic model testing (stochastic assembly models)
We will formalize competing models and fit them to distributional and perturbational data:
- Limiting pool model: predicts coupling between total organelle material and number/size; test via correlations between organelle total intensity per cell and size/number.
- Feedback control model: implement size-dependent growth rate functions; infer from how perturbations shift size vs number.
- Coarsening/fragmentation model: use Smoluchowski-type coagulation–fragmentation frameworks; fit steady-state distributions and infer effective coalescence/fragmentation parameters.
Model comparison will be performed per organelle and across organelles; we will identify shared parameter regimes (“control motifs”).

Omics integration and network inference
- Cell-state covariates: infer cell cycle, stress, growth, and metabolic programs from scRNA-seq (HCA) using established gene signatures and latent factor models (e.g., scVI where appropriate). Map these programs to imaging contexts via shared cell line/tissue annotations and perturbation signatures.
- Perturbation linking: connect Cell Painting/LINCS perturbations to pathway activation using gene set enrichment on LINCS transcriptomic signatures; then relate pathway scores to morphological outcomes.
- Network module discovery: integrate Reactome pathways and BioGRID/STRING networks; identify modules whose activity predicts mean vs variance changes using regularized regression (elastic net), random forests, and graph-regularized models.

Validation using only existing data
- Cross-dataset replication: confirm key scaling exponents and motif classifications in at least two independent imaging sources (e.g., HPA vs IDR; Cell Painting vs IDR).
- Positive controls: known perturbations with established organelle effects (e.g., TFEB-related lysosomal enlargement programs; centrosome cycle regulators) will serve as benchmarks for expected directionality.
- EM calibration: validate that texture proxies align with EMPIAR-derived subcompartment measures for selected organelles/datasets.
- Sensitivity analyses: assess robustness to segmentation method choice, batch correction strategy, and cell size proxy.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble data catalog; finalize marker lists; ingest HPA/IDR/Cell Painting subsets; implement baseline segmentation/feature extraction.
- Deliverable: v0 feature extraction pipeline + curated dataset registry.
Months 7–12:
- Compute organelle size distributions and texture descriptors across initial datasets; implement scaling analysis with hierarchical models.
- Deliverable: preliminary “organelle scaling atlas” (internal) + reproducible notebooks.
Months 13–18:
- Fit and compare stochastic assembly models; define motif taxonomy; begin perturbation-based analyses with LINCS/DepMap links.
- Deliverable: motif classification framework + cross-dataset validation report.
Months 19–24:
- Integrate scRNA/scProteomics state programs; network module analysis for mean vs variance regulators; EMPIAR calibration for selected organelles.
- Deliverable: network-linked scaling atlas v1 + EM-calibrated texture mapping.
Months 25–30:
- Final synthesis, manuscripts, and public release of datasets/tools; host training workshop(s) and working group capstone meeting.
- Deliverable: public atlas + software package + best-practices guide.

Team composition (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Quantitative bioimage analysis lab: segmentation, feature engineering, morphological profiling.
- Statistical physics/stochastic modeling lab: coagulation–fragmentation and feedback model development, Bayesian inference.
- Single-cell genomics/proteomics lab: state program inference, harmonization of scRNA/CITE-seq/PRIDE datasets.
- Network/pathway biology lab: Reactome/BioGRID integration, module discovery, enrichment analyses.
- Research software engineering (RSE) lead: workflow engineering, packaging, documentation, CI/CD.
- Trainees (grad students/postdocs) embedded across tasks; all contribute to shared working-group sprints.

NCEMS’s convening and computational support will be leveraged for coordinated data harmonization, intensive synthesis meetings, and training activities that exceed typical single-lab capacity.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) Organelle Scaling Atlas (public resource):
- A harmonized, cross-dataset compendium of organelle size distributions and scaling relationships across cell types, perturbations, and states for nucleoli, centrosomes, lysosomes, and peroxisomes.
- For each dataset/condition: standardized size metrics (mean, variance, distribution parameters), cell size proxies, organelle count, and mesoscale texture descriptors.
- Rich metadata linking images to markers, cell lines, perturbations, and provenance.

2) Open-source software toolkit for mesoscale organelle phenotyping:
- A reproducible pipeline to (i) ingest HPA/IDR/Cell Painting images or precomputed masks, (ii) compute organelle size and multi-scale texture features, (iii) perform scaling-law estimation and distribution fitting, and (iv) generate standardized reports.
- Implemented as a Python package with command-line entry points, plus Jupyter notebooks for tutorials.

3) Mechanistic “control motif” taxonomy and model library:
- A set of mechanistically interpretable model classes (limiting pool, feedback, coarsening/fragmentation) with parameter inference routines.
- A mapping from organelles and contexts to inferred motifs, including uncertainty estimates and cross-dataset support.

4) Network-linked regulator maps for mean vs variance control:
- Ranked gene/pathway modules associated with shifts in mean size versus changes in variance/homeostasis, derived from integration of perturbation resources (LINCS, Cell Painting perturbations), dependency data (DepMap), and pathway/network knowledge (Reactome, BioGRID/STRING).
- A set of “variance regulators” hypotheses grounded in synthesis evidence, suitable for future community follow-up (without being part of this project’s scope).

5) Training and community outputs:
- Workshop materials on organelle morphology synthesis, scaling analysis, and reproducible pipelines.
- A best-practices guide for reporting organelle size distributions and mesoscale texture features to improve future data interoperability.

Scientific impact: advancing understanding of mesoscale emergent phenomena
The central scientific contribution will be a generalizable explanation of organelle size control as an emergent mesoscale phenomenon. By tying measurable mesoscale substructure proxies to stochastic assembly models, we move beyond descriptive morphology toward mechanistic classification. The project will establish whether robust size distributions arise from shared mesoscale motifs—e.g., fragmentation-mediated homeostasis or scaffold-limited nucleation—across organelles that differ in composition and function. This addresses a long-standing puzzle: how cells achieve reproducible organelle architecture despite molecular noise.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Unification across organelles: A comparative framework will enable researchers to translate insights from well-studied organelles (e.g., nucleoli) to less-characterized ones (e.g., peroxisomes) by identifying shared control motifs.
- Improved interpretation of perturbation screens: Morphological phenotypes from CRISPR or compound screens can be interpreted through the lens of motif shifts (variance vs mean changes), enhancing mechanistic inference.
- Disease relevance: By quantifying “loss of homeostasis” signatures (variance broadening, texture shifts), the atlas can inform hypotheses about how disease programs alter mesoscale organization, complementing transcriptomic-only views.
- Methodological contribution: The project will provide validated, open methods for extracting mesoscale descriptors from widely available imaging, lowering barriers for labs to analyze organelle substructure without specialized microscopy.

Enabling future research
The atlas and tools will create a foundation for future community work, including:
- Extending to additional organelles (Golgi, mitochondria, ER) using the same pipelines.
- Integrating additional public modalities (spatial transcriptomics, multiplexed IF) as they become available.
- Developing predictive models that forecast organelle scaling behavior from molecular network state.
Importantly, these future directions can be pursued by the community using the open resources produced here.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least two manuscripts—(i) a resource/methods paper describing the atlas and pipelines; (ii) a synthesis/mechanism paper on control motifs and scaling laws across organelles.
- Workshops and tutorials: NCEMS-hosted working group meetings culminating in a hands-on short course (virtual + in-person) on the pipeline and modeling framework.
- Public deposition: feature tables, metadata, and model outputs deposited in long-term repositories (see Open Science plan) with DOIs.

Long-term sustainability
- Maintain the software as an open-source project with automated testing, versioned releases, and clear contribution guidelines.
- Archive each atlas release with a DOI (e.g., Zenodo) and provide a lightweight web landing page documenting dataset versions and recommended citations.
- Design the pipeline to be modular and data-source-agnostic, enabling community members to add new datasets via pull requests and standardized metadata templates. NCEMS’s community-scale approach will maximize adoption and longevity beyond the award period.

[Budget and Resources]
This project is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring coordinated personnel, computing for large-scale image feature extraction and model fitting, and NCEMS-enabled convening for cross-disciplinary integration and trainee development. Below is a budget narrative aligned to typical 2–3 year working group activities; exact dollar amounts will follow NCEMS guidelines and institutional rates.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (quantitative imaging + statistical modeling):
  - Postdoc A (bioimage analysis): leads harmonization of HPA/IDR/Cell Painting imaging inputs, segmentation standardization, and mesoscale feature engineering.
  - Postdoc B (stochastic modeling/statistics): leads scaling-law inference, hierarchical modeling, and coagulation–fragmentation/feedback model comparison.
  Justification: the core synthesis requires both deep imaging expertise and advanced statistical physics/model selection; these roles cannot be covered by a single trainee.
- 1 Graduate student (omics/network integration):
  - Focus on integrating HCA/CITE-seq/PRIDE-derived state programs with morphology, and mapping results to Reactome/BioGRID modules.
  Justification: sustained effort is needed to harmonize identifiers, build state covariates, and run network analyses across many conditions.
- 1 Research Software Engineer (RSE) / programmer analyst (50–100% effort depending on award size):
  - Builds and maintains the reproducible pipeline (Snakemake/Nextflow), containers, CI, documentation, and data release automation.
  Justification: software engineering is essential for open, reproducible synthesis at scale and for producing durable community resources.
- PI/Co-PI effort (modest):
  - Coordination, mentoring, working-group leadership, and synthesis writing.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing and/or HPC allocations:
  - High-throughput image processing (feature extraction over millions of cells) and Bayesian/hierarchical model fitting require scalable compute.
  - Funds will support storage (tens of TB where permitted), compute instances/GPUs as needed for segmentation inference (using existing models), and data egress where unavoidable.
  Justification: processing large public imaging corpora and running cross-validation/model comparison exceeds typical lab workstations.
- Data management infrastructure:
  - Versioned object storage for derived features, manifests, and intermediate artifacts; backup and checksum validation.
  Justification: ensures integrity and reproducibility of derived synthesis products.

Travel and collaboration
- NCEMS working group meetings (in-person):
  - Support travel for team members across multiple institutions, with emphasis on including trainees and participants from diverse geographic locations.
  Justification: intensive, in-person synthesis sprints accelerate consensus on data standards, model definitions, and integration decisions.
- Conference dissemination:
  - Travel for presenting results and running tutorials at relevant meetings (cell biology, computational biology, image analysis).
  Justification: broad dissemination increases adoption of the atlas and software.

Workshops and training events
- Two virtual training events + one in-person capstone workshop:
  - Costs include webinar hosting, instructional support, and (for in-person) venue/AV and trainee travel scholarships as allowable.
  Justification: training is a core NCEMS goal; workshops build the next-generation data-savvy workforce and expand community participation.

Open science infrastructure costs
- DOI deposition and long-term archiving:
  - Zenodo is free, but funds may support curation time and potential repository fees for large derived datasets if needed.
- Documentation and community support:
  - Minimal costs for website hosting (if not covered institutionally) and accessibility services (captioning) for recorded tutorials.

Overall justification
Each budget category directly supports synthesis-only goals: harmonizing and analyzing existing public data at scale, developing rigorous and reusable analytical workflows, convening a multidisciplinary team beyond the scope of a single lab, and producing open resources and training that persist beyond the award period. No funds are requested for experimental data generation, sample acquisition, or new wet-lab work.

abstract_original:
Organelle size (nucleoli, centrosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes) is governed by mesoscale substructures—subcompartments, scaffolds, and assembly intermediates (10–1000 nm)—that create emergent scaling laws with cell size and growth state. The emergent phenomenon is that collective assembly dynamics yield robust organelle size distributions across noisy molecular environments.

We will synthesize: (i) large-scale cell imaging atlases with organelle segmentation (Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas; IDR high-content datasets; Cell Painting), (ii) single-cell transcriptomics and proteomics capturing cell state (Human Cell Atlas; CITE-seq datasets; PRIDE single-cell proteomics where available), (iii) known organelle biogenesis pathways and interaction networks (Reactome, BioGRID), (iv) perturbation datasets affecting organelle size (DepMap; LINCS), and (v) ultrastructural datasets for organelle subcompartments (EMPIAR for selected organelles).

We will extract organelle size distributions and mesoscale texture/substructure features from images (granularity, internal puncta, boundary roughness) and relate them to molecular composition and cell size using scaling analysis and stochastic assembly models (nucleation–growth, coalescence, fragmentation). We will test competing mechanistic models (limiting pool, feedback control, coarsening-limited growth) across organelles and cell types.

Key questions: Are there universal mesoscale control motifs that recur across organelles (e.g., scaffold-limited nucleation, fragmentation-mediated size homeostasis)? Which molecular regulators tune variance vs mean size? Do disease states reflect altered control motifs leading to broader distributions (loss of homeostasis) rather than simple size shifts?

Expected insights include generalized principles of organelle size control grounded in measurable mesoscale features, and open tools for extracting substructure descriptors from public imaging. The project will yield a comparative “organelle scaling atlas” linking size control regimes to molecular networks.

This requires team science across quantitative cell imaging, stochastic modeling, and omics integration. NCEMS support is essential for large-scale data harmonization, development of reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to connect mesoscale organization to emergent cellular-scale phenotypes under open science.

title: Mesoscale Emergence in DNA Damage Repair Foci: Integrating Live Imaging, Proteomics, and 3D Genome Context
title_norm: mesoscale emergence in dna damage repair foci integrating live imaging proteomics and 3d genome context
abstract_text:
DNA damage repair foci are mesoscale assemblies (100–1000 nm) where many proteins and chromatin regions co-localize, often with phase-separation-like properties. The emergent phenomenon is that collective recruitment and chromatin reorganization creates threshold responses, pathway choice (HR vs NHEJ), and repair timing not predictable from individual repair factors.

We will synthesize: (i) live-cell imaging datasets of repair foci dynamics (53BP1, RAD51, γH2AX) from IDR/BioImage Archive, including time-lapse series, (ii) proteomics and phosphoproteomics of DNA damage response (DDR) time courses (PRIDE), (iii) 3D genome and chromatin context maps (Hi-C/Micro-C from 4DN; ENCODE epigenomics), (iv) CRISPR screens for DDR genes and pathway choice modifiers (DepMap; published DDR screens), and (v) variant datasets for DDR genes in cancer (TCGA; COSMIC).

We will develop a unified model linking chromatin context and protein network state to mesoscale foci morphodynamics. Imaging analysis will quantify foci nucleation rates, growth/coalescence, and dissolution, extracting mesoscale kinetic parameters. We will integrate these with phosphoproteomic signaling states and with chromatin compartment features at damage-prone loci. Causal inference will identify regulators that shift foci dynamics and pathway choice.

Hypotheses: (1) repair foci exhibit discrete mesoscale dynamical regimes (diffuse recruitment vs coalescing droplets vs stable scaffolds) corresponding to repair pathway choice; (2) chromatin nanodomain topology constrains foci growth and coalescence; and (3) cancer-associated DDR alterations manifest as shifts in mesoscale regimes rather than complete pathway loss.

Expected insights include a cross-study atlas of foci dynamical regimes, mechanistic links between 3D genome context and emergent assembly kinetics, and open pipelines for foci tracking and integrative DDR modeling.

This requires collaboration among DDR biologists, quantitative imaging experts, proteomics analysts, and 3D genomics researchers. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous time-lapse datasets and omics, build reproducible multi-modal workflows, and train trainees in integrative analysis of mesoscale nuclear assemblies.

[Abstract]
DNA damage repair foci are mesoscale assemblies (100–1000 nm) where many proteins and chromatin regions co-localize, often with phase-separation-like properties. The emergent phenomenon is that collective recruitment and chromatin reorganization creates threshold responses, pathway choice (HR vs NHEJ), and repair timing not predictable from individual repair factors.
