We will develop a unified model linking chromatin context and protein network state to mesoscale foci morphodynamics. Imaging analysis will quantify foci nucleation rates, growth/coalescence, and dissolution, extracting mesoscale kinetic parameters. We will integrate these with phosphoproteomic signaling states and with chromatin compartment features at damage-prone loci. Causal inference will identify regulators that shift foci dynamics and pathway choice.

Hypotheses: (1) repair foci exhibit discrete mesoscale dynamical regimes (diffuse recruitment vs coalescing droplets vs stable scaffolds) corresponding to repair pathway choice; (2) chromatin nanodomain topology constrains foci growth and coalescence; and (3) cancer-associated DDR alterations manifest as shifts in mesoscale regimes rather than complete pathway loss.

Expected insights include a cross-study atlas of foci dynamical regimes, mechanistic links between 3D genome context and emergent assembly kinetics, and open pipelines for foci tracking and integrative DDR modeling.

This requires collaboration among DDR biologists, quantitative imaging experts, proteomics analysts, and 3D genomics researchers. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous time-lapse datasets and omics, build reproducible multi-modal workflows, and train trainees in integrative analysis of mesoscale nuclear assemblies.

[Background and Significance]
DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and other genotoxic lesions trigger rapid formation of DNA damage response (DDR) “foci”—subnuclear assemblies in the ~100–1000 nm range that concentrate sensors, signaling mediators, repair enzymes, and remodeled chromatin. These foci (e.g., γH2AX-marked chromatin domains; 53BP1 bodies; RAD51 repair centers) represent quintessential mesoscale structures: too large to be explained solely by pairwise molecular interactions, yet smaller than whole-organellar rearrangements. At this mesoscale, collective phenomena emerge—threshold activation, switch-like pathway choice between homologous recombination (HR) and non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), and coordinated timing of recruitment and disassembly—that are not predictable from the properties of single DDR proteins measured in isolation.

A growing literature suggests that DDR foci behave as higher-order assemblies with features reminiscent of phase separation or polymer–protein coacervation, including rapid fusion/coalescence, concentration buffering, and sensitivity to multivalent post-translational modifications. 53BP1, for example, forms dynamic nuclear puncta whose properties depend on upstream signaling (ATM/ATR), ubiquitin ligases (RNF8/RNF168), and chromatin marks (H4K20me2). RAD51 accumulates at resected DNA ends during HR and exhibits cell-cycle-dependent kinetics. γH2AX spreads over megabase chromatin domains and recruits mediator complexes (MDC1, MRN), creating a scaffold for further assembly. Yet the field lacks a unifying, quantitative framework that connects (i) live mesoscale morphodynamics (nucleation, growth, fusion, dissolution), (ii) the underlying signaling network state (phosphorylation/ubiquitylation programs), and (iii) the 3D genome and epigenomic context in which breaks occur.

Critically, the last decade has produced a vast quantity of publicly available data that, if synthesized, can address these gaps without generating new experiments. First, time-lapse fluorescence microscopy of DDR markers has been deposited in resources such as the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the BioImage Archive, often accompanied by metadata on cell type, perturbations, and acquisition settings. These datasets contain latent information about mesoscale assembly kinetics and heterogeneity across cells and conditions, but are underutilized because they are heterogeneous and require specialized analysis pipelines.

Second, proteomics and phosphoproteomics time courses of DDR activation are available in PRIDE (Proteomics Identifications Database) and related repositories. Such datasets quantify system-wide signaling trajectories after irradiation, replication stress, or chemical damage, capturing kinase cascades (ATM/ATR/DNA-PK), cell-cycle regulators, and chromatin modifiers that modulate foci behavior. However, proteomics is typically interpreted at the pathway enrichment level, not explicitly linked to spatial mesoscale phenotypes.

Third, 3D genome architecture maps—Hi-C and Micro-C—from the 4D Nucleome (4DN) Data Portal and other public studies provide information about compartments (A/B), topologically associating domains (TADs), loop anchors, and contact density that may constrain or facilitate spread of γH2AX and coalescence of repair assemblies. ENCODE provides complementary epigenomic context (ChIP-seq for histone marks and chromatin-binding factors; ATAC-seq/DNase-seq for accessibility) that can stratify loci by chromatin state. While individual studies have linked chromatin context to repair outcomes, a cross-study synthesis connecting 3D topology to mesoscale foci morphodynamics remains missing.

Fourth, large-scale functional genetics resources provide orthogonal evidence for regulators of pathway choice and foci behavior. DepMap (including the Achilles CRISPR screens) and published DDR-focused CRISPR screens identify genes whose loss sensitizes cells to DNA damage or shifts reliance between HR and NHEJ. Yet these screens are rarely integrated with quantitative imaging phenotypes across conditions.

Finally, cancer genomics resources such as TCGA and COSMIC catalog recurrent variants, copy-number changes, and expression alterations in DDR genes. Many tumors show partial DDR rewiring rather than complete loss, suggesting that emergent mesoscale properties—e.g., altered assembly regimes and timing—may be a key intermediate phenotype linking genotype to therapeutic response.

The synthesis opportunity is therefore compelling: by integrating imaging-derived mesoscale kinetic parameters with proteomic network states and 3D genome context, we can move beyond cataloging DDR components toward explaining how collective organization produces robust, switch-like outcomes. This aligns directly with NCEMS’s focus on emergence at the mesoscale and its mission to catalyze community-scale synthesis that is beyond any single lab. No individual group typically holds expertise across quantitative bioimage analysis, phosphoproteomics modeling, 3D genome biophysics, and causal inference from genetics and cancer cohorts—yet all these perspectives are required to understand how repair foci function as emergent mesoscale machines.

This project will leverage and harmonize existing public datasets to build an integrative, mechanistic model of DDR foci emergence. The significance is twofold: (1) fundamental—revealing principles by which nuclear mesoscale assemblies encode decision-making and timing; and (2) translationally enabling—providing interpretable mesoscale biomarkers and hypotheses for why specific DDR alterations in cancer shift repair outcomes and therapy sensitivity. By creating a cross-study atlas, reproducible pipelines, and open models, we also lower barriers for the broader community to reuse and extend these synthesis products, advancing molecular and cellular science through openly shared, integrative inference rather than new data generation.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how emergent mesoscale properties of DDR foci arise from—and feed back onto—molecular signaling and chromatin architecture. The central premise is that foci are not merely “spots” marking damage, but dynamic mesoscale states of the nucleus that implement decision-making (HR vs NHEJ), regulate timing, and buffer molecular noise. We will pursue four tightly defined research questions (RQs) with testable hypotheses and measurable predictions that can be validated using only existing public datasets.

RQ1: Do DDR foci occupy discrete, recurrent mesoscale dynamical regimes across studies and conditions?
Hypothesis H1 (Regime discreteness): Time-lapse trajectories of foci (53BP1, RAD51, γH2AX) cluster into a small number of dynamical regimes characterized by distinct combinations of nucleation rate, growth law, fusion/coalescence frequency, internal rearrangement, and dissolution kinetics. These regimes are not dataset-specific artifacts but reproducible across laboratories after harmonization.
Predictions: (i) Unsupervised clustering of per-cell foci features will yield a stable set of regime prototypes (e.g., “diffuse recruitment,” “coalescing droplet-like,” “stable scaffold-like,” “transient burst”). (ii) Regime membership will be predictable from condition metadata (damage type, cell-cycle proxy, perturbations) better than chance. (iii) Regime transitions within a cell will follow constrained paths (e.g., nucleation → coalescence → dissolution) rather than arbitrary switching.
Validation with existing data: We will test regime stability via cross-dataset replication using IDR/BioImage Archive time-lapse series, holding out entire studies as external validation sets. Positive controls include known perturbations (e.g., ATM inhibition, RNF168 pathway disruption) present in public imaging datasets that should shift 53BP1 recruitment dynamics.

RQ2: How do mesoscale regimes relate to repair pathway choice (HR vs NHEJ) and repair timing?
Hypothesis H2 (Mesoscale-to-pathway mapping): Specific mesoscale regimes correspond to pathway bias: RAD51-dominant regimes align with HR-like states, while 53BP1-dominant stable scaffolds align with NHEJ-like states; mixed regimes reflect intermediate or context-dependent repair.
Predictions: (i) In datasets containing both markers (or comparable conditions across studies), regime features will correlate with HR/NHEJ proxy readouts available in the literature or metadata (e.g., RAD51 focus persistence vs 53BP1 persistence; cell-cycle phase inferred from FUCCI markers when present; replication stress vs IR). (ii) Regime features will predict timing metrics such as time-to-peak intensity, half-life of foci, and time to resolution.
Validation with existing data: We will use imaging datasets with known pathway manipulations (e.g., BRCA1/2 deficiency, 53BP1 loss, DNA-PK inhibition) when available in IDR-linked studies, and cross-reference with CRISPR screen hits for HR/NHEJ modifiers from DepMap and published DDR screens. Concordance between predicted pathway bias and genetic dependencies will serve as validation.

RQ3: Does 3D genome and epigenomic context constrain mesoscale foci growth, spreading, and coalescence?
Hypothesis H3 (Topology constraint): Chromatin topology (compartment identity, contact density, TAD boundaries) and epigenomic state (accessibility, histone marks) impose constraints on the spatial extent and growth kinetics of γH2AX domains and associated repair assemblies, thereby shaping observed mesoscale regimes.
Predictions: (i) Cell types or conditions with more segregated compartmentalization (from 4DN Hi-C/Micro-C metrics) will show different distributions of foci size and coalescence frequency than those with weaker compartmentalization. (ii) Features such as local contact insulation (TAD boundary strength) will correlate with inferred “effective spread” parameters of γH2AX-like domains (estimated from imaging proxies such as focus area growth and plateau). (iii) ENCODE chromatin state annotations will stratify regimes (e.g., heterochromatin-associated marks bias toward stable scaffolds with slower dissolution).
Validation with existing data: We will perform cross-cell-type comparisons where both imaging and 4DN/ENCODE data exist (even if not from identical experiments), using careful matching by cell line and condition. Robustness will be assessed by sensitivity analyses across alternative normalization and matching strategies.

RQ4: Do cancer-associated DDR alterations manifest primarily as shifts in mesoscale regimes rather than binary pathway loss?
Hypothesis H4 (Regime shift phenotype): Tumor-associated variants, copy-number alterations, and expression changes in DDR genes shift the probability landscape over mesoscale regimes (e.g., increased persistence, delayed dissolution, altered coalescence) rather than eliminating foci formation entirely.
Predictions: (i) Genes recurrently altered in TCGA/COSMIC that are also CRISPR screen dependencies will map to specific regime-modulating modules (e.g., ubiquitin signaling, resection control, chromatin remodeling). (ii) Cell lines with particular alterations (integrating DepMap genomics) will show predicted vulnerabilities consistent with regime shifts (e.g., increased reliance on PARP-mediated repair when HR-like regimes are destabilized).
Validation with existing data: We will integrate DepMap mutation/CNV/expression with CRISPR dependencies and, where public imaging exists for corresponding cell lines, test whether predicted regime shifts are observed. Where direct imaging is absent, we will validate indirectly via concordance between regime-modulating modules and proteomic/phosphoproteomic signatures of DDR activation available in PRIDE for similar genotypes.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses aim to deliver mechanistic insight into how mesoscale organization encodes decision-making and timing in DDR. The emphasis is on measurable, cross-dataset predictions—regime identities, transition probabilities, kinetic parameters, and module associations—that can be rigorously tested through synthesis of existing imaging, omics, 3D genome, functional genetics, and cancer genomics resources, without generating any new experimental data.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
We will execute a community-scale synthesis that converts heterogeneous public datasets into a unified, analyzable representation of DDR mesoscale dynamics, then integrates these dynamics with proteomic signaling states, 3D genome context, functional genetic dependencies, and cancer variation. The core methodological idea is to represent each dataset in a common “mesoscale state space”: a set of quantitative features describing foci morphodynamics (from imaging) and network/context features (from omics and 3D genomics), enabling cross-study learning and causal inference.

Specific public data sources (no new data generation)
1) Bioimaging time-lapse datasets
- Image Data Resource (IDR; https://idr.openmicroscopy.org/): curated microscopy studies with metadata and OME-TIFF access.
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/bioimage-archive/): raw and processed imaging datasets.
Targets: time-lapse imaging of DDR markers including 53BP1, RAD51, γH2AX (and related markers such as MDC1, RPA, BRCA1 when present), across perturbations (IR, replication stress, inhibitors, knockdowns/knockouts) and cell lines.

2) Proteomics and phosphoproteomics
- PRIDE Archive (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/): DDR time-course proteomics/phosphoproteomics datasets; reanalysis-ready raw files and processed tables.
- ProteomeXchange consortium identifiers via PRIDE for consistent citation and retrieval.

3) 3D genome and epigenomics
- 4D Nucleome (4DN) Data Portal (https://data.4dnucleome.org/): Hi-C/Micro-C contact maps, derived compartment/TAD/loop calls.
- ENCODE Project (https://www.encodeproject.org/): ChIP-seq (histone marks, CTCF/cohesin), ATAC-seq/DNase-seq, RNA-seq for matched cell types.

4) Functional genetics
- DepMap (https://depmap.org/portal/): CRISPR gene effect scores, genomic features (mutations, CNVs), expression.
- Published DDR-focused CRISPR screens (retrieved from supplementary tables and repositories such as GEO/ArrayExpress where available), including screens for HR/NHEJ pathway choice modifiers.

5) Cancer variation
- The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA via GDC; https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/): mutation, CNV, expression.
- COSMIC (https://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic): curated somatic variants.

Data harmonization and metadata standardization
- Imaging: Convert all microscopy datasets to OME-NGFF/Zarr where feasible; standardize pixel sizes, time intervals, channel identities, and experimental annotations using REMBI-aligned metadata fields. We will create a controlled vocabulary for damage type, perturbation class, marker, and cell line.
- Proteomics: Harmonize protein identifiers (UniProt), phosphosite mapping (PSP/UniProt), and time points; normalize intensities (e.g., median normalization, batch correction with ComBat or removal of unwanted variation) with explicit provenance.
- 3D genomics: Use standardized resolutions (e.g., 10kb–100kb) and consistent compartment/TAD calling pipelines (or adopt published calls with careful versioning). Compute comparable summary metrics per cell type (compartment strength, insulation score distributions, loop density).
- Genetics/genomics: Harmonize gene symbols (HGNC), map variants to genes and functional classes, and align cell line identifiers across DepMap and imaging studies.

Quantitative imaging analysis: extracting mesoscale kinetic parameters
We will build reproducible pipelines to quantify foci morphodynamics:
- Segmentation and detection: Use Cellpose/StarDist (where appropriate) for nuclei; spot/foci detection via multi-scale Laplacian-of-Gaussian, wavelet methods, or deep-learning spot detectors when required, with model weights and parameters versioned.
- Tracking: Link foci over time using probabilistic trackers (e.g., linear assignment with motion models; TrackMate-like algorithms; or Bayesian tracking) to quantify nucleation, fusion, splitting, and disappearance.
- Feature extraction: For each cell and time series, compute: foci count trajectories; size/area/volume proxies; intensity and integrated intensity; growth exponents; coalescence frequency; spatial dispersion; persistence times; and “regime descriptors” (e.g., burstiness, hysteresis-like behavior, relaxation times).
- Regime discovery: Unsupervised learning on feature trajectories using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), switching linear dynamical systems, or time-series clustering (DTW + clustering; variational autoencoders for sequences) to identify discrete mesoscale regimes and transition probabilities.

Integrating proteomic signaling states with mesoscale regimes
- Construct DDR signaling state vectors per dataset/time point from PRIDE phosphoproteomics: kinase activity inference (e.g., KSEA—Kinase-Substrate Enrichment Analysis), pathway activity scores, and module eigengenes from co-phosphorylation networks.
- Map imaging conditions to proteomics conditions by perturbation class, damage type, and approximate time windows; when exact matching is impossible, use hierarchical models that treat study as a random effect and integrate at the level of latent “DDR activation stage.”
- Learn associations between signaling states and regime probabilities using multinomial mixed models, regularized regression, and representation learning (canonical correlation analysis, multi-omics factor analysis such as MOFA+) with uncertainty quantification.

Linking 3D genome/epigenomics to mesoscale dynamics
- Derive per-cell-type chromatin context summaries from 4DN: compartment strength, insulation score distributions, contact decay profiles, loop density.
- Use ENCODE chromatin state segmentations (e.g., ChromHMM tracks where available) and accessibility/histone mark signals to define “repair-relevant context signatures.”
- Test topology constraints by modeling regime features as functions of these context signatures with mixed effects to account for study and imaging modality. Where loci-level mapping is feasible (e.g., γH2AX spread proxies), incorporate published DSB hotspot maps when publicly available and avoid any new mapping experiments.

Causal inference and triangulation with functional genetics and cancer data
- Use CRISPR screen data to define candidate regulators and modules (e.g., ubiquitin signaling, resection, chromatin remodeling). Apply network methods (community detection on protein–protein interaction networks from STRING/BioGRID) to group genes.
- Causal/structural modeling: Apply causal discovery constraints informed by DDR pathway knowledge (directed acyclic graphs with priors) and use targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) or doubly robust methods to estimate effects of module perturbations on regime probabilities, using imaging-derived regime labels where perturbation imaging exists.
- Cancer integration: Map TCGA/COSMIC alterations onto modules and predict regime shifts; validate using DepMap dependencies and any available imaging for matching cell lines.

Validation (all using existing data)
- Cross-dataset validation: Train regime classifiers on a subset of imaging studies and test on held-out studies (external validation).
- Positive controls: Known DDR perturbations present in public datasets (ATM/ATR/DNA-PK inhibitors; BRCA1/2 deficiency; 53BP1 pathway disruption) should yield expected shifts (e.g., reduced 53BP1 stable scaffolds under RNF168 disruption).
- Negative controls: Non-DDR nuclear puncta datasets (when available in IDR) to ensure regime features are DDR-specific rather than generic imaging artifacts.
- Sensitivity analyses: Evaluate robustness to segmentation choices, time resolution, photobleaching correction, and batch effects.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize controlled vocabularies and metadata schema.
- Select and ingest initial imaging studies from IDR/BioImage Archive; set up OME-NGFF storage.
- Pilot foci detection/tracking pipeline on 2–3 representative datasets.

Months 7–12:
- Scale imaging pipeline to broader dataset collection; compute standardized feature tables.
- Ingest PRIDE DDR phosphoproteomics time courses; harmonize identifiers and time axes.
- First regime discovery and cross-study stability assessment.

Months 13–18:
- Integrate 4DN/ENCODE context metrics by cell type; build mixed-effect association models.
- Build module-level signaling predictors of regimes; release v1 of “DDR Foci Regime Atlas.”

Months 19–24:
- Integrate DepMap and published CRISPR screens; implement causal/triangulation analyses.
- Cancer alteration mapping with TCGA/COSMIC; generate regime-shift hypotheses.

Months 25–30:
- Finalize unified model; extensive validation and sensitivity analyses.
- Release v2 atlas, open pipelines, and manuscripts; run training workshop at/with NCEMS.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- DDR biology experts: interpret pathway perturbations, curate DDR-specific metadata, define mechanistic priors.
- Quantitative imaging scientists: develop segmentation/tracking, regime inference, and imaging QC.
- Proteomics/phosphoproteomics analysts: process PRIDE datasets, kinase activity inference, batch correction.
- 3D genome/epigenomics experts: process 4DN/ENCODE, define topology/context metrics.
- Data integration/ML and causal inference experts: multimodal modeling, uncertainty quantification, causal triangulation.
- Research software engineer: workflow engineering, packaging, documentation, CI/CD.
- Trainees (grad students/postdocs): cross-training across modalities, leading sub-aim analyses.

NCEMS support is essential for convening these experts, coordinating community-scale dataset curation and harmonization, providing shared computational infrastructure and best-practice open science workflows, and enabling sustained collaborative synthesis that exceeds the scope of any single lab’s resources or expertise.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables
1) DDR Foci Regime Atlas (public resource): A cross-study, harmonized catalog of mesoscale foci dynamical regimes for canonical DDR markers (53BP1, RAD51, γH2AX) derived from IDR and BioImage Archive time-lapse datasets. The atlas will include:
- Standardized per-cell and per-focus feature tables (with provenance to original datasets).
- Regime definitions (learned prototypes), regime labels/probabilities per trajectory, and regime transition models.
- Dataset-level summaries enabling meta-analysis across cell types, damage types, and perturbations.

2) Open, reusable computational pipelines:
- End-to-end workflows for (i) imaging ingestion → OME-NGFF conversion → segmentation/detection → tracking → feature extraction → regime inference; and (ii) PRIDE phosphoproteomics harmonization → kinase activity inference; and (iii) 4DN/ENCODE context metric extraction.
- Modular APIs (Python) and documented notebooks for common analyses, enabling other groups to extend to additional markers or nuclear assemblies.

3) Integrative mechanistic model of mesoscale emergence:
- A unified statistical/ML model linking chromatin context (3D genome + epigenomics) and signaling network state (phosphoproteomics-derived activities) to regime probabilities and kinetic parameters.
- Quantitative predictions for how specific regulatory modules (from CRISPR screens) shift mesoscale regimes, with uncertainty estimates.

4) Cancer-focused synthesis products:
- A mapping from TCGA/COSMIC DDR alterations to predicted regime shifts (e.g., increased persistence, altered coalescence, delayed dissolution), prioritized by evidence triangulation across DepMap dependencies and proteomic signatures.
- A set of “mesoscale biomarkers” (computable from imaging) that can be used by future studies to interpret DDR rewiring.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project advances understanding of emergence by explicitly characterizing DDR foci as mesoscale states with discrete regimes and transitions—an emergent description that cannot be reduced to single-protein behavior. By quantifying regime landscapes and linking them to network state and chromatin topology, we will provide a mechanistic account of how collective assembly produces threshold responses and pathway choice. The resulting framework is expected to generalize beyond DDR to other nuclear mesoscale assemblies (e.g., transcriptional condensates, replication factories), providing a blueprint for synthesis-driven mesoscale biology.

Broader impacts for molecular and cellular biology
- Resolving long-standing puzzles: The field has debated whether foci behave as liquid-like condensates, stable scaffolds, or context-dependent hybrids. A cross-study regime atlas will reconcile disparate observations by showing when and why different regimes occur.
- Enabling hypothesis generation without new experiments: Researchers will be able to query how perturbations and contexts map to regime shifts, guiding targeted follow-up work (outside the scope of this synthesis proposal).
- Bridging modalities: The project will connect spatial dynamics (imaging) with molecular state (phosphoproteomics) and nuclear architecture (3D genome), demonstrating a scalable approach for multimodal integration.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: At least two major manuscripts are anticipated: (i) the regime atlas and imaging methodology; (ii) the integrative model linking signaling and chromatin context to emergent regimes, with cancer-focused analyses.
- Community workshops: A hands-on training workshop (hosted with NCEMS) on OME-NGFF imaging synthesis, regime inference, and multimodal integration; materials will be released openly.
- Resource deposition: Derived feature tables and regime labels will be deposited in appropriate repositories (e.g., Zenodo with DOIs; links back to IDR/BioImage Archive accessions). Where feasible, we will contribute derived annotations back to imaging repositories.

Long-term sustainability
- The atlas and pipelines will be maintained as versioned releases with semantic versioning and archived DOIs (Zenodo). Workflows will be designed to be rerunnable as new public datasets appear.
- By adopting community standards (OME-NGFF, REMBI-aligned metadata, open licenses), the outputs will remain interoperable.
- The working group will cultivate a contributor model (issue templates, contribution guidelines, code review practices) to encourage external reuse and extension after the funding period.

Overall, the expected outcomes directly fulfill NCEMS goals: community-scale synthesis using only public data; development of innovative analytical strategies for mesoscale emergence; multidisciplinary collaboration; open, reproducible science; and training of a data-savvy workforce capable of integrating imaging, omics, and genome architecture to answer fundamental questions in molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Budget and Resources]
This project is designed as a community-scale synthesis effort requiring substantial coordination, computational infrastructure, and dedicated personnel to curate, harmonize, and integrate heterogeneous public datasets. The budget categories below are justified solely in service of synthesis (no experimental work, no sample generation).

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (computational):
  1) Quantitative imaging + time-series modeling postdoc to lead foci segmentation/tracking, feature extraction, and regime inference across IDR/BioImage Archive datasets.
  2) Multi-omics integration + causal inference postdoc to lead PRIDE processing, kinase activity inference, multimodal factor modeling, and genetics/cancer triangulation.
- 1 Graduate student (or equivalent trainee support): Cross-training across imaging and omics, leading a defined sub-aim (e.g., 3D genome context metrics and association models).
- 1 Research software engineer / scientific programmer (0.5–1.0 FTE): Essential for workflow engineering (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, CI, documentation, data packaging, and maintaining open repositories.
- Partial support for key personnel across collaborating labs (PI/co-I effort): Coordination, domain expertise (DDR biology, proteomics, 3D genomics), and supervision of trainees.
Justification: The scale and heterogeneity of data types (time-lapse imaging, phosphoproteomics, Hi-C/Micro-C, CRISPR screens, cancer genomics) requires dedicated specialists and engineering support beyond typical single-lab capacity.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or NCEMS/HPC allocations for:
  - Large-scale image processing (segmentation/tracking over many terabytes of time-lapse data).
  - Training/optimizing ML models for regime inference and representation learning.
  - Storage for intermediate OME-NGFF/Zarr conversions and derived feature tables.
- Budget includes object storage (S3-compatible) and egress where needed for moving derived products to public repositories.
Justification: Imaging synthesis is compute- and storage-intensive; centralized, scalable compute is required to ensure consistent processing and reproducibility.

Travel and collaboration
- Funds for 2–3 in-person working group meetings hosted at NCEMS (or NCEMS-designated venues) over 2–3 years, enabling intensive cross-disciplinary integration sprints.
- Travel support for trainees and early-career participants to attend these meetings and present outcomes at relevant conferences (bioimage analysis, DDR, 4DN/3D genomics, systems biology).
Justification: NCEMS’s model depends on convening diverse expertise; in-person synthesis accelerates consensus on metadata standards, model assumptions, and shared deliverables.

Workshops and training events
- Budget for at least one open training workshop (hybrid format) including:
  - Instructor time (covered via personnel),
  - Venue/AV support (if in person),
  - Participant support (priority to trainees),
  - Preparation of training datasets and compute environments.
Justification: Training is a core requirement; the workshop will disseminate reproducible pipelines and build the next-generation data-savvy workforce.

Open science infrastructure
- DOI and archiving costs via Zenodo (no direct cost typically) supplemented by:
  - Web hosting for documentation (e.g., ReadTheDocs/GitHub Pages) and optional small costs for domain/hosting if needed.
  - Support for long-term storage of derived datasets and models (mirrored copies and checksum validation).
Justification: Sustained, accessible dissemination of tools and derived products is essential for community reuse and aligns with NCEMS open science requirements.

Overall justification relative to synthesis goals
Each budget item directly supports the integration and harmonization of existing public datasets, the development of reproducible analytical workflows, and the collaborative working group activities required to produce community-scale synthesis outputs. No funds are allocated for laboratory experiments, reagents, sample collection, or any new data generation.

abstract_original:
DNA damage repair foci are mesoscale assemblies (100–1000 nm) where many proteins and chromatin regions co-localize, often with phase-separation-like properties. The emergent phenomenon is that collective recruitment and chromatin reorganization creates threshold responses, pathway choice (HR vs NHEJ), and repair timing not predictable from individual repair factors.

We will synthesize: (i) live-cell imaging datasets of repair foci dynamics (53BP1, RAD51, γH2AX) from IDR/BioImage Archive, including time-lapse series, (ii) proteomics and phosphoproteomics of DNA damage response (DDR) time courses (PRIDE), (iii) 3D genome and chromatin context maps (Hi-C/Micro-C from 4DN; ENCODE epigenomics), (iv) CRISPR screens for DDR genes and pathway choice modifiers (DepMap; published DDR screens), and (v) variant datasets for DDR genes in cancer (TCGA; COSMIC).

We will develop a unified model linking chromatin context and protein network state to mesoscale foci morphodynamics. Imaging analysis will quantify foci nucleation rates, growth/coalescence, and dissolution, extracting mesoscale kinetic parameters. We will integrate these with phosphoproteomic signaling states and with chromatin compartment features at damage-prone loci. Causal inference will identify regulators that shift foci dynamics and pathway choice.

Hypotheses: (1) repair foci exhibit discrete mesoscale dynamical regimes (diffuse recruitment vs coalescing droplets vs stable scaffolds) corresponding to repair pathway choice; (2) chromatin nanodomain topology constrains foci growth and coalescence; and (3) cancer-associated DDR alterations manifest as shifts in mesoscale regimes rather than complete pathway loss.

Expected insights include a cross-study atlas of foci dynamical regimes, mechanistic links between 3D genome context and emergent assembly kinetics, and open pipelines for foci tracking and integrative DDR modeling.

This requires collaboration among DDR biologists, quantitative imaging experts, proteomics analysts, and 3D genomics researchers. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous time-lapse datasets and omics, build reproducible multi-modal workflows, and train trainees in integrative analysis of mesoscale nuclear assemblies.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Patterning in Bacterial Division Machinery: A Synthesis of FtsZ Ring Architecture, Dynamics, and Cell Shape Outcomes

abstract_text:
Bacterial cytokinesis is driven by the FtsZ-based divisome, which forms a mesoscale ring/band (typically ~500–1000 nm circumference; ~10–50 nm filament bundles) with dynamic treadmilling. The emergent phenomenon is that collective filament organization and accessory protein patterning produce robust constriction and shape maintenance, not predictable from FtsZ polymerization alone.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution and cryo-ET datasets of divisome architecture across species (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) single-molecule and time-lapse measurements of FtsZ dynamics (published tracking datasets), (iii) proteomics and interaction networks of divisome components (PRIDE; BioGRID), (iv) comparative genomics of division genes across bacteria (NCBI RefSeq), and (v) morphological phenotypes under gene perturbations and antibiotics (BacDive; published high-content imaging screens).

We will quantify ring architecture (bundle thickness, continuity, patchiness) and dynamics (treadmilling speeds, turnover) and relate these to emergent cell shape outcomes (septum symmetry, division timing, size control). Using statistical physics models of active polymers and agent-based simulations, calibrated to observed architectures, we will infer which mesoscale parameters control robustness. Comparative analysis will test how different bacteria achieve similar division outcomes with different accessory proteins.

Hypotheses: (1) divisomes operate in a constrained mesoscale regime where filament dynamics and crosslinking yield self-correcting constriction; (2) accessory proteins tune emergent ring continuity and force distribution; and (3) antibiotic susceptibilities reflect shifts in mesoscale architecture rather than direct inhibition levels.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of divisome mesoscale architectures, quantitative links between architecture and division robustness, and open tools for analyzing divisome imaging. This synthesis will unify structural and dynamical observations into general principles of emergent cytokinetic machinery.

Team science is required across bacterial cell biology, quantitative microscopy, biophysics, and comparative genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated data curation and development of reproducible pipelines and training for trainees at the interface of mesoscale structure and emergent cellular morphogenesis.

[Abstract]
Bacterial cytokinesis is driven by the FtsZ-based divisome, which forms a mesoscale ring/band (typically ~500–1000 nm circumference; ~10–50 nm filament bundles) with dynamic treadmilling. Using statistical physics models of active polymers and agent-based simulations, calibrated to observed architectures, we will infer which mesoscale parameters control robustness. Comparative analysis will test how different bacteria achieve similar division outcomes with different accessory proteins.

Hypotheses: (1) divisomes operate in a constrained mesoscale regime where filament dynamics and crosslinking yield self-correcting constriction; (2) accessory proteins tune emergent ring continuity and force distribution; and (3) antibiotic susceptibilities reflect shifts in mesoscale architecture rather than direct inhibition levels.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of divisome mesoscale architectures, quantitative links between architecture and division robustness, and open tools for analyzing divisome imaging. This synthesis will unify structural and dynamical observations into general principles of emergent cytokinetic machinery.

Team science is required across bacterial cell biology, quantitative microscopy, biophysics, and comparative genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated data curation and development of reproducible pipelines and training for trainees at the interface of mesoscale structure and emergent cellular morphogenesis.

[Background and Significance]
Bacterial division is a canonical example of mesoscale emergence: molecular-scale polymerization and protein–protein interactions give rise to a robust, self-organized cellular-scale outcome—midcell constriction that preserves size control and shape. The core driver of cytokinesis in most bacteria is FtsZ, a tubulin homolog that polymerizes into short protofilaments and higher-order bundles that assemble into a “Z-ring” or band at midcell. Although the biochemical properties of FtsZ (GTP binding/hydrolysis, polymerization dynamics) are well characterized, the central puzzle remains: how do ensembles of relatively weak, dynamic filaments and diverse accessory proteins reliably generate a symmetric, coordinated constriction that is resilient to noise, perturbations, and species-to-species variation?

NCEMS’ focus on mesoscale emergence is particularly well matched to the divisome. The relevant organizational scale—tens to hundreds of nanometers—sits between individual molecules (FtsZ monomers and binding partners) and organelles/cellular morphology (septum formation, cell elongation, and daughter-cell symmetry). At this scale, the system’s behavior is not predictable from single-molecule properties alone because collective effects dominate: steric interactions among filaments, cooperative crosslinking, membrane coupling, curvature constraints, and spatially patterned recruitment of enzymes that synthesize and remodel the cell wall. The emergent phenomenon is therefore the appearance of robust constriction dynamics and shape outcomes from a fluctuating, heterogeneous, and species-specific set of components.

Existing studies using super-resolution microscopy (e.g., PALM, STORM, SIM), single-molecule tracking, and cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) have revealed key features of Z-ring organization: discontinuous “patchy” rings, variable ring thickness, dynamic filament bundles, and treadmilling motion that guides septal peptidoglycan (sPG) synthesis. Cryo-ET has provided near-native views of filament bundles in some organisms, while super-resolution has quantified ring widths and spatial heterogeneity in others. Time-lapse and single-particle tracking have measured treadmilling speeds, filament lifetimes, and turnover. In parallel, proteomics and interaction mapping have identified a broad set of divisome-associated proteins (FtsA, ZipA, ZapA/B/C/D, SepF, EzrA, FtsEX, FtsQLB, FtsW/I, and many lineage-specific factors) and their regulatory relationships. Comparative genomics shows that while FtsZ is broadly conserved, accessory modules vary widely, suggesting that many bacteria achieve similar functional outcomes through different mesoscale “designs.”

Despite this wealth of publicly available data, synthesis across modalities and species has lagged. Most analyses remain siloed: imaging papers quantify ring dimensions but do not systematically integrate proteomic composition; dynamics studies report treadmilling but rarely connect to ultrastructure; and comparative genomics catalogs gene presence/absence without mapping to mesoscale ring phenotypes. This fragmentation prevents the field from answering fundamental questions about emergence: Which mesoscale parameters are conserved “control knobs” for robust division? Which aspects of architecture and dynamics are interchangeable across lineages, and which are constrained? How do accessory proteins tune collective filament organization to buffer perturbations? Why do antibiotics or genetic perturbations sometimes produce similar morphological phenotypes despite different molecular targets?

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address these gaps because the necessary evidence already exists across repositories and publications, but requires coordinated curation, harmonization, and integrative modeling beyond what individual labs can accomplish. Key enabling data sources include: (i) the BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource (IDR) for microscopy datasets, (ii) EMPIAR for cryo-ET and related electron microscopy volumes, (iii) PRIDE for quantitative proteomics of bacterial proteomes and complexes, (iv) BioGRID (and complementary interaction resources) for curated protein–protein interactions, (v) NCBI RefSeq for standardized genome sequences and annotations across thousands of bacterial taxa, and (vi) BacDive and published high-content imaging screens for morphology and growth phenotypes under perturbations.

By integrating these resources, we can build a cross-species, multi-modal atlas linking divisome composition (genes/proteins), mesoscale organization (ring continuity, thickness, filament orientation), dynamics (treadmilling speed, turnover), and emergent outcomes (septum symmetry, division timing, size distributions, antibiotic sensitivity phenotypes). Such an atlas would enable statistical inference of conserved mesoscale regimes and facilitate mechanistic modeling using active polymer physics and agent-based simulations constrained by real measurements.

Understanding emergent mesoscale patterning in bacterial division has broad significance. It advances fundamental cell biology by revealing general principles of how dynamic polymers and accessory networks self-organize to control morphogenesis. It informs antimicrobial strategies by clarifying how perturbations shift mesoscale architecture and thereby alter susceptibility and failure modes. It also provides a tractable model system for NCEMS’ mission: leveraging AI and data science to unify heterogeneous public datasets into predictive understanding of emergent behavior at the mesoscale.

This proposal therefore targets a clear synthesis opportunity: convert dispersed, heterogeneous divisome datasets into an integrated, open, and reusable framework that explains how collective filament organization and accessory patterning produce robust cytokinesis across bacterial diversity.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address a set of precise, testable questions about mesoscale emergence in the FtsZ-based divisome. Each question is framed to be answerable using existing publicly available datasets and to yield measurable predictions that can be validated via cross-dataset comparisons rather than new experiments.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): What mesoscale architectural “state variables” of the FtsZ ring are conserved across bacteria, and which are lineage-specific adaptations?
We define state variables as quantitative descriptors of organization at ~10–500 nm scales: ring/band width, radial thickness, circumferential continuity (gap statistics), patch size distribution, filament/bundle orientation relative to circumference, bundle density proxies, and spatial co-localization patterns with key anchors/crosslinkers.
Hypothesis 1 (H1): Across diverse bacteria, divisomes occupy a constrained manifold in architectural state space (a limited set of feasible mesoscale configurations), even when accessory protein repertoires differ.
Predictions: (i) Multi-species imaging data will cluster into a small number of architectural archetypes (e.g., continuous thin ring, patchy thick band, helical/distributed structures) rather than showing a continuum; (ii) archetype membership will correlate with cell envelope type (Gram-negative vs Gram-positive), growth mode, and presence/absence of specific accessory modules.
Validation: Use harmonized measurements from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR to compute state variables and perform unsupervised clustering with stability analysis; test associations with genomic features from RefSeq.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): How do dynamics (treadmilling speed, turnover, processivity) couple to mesoscale architecture to produce robust constriction and symmetric septation?
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Robust division emerges when dynamics and architecture satisfy a “self-correcting regime” in which treadmilling and crosslinking jointly minimize spatial heterogeneity in force/cell-wall synthesis around the circumference.
Predictions: (i) Across datasets, higher continuity (fewer/lower variance gaps) will be associated with reduced septum eccentricity and lower variability in division timing; (ii) there will be a compensatory relationship between treadmilling speed and continuity (e.g., patchier rings require faster treadmilling to maintain uniform synthesis), producing similar outcomes via different parameter combinations.
Validation: Extract dynamics metrics from published single-molecule/time-lapse tracking datasets; relate to architecture metrics and to phenotypic outputs (division timing distributions, symmetry proxies) where available. Use meta-analytic mixed models with study/species random effects to account for protocol differences.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): Which accessory proteins act as mesoscale “tuning knobs” that shift the ring between architectural/dynamic regimes?
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Accessory proteins primarily influence emergent behavior by modulating mesoscale coupling parameters—effective filament crosslinking, membrane attachment density, and spatial persistence length—rather than by simply increasing total FtsZ abundance.
Predictions: (i) Presence/absence (or relative abundance) of specific crosslinkers/anchors (e.g., Zap proteins, SepF, FtsA/ZipA analogs, EzrA) will predict systematic shifts in continuity and thickness across species; (ii) perturbations targeting these proteins in high-content screens will disproportionately alter architectural state variables compared to perturbations of unrelated pathways.
Validation: Integrate PRIDE proteomics (relative abundance where available), BioGRID interactions (network centrality/complex membership), and RefSeq gene inventories; link to imaging-derived architecture and to perturbation phenotypes from BacDive and published screens.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Can antibiotic and genetic perturbation phenotypes be explained as shifts in mesoscale divisome state rather than direct molecular inhibition strength?
Hypothesis 4 (H4): Antibiotics affecting cell wall synthesis and division-associated processes induce characteristic trajectories through divisome state space (architecture–dynamics), and these trajectories predict morphological failure modes (filamentation, lysis, minicells) better than target identity alone.
Predictions: (i) Perturbations with distinct targets (e.g., PBP inhibitors vs membrane-acting agents) can converge on similar mesoscale states that precede similar phenotypes; (ii) susceptibility patterns across species will align with baseline mesoscale regime and accessory composition.
Validation: Use published imaging screens and BacDive phenotype annotations to categorize outcomes; where imaging is available, quantify architecture; otherwise infer likely state shifts using trained predictive models grounded in datasets with paired architecture/phenotype.

Research Question 5 (RQ5): What minimal mechanistic models, constrained by real measurements, reproduce observed mesoscale regimes and their robustness?
Hypothesis 5 (H5): A small set of effective parameters—polymer turnover rate, treadmilling bias, crosslinking strength, membrane coupling density, and curvature constraint—can reproduce the empirically observed architectural manifold and predict robustness metrics.
Predictions: (i) Agent-based simulations of active filaments on a curved membrane will generate the same archetypes discovered in RQ1 when parameterized within empirically inferred ranges; (ii) robustness (low variance in constriction symmetry) will peak in a bounded region of parameter space corresponding to the “self-correcting regime.”
Validation: Fit model parameters using approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) or simulation-based inference to match distributions of measured state variables; validate by predicting withheld species/datasets and comparing predicted archetype and phenotype associations.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses aim to transform descriptive observations into quantitative, cross-species principles of mesoscale emergence in cytokinetic machinery, using synthesis and integration of existing public data as the primary engine of discovery.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and working-group structure
This is a synthesis-only, community-scale integration project. We will not generate any new experimental data. Instead, we will curate, harmonize, and jointly analyze existing public datasets spanning imaging, dynamics, proteomics, interaction networks, comparative genomics, and morphology phenotypes. The working group will operate through coordinated “data-to-model” sprints at NCEMS (in-person and hybrid), with shared repositories, standardized metadata templates, and reproducible pipelines.

1) Specific data sources (public repositories)
Imaging—super-resolution and time-lapse:
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI) for raw microscopy datasets and associated metadata.
- Image Data Resource (IDR) for curated, annotated imaging studies and screen data.
- Zenodo / Figshare / Dryad / OSF for published supplementary imaging and tracking datasets (study-specific DOIs).
Ultrastructure—cryo-ET / EM:
- EMPIAR (Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive) for raw cryo-ET tilt series and reconstructed volumes.
- EMDB (Electron Microscopy Data Bank) for derived maps where available.
Proteomics:
- PRIDE (Proteomics Identifications Database) for quantitative proteomics, interaction pulldowns, and global proteome datasets in bacteria.
Interaction networks:
- BioGRID for curated protein–protein interactions, including bacterial interactions where available.
- (Optional complementary integration) IntAct for additional curated interactions.
Comparative genomics:
- NCBI RefSeq genomes and annotations (including assembly metadata and taxonomy).
- eggNOG-mapper / COG annotations (derived from public resources) for functional classification.
Morphology/phenotypes:
- BacDive for strain-level phenotype annotations (morphology, growth conditions, antibiotic responses where curated).
- Published high-content bacterial morphology screens (e.g., antibiotic profiling and gene knockdown/knockout imaging studies deposited in IDR or as open supplements).

2) Data curation and harmonization
2.1 Metadata schema
We will define a divisome-specific metadata standard (JSON/YAML) capturing: species/strain, growth condition (temperature, medium), imaging modality, labeling strategy, frame rate, pixel size, reconstruction parameters (for cryo-ET), perturbations (gene/antibiotic), and reported outputs (division time, size distributions). We will map existing metadata fields from BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR into this schema and record provenance.

2.2 Harmonizing imaging measurements
- Spatial calibration: convert all measurements to nm using pixel sizes/voxel sizes.
- Quality control: automated checks for SNR, segmentation confidence, motion blur (time-lapse), and tomogram resolution proxies.
- Batch effects: record microscope modality and processing pipeline; incorporate as covariates in downstream statistical models.

2.3 Harmonizing genomics and protein identifiers
- Use RefSeq accessions as canonical genome identifiers.
- Map gene/protein names to stable identifiers (RefSeq protein IDs; UniProt where cross-referenced).
- Build orthogroups for divisome components using public orthology resources (eggNOG/COG) and HMM-based searches using existing profiles (no new sequencing).

3) Quantifying mesoscale architecture and dynamics
3.1 Architecture extraction from super-resolution
We will develop/standardize analysis modules to quantify:
- Ring/band width (radial spread), thickness, and intensity profile.
- Continuity/gap statistics: detect circumferential signal and compute gap length distributions, patch size distributions, and circular variance.
- Patchiness indices: e.g., Gini coefficient of intensity along circumference; power spectrum of angular intensity.
Methods:
- Segmentation using classical + ML approaches: U-Net–style segmentation models trained on existing annotated datasets where available (IDR annotations), with transfer learning and careful documentation of training data provenance.
- Skeletonization and circular unwrapping: map ring signal to angular coordinate for standardized comparison.

3.2 Architecture extraction from cryo-ET
From EMPIAR/EMDB tomograms we will quantify:
- Filament/bundle density proxies and orientation distributions.
- Bundle thickness distributions (where resolution allows).
- Spatial relationships between filaments and membrane.
Methods:
- Use existing open tools (e.g., IMOD, Dynamo, EMAN2) for tomogram handling.
- Apply filament tracing approaches (template matching where appropriate, or semi-automated tracing where public segmentations exist). When only derived segmentations are available publicly, we will use them; we will not create new experimental reconstructions.

3.3 Dynamics extraction from published tracking
- Collect published FtsZ treadmilling trajectories and time-lapse kymographs (from open deposits).
- Compute treadmilling speed distributions, directional persistence, turnover proxies (residence time), and spatial heterogeneity of motion.
Methods:
- Re-analysis using standardized tracking metrics (e.g., mean squared displacement variants for directed motion; hidden Markov models to segment motion states).
- Where raw movies exist, apply particle tracking using open software (TrackMate/Fiji, u-track equivalents in Python) with documented parameters.

4) Integrative synthesis: linking composition → architecture/dynamics → phenotype
4.1 Multimodal data integration
We will build a “Divisome Emergence Atlas” with a relational core:
- Species/strain table (RefSeq taxonomy)
- Gene repertoire table (presence/absence, orthogroups)
- Proteomics abundance table (PRIDE-derived)
- Interaction network table (BioGRID/IntAct)
- Imaging-derived architecture table
- Dynamics table
- Phenotype table (morphology, division timing, antibiotic responses)

4.2 Statistical modeling
- Hierarchical (multilevel) models to relate architecture/dynamics to phenotypes while accounting for study-level batch effects.
- Regularized regression / Bayesian variable selection to identify accessory proteins (or network modules) predictive of mesoscale state variables.
- Causal-leaning analyses where feasible using perturbation metadata (gene knockdowns/antibiotics) as “interventions,” with careful limitations stated.

4.3 Machine learning (explainable, not black-box)
- Unsupervised learning (Gaussian mixture models, spectral clustering, UMAP for visualization) to identify architectural archetypes.
- Supervised models (random forests, gradient boosting, or Bayesian additive regression trees) to predict phenotype classes from mesoscale variables, with SHAP-like interpretability to identify key drivers.
- Cross-validation stratified by species and by study to test generalization.

5) Mechanistic modeling constrained by data
5.1 Active polymer/statistical physics models
We will adapt existing models of treadmilling filaments on curved surfaces with crosslinking and membrane attachment. Key effective parameters: polymerization bias, turnover, crosslinking strength, membrane coupling density, curvature constraint.

5.2 Agent-based simulations
- Simulate ensembles of filaments on a cylindrical membrane with circumferential preference and dynamic turnover.
- Output synthetic observables matching measured state variables (continuity, patchiness, width, orientation distributions).

5.3 Parameter inference and validation
- Use simulation-based inference (e.g., ABC, neural posterior estimation where appropriate) to infer parameter ranges that reproduce observed archetypes.
- Validate by predicting withheld species/datasets (architecture archetype and robustness proxies) and comparing to measured values.
No experimental validation will be performed; validation is strictly cross-dataset and out-of-sample prediction.

6) Cross-dataset validation and positive controls
- Positive controls: datasets from well-studied organisms (e.g., Escherichia coli, Bacillus subtilis) where multiple modalities exist; check that inferred archetypes and parameter ranges align with consensus literature.
- Negative controls: proteins unrelated to division (random gene sets matched for prevalence) to test specificity of accessory-protein predictors.
- Sensitivity analyses: re-run models excluding particular modalities (e.g., without proteomics) to test robustness of conclusions.

7) Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Working group kickoff; finalize metadata schema and governance.
- Compile candidate datasets from BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR/PRIDE/BioGRID/RefSeq/BacDive.
- Release v0.1 curated index (dataset registry + provenance).

Months 6–12:
- Implement reproducible pipelines for architecture and dynamics extraction.
- Pilot on 3–5 species with multi-modal coverage.
- Release v0.5 “Divisome Emergence Atlas” with initial measurements.

Months 12–18:
- Scale to broader taxonomic coverage (dozens of species where data exist).
- Perform clustering to define architectural archetypes; publish preprint on atlas and archetypes.

Months 18–24:
- Integrate genomics/proteomics/interaction networks; identify accessory tuning knobs.
- Build predictive models linking mesoscale variables to phenotypes.

Months 24–30:
- Fit mechanistic models; identify self-correcting regime and compensatory parameter relationships.
- Release v1.0 atlas + open tools; submit final synthesis manuscripts; host capstone training workshop.

8) Team composition (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
This project requires expertise beyond a single lab:
- Bacterial cell division biologists (interpretation of divisome components, phenotypes).
- Quantitative microscopists/computer vision experts (super-resolution analysis, segmentation QC).
- Cryo-ET analysts (tomogram handling, filament tracing, ultrastructure quantification).
- Biophysicists/statistical physicists (active polymer modeling, emergent regime analysis).
- Comparative genomics/bioinformatics experts (orthology, gene repertoire mapping).
- Data scientists/software engineers (database design, workflow automation, reproducibility).
- Trainees (graduate students/postdocs) embedded across tasks for workforce development.

NCEMS support is essential to coordinate these groups, host synthesis sprints, provide collaborative cyberinfrastructure, and ensure open, reusable outputs that are larger in scope than any existing collaboration.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables (specific, measurable outputs)
1) Divisome Emergence Atlas (public, versioned)
We will release a curated, versioned, cross-species atlas that links (where available) imaging-derived mesoscale architecture, dynamics metrics, divisome gene repertoires, proteomics abundance summaries, interaction network features, and perturbation-associated phenotypes. The atlas will include:
- A machine-readable dataset registry with DOIs/accessions and provenance (BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR/PRIDE/BioGRID/RefSeq/BacDive links).
- Standardized measurement tables for architecture and dynamics with uncertainty estimates.
- Harmonized metadata and batch-effect covariates to enable reuse.

2) Open-source analysis toolkit for divisome imaging and dynamics
We will deliver a maintained software package (Python-first, with Fiji interoperability) implementing:
- Ring/band segmentation and circular unwrapping.
- Continuity/patchiness metrics and standardized reporting.
- Dynamics metric extraction from trajectories/kymographs.
- Quality control reports and reproducible figure generation.

3) Cross-species classification of mesoscale architectural archetypes
Using unsupervised clustering and stability analysis, we will define and publish a set of empirically supported mesoscale “archetypes” of FtsZ ring organization. Each archetype will be associated with quantitative descriptors and representative example datasets. This creates a common vocabulary and quantitative framework for comparing divisomes across taxa.

4) Quantitative links between mesoscale state variables and emergent outcomes
We will produce synthesis results that connect architecture and dynamics to emergent phenotypes:
- Statistical models relating continuity/patchiness and treadmilling distributions to septation symmetry proxies, division timing variability, and size control measures where available.
- Cross-validated predictors of phenotype classes (e.g., filamentation vs minicell formation) from mesoscale variables.
These results will move the field from qualitative statements (“patchy rings exist”) to quantitative, predictive relationships.

5) Mechanistic models constrained by data: identifying a “self-correcting regime”
We will deliver mechanistic modeling outputs that explain how robust constriction can emerge from dynamic filaments:
- Parameter regimes in active-polymer/agent-based models that reproduce observed archetypes.
- Evidence for compensatory relationships (e.g., faster treadmilling offsetting increased patchiness) that enable robustness.
- Interpretable mapping from accessory protein modules to effective mesoscale parameters (crosslinking, membrane coupling).

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project directly advances NCEMS’ mission by extracting general principles of emergence at the mesoscale:
- It identifies conserved state variables and constrained manifolds—signatures of emergent organization that transcend molecular details.
- It explains robustness as a property of collective dynamics (treadmilling + crosslinking + geometry) rather than a single molecular interaction.
- It clarifies how diverse accessory networks can implement similar emergent outcomes via different parameter combinations (“many-to-one” mapping), a hallmark of emergence.

Broader impacts for molecular and cellular biology
- Generalizable framework: The atlas-and-model approach can be adapted to other mesoscale assemblies (e.g., actin rings, ESCRT systems, bacterial cytoskeletal filaments), providing a template for NCEMS-style synthesis.
- Antimicrobial relevance: By connecting perturbation phenotypes to mesoscale state shifts, the work can inform interpretation of antibiotic synergy/antagonism and failure modes without claiming new drug discovery.
- Community resource: Standard metrics and open pipelines will lower barriers for reanalysis and meta-analysis, enabling future studies to be comparable by design.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: (i) Atlas + archetypes manuscript; (ii) composition–architecture–phenotype synthesis; (iii) mechanistic modeling of self-correcting regime.
- NCEMS-hosted workshops: annual hybrid training on imaging quantification, data integration, and simulation-based inference for mesoscale biology.
- Database deposition: measurement tables and metadata will be deposited in Zenodo with DOIs; code archived via Zenodo releases; pointers to original datasets maintained.

Long-term sustainability
- Versioning and governance: semantic versioning for atlas releases; clear contribution guidelines; issue tracking.
- Interoperability: export formats compatible with common bioimage standards (OME-NGFF references where applicable) and with community repositories.
- Maintenance plan: designate a software maintainer (research software engineer) during the award; after award, transition to a lightweight community-maintained model with documented build/test pipelines and a steering subgroup drawn from the working group.

Overall, the expected outcomes will unify structural, dynamical, and compositional observations into a rigorous, predictive account of how bacterial cytokinesis emerges from mesoscale patterning—delivering reusable data products, tools, and mechanistic insight aligned with NCEMS goals.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy and alignment with NCEMS
This project is a synthesis working group requiring coordinated, multi-institution collaboration, substantial data curation, and shared computational workflows. The budget prioritizes personnel for integration and reproducible software, computing for large-scale reanalysis of public datasets, and travel/workshops to catalyze collaboration and trainee development. No funds are requested for experimental reagents, sample collection, or new data generation.

Personnel (largest cost driver)
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (24–30 months each; distributed across partner institutions):
  1) Quantitative bioimage/data integration postdoc to lead architecture/dynamics extraction pipelines, QC, and atlas assembly.
  2) Biophysics/modeling postdoc to lead active polymer/agent-based modeling and simulation-based inference.
- 1 Research Software Engineer / programmer-analyst (50–100% effort, 30 months): builds and maintains the open-source toolkit, workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, CI testing, and documentation.
- Graduate student support (1–2 trainees across institutions, partial support): focuses on comparative genomics/orthogroup mapping and phenotype harmonization; gains training in reproducible synthesis science.
- Faculty/PI effort (modest, distributed): coordination, supervision, and working-group facilitation; ensures domain expertise across imaging, cryo-ET, microbiology, genomics, and statistics.
Justification: Personnel are essential because synthesis requires sustained curation, harmonization, and software development that cannot be achieved through short-term student projects alone.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations for:
  - downloading and processing large imaging volumes (BioImage Archive/IDR) and cryo-ET datasets (EMPIAR),
  - running segmentation and feature extraction at scale,
  - performing simulation-based inference and agent-based model sweeps.
- Storage costs for cached subsets and derived products (feature tables, QC reports, intermediate standardized representations), with clear retention policies.
Justification: While raw data remain in public repositories, compute and temporary storage are required to reprocess heterogeneous datasets reproducibly and to run computationally intensive modeling.

Travel and collaboration
- NCEMS working-group meetings: support for 2–3 in-person synthesis sprints (e.g., 3–5 days each) with participants from multiple institutions, including trainees.
- Conference travel for dissemination (selected team members/trainees): present atlas, tools, and mechanistic findings at relevant meetings (e.g., ASCB, Biophysical Society, bacterial cell biology-focused conferences).
Justification: Community-scale synthesis depends on face-to-face coordination to align standards, resolve integration bottlenecks, and accelerate cross-disciplinary exchange.

Workshops and training events
- Annual hybrid training workshop hosted with NCEMS support:
  - curriculum development time (RSE + postdocs),
  - speaker/participant travel support (priority to trainees and underrepresented institutions),
  - compute support for hands-on sessions (temporary cloud instances).
Justification: Training is a core NCEMS goal; workshops also broaden the user base and improve sustainability of outputs.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo archiving (no direct cost) but budget time/personnel for packaging releases.
- Domain registration or lightweight project website hosting (if needed) for documentation hub.
- Optional costs for persistent identifiers and long-term documentation builds (e.g., ReadTheDocs-like services) if not freely available.
Justification: Making tools and derived datasets truly reusable requires professional-grade documentation, release management, and stable access points.

Overall, the requested resources directly support NCEMS-aligned synthesis: integrating existing public data, enabling multi-lab collaboration, producing open and reproducible tools/datasets, and training a data-savvy workforce—without any experimental data generation.

abstract_original:
Bacterial cytokinesis is driven by the FtsZ-based divisome, which forms a mesoscale ring/band (typically ~500–1000 nm circumference; ~10–50 nm filament bundles) with dynamic treadmilling. The emergent phenomenon is that collective filament organization and accessory protein patterning produce robust constriction and shape maintenance, not predictable from FtsZ polymerization alone.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution and cryo-ET datasets of divisome architecture across species (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) single-molecule and time-lapse measurements of FtsZ dynamics (published tracking datasets), (iii) proteomics and interaction networks of divisome components (PRIDE; BioGRID), (iv) comparative genomics of division genes across bacteria (NCBI RefSeq), and (v) morphological phenotypes under gene perturbations and antibiotics (BacDive; published high-content imaging screens).

We will quantify ring architecture (bundle thickness, continuity, patchiness) and dynamics (treadmilling speeds, turnover) and relate these to emergent cell shape outcomes (septum symmetry, division timing, size control). Using statistical physics models of active polymers and agent-based simulations, calibrated to observed architectures, we will infer which mesoscale parameters control robustness. Comparative analysis will test how different bacteria achieve similar division outcomes with different accessory proteins.

Hypotheses: (1) divisomes operate in a constrained mesoscale regime where filament dynamics and crosslinking yield self-correcting constriction; (2) accessory proteins tune emergent ring continuity and force distribution; and (3) antibiotic susceptibilities reflect shifts in mesoscale architecture rather than direct inhibition levels.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of divisome mesoscale architectures, quantitative links between architecture and division robustness, and open tools for analyzing divisome imaging. This synthesis will unify structural and dynamical observations into general principles of emergent cytokinetic machinery.

Team science is required across bacterial cell biology, quantitative microscopy, biophysics, and comparative genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated data curation and development of reproducible pipelines and training for trainees at the interface of mesoscale structure and emergent cellular morphogenesis.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of Exosome Biogenesis Microdomains: Integrating Endosomal Proteomics, Lipidomics, and Imaging

abstract_text:
Exosomes originate from intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) within multivesicular bodies, formed in mesoscale endosomal microdomains (50–500 nm) enriched in ESCRT components, tetraspanins, and specific lipids. The emergent phenomenon is that collective microdomain organization yields selective cargo sorting and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual sorting motifs.

We will synthesize: (i) exosome and endosome proteomics datasets (ExoCarta/Vesiclepedia-linked studies; PRIDE), (ii) lipidomics of extracellular vesicles and endosomal fractions (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), (iii) imaging datasets of ILV formation and endosomal microdomains (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR for EM of MVBs), (iv) RNA cargo profiles (exosomal RNA-seq in GEO), and (v) perturbation screens affecting EV secretion (DepMap; published CRISPR screens).

We will quantify ILV size distributions and microdomain organization from EM and fluorescence images using segmentation and spatial clustering metrics. Multi-omic integration will identify latent microdomain states defined by protein–lipid–RNA composition. Mechanistic modeling will connect ESCRT polymerization and membrane composition to observed ILV size distributions using coarse-grained membrane remodeling models. Predictive models will link microdomain states to cargo enrichment patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) exosome biogenesis proceeds through discrete mesoscale microdomain states that determine cargo classes; (2) lipid composition (ceramides, cholesterol) acts as a mesoscale controller of domain stability and ILV size; and (3) cell-type differences in EV cargo reflect microdomain state occupancy more than expression of individual cargos.

Expected insights include a unified mesoscale model of ILV microdomains, identification of compositional signatures predicting cargo selection, and open resources for EV biogenesis imaging/omics integration.

This requires team science across membrane biology, proteomics/lipidomics, quantitative imaging, and biophysical modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize diverse public datasets and establish open, reproducible pipelines and training for trainees in integrative mesoscale analysis of extracellular vesicle biogenesis.
