[Background and Significance]
Exosomes are a major class of extracellular vesicles (EVs) generated as intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) within multivesicular bodies (MVBs) and released upon fusion with the plasma membrane. Despite intense interest in exosomes as mediators of intercellular communication and as biomarkers, the cellular logic that produces selective cargo packaging and characteristic vesicle size distributions remains incompletely explained. A central challenge is that exosome biogenesis is governed by mesoscale organization: nanoscale interactions among proteins and lipids assemble into microdomains (roughly 50–500 nm) on endosomal membranes that collectively drive membrane deformation, budding, and cargo enrichment. These microdomains involve ESCRT complexes (0–III and accessory factors such as ALIX/PDCD6IP and VPS4), tetraspanins (CD9, CD63, CD81), syntenin (SDCBP), and lipid features such as cholesterol, ceramides, and phosphoinositides. At this intermediate scale—between individual molecules and whole organelles—new system properties emerge, including cooperative membrane remodeling, phase-like domain stabilization, and selective capture of cargo classes.

Current mechanistic understanding has largely been built from targeted perturbations and focused biochemical assays, which identify candidate sorting motifs (e.g., ubiquitin-dependent recognition by ESCRT-0, or syntenin–ALIX–heparan sulfate proteoglycan pathways) and lipid drivers (e.g., neutral sphingomyelinase/ceramide-associated budding). However, these mechanisms do not fully account for three persistent observations: (i) exosome cargo is highly context- and cell-type-dependent even when many canonical sorting components are expressed; (ii) ILV/exosome sizes exhibit distributions that vary systematically across conditions and cell types; and (iii) multiple partially redundant pathways yield exosomes with distinct molecular signatures. These patterns suggest that exosome biogenesis is not a single linear pathway but rather a set of mesoscale “microdomain states” whose collective composition and physical organization determine emergent outcomes.

A major opportunity is that the last decade has produced a large, fragmented body of public data that—if integrated—can directly address mesoscale emergence without generating new experiments. Proteomics resources such as ExoCarta and Vesiclepedia curate thousands of EV protein identifications linked to underlying studies; PRIDE hosts raw mass spectrometry datasets enabling reprocessing and cross-study harmonization. Lipidomics data are increasingly available via Metabolomics Workbench and LIPID MAPS, including EV lipid profiles and, in some cases, endosomal fraction lipidomes. Imaging repositories now provide access to raw and annotated microscopy data: the BioImage Archive and the Image Data Resource (IDR) contain fluorescence imaging datasets relevant to endosomal organization and EV-related markers, while EMPIAR hosts electron microscopy datasets that can capture ILV morphology and MVB ultrastructure. RNA cargo profiles are abundant in GEO and SRA, including small RNA-seq and total RNA-seq from exosomes/EVs across many cell types and perturbations. Finally, functional perturbation data—particularly CRISPR knockout screens and genetic dependency resources—are accessible through DepMap, as well as published EV secretion screens with deposited gene-level scores.

What is missing is an NCEMS-style community-scale synthesis that integrates these disparate modalities to quantify microdomain organization and connect it to emergent outcomes. Individual labs typically specialize in one modality (e.g., proteomics or imaging) and cannot feasibly harmonize raw data across repositories, standardize metadata, and build mechanistic models spanning composition and physical organization. Moreover, mesoscale emergence demands joint analysis: microdomain composition (protein/lipid/RNA) must be interpreted together with microdomain morphology (spatial clustering, budding geometry, ILV size distributions) and with perturbation response (which genes shift microdomain state occupancy or alter ILV statistics). Without integration, the field risks continuing to accumulate lists of cargo and factors without a unifying mesoscale theory.

Mesoscale emergent phenomena are important because they represent the “organizational layer” where molecular interactions are amplified into organelle-scale outcomes. In exosome biogenesis, microdomains are expected to behave as cooperative assemblies: ESCRT polymers can generate curvature and scission in a geometry-dependent manner; tetraspanins can scaffold membrane proteins and organize nanoclusters; and lipids can modulate line tension, curvature preference, and domain stability. The emergent output—selective cargo sorting and vesicle size distributions—cannot be predicted from single-molecule affinities alone. Understanding these emergent rules would provide a principled basis for interpreting EV heterogeneity, reconciling apparently conflicting mechanistic studies, and identifying which aspects of EV cargo are robust versus state-dependent.

Existing public data now enable new insights because they collectively span (i) composition across many contexts (proteomics, lipidomics, RNA), (ii) morphology and spatial organization (EM and fluorescence imaging), and (iii) causal levers (genetic perturbation screens). By synthesizing these data into a common framework, we can infer latent microdomain states, quantify their occupancy across cell types and conditions, and build mechanistic models linking composition to ILV geometry. This proposal directly aligns with NCEMS goals: it is strictly synthesis-based (no new data generation), requires multidisciplinary collaboration, advances mesoscale emergence science, and will produce open, reusable resources and training for a data-savvy workforce.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address how mesoscale endosomal microdomains give rise to emergent, system-level properties of exosome biogenesis—specifically selective cargo sorting and ILV size distributions. We focus on questions that are testable using existing public datasets spanning composition, morphology, and perturbations.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): Do exosome-producing endosomes occupy a discrete set of mesoscale “microdomain states” that recur across cell types and studies?
Rationale: EV studies often report partially overlapping cargo sets and pathway dependencies, suggesting multiple stable or metastable organizational regimes rather than a single continuum.
Hypothesis 1 (H1): A small number of latent microdomain states—defined by joint protein–lipid–RNA composition and associated morphological signatures—can explain a substantial fraction of cross-study variability in EV cargo and ILV size distributions.
Measurable predictions: (i) Unsupervised integration of proteomics, lipidomics, and RNA cargo data will yield clusters/components that are reproducible across independent datasets (e.g., ExoCarta-linked studies reprocessed from PRIDE; lipidomics from Metabolomics Workbench; RNA-seq from GEO). (ii) These states will correspond to distinct imaging-derived features (e.g., ILV size distribution parameters, MVB ILV counts, microdomain clustering indices) in EMPIAR and BioImage Archive/IDR datasets where marker information is available. (iii) State assignments will be more predictive of cargo class enrichment (e.g., tetraspanins, ESCRT-associated proteins, RNA-binding proteins, specific miRNA families) than expression of individual genes alone.
Validation using existing data: Reproducibility will be assessed by cross-dataset replication (train on one set of studies, predict state structure in held-out studies) and by stability under alternative normalization/reprocessing pipelines.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): How does lipid composition act as a mesoscale controller of microdomain stability and ILV geometry?
Rationale: Lipids can tune membrane curvature, phase behavior, and line tension; ceramides and cholesterol are repeatedly implicated in EV biogenesis, yet their quantitative relationship to ILV size and cargo is unclear.
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Variation in ceramide species composition and cholesterol abundance predicts ILV size distribution shifts and microdomain clustering metrics, independent of total protein abundance.
Measurable predictions: (i) Across lipidomics datasets, specific lipid axes (e.g., ceramide chain length/saturation, sphingomyelin-to-ceramide ratios, cholesterol-to-phospholipid ratios) will correlate with imaging-derived ILV size scale parameters and with enrichment of curvature-sensitive proteins (e.g., ESCRT-III subunits, ALIX, syntenin) in matched or meta-matched contexts. (ii) Mechanistic coarse-grained models parameterized by lipid composition will reproduce observed shifts in size distributions between microdomain states (e.g., broader vs narrower ILV size distributions; changes in mean diameter).
Validation using existing data: Correlations will be tested across studies with appropriate metadata (cell type, isolation method, fraction type), using hierarchical models to account for study-specific effects. Mechanistic model predictions will be compared to empirical size distributions extracted from EM datasets.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): Are cell-type differences in EV cargo better explained by differential occupancy of microdomain states than by differential expression of individual cargo molecules?
Rationale: Many EV cargo differences may reflect upstream organizational regimes rather than direct sorting of each cargo by unique motifs.
Hypothesis 3 (H3): After controlling for cellular expression (where available from public transcriptomics/proteomics references), microdomain state occupancy explains more variance in EV cargo profiles than expression of individual cargos.
Measurable predictions: (i) State-based models will outperform expression-only baselines in predicting EV cargo enrichment patterns across cell types and perturbations (evaluated by cross-validated predictive accuracy). (ii) Cargoes will segregate into “state-coupled modules” (e.g., ribosomal/proteasomal, RNA-binding, membrane receptors) whose enrichment tracks state occupancy.
Validation using existing data: Expression baselines will draw on public cell line expression resources (e.g., DepMap transcriptomics/proteomics where applicable) and on study-provided input-cell measurements when deposited. Performance will be evaluated using held-out datasets and sensitivity analyses for isolation methods.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Which genetic perturbations shift microdomain state occupancy, and do these shifts explain changes in EV secretion phenotypes?
Rationale: Screens identify genes affecting EV secretion, but the mechanistic link to microdomain organization is rarely synthesized.
Hypothesis 4 (H4): Genes identified in EV secretion perturbation screens map onto specific microdomain state transitions (e.g., ESCRT-dominant to tetraspanin/ceramide-dominant), and these transitions are associated with predictable changes in ILV morphology and cargo modules.
Measurable predictions: (i) Perturbation signatures from published CRISPR screens and DepMap gene effect patterns will associate with inferred state axes. (ii) Genes will group into functional modules (ESCRT machinery, lipid metabolism, endosomal trafficking, tetraspanin scaffolding) whose perturbation shifts state occupancy in consistent directions.
Validation using existing data: We will use gene set enrichment and network propagation on known interaction networks (e.g., STRING, BioGRID) to test whether state-associated genes form coherent modules and whether modules replicate across independent screens.

Together, these questions target mesoscale emergence: how cooperative organization within microdomains produces emergent sorting and geometry, and how this organization varies across contexts. Each hypothesis yields quantitative, falsifiable predictions that can be evaluated entirely using existing public omics, imaging, and perturbation datasets.

[Methods and Approach]
Overview and synthesis strategy
The project will build an integrated, open “microdomain state atlas” by harmonizing public EV/endosome multi-omics with quantitative imaging-derived morphology and perturbation genetics. The core synthesis move is to map heterogeneous datasets into shared latent variables representing mesoscale microdomain states, then test whether these states explain emergent outputs (cargo modules, ILV size distributions) and respond predictably to genetic perturbations.

Specific data sources (public repositories)
1) EV/endosome proteomics
- ExoCarta (exocarta.org) and Vesiclepedia (microvesicles.org): curated EV protein lists with study links.
- PRIDE Archive (proteomics.ebi.ac.uk/pride/): raw MS datasets for reprocessing and consistent quantification.
- (Optional for cross-reference) UniProt for protein identifiers; Gene Ontology for functional annotations.
2) Lipidomics
- Metabolomics Workbench (metabolomicsworkbench.org): EV and subcellular fraction lipidomics studies.
- LIPID MAPS (lipidmaps.org): lipid ontology, identifiers, and pathway context.
3) RNA cargo
- NCBI GEO (gene expression omnibus) and SRA: exosomal small RNA-seq/total RNA-seq datasets.
- miRBase for miRNA annotation; Ensembl for transcript annotation.
4) Imaging
- BioImage Archive (ebi.ac.uk/bioimage-archive) and Image Data Resource (idr.openmicroscopy.org): fluorescence datasets with endosomal markers (e.g., CD63, Rab7, ALIX).
- EMPIAR (empiar.org): EM datasets containing MVB ultrastructure and ILVs.
5) Perturbation/genetic dependency
- DepMap (depmap.org): CRISPR gene effect, expression, and proteomics (where available) for many cell lines.
- Published EV secretion CRISPR screens with deposited results (via GEO, Figshare, Zenodo, or journal supplements).
6) Interaction/pathway context (for synthesis and interpretation)
- STRING, BioGRID for protein interaction networks.
- Reactome and KEGG for pathway mapping.

Data harmonization and metadata normalization
- Identifier harmonization: map proteins to UniProt accessions; genes to HGNC/Ensembl; lipids to LIPID MAPS IDs; RNAs to miRBase/Ensembl.
- Study metadata: standardize cell type/line, organism, EV isolation method (ultracentrifugation, SEC, immunocapture), fraction type (EV vs endosome), and measurement platform. We will adopt and extend community metadata schemas where possible (e.g., MISEV-relevant fields) without collecting new data.
- Batch correction: apply modality-appropriate normalization (e.g., MS intensity normalization; ComBat/limma for batch; quantile normalization for RNA) while preserving biological variance. Use hierarchical models to explicitly model “study” and “protocol” effects.

Quantitative imaging analysis (no new imaging)
Goal: extract ILV size distributions and microdomain organization metrics from EM and fluorescence images.
- EM (EMPIAR): implement automated/semi-automated segmentation pipelines for ILVs and MVB boundaries using deep learning models (e.g., U-Net variants) trained via transfer learning on publicly available annotated EM segmentation datasets when available, and refined using weak supervision (e.g., size/shape priors) without generating new experimental images. Outputs: ILV diameter distributions, ILV counts per MVB, spatial distribution within MVB lumen, and MVB size.
- Fluorescence (BioImage Archive/IDR): segment endosomes and quantify marker clustering (CD63, ALIX, TSG101, tetraspanins) using spot detection and spatial statistics. Outputs: Ripley’s K/L functions, pair-correlation functions, cluster size distributions, and co-localization metrics (Manders/Costes) to approximate microdomain clustering at the diffraction-limited scale.
- Quality control: include image-level QC (focus, SNR), and sensitivity analysis across segmentation thresholds. Where imaging metadata lacks scale calibration, infer pixel size from repository metadata and exclude ambiguous cases.

Multi-omic integration to infer latent microdomain states
We will use complementary integration approaches to ensure robustness and interpretability:
1) Multi-omic factor models: MOFA+ (Multi-Omics Factor Analysis) to learn latent factors across proteomics, lipidomics, and RNA cargo with missing-data tolerance.
2) Joint embedding and clustering: Similarity Network Fusion (SNF) to integrate modality-specific similarity graphs, followed by community detection to define discrete states.
3) Topic modeling for compositional data: Latent Dirichlet Allocation–style models (adapted for continuous counts via Poisson/log-normal) to identify cargo modules and co-occurring lipids/proteins.
State definition: A “microdomain state” will be defined as a reproducible cluster in the integrated latent space with a characteristic signature (top proteins, lipids, RNAs) and associated imaging-derived morphology distributions.

Linking states to emergent outputs
- Cargo enrichment: compute state-specific enrichment of protein families (tetraspanins, ESCRT, Rab GTPases), lipid classes (ceramides, cholesterol esters), and RNA modules (miRNA families, RBP-associated motifs).
- ILV size distribution modeling: fit parametric (log-normal, gamma mixtures) and nonparametric models to ILV diameters; compare across states using hierarchical Bayesian models to estimate state-level effects while controlling for study/protocol.
- Predictive models: train regularized models (elastic net), gradient-boosted trees, and calibrated probabilistic classifiers to predict cargo module enrichment and ILV size parameters from state factors. Evaluate via cross-validation across studies (leave-one-study-out).

Mechanistic modeling (coarse-grained, synthesis-based)
We will connect composition to geometry using coarse-grained membrane remodeling models informed by literature-derived parameters and fitted to imaging-derived size distributions.
- ESCRT polymerization and curvature: implement simplified physical models where ESCRT-III filament properties and scission probability depend on local composition proxies (ESCRT abundance factors) and lipid-derived curvature/line tension parameters.
- Lipid control: incorporate lipid composition axes (ceramide/cholesterol) as modulators of spontaneous curvature and domain stability; fit model parameters to reproduce empirical ILV size distributions per state.
- Model comparison: use information criteria and posterior predictive checks to assess whether adding lipid axes significantly improves fit beyond protein-only models.

Validation strategies (all using existing data)
- Cross-dataset replication: discover states in one subset (e.g., PRIDE-reprocessed proteomics + Metabolomics Workbench lipidomics) and test whether state signatures predict cargo/morphology in independent datasets.
- Positive controls: known EV markers (CD63, CD81, TSG101, ALIX) should load appropriately on relevant factors; known lipid associations (e.g., ceramide enrichment in certain EV datasets) should be recovered.
- Sensitivity to isolation method: stratify analyses by isolation protocol; include protocol as covariate; test whether state structure persists across methods.
- Perturbation concordance: evaluate whether genes from EV secretion screens map to state axes in consistent ways across screens and DepMap dependency patterns.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize metadata schema.
- Build ingestion pipelines for PRIDE, GEO/SRA, Metabolomics Workbench, EMPIAR/IDR.
- Release v0.1 of harmonized identifier mapping and metadata tables.
Months 6–12:
- Reprocess selected PRIDE EV proteomics datasets with consistent pipelines.
- Implement imaging segmentation workflows; extract initial ILV size distributions from a pilot EMPIAR set.
- Release v0.2 imaging-derived morphology feature tables.
Months 12–18:
- Perform multi-omic integration (MOFA+/SNF) to infer candidate states.
- Cross-study validation and protocol sensitivity analyses.
- Release v1.0 “Microdomain State Atlas” (signatures + embeddings).
Months 18–24:
- Link states to perturbation screens and DepMap; identify gene modules driving state shifts.
- Build predictive models for cargo and ILV size outcomes.
- Preprint 1: state atlas and cross-modal validation.
Months 24–30:
- Fit coarse-grained mechanistic models; compare protein-only vs protein+lipid models.
- Preprint 2: mechanistic link from composition to ILV geometry.
- Host capstone training workshop; finalize v2.0 open pipelines and documentation.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Membrane trafficking/exosome biology experts: interpret endosomal pathways, curate biological priors, define mechanistic questions.
- Proteomics specialists: PRIDE reprocessing, peptide/protein quantification, batch correction.
- Lipidomics experts: lipid ID harmonization, compositional transformations, pathway mapping.
- Quantitative imaging/computer vision experts: EM/fluorescence segmentation, spatial statistics.
- Biophysicists/modelers: coarse-grained membrane remodeling models, parameter inference.
- Data scientists/software engineers: workflow automation, containerization, database packaging.
- Trainees (grad students/postdocs): cross-training rotations across modalities; lead open notebooks and reproducible analyses.

All activities are strictly synthesis-based: we will only download, harmonize, reanalyze, and integrate existing public datasets; we will not generate new experimental data or request new sample collection.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
Deliverables (concrete, open, reusable)
1) Microdomain State Atlas (v1.0–v2.0)
- A curated, harmonized, cross-study resource linking EV/endosome proteomics (PRIDE/ExoCarta/Vesiclepedia), lipidomics (Metabolomics Workbench/LIPID MAPS), RNA cargo (GEO/SRA), imaging-derived morphology (EMPIAR/IDR/BioImage Archive), and perturbation genetics (DepMap/published screens).
- Outputs will include: (i) standardized metadata tables; (ii) integrated embeddings and state assignments; (iii) state signatures (ranked proteins/lipids/RNAs); and (iv) morphology summaries (ILV size distributions and clustering metrics) associated with states.

2) Open computational pipelines
- End-to-end workflows for reprocessing and harmonizing proteomics, lipidomics, RNA-seq, and imaging features.
- Imaging pipeline outputs: ILV diameter distributions, ILV counts per MVB, and microdomain clustering indices.
- Integration pipeline outputs: MOFA+/SNF models, state stability metrics, and prediction benchmarks.

3) Mechanistic mesoscale models connecting composition to geometry
- Coarse-grained models that quantitatively link ESCRT-related factors and lipid composition axes (ceramide/cholesterol) to ILV size distribution parameters.
- Model comparison results establishing when lipid information is necessary to explain emergent size distributions beyond protein composition alone.

4) Predictive models of cargo selection
- Models that predict enrichment of cargo modules (protein families, lipid classes, RNA modules) from inferred microdomain states.
- A set of interpretable “state-to-cargo rules” (e.g., which lipid/protein combinations predict recruitment of RNA-binding proteins or specific miRNA modules).

Scientific impact: advancing mesoscale emergence theory in EV biogenesis
This project will transform exosome biogenesis from a collection of pathway components into a mesoscale organizational framework. By identifying reproducible microdomain states and linking them to emergent outputs (cargo modules and ILV size distributions), we will provide a unifying explanation for EV heterogeneity across cell types and studies. The key conceptual advance is to treat microdomains as mesoscale assemblies with state-like behavior: cooperative organization yields properties not predictable from individual sorting motifs. This aligns directly with NCEMS’s focus on emergence at the mesoscale and leverages the abundance of public data to uncover general principles.

Resolving long-standing puzzles using synthesis
- Why do different studies report different “core” EV cargo? Our state framework can reconcile variability as mixtures of states with different occupancy.
- Why do ILV/exosome sizes vary systematically across contexts? We will quantify size distributions from EM and connect them to state composition and biophysical parameters.
- Why are multiple pathways partially redundant? State transitions inferred from perturbation screens can reveal compensatory organizational regimes (e.g., ESCRT-dominant vs tetraspanin/ceramide-dominant states).

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Generalizable mesoscale analytics: The imaging and integration methods (segmentation + spatial statistics + multi-omic factor models) will generalize to other mesoscale organelle microdomains (e.g., clathrin-coated pits, ER exit sites, stress granules).
- Improved interpretability of EV biomarkers: By distinguishing state-coupled cargo from universally enriched cargo, the work will help the community interpret EV signatures in disease contexts and reduce confounding by cell state or isolation method.
- Enabling hypothesis generation for future work: Although this project will not generate new data, it will produce prioritized, testable predictions about which compositional axes control microdomain stability and which genes shift state occupancy—supporting future experimental studies by the broader community.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least two major manuscripts (state atlas; mechanistic modeling) plus methods papers (imaging extraction; integration benchmarks).
- Workshops: annual NCEMS-style working group meetings and a capstone hands-on training workshop focused on reproducible multi-omic + imaging synthesis.
- Community resources: deposition of curated tables and derived features in Zenodo (DOIs), and submission of reusable imaging annotations/segmentations (where allowed) to BioImage Archive.

Long-term sustainability
- Modular, containerized workflows will reduce bit-rot and enable re-running as repositories update.
- The atlas will be versioned (semantic versioning), with clear provenance for each dataset and transformation.
- We will design the resource so new public datasets can be appended via standardized ingestion scripts, enabling continued community contributions beyond the award period.

Overall, the project will deliver a durable, open, mesoscale framework for exosome biogenesis that is only possible through community-scale synthesis and multidisciplinary collaboration, directly advancing NCEMS’s mission to uncover emergent principles from existing molecular and cellular data.

[Budget and Resources]
Budget philosophy
The budget is structured to support community-scale synthesis: personnel time for harmonization and integration across modalities, compute for large-scale reprocessing and imaging analysis, and travel/workshops to catalyze cross-disciplinary collaboration. No funds are allocated to experiments, sample collection, or new data generation.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (full-time):
  1) Multi-omics integration postdoc (proteomics/lipidomics/RNA integration; MOFA+/SNF; predictive modeling).
  2) Quantitative imaging/modeling postdoc (EM/fluorescence feature extraction; spatial statistics; linking morphology to states; mechanistic modeling).
  Justification: The project’s core deliverables require sustained, expert-level synthesis across modalities; two postdocs provide parallel progress and cross-validation.
- 1 Research software engineer / scientific programmer (0.5–1.0 FTE):
  Responsibilities: workflow engineering (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, data provenance automation, packaging and releases, documentation.
  Justification: Community-scale synthesis depends on robust, reusable pipelines and long-term maintainability.
- Graduate students (2; partial support):
  Roles: focused subprojects (e.g., lipid ontology harmonization; perturbation screen integration; benchmarking integration methods), and development of training materials.
  Justification: Directly supports NCEMS’s workforce training mission.
- PI/co-PI effort (modest):
  Coordination, working group facilitation, oversight of open-science compliance, and cross-lab integration.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS/GCP) and/or institutional HPC allocations:
  Needs: reprocessing PRIDE-scale proteomics, large EMPIAR image volumes, deep-learning segmentation inference, and repeated integration model fitting.
  Justification: Imaging and proteomics reanalysis at scale exceeds typical single-lab compute; cloud/HPC enables reproducible, scalable execution.
- Storage and data egress:
  Budget for storing intermediate processed matrices, cached image tiles, and container registries.
  Justification: Ensures stable, versioned releases and efficient collaboration across institutions.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2 per year, hybrid):
  Support travel for key personnel and trainees across participating labs to run integration sprints and resolve cross-modality issues.
- Conference dissemination:
  Travel for trainees/postdocs to present at relevant meetings (e.g., ASCB, extracellular vesicle community meetings, computational biology venues).
  Justification: Disseminates tools and recruits broader community participation.

Workshops and training events
- Annual hands-on training workshop (in-person with virtual option):
  Costs include venue/AV, instructional support, and trainee travel scholarships (prioritizing underrepresented institutions and geographic diversity).
  Justification: Directly advances NCEMS training goals and broadens impact beyond the core team.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo release preparation and curation time (personnel), plus potential costs for long-term archiving of large derived artifacts where needed.
- DOI-backed dataset and software releases; maintenance of documentation site (e.g., GitHub Pages/ReadTheDocs).
  Justification: Ensures outputs are findable, accessible, and reusable, consistent with gold-standard reproducible science.

Overall justification relative to synthesis goals
Each budget category is essential for integrating heterogeneous public datasets into a coherent mesoscale framework. Personnel enable modality-specific expertise; compute enables large-scale reanalysis and imaging quantification; travel/workshops enable the multidisciplinary coordination that makes the project feasible; and open-science infrastructure ensures durable, community-usable products. The requested resources exceed the capacity of any single lab and are aligned with NCEMS’s mission to catalyze collaborative, open, data-driven synthesis of emergent phenomena.

abstract_original:
Exosomes originate from intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) within multivesicular bodies, formed in mesoscale endosomal microdomains (50–500 nm) enriched in ESCRT components, tetraspanins, and specific lipids. The emergent phenomenon is that collective microdomain organization yields selective cargo sorting and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual sorting motifs.

We will synthesize: (i) exosome and endosome proteomics datasets (ExoCarta/Vesiclepedia-linked studies; PRIDE), (ii) lipidomics of extracellular vesicles and endosomal fractions (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), (iii) imaging datasets of ILV formation and endosomal microdomains (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR for EM of MVBs), (iv) RNA cargo profiles (exosomal RNA-seq in GEO), and (v) perturbation screens affecting EV secretion (DepMap; published CRISPR screens).

We will quantify ILV size distributions and microdomain organization from EM and fluorescence images using segmentation and spatial clustering metrics. Multi-omic integration will identify latent microdomain states defined by protein–lipid–RNA composition. Mechanistic modeling will connect ESCRT polymerization and membrane composition to observed ILV size distributions using coarse-grained membrane remodeling models. Predictive models will link microdomain states to cargo enrichment patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) exosome biogenesis proceeds through discrete mesoscale microdomain states that determine cargo classes; (2) lipid composition (ceramides, cholesterol) acts as a mesoscale controller of domain stability and ILV size; and (3) cell-type differences in EV cargo reflect microdomain state occupancy more than expression of individual cargos.

Expected insights include a unified mesoscale model of ILV microdomains, identification of compositional signatures predicting cargo selection, and open resources for EV biogenesis imaging/omics integration.

This requires team science across membrane biology, proteomics/lipidomics, quantitative imaging, and biophysical modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize diverse public datasets and establish open, reproducible pipelines and training for trainees in integrative mesoscale analysis of extracellular vesicle biogenesis.

title: Deciphering the Sequence Grammar of Mesoscale Viscoelasticity in Biomolecular Condensates
title_norm: deciphering the sequence grammar of mesoscale viscoelasticity in biomolecular condensates
abstract_text: This project addresses the emergent phenomenon of viscoelastic transitions within biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). While the ability of proteins to phase separate is well-documented, the mesoscale material properties—such as viscosity, surface tension, and hardening over time—emerge from complex, non-linear interactions that remain poorly understood. We propose to synthesize data from the PhaSePro and DrLLPS databases, combined with structural disorder predictions from AlphaFold (pLDDT scores) and experimental rheology data scattered across literature repositories. The central hypothesis is that specific 'grammars' within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—defined by charge patterning, residue spacing, and aromatic content—deterministically encode the emergent viscoelastic evolution of condensates, distinct from simple phase separation propensity. Our approach involves training deep learning models (specifically Graph Neural Networks) on integrated sequence-rheology datasets to map molecular features to mesoscale material states. We will validate these models by cross-referencing with cryo-electron tomography data from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) that visualizes condensate morphology in situ. Expected insights include a predictive framework for how pathogenic aggregates (e.g., in neurodegeneration) transition from liquid to solid states, an emergent property not predictable from single-molecule dynamics. This project necessitates NCEMS support to bring together soft matter physicists, computational biologists, and machine learning experts to standardize heterogeneous rheological data and develop novel biophysical classifiers.
full_text:
[Abstract]
This project addresses the emergent phenomenon of viscoelastic transitions within biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). While the ability of proteins to phase separate is well-documented, the mesoscale material properties—such as viscosity, surface tension, and hardening over time—emerge from complex, non-linear interactions that remain poorly understood. We propose to synthesize data from the PhaSePro and DrLLPS databases, combined with structural disorder predictions from AlphaFold (pLDDT scores) and experimental rheology data scattered across literature repositories. The central hypothesis is that specific 'grammars' within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—defined by charge patterning, residue spacing, and aromatic content—deterministically encode the emergent viscoelastic evolution of condensates, distinct from simple phase separation propensity. Our approach involves training deep learning models (specifically Graph Neural Networks) on integrated sequence-rheology datasets to map molecular features to mesoscale material states. We will validate these models by cross-referencing with cryo-electron tomography data from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) that visualizes condensate morphology in situ. Expected insights include a predictive framework for how pathogenic aggregates (e.g., in neurodegeneration) transition from liquid to solid states, an emergent property not predictable from single-molecule dynamics. This project necessitates NCEMS support to bring together soft matter physicists, computational biologists, and machine learning experts to standardize heterogeneous rheological data and develop novel biophysical classifiers.

[Background and Significance]
The biological understanding of intracellular organization has undergone a paradigm shift with the recognition of liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) as a primary driver of cellular compartmentalization. These membraneless organelles, or biomolecular condensates, organize reaction centers, sequester stress granules, and regulate gene expression. However, current research has predominantly focused on the binary condition of formation: determining which proteins phase separate and under what conditions. This leaves a critical gap in our understanding of the mesoscale emergent properties of these droplets—specifically their material states. Condensates are not merely generic liquids; they exhibit complex viscoelastic behaviors, ranging from dynamic Newtonian fluids to thixotropic gels and hardened glasses. This material state is biologically decisive; for example, the hardening of FUS or TDP-43 condensates is a pathological hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases like ALS, yet the molecular rules governing this liquid-to-solid transition remain obscure.

This project addresses the 'mesoscale gap' between atomic-resolution structural biology and cellular-scale phenotypic observation. Viscoelasticity is an inherently emergent phenomenon; it cannot be observed in a single protein molecule but arises from the collective ensemble dynamics of thousands of interacting chains. Currently, data regarding these properties is fragmented. While databases like PhaSePro, DrLLPS, and CD-CODE catalog proteins that undergo LLPS, they largely treat the phenomenon as a binary outcome. Quantitative measurements of viscosity, surface tension, and diffusion coefficients are buried in the supplementary materials of hundreds of disconnected publications, often reported in non-standard units. Furthermore, the structural basis for these properties is often hidden within Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs), which defy traditional structural analysis. The recent release of the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, which provides per-residue confidence scores (pLDDT) that accurately proxy for disorder, offers a new opportunity to correlate sequence-level disorder patterns with mesoscale material properties on a massive scale.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to solve this problem. No single lab can generate the diversity of rheological measurements required to learn the 'sequence grammar' of viscoelasticity. By synthesizing existing disparate datasets—linking sequence data, structural predictions, and mined rheological parameters—we can move beyond case studies of individual proteins (like FUS or DDX4) to develop a generalizable biophysical theory. This aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission to understand emergent system properties. We postulate that the transition from a liquid droplet to a solid aggregate is encoded in a 'molecular grammar' of charge patterning, sticker-spacer architecture, and aromatic residue distribution. Unlocking this grammar requires the integration of soft matter physics, bioinformatics, and machine learning to detect patterns invisible to small-scale experimentation. The significance of this work extends beyond basic biology; it provides a predictive framework for understanding how mutations alter the material state of organelles, offering new avenues for therapeutic intervention in diseases defined by aberrant phase transitions.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our research is driven by the overarching question: How do primary sequence features and local structural disorder deterministically encode the mesoscale viscoelastic properties and aging trajectories of biomolecular condensates? To address this, we have formulated three specific research questions and associated testable hypotheses that can be interrogated through data synthesis.

**Research Question 1: What is the sequence determinants of initial condensate viscosity?**
While LLPS propensity is often driven by multivalency, the resulting viscosity of the droplet varies by orders of magnitude. We hypothesize that the 'sticker-to-spacer' ratio and the specific chemistry of sticker residues (e.g., arginine-tyrosine pi-cation interactions vs. hydrophobic patches) differentially dictate internal friction. Specifically, we predict that sequences with uniformly distributed aromatic stickers will form high-viscosity fluids due to network percolation, whereas charge-driven condensates (high net charge per residue) will exhibit lower viscosity but higher surface tension. We will test this by training regression models on synthesized rheology data (inverse capillary velocity, FRAP recovery rates) mapped against sequence features derived from the PhaSePro database.

**Research Question 2: Can we predict the 'aging' potential of a condensate from sequence alone?**
The transition from liquid to solid (maturation) is an emergent property often linked to disease. We hypothesize that the presence of specific 'amyloidogenic gateways'—short sequence motifs capable of forming steric zippers—embedded within IDRs acts as a nucleation trigger for hardening, but this trigger is regulated by the flanking disordered regions which provide entropic protection. We predict that the rate of hardening correlates with the ratio of low-complexity complexity domains to amyloid-prone segments (predicted by ZipperDB). Using time-resolved rheology data mined from literature, we will classify proteins into 'stable liquids' vs. 'aging gels' and validate if graph topology measures of residue interaction networks can distinguish these classes.

**Research Question 3: How does structural disorder confidence (AlphaFold pLDDT) correlate with mesoscale morphology?**
We hypothesize that the 'flavor' of disorder—distinguishable by subtle variations in AlphaFold pLDDT scores and predicted radius of gyration—correlates with the morphology of condensates in situ (e.g., spherical droplets vs. irregular networks). We predict that regions with 'conditional disorder' (intermediate pLDDT) are more prone to forming irregular, viscoelastic networks compared to regions of 'pure disorder' (very low pLDDT). We will validate this by synthesizing sequence data with condensate images from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and Soft Matter literature, using computer vision to quantify morphology and correlate it with disorder profiles.

By answering these questions, we aim to derive a 'periodic table' of condensate material states, moving the field from descriptive phenomenology to predictive biophysics. This mechanistic understanding is crucial for explaining why certain cellular compartments remain fluid to facilitate reaction kinetics while others harden to provide structural support.

[Methods and Approach]
Our approach relies entirely on the synthesis of existing publicly available data, employing a 'Data-to-Knowledge' pipeline that integrates heterogeneous biological and physical datasets. The project will be executed by a transdisciplinary working group over 24 months.

**1. Data Sources and Acquisition:**
We will leverage four primary data streams:
*   **LLPS Databases:** We will ingest the complete datasets from **PhaSePro**, **DrLLPS**, and **CD-CODE**. These provide the ground truth for which proteins phase separate, along with experimental conditions (pH, salt).
*   **Structural Data:** We will bulk-download predicted structures for all identified LLPS proteins from the **AlphaFold Protein Structure Database**. We will specifically extract pLDDT scores and PAE (Predicted Aligned Error) matrices to model domain compactness and disorder.
*   **Rheological Data Mining:** This is a critical synthesis step. We will use the **Europe PMC** API to retrieve full-text articles referenced in PhaSePro. We will deploy a specialized Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline (utilizing BioBERT fine-tuned on biophysics literature) to extract quantitative rheological parameters: diffusion coefficients (D), viscosity (η), surface tension (γ), and fusion times (τ). We will standardize these values into SI units to create the 'RheoPhase' dataset.
*   **In Situ Morphology:** We will query the **Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB)** and **Empire** for cryo-electron tomograms of cellular condensates to serve as morphological validation sets.

**2. Data Harmonization and Feature Engineering:**
Raw sequences will be featurized using a combination of physicochemical properties (charge patterning parameters like Kappa and Omega, hydropathy, aromatic content) and structural embeddings. We will construct a 'Condensate Knowledge Graph' where nodes represent proteins, conditions, and material states, and edges represent physical interactions. This graph structure allows us to impute missing rheological data based on network proximity.

**3. Computational Analysis and Modeling:**
*   **Sequence-to-Rheology Mapping:** We will develop a Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture. The protein sequence will be represented as a graph where amino acids are nodes and edges represent contact probabilities derived from AlphaFold PAE matrices. The GNN will be trained to predict the extracted rheological classes (Liquid, Gel, Solid) and continuous variables (Viscosity). This captures the non-local interactions critical for mesoscale emergence.
*   **The 'Grammar' Decoder:** To interpret the model (Explainable AI), we will use attention mechanisms to identify which residues (the 'syntax') contribute most heavily to the prediction of high viscosity or hardening. This effectively isolates the 'stickers' from the 'spacers' without a priori assumptions.

**4. Validation Strategy (Synthesis-Based):**
Since we cannot generate new data, validation will be performed via:
*   **Cross-Dataset Validation:** Training on PhaSePro-derived data and testing on non-overlapping entries from DrLLPS.
*   **In Silico 'Mutagenesis':** We will feed known disease-associated mutations (e.g., FUS G156E) into our model to see if it correctly predicts the experimentally known shift in material state (e.g., liquid-to-solid transition) reported in the literature, serving as a positive control.
*   **Morphological Cross-Reference:** We will compare our model's predictions of 'solid-like' proteins against EMDB entries. If our model predicts a protein forms a solid, the corresponding EMDB entry should show aggregate-like or fibrillar morphology rather than spherical droplets.

**5. Team Composition:**
The Working Group will consist of Soft Matter Physicists (to define rheological constraints), Computational Biologists (for database integration and NLP), and Machine Learning Engineers (for GNN development). This diversity ensures that the synthesis is physically grounded and computationally rigorous.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will deliver tangible resources and transformative conceptual advances to the molecular and cellular biosciences community.

**Specific Deliverables:**
1.  **RheoPhaseDB:** A standardized, open-access database linking protein sequences not just to phase separation propensity, but to quantitative material properties (viscosity, surface tension, maturation rates). This solves the current fragmentation of rheological data.
2.  **ViscoNet:** An open-source, pre-trained Graph Neural Network tool. Users will be able to input a protein sequence (or a mutant) and receive a probabilistic prediction of its mesoscale material state and aging trajectory. This tool will be containerized and made available via a web interface.
3.  **The 'Mesoscale Grammar' Manuscript:** A synthesis paper defining the specific sequence rules (charge/aromatic patterning) that govern the liquid-to-solid transition, effectively connecting the angstrom scale (sequence) to the micron scale (droplet mechanics).

**Contribution to Emergence Phenomena:**
By focusing on viscoelasticity, this project directly tackles the NCEMS theme of emergence. We will demonstrate how simple linear sequences encode complex, time-dependent material behaviors that only manifest at the mesoscale. This bridges the gap between reductionist structural biology and systems-level cell biology.

**Broader Impacts:**
*   **Biomedical Relevance:** The ability to predict condensate hardening is directly relevant to understanding protein aggregation diseases (Alzheimer’s, ALS, Prion diseases). Our tools could screen for mutations that increase the risk of pathological phase transitions.
*   **Synthetic Biology:** The 'grammar' we decode will enable the design of synthetic organelles with tunable material properties for bio-manufacturing or drug delivery vehicles.
*   **Workforce Development:** The project will train graduate students and postdocs in the emerging field of 'Data-Driven Biophysics,' equipping them with skills in NLP, graph learning, and database management that are highly valued in both academia and industry.

**Dissemination and Sustainability:**
Results will be published in high-impact interdisciplinary journals (e.g., Nature Computational Science, Biophysical Journal). We will host a 'Condensate Data' workshop at the annual Biophysical Society meeting to train the community on using RheoPhaseDB. Long-term sustainability will be ensured by mirroring data on Zenodo and integrating our curated annotations back into the parent databases (PhaSePro/DrLLPS) to enrich the ecosystem.

[Budget and Resources]
The requested budget focuses entirely on personnel, computation, and collaborative activities necessary for high-level data synthesis, with no funds allocated for wet-lab reagents.

**Personnel ($350,000):**
*   **Postdoctoral Fellow 1 (2.0 FTE):** A computational biologist with expertise in NLP and database management. They will lead the mining of literature for rheological data, data standardization, and the construction of RheoPhaseDB.
*   **Postdoctoral Fellow 2 (2.0 FTE):** A physicist/ML engineer specialized in soft matter theory and geometric deep learning. They will develop the GNN models and lead the physics-informed analysis of the 'sequence grammar.'
*   **Graduate Research Assistant (2.0 FTE):** To assist with data curation, visualization, and web-tool development.

**Computing Resources ($40,000):**
*   Cloud computing credits (AWS or Google Cloud) are required to train large-scale GNN models and run the NLP pipelines on thousands of full-text articles. This also covers storage costs for the integrated database and hosting of the web server for the community tool.

**Travel and Collaboration ($50,000):**
*   **Working Group Meetings:** Funds to support bi-annual in-person meetings at the NCEMS headquarters. These intensive 3-day 'sprint' sessions are crucial for the transdisciplinary team to integrate the physics theory with biological data.
*   **Conference Travel:** Support for fellows to present findings at major conferences (Biophysical Society, ISMB, APS March Meeting) to disseminate results and gather community feedback.

**Open Science Infrastructure ($10,000):**
*   Costs associated with open-access publication fees (APCs) and professional services for data stewardship to ensure the long-term usability of the generated databases.

**Total Budget Justification:**
This budget reflects the labor-intensive nature of high-quality data synthesis. The primary cost is intellectual capital—bringing together distinct fields to clean, interpret, and model complex data. The investment in cloud compute and open infrastructure ensures that the synthesis results are not just a static paper, but a dynamic, usable resource for the entire scientific community.

full_text:
[Abstract]
This proposal investigates the emergent rheological properties of chromatin at the mesoscale, specifically how local genomic folding patterns dictate the physical stiffness and plasticity of the cell nucleus. The spatial organization of the genome is not merely a packing mechanism but an emergent mechanical scaffold that influences gene expression and nuclear stability. We will synthesize high-resolution Hi-C and Micro-C data from the 4D Nucleome Project, mechanics data from atomic force microscopy (AFM) studies of isolated nuclei, and transcriptomic data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). The novel hypothesis is that specific topologically associating domains (TADs) and chromatin loops act as 'mechanical springs' whose collective stiffness emerges from the interplay of epigenetic marks and loop extrusion factors, independent of the underlying DNA sequence length. By employing polymer physics simulations informed by real-world Hi-C contact maps and machine learning regression models, we aim to correlate 3D chromatin architecture with nuclear stiffness measurements. We expect to reveal how changes in mesoscale chromatin folding—driven by differentiation or disease—result in emergent mechanical softening or stiffening, impacting nuclear migration and integrity. This transdisciplinary synthesis requires a team of genomicists, mechanical engineers, and polymer physicists to bridge the gap between sequence-based genomics and physical mechanics.

[Background and Significance]
The cell nucleus is not merely a passive container for genetic material; it is a dynamic, mechanically active organelle that must resist physical stress while facilitating the intricate reorganization required for gene regulation and replication. While the molecular biology of DNA and the macroscopic mechanics of the cell are well-studied, a critical knowledge gap exists at the mesoscale—the regime between the 2nm DNA double helix and the micrometer-scale nuclear envelope. At this scale, chromatin organizes into Topologically Associating Domains (TADs), loops, and compartments. Current understanding suggests that this organization is primarily for transcriptional regulation. However, emerging evidence indicates that chromatin folding provides the structural integrity of the nucleus, acting as a 'smart polymer' gel with tunable viscoelastic properties. Understanding this emergent rheology is crucial because nuclear stiffness dictates cellular migration potential (e.g., in metastasis) and genomic stability.

Despite the availability of vast datasets, the connection between 3D genomic architecture and nuclear mechanics remains fragmented. The 4D Nucleome Project and ENCODE have produced petabytes of high-resolution Hi-C, Micro-C, and ChIP-seq data, mapping the spatial proximity of DNA loci with unprecedented precision. Simultaneously, the biophysics community has generated extensive mechanical datasets using Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), micropipette aspiration, and particle tracking microrheology, characterizing the stiffness (Young's modulus) and viscosity of nuclei in various cell types and disease states. However, these two domains remain siloed. Genomicists analyze contact maps to infer gene regulation, while biophysicists model the nucleus as a homogeneous continuum or simple polymer network, often ignoring the specific, sequence-dependent topology driven by loop extrusion and phase separation.

This segregation of data precludes a fundamental understanding of how biological function emerges from physical form. We do not currently know how the formation or dissolution of a specific TAD influences the local mechanical compliance of the nuclear environment. Does the extrusion of a chromatin loop by cohesin create a localized 'stiffening' event? Do phase-separated condensates of heterochromatin act as cross-links in the nuclear gel? These are questions of emergence: the mechanical properties of the nucleus are not simple sums of the DNA polymer stiffness but emerge from complex, energy-consuming loop extrusion processes and distinct folding patterns.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to bridge this divide. No single lab possesses the resources to generate simultaneous high-resolution Micro-C maps and perform single-nucleus rheology across hundreds of cell conditions. However, the data already exists. By synthesizing genomic topology data with biophysical mechanics data, we can develop a 'mechano-genomic' code. This project aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission to address fundamental questions of emergence. We posit that nuclear stiffness is an emergent property arising from the collective behavior of thousands of dynamic chromatin loops. By integrating existing disparate datasets, we can move beyond descriptive genomics to predictive physical biology, solving the long-standing puzzle of how the genome maintains mechanical stability while remaining accessible for transcription. This work will fundamentally shift the paradigm from viewing chromatin as a library of information to viewing it as a physical, load-bearing material programmed by its own sequence and topology.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our proposal focuses on three interrelated research questions that address the emergent mechanical properties of chromatin at the mesoscale. These questions are designed to be answered exclusively through the synthesis of existing data and computational modeling.

**Research Question 1: How does the density and arrangement of Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) dictate bulk nuclear stiffness?**
*Hypothesis:* We hypothesize that TADs function as distinct mechanical subunits or 'springs' within the nuclear polymer network. Specifically, we predict that the density of TAD boundaries (insulation scores) and the frequency of intra-TAD loops linearly correlate with the effective Young's modulus of the nucleus. We propose that the emergent stiffness of the nucleus is higher in cell types with more compact, loop-dense chromatin architectures compared to those with diffuse, compartment-based folding.
*Validation Strategy:* We will test this by synthesizing Hi-C data (calculating insulation scores, loop density, and compartment strength) for cell lines where AFM or micropipette aspiration data is publicly available (e.g., GM12878, K562, HFF). We will train a regression model to predict the experimentally measured stiffness moduli based solely on topological features derived from Hi-C matrices.

**Research Question 2: To what extent do specific epigenetic marks and chromatin binding proteins contribute to emergent rheology independent of DNA sequence?**
*Hypothesis:* We hypothesize that the emergent viscoelasticity of chromatin is modulated primarily by the cross-linking frequency mediated by architectural proteins (CTCF, Cohesin) and phase-separation promoting marks (H3K9me3), rather than the abundance of DNA itself. We predict that regions enriched with H3K9me3 (heterochromatin) will exhibit solid-like emergent properties (high storage modulus), while H3K27ac-enriched regions (euchromatin) will behave as a fluid (high loss modulus).
*Validation Strategy:* We will integrate ENCODE ChIP-seq data for CTCF, Rad21 (cohesin), H3K9me3, and H3K27ac with the mechanical datasets. By utilizing polymer physics simulations initialized with these specific epigenetic constraints, we will simulate stress-strain responses and compare the calculated viscoelastic parameters against existing microrheology data from the literature.

**Research Question 3: Can mesoscale chromatin topology explain the 'softening' phenotype observed in cancer and stem cells?**
*Hypothesis:* It is well-documented that cancer nuclei and embryonic stem cell nuclei are mechanically softer than differentiated, healthy nuclei. We hypothesize that this emergent softening is directly caused by a global reduction in mesoscale looping interactions and a dissolution of long-range compartmentalization, rather than changes in lamin A/C expression alone. We predict that 'mechanical softening' is an emergent signature of specific topological degradation patterns.
*Validation Strategy:* We will perform a comparative synthesis of Hi-C maps from normal vs. oncogenic cell lines (available in the 4D Nucleome and GEO). We will feed these contact maps into our 'Virtual Nucleus' simulation engine to calculate theoretical stiffness. If our hypothesis holds, the simulation (based ONLY on chromatin topology) should reproduce the relative softening trends observed in physical experiments, proving that chromatin topology is a significant driver of the emergent mechanical phenotype.

By answering these questions, we will define the rules of 'Emergent Chromatin Rheology,' demonstrating how local mesoscale interactions give rise to global cellular physical properties.

[Methods and Approach]
To achieve the goals of this synthesis project, we will employ a rigorous data integration pipeline combining bioinformatics, machine learning, and computational polymer physics. We will not generate new data but will leverage the vast repositories of the 4D Nucleome (4DN), ENCODE, and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), alongside curated biophysical datasets.

**1. Data Sources and Harmonization**
*Genomic Topology Data:* We will source high-resolution Hi-C and Micro-C data (.hic and .mcool formats) from the **4D Nucleome Data Portal**. Priority will be given to Tier 1 cell lines (GM12878, K562, H1-hESC, HFF-c6) where data depth allows for 1kb resolution analysis.
*Epigenomic Data:* ChIP-seq tracks for architectural proteins (CTCF, RAD21, SMC3) and histone modifications (H3K9me3, H3K27ac, H3K27me3) will be retrieved from the **ENCODE Project Portal**. 
*Transcriptomic Data:* RNA-seq quantification files will be sourced from **GEO** to correlate expression levels of nuclear mechanics-related proteins (Lamin A/C, B1, B2) with chromatin states.
*Mechanical Data:* We will curate a 'NucleoMechanics' meta-dataset by synthesizing data from **PubMed Central** and **Dryad** repositories associated with seminal papers on nuclear rheology (e.g., data from Discher, Shivashankar, and Lammerding labs). We will extract Young’s modulus (E), viscosity, and deformation indices, normalizing values to account for differences in measurement techniques (AFM vs. Aspiration).
*Integration Strategy:* All genomic data will be harmonized to the GRCh38 reference genome. We will use the `bioframe` and `cooler` Python libraries to create a unified data structure where every genomic bin (e.g., 10kb) is annotated with its contact frequency, epigenetic state, and expression level.

**2. Computational Polymer Modeling (The 'Virtual Nucleus')**
This is the core synthesis engine. We will use **OpenMM** and **LAMMPS** to perform coarse-grained Langevin dynamics simulations. 
*Model Construction:* We will convert Hi-C contact maps into polymer models using population-based modeling approaches (similar to Chrom3D or PGS). Each bead in the polymer will represent a genomic locus (10kb-50kb). 
*Force Fields:* Instead of generic potentials, we will parameterize the bond and angle potentials based on the specific loop constraints identified in the Hi-C data (using `mustache` or `hic cups` for loop calling). Regions with high H3K9me3 signal will be assigned attractive Lennard-Jones potentials to simulate phase separation.
*Rheology Simulation:* To measure emergent stiffness, we will subject these 'Virtual Nuclei' to simulated physical stress (shear and compression) within the software. We will calculate the stress-strain curves to derive the theoretical Young's modulus and storage/loss moduli. This allows us to translate 1D/3D genomic data into physical units (Pascals).

**3. Machine Learning and Synthesis**
We will develop a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to learn the mapping between chromatin topology and nuclear stiffness. 
*Input:* Chromatin interaction graphs derived from Hi-C (nodes = loci, edges = contact frequencies).
*Target:* Experimental stiffness values from our curated NucleoMechanics dataset.
*Architecture:* We will utilize a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) implemented in **PyTorch Geometric**. The model will learn to aggregate local topological features (cliques, hubs, insulation boundaries) to predict a global graph property (stiffness).
*Validation:* We will use Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) on cell types. For example, we will train on GM12878 and HFF, and test the model's ability to predict the stiffness of K562 nuclei based solely on K562 Hi-C data. 

**4. Team Composition and Timeline**
*Team:* The working group requires: (1) A **Computational Genomicist** (expert in Hi-C/Micro-C analysis and 4DN tools); (2) A **Soft Matter Physicist** (expert in polymer rheology and OpenMM); (3) A **Data Scientist** (expert in GNNs and data harmonization). 
*Timeline (2 Years):*
*   **Months 1-6:** Data curation, harmonization of 4DN/ENCODE data, and construction of the NucleoMechanics database.
*   **Months 7-12:** Development of the OpenMM 'Virtual Nucleus' pipeline; initial simulations of Tier 1 cell lines.
*   **Months 13-18:** Training and refinement of GNN models; cross-dataset validation; synthesis of cancer vs. normal comparisons.
*   **Months 19-24:** Final analysis, visualization of emergent properties, workshop organization, and manuscript preparation.

This approach strictly adheres to synthesis constraints by extracting new physical insights from existing maps and mechanical measurements, creating a bridge between the fields of genomics and mechanobiology.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will deliver significant tangible assets and conceptual advances that address the NCEMS mission of understanding mesoscale emergence.

**Deliverables:**
1.  **The 'NucleoMechanics' Database:** A curated, harmonized repository linking genomic topology (Hi-C/Micro-C metrics) with physical mechanical properties (stiffness, viscosity) for over 50 distinct cell types/conditions. This will be the first database to explicitly link these two disparate fields.
2.  **The 'Virtual Nucleus' Toolkit:** An open-source Python package (built on OpenMM) that allows users to input a `.cool` or `.hic` file and output a predicted rheological profile (stress-strain curve) of that genome. This tool democratizes mechanobiology, allowing genomicists to infer physical properties without needing an AFM setup.
3.  **Predictive AI Models:** Pre-trained Graph Neural Networks capable of predicting nuclear stiffness from chromatin architecture, available via a Hugging Face repository.
4.  **Manuscripts:** We anticipate at least two high-impact publications: one detailing the 'mechanical code' of chromatin folding (Target: *Nature Physics* or *Cell Systems*) and another focusing on the methodological synthesis of 1D/3D data (Target: *Nature Methods*).

**Scientific Impact:**
Our work will fundamentally advance the understanding of mesoscale emergence. By demonstrating that nuclear stiffness is an emergent property of chromatin topology, we will solve the puzzle of how cells modulate their physical compliance during migration and differentiation without altering their DNA sequence. This establishes a new feedback loop in cell biology: *Topology determines Mechanics, and Mechanics influences Topology*. 

**Broader Impacts:**
*   **Biomedical Relevance:** Understanding the mechanical softening of cancer nuclei is crucial for metastasis research. Our models could lead to new diagnostic biomarkers based on chromatin topology signatures that predict invasive potential.
*   **Workforce Development:** This project inherently trains the next generation of 'convergence' scientists. Postdocs and students will gain rare fluency in both high-performance computing/polymer physics and high-throughput genomics/bioinformatics.
*   **Sustainability:** By depositing our harmonized data and models in stable, public repositories (Zenodo, 4DN Portal), we ensure that this synthesis effort serves as a foundation for future inquiries into nuclear mechanotransduction.

[Budget and Resources]
The requested budget focuses on the human capital and computational resources necessary to execute this complex synthesis project. As no wet-lab experiments are proposed, funds are allocated primarily to personnel and high-performance computing.

**Personnel (65% of Budget):**
*   **Postdoctoral Fellow (2.0 FTE):** Two full-time postdocs are essential. Postdoc A (Physics/Engineering background) will focus on the OpenMM polymer simulations and mechanical data curation. Postdoc B (Genomics/Bioinformatics background) will handle the 4DN/ENCODE data processing and Machine Learning integration. This cross-disciplinary pairing is critical for the synthesis mission.
*   **Graduate Student (1.0 FTE):** One PhD student will assist with data harmonization and website/database construction, gaining valuable training in data science.
*   **PI/Co-PI Salary:** One month of summer salary per year for the PIs to oversee the working group and scientific direction.

**Computing Resources (15% of Budget):**
*   **Cloud Computing:** Funds for AWS or Google Cloud Platform to train deep learning models (GNNs) and host the public database.
*   **HPC Access:** While we will apply for XSEDE/ACCESS allocations, we budget for local cluster maintenance or priority queue access to run the computationally intensive Langevin dynamics simulations (OpenMM) for thousands of iterations.

**Travel and Collaboration (10% of Budget):**
*   **Working Group Meetings:** Funds for bi-annual in-person meetings for the PIs and trainees to facilitate intense synthesis work and brainstorming.
*   **Conference Travel:** Travel support for the postdocs to present findings at key conferences (e.g., Biophysical Society, ASCB, RECOMB) to disseminate results to diverse audiences.

**Open Science and Training (10% of Budget):**
*   **Publication Costs:** Open Access fees for high-impact journals.
*   **Workshop Organization:** Costs to host the virtual training hackathon and produce high-quality training materials/documentation.

This budget is lean but targeted, ensuring that resources are directed toward the intellectual labor of synthesis and the computational infrastructure required to model mesoscale emergence.

The team validates model predictions through leave one out cross validation and benchmarks against published experimental microrheology data. The project extracts data from the 4D Nucleome Data Portal and ENCODE Project Portal alongside Dryad and PubMed Central. The team aligns datasets to the GRCh38 reference genome to build a unified structure linking physical metrics and epigenetics. The team mitigates discrepancies from divergent experimental techniques by thoroughly normalizing the extracted values for stiffness and viscosity. The two year project advances from database construction to simulation development before finishing with model training and publication preparation. This synthesis of genomic topology and biophysical mechanics demands cross disciplinary expertise in soft matter physics and data science. The team will distribute toolkits and harmonized databases on Zenodo and Hugging Face while publishing in open access journals. The group includes principal investigators and postdoctoral fellows alongside a graduate student to facilitate cross disciplinary genomics training.

Datasets from the 4D Nucleome Data Portal, ENCODE, and biomedical repositories will be aligned to the GRCh38 reference genome and merged to link three dimensional contact frequencies with physical mechanics metrics. title: The Emergence of Metabolic Channeling: Mapping Transient Metabolons via Integrated Interactomics
title_norm: the emergence of metabolic channeling mapping transient metabolons via integrated interactomics
abstract_text: This research focuses on the emergent phenomenon of 'metabolic channeling' arising from the formation of metabolons—transient, mesoscale clusters of sequential enzymes. Unlike stable protein complexes, metabolons are dynamic structures that emerge in response to metabolic demand, creating localized pools of intermediates that increase flux and protect unstable substrates.
